_childDocuments_.review: A lovely game about managing logistics and supply lines. It does become rather grindy towards the end, but there's more here than I expected initially.The Good:It's satisfying to make things run. And watching resources stack up (and addressing the dumpster fire of a supply chain that you inevitably create in the process) is a satisfying experience. The game seems to be stable and, while I may have stumbled upon a few bugs, I'm still not sure whether they were actually bugs or me just misunderstanding why something was happening, regardless they weren't substantial enough to actually impact my enjoymentThe Frustrating:This is going to make it sound worse than it is, I promise, I enjoyed the game. These are just the parts that got on my nerves.The space management on the islands is perhaps the most frustrating part, especially in the late game, many a hour was spent sliding every building over one grid space to try and eek out enough space to squeeze one more building into the bottom corner. Additionally, There is sometimes no good way to get things to do exactly what you want them to (e.g. supply enough to make exactly 1 of something, or prioritize XYZ buildings over ABC buildings), the control over your production facilities is simply too coarse. Finally, some of the pacing is a little funny. The turnaround early on is really satisfying because you make progress quickly and are rapidly iterating and solving issues. By the end, you're making things that have supply lines with really long lag times. This means that problems (e.g. insufficient throughput on an intermediate product or a broken link in your supply chain) don't become apparent until much later. I found that, by the end, the only way to really play was just to let it run in the background and check back on it in a few hours, making it all the more frustrating when you realize you forgot to make a supply chain supplying fuel for the power plant on an island and nothing ran after the first 45 minutes.Conclusion:Overall, plenty of fun at a reasonable price, I would absolutely recommend it if it looks like the type of thing you like to do in your free time
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Its like Forager but... Tedious.. Forager let you build in the space between islands so it became more of a loose suggestion as time went on and turned the initial progression system into an open landscape to fit what you need. Nova Lands has every island have the same exact hexagon shape with no way to expand them. They add logistics to move stuff between islands but with limited space it is always cramped and constantly have to redesign to fit what you want in the limited space. It does this in a very tedious way not the satisfying redesign for maximum efficiency way. Each island produces a unique resource that you need to have in your pipeline somewhere and if you decide you want more of one resource and want to spread it to another island you have to reduce the resource being gathered there... To top it almost all your resources are handed by logistics drones. This isnt necessarily a problem but each island only gets a max of 5 drone slots. Theres also three types of drones. Logistics, harvester and combat. If its an island with enemies you need a valuable slot used on a combat drone or they just kill the other drones and eventually they will repair themselves so it takes a long time. You either lose the slot or run circuits around the map repairing the broken drones manually. If its a resource island you need those slots for harvester drones *until late game* and then you have little room for logistics. So essentially you have to divide islands between logistics focuses or gathering focuses. So you have islands with almost no buildings because they are mainly gathering and moving them to a different island to process where the logistics drones have more work than they can handle.Also who designed the crafting system? It takes every resource to make the next resource up so by the time you get past tier 3 you need 97 of tier 1 with no space to make them. Who in their right mind decided the crafting times as well? Everything past tier 2 takes 10+ minutes to craft. The late game stuff is 38 minutes and 24 seconds EACH. I dont know why they picked that but everything late game take almost 40 minutes per unit.  No exaggeration theres at least 20 lategame products that take 40 minutes to craft. Sure there are speed upgrades. 50% from one thing you can max out and 25% from a tech. Still leaves the late game stuff at 10+ minutes per craft......Essentially they tried to make a factory game and fit it inside the mold of what forager was. Its junky clangy and its very tedious. I find myself taking breaks often to play something else because of how monotonous it is.Either take a forager approach and let us take control of the map to play it a we see fit or add mods so the community can do it for us.

_childDocuments_.review: Nova Lands is a factory building, exploration, and island management game designed around this super adorable pixel space themed universe. In this game, you're a cute little explorer who has just landed on a remote planet, and it's your job to bring industry and grow your community amongst the stars! As you progress through the game, you'll be able to build yourself your own little rocket ship, which will take you to the space station. It's up to you to bring this once thriving intergalactic marketplace back to life! "End game" involves crafting difficult items, shipping them off to be sold, and further growing and developing the space station. Meet cute characters with adorable art along the way!What makes this title different from others in this genre is it really is designed to be casual, relaxing experience. If you've played other automation, factory building or management type games, you may recall that they can be quite stressful and overwhelming. Unlike other titles, such as Satisfactory, Nova Lands isn't as expansive, and therefore, likely much less stressful. It does not require a ton of strategy to master.Beyond factory building, there is a lot more to be done in Nova Lands. As you continue to unlock other biomes and explore the planet, you'll discover monuments and their guardians. These are tough bosses to overcome. Here's the interesting thing about that, though - you don't have to fight them. You can, instead, befriend these guardians. How adorable is that?! There is some combat in this game, but there are ways to develop your gaming experience to avoid as much combat as possible. As you unlock skills each level, you can make certain animals docile, as well as craft fighter bots to do the combat for you. Along with befriending the guardians, you can nearly skip most combat available in this game if you choose to. If collectathons are your thing (games that involve creature collecting, or some kind of collection/museum activity) there is a bit of that too in Nova Lands! Overall, I think Nova Lands is a great introduction to the factory building and automation genre, especially if you haven't tried them before. If you have, but you find those games kind of stressful or challenging, I recommend starting here. This is a great game to learn the genre! Also ALIENS! And space travel! for more cozy game reviews!
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Forager is one of my favorite games of the last few years, and I've been hoping for more games like it. Nova Lands is obviously very heavily influenced by Forager. You go around, collecting resources to unlock new islands, learn new skills, and make higher tier resources. I can't help but compare the two, but Nova Lands does enough of its own thing to make it worthwhile. At first, I didn't like the changes made here to the Forager formula. There are no higher level tools for example. You do unlock upgrades but the difference is not as drastic as it was in Forager. However, as you get further in the game gets more engaging. There is a lot more automation here, and you get access to it earlier on. Things you started off doing on your own are soon handled by robots so you can focus on exploring and optimizing your setup. You'll eventually start specializing your islands, using their limited space and unique resources to make various materials, and then having your bots and conveyor bridges bring those materials to other islands to be utilized there. At this point I can say I'd definitely recommend this game. There are things I wish they would improve. There should be a better way to prioritize where your materials go when they have multiple inputs on the same island, and the game could definitely do with some more content. I'm only 6 hours in and unless the game suddenly opens up some hidden technology tiers I feel like I've already seem a majority of the content here. However, what is here is very fun and I think worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Nova Lands is a cozy factory builder, with inspirations from Factorio, Stardew Valley and probably other games. It's a lot of fun playing the  "minigame". There is a combat system, but it's (almost) never required, which is a nice change of pace! Although... I suck at shooters and yet I found the bosses pretty easy, as long as you go in a little bit prepared, so I didn't bother instead of fighting.While the game is sadly only for Windows, I'm playing on Linux with Steam Play, and save for some very minor visual bugs (which I'm not sure if they are Linux-specific) the game runs flawlessly. Would still love to see support for other OSes.In total: 8.5/10, it is definitely worth the money, especially when discounted.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun little automation game in the vain of factorio but not without it's issues. But most of it's issues don't detract away from the meat of the game.The game comes down to always optimizing your resource production so that you always have enough to make what you need to make. Which for the most part it does a very good job at making engaging, I spent several hours just setting up and tweaking some production lines to make them work as fast as I thought they possibly could.The only part of the game that I disliked is that near the late game some items take so long to produce that it becomes almost mandatory to leave the game running unattended to progress. They player house actually give you a bonus for doing just that. It seems odd to me that the game transitions from something that you actively participate in to an idle game that you leave running and ignore. I think some of those production times may need to be shortened to allow continual engagement of the player rather than forcing the idle transition.That being said; over all I had a blast playing this game, I do recommend it. It's one of the few games on steam I have gone out to 100% so that means something.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a lovely factory game. I haven't yet played Factorio, but i've but significant time into Satisfactory and enjoyed it immensely. Nova Lands struck a very similar chord with me while being distinct enough to exist alongside satisfactory in my brain, rather than taking its spot or being ignored in favor of the former; something i can't say about other factory games i've played.The most significant distinction for me is the separation of the game into multiple hexagonal islands. They're separated by water, but must be scanned by a special device using pre-determined resources to become visitable. I've found that this change has a number of interesting consequences. For one, it de-emphasizes exploration in favor of making further areas another progression system running parallel to the tech tree. I feel like this works quite well, as locking different biomes/islands until a specific resource is provided allows each to be introduced in a pre-determined order, making it clear which area should be set up in/developed next. the limited space of the islands also encourages optimizing for space as much as possible, while also naturally encouaging organizing product per island.Another significant change is the replacement of the traditional conveyor belts with bots. This significantly streamlines the process of connecting devices together, while the limited number of bots per island encourages building across many islands.high recommendation to the factory game enjoyers among you

_childDocuments_.review: basically a sugar cereal of a game. nothing super deep here, but a fun game about setting up supply lines and reconfiguring them when you get an upgrade. definitely not novel, i completely ignored the plot, but i breezed through it and had fun. i also enjoyed the lack of mandatory combat and the fact that most of the grind was totally optional - i maxed out production without going completely bonkers on some of the more boring things. i will say it is slightly buggy, and there are definitely some elements that go completely unexplained. guides are lacking even on steam, there is no discord i have easily found, and i think a few people complaining about excessive idle elements did understandably miss out on some key upgrades. that said i also haven't figured out how a new post-game quest is supposed to work due to that same slightly-buggy sheen and lack of clear guidance.GREAT steam deck game (but controller setup is slightly weird to wrap my head around for some reason). i put in about 20 hours and walked away pretty happy with my experience. not a forever game, just a novel little thing to chew up if you like the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo, and now the full game, and i must say i loved it.It's SO rare to be able to finish a game entirely? I 100% it in less than 24h of gameplay.It has cons, like how cumbersome it is sometimes to just move ressources around... but it's compensated by the fact the quantity of required ressources are quite balanced and does not require gigafactories like Factorio.As a huge added benefit, the game adds a whole side of things to achieve and collect. Let's say there is a big Stardew Valley vibe in here that is very pleasant. I was addicted to really work towards getting everything, fulfilling all quests.Overall, i think i will put a solid 9/10 on it, if not a 10. It's a well made game, no crash, pleasant, only 1-2 very minor bug, achievable... I hesitate to give a 10 only because i wish the way we could handle placement of buildings would be better? Because of the lack of space on the islands, the challenge comes with how and where you produce stuff... and a special item can "destroy" everything on an island so you can do better. But using it with such a limited inventory is just hell.On the bright side, the small size of islands and the constant upgrades to speed here and there contributes to how you should think the links and the production to optimize stuff. Your island is suddenly a bottleneck cause your bots are too slow? you can make them move faster... but you'll learn later that you can also rely on other ways to produce the same stuff, without using robots, and suddenly you feel super smart for basically upgrading your factory. _childDocuments_.review: It's just Forager wearing a fake glasses and moustache.Overall it's a solid knock-off, but with some underlying issues.Some game mechanics aren't clearly explained or demonstrated, and others feel too light.  For example, the oxygen generator limits the amount of time you can spend away from your main island... until it doesn't and you get a basically free upgrade to turn it off, removing it from the game entirely.  There are health kits you can use to heal... but food is plentiful and there are very few enemy monsters that can attack you.  There is a diverse equipment and skill upgrade tree... but the upgrades mostly consist of things which are either so underpowered they barely impact the game, or so overpowered they restructure your entire flow.The best example of the upgrade imbalance is that there are two upgrades for logistics bots, with the first increasing speed by 50%, and the second increasing speed by 400%.  There's nothing stopping you from saving two points, and getting both at the same time, rendering the first one meaningless.The overall progression driver is also a bit too intrinsic.  Most of the driver in the game is "the game wants me to generate X of this resource, so I might as well figure out how to do that".  There's no real narrative, and there's little satisfaction in each incremental expansion.  You get to the end of the game and the ending is basically "congrats, there's no more tech tree to advance, you did it all.  Game done."  It would be better of there were progress points where it felt like something meaningfully changed, even if that change was superficial.  The story opens with you and others crash landing on this strange planet, which is a solid narrative premise... but it very quickly abandons that narrative and NPCs show zero interest in anything other than being a convenient store to sell you upgrades.All those grievances aside, I'm still recommending it because someone looking for this type of game just wants that incremental sim experience of "put simple things together, make big complicated thing", which it successfully delivers.  It won't be a memorable experience, but if you are looking to spend money on an incremental sim, it will be exactly the thing you wanted to spend money on.

_childDocuments_.review: Please, this is a cry for help... Nova Lands has held me hostage for the past week...I guess I should explain how I got into this situation. I bought it initially because people were comparing it to Forager, and I loved Forager, until the dev decided to kamikaze his alleged labor of love into the ground... sorry, besides the point. Just still hurt over that. Anyways, this is not Forager. To compare the two is simply an insult to Nova Lands. Sure, in the beginning, when you're still zapping away at resources with your quantum tuning fork, it's a bit Forager-y. But as soon as that bot goes down, everything changes. My biggest complaint is how this game has kept me from my wife, responsibilities, job, and anything else a grown man should be doing since I booted it up. But what makes it so good, in my opinion? It may not be as complex as other factory games, the NPCs are not as deep as other RPGs, and the story might be a bit vague, but...That's just it. That's exactly the niche I needed filled in my life. Some people don't have jobs, or can't relax, or the can't shut out the yelling of their nearly-divorced parents downstairs, so they need a game so complex or deep that they get lost in it, pushing their brain to its max every waking moment. Nova Lands will not do that. This game, in its nature, simplifies automation to a level that would feel familiar in the early days of 16-bit gaming. It's the reason I prefer the SNES version of Sim City, or the older RCT games. Management gets too stressful for me when I have to run a 1:1 scale theme park, or become a civil engineer just to build a factory. Nova Lands keeps it light enough to not be stressful, but is involved just enough to occupy the unused bits of my cranium. It feels achievable, it feels like I can actually reach the top, get to the end, without too much veins popping out of my forehead along the way. Achieve it, I did. This game is the first game since Forager that I felt motivated to 100%, as I am not one that normally goes for that sort of thing. I play games to have fun, and for once, a developer seems to understand fun. Fun, for those with no lives, may very well be cramping their fingers to get those precise inputs, or solving Sephiroth's anti-life equation to maximize their steel plate conveyors, but Nova Lands doesn't require this out of you. What makes Nova Lands a perfect balance of management and strategy is the limited amount of space. You have a set number of islands which, eventually, if you're trying to produce complex computers quickly, WILL fill up. Sure, you could just AFK and let the computers produce once per irl 24 hours, but what efficiency-obsessed freak is gonna allow that sort of malarkey? None. Thus, by the time you unlock these computation machines in your skill tree, if you made it that far, you're gonna spend a lot of your time figuring out how to reduce, re-use, and recycle.It's so refreshing to see that the devs actually play their game within the game. How do I know this? No, it's not because of the  (which is admittedly cool), rather, it's due to the fact that they clearly knew you'd be using every possible square foot of this planet equivalent to a NY tiny apartment. Soon as you get something that can do the same task, but better, even if the production building is larger, if it produces more resources per tile, you're going to want to rebuild your entire island so that it conforms to this new norm. This will happen many times. This is why, I assume, the devs added a literal wrecking ball. This loop of constantly making the most out of the space you're given, being able to delete your gold farms and replacing it with a drill, then using that newly allotted space to build something else... is soooo satisfying. This exact gameplay loop keeps me building, trying new things, figuring out where to nestle buildings... I mean hell, this autistic obsession has bled into my real life so badly to where I am now figuring out how to best optimize my fridge for frack's sake. Can't say video games never made me a better person now, huh mom?In summary, Nova Lands is an incredibly fun management game in my opinion, one where you can really make the world your own. The satisfactory nature of production is very much present, providing just enough challenge to keep things interesting, but not frying your brain into oblivion so that you can still function as a normal human being while playing... almost. I love Nova Lands, and will be adding it to my top 10 games of all time. Thank you, Behemutt, for this masterpiece. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Harshly addictive, with little to no payoff... but there is a lot of potential.While yes, this game is in a way similar to both Forager and Factorio, I would argue it lands itself in neither territory, offering a fairly unique take with unique problems on the automation genre. For starters, miners and conveyor belts are replaced with handy little robots that function much the same, except there is a limit of 3(+2) per island. What this effectively means is the collection of resources and ultimately the performance of your factories is limited. What doesn't help the matters is the buildings are awkwardly shaped compared to the island (square buildings and grid on a hexagonal island) and the game doesn't tell you the speed at which your buildings work for certain recipes, so optimizing is rather... hard.The game does feature its fair share of charm however and getting through it to 100% was a rather quick but enjoyable ride. If this is your cup of tea, look no further.

_childDocuments_.review: Nova lands is a game that, at it's core, aims to be a spin on forager with a bigger emphasis on automation.# This first section is about how nova lands is as an automation game.A lot of people here in the reviews, and people about to buy the game are thinking of this game like it's going to be similar to factorio, but after beating the game, it's really more like forager. Let me explain:In this game you are restricted to rather small and cramped islands as opposed to factorio and similar automation games letting you build to your heart's desire. As a result, you often have to relocate stuff around - sometimes you'll really need a lot of a resource, but you don't have the space on your island to do that. There are no blueprints or mass dismantling which makes this all more difficult.You are also not told the production rate of stuff. Which honestly sucks, because it means you need to test hypothesis about how many of something you need to set up. For example, if I want to have three assemblers making computers, I have no clue how many assemblers and smelters and refineries making the parts for the computers I'll need.What makes this worse is that, especially in the lategame, stuff takes *forever* to produce. Even when you make all the efforts you can to increase production speed, items are still produced super slowly, which makes testing your hypothesis even harder. And this lets me segway to the next point.In most automation games, you need to deliver 500, 5,000, or sometimes 50,000 of something to progress. That's not the case with this game - to unlock most upgrades, you need 5 of an item. Unlocking most islands literally costs 3 of a resource. Instead of making a ridiculous amount of items and blowing it all on science and building, in this game you'll be making a much more modest amount of items, though it is plenty enough to progress.Honestly, I enjoyed my time playing nova lands, but it is very different from most automation games, so bear all this in mind.# This second section is my thoughts on the game as well, a game.This game is pretty fun! At the beginning there's a lot to do and explore and see, and setting up bots to do things is pretty fun. The game overall is very well paced with how it gives you challenges, introduces new things to you, and gives you more comfort.By far the BIGGEST weakness of this game is UI/UX design. For a game that is actually really juicy and cool looking, the UI is very, VERY half baked. It has no juice whatsoever, it's bland, doesn't have the same personality as the game, and is annoying to work with. When it comes to UX, I almost died from losing oxygen, because the game has no indicator that you're losing oxygen other than a sound effect and a bar that is wayy in the top left, which is a spot you almost never look. Adding some kind of red flash would really go a long way. There are also not a lot of settings - the game pauses when you open machine menus and you can't do anything about it. Wanna change the framerate? Can't do that either.Also, the cutscenes are very very half baked. At one point you fix a guy's spaceship, and when it takes off, there's no animation. Just a white flash and a sound effect. After most cutscenes when you unlock something, there's a really long wait period before you can move again. The lack of cutscene quality really killed me a few times while playing. Again, the game itself is very juicy and nice, but everything outside the game world is very half baked.I really, REALLY wish there were more rewards for doing museum tasks. The only thing you get aside from a cosmetic is a health upgrade, and you have defeated all bosses by the time you have 3-2 islands left. There is basically no point to health outside boss fights, so the last museum unlocks are kind of pointless.# ConclusionNova lands is a neat game, but it definitely needs a UI OVERHAUL, more content, and other adjustments. You are not buying another factorio game, you are buying forager with a bigger emphasis on automation. It is definitely worth $10, not $20, due to the sheer amount of games that offer much longer and juicier experiences for that pricetag. I would give it a mixed review if I could. Hope the devs fix the rough edges!

_childDocuments_.review: Nova Lands is a really addictive game, especially if you are a perfectionist. Even after getting all upgrades and the islands, you can put hours after hours into optimization. The Space Station is well-made. I am happy to see the future content there.The Secrets are fun to figure out. I really love the customizable pet.Some things I wish would be implemented:• The three Bosses get useless after a while. It would be nice if they dropped something only bound to them.• A shop where you can sell all the other materials you have too much off.• The option to organize the Islands better. If you have an Island full of machines, you will lose overview (that some Islands aren't symmetrical is bugging me)• An Option to instantly destroy buildings (similar to Forager, since the game was an inspiration anyway)Summary: It is an awesome game that I would love to put more time into and you should definitely consider buying it if you are into these kinds of games. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo for Nova Lands (then called Nova Islands?) in the recent Steam fest and loved it. They put a lot of care and attention into that; even making a specific quest for the demo to let you finish something (which isn't in the full game). It's very similar to Forager in many ways, but with a little more emphasis on factory building. You produce resources, turn them into other resources, and build up and up until you've got (very simple) supply chains making computers. Each time you discover a new island there's something interesting to do, and it's full of animal and alien NPCs that give you quests. It lacks the proper tools for a scalable factory game, but is great fun.- Beautiful aesthetic- Lots of attention to detail- Has a skill point system that lets you focus early game on different progression areas- You can upgrade your abilities and tools via NPCs- There's a research tree for new technology- Each Island is interesting and unique- You can pin milestones for whatever you're working on- You can have a personal bot to mine and carry stuff- Has museum collections- You can ride some creatures- 3 bosses- There's a space station with a whole load of extra gameplay like new stores and housing- As production chains get longer and you progress, it's difficult to tell if you have a bottleneck and aren't producing enough of something. There's no production overview, and I had to check the wiki to work out the (actually very simple) production ratios- Until you get a specific ability, objects spawn so quickly that on my landing island I barely have time to clear the objects and select something to build before they come back again- Space is at a premium, which is fine - but it's quite difficult to tell which building you're interacting with when they're all close together- There's a Mysterious Tower island, with 5 altars. You can find the solution online, but I can't see any way in-game to work it out- The only way to see where an item is made is to check each machine type- Towards the endgame, there's a lot of just sitting around. There's not really any optimising to do like Factorio, so once you've plonked down as many machines as you can fit, you just wait for it to produce the last item in the chain about once every 10 minutes- The production timers on items are ridiculous. After suspecting that they were taking even longer than I thought, I went and looked it up on the wiki and sure enough, the last item in the chain takes 40 minutes to produce.- I have a gem machine which is meant to increase production speed by 1.5x. The wiki says an item takes 19 minutes to produce. I timed it. Also takes me 19 minutes to produce, so presumably the gem machine does nothing.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Nova Lands is Factorio and Forager mixed into one. Manage resources and building to craft, produce and collect autonomously. With a neat story-line, bosses and a TON of skins to collect, you will spend hours building and managing small islands. I especially like the bots who are programmed to assist you. You can only have 5 bots on each island "with upgrades" so you will have to choose jobs wisely. I do feel multiplayer would have been amazing on this game! I look forward to continues development! PRO:*Runs smoothly with appealing cartoonist graphics. *High replay value. *Achievements & unlocks *Addictive game-playCON:*Hard to target enemies / structures with clutter in the area. *Limited space / small game world. *Single player only.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: You essentially have separate islands and you have to create branching production lines and use bots to harvest and move materials around. I was surprised how addicted I got as the tier progression was really smooth and enticing. It has an AFK mode as well, and I left the game overnight a few times to let my factories run. It's a pretty good value as got 40 hours out of it for a $20 game (afk time included). I don't usually go out of my way to recommend games, but I wanted to give this game some love. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun little logistics / factory expansion game. It provides the excitement of watching your factorys productivity improve constantly and sometimes drasticly as you unlock upgrades and figure out how to organize the space you have access to. It is not very in depth, but if you enjoy the rush of numbers going up faster and faster as your factory becomes more and more lively, fueled by an increasing number of materials being extracted and processed, I would recommend this game. However, the late game is incredibly tedious and boring, with very long crafting times and not much to do while you wait. Additionally, some mid to late game mechanics are very infuriating to deal with, and I feel they could have been easily fixed by implementing a few more upgrades, also helping with the late game issue. Lastly, there are some mildly annoying bugs that manifest somewhat frequently, causing unnecessary frustration, and some grammar mistakes.Despite this, I think the amount of fun, non grindy gameplay this game provides before the late game is worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game. It is a fun little game about automation and I would be lying if I said I did not enjoy it. I finished the main objective (if you can call it that) in around 25 hours. If you are expecting a complex automation game, this is not the game for you. This is a simple game that lets you burn a few hours.It might seem I am very negative about the game, but the things that I don't like about the game are really not that bad. Like I said, it is a simple automation game which you finish in about 20+ hours. Or if you mess around like I did, you can squeeze a bit more hours out of it.Don't expect a complicated automation game that will take weeks of your life. This game isn't that. Combat and boss battles can mostly be avoided and the difficulty is real low. Automation recipes are mid complexity at worst. It is a pretty casual game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: I can recommend this game as an entry-level game to the Genre. There's some good stuff early on and a lot of charm. However, there are a fair few flaws that, particularly to those more familiar with the genre, could potentially sour the enjoyment at the later stages. But asides that, there can be something this game can provide for the right people, but for those looking for their next big factory builder, chances are this might not exactly be what you're after.A lot simpler than most Factory builders tend to be, makes it great for beginners and newcomers alike.Comfy gameplay and art-style.Decent emphasis on Exploration early to mid game.Upgrades come at a decent pace, anywhere from speeding up your buildings, gathering more resources, more and faster robots. It's all there and generally speaking every 15 mins or so I found myself with something new to use and improve the factory with.A lot of in game skins to earn and use. Bunch of neat references thrown in and all acquired in a variety of ways.Doesn't take too much time to beat. 23 Hours was about all that was needed to get 100% of the Achievements in the game and get the Credit Roll.A lot of functionality and information that those familiar with the genre simply aren't there. Ratios don't exist, so figuring out how much of X Building you need making Y to help make Z is going to rely entirely on guesswork. Guesswork that will also change as you get upgrades to your factory buildings. Time taken to produce is also never explicitly given either.Not much of a soundtrack. You will hear precisely a song for the majority of your time playing.Late-game and End-game don't feel nearly as solid and the early and mid portions are. Everything takes an eternity to build, even with upgrades and the use of temporary buffs in Lubricants. And it's stuff you need a fair amount of to boot. A lot of your time is just spamming buildings to make enough of the three things you need to make the Final Building for the "Main Story". There's no new exploration and I would say almost a third to half your time is spent on trying to clumsily put together the right ratios to make the last few items you need.Combat exists. It's very underwhelming. You get exactly one weapon to use and three boss fights which to use them on. Most enemies won't make a point to attack you directly. Feels more like something tacked on for the sake of it rather than it being of significance to the game.No way to get rid of the Feedback Message, at least not from what I can see. Got a bit annoying at times, not going to lie. A toggle for that would've been great.While Logistics Robots come nice and early, they are limiting, even after upgrades. Especially when up-scaling for the endgame. If you're going into Mega Furnaces, make sure you limit their output, otherwise the Bots will be tied down spamming resource delivery for all eternity and your factory will effectively grind to a halt. Don't get caught in that trap!While it's servicable and clean looking, the UI felt a little on the clumsy side. A lot of buttons and icons just don't feel right on a matter of scale. I feel like some bars and buttons could stand to be anywhere from a little to A LOT smaller. There's a good framework there, but it just feels a little hamfisted at the moment. Not a dealbreaker by any stretch, but something to consider, and hopefully something the Dev team might look into later on because I think it's just a few tweaks away from being great and an actual positive.

_childDocuments_.review: Seriuosly great game. Gives a "Cult of the Lamb" feel, but with more logistics. Tons of quality of life considerations too. I never felt any sort of tedium. _childDocuments_.review: Wow!Really really enjoyed my time with Nova Lands. Was a big fan of Forager and have spent time in both Satisfactory & Factorio, but this is the perfect blend that made me want to complete all challenges & collect all achievements! Really fun and chill and I hope they add more to this game in the future! _childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: An automation game that works well with a controller, Nova Lands doesn't do anything particularly novel, but it will absolutely scratch your factory itch. Instead of conveyor belts, you set up friendly bots that run materials to drop points which can be then ferried across the different biomes. It's very satisfying to see long chains of production result in a final product, even if the final products don't do much besides be another type of material. There's always something to do while your factory builds towards its next tier, so I rarely caught myself waiting for the numbers to hit a certain benchmark.I love the miniature ecosystems as animals interact with their environments; sometimes it's best to let nature handle a few things.The game has a definite ending, but it's strangely abrupt and unsatisfying, given its leadup. Still, you can stick around and complete endgame production challenges if you feel like your assembly lines aren't quite as optimal as you can make them. Overall, a fair price for the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game! I'm kinda new/suck at automation games but I'd say this is a great starting point for anyone getting into them. The game is pretty short and once you get to VERY endgame content there's not a whole lot to do but I still really enjoyed my time playing! There's a few things I'd like to see in the game in the future though:-More NPCs/Questlines, I liked the interactions I had it's just a shame they were so short and there weren't many of them-More Islands-Orders for bots (priority list for tasks)-Additional shops/planets maybe?-More bosses-Ability to sell more items & resources -More things to buy with the currency-A more detailed housing system (maybe additional rooms with added benefits/machines?)-More space....PLEASE more space (I get this kinda defeats the premise a little though!)-More useful and beneficial utility items that will help past the midgame point-More puzzles (they were really cool!)-Additional skills to help with very endgame content (more bot antennas maybe?)-Ability to unpack items-Ability to rotate objectsThese are just suggestions, though! It doesn't mean I didn't enjoy the game in any way, just some thoughts I had when playing. Maybe some of these are actually in the game I'm just stupid and didn't realise.Overall, I did thoroughly enjoy the game. In other games like Satisfactory and Factorio I often found myself getting overwhelmed because there was SO much to do and so much going on & this game did an amazing job of keeping me just on that line. I do wish there was more space though, the point of other automation games is a never ending expansion of the factory to keep getting on top of automation and with this game with the very VERY limited space you get it's extremely hard to do that, I found myself having to sacrifice production for important items just to keep on top of others and it kinda killed the rhythm I would get into. It does in a weird way help the game, you have to be very efficient with your space and production but when there are so many components to get, when materials like twigs are still relevant in the end game, it becomes a huge hindrance. Often times I would try to cram as many factories on an islands as possible but I wouldn't be able to use as many as I needed to produce certain things I NEEDED to progress due to the fact that it would kill the resources;  I'd say if you like this genre of game I'd definitely try it out, it's a really good blend of the games around it and it works really well, even if it comes back to bite it in the endgame.

_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting new take on the farming sandbox pixel art game that has taken over the internet for some time now. I personally love sci-fic and think the premisse (although very simple) is cute and works in the atmosphere of the game!The system of customization is elegant: you build and destroy structures very easily, so you can change the biomes fast according to the necessity of the moment. Also, I appreciate that some logistic solutions that are a nightmare to get in other games of the genre appear very early on the gameplay. Not only that, but a smooth evolution is dependent on these solutions: you can automate almost everything and dedicate your time to explorr the planet and administrate the final use of the products you create.I am considering the genre of the game here: we know the grind is real, specially during the early game phase. The difference in this game is that it pays off, since everything is rapid and you can automate a lot of processes quickly.Another interesting point is that you just have skins, because "you can look however you want in the future", and it makes a lot of sense in terms of sci-fic coherence.There are also little puzzles that are, again, coherent to the sci-fic background, afterall you are the one exploring a new planet, so it is up to you to gather information and solve the misteries. At the same time, the puzzles are very lighthearted, even jokes, so it does not become a "hassle".I really appreciate this game and probably will keep playing it for sometime, since it just offers a very satisfying experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Nova Lands is an intriguing game that offers a solid foundation for players to explore, yet it does have a few areas that could benefit from improvement. One standout feature is its commendable automation system, which grants players the freedom to divert their attention to other essential aspects of the game. However, as someone who enjoys the art of base building, I must express my disappointment in the game's lack of any base construction mechanics. This absence leaves a void in my gaming experience, as I yearn to create and design intricate bases to my heart's content.Furthermore, the diamond-shaped islands in Nova Lands perplex me, triggering my OCD tendencies as I struggle to find optimal ways to organize my land. I believe that a game built on a grid-based system should embrace square islands, as they would provide a more harmonious and structured setting for players to unleash their creativity. Additionally, the frustrating process of upgrading or relocating objects within the game becomes a significant hindrance. Why should I be forced to demolish machinery and structures just to reorganize my islands? I firmly believe that the ability to move objects freely should be a fundamental aspect of a grid-based game like this.Despite these shortcomings, I am optimistic about the potential of Nova Lands. It possesses the foundation for an engaging gaming experience, and I wholeheartedly offer it a thumbs up. However, to truly reach its full potential, the developers need to incorporate missing elements and introduce a few key puzzle pieces that will guide us towards a more fulfilling journey. One aspect that could benefit from enhancement is the depth of the tech tree, which currently leaves something to be desired. Nevertheless, I am confident that with time, the developers will address these concerns and propel Nova Lands into a brighter future. Here's hoping for a promising evolution of the game!

_childDocuments_.review: It was fun. Endgame seems like it doesn't exist. Once you beat it, there's no reason to keep playing.Nearing the end, moving all over the map was really slow and annoying. _childDocuments_.review: You'll love it if you love Forager. If you love Factorio, this is a much simpler and faster experience but still scratches a similar itch. I wish it was more procedural and re-playable. Right now there's a set of terrain and progression that is very fixed. But it's worth the money today and hopefully the developers will add more over time.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: I would much rather give this a meh review than a yes but it is competently made and is at least above average so thumbs up i guess.Game reminded me of 'Forager' when it first got teased and when i played the prologue it very much felt like Forager had been an inspiration for some parts. Sadly though it doesnt quite live up. It does however have its own take on automation with robots that you can build, each for their own functions. This does make the game a lot more enjoyable and part of me wishes they had taken this further. My main gripe is the amount of dead time in the game. Im constantly waiting for things to make or grow, the automatic robots are extremely simplistic so while they are fun to watch run around and complete tasks, the tasks are usually go from A to B while taking a resource. Once you get further into the game this just gets worse and worse as everything needs ONE specific item to make, which usually nothing else requires. So you are constantly adding more little bits onto the base, chaining more and more buildings to each other but meanwhile, nothing else changes. The islands are static and boring, no events or anything on most. Most of the resources are so plentiful that you wont have to really search or do any exploration, its all right there. No drops from creatures other than resources. It just gets a bit dull, I find that most of my sessions end in boredom more than any other reason. Im still only around halfway throught the game judging by content to unlock but its already gotten pretty grindy with no real rewards. So far the game has ran smoothly though, the art style is cute and everything works as intended. For how simple the bots are, they do work all the time, Ive never come across a bugged one and anytime they ''stop working'' its usually my own fault. I have also seen that there are more efficient machines and bots later down the line but considering the path to getting them, it honestly feels like this wasnt tested properly. The skill point system is really bad as well, the skills are REALLY specific and because the tree is super tiny, you unlock upgrades to mechanics long before you unlock the mechanic itself. I have no idea what the base speed of some buildings are because i had them upgraded long and was busy waiting out the timers. Like i said at the start, I wish Steam would update this archaic review system to include a Neutral option already. This is a well made game but not a well tested one. It has some fun to it but a LOT of boredom attached as well. If you like this genre and want a new game, go for it, you will probably find enough enjoyment to justify the purchase. If you are new to this type of game and havent played 'Forager', well, sadly I would recommend you play that game first.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Very addictive and very satisfying the automation is straight forward and fun and is very user friendly.Organising all the resources gets progressively harder as the game goes on, but the game has enough tools for you to use to make sure that everything is neat and concise. As you reach the end of the research tree near the end of the game there is a lot less to do, but the amount of content this game currently has is insane. I still think that some sort of coop online multiplayer would be amazing for this game and some kind of boss fight arena or dungeons where you can fight different enemies would make the combat have more purpose. There are a lot of surprises in store when you play this game and the way that the dev put little secrets into the game was really cool. If the devs can keep on updating the game for a few years with new and interesting ideas I think this game would really pop off, it's extremely good as it stands now though. If they add more of what they already have in this game and just make things bigger (bigger islands, more islands, more places to go to more ways to automate bots and gather resources and items to obtain.) I think it will be for the better. Boats and space ships that you can control to explore different places and being attacked by monsters on the way would be amazing.9/10 Epic love you bro thanks for the gift!
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent fun, took ~25 hours to do all the things I wanted with it. Progression is fun, and scratched a factorio-like itch for automation without as much of the complication. There are some UX things I would like to help make moving/building things easier, but given the small space you don't lose all that much time doing that by hand.I've seen reviews that complain about late game being quite grindy, but I found it quite enjoyable to optimize all the production I had to squeak out the stuff I wanted. The limited space and bots instead of belts made for completely different design choices to what you would make in other games. Plus leaving room for natural spawns on the island makes everything a balancing act.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I had been enjoying the game fairly well. And then, I reached the end game.First, the ending portions feel very grind-driven. There's a lot of waiting for resources. If you have the unlocks, there's a space walk function you can participate in, but unlocking it is dependent on waiting for the resources necessary.Then, while making the best of that, I managed to find an issue with one of the later locations — the five-altar island. Clicking in the center asked if I wanted to start a fight, and I pressed B. But... the panel didn't go away. I couldn't close it. So, I left the building. But then, I couldn't interact with any other buildings.Then, the game decided I was going to enter the boss battle anyway, which killed the character immediately.This is the point at which I exited the game, and began typing this review.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exactly what you'd expect, it's like Forager but it does everything just so much better. There is a fair amount of automation to get going and I can definitely see the resemblance to games like Factorio.Plus progression in this game feels really good as you get skills which take away building costs from lower tier buildings, giving you full control over rearranging your islands without having to worry about your resources.Super fun game if you're into more lighthearted building and automation, but if you're looking for something with more of a focus on complexity or combat, this might be the wrong game for ya. But it's worth a try nevertheless!
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Think Stardew Valley, but in hyper mode. Everything progresses very rapidly without too much investment. There is *much* less story and side quest elements, but there still are some interesting side games and a little bit of story. Scratches the itch for "number go up" without too much complexity or repetition, but does get stale after a while. 6/10 overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is [yet] another farming/building/researching game in the mould of Stardew Valley et al. You mind resources, you process them, you advance to a spaceship and doing some space walks asteroid mining if you have a mind to. There are some boss fights if you want; you can get around them. You can take a little pet robot around with you and there is a friendly ♥♥♥♥♥cat that you may find ... and, well, eventually you will get to fill large and slightly difficult orders both for the space station and "back to Earth". And then, that's that.     I have got 65 hours out of this game and started a 4th run (1 & 2 got too messy and were abandoned, 3 I finished, and I even started #4). Trying to optimize. The livestock in this game is different from most of the other games of its ilk, there's no petting your chickens every morning, there's no romancing the milk-maid,  you don't even have a house for most of the run, and you don't sleep overnight achieving a save point: you can save any old time - but there's only one slot for each character you start. No save scumming.     Oh, and, b.t.w. it's kind of nostalgic, BUT: the graphics are like something from a Commodore C=64; chunky little blocks of pixels. Even (or especially) in 2560x1600 resolution. Instead of fancy outfits you can get different heads for your character, but, you can't actually see them in-game, it's just too chunky.All up, the fun and entertainment value of 65 hours play time for what it would cost to go to the movies for a couple of hours: this is very good value for money. It may even invade your dreams, if you really get into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the demo and bought this as soon as it was available. I'm not a min/max-er so it took me a little over a week to finish the entire game, minus getting some skins. If you enjoyed Forager, this game had a very similar feel except everything you need was fully available within regular play (I'm still mad about the legendary gems in Forager). Overall, it's a lot of fun and I'm excited for any future updates!
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Nova Lands is similar to playing Forager with a little bit of added mechanics which are introduced around mid game. The idea of the game is fun; it makes sense and will keep you engaged... until you are not.All in all, the player engagement in Nova Lands is like a rollercoaster; with high engagement and down to low while going back up again once you get the space station. After all that, it will teeter off and become nothing but an idle game. Disappointing part of the game is that it feels somewhat unfinished during the endgame period but I do hope and wish that there are more plans for the game in the future. It's a game with potential; there so much they can do with this and I want more. Still, it is a good start to be a factory/automation based game. Just be prepared to be slogged down midway and at the end for it to be a waiting or an idle game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun game.  It rather short and simple.  Most things in this game are done through automation, so while you will be very active in your first 10-15 hours of play, the later part of the game is just being afk for 20-60 hours while you wait for parts to get made. _childDocuments_.review: very nice game, however here's a suggestionIn order to manage our production, we may need to know the time of each product. Late in the game, when we need to deal with long supply chains, it is important to know exactly how many of each machine is needed. I mean, if there's no way for the player to know the exact proportions of the machines, then the scenario might be like playing on a seesaw: there's always some machine producing too much material, and when we fix it, there's some other machine doing the same thing. In particular, when we need to produce thousands of parts in the final stage, and there is not enough land, a efficient production would become the goal of many players.

_childDocuments_.review: This game should be marked early access.  It is clearly unfinished and the further you go in it, it kinda all falls apart.First 10 hours it's a 5/5 perfect game.  After that and the more complex your factory gets various things just stop ceasing to work correctly and its a real bummer because I felt invested in what I had created.  Transporter arms stop supplying for no reason, bots seem to ignore various devices, and you go to a different island to see what the holdup is and everything has stopped despite ample resources.Many areas are literally half finished.  As you expand the map, islands get more simpler and barren.  The overall map seems half filled, The expansions should have been worth something, 90% of my factory runs on the first few islands. I dunno I knew I would want to keep playing after and ending's aren't really a thing in factory games, but to just finally hit the big peak and it just tell you "lol maybe later" was kinda a bummer.I think this game has massive potential, but it is clear it wasn't close to done and various things stop working to the point I'm not sure you can even complete all the challenges in it's current state, or maybe I just over automated what is capable. _childDocuments_.review: It is a better Forager. It just has a higher level of polish on things like movement, construction, and object spawning. Plus it skips the obnoxious "click repeatedly on things" step, which got old after the first minute or so anyway.The inventory in the game works very well, and your main challenge is inter/intra-island logistics on a very comfortable scale. The game also moves at a very comfortable pace compared to many similar crafting games. You won't feel like you have an overwhelming amount of things to do and instead you can often chill and wait or try and find a clever way to speed things up or both.The game also makes some really smart choices in that you can research the ability to not pay money to build things up to a certain level. This massively reduces the tedium of late game building and honestly is something that every similar game should steal as soon as possible. Though do note that there are other systems in place that prevent free buildings from trivialising the game such as well calibrated constraints on how much space you have to build on each island(plus on many of the islands building more has trade-offs because it reduces the number of tiles that spawn resources).So all in all great game, though fairly short. It is the right length for what is in it though, extending the late game would likely just be adding more tedious tasks.There are a few things that have room for improvement though:* the gem collecting minigame is tedious and repetitive* the combat almost feels unnecessary* not having good indication of build time makes it hard to prevent pipeline stalls in the endgame (as the build times are finally long enough that you can't just count outputs anymore)* could use a better way to clean up items that you don't care about

_childDocuments_.review: Looks like forager but plays like factorio (sort of...). _childDocuments_.review: Nova Lands has a clear Forager inspiration for the island expansion and crafting concept; however, brings a delightful refresh to the genre with complex production chains, resource scalability, upgrades, and plenty of cosmetic skins to collect.I've been able to do a full play through with a second half complete in ~ 20 hours; so, don't expect Nova Lands to be a huge game in terms of time to completion.  However, it's safe to assume the time you do get out of the game will be fun and enjoyable.There are a ton of positives to the game, from the art style, crafting, exploration, farming, etc., that I'll try to focus on the two cons the game has - the inability to set precise production limits and hidden production timers.  Limits are generally set in scale of 1, 50 (half stack), 100 (single stack), 200 (half palette) or 400 (full palette).  This means that buffers can't really be setup very precisely.  Production times are a myth.  There isn't a GUI indicator allowing you to know how long it takes to craft a specific item from a producer - is it 10 seconds or a minute?  Pull out the stopwatch, if you care, because it's a best guess scenario.I found myself constantly over scaling to overcome the buffer and resource production times.  It was plenty fun, don't get me wrong, but it also created a very crowded and very disorganized production chain.For the price, $19.99 (full, non-discounted retail), it's inexpensive entertainment and well worth it.  For the discounted 10% or 15% (if you have one of the package titles), it's a great buy.  At less than $1 per hour of entertainment, you can't really go wrong.  Albeit, if Forager isn't your cup of tea, Nova Lands may not be either.

_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is everything I like, but in a simple package that invites a few minutes of your time, until you realize you've been playing for 3 hours straight :DAt its core, it's an automation game. You start by gathering resources to make other resources, until you can make drones to start automating that work. You gradually unlock other islands with other resources which allow for more complexity in your product chains. HOWEVER: The devs very smartly kept the crafting pretty simple. Unlike other factory games with overly-complicated resource chains (looking at you, Factorio and Dyson Sphere Program), every step in the product chains is used for something. Crafting is done in buildings, so you don't lose context to inventory crafting.And best of all, you're not alone! The other people on this planet are eager to help you in your own adventures, whether by offering upgrades or divulging secrets.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Great factory builder game that has good progression. The end game gets a little time consuming to wait for production depending on your efficiency but it's made fairly easy to manage with the ability to transport goods around. Overall a great experience if you like factory/production style games but want something that doesn't get too complex. For those completionists out there I have basically 100% the game at 24 hours. For some reason I'm showing 38/39 challenges and the game does not list the missing challenge. Everything else is complete.
_childDocuments_.name: Nova Lands

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly this game is like a "lite" version of Factorio/Satisfactory/Shapes. It's got great potential to expand on what it already has, and is off to a great start. With that being said, it does need some QoL improvements I believe.Towards the end game, there is only 1 island for each of the high tier materials, and there is no priority system or able to split your materials autonomously without having to do it manually, so your lower priority builds have the same priority as your higher priority things, and the higher priority ends up suffering. I think a good fix for this would be to add the priority system or even add more islands with more of the higher tier materials so you can build multiple factories and distribute from those.I wish there was a way to make your own Nutritious Egg farm in the advanced farm, somehow. Or allow the animal barn to let the 'bees' inside and farm it from there. as it is a bit of a madhouse on the island where the 'bees' spawn. Would love to see a better system for those.Being able to add more than just 5 bots to an island could be helpful, even if it was just 7 or even 6. Sometimes you just need that "one" more when you're dealing with higher tier stuff or islands that have hostile entities.Some hints on the boss puzzles would be nice. Not sure if they're there, and I just missed them. But it looked like it was a bunch of guessing for the last 2. I'm sure there's more. But honestly it's a great game, and I've dumped 20+ hours in just 2 days. Lol

_childDocuments_.review: Forager may have some more polished visuals and be more popular (for one reason or another), but Nova lands really hits it out of the park on quality of life features.Nova Lands hits automation and expansion on perfect notes than keep the pace and also pushes you to explore, expand, and fiddle just the right amount to get a smoother line going.If you've played the demo, then you know what basis this all encompasses, but compared to the demo, the full release comes with more QOL features (like more automation buildings for making mundane items late game, and drag dropping items onto buildings) and waaay more content.Worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: This gets a thumbs up from me. This really scratches the Forager gameplay loop.The music is fine, but could use a little more variety.The tech trees are spread out across multiple menus/buildings, but mostly draw from the same pool of resources. It's a little confusing (I'm still not 100% sure how to gain level up experience efficiently), but it's still pretty navigable. Aside from research, the rest are just quality of life so it's not the worst to miss them.Menus/automation are a little clunky. You can easily set multiple producers to the same item in a row, but the initial selection doesn't feel that fluid. It'd be nice if you could copy and paste recipes, but I haven't figured out how to do that.I'm not a character customization person, but it's a little weird that a good amount of skin tones/hair are locked behind achievements instead of available from the start. I can understand cosmetics and outfits, but gating character features might not sit well with some folks.With criticisms out of the way, I want to emphasize that the gameplay loop is fun if you like automation games. You get to scale out production to make a lot of resources and unlock even more resource loops. It might be priced slightly higher than its "true value" at $20, but I have been enjoying it!

_childDocuments_.review: What if Don't Starve was relaxed? What if Factorio was cute? What if Stardew Valley was an automation game?Nova Lands feels deceptively simple to pick up and play because it is a distilled format. _childDocuments_.review: This game came at such a perfect time. I recently got the Asus Rog Ally, and this game plays amazingly on it right out of the box. If you like Forager and want something similar with a slight twist, then definitely grab this game. You won't be disappointed.However, there are certainly areas that could be improved. Below is a list of recommendations based on my playthrough of Nova Lands (12 hours in as of this review) so far:: Incorporate a feature into the game that automatically sends picked-up items on an island to any available deposit with the same assigned item on that island. Since inventory space fills up quickly, one way I've found to work around this is toggling off/on auto-pickup. Although I understand that this may be an intended game mechanic, it becomes tedious and distracts from managing the overarching grand automation system aspect of the game.: I believe the game could provide more information on certain mechanics without necessarily complicating the current user interface. Having less text to read is great, but it leaves a lot of room for questions. To illustrate this problem, let's focus on the bot mechanics. You have a collector bot that harvests resources and requires an assigned drop-off location, which can be either the Bot Antenna or a deposit zone. However, when storage space in the assigned deposit zones runs out for a specific item, the collector bot stops working. It took me a while to realize that in order to automate item pickups to their assigned storage, logistic bots are needed to pick up items dropped off at the Bot Antenna. This method works, but in practice, it feels a bit clunky, and I'm unsure if relying on logistic bots to deposit items in storage is intuitive. I think it would be more intuitive for collector bots to handle harvesting and bringing items to deposit zones, while logistics bots feed these items into production buildings. My recommendation is to provide an update where once a collector bot is assigned to a specific item deposit, it automatically knows how to search for other available deposits assigned to the same item within its respective island. This would be a significant quality-of-life update, eliminating the need for manual intervention to specify a new drop-off location for the bot and preventing the bot from becoming frozen.: So far, the leveling-up, tech research, and island research progress seem okay, but I feel that some adjustments may be needed. In my first 12 hours of gameplay, it feels a bit fast-paced and not very well synchronized. I can't pinpoint anything specific, but I often unlock skills related to technology that I cannot research until way later in the game. These skills are often perks for the said technologies so I feel that I should have unlocked it first prior to leveling up to acquire the perk for it. As a side note, I don't think I'm necessarily playing this game in any special way that would bias me from leveling up faster than tech unlocks. : This suggestion is pretty self-explanatory. I would like a mode where there is a higher level of threat and challenge.All in all, though, this is a delightful and addictive game that I would wholeheartedly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted more automation in forager from early in its' lifecycle to the very end, so this hits the spot.  Nova Lands does a very good job of distinguishing itself from similar games while still presenting familiar-feeling progression and ui/ux.  Aside from a little bit of timing weirdness when you get over three digit furnaces on an island, it runs perfectly fine, which is great for a game with so many moving parts.  If you're a pacifist, there is a route for you to do that in this game.  The combat feels like a streamlined version of forager's, but where it really shines is in how early and effectively you can automate the production of things you don't want to have to do a million times by hand.

name: Lords of the Fallen
detailed_description: Lords of the Fallen introduces an all-new, epic RPG adventure in a vast, interconnected world. Aeons after his defeat by the hands of man, the demon God Adyr’s resurrection draws nigh. As a fabled Dark Crusader, journey through the realms of the living and the dead in this expansive RPG experience to overthrow Adyr once and for all. Featuring colossal boss battles, fast challenging combat, and deep, immersive storytelling. Explore A Vast, Interconnected World Journey across two expansive, parallel worlds - the world of the living and the dead - with each harbouring its own pathways, secrets, treasures… and foes. Master Fast, Challenging Combat Choose from 100s of unique weapons, from heavy-hitting flails to rapid-fire crossbows, or forgo metal for magic with devastating attacks of the arcane. Customise your Journey With the Advanced Game Modifier System, fully customise your gaming experience, including enemy density, randomised loot, pre-upgraded weapons, permadeath, and more. Define Your Legend Personalise your character’s appearance before selecting one of nine varied character classes. Whichever starting path you take, develop your own playstyle by upgrading stats and weapons. Unite in Online Multiplayer Experience the campaign alone, or unite with other players in online co-op. You’re free to journey together for as long as you desire, with guests able to collect vigor (xp) and any gear that enemies drop, though only the host will retain world progression and quest items. Post-Launch Updates Over 30 post-launch updates have been released, vastly improving the experience with significant performance enhancements, rigorous difficulty balancing in response to player feedback, multiple new questlines, and a number of new Quality-of-Life features. Key Features: Journey across two vast, parallel worlds Fully customise your experience with the Advanced Gameplay Modifier System (immediately available) Master a fast, fluid and challenging combat system Overcome epic boss battles Wield devastating magic attacks and character buffs Invite a second player to join your campaign in uninterrupted, online multiplayer with crossplay functionality (only host saves world progress) Encounter a wide array of NPCs Choose from 9 starting character classes, including Knight, Rogue and Fire Apprentice Replay any boss in ‘Echoes of Battle’ mode (accessed at any vestige) Face the ultimate bossrush challenge in ‘Crucible’ mode (accessed at any vestige)

_childDocuments_.review: Lords of the fallen is a fantastic change to the souls like genre. There are some issues, performance seems to be something people are struggling with. But I have yet to run into a crash nor any performance issues that couldn't be fixed. I am playing on Ultra with Global Illum set to medium and i am getting 90 frames on a 2070 Super.This is a big change in mechanics, i feel bosses are a slightly more difficult than DS3, but harder than elden ring. The lantern mechanic works as a puzzle solver aswell as a boss/mob stunner which can be improved. The world design is gorgeous.My big complaint is multiplayer being ... interesting, they make the joining and hosting of games a lot easier than most but the actual gameplay and QoL a nightmare. There is hardly any incentive to joining a game unless its to pvp or to play with your friend and not care about progression.i give it a 7/10, if they fixed the multiplayer id say 9/10 as its just fun to look at and fun to play. I am pretty confident this dev group is open to change, they've been helpful and communicative. Feel free to debate me if you feel otherwise :D

_childDocuments_.review: If you want an Update after the game got a bunch of patches that some people insist "fixed" the game, I want to warn anybody against playing it still. The fundamental problems with the game quite simply can't be patched.I played up to the first of presumably 4 major beacon bosses, and while some issues have been fixed (Performance drops in particular), the game is still just the least balanced and fun of all soulsclones out there. Fighting the Hushed Saint for 30 minutes, really brought back everything that is terrible about this games boss design. AoE explosions after every attack to punish you for parrying. Perfect tracking on every attack to punish you for dodging. Absurdly inflated health pool to make sure you get to enjoy this for the maximum amount of time.Aggressively linear (Discounting the ability to go into one late game area early... where every enemy will then one-tap you), with boring world design, boring encounter design, awful bosses with maximally annoying boss runs and an annoying as all hell duo-world mechanic the game insist on forcing upon you constantly.The last part in particular is what just irks me out of my skin. No, it is still not fun to have to look for a worm thing inside a boss arena by pointing at it with my lamp, while the boss is already active and trying to kill me. No it is not fun to fight the literal same 3 enemies copy pasted over, and over and over while im in there. Yes its still lazy to literally copy paste certain bosses literal seconds after you fight them, but as regular enemies this time.If you're looking at this to scratch that souls-itch: Go play Lies of P. If you already did, play it again. Or just reinstall Elden Ring. The only reason to buy and play this is if you are genuinely so bored of the alternatives that you don't mind playing the same thing but worse in every way.
