_childDocuments_.review: Lords have honestly perfected the souls co-op. It is seamless, ignore aall the negative reviews saying otherwise, yes the game released in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ state where co-op didn't even work. Well they fixed it, and its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fantastic. So let me go into detailsIf you join a host, and you die, they can ress you once. If you die again, you simply follow their camera and wait till they rest.You heard that right baby, you can rest at bonfires (Vestiges) together with your co-op partner, both can use it, so you can both level up together as well. When you kill a boss, you do not get sent home and have to go to a tedious procress of being re-summed in a new area, nope baby, you continue on together, rest at the vestiges, refil your cross and go on your marry way together.Honestly I don't know why dark souls or Elden ring or any other DS clones out there haven't been able to do this, it makes the game so much more fun now that you can play from start to finish with your friends if you desire it. I have yet to try the pvp so I cannot rate that, but the co-op is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fantastic.The game itself is beautiful and haunting, great enemy designs, and has the BEST FASHION CHOICES in a souls game in a very long time, like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You can look like a bad ass crusader, a phsycopatic pyromancer, a lame dressed priest, or a degenerate wearing a gaddamn BELL as a hat with a cross weapon going around teaching people why they should follow jesus christ or get a cross through their damn mouth. Combat is actually quite nice, there is combo's, and at first I didn't really use them, thinking they were pointless. They - are -not. You can go swinging through enemy hordes with a light to heavy combo starting to spin, you can go smack smack THWACK, its a simple system, but adds a lot to the combat just giving you that little to work it. And magic? hoh boy magic is a whole else kind of awesome. I will say though they do mistake -difficulty- for tediousness at times, you'll go long ways without any vestigaes to rest at, but you do get introduced to a system of making your own spawns. These resources are usually obtained by killing a mob you can find around in the dead world, or co-op. You also get them from bosses, so it can work around the tedious loop of not finding a vestige. All in all I'm GREATLY enjoying this game, and can highly recommend it. Though its a big change to normal souls games, making their own twist on it like they tried last time, and honestly? This time I think they nailed it. There's room for improvements, but other than that, I'd give this a solid 8/10 with what I've played so far.

_childDocuments_.review: So. ProsThe game introduces several mechanics that stand out positively. The parrying system, similar to Sekiro, feels incredibly satisfying and is a welcome feature. The ranged attack mechanics are both unique and interesting, and the Umbra lantern mechanic is simple yet refreshingly organic, fitting seamlessly into the game.The first real boss, an angelic woman with clearly telegraphed attacks that can be parried, is an excellent example of a well-designed boss for this type of game. The decision not to give this boss a second phase was smart, as the initial fight is challenging enough without unnecessary complications. Design-wise, the boss might seem cliché, but it’s still very well done. Additionally, it’s great that this boss continues to be a character after her defeat, switching to the player’s side. Stories of characters losing their way but later realizing their mistakes resonate well, though the transition happens too quickly after the boss fight. It would have been better to allow some time before she becomes an ally.One of the game’s standout features is how it handles magic. Without irony, the magic system here is better than in Elden Ring. Although you have few slots, pressing a button lets you switch to spell-casting mode without having to change your weapon - everything is within reach. This is both unconventional and highly convenient. The way the game handles world-crossing, both for platforming and combat, is also very well done. Sometimes, you turn on the lantern and see a horde of enemies approaching, but switching it off keeps you in your world. The rendering of two worlds simultaneously is excellent, although occasionally it feels cheap. The game also offers satisfying environmental and level design. While it doesn’t reach the genius of Dark Souls 1, it does a commendable job of linking locations on a large map, leading to moments of discovery when you find a door at the beginning of the game that you can’t open until 20 hours later, from what seemed like a completely different location.The combat mechanics add layers of depth, such as enemies dodging charged heavy attacks, which brings additional challenge and realism. The variety in the move sets, despite the game's somewhat slow pace, makes it feel like a slasher at times, which is always a positive. Ranged attacks can be used from a long distance, and while enemies can also attack you from afar, it’s a fair balance.Another aspect worth noting is the interconnected world. It’s satisfying to explore and find paths that loop back to previous areas. The New Game+ mode with multiple modifiers and world-reset options at different difficulties is a fantastic addition. It slightly simplifies the game but adds replayability and keeps things fresh. The inclusion of a built-in randomizer is a particularly brilliant idea, offering a unique challenge and encouraging multiple playthroughs.But, consDespite its many strengths, the game has significant drawbacks. It is overloaded with mechanics, and at the beginning, you’re constantly bombarded with tutorials—how the lantern works, how to travel between worlds, and so on. Unlike games where you adapt over time, here the mechanics remain overwhelming, and you can easily lose track of what to do or press. This isn’t helped by the need to hold down keys for many menu and inventory functions, which feels unnecessary and cumbersome.The «first» boss, whom you’re not supposed to defeat, is incredibly frustrating. Unlike Sekiro, where you have a balanced fight with Genichiro, this boss kills you outright, making it nearly impossible to win. This is a weak narrative-gameplay device, and it’s disappointing to see games still using it. Death from falling is also poorly handled. Some might argue that falling should result in an instant game over, but we’ve seen better implementations in Sekiro and other games, where falling results in a loss of health. Here, the character dies but respawns in the world of Umbra—a cheap move that would have been better handled like in Sekiro, especially given that the game includes platforming sections, particularly in the early levels.The mimics in this game are another major issue. They have no indicators, are scattered in random locations, and the only way to identify them is by using the lantern - but you can’t distinguish a regular item from a mimic, and they kill you with one hit. This feels like a deliberate attempt to frustrate players, and the lack of a proper counterplay is a significant design flaw.The game also suffers from a lack of originality in certain aspects, borrowing heavily from Blasphemous in both design and narrative, to the point where it feels like blatant plagiarism. While inspiration from other works is common in gaming, this game takes it too far. The armor-changing feature is another unnecessary addition, and it’s unclear why many menu and inventory functions require holding down a key instead of a simple press.Additionally, the game’s decision to make most important characters and bosses women, while perhaps a nod to diversity, feels out of place in the grimdark fantasy setting and can break immersion. It becomes almost comical at times, especially when you realize that many of the bosses who feel the same in terms of design are simply copy-paste female knights. The inclusion of a burly German woman as the blacksmith, for example, feels forced and detracts from the overall atmosphere.The game’s environmental design, though visually appealing, contributes to gameplay that can feel jumbled and disjointed, making it easy to get lost or confused about what to do next. The maps, with their primitive sketches, seem like a joke designed to tease players, and it would have been better if they weren’t included at all. The final boss is another letdown, feeling like a dull gimmick battle akin to the Deacons of the Deep from Dark Souls 3, and the underwhelming pre-final boss doesn’t do much to redeem the situation.In conclusionLords of the Fallen 2 is a game that’s difficult to pin down. It features a mix of interesting and unusual mechanics - some that work well, and others that fall flat. While the game is overloaded with mechanics and makes some questionable design choices, it’s also a game with a lot of heart and ambition. The evolution from the first, frankly awful, Lords of the Fallen is evident, with clear efforts to innovate and experiment. Despite its flaws, it’s a game that doesn’t deserve harsh criticism. The developers took many interesting risks, and for that, they deserve praise. For fans of the soulslike genre, this game offers a unique, experimental experience that isn’t overly long or repetitive. It’s not the best game, but it’s certainly an interesting one, and it shows the potential for growth and creativity in future titles from the developers.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but there are many things that just are not fun about the game that end up spoiling the experience.The art direction and graphics fidelity of the game are phenomenal. Whether it be the many vistas you find yourself staring out upon, the areas you travel through, the enemies design, or even the pieces of gear you acquire, all of it looks incredibly and can really pull you into the experience. What's helped more is that the levels can be quite fun to explore, and it feels like you're rewarded for walking off the (admittingly linear) beaten path, with items or equipment.However, many other things will pull you back out of the game. I experienced decent performance overall, with only certain areas having an unsteady framerate (one being a boss arena), but overall these feel greatly exaggerated. Combat, however, does not feel great at all. It feels floaty, as if you're not in direct control of your character. The animations and sound design do not help, as it both makes it feel like there is a lack of weight behind you attacks. The animations of enemies and bosses feel cheap too - their attacks feel poorly telegraphed a good portion of the time, making it frustrating to fight them as you cannot tell when it's a good opportunity to avoid damage or take the offensive, or sometimes you just take damage because the animations are too stiff or quick to even know what's about to happen. Not only that, this game confuses difficulty with high densities of enemies and sometimes enemy/boss sponginess. Some places spam enemies, sometimes plants a few tanky threats in there to be frustrating, and sprinkles in a hard to reach ranged enemy that takes chunks out of your HP per attack. Other times, you'll find enemies hidden around corners or behind breakable objects, which also adds to the cheap feeling of enemies who constantly catch you off guard. On another note, I have not seen this spoken about much but this game has a very aggressive buffering system to moves. Oftentimes, I would find myself be trying to dodge an enemy, be hit and put into hitstun, before dodging once again without pressing anything, because I had maybe pressed the dodge button a few too many times before being hit, or once during being hit. This further adds to a feeling of not being in full control of your character, in a genre where you really want to be in full control of your character.Overall, I cannot recommend this game - more often than not, you'll find yourself frustrated with many aspects of the game, in between the few moments of joy the game brings to the table.

Don't get me wrong, combat feels pretty good most of the time, but sometimes when actions get queued up, it's like Jesus takes the wheel, and he can't drive at all. You can watch your character do 2 attacks missing the enemy, do a 180 and make another attack missing the enemy, or roll backwards towards the danger you were trying to evade.The camera does you dirty sometimes, but steps were taken in the right direction by the devs, as it also zooms out in some boss fights to let you see more.Music... must have been forgettable, since I can't recall any aside from the intro and main menu.The story and lore are great, I don't think it was a great idea to hide lore behind stats half the players will never invest in though.As of writing the difficulty felt just right for a melee user. _childDocuments_.review: Lords of the Fallen might just be the best souls-like I've played, outside of From Software original games within the genre. Its dark fantasy theme and world is lovely, with the story being as convoluted as any Dark Souls game.The second wind mechanic - that lets you fight your way back to life, through the deadly parallel shadow realm "Umbral" - is a fun and rewarding way to smooth over the mistake that made you fall the first time. The character's weight and feel is a bit different from the From Software games, but not at all bad as some other reviews seem to mention. For me the movement and game combat clicked when fighting the game's first proper boss, as it forced me to properly get the hang of how to time the parrying and dodging in fights.However, a few of the bosses feel a bit broken and unfair. Especially a certain giant demon baby later on, that one shots you with its slap attacks, which tends to teleport you back in after you successfully dodged past it.Regarding the game's performance on Linux machine (through Proton Experimental) with Ryzen 5 2600, 6650 XT, and 16 GB of RAM: It has maintained around 60 FPS at 1440p with FSR at set to quality, with some dips. No crashes so far. I've put the graphic settings on high (except the illumination/reflection, which I put on medium to turn off the ray tracing). It seems like multiplayer isn't working on Linux - I think - as I've yet to be invaded (phew!). But some online functionality works, like the ability to avenge other player's deaths.While not as polished as the games by From Software - that made the genre - Lords of the Fallen stands as the best Souls-like in my opinion. With all this said, I can wholeheartedly recommend Lords of the Fallen to any Dark Souls fan!

_childDocuments_.review: Lords of the Fallen stands out as a solid Souls-like game, heavily inspired by the original Dark Souls. The game has stunning graphics and an immersive atmosphere, though the optimization issues initially hindered mine, and the experience of many other players. Recent patches have addressed these concerns, making the game more accessible to their audience.The exploration and gameplay mechanics are satisfying and enjoyable. However, the bosses often disappoint, lacking the complexity and excitement expected in such encounters. The very first boss still almost feels like the best one, throughout the entire game, which should not be the case. You would expect more from a game, that is heavily inspired by the Dark Souls franchise, since it’s a crucial point, and should be something to look forward to.Despite this, the game introduces a unique mechanic with its Umbral world concept. The ability to transition between realms adds depth to exploration and introduces new challenges. The Umbral lamp mechanic allows players to manipulate the environment and find more ways to explore. One can either choose to enter the Umbral world by will, or will be dragged into it after death, and therefore will be granted a second chance. While in Umbral the world not only changes appearance, but there will also be new and more enemies, which become aggressive the longer you stay in Umbral. I think it makes the exploration unique, although it makes you feel like you’re missing out on items whilst you are not in the Umbral world. You even have the possibility to place your own safety points with so-called “vestige seeds”, which can make boss runs very accessible and exploration way easier if needed.Unfortunately, the multiplayer aspect of the game isn’t really the most pleasant thing about the game. While the option to engage in multiplayer activities is easily available, there are quite some issues with the matchmaking, but more so the players. Even after waiting for a very long time, I have not managed to join any other player and help them out in their world, and that one time I did, I got disconnected. Invasions are even worse, most players either disconnect shortly before dying to deny you any rewards, or disconnect as soon as you invade, it goes for both sides. For the co-op, I have to admit that the game does a really good job. It never disconnects a player from the host, even after defeating a boss, you even have the possibilty to rest at a verstige. You could basically play through the entire game as co-op in one run, which I think is very cool.Despite all of this, Lords of the Fallen stands as a worthy entry to the Souls-like genre. Although the bosses aren’t the most notable thing about the game, it’s still a worthy recommendation for players that seek a dark and challenging adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: LotF has a lot of things in common with Elden Ring, but it's also unique in its own class. I can't help but feel the Elden Ring vibes as I've gone through the tutorials, the areas, and the few bosses I've faced. Instead of Scarlet Rot, you're always in between the living world & the underworld. I appreciate this approach from a puzzle perspective. Some obstacles are removed by holding up your lantern to determine if you can continue in the underworld. It's been good so far, and I feel like the customization of the weapons will be fun to play around with.7.8 Hours in - The nuances of LotF are growing on me - I've tackled 4-5 bosses, each taking 1-3 attempts to finish. I'm currently running the Deluxe Edition starter build - Str/End/Vit. It's been enjoyable so far, and I've been able to scour the map for some other weapons. I look forward to changing into a Radiance build later on, but really want to Unga Bunga for a few just because it's a DS game. There are some elite enemies that irritated me for a bit, but once you learn their patterns, they're less troublesome. There's a good variety of melee/ranged enemies that you encounter.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to Lords of the fallen 2.0 where a character's story line can be messed up by opening a door in an area where the character does not reside, or by using an elevator, for example.The game that took an extravagant approach to the old fashioned method of adding new stuff to your ng+ playthrough. Instead, this time we're taking away your checkpoints. Truly revolutionary, I have to admit. And if you don't like this, sorry, you're just part of the loudmouth minority. If you've ever wondered what individual would put a seed right next to a vestige, now you've got the answer.The game that released 7 stability patches in the first week after its release. Technically, they were 6 as the changes of one of the patches were  reverted due to causing ever more issues. Only if they were so dedicated to making the damned lock on system work properly, as sometimes it feels like the only AI in this game that functions properly, even though it's often to the detriment of your experience.The game where you can find more success in using metric system in the U.S. than using the maps found in the world.The game where the shortcuts are often so useless that even the devs didn't bother programming the enemies to react adequately when approached from behind.The game where a successful parry sounds like a fairy fart.In light we walk indeed, as long as we're on the same platform, as cross-play is temporary disabled. It has not been enabled yet to be exact.The game that makes us install Dark Souls 2 again. Dark Souls 2 wasn't a bad game, to be fair.I can appreciate the creative approach when putting the world together, but to me at least felt the entire game is one huge Shrine of Amana. Most areas just blend together, which along with the fact that they're pretty big makes them feel like a maze at times. Lower Calrath, Forsaken Fen, Sunless Skein and Revelation Depths stood out as the most unpleasant places for me. Not to mention the enemy density. Not to mention the range of some ranged attacks. Not to mention my thoughts on the platforming in this game. God forbid if you need to lock on a target while on a platform.Played this game right after Lies of P, which was way more linear (for the most part), and also struggled with the lack of enemy variety. However, the enemies (and the overall world) were put together in a smart way, so fighting them over and over again didn't feel like a chore. This time around the enemies you're seeing in the 1st hour will be the same enemies you're seeing right up until the last boss. "Nah, mate, 5 total enemies for the umbral world is good for us, we're releasing the game like that". Just make sure that the melee enemies spawn as fast as possible.Also, I thought I'm the only one who can easily stuck between environmental objects. No, even the enemies are not safe from the unreal engine/the development team.After playing Lies of P, the bosses here felt way easier. That's not necessarily a bad thing, though, as most enemies in the world hit like a truck. So I guess one thing compensates for the other. There's a lot of stuff to explore. And I believe that this is the game's greatest strength. There are a lot of secrets, a lot of weapons, rings, pendants etc to find in the world, making you come back to reclear old areas again. This honestly felt awesome, kind of making up for everything mentioned above. I was pleasantly surprised by the amount of builds you can make. When it comes to that, the developers definitely put a lot of time and effort.Also, the co-op, since it's way more stable now, is probably the best out of any souls game so far. The visitor does not disappear even after the host dies, which makes for some majestic jolly cooperation.When it comes to Lords of the fallen 2023, what's good was taken straight out of Miyazaki's notes. Unfortunately, most of the devs' innovative ideas must be put back where they came from. No matter how much content you have in your game, at the end of the day, the player must be incentivised to consume it.Even though most of my complaints can be fixed with patches, I can only judge a product for what it is, and not what it could become. As such, this is a very solid meh/10.Edit: 108 hours later the game still feels like a Dark Souls 2 DLC expansion based solely in frigid outskirts.Please add adaptivity stat :3

_childDocuments_.review: I am a veteran of the souls games. 100s of hours on dark souls 1 2 3 and Elden Ring. I am Still on first playthrough of Lords of the Fallen and not even halfway through the game so treat this as more first impression than review. This game is fantastic so far. the combat is fun and satisfying and all the weapons Ive tried have interesting movesets. The world is very interesting and pretty. Enemy variety has been great so far but ive heard that it gets stale later on so that could be the case. mob density can become an issue at times but has not been a problem for me personally. Most complaints Ive read about this are due to the player staying to long in the umbral world. Literally the point of the umbral world is that it spawns more and more enemies the longer you stay in it. The performance issues people have been having is a shame personally the game has ran fantastic but I seem to be in the minority there. Hopefully devs get the game in a more stable playable state quick cause this game is a Fantastic SoulsLike and is very much needed. FromSoft can learn allot from this game. If this game will run for you Its a definite buy from me but since theres been so many issues others have been having Id say wait a couple weeks and see how things develop.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a great souls like. Many complain about the co op which, while in co op, only the host progresses the story and gets key items. The combat is fluid and feels much like bloodborne did to me. The umbral world provides interesting puzzles and a constant pressure of increasing enemy spawns and difficulty. This makes you feel the pressure of time while in the umbral realm adding another dynamic to the game. since recent patches the performance issues have been fixed. No problems in multiple hours since the patch.The game is good, especially if you look past some of the co op progression issues ( ignoring progression I like the co op). I feel due to the pre release hype many have been overly critical of the game. Look at first area gameplay to decide for your self!

_childDocuments_.review: False and misleading advertising surrounding the seemless co-op experience. In 2023, I would have thought devs coukd implement a decent co op system. A small company like Gunfire games can implement a simple but meaningful co op experience. Hosts world progresses but the guests doesnt but they keep all exp, items, can interact with the hosts world and then when they return to theirs they have all exp, equipment etc. This game does not have anything like this at all. Terrible decision by devs.EDIT: Nice work on the copy/paste reply marketing team.UPDATE #1: After numerous patches, the games performance has gotten worse. High frame drops even using low settings. When playing at launch, i was using everything on hight settings and there was no problem. How can you make a game worse after patches? Atrocious.Update #2: Months later I decided to give this game another try. Looks like there has been, yet again, no performance updates. Absolute lag and stutter fest. With the lies of seemless co-op before lauinch and now this... I wish I could have got a refund on this abysmal game.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I’m going insane with how negatively this game has been reviewed. The devs made some mistakes but they almost always immediately respond to feedback and get a patch for issues out as fast as they can. I love soulslikes and have played every major one and even niche ones. This one has become my second favorite (behind only Lies of P) one I’ve played that isn’t released by From themselves. The combat is super satisfying and feels great, the large dodges are amazing, and I love that when locked on you sidestep like in Bloodborne. The world/story is also super interesting and I read items more than I do in actual FromSoft games. The umbral mechanics are also awesome and the simple yet fun puzzles that you need to transform to it to either progress or for a valuable item never got old.I play on the Steamdeck and while playing on low everything kinda sucks due to how visually stunning this game is on higher settings, it still manages to run decently. I’m on my second playthrough with a new character that I started immediately after beating the game with my first, and I’ll probably go for the third ending with one of them after this run too. If you enjoy souls games, I recommend this 100% and praise the devs for their hard work and how great they are at listening to the community.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a good combat system, amazing visuals and really great level design. One of the best level designs I've seen in soulslike games. But a big but... unfortunately the game has a big issue that makes all these great features unenjoyable: enemy placement and density. Maps are filled with tanky enemies and usually paired up with ranged snipers... After a point I just found myself running arround trying to get to the boss because of this... Devs seems like listening the feedback at the moment. I will definetely visit the game again in the future but as it is right now I can't really recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Very poor performance, low mob variety, way too high mob density, map layout is absolute trash and annoying and feels like a labyrinth at times as to what is the correct way and which isnt. Not sure why they have a jump mechanic if you can hardly jump at all and it feels clunky. Bosses are pushovers for the most part, Lantern mechanic is basically useless as you usually play in the death world anyway for the majority of progressing as its not worth to constantly switch in and out. Too few vestiges, even with seeds, since you can only have one up at a time, it still makes for lots of running through areas. Items on the ground are mostly trash stuff and only very few are worth picking up. Damage scaling through stats felt bad, hardly felt any difference really. Coop was not that seamless as only the host is able to pick up items (other than mob drops) and progress with the game.So all in all its a pretty ambitious Souls Like game with too many flaws and bad execution all around the board but a Souls Game nontheless.Game is not worth the full price and i would recommend to wait for a hefty sale

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game, I honestly really enjoyed it and not sure I quite get the mixed review status. It does seem the game may have had a lot of bugs on release but I played it about 3 months after and I hardly had any.Its a lot faster paced than DS, so thats a change but it is very much so a DS game. The visuals are dope and the combat is fun, again its pretty faced pace.I think it does need some work, I think the lock on system is pretty bad and sometimes its just a chore to lock on to something right in front you. The collision also needs work, I cant tell you how many times I died from simply getting stuck or pressed up against a wall from an enemy. Also the final boss.... was a bit of a let down.Overall however I think the game is fun, I enjoyed the story and it has some really awesome bosses and environments as well. I liked the weapons and armor choices as well. At first I wasent a huge fan of the umbral world but it really grew on me by the end. I think if you are fan of good souls like or DS games in general this is a solid choice, I really also hope they plan to make a sequel with a few simple fixes I really think this game would be amazing.As it currently is, I say an 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Quick update: Encountering your first boss in the Fief area, which is a big dude with an axe with projectiles, three dogs that spawn spikes, (both the boss and dogs are invincible until their parasite is removed and you can imagine how fun that is to get rid of when surrounded by 4 enemies) a pool of water that you can't move properly in (unless you're in Umbral), and to top it off, a mini-boss spawns in when you're in Umbral when you've already got a boss and dogs to deal with. I'm all for a difficult game but when it's this BS to the point where it's not fun to even try and attempt? I'm just not gonna waste my time on it.I really tried to like this game. The world is pretty to look at, venturing between Umbral and Axiom is a neat idea, the game has some good ideas overall. I've played, completed, and done challenge runs on all of FromSoft's souls games plus Sekiro and Elden Ring and I never got tired of or annoyed at those games in the slightest. Lords of The Fallen is a different story. This game is just so tedious and so unbearably annoying to the point where I just can't recommend it. Enemies for some reason kill you in one or two hits no matter how big your shield is or how tanky you are and they home in on you from miles away. Some specific enemies and their spawn placements just do not feel fair. Once you finally do get through the area there's just no satisfaction to be had. You're just filled with dread at whatever nonsense is coming up next.Picture this, you're in a tight area/corridor, you get killed by some tough enemies in Axiom, so you come back to life in Umbral but surprise surprise, there's an abundance of Umbral enemies and even some grim reapers ready to launch themselves at you, AS WELL AS the enemies that killed you in Axiom. You try your best to get through it but you inevitably die due to the sheer number of enemies combined with all their extremely annoying attacks that wither your health away and make you use up all your heals. Rinse and repeat till you start exhaling so hard in annoyance that your lungs might just pop out. At least in Dark Souls, whenever you died it felt warranted, you messed up your crowd control or you just messed up a timing and got punished for it. It was difficult but it was FAIR. Lords of The Fallen is difficult but not in a good way, it's more in the kind of way that makes you want to bash your head into your desk and just nuke the entire area so you don't have to deal with such obnoxious enemies for the next few minutes at least.I commend the devs for releasing constant patches to address optimisation issues. I personally never had such issues but it's nice they're working hard to fix it. You can tell they really put a lot of effort into making this game and there are some really cool aspects of the game. I'm glad people are enjoying it but for me, it's just not scratching the itch I have to tide me over till the Elden Ring DLC releases. The game provides more annoyance than fun, so I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: So review of the game Lords of the Fallen (2023): I really liked it; Best non fromsoft soulslike I have played to this day! (I really enjoyed my coop run, better system than what fromsoft does, although perfectible)But although I do recommend it there are flaws I must mention before talking about the positives.Negative points:-Enemy density and placements could be better (often too close to DS2 to my liking)-The weapon movesets is lacking in variety (but apparently there will be a rework of boss weapons so it could be fixed soon)-The main bosses are a bit too easy. You could make some a bit faster and allow some more mix-ups in movesets (and WTF were  fights?!).-The performance could be better (but it has been steadily increasing since lauch so it won't be a problem in a close future)Good points:-The ranged weapon and spell systems are litteraly better than any soulslike I have played INCLUDING FROMSOFT!-The Art Direction is top notch! (Lies of P has a better palette & some chara designs are better but LotF is better in everything else in this department)-The soundtrack is very good with some OST being amongst the bests I've heard in gaming! -Enemy density & placements aside the levels are beautiful and well designed!-The combat system is enjoyable and offers a lot of variety.-Although the average boss experience is mid, the best of them are awesome in my opinion!In short, if I have to rank it alongside the soulslikes I played:It's on par with DS1 in my opinion; but below Elden Ring, Bloodborne or DS3.

_childDocuments_.review: Has the potential to be a really good non-FROM souls title, but it's ruined by hilariously bad performance, recommended specs on the store page are an outright lie.Paired with atrocious online, invaders hundreds of levels above you killing you in 2-hits whilst you do absolutely zero damage to them. Terrible netcode means playing with my friend is unbearable, up to a full second delay on dodging and parrying means I have to try to dodge things before I even see the attack for it to count.Also a dev responded to my friend's review and said they're making matchmaking better by 'prioritising good ping'?? Okay, what about friends who are playing together and have the same ping no matter what?? What a stupid nothing burger of a response. Fix the damn netcode or this game's online won't last a year.I picked this up specifically to play with my friend, but as it stands I can't bring myself to do a second run of the game, which is a horrible shame since the draw of these types of games is doing multiple different builds and trying new gear.The netcode needs redoing from the ground up, non-hosts need to have some degree of agency over whether they dodged/parried something, because having to dodge a full second earlier in my friends' world is laughably bad and really doesn't make us want to replay this game for a second run when we spend 50% of our run in the other persons' world unable to properly dodge or parry.Also can I just take a moment to say, whichever dev also said to use the 'auto' function because of my friend's complaint about bad performance.. you really have no idea what you're talking about.I'm over the 'recommended' specs and my buddy is rolling a 4090, the 'auto' sets me to high and him to max, and runs like complete garbage. _childDocuments_.review: The combat of this game will be very familiar at a base level for those who have played any of FromSoftware's Souls games or Elden Ring.Ontop of that it has a few added mechanics that make it feel a bit different but you know what you are getting into. The main new mechanic is the Umbral Lamp, this allows you to traverse the terrain (more on that later) and also use a special ability to tear out the soul of the enemy to deal some damage to them.The sheer build variety of this game blew me away, it's on par if not has more options than Dark Souls 2.The main negatives about the combat is that it can feel a little floaty with how dodging works and some enemies feel like they skate along the ground toward you from 100 meters away, I didn't have much of a problem with this myself but I could see it being annoying. Oh boy, I know there's ALOT of people that weren't a fan of this, but I absolutely adored finding every little secret, shortcut and alternate path. Every one filled me with a sense of joy and achievement that I've only had in the Dark Souls games, no other Soulslike has managed to capture this as well as Lords of the Fallen has.It has the normal exploration that other soulslikes have, yes, BUT it also has one other very interesting mechanic which is that the game has two worlds in parallel with each other. The normal world is Axiom and the realm of the dead is Umbral.You can use the Umbral Lamp to look into the world of Umbral at any time to see if there are extra paths, treasures etc, but if you aren't careful enemies in the Umbral realm can hit you while using the lamp and drag you into their world.A lot of the traversal requires you to swap back and forth between the two realms to find your way through the game or to find extra treasures/side bosses. While this isn't an entirely new mechanic in games (last one I played was Legacy of Kain Soulreaver, give remake pls.) but it's the only one in recent times that has done it so well.The story and lore is laid out mostly the same way as the Dark Souls games of old, through item descriptions, NPC encounters etc. It also throws in memories that you can view using the Umbral Lamp to get more tidbits about characters or what happened in the area you are exploring.The environmental world building, interweaving between Axiom and Umbral is in my opinion the best I've seen in these types of games. I'm not saying I think the story is better than souls, because it's not, but the way they use the environment to tell the story is.This game is absolutely beautiful, it's the first fully fledged UE5 game I've played. I very rarely found repeated assets in the game, most statues had something unique about them, especially with the way the doodads in the Umbral Realm were laid out.Onto performance, it released in a pretty poor state, crashing for lots of users and very low framerate or frequent frame drops. Now for me after updating the drivers and realising that Shadows, Lighting and Reflections above medium settings actually turned on Raytracing, performance shot up for me and I rarely had issue after that. The dev team has been very hard at work listening to feedback, collecting crash reports and trying to squeeze more optimisations so that everyone can enjoy the game. I have a fairly beefy rig (5800x3d/3080) so I imagine those with lower specs might have more issues.So, and this felt the same as Dark Souls 2 for me again, all of the bosses were EXTREMELY easy.Outside of  the tutorial boss you aren't supposed to beat right away and one other, I beat every boss on my first to third try. The areas inbetween bosses are absolutely brutal at times, again akin to DS2.While in the Umbral realm, you are on a pseudo timer in that you have an eye meter that builds up over time, slowly opening. Once fully open, an extremely difficult enemy spawns that for most of the early game at least will generally one shot you and has an absurd amount of health.This could be frustrating at times, but I found there were enough emergency umbral exits that I didn't have to worry about it a huge amount, and by the midway point in the game I was able to kill it fairly efficiently.Again, just like Lies of P before this, I'd say this is a must play for fans of Soulslikes, ESPECIALLY if you liked Dark Souls 2 as much as I did. This very quickly took over for me as my personal game of the year, and it has the best aesthetic and gear/weapon design of any game of it's type. The only game I think that beats this in terms of that is Bloodborne.I really hope that the devs develop DLC for this game or even a sequel in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: The game is very good, technical issues have been or are being fixed daily. If you like Fromsoft games and are looking for a souls-like that does most of what they do (sometimes even better), a few things of its own and don't mind it stumbling a few times along the way, you will enjoy this.It saddens me to see this game stuck at "Mixed" reviews, for this is, imo, the best souls-like currently on the market.It is true, the game launched with technical problems and would really benefit from a month or two more in the oven, but even with my specs, I only had two inconsequential crashes and occasional frame drops in certain areas. This is not in any way worse than Fromsoftware games and it is certainly not yet another Redfall. The game is feature-complete and the devs have been patching the game literally every day and, for me at least, the performance has only been improving.Lords of the Fallen is a souls-like almost to a fault. It is evident that the devs are huge fans of Fromsoftware games and, quite frankly, ape their games. To someone like me, who likes Dark Souls, Elden Ring and Bloodborne and basically wants more of that, this is, by and large, a positive. They took all the good (like the combat, the level design, the interconnectivity of the world, etc), but also took the bad (like the obtuse quests, a thread of which is very easy to lose or the dialogue that you have to spam a button through). None of the negatives are a deal breaker for me, personally. A quirk of the game's combat system is how your weapon swings propell you forward way further than you'd expect. That sounds like a huge problem, but it was surprisingly easy for me to get used to it fast. Same rule applies to enemies too, so you just have to keep in mind that the range of your and their attacks in effect is longer than you think. It has advantages and disadvantages and generally it isn't an issue and only caused a fall off a cliff once for me, but it's something worth noting.With that said, they do try their own things too, like ranged and spell system. Ranged combat (that is bows and throwables) in Fromsoftware games is an afterthought, a tool only useful for pulling enemies from afar. Hexworks tried their best to make actually compelling and functional ranged combat that can stand alongside mele as a legitemate way to play the game. You have of course your bows and crossbows, but it's the throwables that stand out. You have your javelins and knives for pure damage and status buildup, but you also have standards for buffs, grenades for debuffs and damage and many other niche and utility options, of which you can have up to three slotted to be switched between on the fly. You have a wide variety of spells as well, of which I won't write much, but they are performed under the same system as ranged, making spell casting a fluid and enjoyable experience.A little more about the world: the game is pretty long with around 16-17 zones, a couple of which are revisited. All of them have plentiful shortcuts, side areas and secret passages. Exploration is one of the strongest pillars this game stands on and you will feel right at home if you've played other games in the genre. If there is one criticism I had about the zones, it's that a big chunk of them are a "city" biome, as it were. A little more variety would break the samey feeling mid-game. That said, a few times you will have a choice between which zone you want to tackle next, so that could help.One problem the game does have is the bosses. I'm not the "git gud", "hard = better" type of player, and although fighting Gale, Ludwig or Orphan of Kos was the most joy I've had in a video game, I don't believe that difficulty is the most important part of Souls-likes. However, Lords of the Fallen bosses are very easy and I can't quite point my finger at what exactly is the issue. Perhaps the attacks are too weak, perhaps the hp is too low, perhaps the combos are too short or telegraphs are too, well, telegraphed. When I fought the first six or so bosses (including important ones), I thought the difficulty was appropriate for the early game as it wouldn't discourage newcomers. Unfortunately the trend continued and hardly any boss required more than two attempts. It was still enjoyable, but I wanted more of a challenge. Perhaps NG+ will be different. Mind, Getting TO a boss is still, more often than not, a challenge, but I wish it was a bit more evenly balanced.A word about Umbral realm (Ah, devs, I see you know your Soul Reaver well!). Don't write it off as a gimmick. This is an integral part of the game and a masterfully implemented one. Not only the visuals are stunning, but it also makes you think differently about how you navigate through the zones. You can drop into it at any point, but getting out is only possible at specific effigies scattered around a given zone or through ones you create at the cost of a scarce item. The realm introduces extra enemies that complicate the area further and you have to be more careful. My only problem with Umbral is the constantly spawning weak enemies become a real annoyance and at some point I just get tired of mowing through them.Lastly, visuals, and I'm not talking about the graphical fidelity. Some would argue that art direction of a game is one of the least important things when it comes down to playing, but I strongly disagree. The visual style and art direction, when made with thought and a consistent vision is one of the core aspects that make the whole thing work. The art team has set out to create a dark, opressive, suffering world that hates its people and they absolutely nailed it. Partly thanks to the worldbuilding and the lore (of which I, admittedly, neglected to talk about, but it's good!), you get immersed in this world in pain and on the brink of collapse. It is unpleasant in the best possible way.To close this off, it is rare for me to enjoy a Souls game not from Fromsoftware. Something always feels off, be that speed, the combat animations, telegraphs, the disconnect between a swing animation and actual strike connecting. In Lords of the Fallen, everything just clicked perfectly within the first hour or so. It is a great game, a real product of passion and love for the genre from a team that truly wanted to make something they themselves like playing. There are many more good things I haven't written about, because I was just putting in stuff off the top of my head, but trust me, a random talking head on the internet, when I say that the positives outweigh the negatvies. Come with an open mind, abandon your preconceptions and you might just enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've given this game far more chances than it deserves, waiting for the fun to happen, but it never does. So many questionable design choices — the fact that mob density is an actual feature just baffles me and at times I wondered if I was actually playing a Musou game. To make it worse, when combined with the lack of enemy variety, every encounter is basically you rushing to kill off the snake archer that is WAY too powerful before he kills you. I don't think I've ever played a game where the parry is this badly designed either. In games like Sekiro, you get this wonderful visual and audio cue of your blades clashing, but in Lords of the Fallen you get a soft sound of a bell chime. Why?Combat feels floaty and awful - dodging or swinging of your weapon sends you 2 meters forward. It's just hilarious to me that the biggest challenge of the game isn't the bosses or enemies but rather how often you fall to your death. Bonfires are replaced by the vestige seed system, where you get to 'plant' your own bonfire that's scattered throughout the level, keeping the player guessing on which ones they should use. Sounds neat until you realize that some vestige beds are placed literally right next to checkpoints, so you've just wasted your seed.. WHO designed this?? I could go on and on about the terrible level design, atrocious lock-on, performance issues (the stutters are too real), unrewarding exploration, enemy souls not scaling, awful enemy placements and getting sniped from half a continent away.Imagine getting a second chance to reboot your franchise with years of valuable feedback on what NOT to copy from the worst part of previous souls game and still failing in so many aspects of game design. The only redeeming quality of this game is the environment and graphical fidelity — there are gorgeous vistas, but good luck appreciating them when you're constantly swarmed by enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the hype train when I bought it. I tried really hard to enjoy this game but I can't get the game run above 25 fps with a 3060ti gpu. Lower graphics settings don't change anything, only lower gpu usage and missing textures. In some areas fog is a giant rectangle on low settings. Oh, and it's a gamble of 50-50% whether or not the game corrupts your save file,  Ye ye then backup your saves manually, of course it's definitely something you would expect from a 60€ game.Let's not forget that the devs set the expectations high:  and of course the very NOT suspicious and definitely NOT paid positive reviews on release day of a half-finished broken game. Oh and they really do co-operate with the community, they delete the negative comments about performance if they can, and only keep the positive ones. They don't give a single f about the community because it is clear what orbitally big issues the game has, and what do they do? they launch a halloween event or nerf boss weapons so that everyone, who grinded for hours to get the mats required  is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ because the upgrades are reverted and the mats are taken away without compensation. Oh and if you had runes in those weapons, those are deleted as well. But then they said you can buy those materials from the coop vendor. Yes, for a currency which you get if you play coop and even if you manage to connect to someone, it is with insane lag. And you have to kill 15 bosses like this to buy one of that crafting material. Instead of 30. Temporarily. As a compensation for taking away something you worked hard for, you can work even harder to get it back :))) Inventory is limited yet we get no storage, so if you go past the limit,  Pvp was (and is) trash so what did they do? Nerfed pve weapons and skills so that pvp is still trash but now pve is as well. Millions of micro patches that make the game worse but they can't address the most basic issues like performance and stability. Game crashes like crazy yet they very much emphasise that only a very small percentage of players are affected by performance issues. Both my SO and I experience gamebreaking performance issues, but we are definitely the 0.1% exception as the devs say.And please try to recognise thatThe game is not hard. Bosses can be insanely easy especially if you don't rush through the game and take your time to explore and get some exp. Not much after the tutorial you will be able to one-hit-kill almost any mobs that try to attack you. The problem is that it was not once that I died because mobs swarmed me and couldn't move. I wouldn't have a problem with this, but why is that I don't die to bosses yet small mobs keep making me die? Pushing me off ledges or jumping on my head is not difficulty, it is annoying.Devs don't care about the community, they don't care how much time you lost because of their incompetence. All they care about is money. Keep ruining your game devs, it was a big slap in the face for almost everyone who bought the game just after release. And don't get me wrong I am not biased. I was hopeful, I was actually defending the developers, because  I actually tried enjoying the game, looking past all the issues it has. My head hurt because of the low framerate and not once did I ragequit because I died multiple times caused by the stuttering and framerate drops. I couldn't use flashier builds because the effects killed my game. But hey, I liked the idea, combat was more fluid than it is in let's say Elden ring, the umbral world is an amazing concept, and the art style is eerie yet beautiful dark fantasy, the co-op system would be good, better than any of the souls games had to offer as you are able to finish the game from tutorial to the ending in one session with your partner  so I sticked around. The game had potential but the execution is bad, and let's not talk about the attitude of the developers.But it is getting clearer and clearer that they are incompetent. I won't say I wasted my money but I definitely feel scammed and lied to. They had the chance to make things better and they decided not to. Looking past the issues got very exhausting and I just gave up. Uninstalled the game and I will check back when it actually gets playable. And they have the audacity to ask for a GOTY vote. Keep dreaming.

_childDocuments_.review: After completing the game, I have a generally positive feeling overall. Does the game have some annoying quirks? Yes, but I can say the same for all of the Dark Souls games. In the end, between the cursing when I died for the Nth time, and the glowing satisfaction I felt when I finally managed to survive to another vestige, it felt like I was playing Dark Souls 4. I honestly prefer this game to the Nioh series, because it's so much more satisfying to find hand-crafted gear than gear with random stats assigned. I would put this alongside Lies of P as the best non-FromSoftware souls-likes so far.I played it starting day one and didn't have any hard crashes, but I did have consistent frame drops. After all the patches, I'm not sure the frame drops really improved, but it was never really game-stopping on my relatively-strong system anyway. Props to the devs for their fast updates, I've never seen a dev pump out that many updates so quickly. Hope you guys kept up on your sleep. System specs: 4k 120Hz VRR display, RTX 3080 Ti, 5800x3D, PCIEGen 4 drive. Settings were on high with DLSS on performance mode.I think the game is fairly good for replayability, although I'll be starting fresh with a new character instead of playing new game plus. I'll let it sit for a few years and run through it when I'm doing yet another Souls marathon. There's plenty of different character builds and items to use, so I think it will be fun to try a different build.They are reducing mob density in certain areas, although that never bothered me since most of the weapons are built to deal with crowds. I guess this is highly subjective, you'll either not care or hate it.Some enemies were definitely over-tuned with their scalars, such as the crossbowmen who kill you from 10 miles away in two hits regardless of armor or level. Some of these enemies have been tuned by patches, but I'm already past that part, so I can't comment on the impact.Boss fights were probably the most polarizing part of the game, aside from the crowd density. Some boss fights were incredibly meh, like the last boss, or they were incredibly annoying, like the first boss in the ice area that had deep water to slow you down, a boss with a two-hit medium ranged attack, a bunch of wolves, a stone head mini-boss, and a parasite to protect all of them in the same room. Ugh. However, some of the bosses were pretty fun to fight, like the first two bosses, the crow boss, etc.The only complaint I really came away with was regarding the monsters disguising themselves as items. Because they look like normal items instead of chests, it's incredibly easy to just wander up to an item and click on it with muscle memory before the brain kicks in, then you're dead. I prefer the mimic in DS games since chests are more rare, and the mimic is a tough fight even if you realize it's a mimic. The item mimic in this game was just annoying instead of fun, since it's incredibly easy to kill but you probably won't realize that it's a mimic, especially if you only play the game every few days and forget that the mechanic exists.My final suggestion would be to buy this game if you have a decently-strong system and you like Souls-likes. Don't have a strong system? Be ready to possibly refund since UE5 is a demanding game engine. Of course, at the rate the developers have been pushing out patches, this may be the most polished UE5 game outside of Fortnite by the time the first sale comes around....I'll leave the comments on because I want the salty players to come to me. Shed your tears upon me while I praise the sun!

_childDocuments_.review: My first review of the game was mean spirited, so I removed it. Now, let me explain why I changed my mind:Lords of the Fallen is a Soulslike.  Let me remind you that a Soulslike is a game like a souls game, but not exactly the same as one.  Once I came to terms with that, everything clicked for me.  Lords of the Fallen is similar to dark souls in that you have a currency you lose on death and have to retrieve, bonfires, stamina based combat, etc, but that's where the similarities end and where LotF decides to be its own thing.Lords leans heavily into the action aspect of action RPG.  You are constantly fighting against two, three or more opponents at a time.  Thankfully, the game's movement and dodging systems are made to compliment this fact.  Movement is fast, and rolling provides huge distance, which you'll need to handle the swarms of enemies, yet make sure to watch your surroundings as well.Let me mention the elephant in the room that's been going around online as more people play the game: New Game + removes all hard checkpoints outside of the hub area.  Yes, the developers originally designed the game this way.  Yes, I think it's silly and should be changed.  Despite this, something that only happens in an optional new game + mode has not affected my experience in standard new game.Performance wise, with an nvidia 3080 TI I haven't had any issues running at 60FPS after setting shadows, foliage, and a bunch of other performance heavy settings (depth of field, motion blur) to low/off, while everything else is on Ultra.  YMMV, you'll need more than a 4080 TI to do everything.  If you go with the game's auto-detect settings or just use the preset option to go to High or above the game automatically introduces raytracing.  Now, let's talk about the negatives and things the game can improve on.The developers are constantly patching and fixing this game.  I've seen multiple patches a day, even.  Despite this, there are a few glaring issues that may end up being a deal breaker to some.  PVP Invasions range from very laggy to smooth as silk.  You'll be rubber banding into the host's attacks and killed without a way to defend yourself often.  If you're the host, the invasions run smoothly with absolutely zero issues, however.The game has seamless co-op, however only the host is able to interact with world items and progress their world state.  Once the co-op buddy returns to their world they're back to whatever state their game was in.  I don't mind this, but I'm aware some people very much dislike the idea of "losing" progress.There are also a few technical issues that will lead to more than a few "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" deaths.  Enemy archers/mages can and will target you from across the map and hit you 99% of the time.  Enemy projectiles can and will track and turn mid-flight to hit you, meaning simply strafing isn't an option.  Enemy projectiles can and will clip through walls and hit you.  I believe this is due to the dual world nature of the game, still a rage maker.  The lock-on system is odd and will lose target constantly.  Sometimes it works perfectly and sometimes the game will lock onto something on a rooftop 20 feet away while you're fighting five guys in front of you, which causes your camera to jerk to one direction and disrupts the flow of combat at best, gets you killed at worst.  Finally, the last negative on this list is the rolling.  Throughout my entire playthrough I've learned I can't trust my rolls.  If I'm locked onto an enemy, hold my control stick straight backwards and roll, 7 times out of 10 my character will roll either to the enemy's left or right.  This is the biggest issue I have with the game, that the dodge roll seems to be based on your lock-on target, rather than your character.  This takes away control of your character and leads to a whole host of other "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" moments in an otherwise fine game.Despite all this, I do recommend the game.  Lords of the Fallen takes enough from Souls to be familiar, but then it immediately branches out to be its own animal.  The best advice I can give to someone playing or interested in the game is to not treat this game like dark souls.  If you treat the game like dark souls, you're going to be disappointed, like I was.  Treat the game like Lords of the Fallen and play into all the strengths you're given and the game is great.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to say about lords of the fallen (LOTF from herein), but I'll preface this by saying that it's so close to being a good game that it's downright frustrating to downvote it like this. LOTF is another entry in the 'git-gud' souls-like games and combines elements from almost every single one; posture gauges, a "second life" mechanic and an open-ish interconnected world with tons of explore. Let's start with the good; the whole concept of having a second version of the world going at the same time is really well executed. It's polished and looks fantastic to change between worlds to cross gaps in the terrain, find hidden items and the likes. The enemy's visual design is very distinct between both and the game is usually very good about letting you know that there's stuff going on in umbral.The game has a lot of redeemable qualities in the combat department as well -- the lamp is a cool mechanic that allows you to pull/push enemies around on some regenerating charges and there's a certain sadistic joy in flinging enemies -- or players -- off of ledges with it. A lot of maps feature these insta-kill pits or very high drops that are guaranteed to be fatal to any rank and file enemy. Furthermore this mechanic is even useful on bosses that -- while they can't be flung -- will deal considerable posture damage to them. Weapons are varied and the ability to dual wield, power stance and one hand weapons seamlessly mid combos is really cool and feels great to use. The visual design of these weapons is well realized and most of them feel great to use.Ranged combat is also very well implemented -- a mixture of mana bars for casters and an ammo counter for physical damage dealers means you aren't constantly buying arrows or wasting precious flasks just for a bit of extra mana. The consumables needed to replenish either of these are plentiful and very cheap to replenish even in the early game.However, all of this has a certainl cost associated with it, and this is where the bad stuff comes in;LOTF suffers from having combat that is both incredibly slow and methodical to pull off, but also marred with inconsistent hit/hurt boxes for enemies. Some attacks are very well telegraphed, some are downright instant and offer you almost no breathing room at all. There's also an issue with enemy placement; yes everyone complains about every zone past the introduction being utterly flooded with archers and casters in every ledge this side of the planet. These are countered by just using the game's generous ranged opportunities to some degree -- but the sheer number of enemies that are usually in every little portion of the game really harkens back to the feeling of "monster closets". More than once -- even in the early game -- you'll find yourself walking into a new room with two, three or four enemies who lock on to you while one or two enemies pelt you with ranged attacks from afar. It's tiresome, and often a single mistake can leave you completely stunlocked for the rest of your meager life.Secondly, there's an issue of balance -- most standard enemies feel relatively well balanced, but a few "tough" enemies are thrown about that are extremelly spongy, not to mention they can empty your entire lifebar in two to three hits. Blocking or parrying works wonders if they're isolated, but as the point above stands; this is rarely the case. You'll find yourself surrounded trying to clear the smaller enemies while being assaulted from all sides. Careful preparation is a godsend in getting through some of these areas, provided you don't accidently step off a ledge, get knocked over and stunlocked, or simply run out of stamina while trying to dodge and find better footing.Weapon balance is utterly out the window. Some weapons are downright garbage, there's no reason to have or keep them. Save for a few instances, you'll find yourself relying on the same weapons you see other players use.The umbral realm -- while a stellar idea on paper -- comes with a significant problem; endlessly respawning enemies can be a great source of regenerating your "withered health" -- but they're also a constant nuisance, adding to the already extremelly busy monster closets you fight your way out of. On top of this, the umbral realm also usually contains even more enemies that aren't present in axiom. One would think that shifting between realms would offers a different set of enemies, but unfortunately this is not the case; enemies from umbral are added on top of those that already exist. This means that if you find yourself mobbed and in a bad spot, you can expect things to get even worse once you switch over.Secondly, on the topic of umbral, certain sections "force" you into being in the umbral realm, which takes away your "second chance" mechanic.Lastly, the quests; the game has three endings. Doing a certain thing near the end of the early game locks you out of all but one ending. Certain items needed for quests are hidden in sidepaths that are super easy to miss, and NPCs will rarely -- if ever -- give you any real directions on what they want and where to find it. The third ending is so convoluted that it's ultimately recommended to grab a guide to get it.Conclusively, LOTF has a ton of potential. It has so many good ideas and is an incredibly polished game with a lot of charateristics that should make it a smash hit. But some of the level design decisions, and the interaction between some of these mechanics make it a soft pass for me at this point. Worth getting on sale, but hardly at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a mixed bag of good and bad mechanics that leave alot to be desired.The ending feels unfinished, is very disappointing and not something to look forward to either.Skip until fixed, if this can even be addressed.Let me preface this with the following:I have played my fair share of Soulslikes on PC and console, but this game is unfortunately a mixed bag for me.There are a few things that it does really well, but there are also a bunch of things that it doesn't do well or are outright poor.I have also played through the game and did the radiant ending. It disappointed me so much that it brought me to let out my frustration with a chunky review, that i'm usually too lazy to write down.The Manse of Brothers and the rest of the Holy Grounds till the Judge and thus the end of the zone were the most fun i've had in the entire game. It was the only area where i can give cudos to the devs and designers honestly.Also being a Hammermancer is fun. Throwing is probably too strong compared to alot of the early spells you can get in the game, but its fun.I played through the game solo, so i only have limited online experience. I was constantly online and was only invaded once in my entire playthrough. This is not suprising if you take my experience with me invading into consideration.The Invasions in this game are just not happening alot of the time. It either doesn't connect and when it does you often get choppy connections. Often times though the enemies quit out to the menue causing you to instantly dc upon loading in. Which is probably due to the vestige and seedling system together with the enemy density that causes people to just dread the runback.The few times i tried to  a friend to buy an item from an NPC that was dead in my world it straight up wouldn't let me connect except once after trying for about 15 times.I was at a point at the end of the game, where i just wanted to be done with it, because it felt more like a chore than a game to have fun with, but i wanted to finish it to give my honest thoughts about the entirety of the game. The last zone, Bramis Castle, is bursting from the seams with elites, rangers, mages and fiery dogs ready to turn you into a pile of ash. So everyone i know just sprints through Bramis castle to the final bosses.Only to be greeted by two bosses that shouldn't even be called that. Those two fights were the most boring fights i have had in any Soulslike to date. It feels like they ran out of money at the end.If you are expecting Pieta fights all throughout the game then you are sorely mistaken. There are only a handful of fights that are fun and challenging.The last boss in the radiant ending is just a dude holding a monologue while you kill some boring adds that damage the boss upon their death.I'm honestly disappointed.Despite so many Cons i believe this game is close to being good and recommendable, but it is missing alot of polish to be worth a thumbs up.Many people describe this game to be the successor of the original Dark Souls 2 Shrine of Amana and it does fit that description very well in the positives, but also in all of the negatives.This is probably why the game feels very anti-player.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend but with some strong caveats (Original review is after Update 1 and Update 2 sections)I reinstalled it. I hate not giving a game it's fair shake so I powered though.Overall, this game isn't bad. I wouldn't recommend this over Elden Ring or Lies of P, but I feel it's worth a play-through once it's available at discount or via subscription service like Game Pass.Very linear, but confusing at times. I got lost a couple times and had to look up where to go. The lack of detailed live maps in this game is a very large con, IMO.I still maintain the combat is floaty and unsatisfying. I played a sword and board build with Pieta's Sword and it never felt meaty or impactful when I struck enemies.Parrying is easy in this game, so easy that it feels like a cheat code to reduce difficulty, and I'm terrible at parrying (Lies of P was a nightmare for me but I enjoyed every second of gameplay).Fine but the unvaried throughout the game. Most of the enemies you fight in the tutorial and Pilgrim's Perch areas are the ones you face throughout the game, except in the end-game castle, and then only a few new ones are introduced. Difficulty is scaled via enemy damage and HP, not by introducing more varied enemy types with different move sets.Easy doesn't describe to how easy the bosses are. I don't think I struggled with a single one (maybe Lampreaper? Lightreaper? The dragon-rider demon guy), beating most of them within a couple tries. Their move-sets are few, slow, and easy to learn. Parrying often reduces these fights to simply waiting for them to swing their weapon.Many bosses are actually dull affairs (the Progeny fight leaps to mind) where you spend a good deal of time waiting for the enemy animations to finish before you can start damaging the boss again. The final boss of the game (POSSIBLE SPOILER) is a particularly anti-climactic and dull fight, especially since it's the big bad of the entire story.I maintain this is under-baked. There is a single fight in which the Umbral Realm played a part, and it felt more gimmicky than fully fleshed out. See Original Review below for my thoughts.It's a fine game, but in a genre with gems like Elden Ring and Lies of P with which to contend, it's unfortunately in the bottom tier of recent releases. I don't want it to come across that I don't like this game because I do. I like a lot of the ideas and gameplay choices here but they feel like they require a few more passes before release and the insertion of more enemy variety and a pass on the boss encounters to ensure they were up to standard.Some may disagree, and I don't say they're wrong. These are simply my thoughts and feelings after completing this game as it stands today.Before I go, I want to shout out the dev team. The sheer number of updates and patches put out in the first few weeks since release is staggering and I look forward to anything they put out in the future!I'm uninstalling it.Some may say "get gud" and while they may have a point, I find this game to be tedious. After devouring ER and LoP, I don't want to put in the effort required to complete this game, and will return to those until the ER DLC drops.Cheers to those that love this game, more power to you and enjoy!In true Souls-like fashion, the game mechanics are introduced to you in the first minute of game play and are never brought up again, so if you don't take copious notes, you'll miss out on some key mechanics.Everything is pretty linear, which is not a bad thing; Lies of P is a great example of linear level design and clear direction of where to go. Despite the branching linearity of Lords of the Fallen, it's not evident which paths will progress you along. I find myself wandering down paths killing enemies with no real goal made clear to me, hacking and slashing my way down one path or another not really sure whether I'm making any real progress, and dying repeatedly in areas for which I could be under-leveled but don't have the information to know whether I should even be at this part yet.There are maps to point you in a general direction, but they lack detail and landscape, having just a series of pictures with arrows and descriptions in indiscernible in-game languages.Once you get past the tutorial area, checkpoints become extremely sparse. You can play 20 minutes or more in the Pilgrim's area, filled with precarious platforming while ranged-attackers take potshots at you from seemingly everywhere as you fight melee tanks, and not come across a single checkpoint. They kinda-sorta address this with a seedling mechanic, but those seeds are preciously rare and overwrite each other as you plant new seedlings. So if you plant too often, you won't have any more seedlings and you'll be at the mercy of the out of the box checkpoints.    UPDATE - You can purchase the seedlings for 2500 vigor at Skyrest.Combat is fine, and that's actually a shame. In a genre that prides itself on combat, it doesn't have the polish of a Dark Souls, Elden Ring, or Lies of P, and feels floaty (a common complaint in other posts). As you swing your weapon you can dart around and behind enemies. Whenever this happens, a delay in the camera causes it to lose focus on your locked target. Once the target lock resumes, the camera whips around seemingly out of control. It's very disorienting, and has been the cause of more than its fair share of deaths.Speaking of the camera lock, if you change targets in combat, it's crazy fast; disorientingly fast. Slowing this down a bit would make for a smoother experience and make it easier to track your physical space during combat.You can also swing your weapon and stop off any platform edge you're near. No safety guardrails in this game, just FYI.A mechanic that is incredibly spotty is the "soul ripping" function of the Umbral Lamp. It works in the tutorial, but only works every 1/3 time in-game, even if you have full charges. This needs to be addressed as it's one of the main ways to defeat some tanky enemies during platforming.The Umbral Realm is a good concept but feels under-baked. It serves mostly as a puzzle mechanic to push or pull a platform across a ravine to access an area or to "soul-rip" a series of connections to unblock a door, then you exit into the real-world as soon as you're done with the puzzle. The 2nd life in the Umbral Realm is a real chore, and I do not find it enjoyable. Instead of exploring or soaking in the incredible work put into this parallel world, I find myself bee-lining it to the nearest extraction point. It feels oppressive and you're constantly harried by trash mobs that do an inordinate amount of damage, especially if you get cornered. Additionally, stay more than a minute or two and a reaper comes to 1-shot you. All nudges point to a quick exit.I find I must to force myself to play the game rather than having the urge to play it like I typically do with a Souls-like, and I find that disappointing. Whenever I die in a Souls-like, I can typically understand why; I mistimed a dodge, I should have parried rather than blocked. Every encounter and enemy has a solution, I just need to find it. Here, I can't tell you why I died most of the time, and don't know what I need to change to be more effective.I'll continue to play and finish the game but as it stands today, this won't be a Souls-like I revisit after completion.
