_childDocuments_.review: The thing with "Batora: Lost Haven" is that, albeit the gameplay is solid, the storyline, character development and overall plot is just too ridiculous to take seriously at any given point.You take control of Avril, a girl who has lost her homeplanet of Earth because of a sundering and is sent in a grand quest throughout the galaxy by the elden protectors of Earth, Sun and Moon, to retrieve four cores from other planets that will revive Earth. With her friend Mila, and other friends from different species that she'll meet along the way, Avril must show a great deal of bravery to make choices that will inevitably either destroy what's left of Earth or the rest of the galaxy.And that's basically it! The graphics are neat and the gameplay is really innovative. Avril can switch between two forms, Sun and Moon; while Sun form deals a ton of damage to Yellow enemies, Moon form is a spiritual form that destroys the Purple ones at range. Those two forms merge to give you an Ultimate Ability that you unlock later in the game, and for each form you'll learn specific skills to use in combo that are really fun to master. There are a lot of bosses that encompass both those affinities, with other enemies behaving as such called Hybrid enemies. In a very unorthodox manner, you level up by equipping runes that take up your runic knowledge slots; there are three kinds of improvements here, the Defender, Neutral and Conqueror sockets... You get more of each by taking the appropriate decisions that will affect the grand scheme of things... The only problem is that THIS grand scheme of things is actually uninteresting, lame and sometimes so boring that you'd be grinning through your teeth during a scene that's supposed to make you cry! At world three, I found myself just skipping most of the nonsensical dialogue, as if this was my second playthrough! Hint: IT WAS NOT. Batora: Lost Haven is a  game with great fighting mechanics, but a horrible storyline with nothing interesting or even remotely redundent going on! There are four endings, but you'll be like "Meh" most of the time that you'll be satisifed with THE ONE you get first. Play it once and drop it, thank me later!
_childDocuments_.name: Batora: Lost Haven

_childDocuments_.review: It's a shame that a game with such beautiful visuals and art style has nothing else to offer.The story is trivial and unengaging, the characters and plain and cliche, the dialogues are long and boring, and, worst of all, the gameplay and combat mechanics are simplistic and repetitive. You get a mission, you run to a point on the map, a few enemies spawn, you kill them and run back, then a few more enemies spawn. That's it, exploration is non-existent, since there's no interesting side activities, hidden loot or narrative storytelling. Just tons of backtracking and identical fights.This could still be ok for an indie game if the combat was good, but it's not. You can switch between physical and spirit versions of your character, and the enemies also come in these two variaties. Sounds interesting on paper, but comes down to this: attack orange enemies in physical form and attack purple enemies in shadow form, otherwise you deal little to no damage (depending on the difficulty settings). Actually, you can disable this and deal full damage regardless of enemy color, but that completely destroys those few interesting ideas the game has.Speaking of combat, each form has an evade, a basic attack, and a couple specials with cooldowns. So all fights boil down to evade, use cooldowns, and then basic attacks until cooldowns are restored. Even boss fights follow the same pattern, but you also have to evade ground attacks and other aoe effects. That's it, very basic and uninspired, especially given how many of these identical fights are in the game.If one removed some of these repetitive fights and boring dialogues, game could be ok (and 2-3 times shorter), and it would make sense to play it just for the visuals, but alas, the developers decided we would be interested in all these mundane activities. And I decided not to waste my time on this.
_childDocuments_.name: Batora: Lost Haven

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface by saying that if I'd played this when I was younger, and my standards were lower, I probably would have enjoyed it. I really don't mean that as the kick in the teeth that it sounds like tho. This game feels like someone's passion project and there is a lot to like, but my main take away is that so many other games have done this exact thing but better.As a player, I prefer story blended with gameplay rather than what Batora does which is interrupt gameplay with story. This would be somewhat forgivable if the story was good but it really isn't. It's a pretty standard fantasy setup with a chosen one who can wield two opposing forces (read combat styles) and she needs to kill a big bad to stop a planet from being destroyed. She has a friend to save and there's a token moral choice thing running through the story that adds nothing. By the 20 minute mark I was already just mashing the skip dialogue button every time a cutscene would play which had the dual benefit of me not being subjected to the kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥ voice acting.Now I can hear what you're thinking... all of it, actually. You really need to see a therapist. But also I can hear you thinking that if all I did was skip story beats, then what right do I have to complain that the story is boring. That is actually a fair point and if you have more patience than me, you might enjoy some of the character moments.I have more nice things to say on the gameplay side. Combat feels smooth and intuitive, and the arenas are at the very least functional. There are two types of enemies that have different elemental weaknesses, requiring you to change combat styles on the fly in response to what enemies spawn. Sounds cool but in practice it just boils down to hitting the red dudes with your red sword and the purple dudes with your purple fire. Enemies get suuuper spongy pretty quickly too. Not threatening mind, just annoying. Hmm, maybe I don't have that much nice to say, actually.The fights are all so repetitive. There's no interaction between combat and environment, so all the fights may as well be taking place in an empty white square. The enemy AI doesn't do much but spam attacks and vaguely walk towards you. There is a token badge system for mixing up your stats but barring a few totally broken badges you get during story beats, none of them are worth equipping. This means that I have no reason to interact with vendors, so the world ends up feeling superfluous. Not to mention it leaves me wandering around with squillions of dollars in my bag that I have no interest in spending.Again I want to stress that I think it would be very possible to have fun with Batora. It's an uncomplicated little distraction with enough passion to hold it head and shoulders above most soulless triple A garbage. If it looks like your kind of thing, go in with low expectations and I'm sure you'll have a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game does a lot of stuff pretty well, but it's hard not to see the places where it falls short.The two-mode combat system is interesting, but combat upgrades are doled out at specific points in the story rather than according to your level, so the progression systems can feel a bit meaningless, and almost all the runes are just stat changes, so your ability to customize your playstyle is limited.The story's alright, but it feels pretty rushed. The game sets up this big elemental cosmology but rushes you through each world. To its credit, your character  feels like she's being rushed though things, but it still feels like it would've been better to let you really explore and get to know each world. That goes double or triple for Earth itself—it seems like the devs made the classic mistake of assuming that players would have a natural inclination to value Earth just because we're, you know, human, but I didn't really get a sense of who our character was fighting for back home.The dialogue and codex entries could also use an editor—there were numerous grammatical and spelling errors throughout. They were generally pretty minor, but the quantity was rather surprising, given the otherwise pretty good production value. Likewise, I found the voice acting pretty solid in most places, but there were a few spots where it seemed like the actors weren't given very good direction.Overall, while I'm not sorry I played it,  just left me a bit underwhelmed.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, gameplay-wise it's fine. Not great. Not even good. Just fine. Issues are as follows:2 types of attacks are weird. You have button-press attacks, which go in the direction you're facing/running, making them dangerous to use in many cases. And twin-stick shooter attacks, which let you aim but are much slower, and in the case of the sun attack really annoying and more likely to get you hurt than to do much against the enemies. Your dodges are largely ineffective, with the exception of some environmental hazards and telegraphed boss attacks. If you try to dodge while an enemy is winding up to attack, there's a good chance they'll turn on a dime and hit you when you come out of your dodge. It just doesn't do a good job of its main function.Storywise, it's mixed. The basic premise is fine, but the characters themselves are super inconsistent and weird. In chapter 1, you've barely known Sun and Moon long at all and Moon suddenly refers to you as "beloved." Weird. Also, there's a particular character near the end of the chapter - I won't be more specific for spoiler reasons - that mentions that he was tricked and used by someone, and your character seems sympathetic . . . then all of a sudden she's yelling and berating him as if he did what he did on purpose, and he's responding as if he actually did do it on purpose and wasn't tricked into it at all. Just a total tonal shift mid-conversation that contradicts things said less than a minute beforehand.Still, the game isn't terrible. But it really needed more playtesting to get the annoying elements of combat ironed out and to have a proper editing job done on its dialogue. It really feels like there were 3 or 4 different writers working on this who didn't bother communicating with each other.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, the effects looked quite nice, but that's all there is to this game. You'll be stuck in a never-ending cascade of pretty but quickly boring landscapes with nothing to do but roam and have a truckload of endless loading screens despite having a pretty good machine, weaved with an incoherent story and a bit of combat in between.The story takes place on a post-apocalyptic Earth, where Avril, the main character will suddenly becomes a Champion for 2 gods, Sun and Moon and gets infused with super powers. The how or why literally doesn't matter and you'll have no explanations for this. You fall down a weird waterfall and pop comes the powers after finding a statue of the gods. Then you'll be transported to other worlds... I would have liked to see more of this Earth, where people say it's dangerous, but you'll see none of it except the tutorial, not even any of the problems mentioned.You'll basically be transported to lands of each element: Earth, Air, Water and Fire (in this order), beat some enemies senselessly, resolve a couple of quests, beat a boss, get transported to the next world where your friend will (almost) ALWAYS land somewhere away from you where you have to find her... Come on.The dialogs have a funny touch sometimes, but I found that the attitude of the main character completely derailled after 2 or 3 dialogs and she just went with rolling a die to determine her mindset for the next line of dialog with no consistency what-so-ever.Sometimes the game will ask you to make choices according to two trends: Defender (one would think the sacrifice oneself for the others way) or Conqueror (I'm gonna punch everybody's face in). First of, those 2 paths do not correspond to the main character who seems adventurous and curious, but want to help her friend. From time to time, you'll have to make a choice towards either of those directions, but none of them are what you want or seem to correspond to the actual trend and several times I actually stopped for a moment with a "wow, wtf?" moment. The choices you make along the way do not seem to really matter, just affecting the story slightly and you'll still end up having to roam around, fight baddies or solve a puzzle.What brought me to this game was the visuals: a nice whirlwind of purple in orange around pretty landscapes. The character design is also very impressive and I love the art in the game. The effects overall are pretty well done too.With the 2 forms (Body/Spirit or Sun/Moon), your character aspect will change appearance and that's a part that's quite well done visually, each skills is and feels unique.The landscapes left me breathless the first time I arrived in each new world, there was some nice details put in them that leaves you pin point some things and want to discover. But make about 10 steps and you'll quickly realise that what you saw will be the only elements you'll witness in the whole level, making it ultra-repetitive and boring.The enemies are... inconsistent. One can barely see what they are as they always blend a bit in the environment. They split their attacks between either body, mind or sometimes both for the bigger ones. Unless you spend time to learn each of their attack patterns with diligence, they will just be a blur with almost no way of distinction between their attacks.The game presents you with a duality of Body and Mind where each have their own attacks and health bars and you can switch at any time during the game. Enemies are also split into those 2 like described earlier. This was actually great and felt pretty creative, as you have to shift regularly to defeat your enemies. In normal play, attacks you make with one of the aspects inflicts half damage on the monsters of the other aspects.The fighting had a great touch and requires you to react in a matter of milliseconds to avoid attacks, because as described earlier, you will not see what will be happening until you see the attack, which is sometimes the enemy charging you with ludicrous speed. The biggest complaint I have with the fighting is that the Body form and its sword felt underwhelming. If you bash your enemies, you'll get damaged because of the animation time and the lack of visibility.Each bosses felt mostly unique, with a good mechanic of the 2 health bars for Body and Mind that you have to grind down, but not too much, because as soon as one segment goes out, you have to destroy the rest of the other form's segment quickly or everything heals, forcing you to use both forms to fight the boss. Also, they also have two forms, but they are immune to the damages of the other and have their own set of attacks for each.The puzzles are neat, requiring you a bit of thinking sometimes, utilising both forms Body and Spirit. Some platforms will only be "walkable" according to the form you're in, you'll be able to remote control balls to go to switches and levers, moving platforms and all. It started very well until the level designers put platforms that overlapped between Body and Mind, making them extremely difficult to determine what was happening. Just put them as plain platforms if the form doesn't matter...Finally I have to mention the zoom mechanic and the camera: you can zoom out or zoom in with 2 levels of vision while you play, where one is supposed to help you better see the landscapes and the path, and the other one zooms in to help you see in a fight. Problem is that the fight arenas are either too big so to see the enemies that will shoot at you you'll have to zoom out, but if you do so you'll lose proper vision on what's happening right around you. An in-between view only would have been better. As for the camera, I think it's a lesson that was learned a long time ago: don't lock the camera! This was so frustrating, exceptionally against bosses where their attacks would pop at the front of the scene, monopolising half of your screen.The game offers a character stats customisation via a system of points of differnt kind with which you can slot runes. You can directly feel this aspect was half baked in the game as the interface is barely there for this: there's only one bar where you'll slot all your runes and there's no filtering (at least by type of alphabetically, guys, come on). You quickly understand that runes are not upgrades, they just let you trade one stat for another, only a handful will be a straight up bonus. In the end, I didn't feel any difference while playing with the runes and no real "build" can be made.The voice acting is properly done, props to the voice actresses who had to follow the constant mood change of Avril and Mai. On the other end, the big entities are voiced quite poorly, barely audible over the music because of some reverberation.I didn't notice the music too much and apart from some dialogues, it never got in the way of the game, so I'd say they did a good job for this.I'll say this once: . Oh the amount of loading screens, knowing that all require you to press space to continue but still they take several seconds, and sequences that will prevent you from playing (looking at you stupid quest update messages), it was sooooo frustrating!

_childDocuments_.review: Good plot line with likeable characters and humorous cut scenes. The game mechanics of having two disciplines of a attack to switch between while battling makes it more interesting. The visuals are stunning even on a non-RTX GPU so I'll check it out later on my laptop to see the difference with it turned on.On the graphics there's some strangeness...The choice of imposing a 60fps frame limit even with V-Sync off is odd. I'm not sure of the reasoning behind this because the GPU was pretty much idling playing the game on Ultra settings at 1440p without ray tracing. It wasn't CPU bound either. Additionally while DX11 is recommended for some reason over DX12 there was no difference in performance or stability between the two.I tried with my GTX1080ti which can technically do ray tracing via cuda core brute force rather than dedicated RT cores, but it struggled to render with RT on at native panel resolution as I really expected it to. I just wanted to see how intense the game could actually be on that system 15fps was the answer.Running at 4K (DSR factors) loaded the same GPU up to 80% instead of 45-50% for normal 1440p usage but even then the frame rate still stayed steady at 60 fps.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all this is not a “Diabloid” as someone may think after watching demos. This also can not be called an RPG. The correct definition would be an “isometric action” game.There is no actual character development. Despite our character gaining experience and level-up, we are unable to influence the way she evolves, such as distributing attributes points, choosing abilities or anything else. All skills are unlocked automatically as the story progresses.There is almost no inventory: we can not obtain new weapons or armor. The only thing available are rune-stones, which enhance the character in different ways.We have 2 forms: physical and spiritual. In physical form our character uses melee weapons and skills, in spiritual - rong range magical projectiles. There are also 2 different health pools: physical and spiritual. Enemies differ in the same way by types: some use physical attacks which depletes “physical” health, others - cause spirit damage, which depletes “spiritual” health. When either of the health bars reaches zero - the game is over. The “physical” type enemies are vulnerable for physical attacks and resistant to the spiritual ones and vice versa. Thus in combat we have to evaluate the situation and switch between different forms in order to get victorious. It may sound to be an interesting mechanics, but, at least for me, it does not actually feel like it. First of all, enemies are simply highlighted according to their alignment: orange - for “physical”, violet - for “spiritual”. Thus you do not need to study foes, searching for the correct tactics. Also this is quite a stupid way to combine melee and ranged combat. You can not deal with “physical” enemies from a distance, and can not quickly slash “spiritual” in melee. It's like we have 2 different combat systems, which we are forced to switch between all the time.A significant part of the gameplay is puzzle solving. And this is almost the only thing, which feels actually good. Puzzles are well designed and look really fresh. They often require switching between “physical” and “spiritual” forms, creating quite a unique challenge. They are well balanced, requiring deep thinking from you without breaking your head.Also bosses are quite interesting. They also have 2 health bars, but unlike it is for our character, both of them should be depleted before they die. Bosses are quite different and change their behavior during the battle.Overall the game feels like “Darksiders: Genesis” but in very basic form, stripped from many features.Story is disappointing. The heroine - Avril has been chosen by god-like beings to save the dying Earth, and they granted her supernatural powers to do their bidding. I can not say that the story is completely hackneyed, but it is close to it. It has a twist near the end, but that one is quite predictable.Main character's personality is also quite disappointing. Her planet is almost destroyed, shattered by the earthquakes, her friends and relatives died in the process, the food should be scarce, but she has an attitude like “let's go search for some strange voices underground, it will be fun!”, cracking jokes along the way. There is nothing bad having a cheerful heroine, but it simply does not fit the scenery.Overall it all feels childish and well…stupid.The game claims: “your every decision will have consequences” - well, not really... We are not allowed to return to the worlds we visited to see in which way they were affected. There are no actual forks or significant choices. The only notable difference is which exact ghost will haunt us during the spirit trial at the last stage. At the very best the last boss may be different, although I have not checked this (may be it will not). We can choose between “conqueror” and “defender” alignment, which affects which runes we can equip and nothing else.There are several possible endings, but I feel no desire to uncover them.Game is quite short. Each planet provides a relatively small gameplay area. There is no significant difference between worlds. The most bright example is the one with the underwater city, where neither our character nor enemies are able to swim. They walk and run around, like there is thin air around them instead of water. You do know the water has higher density than air, don’t you?..The Graphics are basic, cartoon-styled. It appears like “Torchlight”. It is not highly detailed, but it is well enough for the gameplay.Animations fit the graphics: not very detailed, but smooth.The dialogs are made in “visual novel” style almost without any cutscenes.Camera has only 2 options of view: “far” and “close”. We can not rotate it or choose an exact zoom. Although It is positioned well enough, I can not remember cases when it caused troubles.Music is unremarkable. Although I can not say it is bad.Overall it is 5/10.“Half of the game” is an exact definition for this. In comparison to previews and advertisements, this is a huge disappointment. “On the paper” it appears much better than in reality.For the small development team, this game may be considered as an achievement, but you can find much more interesting products on the market. It is not worth the money, it is not worth the time.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Neutral game, not bad or good. Play this if you don't have any other game you want to play. Buy it when on sale or as part of a bundle.Story is one of the weak points for Batora. The story is not interesting with dialogue that I would like to skip.The game mention that there are multiple paths you can take and, according to their website, there are 4 endings you can see, but after only completing one ending I don't feel like I would like to go back and replay them. The story is bland and nothing make me feel hook to them, so replaying them to see other endings feel like a chore more than playing.Pacing is also bad. The last half of the game go by very quickly compare to the first half, about 2 times faster. Make me feel kind of off due to this inconsistent pacing.Characters in this game are forgettable. You will be traveling to multiple worlds and each world will have characters that you will be introduced too. There are nothing that make me feel connected to them because only small background is given to each character. Most of them just feel like they are there to give you quest.If your game have bad story, then you should make it up with good gameplay. Sadly, Batora is not able to achieve this.The combat system is interesting and provide a new experience. You will have 2 types of attack, sun (melee) or moon (range). You can switch between them during combat and each enemy will be weak to certain type, so you need to select the correct type to deal damage to enemy.Although, the combat is interesting, the execution is poor. Combating in this game can sometimes feel frustrating. Dodging is not that responsive, range attack don't have aim assistance so if you play on controller you will have a nightmare. I need to switch to mouse to complete puzzles that need to use range attack because the aim is so bad. Talking about puzzles, they are very simple. Just simply walk here, shoot there, hit this, move that. I don't really hate them but you may not like it if you want something more challenging.Enemy types are small, bosses are okay.Batora is an average game. It has a bland story, interesting combat but poorly executed. I want to give this a neutral score (5/10), but steam only have recommend or not recommend, so I choose to recommend because it can serve as a pass time if you don't have any game to play. Just make sure to buy this during sale or as part of a bundle because I don't feel like the full price will be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Batora: Lost Haven is an action GDR story driven, notable on many aspects. Maybe art and cartoon-style graphics resemble games like Diablo series, this game by Stormind has got an original and satisfying gameplay. Avril (the protagonist) can attack melee or by distance, so she can adapt to several combat situations and you have to switch or combine these mechanics to handle all the enemies she faces. And it’s all quite satisfying. The world is stunning, with a great use of color and lights, and also there’s a pleasant sound track.Another thing I appreciated is the way the storytelling affects gameplay (and vice versa). Moral choices of the player will bring Avril to specialize in different branches, thanks to Rune System, which can be equipped to change passive and active attributes. Also, the choices affect the storytelling and the player experience, so be conscious of what you choose!Obviously there’s not a wrong choice, but you may regret on some of them, especially if you wanted to role your character.I suggest everyone trying this game, for several hours of fun. Maybe I’d have preferred more action than puzzles, but I loved the importance of the plot and ethical choices. My compliments to this italian team and this lovely indie game. Go on!

_childDocuments_.review: Though an overall enjoyable experience, it's hard to actually recommend Batora. Everything it tries to do, a lot of other games have done, and better. The game does have an amazing character design, really enjoyable (if a little bit hammy) voice acting, and a decent overall idea. It's just let down by very lacluster combat, slight issues with pacing, and a general lack of overall polish. By the end of the game, I saw no reason to use the physical (i.e. melee) attacks. Ranged attacks against you are easier to dodge than melee, and are just as easy to hit. The only issue is that it will take slightly longer to kill the enemies of an opposing type (ranged attacks work better on ranged enemies, melee attacks work better on melee enemies). Either way, it feels a little 'bulley'-spongy.The story isn't particularly complicated, and it feels as if it's on its way to being something great, just needs a little more subtlety and nuance. I might get around to 100%ing it, seeing all the different story endings - perhaps a lot of the polish-time was devoted to actually crafting multiple endings with differences that do actually matter. Either way, it's not particularly difficult, just a little tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: Right, so I've just wasted several hours of my life on this game that somehow managed to be slightly less terrible than I expected. Which, let's be honest, is like saying this headache isn't as bad as my migraine - it's still bloody annoying, isn't it?They've gone and voiced every single line in the game, which would be impressive if half of it didn't sound like they recruited their voice actors from a drunk karaoke night. The combat's got this thing where you switch between Physical and Mental powers - which are actually decent and the visuals are all bright and colorful, like a children's paint set exploded all over your screen. But Christ, those controls. Moving diagonally feels like trying to walk straight after a night out with my mate Johan - technically possible but unnecessarily difficult.Look... ... let me tell you a little story about this game. It's like when you're at a party, right, and there's this person who's not particularly attractive, not particularly clever, but they're trying so bloody hard to be liked that you end up having a decent time with them anyway. They're telling these mediocre jokes, stumbling over their words, spilling their drink a bit - that's the wonky controls and technical issues for you. But then they'll occasionally say something properly interesting or show you a cool party trick - that's the combat system and those rare story moments that actually work.And by the end of the night, you're sitting there thinking, "You know what? That wasn't half bad." Not because it was actually brilliant, mind you, but because your expectations were so low that anything above absolute rubbish felt like a win.So would I recommend it? Yeah, like I'd recommend that party acquaintance for a pub quiz team. They might not be your first choice, but when your usual mates are busy and you've got nothing better to do... you could do worse. Just don't expect them to be the next Stephen Hawking of gaming

_childDocuments_.review: I tried. I really did. But sometimes you know right away that a game is not for you, and this is just not the game for me. On paper, it's tagged as everything I love the most. A story-rich RPG with a strong heroine? Yes please! But it just ended up falling flat on its face. I will give it the benefit of the doubt when it comes to story-rich as I didn't make it more than twenty minutes or so into the game. But from what I did see, it didn't deserve that tag. The story is boring and cliched, the voice acting weird in places, and the writing is bland and uninteresting. I don't care about the characters, and in fact I find them, particularly the heroine, annoying and whiny. Where are the RPG elements? You're just clicking through cutscenes and there are no choices to speak of. The combat is repetitive and does not feel satisfying or varied. Overall, it just felt like a slog. I was so disappointed and I felt every second of the twenty minutes I played this game, until I finally decided to put it down and uninstall. It just was not the game for me, and I honestly don't see myself recommending this to anyone either.

_childDocuments_.review: It starts ok but at the time you reach the third planet/chapter you realize that the story isn't much and the protagonist is very gullible and at this point she also becomes very whiny. The gameplay is kinda repetitive and doesn't offer you much reason to go further. I played it to the end for achievements, at least it's not very long after that chapter.I also have some issues with the combat: your most powerful attacks are either delayed (the physical one) or static (the mental one) so good luck convincing the bosses to sit in one place when you cast them. Not that are completely useful but... meh. And if the mob you kill ends the battle (it's th elast mob in the group) the game locks you in place and show you a "death animation" which is not even so interesting the hundred time you see it. And if that last mob shoot projectiles just before its death, you'll get them plenty. I died a few times like this.

_childDocuments_.review: In Batora: Lost Haven I found a game with an interesting mechanic to switch between different fighting modes, beautiful sound and graphics design and a captivating story. The world is filled with information to learn more about the environment and the pieces of information to be found are well written and present an in-depth view on the world of the game. So if you play the game, I really recommend to look through the codex and to read the information you get on the world.Sadly some of the fights nearly got me to quit the game early and stop playing but I'm happy I've made it through those passages as the story, world and sound design are really worth continuing to play.Overall: Clear recommendation for this game though you should bring some frustration tolerance for some passages.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all this is NOT a roguelike/lite, if anyone was wondering, despite it's combat encounters and map transitions action fighting and such kind of giving that impression, like say hades.The game is completely linear, there aren't side quests or collectibles or optional boss fights(just optional major story events that can lead to missing some fights your first play threw).It will take around 6 hours of play time to complete the entire game form start to finish assuming u don't read dialog very slowly, or have trouble grasping the combat and puzzle mechanics(which are rather straight forward with good explanation tutorials and forgiving for failure), however it is worth playing threw a second time due to the way New Game+ effects the game and to do the other story choices you didn't do the first time threw, so it'll be at least 12 hours of game play give or take. Personally i have played threw it three times as of posting this, cuz i love the combat in new game+ play troughs.The story choices, being only two at every major event, including the end, ultimately do not change the endings, my 1st play threw i chose what i want, the 2nd i chose what i didn't my 1st, the 3rd i did all of one type of choice to try and get the maximum effect of a speific type of choice, but it resulted in nothing different that i hadn't seen in my other two plays, despite their being a tracker of how many choices you've made of the 2 diffrent types.While disappointing, having played under tale for example, that there isn't much impact in your choices, just different events to encounter, to the point to make a 3rd 4th or 5th play threw meaningful for new experinces, new game+ on 3 or more play threws does let you play threw the game difrently from a combat perspective if u want to try beating the game in new ways. The combat is more exciting from your 2nd play threw and onward using new game+ than it is your 1st time threw since u don't start with next to nothing and slowly build up threw the game but start with almost everything from the start and enemies that can survive it and still kill you as well as more diversity in the way you change your stats or the way skills work having brought some stuff from previous attempt along with you.The only issues i have with the game really, is on new game+ QoL wise, or for speed running a fresh play threw, there is a lot of dialog u can only button mash threw and not avoid entirely, and some cut scenes u can't skip because they are basically used as loading screens leading into dialog, as well as the fact the mandatory puzzles can't be skipped if u have already done them(tho this is less relevant for speed runs which would still want to do the puzzles), which results in making a new game+ only slightly faster than the 1st time threw, more so on your 3rd time or more where u have done both choices to every event and just want to experience the combat.The main issue i have that isn't simply QoL experience would be the A.I that follow and fight with you at some points in the game dying too easily, more so on New game+ where enemies are higher level, on occasion sometimes nearly instantly in multiple round fights before u even kill the first wave, making you have to play more dangerously to protect them or risk them dying, which isn't that fun, which, if they die, it results in you failing as if u had died, but the setback to dying is about as stressful as the setback to failing a part of the puzzles, and doesn't really result in much loss even on purely auto saves due to the way checkpoints are done.There is no loot or grind, all stat changing things are pre-determined at points throughout the story so you can flow threw the game from one point to the next only backtracking because the story tells you to, there are some chests to loot for currency for shops and sell-able junk which u don't really need to go out of your way to get a lot of.boss fights don't change on new play threws(tho you can't encounter them all in one), though they do gain more health and damage on new game+ cuz levels keep going up(but should max out after your second, making your 3rd max level form the beginning, so combat wise a 3rd time can be fun), which can make you change your fighting style.The orange/purple physical/mental melee/ranged swapping combat is rather unique and well done, while matching the color of your enemies does more damage u can do dmg with both, except for most bosses you have to match but they have health of both types, and some enemies are multi colored. you also have a different health bar for taking physical or mental damage regardless of the form you take it in and die if either gets depleted not both. The puzzles also utilize the swapping system in various ways. Ultimately the game isn't very difficult just fun.I do think 25$ is a bit much for only 6~ hours of gameplay, 12~ if u play twice for full experience, there isn't much that can change how much time it takes to play it. but the story and combat is worth playing. Buy it on sale. Hopefully they will add more endings/New game+ experience in the future or extended content/features with DLC. However i would expect a sequel or expansion continuing the story after the ending, telling the story that came before the start of the story, or the same theme universe and combat in a completely separate game with different characters like final fantasy does. more than alternate endings alternate paths or new features since this is a liner story with completed beginning and and end not a rogue like. Great game regardless, while you could simply watch the story on a let's play and get as much out of it as playing it, the combat however short lived is fun to do yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Free will, good or strong, bravery or empathy, Sun or Moon. There are also runes to boost your stats (which I couldn't yet analyze much).Also, some puzzles break the normal flow, and add more fun.Avril goes through worlds and, at least for the ones I visited at the moment, they're stunning and show lot of originality.This game has got personality. _childDocuments_.review: This game demonstrates why not to put the fate of the universe in the hands of a teenage girl.I join the deluge of recent reviews from people who played Batora after getting it as part of the  Humble Bundle bundle.I have really important games to play, and not much time left to play them, so I really shouldn't have been messing around with Batora.  I tried it because it was built in UE4, making it a candidate for viewing it in stereoscopic 3D with my VR headset and the .Not lie gonna, I got off on the wrong foot with this game.  The main character, whose name is not Batora, was a cocky, childish, and reckless, tomboy named Avril.  I wasn't looking to play a game with a character like this.  Avril had all the characteristics of an insufferable "mary sue" character who gains immense power with no effort, and is little miss perfect.But I wanted to take a break from the 30+ hours I'd blasted into my playthrough ELEX, so I decided to see where Batora would go.The first impression this game gives almost made me decide to quit.  But as the story unfolds, Avril's initial immaturity is whittled away as she is deeply affected by what's going on and is forced to take things more seriously.  There's real story-telling going on here, not only with Avril.  A larger mythology is built up across the worlds she visits and the peoples she meets.The game isn't mature, but it's also not for kids.  It has high stakes and often brutal consequences.Batora is focused on the choices people make and their personal willpower.  Do writers realize just how heavily they all draw on these ideas?  Why is there such an fascination with the supposed righteousness of an individual making decisions for himself, according to his own morals?  As long as a person made a decision freely, we're all supposed to accept it - no matter the consequences.Well, Batora takes these concepts to absurd lengths by making the 16-year old Avril arbiter of the course of the entire frickin' galaxy.  Whatever she decides, is what it's going to be.  It's bizarre, but even though it's mentioned a few times, it goes mostly unexamined.The gameplay isn't deep or engrossing, but it's fine.  Read another review if you want more details.In addition to my own impressive determination and willpower, the lovely visuals are one of the things that helped me get through the initial feeling that I was playing a cringe-worthy game not worth my time.  Viewing the imaginative and pretty worlds and characters in stereoscopic 3D enhanced enjoyment even further.  This is the first time I've played a game with an isometric perspective using the UUE4 3D fix.The game switches perspectives often, defying the ability to use a static convergence value that works in all scenes.  Thanks to the auto-convergence feature, it kept things looking good.  This is the first time I've used it and it worked miracles.The game can certainly be criticized for shallow and repetitive gameplay, simplistic puzzles, an unappealing introduction to the characters, and contrived situations for the decisions.  But I decided to see this game not as a AAA extravaganza.  It's a decent AA gaming experience aimed at kids half my age.  I didn't take the game too seriously.  It was a silly diversion for a few days.  I can recommend it.This review is over.  Now, back to that ELEX playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Batora: Lost Haven is the first ever game to portray a character commiting double genocide as a pinball minigame!In all seriousness though, I would recommend this game, but if steam had a percentage rating system, this game would definitely fall somewhere around the 45% mark, so dislike it is.Don't get me wrong, the game isn't bad, it just isn't that good either.TL;DR:Graphics: 9/10Story: 2.5/10Puzzles: 1/10Combat: 6.5/10 (protagonist: 8/10, enemies: 4/10)Game progression: 3/10The graphics are good, probably even the thing that got me to rate this game so well. The artstyle is very enjoyable, there are plenty of well animated cutscenes, and the character designs are insanely good. (I absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love the lizards' design!)The story is pretty bad. It's basically as generic as it can get; the protagonist gets chosen by gods to *save the world* and gets a buncha cool powers on the way.There is also this "karmic balance" aspect to this game's choices (that is drilled into you for the whole first world by the two gods), which I can't call anything other than ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid. You are basically told that you are a "keeper of balance," implying you should try to keep this "karmic balance" thing y'know, , but even though some choices are good and question your morals, most are just "be a ♥♥♥♥ for no reason" or "be respectful."Example (world 2, minor spoiler): . This whole choice thing is a giant joke. The puzzles are so bad I don't know whether to laugh or cry. You could probably put a 6 year old in front of the computer and they would be able to solve them. Most of them aren't even making you think, they are literally just "walk along a path and hit this conveniently placed switch with the correct color." Oh yea, and also the thing I said at the begining of this review... the worst possible place you could ever put a pinball minigame, jesus ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ christ.The Combat is pretty good. Near the start you have pretty limited arsenal, but slowly it gets a bit more diverse and you will be running around doing a lot of cool moves. I also quite like the different damage types for enemies.The enemies though, those are rarely challenging, with most of the challenge coming from unreasonably large healthbars and bad attack indicators which, instead of telling you that an attack is about to deal damage, tells you that there is gonna be an attack directed , sometime between the next 0 to 3 seconds. (Oh yea and you spend so little time in each world that you don't get the chance to memorize the timings)The game progression, as most of the game, isn't that bad, but it lacks challenge; you basically just buy a bunch of upgrades when you get the chance and slap them onto your character. The enemies also slowly level up with you so any sense of progression is only indicated by larger numbers appearing when you deal damage.  Nevermind that, after playing a bit more, the game started giving me the MMORPG treatment; enemies with unreasonably large healthbars that even a fully attack-focused build has trouble killing.

_childDocuments_.review: Batora: Lost Haven is an isometric action RPG where the primary conceit is that the player character has dual natures and can switch between them at will. Each nature does a different type of damage and has its own health bar.There's a very dramatic plotline about reversing the destruction of the earth - it's apparently loosely based on a , and I really got the feeling there was a ton of lore that they thankfully didn't dump on me.It's clearly an indie game, but it's very well made, and there were only a few areas I felt could use a little more polish (e.g. copyediting).The dual-combat thing was interesting, but even with the addition of extra abilities and powerups, I found it somewhat tedious by the end - I would have liked the option for more puzzle mazes instead.Overall, I had fun unwrapping the story - it was time well spent.

_childDocuments_.review: ---Summary---Although it doesn't stand out for its story, Batora is a solid game with enjoyable graphics. Progression requires a mix of combat, simple puzzles, and story choices. Recommended for people looking for a straightforward adventure who don't mind predictable story elements.---Breakdown---Graphics: Fun and stylizedOptimization: Runs well. I encountered no stuttering, crashes, etc.Dialogue: Cheesy and predictable. If you take certain choices it devolves to cringeworthy.Voice Acting: Pretty good, albeit anachronistic (you're all supposedly from England, but you wouldn't know it if the game didn't tell you)Controls: Designed with a controller in mind, but I had no issues with KBM.Story: Fairly predictable. There are technically four endings, but it's really two endings with minor variation. The morality system (defender vs. conqueror) is set up with a "there's no wrong choices, only consequences" theme, but at the end of the day, there's definitely a bad/selfish vs good/self-sacrificing theme going on. The major morality choices are really the same choice over and over again with variations in framing.Gameplay: Isometric ARPG. There's an interesting system here where you swap between melee and ranged throughout every fight. You have two healthbars, which can be tricky to balance in the early game, but becomes much easier when you get your endgame abilities. Overall, I found the combat enjoyable. The puzzles were straightforward, but a welcome break. There's a NG+ option, which is necessary to use for at least one achievement (reach Level 25).

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed it. The story, dubbing, automatic dialogue continuation and even cinematics were all incredible and kept my attention locked in, like a built-in movie 👍Combat was enjoyable even if the amount of available moves/attacks got a little overwhelming towards the end. I liked character upgrading with skill points and picking orbs.The difficulty scaling was fine, pretty much linear maybe you get a but too powerful towards the end. And also it was just weird that the final bosses were straight up easy for some reason, both one-shot without issues and I have to say that even some "normal" mobs before the final fight gave me bigger struggle 😅 Whatever.If I had to nitpick one thing it would be the escort missions where it sometimes just felt like RNG, if the f*cker you're supposed to keep safe catches agro or stayd in the area of a charge attack, you are done. Ok New Game+ it's even worse. Fortunately these situations were quite rare and even when unlucky you can get through after few tries. Just a little frustrating.Technical notes:- runs great on Steam Deck - surprisingly best performance was with Direct 12, which was supposed to be experimental, otherwise default setting, yeah the battery goes down quite fast, but you can always tweak it- fast loading- 100% achievements are very attainable with little to no replaying, achievements you will miss during gameplay can be easier got after loading so-called "turning point" saves, which are automatically created (much appreciated), and choosing the 2nd option. Or you can replay the game with "New Game+" if you want to.

_childDocuments_.review: 4/10.The gameplay itself is fine; as others mentioned, it's got a quirky combat system that feels fresh at first but slowly gets a little annoying. The moral decisions (at least the few I saw before dropping) are gray-area but designed to make you feel bad if you don't pick the 'right' call, after first telling you that there's no 'right' call and to make your own decisions. Reminds me of Spec Ops: The Line, only that one at least had a reason for it and kept the making-you-feel-bad part to the end. This one hits you in the face what feels like moments after you make a decision.The problem for me was it felt vaguely racist when I hit the second 'planet'. Maybe I'm reading into this too much, so make your own call on that front... Lizard people talking in broken English (with a simlish-type speak behind it sounding vaguely like the voice actors may have been paid to try to sound as close to stereo-typically Chinese as they could without actually speaking Chinese), using a few iconically Chinese terms (the "Wuxian" desert, the "forbidden city"), some Chinese names (Yu Xuan tribe, Li Feng....),...Yeah, pass.

_childDocuments_.review: You ever question how much your decisions actually change the story for the game you're playing? Every choice has a consequence, but really, how much of a consequence are we talking?I uhh... I got myself exiled from an entire planet. I didn't even see it coming. All the chaos I caused had some actual consequences, apparently. I was not the defender, but the Conquerer. Oops...? Besides being a game of choice and storytelling, Batora: Lost Haven is a classic twin-stick shooter combined with a hack and slash. Both of the natures of the game are represented through two "class" styles that you can change at will. One is wielding a giant sword and swinging it with reckless abandon, and the other is shooting some magic missiles. Both, of course, have some other skills and attacks once you level up. The fighting styles can be changed on the drop of a dime in the middle of combat (and if you want to live, this is encouraged) as the enemies also differ in nature, and are much weaker to one style over the other. Puzzles also come up throughout this game, and many of them also require different natures for the different effects on the environment, switches, or the way the attacks may trigger a specific event. There are also some riddles to work with as well. Due to the way leveling works, achievements to be earned, and the different paths your story can take, the game is definitely something one could replay a couple of times. The game itself played pretty smooth, and even having played this before the release, I hardly encountered any bugs. Pretty neat game.

_childDocuments_.review: Batora Lost Haven is the right mix of multiple genres that creates a perfect isometric action RPG. If you are a lover of the genre, or if you want to try a new videogame, you absolutely must play Batora!

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really like isometric games. I approached Batora with this mindset and I have to say that the game is making me change it as I progress through it. I just had a boss fight on the first planet, which I found challenging and never boring. The game aims for dynamic gameplay that manages to satisfy the player when effective combos are cast against physical and mental weak enemies, using the power corresponding to the shown color. The character duality is certainly not an innovative idea, but it is part of the right mix that makes Batora: Lost Haven truly intriguing and never predictable for now. I appreciate the plot choices dynamic that manages to make the player identify with Avril, the protagonist, by placing you in front of important crossroads with consequences or rewards that you will carry with you during the adventure.I have played with joypads and I have not encountered any major issues, the directional attacks are a bit challenging, but you get used to them easily. The enemies are diversified and rewarding to eliminate, with a few exceptions that may make you die sometimes, but which do not consist of real unbeatable threats. The RPG system is characterized by the presence of runes that provide situational buffs and debuffs to skills, life, and the unique characteristics of physical and mental powers. Initially, I did not expect a similar system and I was annoyed a little bit, but I have to say that you can manage it really well, with the possibility of buying and selling in the various shops on the map. Well, Batora surprised me, I had created a much lower expectation that was greatly exceeded thanks to the technical and narrative qualities of the game. Give it a chance, you will not regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this new indie game made by Stormind Games. It winks an eye to titles like Bastion or Transistor, but finds its originality in a more consistent plot.Earth is on the verge to collapse and everything is in ruin. Two gods (Sun and Moon) lend her their powers and she becomes the hero whose task is to collect powers from other worlds cores and, by doing that, heal her own planet.The two gods, in terms of gameplay, let her switch between offensive melee attacks (Sun) and long range magical shots (Moon) and, as the story goes on, she learns new abilities and get more powerful.Regarding the plot itself, in many occasions she can respond with a strong and almost arrogant way (inspired by the Sun), or with a meditative and sensible argument (Moon, of course). This probably lends to different scenarios in the game (I'm not yet sure), but it's a promising feature.The art is stunning and impressive: each world has its own style, characteristics and inhabitants. _childDocuments_.review: I'm an hour and a half in.I really wish this was in early access because it still needs a lot of love. And by "It needs a lot of love", I mean it: this game feels like it's an action RPG made by people that don't like action RPGs.The story feels like it's been written for kids, which could be fine, but with a crude gameplay that kids would find too difficult or annoying.This game contains a LOT of pace breaking unskippable dialogs (unless you consider button mashing an acceptable skip method). Invasive tutorial windows keeps popping up to explain very basic stuff, again breaking the pace of the game.Combat has interesting mechanics requiring you to switch between two combat mode (melee and range), but both feel underwhelming, and the melee mode lacks fluidity and is straight up not fun.Overall, the experience feels like this: You get 5 seconds of walking your character, 5 minutes of unskippable dialog, followed by another 5 seconds of walking, 2 tutorial popups that pause the game, then 15 seconds clunky combat, another 2 minutes dialog, then you pickup an object that triggers a very slow animation. Repeat this 20 times while doing back and forth in a linear world with loading screens.If I had one advice for the devs: ask yourself who you are making this game for, and what type of game you want to make, because it feels like you don't know. It goes halfway in every direction without leaving a satisfying experience on any aspect.

_childDocuments_.review: My biggest problem with Batora is the camera controls. Neither can you move the camera angle freely, nor zoom smoothly. Only switching between two fixed zoom levels is possible, but that’s more like “camera far away” and “camera very far away”.And in the dungeon passages, especially when you have to run down, this “very far” is still somehow too little for my feeling. There you run mostly into the unknown and can not see well where the character is heading. Sometimes there are then automatic adjustments of the distance, which are mostly helpful, but sometimes they are not.Graphically, Batora is often really pretty, and then again it has passages where it tends more toward “mediocre”. The game offers a very unique style, which is also used consistently. So the developers can really do great things graphically, but somehow they didn’t implement this well throughout.Some textures unfortunately look a bit boring and muddy. And many details of the models for characters and monsters become clear only in cutscenes. Because in the normal game, the camera is just so far away, so the details are often lost here. But it is a graphically good average to a little above and altogether this is already on a good level. But still, there would simply be more in it, Stormind regrettably gives away some points here.No video for now, might come laterGenerally, some of the fights still seemed a bit badly balanced to me. Obviously, you should use the various skills, shields, combos, and self-heals skillfully. And if you pay attention to all this, you can also take care of yourself quite well. However, if it then happens with the companions in the fight constantly that these stand around bluntly in the middle, and are collecting all area damage from the opponents, and then falling down quickly, it can sometimes become frustrating.Here, I would have liked companions to just pass out and get dropped as help until after the fight. But having a companion die in combat and then trigger a game over didn’t sit well with me at all. I had some frustrating moments there, which are also very hard to avoid, even when you try to draw the enemies’ aggro on you.The balancing of some boss fights was still a bit too much on the difficult side for my taste. But in boss fights, I can still understand it best. But when even the “normal” monster groups sometimes knock you off your feet 5-6 times in a row, or constantly kill your companion, then the line between fun, challenge, and frustration is reached more often than is good for the gameplay.Thus, I think the game overall lacks a difficulty slider and more gameplay options to adjust to one’s idea of difficulty and enjoyment. Gamepad acrobats might find themselves challenged, but for players with slightly slower reflexes or even limitations, this could become a problem and a source of frustration.Great Story – Characters with PersonalityI really like the story of the game. There is an interesting mix of post-apocalyptic sci-fi, magic, and alien stories here. The story is roughly based on a book also called Batora, so if you really like the game, you can go deeper here.You can also tell that the world and characters have a bit more substance to them here than in many other action-adventure games. The main characters have strong personalities and occasionally babble a bit away from the exact main story, and even some of the side characters have fun idiosyncrasies and a few small, but powerful appearances....The Design Unfortunately a bit Too LinearHowever, I must note that both the level design and the story progression are actually absolutely linear. Apart from a few small roadside stashes, there aren’t many opportunities to take different paths. That’s actually quite a shame because a little more freedom would have added a lot to the game.For $24.99 or €, Batora offers roughly 15-20 hours of gameplay, depending on combat skill and the number of deaths. Should one skip all dialogues, this can be shortened dramatically. But I really can’t recommend that, because then you would miss about 70 % of the game because Batora is very story-heavy.Batora is not a real RPGThe replay value is unfortunately limited by the somewhat low role-playing depth and the linear structure. You do have some decisions to make, and there are different endings to the story. I haven’t had a chance to try them all out yet. But I don’t think these have such a strong impact that this alone provides motivation for multiple playthroughs. With a skill tree and more freely distributable stats, the game could have gotten much more depth and fun here. Unfortunately, the developers at Stormind missed an opportunity here to make the game even better.When I put into perspective the fun and length of gameplay offered, as well as the original story and special game features, I would like to give Batora Lost Haven a base rating of 85 %.For the slightly too linear game design and the limited role-playing system, I deduct 3 %. Slight flaws in the balancing of the battles, especially with the companions and the lack of a difficulty slider, deduct another 2 %. With that, Batora Lost Haven gets a final rating of 80 % from me.For a higher rating, the replay value should have just been better, and fewer frustrating moments while fighting would have really enhanced the experience. With good updates, I think Batora could still pull out 5 % more.EN DE

_childDocuments_.review: ✅Choices and consequences✅Solid graphics/artwork✅Smooth UI✅Character development (plot)➖Cringey hit-or-miss zoomer dialog➖Nonsensical plot➖Shop UI is a pain for rune slots➖Puzzles➖BuggyGame World: In Batora: Lost Haven (BLH) the game world is presented as a top-down map similar to APRGs like Diablo. You visit a wide variety of areas made up of different environments. Unfortunately, the world seems to be fairly linear so there isn’t much option for deviation. What’s more is there is plenty of backtracking so it's not uncommon to have to slowly walk across the same zone a couple times. You end up visiting a variety of worlds - sand, ice, forest, each world may look different aesthetically, but it's made up of the same linear paths. Narrative: The plot in BLH I found disjointed. First of all, the game starts with some horrible catastrophe befalling Earth, but you are given literally zero backstory to anything on your planet as you randomly become a superhero within the first 10 minutes of the game. I’d have loved a bit more backstory for the characters and Earth so as a player I can understand at the very least what the main character is fighting for. You play as Avril, who stumbles upon the powers to harness the sun and moon. I’ll cover this more in the mechanics. Anyways, your goal is to heal other worlds by venturing to their cores in order to restore Earth to whatever damages happened there. There is no explanation of these random planets and some hastily made up backstories of the denizens who reside there. Throughout the story,  you’re left with making some significant choices that greatly impact the inhabitants of these planets. Despite the gravitas of these decisions, it still seems inconsequential because you never see any future effects of your actions. Whatever you choose, you get a couple of lines of dialog, Avril goes emo for a bit, and the journey continues. The only reference you ever get back to your choices is . At the end of this through all these decisions, you will see Avril grow as a protagonist, which is nice to observe, even if the .Length: I finished 1 playthrough in 7.5 hours. Controls: I chose to play with KBM since it's heavily based on Diablo, the controls were just ok. Melee as Sun feels messy, inaccurate, and tough to actually avoid damage. Ranged on Moon feels good enough. Mechanics: If you’ve ever played Ikaruga, you’re familiar with dual color mechanics and how annoying they can be. Thankfully, this game is nowhere near as hard as Ikaruga, but the concept is still there. You swap between Sun for melee attacks and Moon for ranged attacks. Each enemy has their own element that you need to attack for maximum effect. You gain MOBA-like abilities for each stance - as a sword you’ll get bladestorm, a charge, and a shield, as ranged you get a damage wave, tornado, and reflection shield. You do have a heal that you can use but to charge the heal up in melee, you must be doing damage in ranged, and vice versa. Lastly, you do have some stats you can impact, like attack, health, and critical damage. There is no gear, only runes you can equip. The majority of runes have a negative effect though, so it's common to see ones with +50 attack to sun -5% critical change on moon, or something like that. Moving on from your character is the puzzles. They range from okay to bad. The worst ones are moving a lot of balls, like Marble Madness. The better ones are only a few where you get to play a giant game of pinball. I did not really enjoy the puzzles and they seemed arbitrary to the game and nonsensical to the plot. Overall, the combat and equipment mechanics are a letdown. Combat is just okay, while the runes are meaningless at best and annoying at worst. Difficulty: I found Batora to be around the middle in difficulty, leaning towards hard. Towards the end some of the abilities the enemies do are just unfair and janky, meaning you still get hit no matter what. I died maybe 10x during my playthrough. Quality: Pretty good. Aside from the overhead Diablo look, most of the cutscenes remind me of something like a Pixar movie. The characters look good. UI: Hit or miss. The GUI during combat is smooth and well done. Love the way it looks. The rune menu is just okay, could definitely be better. The shop menu is atrocious. You have no idea how many open rune slots you have when you’re looking to buy a new rune, so you need to exit the shop and go back into your inventory to see. Really needs a QoL update here. Performance: I have no issues with how the game runs, as it was always stable on my desktop PC:i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSDI did run into many bugs as I played it. From things like subtitles remaining on screen long after the cutscene ended, to more harmful things like NPCs bugging out and my abilities not aiming correctly. Sound Effects: The voice acting quality is good here. The sound effects are fine. Music: Okay, there were a couple songs during boss fights I thought were good, but other than that, pretty forgettable. Good, you have 4 or 5 major choices to make with 4 different endings. There are also achievements and NG+ so you can jump back in and see the choices you didn’t make with your current setup. Overall mediocre at best. The strongest point of the game, the plot, didn’t really interest me. The combat/gear mechanics were not that fun, or barely even present, respectively. I powered through to finish the game, but was close to retiring it multiple times. You can find my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: I have never done something similar. I have finished this game on my switch a couple of days ago. It was buggy, unpolished and somewhat chaotic but I liked it so much that I decided to buy it here on Steam as well and played once again all the way to the end (I also got a different ending). My hours is low here because I have skipped most of the cutscenes. It is not the definition of an indie gem, but still a very fun game, if you are able to look away from its faults. My short review: + Very good, satisfying combat - the continuous switching between two elements makes it very interesting and sometimes challenging. + I liked the puzzles very much. I have played both BOTW and Fenyx Rising, but I liked the puzzles here more. They were clever and funny. + The story is a plus, although it is not the strength of the game. But it kept me going. I really liked the different worlds we visited though. + It has multiple ending (4 to be precise), based on choices. + I have read that the protagonist is hated generally. For me, it wasn't as bad as in Forspoken. Not the best protagonist ever, but not that bad. - There are bugs, some pretty annoying ones. For example. I had to redo the last boss 3 times. The only reason I didn't ragequit was that I really liked the combat. Also at one time mobs appeared right before the cutscene started and they started to kill me. The screen was flashing red and I was dead after the cutscene. - There is also one annoying aspect of the combat. You cannot jump "through" enemies, they block you. It was pretty annoying when I was surrounded and couldn't not escape and died because of that. - The story and the lore could be explained better. The game gives you many lore pieces which you can read for plus info but it could be integrated into the story more organically. - Graphics could be better. - The writing is pretty bad sometimes.Overall, the combat system and the puzzles carried this game very much for me. I recommend it, especially on sale. You have to keep in mind that this is not a AAA production - it feels more like a love-child indie game. If I should rate it objectively, I would say: 7.5/10. But for me personally it is 9.5/10, I liked the good aspect that much.

_childDocuments_.review: has a lot going for it, but ultimately I just didn't found it fun to play.Let's look at the positives first. The game has a really cool art style, great music, amazing setpieces with a very distinct look and feel, and a lot of replay value thanks to the decision system, a New Game + mode and four different endings. It offers fast-paced, colorful combat as well as numerous neat puzzle sequences, both built around the game's fairly unique duality system. It also has an interesting story that, although frequently advertised as science fiction, is actually closer to traditional celestial fantasy fare with some inconsequential scifi trappings around the edges. All in all there's a lot of great stuff in here, so why didn't I enjoy it?The first and most important facet of the game that fell flat for me was the combat. It's a really interesting system that makes full use of two very different forms your character can take (one for melee, one for ranged combat), both of which have up to four broadly similar yet distinct abilities that run off of a cooldown mechanic. While well thought-out overall, it just felt extremely unbalanced to me. For starters, I found it punishingly difficult. Maybe I'm just bad at it, but I normally don't have major problems playing twin-stick shooters, so that can't be the only reason. Enemies always appear in packs and can take up to a dozen hits to kill each, all the while your character goes down in two to three hits from anything stronger than the most basic cannon fodder mook. Needless to say the (admittedly awesome) bosses can kill you in a single attack if you screw up even once, and these battles can drag on for 10-15 minutes, forcing you to start over from scratch every time you die. This isn't helped by the fairly lengthy cooldowns on your combat abilities and the near-total lack of reliable combat healing options.It's made even worse by the annoyingly frequent escort missions. An estimated 30% of combat encounters in the game pairs you up with a companion, which is invariably a suicidal POS without an iota of self-preservation instinct that happily runs into enemy AoE attacks without a care in the world even when they aren't actively being targeted by hostiles. If your escortee dies, you get a game-over and have to restart the section. So you don't just have to keep yourself alive somehow, but also the idiot of the day that decided to tag along without an invitation.Leveling also seems to be off. It starts out well enough, with you and your enemies' level being evenly matched most of the time, but the further you progress in the story, the more enemies begin to outlevel you, which almost certainly plays a part in why I found the combat so tough. There were sections where I was level 18 while the enemies were around level 22-23 out of a maximum of 25. Level grinding doesn't seem to be a thing, and I'm pretty sure I killed everything I could, so I can't help but blame this on the game itself. Story-wise, while I very much appreciate the impact of the decisions you have to make, much of it still feels... I don't know... weird? For instance, the game starts with Earth mostly destroyed and the survivors hanging on by a thread, but your player character and her best friend are introduced cheerfully cruising through the ruins of London like a pair of 1980s highschool students exploring the woods around town. They're also dressed in immaculate, trendy street clothes and hairstyles, with your gal pal rocking a skintight top that bares one of the most bodacious midriffs I've seen in a while. Now there's absolutely nothing wrong with bodacious midriffs being bared, but neither of these is exactly conducive to building a postapocalyptic atmosphere. Nor does the characters' constant childish banter. I know they're teenagers, so this was to be expected, but the game tries to tell a serious story about tough decisions and the weight of responsibility, which just results in a massive, constant clash of emotions I found hard to reconcile.The puzzles are another one of these things that could've been great but suffered from incompatibilities with the gameplay; in this case, the controls. These are clearly built around console controllers while the puzzles are all about speed and precision maneuvers, two things that just don't mix all that well. The game switches seamlessly between controller and mouse/keyboard on the fly, so that's a plus, but it still kinda forces you to memorize two completely different control schemes for the same game. Nothing insurmountable, sure, but certainly not an advantage, either.One last point I need to get off my chest although it has no real influence on my final verdict: why in hell is the game named after an ultimately inconsequential side character? You'd expect it to bear the name of the protagonist, or the most important locale, or maybe even the main villain, but no, it's the name of some weirdo who pops up every now and then and, despite being somewhat important to the story, does ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to actually influence it. Of all the design decisions I can't quite get behind in this game, this is easily the one that sticks out the most.All in all, if I had to rate  numerically, I'd give it a 7 out of 10 overall, but the extremely unbalanced combat pulls it down to a 5 and thus a thumbs-down from me.

Main issue with the combat is that with every encounter you are locked in a confined space with the enemies, you cannot fall back and disengage, or kite the enemy, which OK. _childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for playing this Italian indie game ever since it was first announced during a Steam Next Fest last year. Now that the game is finally available, I can say it was worth the wait. I streamed this game on my Twitch channel, and thoroughly enjoyed how the plot evolved. For my first playthrough, I went full Defender, picking only the more cautious and less impulsive choices.It's a solid hack-and-slash action game, and it's interesting how moral choices have been written and portrayed in the story. There are no good or bad choices, just the choices that we consider right, and even the consequences are unexpected. The art style is phenomenal, and every world we visit is fleshed out in a compelling way. The Codex feature is also a chance for lore enthusiasts to delve deeper in the worlds and cultures of the universe. Puzzles can be a bit frustrating in some parts, but they're not too difficult to solve.There are only two negative aspects I can say about this game. The first is that the combat system can feel a bit boring and repetitive, especially in the first part of the game when we can only rely on basic attacks. The second is the lack of a beastiary gallery, featuring the monsters we fought during our journey.Overall, Batora: Lost Haven is a very good release. If you like hack'n'slash games, some good worldbuilding or you just want to enjoy an emotional adventure, then this is the game for you.
