_childDocuments_.review: The recent surge of Kaiju-centric games has been a pleasant surprise for me. Before Pacific Rim, I didn’t have much interest in them, but now I love the idea of taking on a near-unstoppable force whose only motivation is raw destruction – or taking on that role myself. Kaiju Wars puts you in command of the forces responsible for stopping rampaging Kaiju in a turn-based strategy that will challenge your tactical capabilities.Abbreviated Review:  In Kaiju Wars’s narrative, you’re the mayor of a coastal super city. One that is attacked almost as soon as you show up. For whatever reason, you’re also a mayor that has the skill and responsibility to command the military. A military that isn’t particularly robust and is generally ineffective at taking on a giant monster with the will to kill. The ace up your recently elected sleeve is a scientist that, within every level, must develop a new Kaiju repelling concoction that sends them back to the depths. So, in essence, just about every encounter is a countdown to a science victory. This may sound similar to Into the Breach, and it definitely has plenty of parallels, but it does feel distinctly different in a lot of areas. For instance, rather than pushing a squad of powerful units into each round, you’re relegated to spawning a larger supply of generic tanks, missile launchers, bombers, and so on. These require money which is generated by the buildings on the map. Buildings that the Kaiju specifically target each turn. The “science” is generated much the same way from a special subset of buildings and added to the pool each turn until enough “breakthroughs” occur to put the monster down and achieve victory.This creates a system where you’re playing a game of attrition where the goal is slowing down, redirecting, and temporarily halting the Kaiju’s efforts for as long as possible. Each unit you have can do a tiny sliver of damage with an attack, but can also add to that damage when “countering.” This process requires the unit to be in the path of the beast as he moves to his next target – which is possible to predict since they (usually) go for the nearest building and the probability of each step is displayed on the map grid. Often, the path to victory involves a combination of attacking with offensive units while also placing stronger countering units in the predicted path of your enemy to double down on the damage and trigger additional inhibiting factors. The tactic of damaging and slowing down the attacking Kaiju (or Kaijuis as some maps feature more than one simultaneously) is the cornerstone of the gameplay. However, it’s not the only ingredient in the recipe for success. The buildings on each map generate nearly all of the resources you obtain and use to accomplish your goals. Some buildings create money that is used to buy and repair units, while others spawn the science resource that leads to your victory. On top of this, there’s a “breach” meter that counts down as unseen forces try to push the monster in the right direction. Once enough of these occur, the Kaiju will suddenly lock in on your scientist and, if successful in tracking her down, you’ll face an abrupt end to that level.Unless you’re able to slow or temporarily stop the creature by stripping its health – from which it recovers very quickly – you’ll have to evacuate the scientist and run her to another lab to continue her work. This is usually only a minor inconvenience, but it can mark the difference between a quick victory and a much longer and less rewarding battle. Usually, each map has a special bonus if completed in a certain number of turns. This gives you an additional resource – medals – which are used to upgrade special units and unlock perks as you progress. Winning each level rewards at least one medal, but several more can be gained from quick victories, completing a level on ‘hard mode’, or other challenging criteria. You can even earn more of them with special optional levels that sometimes play out more like a puzzle than the rest.What this adds up to is a fairly deep strategy experience that explores the many different types of units with unique abilities and the handful of distinct Kaiju that also have abilities and skills that distinguish them. While the variety of map tiles is a bit limited and the objectives for each level are mostly similar, there is still enough here to make levels noticeably different and deliver a sense of progression – even when I didn’t make much progress. While it may be easy to lash out at a game over simple stuff like a color palette that looks straight off the Commodore 64 or a painfully slow turn phase for the Kaiju (which has been addressed with great updates since launch), I can just say I suck at it. There were maps I tried up to five times and still failed, and that’s rough to repeat in a turn-based game. However, the fact that there’s a leaderboard showing how quickly some people succeeded on the turn counter, kind of gave me a light at the end of the tunnel. It didn’t make me suck less, but it made me feel ok about it. Even when I’d finish and be 250+ places down that leaderboard. The aesthetic of the main gameplay can be a little tiring after a while though. Which is sort of disappointing since you get glimpses of great design in the comic book presentation of the levels across the six chapters. There are also a lot of neat little interactions in the main menu including a wall of television screens that have things like faux news clips about monster attacks and links to public domain classic Kaiju movies. Those details along with the ability to access weekly challenges, player-made maps, and the option to make maps yourself leave Kaiju Wars feeling robust for its an indie game at this price. So it’s easy for me to recommend this challenging yet well-made game that I will probably never beat. But if I had fun, people that are better strategizers than me will probably have a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: The #1 issue with the game is that it is just painfully slow. Even after disabling all possible animations and speeding it up as much as possible.The game plays out essentially like a puzzle game, with preset scenarios, however with some RNG thrown in for seemingly no reason. This means you can fail based purely on chance even if you play perfectly. It also means due to how insanely slow the game is, upon failing you will be forced to play through essentially the same sequence over and over again praying for a different result. The game has just enough RNG to be annoying, but not enough RNG to actually be interesting.I would be tempted to grind out a few more stages to see if it changes much, but based on the other negative reviews with 8 hours and even 40+ hours of playtime saying largely the same thing, I'm gonna go ahead and assume it remains the same throughout.Would highly advise you just go play an actual puzzle game or a more interesting strategy game instead. Would suggest Baba is You and Into the Breach.

_childDocuments_.review: Way too slow, both from an animation and gameplay perspective. The only challenge is figuring out the new abilities of the kaiju and then ignoring it while maximizing science. Almost more of a city builder than strategy game. Similarly, the campaign is flawed with the ace units and researchers. You'll either find a mission way too hard or way too easy depending on how many medals you have. Conceptually and thematically it's neat but the gameplay is just flawed, this isn't into the breach or advanced wars even but some sort of slog where you mostly will be sending units to stop flames on your production buildings rather than fight the kaiju.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'll preface by saying I've always been a big kaiju fan, and thus the concept itself was already appealing to me. And for any fan of the film genre or just giant creatures in general they'll find a ton of enjoyment in this game just like I did. As the gameplay reflects quite a bit of the feel of kaiju movies.You play as the mayor of a city now suddenly under siege by kaiju and commanding the military forces to defend your people. For the most part, your units are woefully outmatched by the kaiju, who destroy almost everything you can throw at them in one hit and have big health bars. But the strategy is there still. As careful placement of bases can lure kaiju around the battlefield where you want them to go. Some units do more damage when they're attacked and destroyed. Some don't do any damage if they're attacked. You have special super science units like mechs and masers that can sometimes take more than one hit, and do a lot of damage. But they take awhile to produce unlike your standard units.There's even much more than this. Managing resources. Keeping your lead scientist from being attacked. Project cards used by you and the enemy to alter things on the battlefield. Even special abilities for the kaiju that vary mission by mission, changing their capabilities and behavior. As well as optional missions that place strange conditions on you to make them into special challenges. There's a lot of depth to this game.Further, the aesthetic is fantastic. The vaguely retro graphics and optional fuzzy video tape overlay lend it a lot of personality. Which is only built on by the writing. The game doesn't take its story seriously. It's there to poke fun and celebrate the genre. With bits of humor and character archetypes that are common tropes to the kaiju genre. It even has a few live action newsfeed cutscenes that come off as intentionally stilted, but they are rare enough to not overstay their welcome.The creature design I won't lie and say is amazing, but it is far from bad. They look, at least, more interesting than some of the original kaiju presented in Legendary's Monsterverse, and the references each one is to real cinema kaiju is usually pretty easy to guess.The only real negative I have found so far is the menu. It's cool and creative, but it's also a bit difficult to find your way around. As there's a handful of different objects to interact with for fun, and a lot of the various options don't have their name displayed until you hover your mouse over them. This makes the menu navigation a little annoying.As far as length goes, I can't judge that yet, but the game outright says early on there's fifty missions in it. And there is the ability for players to create their own custom missions as well. Though I haven't delved into that to judge it either. But point being, from what I currently know the length of it seems well worth the price.TLDR: This game is clearly a work of love. The entire vibe and feel of the game is that of a classic kaiju movie with a bit tongue and cheek humor. The gameplay has a surprising amount of depth, and can be challenging. If you love kaiju you'll love this. If you don't you still might find it a fun strategy game. If you dislike the kaiju genre, however, the feel of the entire thing is definitely not for you, good game or not.8/10 in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: from the moment you start a fight and until it ends you feel like you are losing and you only truly win by science. to push this fact even if you do take out the kaiju you still need to complete the research to finally end a fight. this leads to sometimes it being better to just slow the kaiju over going all out on damage. you are given a limited number of units though they can be repaired any number of times and you can upgrade each of their 4 states once with medals (land A, air A, counter, and speed ). money and research work like advance wars where you get cash from building and research from labs. build base to build specific units (land, sea, air) and you also get 1 of 3 random buffs each turn (+attack/speed, +cash, +research, build a free unit/building, and many more). the game feels like there is an optimal way to do each level so i don't feel like i have freedom to do as i please. then you have optional mission that are strait up puzzles.the games not bad per say but it is frustrating even when you're winning. yes, i get thats how the humans in a godzilla movie must feel but i don't know how i feel about it for a gameplay loop. i'ed like to go neutral on this so you could decide yourself but here we are on steam with binary choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Godzilla 2 (yes they even admit it in the game!) and a bunch of decent original humor things with a couple of inside jokes (memes) thrown in for good measure. Very pleasant. And I love the sketchy 2d animation of the kaiju. They're hand drawn and a full good rate drawing FPS animation. (seriously they're really fun to watch)Lots of potential when you play too cause you can upgrade units, get turn bonus cards.. even a local vs multiplayer with one person playing the kaiju! It's really well made.EDIT: I tested the local multiplayer versus... it's actually very limiting to the second player (Kaiju player) So I can't recommend that mode. Maybe later on at the later levels maybe? or if someone makes a more multiplayer friendly custom map?Note: this  more plays like a puzzle game in a lot of ways rather than an advance wars style game
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Playing as a completionist, after beating some missions on Normal (and somewhat enjoying them, but finding them too easy), I thought I'd give a go at Hard, for more of a challenge. I didn't want to miss out on medals to upgrade Ace units.... However, Hard Mode missions aren't so much of a challenge as RNG suffering simulators. In order to win in hard mode at all, it seems you HAVE to roll multiple 50% or lower chances to even have a shot at success, much less something worthwhile on the leaderboard. I replayed a hard mode mission multiple times with an optimal strategy, and it's just straight up not fun redoing the same actions, watching the same (sped up, but still too-slow-for-this) animations over and over waiting to see if RNG would let me clear the next hurdle. Repeatedly it didn't, with, often, 50% rolls being the _highest_ chance, plus the fact that you have to clear 5+ of these rolls per mission going _exactly_ as planned to have a good shot at victory? Ugh. No, not worth it at all.If not clearing hard mode missions won't bother you, this game is honestly still worth a shot. It's a veritable love letter to the kaiju genre and drips with style, but there's a big reason other similar titles like Into the Breach made their gameplay as deterministic as possible.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Very enjoyable strategy/puzzle game with a pleasing old-school aesthetic to the graphics with its colour selection.And of course it goes heavy in its love for the classic giant monster genre with its flavour displayed in every detail, particularly if you look at the background of the main menu area (Little tip, you can turn left and right in said area using the A and D keys, only found out out awhile into my playtime).The plot and its cast is more for humour and to function as a framework for the game (which could otherwise just be a string of challenge stages with a simple text blurb at the start) but is rather decent & does its job in bringing amusement.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Are you looking for a tactics game but with Giant Kaiju? If so, this probably isn't the game for you.Are you looking for a puzzle game but with Giant Kaiju? Then this IS the game for you!What I gathered from the tags and inital viewing of the trailers was that this was going to be a strategy tactics game, but after playing the first few levels of the game that impression quickly disappeared. How the game works is you must lure the Kaiju around the map using your buildings as bait, until you can earn enough breakthrough through a combination of defeating the Kaiju and accumulating enough science. Buildings can only be built in set locations dictated by each level and the unit and project pools are limited to what each level dictates. So while the pool of units that the game gives you on later levels does expand, it is in a constant state of flux in both amount and variety of units and projects, particular to that level. So it really does feel like a puzzle game where you're trying to use the tools that are provided to you to reach the breakthrough goal.I personally found the game to be quite challenging, particularly in the later levels. So if you're a big fan of puzzle games that make you think, I think you'll have a great time! The characters you meet along the way have some fun banter and lots of references from characters to one-liners. The dialogue that pops up from positive and negative events is also quite charming, so be sure to pay attention to it every now and again!Final note: While I was playing the game I did encounter quite a few game breaking bugs, a lot of these were caused by the Twitch Integration so if you're having troubles with the game locking up, disable that. Also the developer did take note of these bugs, so I hope they'll sort those out!
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: A tough but not unfair game of battle chess that pits the player in an asymmetrical war requiring actual tactical thinking and forethought.You can ignore the negative reviews, they all complain about the same thing. It's a slow-paced game on purpose, so one turn doesn't make-or-break you, and means the game is more about setting up elaborate strategies and responding to an evolving battlefield. The game has so much more tactical depth because what worked on the first wave won't necessarily work on the second wave of kaiju attacks, and you have to think further ahead than just your next turn. That being said, the game isn't actually *that* slow. Except for a couple act finishers, most maps end in 10 turns or less, with plenty of in-game options for speeding up turns if you're really in such a rush. Most the other negative reviews just don't understand how tactics games work.The game is tough, no doubt about it. It's really only worth it if you're really a fan of the genre. There are some problems with the game not properly conveying information before a mission that you'd expect to be there, meaning sometimes a quick restart is in order. And that's not great, I admit. But if you put up with a little bit of clunkiness, each mission presents a unique challenge to solve, requiring you to optimize the loadout at your disposal. The replay options in Hard and Freeplay really test your mettle too.All in all, Kaiju Wars is underrated. It's a game with far more tactical depth than many in the genre, it just had the audacity to flip the script on gamers used to having the upper hand on enemy forces.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Ultimately comes short of the delivery and feels frustrating and unsatisfying. The theme and presentation is great, but each mechanic introduction just gets in the way, and just the base interaction feels slow. The goal isn't killing monsters, which is fine, but the scientific victories feel unsatisfying while also taking extremely long to fill, and failing means starting over. Unit movement feels stifling, and engaging with a kaiju is exceptionally uncomfortable, even without the grid selection issues (thankfully there are free undos). Weirder units seem to handle their edge cases in the most player unfriendly ways, and they aren't predictable until the bad outcome has already happened (For example: why does a transforming unit not transform in the square it is in, but instead moves to a random adjacent square?).The writing and presentation are enjoyable enough for the obvious constraints but running jokes run aground early and it wasn't enough to push through the mechanical frustrations. The player input strings were a great touch, and the soundtrack is servicable.The feeling of being on the back foot from a rampaging kaiju is great and an interesting framing. The process to turn the battle and then win the fight doesn't feel like I've overcome through tactics, but that I just waited long enough to gain the VP for credits to roll. More elements around a science victory to make it feel satisfying would have gone a long way for making it an engaging way to achieve success. As it is, the experience of a battle comes up short.I recommend trying the demo to see if you have more patience for the combat quirks than I do, or picking it up on a sale to give it a spin. Hopefully it gels with you more than me.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: A turn-based tactics game in which you fight off giant monsters ("Kaiju") by tactfully throwing ineffective military equipment at it while your scientists work around the clock to find a more permanent solution.The game takes some pages from the holy book known as  (praise be) but adds its own spin to it. Kaiju can have different abilities and may retreat into their lair periodically, while you have special superweapons you may be able to deploy.Unfortunately the game also adds some - in my opinion - unwanted factors into the mix. For example, it's possible to give some of your troops - your Aces - some minor upgrades between missions, but you won't know which of these Aces you'll actually want to deploy during the mission. Sometimes you're also able to select your own event cards to choose from. In both cases it's best to play the match for a few turns to see if you're up against a flying Kaiju, what kind of Dark Projects the enemy has access to, etc. and then quit to the main menu, upgrade your troops accordingly, selects the events you want to have in your deck, and then restart the mission. Either this information should be available up front or the (lackluster) upgrade system should be scrapped altogether. As it stands you either force yourself to play with a terrible team composition or useless event deck, or you accept that you're going to lose a few minutes each match 'scouting ahead'.The main menu seems to be the primary reason for why this game has a remarkably long load time whenever you boot it up. Unlike everything else in the game it's completely 3D animated and there's huge amounts of visual clutter for no apparent reason. I had to click around for a solid minute before I was able to find out how to start the campaign. The 3D effects can be turned off in the settings but this makes the main menu a very dark void, which is even less pleasant to navigate and does nothing to improve the boot time. A baffling choice to include in an otherwise highly stylized 2D experience.I threw the towel in the ring when on one particular mission a randomly aimed beam attack from a Kaiju destroyed the target building it was headed for (a 25% chance it would target that square), thus forcing it to immediately choose a new target (50% chance, two buildings to choose from), immediately moving there in the same turn and choosing the most out-of-the-way route to get there (a 12.5% chance), which resulted in it stomping on the lead scientist I had to keep alive. A 1.56% chance ended the 40 minute/30 turn match i was otherwise just about to win. With zero intentions of going through the whole process a second time and without any sort of Autosave systems to fall back on I called it quits. You can't force players to sit through overly long missions and then throw random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at them and expect them to think it's both fun and fair.There's a good game in here for the right person. I am not that person.

_childDocuments_.review: I can tell the devs really poured their hearts into this game. _childDocuments_.review: There's a good game in here, but it's hampered by an extremely poor user interface that often has units move to completely different squares than you selected and seems to want to spend 90% of its effort on "looking cool" and 10% on "actually telling you what you need to know to play the game" :/. _childDocuments_.review: Painful gameplay. Imagine playing Advance Wars, but all your units including the air have reduced speeds. Often my units just chase the kaiju's for several turns as it destroys stuff before they can finally catch up. Even with the upgraded units later on. One Kaiju abilitie destroys units not even in the path so once it finally catches up it'll get one attack and then die.Animations are slow, loading is slow, the dialogue is a slog to get through. _childDocuments_.review: Kaiju Wars is fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: Buy it for the many references, stay for the gameplay.I'm not joking, this game's has got a good amount of strategy. You're not here to defeat the kaiju, you're here to slow them down as much as you can until you gather enough research points to win.I really recommend it for the gameplay. _childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Not really my pace, but I'm still recommending it because there's nothing actually wrong with Kaiju Wars.The visuals are charming and the music is pretty nice. If you like the idea of slowly building up resources to fight powerful kaiju, then check this game out when it's on sale.However, despite no true flaws, I felt the pacing of the game to be too slow for my liking. The economy system feels like it makes things too gradual. When a kaiju is attacking your city, it seems odd to start building tanks and planes at that point. The military should be ready to go and not need to wait for individual dollars from the economy phase. I get that this is a usual trait of many strategy games, however, I feel like the money and unit deployment systems could have been streamlined a bit to make the game feel more exciting.With that said, if you like slow-paced strategy games, then give this one a shot. The animations are all pretty nice and the gameplay is solid. I didn't care much for the dialogue or characters, but you might! Not a bad game at all, so kaiju fans may want to check this one out.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay loop feels extremely suffocating,Constant crisis that blocks paths indefinitely and some essential buildings relegated to special cards that show up at random is very frustrating.Optional mission has most of the time only a single way to finish it, so basically you will have plan ahead upto 5-10 turns or end up losing ~20-30 minutes of game just because you made a mistake early on.I dislike the fact that none of the units have any type of ranged attack so either your units attack the kaiju by placing them next to it and lose them in the next turn or use them as a sacrifice by tying it up to a building for a counter.I like the layout and where this gameplay could go but I might consider trying different Turn based strategy games instead of this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Snappy Kaiju-fighting tactics featuring a variety of units which appropriately die in one hit but have various capabilities that you'll need to counteract the Kaiju's own abilities, as well as a deck-based system where both you and the Kaiju's side play cards to benefit from special effects each turn.The game also has a great aesthetic that celebrates its inspirations, and an awesome soundtrack. I'm glad I didn't miss this gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: RATING - Bad: 4 / 10WHY?- This game has BUGs and some BAD DESIGN DECISIONs that make it BROKEN !- The devs have been informed of such game breaking designs and said bugs. They are nice and I am waiting to see if they will act. DEVs PLEASE FIX THE GAME! BAD DESIGN & BUGS- I will give one common example: If you want to complete in-game missions and achievements, you will be stuck in the stage "Big Game Hunters" because defeating the kaiju (monster) before the requested turns should end the game, but it won't. Due to a game breaking design decision, the game doesn't end when you kill the kaiju (only when science completes) and in this particular stage the kaiju returns from death buffed to the max gaining extra bonuses every turn while you will not get any more bonuses. Not only that, but the kaiju will go straight to your lab (if it destroys the lab, it's game over). Besides that, the buffed kaiju bonuses will make the monster recover more HP than you can ever inflict, so it is going to destroy the lab for certain. You may escape with your scientist, but there is no other alternative to gather science and the kaiju will destroy everything with its buffs, killing the scientist about 20 minutes later. If you want to beat this stage, your only option is to not fulfill the extra mission and leave the kaiju alive with low life and low movement while your science goes up. I have tried this and it is such a bad design decision... a lot of time wasted because of such a broken game!- This same game breaking design happens in many stages and there are people in the forum asking the devs for a fix...- Another terrible bug is that story videos are not working on Steam Deck and Linux PCs (I don't know about Windows or Mac). This includes the news from first page and all stage introduction videos. Devs know about this, know the way to fix it and I hope they implement the solution!THE GAME- The game itself,  apart from game breaking design and bugs, is a lot of fun, but brutally difficult. Especially on hard mode, where you have to be "pixel perfect" (or move perfect on this sense) to beat the stage. By the way, you will only know the specific set and order of moves if you play and die, so expect to play the same stage many times, which is a dread because the pace is very slow and you always have to start from the beginning (at least 10 minutes per attempt just to watch the same animations and doing the same movements until you can try the next variation of your strategy).POSSIBLE IMPROVEMENTS- Fix game breaking design and bugs! I have sent the devs some fix suggestions.- Fix video codec!- Include the option to rewind your game per turn, that way players won't have to replay and rewatch everything just to try a different move wasting 10 to 15 minutes everytime they do it.-   - implemented! - Allow to skip animations - I would say to redesign stages so that the solution doesn't become "pixel perfect" but that may be something for future games or releases.CONCLUSION- There are bugs- There are game breaking designs- Devs have been informed of game breaking designs and bugs... still waiting for fixes...In the end, this is still a broken in development game. The ideas, graphics and soundtrack are good, but there is work to be done! It's an unbalanced tower defense that requests a specific set and order of moves to win on harder stages. Make a mistake, and you have to replay and rewatch the last 10 to 15 minutes (sometimes more).I am willing to revisit this if the game breaking designs and bugs are resolved and the improvements are implemented. Currently, I wish I hadn't bought this one in a bundle... some issues are really frustrating... but at least the devs are nice and I hope they fix the issues!DO NOT BUY! WAIT FOR FIXES!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're at all interested in turn-based, tactical games, do yourself a favor and pick up Kaiju Wars. It plays a little bit like Into the Breach, in that you command military units and try to stop Kaiju from destroying a city. The scale is bigger though, since you command an entire army, and you can replenish your units throughout the fight. There's no such thing as a "perfect run" in Kaiju Wars either, since the whole point is that the Kaiju are vastly powerful and will stomp all over your city no matter what you do. In a similar way to Into the Breach, though, the goal and the fun lies in using the tools you have at your disposal to figure out how to stop the Kaiju long enough to win the mission. ItB is one of my favorite games, and Kaiju Wars scratches that same itch like no other game I've found. I highly recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: Mild to decent recommend.  Scratches the same sort of itch as Into the Breach and Atom Zombie Smasher, a game that's part tactics, part economics, and part puzzler.  Balance between those categories varies from mission to mission, as well as what difficulty you're playing at.  I'd say they do a good job and that keeps it interesting but this format might not be for you, while I haven't found any mission controller snapping frustrating (yet) there have been one or two that have annoyed me a little.  Overall it's not the most brilliant or heaviest game ever, but it's not trying to be and I think it does an excellent job for its weight class.  It's nice to see a smaller studio do something this polished and stable rather than pushing early access with a pre-alpha build.Side note: I liked it's sense of humor, and think it's probably the best way to go given the subject matter.  But I didn't LOVE it, parts of this might grate on some people.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I think the game is pretty great. One can see that the devs love the Kaiju genre. There is so much stuff in the game that is there just purely for flavour (e.g., the news broadcasts), and I love that sort of world building. The story is compelling and the graphics as well as the dialogue brings it to life in a really nice way. The game also does not mess around and "defeating" the Kaiju is not the goal since they cannot be killed. So the player essentially has to slow down losing the game. The main characters are all unique and likable in their own way. Some follow established tropes (but that does not have to be a bad thing) and in general the game does not take itself too seriously. There are a lot of features that encourage players to replay the game (e.g., community maps, trying out different units or researchers), which I appreciate.   Annother thing I think is worth mentioning is that it runs smoothly; even on my laptop that is running on life support.[Disclaimer: I may be biased since I like the devs, did some testing on the game and some language work. Still, I did not get the game for free and bought it on release because I like it.]

_childDocuments_.review: I have to be honest: The presentation of Kaiju Wars kind of rubbed me the wrong way. I just didn't vibe with the art style. In fact, maybe I still don't. But there's a solid game here.Imagine Into the Breach, but instead of having mechs at your disposal that can match and exceed the Vekk blow-for-blow, you mostly only have conventional military hardware. That means instead of dispatching multiple monsters every turn, your forces can only hope to slow it down - or at best, send it back to its lair to heal for a few turns, before it returns stronger than ever.I'm about a dozen hours in so far, but only about a third of the way into the story, owing to my completionist tendencies. There's a lot of content here, including a map editor, and everything seems very thoughtfully tuned. Plus, if you're not sure whether you'd like it, you can try the demo free of charge.Normally I'd complete a game like this one before reviewing it, but since there aren't too many reviews at this point, I'll go ahead and say:Highly recommended if you're a fan of turn-based tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: Video Review: Steam Curator: As an Into the Breach addict since 2018 and a diehard Godzilla fan since uh... birth, Kaiju Wars is the 2D turn-based strategy game I never knew I needed. It combines immediately accessible yet surprisingly deep turn-based tactical gameplay with a fun, lighthearted B-movie storyline, then renders all of it in high-quality pixel art and slaps a deliciously cheesy synth soundtrack on top. If all that didn't sell you, I’m not sure what will, but for you weirdos still on the fence, allow me a few minutes to unpack Kaiju Wars’s Story, Gameplay, Content, and Style, after which I hope you’ll have a better idea of whether this game is right for you. STORYQuirky, wholesome, and genuinely funny, Kaiju Wars’s absurd plot, characters, and dialogue left me uniformly impressed, perhaps because I, admittedly, expected so very little in the way of narrative value from such a silly premise. The storyline follows your mayoral administration and its cabinet of hapless yet loveable kaiju-hunting cliches, from the uptight, science-obsessed Dr. Wagner to your right-hand military man, Major Danger, an overly-macho, machine-gun toting simpleton. Together, and along with a handful of memorable supporting characters, you’ll battle kaiju (and, more lethally, bureaucracy) across the globe from America to Antarctica. A mildly interesting alien-infused conspiracy runs through this cheeky narrative, and the game’s relentlessly self-aware dialogue makes the story of Kaiju Wars more enjoyable than it has any right to be. GAMEPLAY & CONTENTBut enough fluff—how does Kaiju Wars actually play? In a word: well. Kaiju Wars is fairly refined as turn-based grid combat goes. Essentially, your administration faces between one and five near-indestructible kaiju each level that spawn and move semi-randomly across the map. Dr. Wagner and her squad of scientists predict RNG paths of said kaiju on their way to destroying whatever building is closest, each of which carries a different function. Most important, here, are labs, which churn out science points necessary to creating kaiju repellant serum—because you can’t stop these beasts; you can only hope to contain them. Allow the kaiju to destroy too many security buildings and the monsters will plot a direct course to Doctor Wagner’s location, and her death means game over man, game over(!) for without her housed safely in a lab, your administration will produce neither money nor science. Luckily, labs aren’t your only means of defense, here, as the foundations in each level can also be turned into army or air force bases. Pump kaiju full of enough lead and they’ll lose health bars, each of which grant the big bad guys an additional move space per turn. Thus, your role as mayor is to distract and deter kaiju long enough for your labs to pump out the science points necessary for victory. As if all this this wasn’t enough, Kaiju Wars also allows both humans and kaiju to draw a special card per turn—you may gain extra science points, money for troops, or the ability to build a free base, while the kaiju may replenish health or even gain a new power, some of which can prove quite devastating to your puny human ambitions. So, as you might imagine, there’s a considerable degree of depth to each level, all of which contain unique map arrangements and objectives—for example, some missions find you without access to military units, period. You’ll instead have to build productionless decoy buildings to lure kaiju away from labs long enough for your nerds to pump out the requisite science points for victory. Other missions emphasize anime-esque special units, unique environmental hazards, or introduce brand-new gameplay mechanics, like buff-bestowing researchers. After a successful mission, you’ll gain performance-based medals that you can then pump back into troop stats, adding a nice sense of personal progress to the 20-or-so-hour campaign. After that, feel free to swing by the map editor and give your own kaiju simulation a spin, then publish it for others to try and probably fail because you gleefully added too many overpowered kaiju to one map. STYLEFinally, a quick word on style. Kaiju Wars is, if nothing else, darn fun to look at. Over-the-top visual flourishes, like the entire map rumbling when kaiju emerge from their lairs, gives the game a nice sense of scale, despite the small levels. My only critique, here, is that each chapter of the campaign is really just a color gradient reskin of the last, so you may grow tired of the overall aesthetic. Ditto that for the soundtrack; while each chapter adds a new song or two, all of which are ridiculously catchy, Kaiju Wars could benefit from a little more everything, kaiju included. CONCLUSIONThis said, Kaiju Wars is still a pretty much perfect love letter to PC-playing, kaiju-loving man children like me. And while I wasn't blown away by any singular aspect about the game, Kaiju Wars does so many things so well that I can’t imagine anyone not at least casually enjoying this Godzilla-gone-goofy strategy game. Not that Godzilla wasn’t already a complete goof: .After averaging up our micrometrics, Kaiju Wars earns a very solid MEGA score of 3.87/5 and is my favorite game of the year to date. Until next time, this is Scope, and thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for this game. I'm undecided after my first session. If into the breach is a perfect game with modest goals, kaiju wars seems to be a slightly scattered and ambitious project.I played on hard mode and it felt a bit railroaded, maybe that means I can improve by reading more deeply. The cards felt bad, eventually the kaiju is just healing faster than you can damage it which felt like a weak fix for the game being too easy somewhere along the way. Maybe later when there's more card variety it'll be more interesting but I'm already not loving the rng after you make your decision model.the visual are really charming, but the charm wears off soon and I was in the menus looking for a way to turn off all the cut scenes to make the game feel snappier. there's lots of option for that but not enough, and obviously so much work went into making these visuals the game doesn't feel right without them either.  there are also bugs and heavy graphics here and there but my machine is garbage so it could be a me thing. in general the game looks very cool, though, some of the art would be better left out (economy, military panels feel slow and some are much better looking than otheers)I'm recommending because I want it to be good, and if it became even slightly better I think it would be, so I'm reserving judgement and cheering y'all on! _childDocuments_.review: I was mostly enjoying the demo but the full game added a terrain hazard mechanic that I'm just not willing to deal with. I don't like the ace unit mechanic as it keeps me from improving units as a whole. I would just use air units if the game would let me as they are clearly SUPERIOR to ground units due to the far better movement. Allowing the upgrade of units as a whole instead of having the ace vehicle mechanic would help fix this. Ground units have no positives over air units. They have less movement than air units, are negatively affected by terrain and don't gain any movement by using roads. The ability to slow down kaiju after being stepped on is underpowered compared to just doing damage to a monster. Getting a permanent reduction to the kaijus movement by doing enough damage to remove a healthbar is always going to be a better option than sacrificing a unit to slow it 1 square(at least it has been so far in my playtime). Doing damage is also one of the two ways you can beat a mission so you have double the reasons to spring for higher damage units over trying to slow down a monster. Even when you have the kaiju at it's weakest and it only has 2 movement left, you can't keep it from destroying a building without having two units with the slow ability in it's way. This is asking too much when the units with the slow ability can only use it on either a ground or flying type monster exclusively and those same units are also quite slow themselves making positioning difficult. I also found the card system to be underwhelming. It doesn't really change the way the game plays and while something like getting a free base at random is nice, it isn't really exciting. I think in this case I would rather be able to choose from the pool of cards directly rather than from a random set of 3. If you have played the advance war games on the gameboy then you know the different abilities of the characters really change how you play the game. You can have somone who makes all units cheaper to produce but with lower stats, you can have inafantry gain passive buffs to make them perform closer to vehicles and you can have other abilities like striking enemy units with a missle. Kaiju wars just doesn't have anything that changes the game up like that so far. I like the art style, I like the simple story premise and I like the core turn based gameplay, but the execution just isn't there for me. Oh I almost forgot that there isn't a single ranged unit for you to use. At least not to begin with. You would think that the missile launchers would be ranged but nope.

_childDocuments_.review: Having thoroughly beaten the campaign and gotten all of the achievements not related to making custom maps, I can comfortably say Kaiju Wars is a great tactical strategy game.Don't be mistaken; this is NOT Into the Breach, XCOM, or any other hero-based tactical game. You have only regular army units (and the occasional sci-fi superweapon) at your disposal. Units WILL be crushed, cities WILL be wrecked, and the game is about getting your units stepped on and cities wrecked in such a way as to slow down the monsters and chip away their health, bit by bit.Killing the monsters usually isn't the goal, though - you need to produce Science, which can be done in a variety of ways to allow for different strategies and some creative missions. In general, the missions aren't super difficult, but optional objectives, hard modes, and freeplay modes create more challenge if you want it.On top of this, the artstyle is pretty cool and definitely distinctive, and the writing and characters are fun, if nothing earth-shatteringly creative.If you like tactical strategy, or find yourself feeling bad for the doomed army guys in the first half of a monster movie, I definitely recommend Kaiju Wars.EDIT: Also, it's Canadian! Super cool to see such a neat game coming out my home country.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: If you came to this game expecting Advance Wars or Fire Emblem, yeah you'd be disappointed.You're not the glorious heroic army that will save the world from the evil empire, no, you're the hapless self-defense force, the doomed army in monster films that gets slaughtered to the last.  Remember that scene in the Animatrix where humanity's finest marches off to fight the robots and all die?  Yeah?  Yeah that's what you are in this game, the General who will die standing with themIf you wanted victory, if you wanted glory in battle, you should play any other tactical RPG.  Symphony of War here on Steam is a nice alternative.  But for a grim and unique experience that's a lot less serious than you figure it'd be, play this one!Not to mention, the side content includes a bunch of old kaiju films, including the infamous North Korean one Pulgasari.  Surely that's worth $5 on sale?But yeah, I need to emphasize that this is not a typical tactical RPG.  Victory is not the point, the point is to delay those monsters for as long as you can.  Defeat is constant, but as long as some humans can escape, as long as our species can continue to exist after the battle, then you've won.  Get out there, soldier.  For humanity!
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent tactics game, though unconventional because of its reliance on a counter mechanic. Unlike most tactic games, the goal is not to kill all the enemy kaiju on the map, but instead to hit a certain number of 'breakthroughs', which are earned in part by economy (buildings producing science) and only partially by killing kaiju (worth 10 science production). This creates an excellent depth between going for kaiju kills (which can get very difficult due to the kaiju having abilities that can sweep your units off the map prior to combat) and simply trying to delay them, bait them into going other places, or last-ditch moving the kaiju objective (Dr Wagner) to another lab. Two principal criticisms - there is a pretty significant progression aspect to the game in that your units are very, very weak at the start. Buying your 'ace' units their movement upgrade at a minimum is absolutely vital, and fully upgrading them is critical to many maps. Don't try to do the hardmodes or even some of the turn based challenges of the early maps until the units you have available for the map are upgraded. In addition, you never have access to everything all at the same time - each map has a different selection of ground units, air units, and experimentals you can build on the level. Ground and air units are displayed in the preview, but your 'project' deck is not - which is a major factor in how good some of your units are and which experimentals you can deploy (Missile units become extremely powerful once you can stack project buffs like +1 rng +2 attack when still +2 attack on hills). This leads to a cycle where you go into a map blind, get wrecked a bit, then after you know what's available you can highscore the map easily. Related to this is the fact that some maps seem balanced around drawing specific projects so that the map gimmick functions (for example, an all-jungle map where you have a project that gives your units +2 counter in jungles). To even attempt this map properly requires restarting the level until that project gets drawn on the correct turn - easier to just have the project be guaranteed on the draw.There are a lot of levels, and I kind of don't want to unlock every single medal on every single level, but there's definitely enough content here for anyone to just chew on for 25+ hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Clearly developed by people that genuinely love Kaiju movies and turn based tactics games. It shows in the level of detail, both in the game play and in the presentation. Recommended for people who are a fan of Kaiju or turn based tactical games, and damn near essential for people who are fans of both!

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent. Two reasons:1. The StyleI have 7 hours of play time and the moment on each level when the kaiju appear from the ocean still impresses me every time; the banter between the characters is exceptional, big fan of the synthwave-lite art direction as well. I like playing games with podcasts in the background. Not this one. Why? I can't miss out on the soundtrack. I love it.2. The Gameplay"Easy to learn, hard to master". There are multiple easily understood mechanics that interact with each other in interesting ways to keep each map fresh, without ever feeling like you need a PhD in Kaijuology yourself.Addressing some complaints I have seen in other reviews:1. The game is not RNG dependentOn occasion RNG can in fact make a level more difficult than otherwise, but this is uncommon. The campaign difficulty seems well balanced to me so far, as well.2. The animations are not too slowWhy would you ever want to skip them??? They're excellent! I love the animations!The game has a slider that lets you accelerate the kaiju's movement animations, I keep mine at like 1.25 or 1.5. Reviews complaining about this not being in the game may be from an earlier patch. I bought it on sale, but if I bought it for the current list price of $20, I still would be happy with my purchase. If you like strategy games or the film genre (and especially both!), you will be happy with this game. It's like being a kid playing one of those Game Boy Advance strategy titles again. There's something magical about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. The campaign will last you a good, long while, especially if you're trying to 100% it or play through starting on hard mode. It also does a good job of introducing new concepts at a decent clip, and giving you side missions to change the game up a good bit.Once you get what feels like a full arsenal and are handling it, you get a good challenge. Then in the next chapter, some of the units are changed up and new ones get introduced. This fits and feels good all the way through, especially with the rewards system for beating a mission, doing it in a certain number of turns, doing it on hard, and in many cases, doing it with your won custom setup rather than the premade one- that last one lets you have some real fun changing up how the mission works, and lets you get that "I'm a badass" feeling from either coming up with a new solution to the mission, or being able to dominate a mission that *was* a challenge.Definitely a worthwhile game, *especially* since you can turn certain animations on/off or have them only trigger the first time used per mission, *vastly* speeding up gameplay once you feel like you've seen everything. AND  you can do it mid-mission without having to restart the game.10/10, highly recommend. Great example of good *game design* at a campaign level *and* at a singular mission level.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an enjoyable strategy game about using a swarm of weak units to overwhelm an overpowered foe, though some of the design choices (mostly missions that rely heavily on RNG) are a little questionable. _childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Solid turn based game apparently based off a Godzilla SNES game I have never before heard about. You play as human military facing off against a handful of kaiju that reappear on different occasions. The flavor of the game comes in the form of projects, dark projects, medals, scientists, kaiju abilities, and map layouts some of which I will expand upon.Projects and Dark Projects are essentially the same thing, a deck of cards for the player in the form of projects and a deck of cards for the enemy kaiju in the form of dark projects.The objectives of every map is going to be to slow down the kaiju to the point where it retreats or you manage to gain enough research to obtain science breakthroughs. All throughout a mission, projects will give bonuses to you either temporarily or throughout the entire mission, likewise for the kaijus. On a side note the story is super cheesy in a very good way, chalk full of humor and definately plays on kaiju movie tropes, game is worth buying for the tongue n cheek humor alone.Back to projects, bonuses can vary widely from being able to deploy units for free, instant massive injection of funds to top secret weapons and tactics. Dark Projects will mostly speed up kaijus and spread devestation accross the map, basically fire tiles which can kill your units if you end turn on them and prevent income/science if they land on specific buildings.The game is very challenging as you definately feel yourself trying desperately to fend off giant beasts tearing down your city. This is especially true as kaijus unlock abilities which will make it harder for your units to attack a given kaiju e.g. one of the kaiju requires radar to be detected or else only counter fire can damage him.Although there aren't many kaijus their varied abilities and map designs will keep the game fresh along with plenty of military units/scientists being introduced  as the campaign progresses.Upon the completion of a mission you are awarded medals which you can spend upgrading your troops or purchasing new scientists or unlocking easter eggs. It is worth noting that you aren't upgrading all your troops by spending medals more like the Elite troops which are one off versions of a unit which will have stat increases as you invest medals e.g. in a mission you may be given 3 infantry squads but only 1 of the 3 will have its stats boosted.Equally important is spending medals on scientists which can help you generate science faster in order to win a given scenario faster. Some will allow you to generate more science if a lab is constructed close to a forest tile or a volcano, others will be from having a specific building within 2 tiles from a lab, others from attacking with experimental weapons etc.There are 6 Acts in total with about 5-6 main missions peppered with optional missions so there is plenty of content to go around (Im still not done the main campaign as of writing this though very close). On top of lots of scenarios there are different play modes such as being able to pick ur project deck, and hardcore mode, both of which acquire you extra medals upon completion. Moreover there is a hotseat mode which I think allows you to play local only, thought it is an aspect of the game I have not yet explored.If there would be things to improve I'd say perhaps having more kaijus or more varied dark project deck, but considering it's an indie from a small studio I can't bash it too hard. Maybe an online multiplayer would be nice for those missions you can hotseat.  Otherwise, graphics are superb with really nice color and a retro tv monitor filter that you can turn on and off. Soundtrack is pretty solid too with nice 8bit songs accompanying every different acts of the game. Also very nice touch is the interactive menu which also show cases Kaiju movies that are now public domain, this feature alone has made me start watching giant monster movies I never heard of nor never really watched like Godzilla, Yangary, Gammera and PulgasariOverall 8/10 really impressed, hopefully Kaiju wars 2 sees the light of day at some point.Now buy the game so you can nickname all the monsters as the N-word or wtv gamer profanity you can think up
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo back during steamfest and loved everything I saw. Of course there were a few placeholders and some things to iron out then, but now the game is released and I lvoe all the extra art and music and the way some levels were redesigned. If you liked into the breach, then give this one a shot for sure! _childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Kaiju Wars is a turn-based tactics game where instead of fighting many units, you fight a big Kaiju!Some of the core mechanics of the game would be:You vs. One instead of many. You fight Kaijus, which can't be killed, only forced back! They have many abilities and huge health bars and destroy everything in their path.Victory Condition. Each level requires a certain amount of "breakthroughs" to win. You get these by getting 10 science (labs produce these, as well as some cards from the project deck) and you also get 1 by reducing a Kaiju's heath to 0.Project Deck. Each level has a "deck". You draw 3 per turn out of 14, and they do many things like "build a lab" or "next unit you buy is free". The normal mode of levels have a pre-built deck, but freeplay versions of missions let you customize the deck.Researchers. You can bring up to 3 researchers to missions. They give you additional science for playing a certain way/synergize with certain Project cards.Counter. Certain units when destroyed will do damage to the Kaiju, so positioning units in the path of destruction is a big part of your strategy, which I find fun.Things I love:- Disposable units- The twist of fighting an enemy that can't be killed- No "combat RNG".- Art Style/Theme- There is a complete remake of NES Godzilla 2 in the game- So much content. All levels have a normal and hard mode. Some have a freeplay mode as well, and there are optional missions too.- The quips. When events happen you get cute quips, which really add to the experience for me- The story, for what it is I'm enjoying it, short and sweet- Map editor/steam workshop sharing of levels- Weekly challenge missionThings I'm neutral on:- The project deck- Science seems to trump combat in terms of winning (slamming labs is my go-to strategy)- Spending medals to improve units/gain researchers (you want to refund you medal purchases and re-spend them before every mission, since the units you can bring each time is different, which I find a bit tedious)Things I dislike:- After 11 hours in, the game is starting to feel a bit slow with certain animations, turns can take too long- Missions generally always feel like first try you fail because you don't know what units you get for it/what the project deck will have. I wish on the map preview screen it showed me what units I could deploy.Overall I'm really enjoying this game. A huge amount of content for $20 base price. If you enjoy turn-based tactics games you will enjoy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Fun art style and concept. Several clever design choices that make it feel like a game with 10X the budget. The Kaiju follow very specific rules so it is easy to plan ahead. That also means there's no brain dead AI like in most strategy games. You never feel cheated either. All of the information is laid out in front of you. Also, the developers are very responsive. While there are a couple of issues, it is great value for $20. If you can get it on sale it's an absolute steal.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If a tactic game enjoyer, youll enjoy this one, auto buy at full price imo.To temper expectations a bit, a lot of comparisons to Into The Breach can be made, but this game has not achieved the same "perfect information" that ITB has. Some of the RNG added into the formula is fun, a card system that is fun to play with. But some of it feels unnecessary and a step backward for the genre, It feels frustrating when your success or failure balances on a monster taking a 50/50 move between two equally close buildings. It would really be as simple as that 50/50 decision being made BEFORE its turn and the game telling you it. Would remove all RNG but would be pretty close. But none of the games flaws could possibly hold back the sheer amount of content, tactical decisions to make that are within your control, and awesome flavor the game offers. One of those games you play and the passion the devs had for it bursts out of every orifice.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: I meant to post my review two days ago, but every time I had enough free time to write it, I decided to just play the game instead. That's how addictive it is (for me, anyway).You should play this game...-if you like LOADS of content (long campaign, map editor, optional maps, weekly challenges, etc.)-if you like elegant turn-based tactics games with shrewd pacing and incremental depth-if you like isometric tilesets, pixellated retro graphics, comic-book-style animations, and clever palettes-if you like driving, synth-y, earworm-y, atmosphere-building music (each kaiju has a unique theme!)-if you like the kaiju genre (the background movie clips, palette based on old posters, live-acting segments, and retro map re-designs from Godzilla 2 for the NES really make this a love letter to - and affectionate parody of - the kaiju genre)-because the monster designs are charming (and somehow *never* get old despite the small roster)-because the dialogue is clever and flavourful, and the in-mission quips are hilarious-because the developers are engaged and unbelievably responsive to feedbackYou should not play this game...-if you hate turn-based tactics games or kaiju, I guess?-if you're going to let the main menu scare you away from the meat of the game (it's not bad by any means, just a bit stylistically inconsistent and not as good as everything else the game has going for it)-(I was going to say something about optimal play, but it's not really an issue because there's a lot of flexibility in how each person will play the game; you can skate by missions barely, replay them with more information for high scores and medals, or play again on hard or free-play or PVP modes)Really, I don't have much negative to say about this game. I suppose it needs a tiny bit of polish (e.g. bug-fixing) in some areas, but as I say above, the developers are really responsive, so any minor rough spots are going to be fixed soon enough. A final note: I love the "little touches" that show the Foolish Mortals signature style, like being able to name the kaiju and write a speech to the citizenry in some of the missions (the quips during the mission will then be based on the speech you wrote - this had me dying laughing). My kaiju names...-water kaiju: Aquossum-volcano kaiju: Fryvern-ground kaiju: Mandiburrow-forest kaiju: Huggy

_childDocuments_.review: A fun and retro-style Kaiju killing game! A straightforward strategy game that tasks you with either fighting a giant kaiju off long enough for research to be completed or to kill a giant kaiju. The game feels well balanced in terms of the different qualities that various units have, some have a higher level of damage or counter damage, etc. The soundtrack is a bonus as it blends great with the on-screen action during a mission :) This game so far has done a great job of not only giving me the exposure to a hard working and passionate developer but also other games that are just as fun as Kaiju Wars! I love this game and I really hope the success of this one will be able to afford the developer to make a second installment for Kaiju Wars, I give Kaiju Wars 9/10 Specium Rays!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously a labour of love for people who like Kaiju (giant monsters like godzilla) retro and tactical games.In this game, you are tasked with putting kaiju back to sleep. You can't kill them permanently so you need to either force them to retreat for a few turns by dropping their health bar to 0 or to stall them while you do research. The basic flow is that you build research everything turn until you reach the required amount and win the map. Harder difficulty modes let you keep going until the monster eventually wins and this puts you on a leaderboard in the game. As the game goes along you unlock unit and abilities. Unlockables include a deck you have to give yourself various boosts and using medals you get by beating challenges to get power ups. The game has veteran or elite units but these are available from the start of maps rather than by having your units deal damage and survive. The game also has a bunch of other extras in the interactive main menu like public domain kaiju movies, a map editor and daily challenges.The story is pretty basic. You can customize various texts in the game like how you are addressed, unit names and even speeches you deliver. The game has a bunch of one liners from gaming pop culture like "more pew pew less QQ". A fun package with a lot of content. It has a lot of replayability with its various modes. You can replay maps with custom card decks, a hard mode or even a vs mode where one player is  the kaiju. There are also a lot of unlockables.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: A neat, unique tactical game. I don't know that I've ever seen a game where my own units are just so darned... expendable. Placing fodder in the way of giant monsters has never been so much fun. And the game oozes kaiju-based personality - it's pretty charming stuff. I don't think it'd be for everyone (and I don't think it's trying to be), but it really nails a kaiju-tactical battle niche. Worth trying for anyone who's a fan of tactical battle games just to check out what it does differently.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Play out a Kaiju movie as the (hopelessly) outclassed military in this stylish 2D turn-based strategy game. Construct buildings and defend your city with cannon-fodder tanks, jets and more as the devastating kaiju grow in power with every attack.
_childDocuments_.name: Kaiju Wars

name: Erica
detailed_description: Prepare to immerse yourself in an interactive live-action thriller, merging the world of film and game like never before. Erica, a young lady plagued with nightmares of her father's murder. With the traumatic events of her childhood dragged back into the light via grisly new clues, it's up to you to unearth the shocking truth. Explore the enigma of Delphi House where every choice you make influences how the game develops, with multiple endings awaiting you at the finale of the gripping branching narrative. Ground-breaking live-action technology Immerse yourself in a feature-length cinematic experience where you affect the action playing out on-screen, merging high-fidelity Hollywood production values with engaging, tactile gameplay. Make key choices via interactive storytelling Alter the path of the game's branching narrative by making meaningful decisions that have a profound effect on how the story plays out. Choose how Erica interacts with other characters through conversation, and shape her relationships with them. A filmic score filled with tension Get wrapped up in every moment via a haunting soundtrack from Austin Wintory, the award-winning composer of games such as Journey, The Banner Saga 3 and Assassin's Creed Syndicate.

_childDocuments_.review: Erica is a modern and fresh addition to the FMV genre. It feels like a feature film with its excellent cinematography but with many branching paths and choices for players to make. It is priced extremely fairly but I found it to unfortunately suffer with awkward controls and bugs, which incessantly hindered my experience.+ Excellent automatic save system.+ Many branching paths with a plethora of different choices to encourage replays.+ Steam achievements.+ Excellent cinematography.+ Fair and decently priced ($AU16.95).+ Interesting story with a few twists.- Multiple frozen screens.- Controls were awkward with many of my clicks not registering or were very delayed.- No option for manual saving.Erica is named after the protagonist who shares her name with the title. She suffers from strange nightmares and trauma from witnessing her father’s death as a child. Now a young adult, Erica's childhood is suddenly upheaved once more, but new clues surrounding her mother’s disappearance and her father's murderer have been brought to light.  After being sent to Delphi House, a reformity for young girls. Erica connects with the other troubled young woman and finds a shocking connection there with her long-lost mother.There are various endings and differing choices along the way that critically impact the story, with a strong recommendation at the beginning of the game to replay at least once, as the story is not fully told in just one playthrough. Averaging about as long as the standard film (1.5 - 2 hours) and being of the same high filming quality, Erica's story feels exactly like an interactive movie and a move in the right direction for the modern day FMV title.I am a considerable fan of FMV titles, both new and old. Typically, their old school vibe and interesting methods to tell a story always intrigued me and keep me more captivated with choices, as opposed to just sitting back and watching a movie. Erica fits exactly this, except it manages to steer away from the long-established and conventional methods of the genre, giving it a more contemporary feel, which I definitely appreciate.Surprisingly, the game is a whopping 37GB. This is not something I expected for a short 2-hour game, but it is dubbed in 7+ languages and features very high-quality filming, so I suppose this is more understandable. But for those who may be running low on space or those (unfortunately like myself) who are limited with awful internet, this may be important to note. Erica is unique in that the game saves automatically at essentially every single screen, most likely due to the sheer number of choices that quickly alter the story. However, for those quickly looking to replay certain sections, curious to see where the opposing path leads them, this is impossible. The entire game must be completed again, from the beginning. There is no chapter select or manual save slots, players must sit the games entirety if they wish to see other endings or specific choices. Perhaps this is due to the changeability and volume of different decisions made throughout one playthrough. However, I would prefer to have the option to manually save my game at any given points, if I just wanted to see the result of one single choice. Even if they are all connected as one complex cascading story, having this option would be beneficial. For those who are not well accustomed to this style of game but are enticed by Erica's modern approach, this section may assist you.  The game is essentially an interactive movie. Certain scenes like flicking the mouse to swipe through pages of a book, opening a letter or choosing dialogue options under a designated time limit are all very standard FMV procedure. Erica also incorporates many different areas to choose from, each choice such as choosing to exit through the door or explore a prohibited area, all branch players down a different story route which heavily encourages multiple replays. Unfortunately, my experience was hindered by multiple bugs and was not very smooth. I encountered at least 2 frozen screens where the audio continued but the motion picture did not. Completing simple tasks such as clicking on specific hotspots could be quite the chore, with my clicks seemingly either not registering or being quite delayed. This caused me to frantically click away, trying to trigger it, as most scenes and choices are timed.Furthermore, certain scenes like even right at the beginning of the game where players must light a lighter felt like a boss battle. I am unsure why it was so difficult as I tried clicking downwards at varying speeds and matching the display onscreen to no avail. It just seemed as if the game was not properly optimised for mouse which may be the case as it was first released for PS4 in 2019, then ported to iOS earlier this year. I did get the feel a touch screen would be easier to play this on. Fortunately, the developers are actively patching these issues and have already fixed a bug where players with high refresh rates could not bypass a specific scene. Perhaps this is the reason why I struggled so much throughout the game as well, as my monitor is 144HzThis is where the game exceeds similar titles and stands out amongst others in its genre. The interactive storytelling is portrayed in HD and to a very high standard, with exceptional cinematography skills on display from start to finish, across a surplus of different locations. It is exactly what one would expect from a modern-day film from Hollywood, except that it features tactile gameplay.   Similarly, the soundtrack is also to a high production value. Featuring the well acclaimed composer from games including . Its haunting story and decent acting are brilliantly matched with the accompanying sounds that all made me feel like I was watching a newly released movie. Erica is an excellent, modern addition to the FMV genre with an eerie narrative that features upstanding cinematography, a plethora of choices and multiple endings. Unfortunately, I did encounter a handful of bugs and controls were not as smooth as I had anticipated, but developers are actively implementing fixes and it is priced extremely reasonably at $AU16.95. I recommend this not only to long-time fans of the genre, but also to anyone who is curious to try it out. Erica's modern style and approach make it an excellent FMV to begin with and there is plenty of value for money with its focus on replayability.This review copy was provided to the Devils in the Detail curator.
