_childDocuments_.review: Edit 22/07/2022 - Original review is still below, however I realised I did need to update my opinion.[my only review which people ever found helpful will now have those ratings cleared :( ]It took some time (over six months iirc) but Capcom finally addressed my main gripe of this - that the games weren't available as individual titles - although it took them a long time to do so.  They also added quite a few more features; although had these been implemented from the start then they may have found this reviewed a lot more favourably than it was.There are a number of online challenges now available for each game, with 'CASPO' points to give people a secondary goal if they find themselves tiring of the games.  Game difficulties/lives/etc. can now be changed to make a game less frustrating or give you more of a challange - an unexpected bonus I was pleasently surprised by, even if I won't be using itNo online co-op still though, which is a shame and we still can't remap controls, which is - quite frankly - ridiculous in this day and age.I would now recommend this product, although I still do have some reservations with how much of a cack-handed job they made of it initially.  Like some other Capcom products (SFV springs immediately to mind with it's ignorance of what casual players wanted), they seem to be oblivious to what their consumers actually want and now spend the early days of their products stubbornly believing that they know best before finally caving and making the changes that should've been their from the start.To be completely honest, Capcom Stadium Arcade is a good example of why Capcom have earned themselves such a poor reputation and causes me concern that things won't change with them.  Hopefully I'm wrong though and they improvements made since release mean that there ethos towards their customers has changed.  Only time will tell.---ORIGINAL REVIEW:What could've been great is ruined by greed.So, we get the base launcher (for want of a better word) and 1943 (the sequel to 1942 if anybody cares) for free! Yeah!  Great, now to pick up 1942 (the sole reason I got this) and I'm set.  Except if I want 1942 I have to buy it as part of a bundle for a minimum of £10.  Hmmm...Now, I can understand the bundles but the fact that only one game (which many people have stated they preordered for free yet have had to pay for to access...) is available on it's own is, quite frankly, a joke at best.  Why you have to buy bundles and not individual games is beyond me.Put simply, this is nothing more than a fancy version of MAME tbh.  You can change what the arcade cabinets look like, whoopee!  You can also upload your high scores and view them online.  Pretty neat I guess.  That's it though.  No online co-op, no button remapping (why must I use RS3 for 'insert coin' when there's half-a-dozen other buttons not in use).This smacks of a desperate money grab tbh.  Capcom have seemingly done as little as possible with these ports and structured the DLC in such a way that the majority of people will have to pay well over the odds for the few games they want.The lack of extras, current modern gaming options (i.e. online co-op) and so forth make this unattractive as it is to anyone who deosn't want to play some old arcade games, but sticking every game bar one in a 'bundle' to buy - instead of allowing them all to be purchased seperately is nothing more than a con.  Due to this, I would advise anyone to stay well clear of this and just use MAME for your arcade needs.I'm going to give it a week - in the hope that the lack of individual games available is an oversight - but will be uninstalling if not.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay then: back when this first came out and most of these games could only be bought in pre-set packs, I left a negative review and said I'd reconsider if an "a la carte" purchasing option was made available across the board. So here we are, and as promised I've picked up a few things (all scrolling shooters, so note that my perspective will draw from that particular genre's experience herein) and given the collection an honest go; still not sure why this seemingly bog-standard setup wasn't included from the start (except perhaps to prey on some buyers' impatience), but, well, better late than never. I'll spare you my thoughts on the individual games, and instead highlight a few items concerning my overall experience with the collection as a whole:- Some folks have complained that the RE Engine stresses their computers - and I do have to agree that it seems silly to use a relatively new and demanding framework to run such old games - but I can at least say that my laptop, whose specs are a little ways above the recommended ones, didn't seem to have any trouble with it.- A decent number of display options and filters are available and gradually unlocked, though many of the former are just "waste screen space with cabinet edges" variations; on the other hand, vertical-screen "tate" orientation is available for titles which utilize it, a rarity in older compilations. I've read accounts of graphical hiccups in some games but nothing so far has managed to catch my attention on that front.- A third-party XBox 360 controller worked without issue, though a Hori PS4 pad was not detected. Dedicated "rapid fire" buttons are available on all of the shooters I acquired, which my hardware and fingers both appreciate.- The "main" play mode, in which you can freely adjust the usual DIP switch settings, doesn't save high scores by default, though you can create a save state or two as a workaround. The "challenge" mode, in which you're locked into default settings and a single credit to have a go at the online leaderboards, only saves your single highest score for each game.- Most titles allow you to switch between the US and Japanese versions, though note that separate "challenge" mode scores are not saved for each.In a nutshell, while not the most full-featured "classic" game reissues out there, I'd say that what's on offer here is fair for what's being asked, now that people who already own or aren't interested in most of the "bundled" items can pick and choose alongside those who are up for grabbing a bunch at once. The question going forward, of course, is to what extent, if any, Capcom intends to follow up on its initial 32-game roster, for while there are certainly some classics and gems in here there remain plenty more such veins to mine: whatever your favored genre, there's assuredly at least a few titles you (and I) would like to see make a reappearance in the future. Here's hoping we do eventually get something resembling a "definitive" place to revisit the cabinet-laden days of yore; even for the moment, though, I think a good amount of folks will find it worth popping a few proverbial quarters in to pass the time.

_childDocuments_.review: What's good: almost complete collection of the 1942 games and other good vertical shooters, including Vulgus. There is a good variety of games which should be blasts from the past. There are several Street Fighter games, but also other beatemups including about 3 with Mechs in like Cyberbots for '90s excess.Good pickup and playability, plus local coop, up to 3, but mostly 2 player. With the emulation side, you can put lines and screen curvature, nice touches. Complete screen art to go on either side is a 79p DLC. For me those were worth it and that implies some sort of effort with emulation on the part of Capcom.There is some nice additional gameplay with a points system based on time played and various challenges and modes (Three, Time mode, a points mode and a special challenge mode based some variables unique to each game). I personally don't mind just vanilla pumping some coins into a game and just playing until I do something else.What's bad; you just get 1943 to play for free and everything else has to be bought separately as DLC. However, they are cheap. Altogether, it's like 40 quid. But I spent about 3 years getting most of them and am personally content. Some people complain about the collection being heterodox, and it's true with such a wide remit over 2 decades, you risk being a jack of all trades, master of none. Just buy what you like at first and either keep your commitment low or go for the virtual arcade they make some effort into making it feel like. As for the censorship, well, the flag that they used to bomb Pearl Harbour with or a colonial flag with Hong Kong, and it's Americans complaining seems a bit hypocritical to harp on about from where I'm sitting as a censorship issue.I played 1942 in arcades in the 1980s, but later on I played 1943 a lot. When I was 15, I'd go to my local arcade and put 50p in for 3 credits and get as far as I could. Times changed and there was home computing, but 1942 games were hard to find. In the late 1990s, my friend took me to Full Tilt in Camden. It was all grunge and a bunch of music I wasn't interested in, but upstairs there were some cabinets, and 1942 was in there. That was my biggest memory of the night was playing that again, but I must admit I hate grunge too, so it was a nice break from that. Even later came rasberries and other emulators and I was interested, I wanted to play Strider and 1942 again. Strider was another favourite game from when I was 16 in arcades, the sound design and gameplay was amazing for its time.Capcom Arcade Stadium had both of those games and more that I used to play, but those Two were the first Two I got for it (1943 comes free, I spent a whopping pound and some change for Strider, and left my Capcom arcade like that for about a year, only adding more 1942 games as I felt like). I like making the screen look like the old screens back then with lines and curvature, those are nice features.It was great to discover that after all these years, I'm terrible at these games compared to when I was younger, but it's worth learning to play them again, and it's nice to do so on my own time. I use these very much as pick up and play for short sessions.Obviously these are very specific to Gen X'ers. It's not because I think that time is special to casual readers, it's more like this would probably be understandably boring to other people, the games are limited, and some of them are notoriously hard, like the first Ghosts and Goblins, these are games designed to make you drop coins in them they're seemingly pointlessly hard, the gameplay will seem very limited or simple, because it was early days. I'm personally glad to be reminded, and despite my seemingly decrepit reflexes now, I still know where the secret cigars and cows are for the bonus points.However, if you like bullet hell games, many of these are for you too, there are also lots of good anime references regarding the art styles for modern gamers.The other advantage that Arcade 1 has is a few early Street Fighters, so with that and the other games there is local coop potential, there is a nice collection of the 1942 series with 1943 Kai in Capcom Arcade 2 for the complete set, that for me was worth buying. I definitely played that in an English ROM in the Uk, but Japanese ROM only is available in Capcom Arcade 2. There are also the Dynasty Wars-style games and mech beat 'em ups like Armored Warriors, which I also like There are also conventional beat 'em ups as well (Two), plus Section Z, which everyone likes a lot, but I prefer Sidearms on Capcom Arcade 2 for the same Side-scrolling gameplay, but reskinned with mechs.Just take your time and buy up the roms on sale, they're cheap either way. I probably would not even be on Steam if it wasn't for some of these games, I personally enjoy being able to play them again after specifically missing them, so if you feel the same way, you'll probably get the same nostalgia playing these and satisfaction collecting them.Overall I do like shmups for pick up and play between serious gaming, and these are it, there is also good local coop potential and you're getting complete games, not just another roguelite shmup, like they all seem to be now.Looking at the other reviews, IDK, I personally did not mind the long spend with this one, buying up the roms on sale when I wanted to. Yes, it's annoying that it tries to remind you of the games you don't have (you can set it to show only playable games and it usually remembers that setting), but is it as bad as microtransactions games that are play to win, no, not at all.I don't notice any performance issues, have played these over 3 pcs. Is it a very good collection, I don't know, I hate the Pirate Ship Higimaru one and Wings of Fate from back then, I just don't buy those roms, but Vulgus is a classic vertical scroller and Capcom are right to be proud of that to include it, I can personally see how we get from that to their other vertical scrollers with the similar cute secret bonuses.Is it overpriced for an emulator, probably, but I've wanted to play Strider and the 1942 games for a long time and even my phone version of 1942 just is not as good as the original, I liked the initial convenience of just having that in my steam collection. I just presumed that other people would make the same kind of calculus with that. I think this parallax model of getting you with the DLCs is not as bad as microtransactions.Of course people should vote with their feet and I'd personally really like to play Shinobi and Tigershark again, but for now and for me, this is good enough on the balance of probabilities.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't in any way shape or form qualify to judge or criticize this game (or collection of games rather) since I'm indeed outright not a part of the intended audience, not even close and yes, I did get it after the free Street Fighter 2 DLC and just that one alone, but at the very least I think I can appreciate the way they chose to go with it. The whole customization aspect of your very own arcade, even if it doesn't go as deep as it can, is a fun little aspect. It may not be the best looking game out there but I like to think they've managed to use the RE Engine in a way that I can excuse any and all minor faults. Maybe if they could, it would've been better for them to not use the same UI elements like the ones from Resident Evil 7 and the later entries but that doesn't matter much. But maybe I won't get lynched for saying that in a game of this kind I really would not like to be reminded of the feeling of intensity of a survival-horror title with similar UI elements, it just felt slightly out of place and contrary to the the game's overall visual style. But at least the in-game customization options seemed plenty and sufficient. And lastly I don't know how it feels like for people who value the games in this collection but charging for each and every game in the collection for some reason felt a bit scummy, this game didn't need to be free I feel, it almost feels like a scam considering the fact that isn't really plastered on every single place, feels a bit deceitful. _childDocuments_.review: It's Capcom, so this kind of thing is kind of what I expected from a free product with their name stamped on it.For anyone wondering, the "free" part is  an unnecessarily-bloated launcher with one of the worst game selection menus I think I've ever seen in...well literally anything.  It pops things up that you just want to close when you first start it because you haven't even had a chance to get your bearings. The rest of the games are all locked until you buy them for about $2 a pop.  That might sound okay at first, but consider that these games are a thousand years old at this point, and if you intend to try most of them or fill out your library or whatever, that's going to add up really quickly.   In an age where there are countless numbers of free (and better) games out there just waiting to be played, its hard to justify recommending this to anyone short of the most die-hard arcade game nostalgia seeker.I really liked Capcom's games as a kid growing up, but my god they're such a terrible and shady company in the modern age that really doesn't deserve your money.  It's time for them to get better or get lost.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I got this game for free with a DLC and wish I hadn't because installing it and trying it out was a complete waste of time.I understand what Capcom were trying to do here, but they failed horribly. They probably saw people saying that they pirate old games because they're not being sold anymore, so they tried to create an emulator for those games so that they could sell them to people again, but I don't think they've ever seen any emulators before because this is missing some features that are pretty important to me.The keybindings in this game were probably made for QWERTY keyboards, and even if you switch to QWERTY, they feel unnatural and weird. Switching to QWERTY isn't a problem for me if I don't have to type anything - I use Dvorak because I find it more comfortable. Some of the emulators I've seen let the user change their keybindings. CAS doesn't let you do that from what I've seen, or at least I couldn't find the option to do so.This game is for Windows only, which isn't a problem for the majority of people, as almost 97% of Steam users use it, but I use Linux, and, hear me out, most games (about 92.31% of all tested games) are playable on Linux even if they're Windows only thanks to Valve's Proton, which is a modified version of Wine, which is a program that lets you run Windows applications on Linux. This one, however, crashes upon launching unless you launch it with a specific unofficial version, and even then crashes (at least on my PC) when launching an arcade game unless I set the game to run in a borderless window., BUT if your priority is to create a game that would stop piracy of your old games, you should try to make it accessible to everyone.(Also, Resident Evil Village runs just fine via Proton, so it's not because "the game's too complex to run on a non-native system" or something like that)Another thing that was a bit weird was that you can't set the audio volume in the settings. Had to do that in my PC's audio volume settings.

_childDocuments_.review: [This review is based on my exploration of the app, testing a couple games I have purchased, and a complete playthrough of 19XX: The War Against Destiny]Capcom Arcade Stadium is Capcom's latest compilation of arcade games.The initial presentation when you first launch the app is a bit frontloaded as you are given pages of tutorials to explain the game gallery. But after you read through the pages it's fairly straightforward. 1943: The Battle of Midway, the free game that comes with the app, and any purchased games are displayed in Capcom's Impress Candy Cabinets, though there are additional options, such as the Cute, the Status 18, or Generic Upright cabinets. Sadly none of the game have their original cabinet, but seeing how this layout is meant to be based on Japanese Game Centers, it makes stylistic sense. The app does show games you don't own as a means of persuading you to buy them, but you can switch the view to 'Playable' games to show only the ones you have.Gameplay Wise, it's as one would expect of an arcade compilation, the gameplay appears to be accurate. Bringing up the pause menu allows the player to change settings such as difficulty, lives, game specific settings; but interestingly, it seems that key-bindings/controller bindings is per game, so you will have to open up each game to change them. It's not a bad way of doing it, but having it tucked in such a manner made it easy to miss.While there isn't official online multiplayer in this game, this game does support Steam's Remote Play Together, however I have not been able to test this myself just yet.Capcom's decision to bundle games into packs is off-putting if you only want specific games; but for people who prefer having a collection to playthrough or visit, it might be worth checking out a bundle.Those looking for historical information like flyers, artwork, videos, and such for the games will be disappointed as there doesn't appear to be any in this app. This is a straight forward game collection.My Recommendation: If you don't already own these games in another bundle, check out the free game first to get a feel for the app to see how it plays on your system. If you know what you're getting into, it does seem to be pretty good. I've had no issues with the games so far.As for myself, I got a couple arcade games I wanna play for the first time, and some I wanna revisit again.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a collection of old arcade games, some of which have aged better than others. Whilst it was originally released as bundles of DLC where you couldn't choose individual titles to buy, they have now changed that and each can be bought separately. Ghosts n' goblins, strider, ghouls n ghosts, forgotten worlds - these are titles I have fond memories of, and for a couple of quid feel they are worth buying. From what I've played (Ghosts / Strider), the emulation is excellent and the games run very smoothly.Though I would also have to admit there are some indie games that aren't much more expensive, that will beat most of the games here due to being released more recently. I'd imagine the beat-em-ups still play pretty much the same (it's not a genre that's seen much improvement in 30+ years), but the vertical / side-scrolling shoot-em-ups are probably nowhere near the intensity of the bullet-hells that have come along since. Under £2 for an old shooter? Or £7 for Ikaruga? If you have that extra fiver, then the choice is easy.Same goes for the action platformers, such as Strider, which has been surpassed in the genre. Titles like G n' G, and...uh...the other G n' G, have aged better, due to being simple games trading on a tough challenge. Most are still worth a play-through for the cheap price, but every single game here most likely has a more advanced recent alternative that's not hugely expensive by comparison.  Now that they've changed the pricing structure and availability of the games, if they could just get rid of the f***ing awful, limp-wristed pile of fetid sonic cheese that passes for music on the title screen, it would be better.

_childDocuments_.review: My review here is actually pretty mixed, but I'm choosing the "Recommended" overview option to try and contribute to a more balanced element of feedback to the store reviews, which is mostly negative at the time of writing this.I actually understand why people are pissed. There is one game, 1943 - Battle of Midway, that you can play for free that comes with the arcade download. On the Switch version, your free game was Ghosts n' Goblins, which I can't help but think I would vastly prefer, personally. I'm not alone, and the way it's packaged is pretty scummy. Having bundles for different collections of these games as options is one thing, but other than an individual purchase for Ghosts 'n Goblins (which is roughly 2 dollars, currently 1, not free as currently marked - I think it's only free as part of the bundle?), these games do not seem to be available as individual purchases. Rather than the few dollars you want to spend on the odds-and-ends games you might have personal interest in, it's upwards to $50 between the different collections, depending on which ones you want.So, I get it. The bundling/pricing system is kind of messed up. And I wanted Ghosts 'n Goblins free, so disappointment there too. That being said, there are positives too.It's great ROM access that's actually legal. There are a handful of titles I wouldn't mind checking out for the first time, many of these games being before my time, and I'm sure there's nostalgia for people who actually lived through this era of gaming as well. And I'm not someone that takes notes about a lot of technical aspects, but apparently it runs better on here than it does for the Nintendo Switch, so this is the copy of the game with better performance.I would go about this release a different way, namely mostly where the pricing was concerned, but overall the product seems to play perfectly fine. Just go in informed.

_childDocuments_.review: This collection has some issues, but it is overall quite good. On the plus side, there's the gameplay itself. Emulation is good with very little input lag. Online leaderboards are great for most of the games on here, and you can just buy the games individually for really cheap to play just the titles that interest you. The selection of games is great, with some such as Progear having never received home releases before this collection.Having different cabinets to play in is cool, but is ultimately a novelty that you'll play around with for about 10 minutes before switching to a regular display (Was this collection intended to be playable in VR? The virtual cabinets would make a lot more sense there.)The issues can't be ignored, however. The UI has some big problems. You can't rebind or even view the controls until you start up a game. Most of the tabs in the game selection menu are near-useless unless you own most or all of the games in here. The score attack focus of the collection makes some of the included games seem odd. Anyone interested in Street Fighter II likely cares more about online versus than online leaderboards, but a Capcom arcade collection would seem incomplete without it, I suppose.The limited-time Special Challenges rub me the wrong way. Why not just have them permanent?The gripes I have may not be small, but I believe the pros outweigh the cons, as the games themselves are excellent.

_childDocuments_.review: Giga Wing on Steam. This was the driving factor of my interest in Capcom Arcade Stadium. The game that originally solidified my interest in the shoot 'em up genre finally available on the gaming platform I use daily.I will be honest, I initially planned on solely purchasing Giga Wing but, when I found out it was only available as part of a bundle, I had no problem purchasing that instead. I would have paid the price of the bundle for Giga Wing alone so, for myself, the bundle was an amazing value. And not just an amazing value, but an opportunity for discovery as well.Game selection in Capcom Arcade Stadium is marvelously laid out. Scrolling through games moves through both their logos and cabinets, with the games running on the screens. In the same way one would walk through an arcade and be drawn in by the various logos and cabinets, one can be drawn in to unknown games (or old favorites) by scrolling through the game selection, which is exactly what happened to me with Warriors Of Fate.While there are many games in Capcom Arcade Stadium that I recognize from the past, Warriors Of Fate is not one of them. The logo caught my eye as I was scrolling to Giga Wing as usual and, after playing it, the game has quickly become one of my favorites from the bundle. If purchasing Giga Wing alone was an option, I may have never stumbled upon this excellent game.Capcom Arcade Stadium is more than just a launcher for a plethora of games. The suite itself is loaded with features and presented in a quality fashion. On a per game basis, both controls and display options can be customized. And, for purists like myself, the option to play the games fullscreen at their original aspect ratio, with black bars and no filters, is available. It is also possible to unbind the various buttons that did not exist in the original games.Leaderboards are present for either score or completion time (depending on the game), with both all time and weekly rankings. Leaderboards use a separate ranked mode with game options, such as difficulty, preset, creating a level playing field for everyone competing. Additionally, there are special challenges that occur only for a limited time period, with differing game options from the standard ranked mode, and these have their own leaderboards as well.To bring it all together, there is an overarching profile system, with stats, such as personal best scores and most played games, and levels (including content unlocks as one moves through them). There is also a leaderboard for accumulated profile points, giving recognition to the most dedicated players, regardless of game.The free to play version comes with 1943 which, for a shoot 'em up fan such as myself, not only offers enjoyable gameplay, but also a glimpse at the roots of the genre from before my time. With support for 1440p and the PS4 controller via Steam Input (the gamepad config works well), the game is fully playable on PC. The combination of stellar games and a full-fledged, modern environment to play them in results in Capcom Arcade Stadium being the best presentation of classic games I have played.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Finally managed to get it up and running so I guess I'll keep it, and I'll change to a positive recommendation, but I'll leave my initial review up to reflect the frustration of initial setup.First up... set your expectations of the package relatively low. Capcom hasn't re-invented the wheel, there isn't much here that can't already be done with a mame setup. This is essentially some form of emulator for existing roms. What this package does is provide a decent front end for a large selection of games, and legitimize the roms.One thing I do give them credit for are the display options. Portrait mode options are decent... for 1943 you can select Full Screen (stretched up/down), Full width screen with borders at top and bottom, or one of several "3D" options that wraps the game screen in a digital upright console.ORIGINAL REVIEW:Less than an hour in, and I'm debating whether or not I just want to return it.Control settings are an absolute hot mess! It will apparently only recognize an XBox style controller so my custom zero-delay joystick will have to be custom set in steam? (I finally found the controller mapping option, but it doesn't recognize the fire buttons I have set up, it will only let me use the trigger buttons which on my setup are being used as pinball flipper buttons on the side.....Any game that still has me scratching my head on controller configuration after 30 minutes has something seriously wrong with it.I'll give them credit for having their display system automatically adjust for play on a portrait mode monitor, and after a bit of cursing it finally started respecting the windows "norm" of opening fullscreen on whatever monitor the shortcut is placed on.I really wanted to like this package as I believe in paying for content as opposed to pirating it, but they're not making it easy....

_childDocuments_.review: Tested the setup with the free copy of base Street Fighter II.  This is really good emulation.  Expect to get your butt whipped in some of these games, even if you set the difficulty to easiest.  Has a lot of options for speed, difficulty, etc.  Can use infinite credits, since it's a button press to get one.  Some people say you can't rebind controls, you can, once in a game (not on the game selection menu), hit start, go to controller settings, you can change it there on a per game basis.  Basically there are 3 tiers of menus, after you load up the arcade selection screen.  One on the arcade selection screen, one after you select an arcade (this is where you get game settings for things like speed and difficulty), and one after you hit A after selecting an arcade, which launches the game - this is where you need to be to rebind controls.  Has a rewind feature and save states.  I don't notice any input lag.  Got the 3 bundle set for ~$25CDN on a 50% off sale.  Lots of coop games, both same time and take turns.  Going to have a lot of fun with this.

_childDocuments_.review: Title: Capcom Arcade Stadium: A Nostalgic Blast From the Past with Modern FlairIntroduction:Capcom Arcade Stadium is a love letter to arcade gaming, bringing together a collection of classic Capcom titles in one exciting package. This retro compilation doesn’t just serve up the hits—it adds modern features to enhance gameplay, making old favorites feel fresh while keeping their vintage charm intact. Whether you're a long-time arcade fan or a newcomer eager to experience the magic of retro gaming, Capcom Arcade Stadium has something for everyone.Gameplay:The core of Capcom Arcade Stadium lies in its wide variety of games from Capcom’s rich arcade history, spanning genres like shooters, fighting, and action. Included games like 1943 - The Battle of Midway*allow you to team up with a friend in classic co-op gameplay, offering an authentic arcade feel. One of the standout features is the inclusion of modern gameplay tweaks—such as a rewind option to correct mistakes, speed adjustments to control the pace of play, and save/load functionality—so you can approach each title on your own terms. These quality-of-life improvements make the experience smoother while maintaining the challenge and excitement of the original games.Graphics:Capcom Arcade Stadium nails the aesthetic of an authentic arcade experience. The 3D-rendered arcade cabinets and customizable display settings, including scanline filters and aspect ratios, allow players to tweak the visuals to their liking. The retro pixel art of each game is wonderfully preserved, but the new graphical features let you polish the games with a modern touch, keeping the nostalgic vibes intact while offering a smoother presentation. The attention to detail is fantastic—each title looks as crisp and vibrant as it did back in the golden era of arcade gaming.Conclusion:Capcom Arcade Stadium is a must-play for fans of retro gaming and arcade enthusiasts alike. It brilliantly combines the best of the past with the conveniences of modern gaming. With a rich collection of Capcom's classic titles, new features that improve accessibility, and a polished visual presentation, it offers an engaging way to revisit some of the best games from the arcade era. The addition of online leaderboards provides extra incentive to perfect your skills and rise up the ranks, giving these retro classics new life in a competitive arena.Rating: 4.5/5 – A Stellar Revival of Arcade GlorySummary:Capcom Arcade Stadium brings the timeless appeal of classic Capcom arcade games into the modern age. With customizable visuals, gameplay enhancements like rewind and save functions, and a wide selection of genres, it offers an arcade experience tailored to every kind of player. Whether you’re here for the nostalgia or curious to explore retro classics, Capcom Arcade Stadium is a brilliant and polished collection that honors the legacy of Capcom’s arcade legacy while adding features we only wish we had back in the day.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I can rate Capcom Arcade Stadium as Positive with some caveats:Pricing structure:  Capcom's approach here has made the whole situation somewhat disconnected at best and a confusing mess at worst.  Though initially unavailable, Capcom has allowed the purchase of individual games alongside the decade-centric and "all games" packs. However, with the additional sound track offerings and in-game enhancements, the collection of DLC options here remains somewhat challenging to navigate.UI:  I can't help but think that the use of the RE Engine here was overkill.  Capcom had a perfectly sufficient interface that was fine for both Street Fighter 30th Anniversary Collection and the Beat-em-up Bundle: straightforward, effective, simple.  While certainly looking fancier than those releases, the UI here provides a level of bloat not commensurate with the overall experience; the cabinets all look uniform, the "attract mode" for the games is pre-rendered video, the in-game features don't seem to require this level of technology, and the navigation appears overly fixed / locked-in.  Added to which, I've noticed that as with the prior Switch release the RE Engine-based UI introduces occasional graphical and performance anomalies to the games during play that would otherwise not occur.On the far more positive side, the games generally seem to look good and play well overall.  The rewind feature is a welcome addition and the different border/filter types will likely succeed in getting the game to look the way you'd like.  The selection of games provides a nice variety, encompassing everything from side-scrollers to shmups, VS. fighting games, and everything in between.  While you're bound to find a game or two that's  from this lineup, all the major releases seem to be covered and do a solid job representing what Capcom was going for with their arcade offerings in the 80's and 90's.Once you get past the multitude of pricing options and the bloated UI, Arcade Stadium is a pretty solid release.  This is especially true if you don't have these games in other collections released over the years, both on Steam and elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I love it. I bought it on Nintendo Switch and I loved it enough to buy it again on Steam. Granted, I didn't buy everything. I'm content with just the Dawn of the Arcade Pack and Ghosts 'n Goblins. Before I played Capcom Arcade Stadium, I wasn't particularly interested in arcade games or older video games in general. There was some event when it was first released on Switch where you could get Ghosts 'n Goblins for free. I thought to myself, "Huh, I might as well try this and see what it's about." So I had two games: 1943: The Battle of Midway, and Ghosts 'n Goblins. I played 1943 and realized that these arcade games were fun. I played Ghosts 'n Goblins and realized that the games didn't look nearly as bad/old/primitive as I thought games from the 1980s would look. So I bought the Dawn of the Arcade Pack, because those first two games sparked my interest. (And that's also sparked a wider interest in old-school video games from  before my time.)I do not regret my purchase. My favorite of all these games is Commando from 1985. There's a score challenge mode, and it's what it sounds like: you try to get a high score, and if you pass a certain threshold, you get ranked on the leaderboard, and you can see who else is ranked. I had gotten ranked for some other games, and since Commando was my favorite, I decided I would get on that leaderboard. I played Commando for two or three hours straight in my determination. By the end of it, my hands were shaking. But eventually, I did it. And I'm already on my quest to do it again on the Steam version.Now for some reason, the game Trojan is only available in its Japanese version, called Tatakai no Banka. I'm not sure why that is. (This is also the case for the game Mercs from the Arcade Revolution Pack. It's only available in the Japanse version, Senjo no Okami II.) Bionic Commando is only available in its English version. Not to talk about some of the gems of the crown, like the CPS-2/Dreamcast Giga Wing and the incredibly beautiful pixel art of Progear. The "full package" comes with many surprises and undiscovered gems (like 19XX, one of my favourite shmups that I tried this year). Usually this kind of compilations include more "known" gems than unknown, but in this case we finally have BOTH.We "secure" the collection because we could enjoy our Street Fighters, our Captain Commando (which is another timeless classic, fun and incredible as the first day), our Final Fight, our Strider, our Makaimura/Daimakaimura (Ghost n'Goblins, Ghouls n' Ghosts) and our beloved Bionic Commando as well, but also we got more than amazing games to discover like the outstanding Chiki Chiki Boys/Mega Twins, the great 194X series and all the above-mentioned "selected" gems that I commented. Please, forget all reviews that just tried the free-to-play game and gave a bad review because they hoped to have the full collection unlocked.This compilation is AMAZING and we've got rankings,  cosmetic stuff, modes, leaderboards and weekly challenges for every single game. CAPCOM is right now one of the best game companies (definitely, they are right now living one of the best times of their long history), but this is a reminder that their legend is not made out of nothing. Give it a try if you really love video games.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, the arcade classics Ghosts'n Goblins and Ghouls'n Ghosts were not available on Steam and Cursed Castilla had to act as a replacement. Capcom has finally changed that and some of the arcade cabinets that stood in the lounge of a gym in my hometown in the late 1980s can now also be played on the PC.As of 06/2021, most of the negative reviews are unjustified, as they only refer to the fact that the games cannot be purchased individually or played for free, or that you do not receive a fixed monthly salary for playing these games.This is a very good collection of 32 Capcom arcade cabinets that hit arcades between 1984 and 2001. That's a lot of content and game history. The collection is a good mix of SHMUP, action platformer, brawler, fighting game and top-down shooter with local multiplayer support.On Capcom's website for the game, the 32 game titles are listed in chronological order as are the arcade cabinets in the Capcom Arcade Stadium. Here becomes visible how from the first arcade cabinets in 1984 to the last in 2001 the screens got bigger, the picture format changed and the graphic quality got better and better.All settings can be made individually for each of the 32 games. In the display settings, you can either set the screen size and frame, or alternatively select an arcade cabinet to display the game.The rendered arcade cabinets look amazing and it looks outstanding to play in the arcade cabinet view. The Candy Cabinet provides the biggest screen size. However, there is only one zoom level for this view and the screen is therefore quite a bit smaller compared to the full screen setting. Three filters are available for emulating CRT monitors: scan lines, curved screen and a slightly blurred screen. The combination of these three filters creates a really good retro feel and they can be used in full screen as well as in arcade cabinet view.Capcom has also thought of gamers with arcade sticks and the key assignment can be configured for two game controllers per player. You can save at any time, change the game speed and rewind in game. For a retro game feel and to be listed in online score lists, such cheating is not advisable. Since these are original arcade versions, the continue system known from arcade cabinets is included in every game and should be sufficient to simplify the game. After all lives have been lost, you have 10 seconds to insert a coin in order to continue playing with the current progress. It would be nice if the maximum amount of continues or coins could be configured.Capcom did everything right with this nostalgic collection of arcade machines.

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom Arcade Stadium has been a.. "controversial" release to say the least, and I feel most of the reasons cited for it are a tad undeserving. The collection uses Mame, a free and open source arcade emulator, the absolute best in class, which is reflected here. (minus one 1942 logo bug that Mame fixed but is still broke here) This is huge, as not only did Capcom PROPERLY FOLLOW THE LICENSE OF THIS ONE (looking at you final burn alpha), but it shows that the efforts of the Mame team are now even recognized by companies, and that free and open source emulation is here to stay, and is welcomed by the systems they emulate (baring you Nintendo) The emulation as I stated, is perfect, all the dip switch settings are available to you, tate mode for those vertical games, and the sound is now perfect too (Mame at the time of the switch version did not have sound cores that could be used commercially, so Capcom made their own, really bad ones, they have since replaced them with the new Mame ones, and they sound fantastic.) Input lag is non existent and it even has default controls for both controllers and arcade sticks!The fronted is powered by re engine, and its alright, its smooth, the games show attract videos, and unlike Mame, navigating the options doesn't make you wanna blow your own head off with an awful outdated ui. My main gripe is you cannot make the machines look as they actually did, no original artwork, no custom models, just generic bland trash.So why the hate? If the emulation is rock solid, supports the community, and is improving with updates, why do 64% of Steam users not recommend the game? I've complied the main points I've seen, and will try to answer them.You can also pirate the collection too if you felt like it, just because Mame exists (which need I remind this collection uses.) doesn't mean official releases are simply just not allowed to exist. Mame is in a grey area legally, while other emulators can throw up the "We tell everyone to only use their dumped games and we wont help pirates!" shield, Mame cant. Mame is the one emulator where you HAVE to pirate the games, usually the whole damn 50gb of it if you want to ensure it works. I am absolutely for the free sharing of roms, in an age of DRM and abandonware, so many games would be lost to time if not for roms, but getting free roms through piracy does not make an official collection have less value.I agree, 50 bones for some roms and an emulator they didn't make is steep as hell, and while Capcom has stated they will sell them individually, (the price of each game was listed as $2.50 on Steam before Capcom hid them) there's zero reason why it should not have been a day 1 option.1. Remote play together2. I'm sorry but, how often are you really going to use it? The online in these collections ALWAYS dies instantly. Check out that Street Fighter collection, or the Samurai Showdown collection, the Beat em Up collection. Or that time players said they wouldn't buy an XBLA port of Golden Axe unless it had online, which on launch, had 2 total players online. All dead onlines that players begged to have in. I get there are people would genuinely use it once or twice, but its just not worth it. If you want online, use Fightcade, Retroarch Netplay, or Steam Remote Play Together. All great options (with fightcade having that rollback netcode everyone loves.)N-no ♥♥♥♥? They advertised 1943 as being free. get your head on right.The primary complaints about this collection really boil down to "price too high" which while a fair point, do not automatically make the collection itself bad, Capcom making the game free really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ this up as any brainlet can download it, get upset its not free, and say it sucks, which is just absolutely unfair.Capcom Arcade Stadium features perfect emulation curtsy of the Mame team, the ui is snappy enough to use, and all the options you will actually use are there. But its price is just too much, so hopefully they can sooner rather than later get these games sold separately. If using Mame scares you, you want to encourage more companies to use free and open source emulation (that's me!), you feel guilty about pirating them for all these years, or you just see the flashy ui. Capcom Arcade Stadium itself, is a great product.

_childDocuments_.review: The undying fashion for retro makes dinosaur publishers compile nostalgic collections of their former hits - and they do it with varying success. SEGA had the SEGA Mega Drive Collection, Konami had anniversary reissues of Contra and Castlevania, and Capcom had already turned to the Megaman collections and Walt Disney's cartoon legacy in the Disney Afternoon Collection. Now they have also presented to the public CAPCOM Arcade Stadium – another set of great (and not so great) classics of the era of VHS cassettes.They won't be ruined by the visual presentation either. All games lend themselves to flexible display settings, including an imitation of an arcade machine booth with a tilted screen. And a large set of special filters will easily turn your modern 4K TV into an old father's "Ruby" - and no one will tell you that you can plant a kinescope.Finally, following all modern trends, Capcom tied high score tables, special tests, user-friendly manuals and achievements to the game. From the generosity of the soul, we even brought a choice of ROM – most of the games are available in two versions, English and Japanese, and some are available only in the original.Capcom Arcade Stadium itself is just a platform, only one game is built into it for free – the legendary Ghosts ‘n Goblins. All the others can either be purchased separately or as part of three thematic packages. Gamers in a rage have already condemned the publisher for greed, although let's be honest with ourselves – most of us and our parents did not have (money and opportunities) then in the 90s to buy a licensed cartridge from the NES or SEGA Mega Drive. Now we can honestly pay Capcom for a happy childhood – except that the sale of invulnerability mode and design frames looks very greedy and stupid.As for the games themselves, then, probably, it is not necessary to say once again how outdated almost all of them are now, both morally and even more physically. It is currently not possible to perceive most of the 30+ games without condescension and irony. And even then, perhaps, not all games from the list can be called examples of art.There is no great reason to talk about each game – even a simple enumeration of them with an extremely brief synopsis would take a good couple of pages. Almost all the games from the set can be divided into four categories: fighting games, action platformers, bitemaps and arcade scroll shooters.The former are represented primarily by as many as several versions of Street Fighter II, including Super Street Fighter II Turbo, released on the first PlayStation and Sega Saturn. Another fun addition is the game Cyberbots: Full Metal Madness, which in fact did not leave Japan. There is no practical value in this clone of the "Street Fighter about Mechs", but it is interesting to look at it.There are also quite a few bitemaps in the set – from the legendary Final Fight to the lesser-known Captain Commando and Battle Circuit. Since over the past years the genre has almost died and only recently showed signs of life, even these ancient hits of the past are now being played quite fun and funny.The absolute winner of the collection by the number of representatives of the genre was a variety of scrolling shooters of all varieties and colors. The 194x series was the luckiest of all – it was added here almost in full, from the most ancient parts that came out in the mid-1980s to those that appeared already in the midst of the 1990s. Most of them are arranged according to the same principle, and therefore if you played one of them, you get the feeling that you saw literally everything. Nevertheless, these are still pleasant, and sometimes very exciting arcade games.The smallest and most interesting in the entire collection would like to call platformers, among which two (or rather three) stand out: Strider is a dystopian hack-n-slash that became a kind of progenitor of the God of War and Devil May Cry series and the stylish, dark and incredibly hardcore Ghosts ‘n Goblins with its sequel. These three games are rightfully still considered iconic and there are many reasons for that.Capcom Arcade Stadium is a convenient and comfortable collection of three dozen classic arcade games of a bygone era. Even if not all games have survived to the present, curious and retromans should definitely pay attention to such an offer.Rating 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom Arcade Stadiumby Capcom (obviously)Genre: Arcade collectionRelease: May 24, 2021-----EDIT: CAPCOM HAVE NOW SET THEIR GAMES HERE AS INDIVIDUAL DLCs. YOU DON'T HAVE TO BUY PACKS ANYMORE!!! This alleviates the major gripe that people have about this collection. It's my hope that people will go and edit their reviews and change back to Recommended if they feel moved to do so.Now begins my review proper!So, what is Capcom Arcade Stadium? It is another in the long line of collections of retro games available on Steam, this one focused on arcade games developed by, well, Capcom, ranging from the early 80s up through – all of the 90s and even some of the 2000s, surprisingly. This is probably the furthest-reaching collection of this type that I've seen, but that's definitely okay.What's in this set? Well, there are the Shmups: the vertically- or horizontally-scrolling shoot them ups usually involving a ship or plane as your character. These would, from my observations anyway, actually be the most numerous in the games in the collection: from Vulgus as the earliest example, five of the 19 XX series of Shmups starting with the classic 1942, up through some games that use the Capcom Play System 2 board, that I have not even tried yet. But I look forward to it!There are simple side scrolling shooters and brawlers (that do not necessarily count as Shmups due to their makeup) that were some of the most prevalent back in the day. These include Trojan (only currently included here as its Japanese equivalent, Tatakai no Banka), Ghosts ‘n Goblins, and many more.There are the more “built” brawlers that have more fleshed-out systems and thus better-known, like the classic Final Fight, Warriors of Fate and others.There are fighting games! These actually have an overlap with another great retro game collection called Street Fighter 30th Anniversary Collection, as three games here are also present in that collection. So you can choose which ones you want to play where, but there are also others.There are the other high-profile games that don’t REALLY fit into the above-mentioned categories but are well-known and loved by classic game enthusiasts (or else should be!), like Bionic Commando, Pirate Ship HigeMaru, Mega Twins, and a few others.I can say that there are a couple of Capcom games that are missing from this collection that I would love to see as DLC – these include Magic Sword, the side-scrolling RPG-like brawler/hack-and-slash; Willow, the side-scrolling magic-slinging game licensed from the epic fantasy movie; SonSon, what seemed to be Capcom’s answer to Psycho Soldier (or the other way around!), an auto-side-scrolling multi-level-jumping shooter.All in all, a great collection – one that I highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: This game saved my life.I am 44.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.Today, I am now am a 45 yo father, probably one of the oldest people playing this game. _childDocuments_.review: Capcom Arcade Stadium is a retro compilation that brings together some of Capcom’s most iconic arcade games from the 1980s and 1990s. Offering a nostalgic journey through classic titles, the collection features favorites like Street Fighter II, Ghouls 'n Ghosts, and 1943: Battle of Midway. With updated features and modern enhancements, this collection aims to cater to both old-school fans and newcomers looking to experience arcade history.The compilation includes 32 games, divided into three separate packs based on their release years: 1984-1988, 1989-1992, and 1992-2001. Each game retains its original arcade mechanics, offering a mix of beat 'em ups, shooters, and fighting games. The classic gameplay has been preserved, capturing the authentic arcade experience with its challenging difficulty and fast-paced action.New features like rewind, save states, and adjustable difficulty settings make these old-school games more accessible, allowing players to overcome their steep learning curves. The rewind feature, in particular, is helpful for mastering difficult sections without the frustration of starting over.Capcom Arcade Stadium uses a virtual arcade cabinet presentation, allowing players to choose different viewing modes, including scanlines and CRT filters that replicate the look of classic arcade screens. The games have been faithfully emulated, with smooth performance and crisp visuals that maintain the original pixel art’s charm. The nostalgic aesthetic is enhanced by the customizable display options, making each title feel like a true arcade experience.The collection also features a dynamic UI, with each game’s cabinet and marquee art adding a touch of authenticity. The visual enhancements breathe new life into these classics while respecting their original design.The lineup offers a good mix of genres, from fighting games like Street Fighter II: Hyper Fighting to side-scrolling action games like Strider and shoot 'em ups like 1941: Counter Attack. While many of the included titles are iconic, the selection also includes some lesser-known gems that will be a pleasant surprise for fans of retro gaming.However, not all games are available in the base collection; players can purchase additional packs or the full bundle to access the complete library. This piecemeal approach may feel restrictive to some, as iconic games like Street Fighter II are only available in specific packs, potentially limiting the experience for those who don’t want to buy the entire set.The addition of modern features such as save states, rewind, and speed adjustments makes the compilation more accessible, especially for players who might struggle with the high difficulty of classic arcade games. These features allow for a more forgiving experience, letting players enjoy the titles without the frustration of losing progress. The online leaderboards also add a competitive edge, letting players compare high scores globally.Many of the included games feature local co-op or versus modes, which retain the fun, competitive spirit of arcade gaming. Local multiplayer works smoothly, capturing the social element of classic arcades. However, the collection lacks online multiplayer, which is a missed opportunity, as it could have added replay value and connected players worldwide.Capcom Arcade Stadium runs smoothly across all platforms, with minimal issues. The emulation quality is excellent, faithfully reproducing the original gameplay. The game’s interface is user-friendly, and the transition between games is quick, allowing for an uninterrupted experience. The visual filters and display options perform well without affecting frame rates, even on the Nintendo Switch.With 32 games to choose from, the collection offers substantial replayability, particularly for fans of retro games. The variety of genres ensures there’s something for everyone, and the addition of new features makes revisiting these classics enjoyable. However, the difficulty of some games may deter casual players, as many titles remain as challenging as they were in their original arcade releases.The leaderboard system adds an incentive for score-chasers, but the lack of online multiplayer limits the social replay value.Capcom Arcade Stadium is a well-crafted compilation that celebrates Capcom’s arcade legacy, delivering a faithful and nostalgic experience with modern enhancements. The selection of games, along with the customizable display options and accessibility features, make it an appealing package for both retro enthusiasts and new players. While the piecemeal content approach and lack of online multiplayer are drawbacks, the overall experience is a fun and engaging tribute to classic arcade gaming.- Faithful emulation of classic Capcom arcade games.- Modern features like rewind, save states, and visual filters.- Wide variety of games and genres, from beat 'em ups to shooters.- Nostalgic presentation with virtual arcade cabinet aesthetics.- Piecemeal game selection may feel restrictive.- No online multiplayer support.- Some games may be too difficult for casual players.Capcom Arcade Stadium is a nostalgic and enjoyable collection that offers a great way to experience Capcom’s arcade classics. Despite a few missed opportunities, the compilation delivers a polished package with plenty of content, making it a must-play for fans of retro gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, this "collection" has a lot of good and a lot of bad, so let's start off with the positives. The games here range from alright to amazing. There are games like Strider and Final Fight that capture the true essence of 80's-to-90's Capcom, and then you also have games like Ghosts and Goblins that throw everything and the kitchen sink at the player in an attempt to suck quarters out of their pocket. If you choose which games you get wisely, you'll have a great time.But that leads to one of the major points of contention: the fact that you need to buy the games with your own money. Before you get the DLC games, Capcom Arcade Stadium is nothing but '1943 -The Battle of Midway-' with some shiny new packaging. Unless you read the"About this game" section, this won't clear in any capacity, so you might feel ripped off when you first boot up the game.And then there are the new features. You have some cool ones like Speedrun mode and Score Attack, but the others have been done already. You have rewind, fast forward, fast rewind, faster fast forward, the ability to change the game speed and difficulty... These are all emulator features. And to rub salt on the wound, a some of the games are censored/have their NA versions missing. If you want these games on modern hardware, just use an emulator and save your money. There isn't enough to make this "bad" per se, but you are paying Capcom to play games that you can find on an emulator. 7/10.TL:DR: Some of these games are good but lack variety. You need to buy every game separately, which defeats the entire purpose of the collection. The games are censored with missing versions, and it is abundantly clear that you are paying for an emulator that costs money. It's not bad, and the games here are fun, but Capcom could've made the advertisements a little more accurate to avoid confusion.

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially put off by the free-to-play tag for what amounts to a lobby that you have to buy collections for.  However, when the three packs were on sale, I picked all three.  Even as a fan of classic games, I think the first is the weakest.  The second arcade is probably the best for varied selection, but the third one has a lot fun games too.The majority of the games seem to be either shoot 'em ups or beat 'em ups.  With a few overhead run-n-guns, side scrolling platformers and Street Fighter II of few kinds.  So, for me to truly recommend these collections, the player must be a fan of shmups or beat 'em ups.  Or there may not be that much of interest.That said, there are a bunch of shmups and beat 'em ups really worth playing.  With fair range of skill levels covers, but these are still arcade games meant to munch quarters.  Though, these games often let the player to keep pumping the virtual arcade machines with pretend quarters (or Yen for the Japanese ones).The collection is very much setup like an arcade.  With cabinets and default to cabinet view of the games during play.  Though fortunately, this can be turned off in the options.  Additionally, the collection features a rewind, fast forward and (I believe) slow-mo.  The player can also customize their arcade by choosing what type cabinet each game is in, but this doesn't really affect the game unless you play the games in the default cabinet view.The biggest complaints I have are more of nitpicks, You have to switch between regions (such as the Japanese only games) to play a couple of the games.  This is simple enough with the toggle of a button, but I don't really care to have to toggle between regions for the few games that are multi-region.  The other is quitting, or leaving if your prefer, the arcade has the player back out of the game to the arcade menu and to the title screen (pressing a different button) and this selection 'Quit" where it asked if you want to quit.  That's a few more steps than I'd like.  Like I said, nitpicks.  Otherwise, I have been quite impressed with the collection, and I hope future additions occur.

I got tired quick cuz I've already played all of this games before. But please buy the game and support Capcom. Don't download pirated emulators over this one. I know that struggle because I am a Game Developer.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good thing I didn't have to pay to get this game, it just refuses to work on my system, it keeps crashing constantly during game startup, tried everything, and I do mean absolutely everything, nothing helps.It runs fine on my brother's gaming laptop though, both running Windows 11, so that isn't the issue, my best guess, the game's got some problem running on newer hardware, I give up, unless by some miracle someone manage to give me something new to try, this thing is scrapped as far as I'm concerned.Do yourself a favor, don't try it if you're running an AMD based system with Ryzen 3000 series and B550 Mobo or newer hardware, you're probably not going to get it working.

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom Arcade Stadium is a really fun way to play all those arcades, especially the challenge mode where you compete against players around the world.I really don't get it, about all the negative reviews. The base (free) game clearly states it includes one game - 1943, which is actually pretty good. The price for the DLCs is more than fair, the emulation is decent, and the challenge mode adds so much fun! I just hope Capcom has more games for DLC Pack 4 to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: After reading the mixed reviews, I decided to give it a try. I bought Ghosts 'n Goblins which is on sale. As starter you get 1943 game for free, the rest you could buy as bundle or buy them separately. As for my case, I already got Capcom Beat em up collection & Street fighter collections, so options to buy individual games is a good solution.This game really makes you feel like stepping into an arcade, you could change to whatever display setting that suits you. The rewind buttons is the most helpful, I'm gonna try 1 cc Ghosts 'n Goblins using rewinds. Another plus is you can save your game anytime for busy people and load them whenever you have time to continue playing. Overall a Yes from me. Please give us AvP, Punisher, Cadillacs and Dinosaurs, etc. on the next updates
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10This compilation/emulator has some of the most influential games from my (wasted?) time in arcades.Ghosts and Ghouls/Goblins and Final Fight have taken a fair chunk of my time and money.  Over the years there have been very good versions - and some exact.  The 8 bit Spectrum versions have the highest sentimental value for me - but this is the first time I have seen an emulator with such solid features as Rewind and saving.  I may be wrong but these features are pretty unique or at best underused.  Some games from this period have quite a steep difficulty level and getting through them using the Rewind is a - perhaps guilty - pleasure.  Like most things, this package has some odd flaws.  It does freeze a fair bit which makes restarts common.  The biggest one is the lack of other games reportedly to be added.  The internet at this point is hinting to a sequel rather than other games being added to the stadium.  If that is the case, what is the point of setting it up in this manner?Hopefully that will become clearer.  It is a great compendium that has extremely playable games which in places put a lot of guff being sold to gamers to shame.  I do find it odd that some of these are officially antiques.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR Arcade Stadium is a middle of the road Capcom version of SEGA Mega Drive and Genesis Classics. OK ports, acceptable controls, passable graphics, less than stellar pricing model.I really like 1942 and Dynasty Wars; so it was awesome to see Capcom release them officially with a ton of other great classic titles like Ghosts and Goblins, Commando, Final Fight, and Strider. I could personally do without yet another Street Fighter II rerelease; in this case 3 of them but it is nice to have available anyways.I think the overly complicated means of buying all the games is unacceptable, but Capcom do as Capcom does. Selling Invincibility as a $0.99 DLC is pretty scummy and having a small selection of music sold as 'mini-albums' is outright the worst thing I've ever seen. Many compilations games of the past would've included a side mode with a sound track listening option and concept art and I must say I don't like the direction many recent classic retro game packs are taking.For effectively being a dump of old games' ROMs with modern controller support and a basic UI Arcade Stadium is a bland, unoffensive title. They have some notable fan favorites as expected, a few lesser known titles making appearances, and another rerelease of Street Fighter II that nobody wanted; especially in this manner. It's a mediocre offering; best bought for only the games you actually want it for. I can't recommend against it due to the games being only $1.99 each; but I will say this isn't the most lovingly crafted game Capcom could have made. Clearly they didn't show too much love towards their older IPs or they wouldn't have shipped Arcade Stadium the way it is.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: Navigating the menu to the game I want to play is annoyingly cumbersome and there doesn't seem to be a way to launch directly into a specific game, game roms aren't directly accessible to play them in another emulator and downloading 1.5gb  to play games where the rom files are around 20mb is peak bloat.I'm still giving a thumbs up just for making Progear legally available for 2€ and because Capcom got their ♥♥♥♥ together and started selling the games individually instead of forcing you to buy bundles of games when you are only interested in a single game, and technically everything just works.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: A collection of fun classic games suitable for all ages and skill levels. Has a variety of customization options for the games and the arcade hub. No online multiplayer, but there is local play, online ranking and challenge modes. Pay for the games you want, or get the game bundles. Solid games that are worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of fun to be had here with these retro games, brings back some good memories. The cabinet graphics take up a little more of the screen than I would like, and the keys need some remapping when you first get in there. But for the games themselves, which is the real highlight, if you are into retro games, you can't beat this as a one-stop retro arcade machine. Packages and deals are good too. Highly recommended :)
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from both a Nintendo Switch background and a lifetime Capcom fan, both with its ups and downs on the long-running company, this collection felt like a love letter to everything I hold dear with the 40+ year-old company. On the Switch, I purchased all the game packs at once for the whole experience and can happily say that I can finally play Strider again on modern legal hardware. This collection has also introduced me to other franchises I would have passed over any other time. Warriors of Fate, Captain Commando, Cyberbots, and Battle Circuit all were incredibly vibrant and fun to play for the first time(s). Online features I could care less about other than leaderboards, which tends to get hacked with 00.00.00 times at the top, oh well. The artwork and selection of overlays available are a nice touch to an already robust package once purchased. I hope Capcom pulls through with their intentions to add more games to the program as I am also among the many that would like to see titles like Darkstalkers and Rival Schools in some way weaved into this.It's a callback to 80s-90s arcade playgrounds everywhere and definitely deserved my money. Great package altogether nonetheless! Easily recommended for any arcade/ Capcom lover
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: Looked at the demo, scrolled through the games and said to myself i own that, that, that, that already, half the games are almost identical. They are selling back to you what you may already own at silly cost.The only decent game on there i would have bought would be mercs as it was known on the megadrive\genesis.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, the lack of Street Fighter II': Champion Edition or Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers is a bit of a blow in my opinion. Not fond of the "alternate costumes trend" that Capcom loved so much back in the day. However, now that you can pay for games individually for relatively low prices, this is actually a pretty solid collection, especially if you're not willing to pay for the SF 30th Collection or the Beat 'Em Up Bundle. Street Fighter II, Final Fight, Captain Commando, Mega Twins, and Battle Circuit are my favorites. The emulation is good, and the invincibility option and additional controls give many of the games much-needed balance and replay value.The challenges can be pretty difficult though..
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Arcade Stadium

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom Arcade Stadium is filled with features. My personal favorite are all of the challenges. Every week certain games will have challenges to keep everything interesting, complete with leader boards. It reminds me a bit of Game Room that was on XBox and GFWL a decade ago, which honestly did this a little better (individual purchases, better decorations, features involving friends, etc.). This does things differently, but it's still a great way to do it.Something to keep in mind, as of 7/19/21, 411 people liked this compilation whereas 741 don't. But those 741 are mostly people who have not paid, reviewing it negatively because individual games were listed as $1.99, marketing the $15 packs as a discount though the bundle was the only option (among others, but that's the big one). It's a valid critique. That said, reviews of the console release have been good and Steam players who wanted it regardless and bought it comprise most of the good reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good little emulator but it only comes with 1943 right now..It's pretty ridiculous that you have to buy the games all in one package but I'm sure capcom will (hopefully) break up the games so you can buy them individually and in smaller packs..The emulator runs well, i noticed a lot of people talking about how great the sega emulator is and it is pretty cool but it the sega emulator's front end ran really slowly for me. _childDocuments_.review: I'm an arcade fanatic and I have to roll my eyes at yet another attempt to bundle and re-release classics is fumbled. Why is this concept so hard to do for game companies? Why? Just, make a fancy menu, have some historical exposition of depth for the games, have a healthy selection of classics and give people the option to pick and choose what they want. Why is that so hard?Out of all of the platforms of gaming to get disrespected the most, I have to say Arcade gets a lot of undeserved neglectful treatment. It isn't like you can just buy arcade cabinets laying around without having to pull a loan to afford one to have the experience again. The age of digital releases should be a thriving time for arcade classics to be re-released, but it just seems like there's no good faithful treatment of respect to them. From companies like DotEmu ruining the emulation of arcade games to now Capcom just making bundle packs, robbing people of choice as to what games they'd like to revisit again.I can't say that the presentation demonstrated here with Capcom doesn't have the love and care poured in to attract you to these games. Aside from maybe a lot of annoying screens and tutorials jumping out at you. But, that pushed away, come on Capcom. You are just one or two fixes away from being on a list of companies that are doing this right. You've done well with your previous arcade bundles. Just give people the option to buy separate games to have here.Otherwise, you're giving people reasons to pirate. Which is the antithesis of giving people a reason to go the route of the legal alternative to buy games like these.

_childDocuments_.review: Jam packed with some of the most legendary titles ever created both english and japanese versions available,has tons of options ranging from scanline effects, screen orientation, custom keybinds, rewinddaily challenges and more, the PC version has some additional options for the front end.This collection is a must have for anybody interested in playing arcade games, and it has PRO GEAR which never saw a release outside of the arcades until now!Very low input lag compared to the Nintendo Switch version which hovers around 5-6 frames of lag with alot of the games,different controllers and arcade sticks are supported, so this would be the goto version.

_childDocuments_.review:
Relive the Capcom classics!1943 -The Battle of Midway-comes as a free download. Shooters, fighting, action—all your favorite genres in this exciting collection! Capcom Arcade Stadium brings back all the nostalgia of the arcade, while adding in new and exciting features you'll wish you had back then. Just Like the Good Old Days
