_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed my time with Schim, a funny looking blob that represents the inner essence of our protagonist that is ripped out of him during a particularly stressful period of his life. It is up to us to get back to him and rejoin as one. As we follow him around, watching his day to day occurrences, like going to work, travelling around the city, and attending social events, we skip from shadow to shadow in pursuit of him. I really enjoyed this interaction with the character. It added a nice  story element to the game which I wasn't expecting, and even though stories without words can often be problematic to understand sometimes, this story made perfect sense and was quite emotional. The different locales he finds himself in make for some really imaginative and original puzzle playgrounds, jumping from shadow to shadow in zoos, playgrounds, factories, on the street, and many other interesting places. The world of Schim is quite entertaining and feels alive with people going about their business, and finding visual treats off the beaten track like a fireman rescuing a cat can feel rewarding and encourages exploration. Everything just looks amazing with an innovative aesthetic that is so cool. Even though it looks basic in a way, there is so much detail everywhere that places just look real. Game play is as simple as jumping from one shadow to the next in pursuit of your other half. Things start off quite simple, and I was worried that the game was going to be too easy, but the difficulty does ramp up when you have to interact with objects to create shadows, and manipulate objects to get things moving so that you can jump on their shadow. There's puzzles like changing traffic lights to get pedestrians moving, so you can hop into their shadow, or hitch a ride on a moving vehicle. There are also unobtrusive objects like parasols and washing lines that can propel you over greater distances. The majority of the game does involve just finding a path to your next destination, but I never got bored jumping from shadows as there are some original mechanics and interesting objects to interactive with. I think there could have been more manipulation of objects to make the puzzles a little more difficult. I did get stuck a couple of times in the game, but that ended up being because I wandered too far away from the path I was meant to take and couldn't get back. There is a restart button but it does take you back to the start of the level, but because levels are broken up into tiny sections, it's not too much of a pain if this happens. There are other Shims in the game, and you will see them as you travel around places. Sometimes, they appear when you find hidden objects, usually in out of way places, and other times finding these objects creates shadows you need to progress. The other Schims really confused me and I wasn't sure what I was meant to do with them. There is an achievement to reunite them all, but reunite them with who and how? There is an interact button but it didn't seem to do anything so I really don't know what that was all about and I feel like I have missed out on a facet of the game because it wasn't explained in the short tutorial at the start. There are also achievements for finishing the game with only one jump allowed, which makes it much harder, and a risky mode where my understanding is that you have only twenty lives to complete the whole game! It is a shame that you cannot play chosen levels after you complete the game for mopping up achievements. As far as I can tell you need to play through the whole game again which I find frustrating and needless.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: Concept is very cool, and is a lot of fun for the first 30ish minutes, but unfortunately after 2,5 hours there is no drive in me left to play any further. The story drags on for too long, and can be very frustrating. Often there is no clear path where you have to go, and then get "stuck". Definetly recommend playing the demo beforehand. All in all a nice little game with a new interesting game mechanic, but after 2 hours too dull to keep going. Oh, and also maybe it would be better splitting the story into smaller bits and releasing them separately for a lower price.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: Many hours, hard to say how many because of the "Risky" achievement 9/10 3 or more Tasselfoot and I wrote  No No, there is level select No No No No No Yes, after completing the story at least once some extra difficulty settings unlocked NoI'm so torn apart by writing this review. The game concept is awesome, making a platformer out of jumping through shadows is such a cool idea! And it was so nice to see the Dutch lifestyle and environment in a video game, which felt so familiar as a Dutchy. However, the game is long with 65 levels... too long in my opinion. What doesn't help with this feeling is that you lose your human very early on and you'll trying to catch up with him the rest of the game, which gets a bit depressing, as his mood is quite depressing. Around level 30 I was so ready to get reunited with my human, but I had to wait another 35 levels before that happened. Normally more content is a good thing, but there is a limit before something grows stale. don't get me wrong, none of the content felt like filler content to me, it tells a story, and later on, going back to familiar settings was nice. However, I think it should have been quite a few levels shorter, especially with the challenging modes that unlock after completion. I felt no desire to go through all the levels again after taking my time to find every collectible. So what did I like about SCHiM, the concept is so strong, and in the beginning, the game is so happy and funny. (This makes me wonder how much influence the mood of the human had on my feelings toward the game.) It is so clear to me that there went so much love into this game with how many details there are and how you can interact with so many items. Some just make a noise and have a visual effect, others even let you play around with them. Also, all the little details as the color scheme and the size of the shadows during which time of day the level was and how that changed were so nice to see and notice. SCHiM has a wide range of achievements. A lot of them are for doing different things in levels, for example using the hoose on everybody in a garden in one of the earlier levels. There are also achievements for interacting with every type of object, interacting 50 times with animals, visiting 1k shadows, traveling 500 meters with vehicles, and using a car honk 250 times. Gladly most of those don't have to be different items, you could just jump into the shadow of a car and honk it 250 times in a row to unlock that achievement. What was very nice to see is that most of those achievements have a progress bar on Steam so you can see how many times you did that already and how many times is left. SCHiM also has a bunch of quite challenging to even very difficult achievements. As stated above, after finishing the game you unlock some new game modes. One of them is the one jump mode, and there is an achievement to complete all the levels with this mode on. There is also a mode where you don't have checkpoints, so you have to complete the level in one go. The hardest one is "risky mode' which gives you a maximum of 20 respawns to get through 65 levels. Getting all the achievements in this game will test your patience and skill level. I give SCHiM 3 out of 5 stars.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: I want to recommend Schim because it's a cool and interesting game that others might enjoy. However, the game is not for me. I wanted to like the game as I had followed its development for a long time, but the game drags on for too long doing the same thing (more or less) and it can be quite frustrating at times. The first hour or so is great, but it then gets increasingly frustrating and at times unclear what you're supposed to do to progress - sometimes I got stuck and had to reset the level. Couple that with sometimes harsh checkpoints or tedious moments of waiting, it can quickly become too frustrating if you're not the most patient person. One day I might revisit the game just to finish the story elements, but most likely not.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: SCHiM gives me mixed feelings, but not enough to give it a thumbs down or a straight up Do Not Recommend.65 levels jammed into this game, but at least a quarter of them were 2 seconds long and should have either been combined with another level or omitted entirely. It felt like padding to extend the length of the video game rather than the intended sense of continuity. The levels felt too similar and repetitive after the first 30, but the ones that stood out were fun, even if they were a little janky (the lightning was as cool as it was irksome, to say the least.)There are unskippable cutscenes that make replaying this game a slog, and cutscenes woven into gameplay every 10 seconds that will reset your camera angle and disorientate you. The objective button is a good idea, but it stops being a good idea when it tries to give you hints that mislead you instead of just showing you the endpoint or its general direction. Incredibly misleading and overall frustrating to use. This could be fixed by simply allowing players to control the camera to view the entire stage instead of limiting their FOV.I also didn't realise there was a collectables counter for each level until I was 20 levels in. Just add the collectable counter to the bottom of the UI, I promise it won't ruin the vibe!Am I saying you shouldn't play it? No. But what I am saying is that it has some problems that, until addressed, will dampen the experience of an otherwise decent little game. It's cute and has a great concept, but needs some real quality of life improvements to be a good game.Also, this game's title sounds like a transphobic slur and I wish they'd named it something else.

_childDocuments_.review: For what I have noticed the game has no replay value; spending 25 euros on just  good art and good music is maybe a bit muchI did enjoy the four hour game play I had on it; but wished it had more to offer You just get the illusion on choice; I would have liked multiple paths so you can see more of the art. would also increase replay valueWould love to get the OST

_childDocuments_.review: This game's selling point to me was the idea of playing as a character that has to jump from shadow to shadow. It reminds me of something I would try to do as a kid or something, trying to go from one place to another by only standing on shadows. I think the game pulls this idea off very well, but I have some criticisms as well. The gameplay is very responsive and feels good to play. The layout of the objects in game feels natural but also convenient enough to provide you the means of getting from one place to another, which I'm sure was a difficult balance to strike. One of my biggest issues with this game though is the lack of variety of the environments. The street of a town or general park/public area is by far the most common setting in this game and eventually you start to really notice how many times you've been to certain areas. That being said, there are areas I won't spoil that are incredibly creative and impressive that I wish we got more areas like them or at least got to them a little faster. I'm surprised I beat the game in 3 hours, because it felt longer than that. There is a story, and I liked it! They attached a nice little message to the game and I liked that. Also the player character is adorable. I'd recommend this game, just with the little note that if you start to feel the pace dragging, the last few areas are worth getting to.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: The idea for this game is neat but the gameplay is rather shallow. The first 80% of the game is essentially the same. The last bit becomes more complex, but not in a way that I find satisfying but rather in a way I find frustrating because it's introducing gameplay elements that seem like they weren't introduced prior to the very end and are never explained well. There are a number of 10 second levels because the game wants to tell a story, but the story is an inch deep. The visuals are really top notch here, but that's about all I'd recommend the game for.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: I haven’t finished the game yet, but probably a bit of the way through.Lovely game. Fun traversal of an environment.Would highly recommend as a sort of therapy. You can tell the devs put a lot of love into this game and I really appreciate it. It feels warm to the touch, with a sprinkling of melancholy.If you can’t tell, my favourite games do not include sprawling open worlds, or things that explode. I’m more into stuff like Manifold Garden (although that is more challenging), and Rez, or Untitled Goose Game.All of them scratch a weird itch where something is quirky, inventive, and offer a new and great experience.Highly recommend, but look away if you are expecting serious games with fireworks.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: I have SCHiM on my shortlist of the most beautiful art style games that I love, alongside Islands: Non-Places, Windowsill, Donut County, Mosaik, and Untitled Goose Game.There’s a lot of love and attention to detail in its visual narrative approach. The music adds value, being well-composed and produced, orchestrating an overall sweet, emotional feeling that gives off very good vibes.To me, SCHiM feels like an interactive, playful, and beautiful environment that keeps drawing me back. I find it to be a truly touching experience.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: I admit, despite me saying this is recommended to play, that's only going to be a subset of players out there from day one. It's one of those games where despite some moments of intrigue and a concept of shadow jumping that is interesting on the surface, it doesn't hit the heights that I really think it could given enough time and resources. Don't get me wrong: the game when it's firing on all cylinders and using things like night flickering lights and playing around with moving people, it can be a bunch of fun. The visuals are sleek and the animation work is great, and there's some very charming moments in the game. There was obviously a lot of effort put into it, and there's a baseline it hits that's satisifying from a platforming perspective.It's just that, I couldn't help shake the feeling that it was meant to be a lot more. It doesn't explore some out there ideas with the shadow based platforming that would have taken it to the next level: things like a rave or even sudden rain clouds and storms that could have been interesting. The story that it tells is a little confusing, almost forgetting about the character of the shadow you are playing as, and again, feels like it misses the mark because there's some gaps that don't make sense. The pacing is probably the worst part of it: you could go from a level that is tremendously long and frustrating, and then follow it up with something that's 20 seconds. The last half of the game has parts that feels like filler at times, and in a game that does the same thing a lot that can be killer.The elephant in the room is the price. Look, I'm going to say from the get go that for me, games are usually under priced. I know that's controversal, but for the amount you get out of them a lot of the time and the cost to make them, I feel that yes, in most cases it is. But it's hard to sit here and look at Schim at that launch price, and not recommend games in the alternate platforming genre before it. It's just a hard sell at that point, and for some it's going to be a game you put on your wishlist and wait until it's at a deep sale. Did I have fun? Yes. Do I think the game has problems? Yes. Is it worth playing? Eventually, for the price you're comfortable in buying it at.:

_childDocuments_.review: I received a free review key, and completed the game 5 times during playing (for challenge mode achievements).SCHiM is a worthy experience on your first, casual playthrough.  The scenes are lovely, the sad story-telling is incredibly well done with no text or voiceover, and the exploration is a ton of fun.  About 4 hours for a casual completion.

_childDocuments_.review: SCHiM attracted my attention at first glance two years ago. The art, the style, the idea—all of it immediately convinced me. Happy in playing it now : )Even from the intro of SCHiM, it's clear that this game is much more than just a platformer. Its unique mechanics, astonishing visuals, and poetic backbone, combined with a narrative approach, create a truly unique interactive experience.Starting with the playful idea of a cute frog-like creature that jumps from shadow to shadow, the game expertly handles the themes of continuity and bonding in the context of the pursuit of human relationships.Carefree, happy moments alternate with significant events of adulthood. Daily little details and unexpected happenings trigger a variety of emotions and evoke memories of beloved artworks from our personal memory archives.The elegant and modest visual style references a charming old comic style, adding a romantic signature topped with a fresh, unique polished layer. The music adds extra value to the overall experience. Featuring a unique flavour of old-style clear motifs, well-structured, and perfectly aligned with the changing moods of the narrative.

You really feel a sense of kinship with your schim, and you want to see him returned to his master. a lovely, sweet game about picking yourself up while you're down and never giving up!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing art style, a playful idea with the shadows, great audio, good direction, fantastic experience! _childDocuments_.review: If you like a cute and quirky platformer, with a stunning style: SCHiM is the game for you. _childDocuments_.review: What can someone say about this game?Well first and foremost, it is a cute little 3d, 2.5d plattformer game, with a cool story.But there is a lot that kinda gets annoying after a while and really kills a lot of fun.In many levels you need to wait for the shadows until they arrive, that kills the flow. _childDocuments_.review: SCHiM is overall a positive experience, before everything else it's a successful execution of one of those video game concepts that many people have probably thought about but never materialised until now, somehow. Swimming through shadows and hopping between them as if they were pools or puddles- it's kind of a perfect video game concept.Aside from that, my feelings go back and forth however. The aesthetic is great, both the music and visuals are satisfying but some of the colour palette choices strain the eyes after a while, especially on longer levels. There is a feature for modifying the colour palette for stages that aren't comfortable to look at, but I feel as though that feature should be streamlined or there could be a better solution. I found myself remembering the feature after clearing a level and reflecting on it, but maybe that's my issue for not thinking about it proactively (I would argue that I shouldn't have to think about it.)Level design for this game struggles in larger levels and in terms of variety. This is ultimately a narrative game with no dialogue, not a puzzle platformer as I initially hoped it would be. A lot of the larger levels struggle with the game's camera not showing as much as you'd like or navigating over certain finicky obstacles; pedestrian or vehicular traffic can be especially frustrating to navigate reliably as it seems to be generated randomly and you often find yourself impatiently waiting for the next "good" shadow to pass by, the game has a lot of frustrating waiting around. Checkpointing and certain optional sections can be frustrating to navigate if they are just on the edge of your jump range and some difficult jumps send you back several shadows instead of more logical checkpoints.The shorter levels are more fun to rapidly leap through and get into a flow, but especially later on in the game it repeats several of them- primarily for the sake of a callback, but admittedly they do get a bit repetitive. Additionally for the sake of the narrative, shorter levels keep the pace going reliably but the larger stages at times cause you to forget where you're going and why you're there; the last large level was particularly fun because it had a lot of unique things to interact with, it's a shame it shows up so late in the game. I can't say the same for a certain factory/shipping stage or highways that really derailed things early on.You can interact with any obstacle but the feature is 95% fluff and few interactions are actually productive- on one hand this fits the game's whimsical presentation, something akin to a less chaotic Untitled Goose Game, but the problem is that over the game's length you eventually kind of give up on interacting with things and when the game throws an obstacle at you that can only be surpassed by interacting with a never-before-seen object...Admittedly I had completely stopped bothering with the interactions because they no longer felt rewarding and that caused me to get stuck for a moment. I feel like more interesting and varied level design that focused more on problem-solving and fun interactions rather than simply challenging the player to get from point A to point B would be a more engaging and satisfying loop- the existing pace of the game gets exhausting. The game ends on a particularly strong note in this respect, with many small levels requiring intuitive interactions strung back to back as you're on your victory lap.There are also several minor bugs with detecting when you land in shadows, or when moving shadows overlap static ones, but most of these are minor. I encountered one significant issue where pedestrians stopped moving in a stage and I had to restart it, and one somewhere in the middle where the destination preview started going backwards so I had to wing it through the rest of a large level.It's about 4 hours in length for a casual playthrough with consistent attempts at searching for collectibles, probably 5-6 hours if you want to hunt them all down and there are still additional challenge options to turn off your extra jumps out of shadows, checkpoints and even a limited number of lives across the entire game.I still want to recommend the game for the experience, but I think it's important to temper expectations. This game relies a lot on its core concept remaining endearing for the entire length, and I think there's a scale balanced between one's appreciation for the aesthetic and general coziness of the game versus the steadily-mounting frustration from the level design as it progresses. It starts and ends in satisfying ways, and there are certainly solid levels in-between, but if I had to give the devs a recommendation I would like to see more puzzles in gameplay (similar to the final levels) and less large, empty stages that end up testing the player's patience and gradually wearing away the game's plentiful charm.
_childDocuments_.name: SCHiM

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend this as it is a very cute game, but despite the fact that it took me about 4 hours to beat it, it still managed to overstay its welcome.Its main mechanic- jumping from shadow to shadow- is novel, but unfortunately the game does not iterate enough on this basic mechanic. In its span of more than 60 levels, there are quite some levels that I can only describe as filler: short levels that only contain basic hopping from shadow to shadow. Other levels contained some manner of environmental manipulation, such as using an umbrella to launch yourself across a large distance or raising the forks on a forklift to extend its shadow and allowing you to reach new places. Some of these mechanics stayed common, others were rarely sprinkled throughout the game. Unfortunately, despite these novelties here and there, the game never quite dared to toy around with these other mechanics. There's potential here that the game didn't fill. In that regard it's a bit ironic that the game starts off with you being "chained" to your person, only to then spend the rest of the game unchained from him. I feel like that was exactly a mechanic that could've been explored further.Some objects also shared mechanics- umbrellas and signs being noteworthy ones- so what appears to be a new object to toy around with may actually just be a mechanic you already knew in disguise. This quickly erodes the novelty of such mechanics as well. The same counts for the level design: a lot of levels are simply streets, so prepare to see the same set of objects a lot. The level design does feel a bit like it is all over the place though: you get the feeling that they ramp up the difficulty as you progress, but many "endgame" levels were as easy as the first levels.One aspect that kind of annoyed me throughout was that the game breaks the "flow" quite often- especially for story reasons. One way that this happens is that you sometimes have to wait for a vehicle or pedestrian to appear so that they can carry you across some distance. This can take some time, so it can happen that you're chaining together a bunch of leaps and jumps, only to come at a dead stop because you have to wait to hitch a ride on a vehicle's shadow. In one level, I actually managed to get "stuck" this way once, not knowing how to progress: after jumping back and forth a few times, suddenly a pedestrian appeared and walked right to the place I needed them to be to progress through the level.The game sometimes also directly takes away your control for narrative reasons: you're the "schim" of a person, living in his shadow, and throughout the entire game you try to get back to him. Your person is going through a rough time in his life, so occasionally the camera forces you to a stop and pans to him to show what he's going through. Again, if you're going through a satisfying series of leaps and jumps this can get quite annoying.I liked the art direction: despite the game's limited camera angle and colour palette, I could easily tell that I was in some Dutch town (minor point: if only there were not so many American muscle cars and pickup trucks). Some colour palettes were a bit harsh on the eyes, but you can change the colours yourself! From an accessibility standpoint, this is a really nice feature.TL;DR: Cute little game with a nifty art direction, but unfortunately I cannot recommend this because it doesn't really iterate enough on its main mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: A Masterpiece in Minimalism!SCHiM is an innovative and creative indie game. In this game you control a charming little creature, a Schim, that jumps from shadow to shadow. With its minimalistic style, touching story, and unique gameplay mechanics,  SCHiM knows how to captivate you.Art StyleThe visual appeal of this game lies in its minimalistic design and in the intriguing palette. Every scene feels like a piece of art, with clean lines, thoughtful compositions, and broad strokes of colors. The absence of unnecessary details allows the core to shine and allows to focus on the shadow-to-shadow jumping mechanic without annoying distractions.As a bonus, it shows a rare and faithful representation of Dutch scenery and culture. The game beautifully captures the essence of the Netherlands, from its iconic canals, to the charming architecture, to the bikes scattered everywhere. Funny and sad moments, like seeing bikes stolen, add humor (and realism!) to the game.A Touching StoryI was not expecting a moving story! But it fits perfectly. As you guide your Schim through its journey, you uncover a narrative filled with emotion, trying to reconnect to your human. THe narration happens through scenes and transitions, with no lengthy dialogues. A great example of how sometimes, less is more!Did I Mention the Unique Gameplay Mechanics?Moving in the shadows and controlling characters by being in their shadow is as innovative as it is engaging! (pro tip: you probably want to use a controller rather than a keyboard, because of the isometric navigation) The main mechanic is visually striking and cleverly designed, turning the game into a thoughtful puzzle game. The levels and puzzles are forgiving, so they are perfect if you are looking for a more laid back game where you can enjoy the story progression, the scenery, and the playful exploration.And don't forget to interact with everything you come across and to have fun! The world is filled with little interactions and surprises! :)

It never gets truly difficult, making it a very enjoyable experience for younger players as well. In short, a shadow play that deserves to be experienced.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by saying that the art style and the actual gameplay is quite enjoyable in small doses.  There are some pros. There are some cons. _childDocuments_.review: SCHiM is a very unique 3d platformer where you jump from shadow to shadow as a tadpole-like creature: a schim (shadow/ghost). Will you be able to create new opportunities for them and let them follow their dreams? The mechanics are super fun to play around with and are something I have never seen before in a platformer game. They are also easy to grasp and make sense. Everything works very smoothly and the level designs are great. There are a bunch of collectibles to find on almost every level, which makes the game even more interesting. The art is very beautiful and I love the different colour palettes so much. The storyline is told very well through the animations. I love the environments, they’re very Dutch and make me feel right at home, since I am Dutch as well. I highly recommend you try SCHiM and I hope you’ll enjoy yourself as much as I did. _childDocuments_.review: SCHiM is essentially a puzzle game where out character is basically a shadow.The levels are super meat boy-ish style except we do play in a isometric view, there is checkpoints and our objective is to jump from shadow to shadow until we reach another point of the map.Where the princ "couch couch", the shadow owner will always be in another cas..." couch" level.The levels are mostly easy and some of them just exist for story porpouse and don't pose too much of a challenge.There is optional stuff to collect inside the levels that increase a little bit the difficulty but it's mostly easy.The levels are quite dynamic since many times we need to jump from shadow to shadow through moving persons, cars, flickering lights or even storm shadows, so it's not just pre-defined shadows.It should take around 3 to 5 hours to finish the game and collect all the optional stuff.After the game is finished we do unlock additional challenges like, disabled checkpoint system inside the levels, Disable the double jump system and also a risky mode which you only have 20 respawns for the entire game (this one is crazy).The game have an insanely great art style and can run in any potato pc, make sure to try the demo though.There is a bit of story related to difficulties, expectations and overcoming difficulties and the way we look into the life.I will gladly recommend the game, for what it is, but it will depend on how much expensive or cheap it will be.

_childDocuments_.review: SCHiM is a puzzle platformer with snappy controls and a stellar presentation that's a must-play for fans of the genre.In SCHiM, you play as a living creature who can best be described as a shadowy frog. Living in someone's shadow (literally), this creature represents the soul and spirit of the creature that it inhabits. At the start of the game, you're unfortunately separated from your young owner. Through the game's sixty-five levels, it's your job to make your way back to them. It's almost like Homeward Bound but in this case, you play a shadowy little frog. Without going into detail about the game's story, the narrative happens without dialogue but tells a story that's worth paying attention to while you're playing.In practice, you'll start each level of your journey on one side of a level and be asked to jump between the shadows in the level thrown by various objects within it to make your way to your objective. The end of the level usually gets you a step closer to a reunion with your human. Shadows are cast by a multitude of everyday objects; everything from a park bench or a garbage can to living creatures like birds and other humans.Most of the levels were perfectly sized and didn't overstay their welcome. However, there were 1-2 levels in the game that were very large and I wish that they could have been split into smaller chunks.Genre-wise, SCHiM is a puzzle platformer that's light on the puzzle and heavy on the platformer.Each of the levels is a small community inspired by rural European towns. The game's levels start relatively simply; small levels with a pretty straight-forward path. However, as you go, layers of complexity are added. You might be asked to affect traffic lights, for instance, to affect the flow of traffic in a busy intersection or jump into a car's moving shadow to cross a wide street. You will also quickly be asked to interact with objects in the world. These interactions can sometimes be for laughs. You'll shoot garbage out of a trash bin, you'll make a cat meow or jiggle a lamp post. Some of these interactions can meaningfully affect your traversal. You may be required to catapult yourself across the level using a beach umbrella, jump onto a trampolining clothesline or even jump into a fountain to make your way across a shadowless part of a level.One of my favourite parts of this game is how breezy the game is to play. The controls on this one are perfect. They're incredibly tight and any mistake on your path is a player error. Your shadow creature can't survive outside of the shadows for long. Your SCHiM can spend a few seconds outside a shadow and in that time, they can make a single additional jump. This additional jump adds a fun layer of strategy to the gameplay. Many times through the course of the game's Dutch-inspired locales, I would ask myself: can I make that jump? And the answer was usually: "let's try it," because the consequence for jumping poorly is that you reset yourself a few seconds back with no load times. I will say that the game's checkpointing system wasn't perfect; I found myself being put backwards a little further than I should have on occasion, but this was nothing but a minor annoyance.Apart from making your way from start to finish, most levels have one or more collectables within them that are usually tucked away in a corner or off the beaten path.My other favourite thing about SCHiM is the game's presentation. The art is charming and the keyboard-heavy soundtrack just made me happy as I bopped between the different shadowy sections of a level. Diving deeper into the visuals, you can tell that there was a lot of care put into this one. Each cel-shaded level had a deliberate choice of colour palette that matched the action. If you were by the beach, you could come to expect a light brown hue representing sun and fun. If you were looking for alley cats in the evening, the colours were much darker. And the style also bled into the interstitials between levels.Most objects would cast shadows, but as objects and light sources moved around, their shadows dynamically changed shape. For a game with a scope like SCHiM, it was impressive to see it in action. Occasionally on Steam Deck, some of the shadows looked a little jagged. This didn't detract from the visuals, however. It's worth noting that at the time of publication, this game was not approved on Steam Deck. Did I mention the buttery-smooth movement?The music and audio design for this one helped me fall into a meditative state while playing. Hats off to the team at Moonsailor, whose previous works can be found in games like Dungeons of Aether, VALORANT and Mullet Mad Jack. They have created a soundtrack that always seems to match the on-screen action and provides some satisfying sound effects as you bop around the map with your little SCHiM. If you press the action button while sitting in a human's shadow, they would usually sneeze. Little details like this set the game apart.My only real complaint with the game is that it can become a little one-note over time. I noticed as I entered the back third of the game, I had sort of already seen everything that the game had to offer. I wish that the game would have been about 10 levels shorter as I found over time some of the locales were repeats without much in terms of variety between repeated sections. You visit a grocery store twice, you'll visit parks that feel similar and at the end of the narrative you'll stick around one particular neighbourhood for a while. This last one makes sense in the narrative but doesn't lead to the most engaging gameplay.SCHiM is a game best played a few levels at a time over a week or more. If you're looking for a great puzzle platformer to zone out to for thirty minutes before you go to bed every night, SCHiM is 100% that game. Between its tight jumping gameplay and stellar presentation over the game's 5-6 hour runtime - SCHiM is worth playing.

name: Goblin Stone
detailed_description: Goblin Stone entrusts players with the fate of the last goblins to escape annihilation by cruel adventurers. To avoid extinction, they must build their numbers, venture back into the world, and put an end to the adventurers who hunt them. Embark on a heartwarming journey to rebuild a goblin lair and help them thrive in a turn-based roguelite where every decision counts. Craft the perfect goblin party by mixing classes, abilities, and genetics. Experience an innovative turn-based combat system, where the order of actions is determined by the strategic positioning of combatants. Guide a merry party of goblins as they battle relentless adventurers, pompous elves, and surly dwarves. Dive into a world with nostalgic, storybook-inspired visuals, accompanied by an epic soundtrack composed by Hearthstone's Peter McConnell. Manage a thriving goblin colony and build your lair chamber by chamber, from the Barracks to the War Room. Carefully breed your favorite goblins, combining the finest genes and traits to cultivate a formidable lineage. Venture through procedurally generated adventures, where permadeath heightens the stakes. Difficult choices await as you decide which path to take and which goblins to sacrifice for survival. Receive exclusive news, updates, and perks by joining our active community on the Goblin Stone Discord.

short_description: Goblins have been hunted to extinction by cruel adventurers. Embark on a heartwarming adventure to rebuild their lair and help them thrive in this award-winning turn-based RPG where every decision counts.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly can't recommend as a big fan of the turn-based roguelike genre. Bugs and performance issues aside, which will be hotfixed eventually. Gameplay loop & combat is similar to darkest dungeon alternating between adventure -> basebuilding/recruiting -> adventure etc... forming it into one bigger campaign with an actual story rather than being a fast paced in and out kind of game, if thats what you are looking for.While combat itself can be very unforgiving, you don't feel any pain in loosing a companion, as the game is designed for you to constantly replace your goblins, and with deaths shortly buffing the remaining members it will be very common to loose a few goblins in a run, while making it almost impossible to not finish the job with the remaining few. When out adventuring the only ressources you take back home are for basebuilding, upgrades from loot and through random event markers, !which usually are THE gamechangers in roguelike!, will only affect the current adventure and will not carry over (*a single exception). Thus permanent upgrades solely stem from the basebuilding, discouraging you to ever choose the event options on the crossroads and always opt for the ressource markers.The combat mechanics are kept simple but fine. You can exchange between a small selection of skills for each class before venturing out, but each goblin of the same class will share those skills, which gives less room for costumizing your playstyle (can't run both a dps and supporter shaman at once f.e.) The variety of enemies and equippable weapons is rather small. A new area only introduces upgraded versions of the same weapon types, with up to 2 straightforward enchantments. Do not expect any common-legendary type of loot. While the bossfights have a unique design so far, common enemies in a new area only seem to be stronger reskins and even the "tough battle"map markers are just adding quantity instead of introducing elite monsters.The upgrades for each facility seem to provide a reasonable boost. If you want to upgrade everything you need to repeat farm old stages, which do display fixed clear rewards giving farming good consistency. Sadly the monotone mobs and dissmissable map events make farming no fun. Now to the 2 biggest problems in the base; Camp/Merchant + Breeding Grounds; which both result from the same fundamental problem: :A new class in camp will only appear after you beat a story boss, all other recruitable goblins will have a statcap and genepool based on story progression. The merchant completely replaces the weapon stock after certain story points. You cannot discover new Gene Mutations through breeding, breeding can not randomly overstep the parent's statcap. The genepool expands through freeing captive goblin on adventures, yes. But mutations that these captives can have are based on your story progression too. Hitting the story-statcap of 6/6/6, 7/7/7, 8/8/8 + 2 optimal mutations is always the best you can get. If 2 perfect parents breed a new child, but you did not continue the story, the child will most likely be weaker or equal to the parents at best, destroying the whole gimmick which could make the game unique. You don't get a choice to play the game at your pace. You are either too weak and need to grind or you are exactly reaching the current limit set by the game.Even though the devs choose "mass instead of class" befitting the goblin's nature, it makes grinding painfully bleak knowing there is no room for improvement for individual goblins. You cannot get attached to any of your current goblins as they will be outscaled no matter how many battles they survive, neither can you look forward to your new creations as they can not exceed your expectations through stat breakthroughs or new gene discoveries. The map generation and loot pool is very poor and can't surprise you nor give you a significant change in your permanent powerlevel. In the bigger picture there is no actual RNG involved, you won't ever get the feeling of "damn i'm having a lucky run right now" or the thrill of finding a 1/100 item or perk. While this kind of consistency can be appreciated for certain types of players; for me personally from both an RPG and roguelike viewpoint, it completely misses the mark. If i could decide on the tags, it would be "Turn-Based Combat, Story-Driven, Adventure" if anything.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot in all good faith recommend this game to anyone.  Don't get me wrong, its a fun game, has a charming art style and interesting mechanics.  Sadly though, its not done.  There are tons of bugs, ranging from visually annoying, to mechanics not working right, to just flat out game crashing.  This was rushed out the door before it was done, which is truly a shame as if there weren't so many of them, this would easily be a top tier game.  Give it a few months, let them iron out the kinks, then maybe give it another look.Update as of 4/12Ok, its been a bit after first major patch and it does seem they polished out some of the bugs, my game is still locked on a late chapter bug that prevents progress.  Seeing as I am 60 hours into a game and have NO desire to do the whole thing over, i'm gonna wait till they fix that before updating again.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really fun to play.  Very Darkest Dungeon like, which is a good thing.  The bad things are the bugs.  This is not a 1.0 release game despite being given the 1.0 since it is nearly unplayable.  Your game will on occasion soft lock (typically when goblin breeding.).  No big deal though since the game touts how it is constantly saving so your choices are permanent (which is great in theory) ....right???  That's a yes and a big no my dude.  Load back your a game from either a normal exit or a crash and good luck on telling when the save is from.  Could be from when you last clicked exit or it could be from the start of the day after spending said day playing this game (it is fun when it works).  You'll lose hours of game play just from exiting the game that "saves"  all the time and loading it back.  If and when these issues get fixed, get the game since it is really good.  Until then, stay away from this cluster f....  far far away from this game....

_childDocuments_.review: There is no true progression aside from chapters, random shop weapons and shrine bonuses that can lead to losing a goblin at any %. Every chapter has a cap for goblin stats to max out. There are weapons you can randomly buy that can give an edge. You can filter breed to get traits to minmax. That's it, just a single loop that gets harder every chapter you get to. And then there are the bugs and game ending corrupt save file incident. I'm not going into my app data and deleting an auto save to roll back only to lose hours of play. This isn't early access, played up to 26 hours only to get the breeding grounds glitch that resulted in my save being bad.  You're supposed to kill, retire goblins off to advance so no naming or getting attached. That doesn't matter when you max stats with same traits only to retire to do it all over again on next chapter with higher numbers. There just numbers to an ends. The only real edge I felt was with the shop weapons that added to a goblin's abilities. Shrines that give permanent bumps to stats can corrupt and ruin a goblin at any %. Feels like there's a memory leak and game chugs along unless you reset.  Repetition even the narrator repeats the same lines over and over again. Every run you are given bonuses to cards, stats and random weapon drops all of which go away at the end of a run. Only thing that stays are the corrupted shrine bonuses (if you don't lose a goblin to %) and any loots found or bought from merchant.   Great concept, Darkest Dungeon goblin edition but minus everything that makes Darkest Dungeon great. Side by side Darkest Dungeon is the super deep swimming pool with an Olympic diving board and this game is the two inch kiddie wading pool with a hole in it and almost empty of water.
_childDocuments_.name: Goblin Stone

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:1. Awesome Voice acting.2. Great Story line, including a unique "start" of the campaign.3. One of the best ways I have seen a game deal with "death" of characters.4. It's very challenging.The Bad:1. There is a memory leak in the game, only thing I can think of, as this game will max out my 2090 TI - even though this game isn't some graphically intensive game. This happens mostly in the menus, even if I turn the graphics down to low and limit the FPS.2. Practically no "loot" in the game. When you go out on the "small adventure" or "location" almost everything you find there is temporary. So if you find a weapon? Temporary, it's gone after the short adventure. Buffs don't follow after the adventure, you can upgrade your attack cards via a "battle guru, orc, well that is just for the small adventure as well. I think it's a terrible way to have a game played, as I have no real "reason" to want to go through these adventure locations, other than to move the story forward. I have been playing for a while and i still only have the weapons the game starts you out with.3. The only thing that is permanent in the adventure locations are death and near death. If your goblin hits a really low HP, they get "mortally wounded" which is a death sentence. IF they survive, they get 50% max health forever, so it makes them kind of useless. At this point it's either let them die, dismiss them, or retire them, they are no long a "viable" team member.4. There isn't any kind of experience or levels/any kind of progression of the goblins as well.5. This just makes it feel like I am doing the same thing on repeat, even after the third location. It just makes it feel very disconnected in my opinion, I would rather get through the map as quickly as possible, knowing that unless i find a treasure chest that has materials in it, it's all just worthless after the run is done.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely write reviews, but this game has been such a letdown I just have to. It could be so great. The artwork is awesome, the premise and storytelling are enjoyable, but... it's just such a slog. Gold becomes pointless, there aren't enough persistent upgrades to make farming enjoyable in any way, your lair and the upgrades are nice, but it's so hard to farm for the upgrades (and again, farming is just a chore) and they made breeding for genes and stats boring somehow. I really really wanted to like this game. I got to the last area by pure persistence and I'm just so bored playing this game that I probably won't finish it, despite how much that will irk me.If they tweak this game and add in more reasons to want to farm, add more persistent upgrades and change the ridiculous mechanic where you are locked out of upgrades and genes, this could be one of my favorites. Until then, it's just a big slog and a bummer.

_childDocuments_.review: (Maybe I've been unreasonably fortunate, but I purchased on release day and haven't encountered any of the game-breaking bugs and crashes people seem upset by in the reviews. I'm only about 20hrs in, and there are a few minor things which need tweaked (e.g. a few menus that are annoying to navigate out of) but I really haven't run into any major issues at all.)I think the comparison to Darkest Dungeon is probably roughly fair - though the pacing appears designed so that a) a single run is designed to take a long time and you're not going to be racing through multiple iterative play-throughs  of the game and b) your individual goblins are designed to be expendable and retired as you breed slightly better ones. I'd definitely primarily genre the game as something "turn-based tactics with base-building elements" more than thinking of it as a roguelite where you're expecting to fail a bunch of runs.The art-style and theme are excellent and personally, I am really enjoying getting revenge on all those pesky halflings and humans for their crimes against Gobbo-kind.  Also having a ton of fun with the breeding mechanics and seeing what kinds of fancy goblins I can create. I can't yet comment on the real longevity of the game and whether I'd want to do further full play-throughs (unless everything goes wrong and I fail, of course) - but after 20hrs on this initial run I'm still having fun and there appears to be plenty content left that I haven't got to. I'm not yet certain if there is true meta-progression between full runs of the game, but there's  lots of things to progress at your base by upgrading rooms, unlocking classes, buying weapons and breeding better goblins and such, so you can feel the overall progression slowly as you send your teams out on their missions.

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to say this, because this game has so much potential, but its not worth it at the moment. _childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of the art and the round-based strategy combined with the lair building and played through every similar game starting from darkest dungeon. Initially, I was in love with the game. The basic ideas are great and new concepts such as genetics and breeding brought new aspects to the genre. Furthermore, the art style is amazing as well, especially the crazy variants of goblins one can gather!Over time, however, some of the negative aspects took the fun out of the game for me. It started with a lot of bugs, I had to restart my run twice because my lair got bugged or the game stuck in a fight. Later on, some mechanisms were not working accordingly. For example, freezing an enemy bugged out and did not work in a certain run anymore. Another thing was that certain 20% hits (shield, bleeding) always resisted when they activated even if the opponent had no resistances.After 30 hours the game got also quite boring and repetitive. I think on a typical run I spend 70 % of my time doing my breedings and dismissing goblins after a run to get my 6 souls (highest soul farming efficiency.) This process is however tedious after a while. The lair is also fully upgraded at 50% of the story so you do not have to farm resources or souls anymore. I still want to play efficiently but you just pile up stuff which you do not need. The same goes for gold. Sitting on 60k after purchasing all the rooms. One can buy a weapon here and there but a challenge run is usually better for rare stuff. Once you get through all the grinding the run itself is in my opinion way too simple and repetitive. Compared to darkest dungeon you can not lose a run or even a fight. Overall I think I lost 2-3 goblins in battle and sent away hundreds after runs for soul farming. I think it would be better if more difficulty options were available from the start of the game maybe combined with multiple run slots.
_childDocuments_.name: Goblin Stone

_childDocuments_.review: The first 2 hours are great. You get charmed by the art and you discover and unlock new things at a nice pace. Soon after, you get over the art and the pacing feels like a f2p mobile game. It's slow and grindy and the combat gets repetitive quick. I might continue to play a bit, because I still have many classes to unlock, but I doubt I'll ever get to the end of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: 20 hours in and all i can say is... i don't feel compelled to finish the game. I really wanted to like this game as i've been following the development in discord for about a year now. here are some of my issues:- I wish the narrator wouldn't speak every. single. time. i pick up some loot. It stops me from accessing my inventory until he finishes speaking and its frustrating. It would be okay (i guess) if he had more than 5 lines of dialogue when i picked up something but it gets repetitive. - I succeeded at failing a 3% chance of failure and lost my best goblin right before a boss fight. - The merge options for the main base are limited, i have LOADS of space for repeated buildings but whats the point??? - In my opinion it takes WAY too long to get access to the other units. - Breeding can be a huge hit and miss, whats the point of showing 3 different potential spawns and not getting any of them, or even close for that matter. - Traps  DO NOT have a 50% chance of going off on hits.... i know it isn't impossible for these to fail 8 -10 times in a row... like i'm sure i can flip a coin to land on heads 8 times in a row... eventually... - The art style is nice and i liked the writing. - I haven't run into any save corruption issues like some others have in their comments...sounds like a bad time. So no issues for me there.- The weapons felt punchy but there was definitely a lack of options in weapons and attacks that made an impact. There was really only 3 'attacks' i felt useful for a couple classes.... not to mention the fact that some cool weapons i found along the way i cannot bring back with me... like... what? Why? I already have WAY too much gold and the merchant never has any good weapons so why cant i keep my loot i found while exploring? I just wish there was more reason to keep playing other than grind for materials to eventually get a new class to only be let down again by breeding over and over again. It just feels too slow. I dont know if this is supposed to be a long game or a short game and i don't feel like some of the devs did either :( Sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: : I haven't played the game since I posted this review which was a good 4 or 5 days ago. During that time I have now realized what is "wrong" with this game. And it is not that  , It is not that the base building aspect is  like the fact that having goblins in the base will be just that, goblins doing nothing in the base and  "One goblin will defend or be the lookout, this goblin will do blacksmithing, this one will clean etc." is such a missed opportunity.. What is the most important thing when playing Rogue-like games? It is the randomness of each game and encounter and all the things/upgrades/loots you get and it becomes a dopamine hit and release that you keep playing. It becomes a 'one-more'... until next thing you know its been 12 hours and the sun is almost back up. Don't get me wrong Goblin Stone does have rogue-like aspects to the game but it does so differently than most game. But do keep in mind that this game is also a turn-based RPG so to be honest it can do away with the whole Rogue-Like mission maps and it'd still be the same game. Repetetive and boring and here is why:. What makes a Rogue-like? It is the crazy upgrades you get that last until you face off with the final boss or you die and you start over again getting probably different set of crazy upgrades or whatever the gimmick of that rogue-like is. In Goblin Stone Rogue-like upgrades only lasts for the duration of the mission and any good loot you get while in that mission is also only usable until that mission. Also you don't die a lot but your characters do. And I think some degree of attachment to your character is necessary specially for the RPG aspect of it. After I unlocked the next 3 rows of genes I've become desensitized with losing goblins and it just feels ehh.

It's just that the game is not that fun; every run feels sameish. You have zero agency on what kind of permanent upgrade you have on your weapon. _childDocuments_.review: I  wanna like this game.It's cute, the general idea is good and the style is quite unique.The fact that the performance isn't perfect - fair enough.Unfortunately, Goblin Stone is  (unnecessarily!) clunky!The menus are a horror in almost every way and the whole thing just continues with the movement of the goblins...Normally I don't write a negative review "just" because the user interface isn't perfect.But here I'm so offended by it that my enjoyment of the game suffers.I'm ready to change my mind immediately if there are any major improvements!

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying the game is pretty fun. I see a lot of people comparing it to Darkest Dungeon in a bad way, but I think it is like Darkest, but with out some of the annoying management things and negative perks.The reason I can't recommend this game is due to the bugs and how long it is taking to resolve them. Some passives (genes) have not worked since launch and still don't work. Game breaking bugs occur often, like lost saves of bugged quests which don't allow you to continue. Only the bugs that they say they are working on or look fixable get replies on the official discord.The game should be in early release with an early release price until the bugs have been worked out and the game is complete.Avoid this game for now

_childDocuments_.review: "Exit to main menu? (All progress will automatically be saved)"Automatically saved my ass, that's how I just lost 30 minutes of progress. I'm so done with this game.Bugs after bugs after bugs. Some are minor, some require you to find a workaround, some makes you think why this game isn't in early access. I'm about to pull my hair out.The gameplay doesn't even make up ♥♥♥♥ tons of bugs you have to bear with.Contents are severely lacking. I'm 5 hours into the game and I'm still using almost the same gears and skills 3 hours earlier. Battles are really slow with most enemies being damage sponge. I wish there's a 2x or 3x speed option.Base building is lackluster and nothing to be excited about. It seems to be inspired from Fallout Shelter except it's nothing like it. Your goblins doesn't interact with each other, your goblins have no personality. Your goblins doesn't even walk around from rooms to room. Everything is just for show.User interface is extremely clunky which adds further frustration when you need to manage / breed / change jobs / equip your goblins. I wish I could still refund this crappy game, but at least I have a chance to persuade you from avoiding this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really would like to recommend this game but I sadly am unable to do it in good faith.While seems fun at first cutesy & bright kind of Darkest Dungeon the game quickly becomes... not fun & repetetive. I will not mention the bugs that are still out there (my main one is where I am unable to dismiss or hire new goblins thus making breeding new goblins impossible).Additionally I feel that almost every thing out there is made to inconvenience the player. Whether it is UI stuff, moving on the map, animations, cutscenes, small icons you have to click with precision on the map.  (Fixed) or merchant interactions are especially frustrating. The upgrades all need the same materials thus you have to repeat a mission multiple times for an upgrade. Gold while important at first quickly becomes thing you actually do not need, have heaps of and cannot actually do anything with.The combat while interesting at first features many similar type of enemies (Halfling, Halfling Warrior; Purple Ooze, Yellow Ooze, Green Ooze) which do not have that much different strategies and feel like copy + paste with different colour palette.  The enemies are almost the same so you do not need to think up of new strategies of dealing with them (though there are some strategies particularry effective against some types of enemies). The bosses either are easy as heck or very hard and usually very very long.Whole content of this game when it comes to combat and exploration feels like unfinished product.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on this review.The game-play and mechanics seem great.  There are so many bugs.  This should be an early access title.So many quality of life features should be added as well.The UI is TERRIBLE!  They dropped the ball here.  The UI will show some but not all the stats for a goblin when you are trying to breed.  So you have to manually go through each and every goblins stats one by one until you find the perks you want.  Once you find said goblin, you must remember it's name because you can't select it for breeding until you exit the stat screen.  Oh and the stat boxes randomly break.  You try to open stats and a wood panel never opens.  This means that goblin is broken and you can't even equip their gear.  I end up dismissing them because I can't even sacrifice them for souls.You can't play with gamepads, even though they are supposed to be creating that feature in the future.The mouse cursor is so small and dark in color, I it's nearly impossible to see.  I have to wiggle the mouse around forever to locate it.In a fight if you want to heal another team mate there is a giant stat box blocking health bars at times, which makes it really hard to heal the right goblin.The game does not seem to be balanced.  I'm in chapter 3 and only party wiped twice.  The problem is you need to kill some goblins to upgrade your main building at your base.  I never have enough souls.So I'm giving this a negative review as the developer did not release a complete game.  This game has a lot of potential and I have had quite a bit of fun with it despite all the flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Great game for the first 25-50%. This game starts off great. Endearing graphics, a story that challenges norms, and familiar-yet-novel gameplay. When the player uncovers the last classes, soon thereafter maxes out their base, the gameplay becomes entirely redundant. Also, the story that started sweet and counter-culture drags out thereafter. Meet a new NPC? Great! Chase them, protect them, and get their back story. How you ask? The same 20 minutes of gameplay repeated thrice more, naturally. I rarely leave a campaign incomplete -- I come here for stories and experiences! -- but I couldn't finish this one. That said, the first part of the game was still lovely; later rambling and dragging won't undo that.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, I have to give this delightful gem of a game a negative review. The theme and gameplay are great, the music and narration on point, but the experience is so badly marred by the bugs and various QOL issues that are too frustrating to look past. Softlocks on certain screens requiring frequent alt-f4s, restarts, and a a false warning of "your progress is saved at every decision" that turns out to very much not be the case when you lose all your progress. _childDocuments_.review: I heard people compare this to Darkest Dungeon and while there are similarities, it's the differences that separate the 2 games.For example, if you lose a character in DD, you lose all the time and effort into levelling up that character.If you lose a goblin in GS, you get rewarded for it. In fact, you can't progress unless you retire your goblins, or lose them in the dungeon.Another difference is the classes. In GS, some aren't unlocked until you get to certain points in the story. In DD, the classes are random stagecoach selections. In DD, you can stay with a single comp, but different areas will be more difficult (like a bleed team in the Cove) so you'd start looking for other strategies to use. In GS, once you have a good comp, you don't want to change it. I've been running 3x hunter and 3x shaman for the last 15 hours and the game is a breeze. If you don't like grindy games, this isn't for you. The lack of wood and fibre will stop your base from improving. The game would be served better if they doubled the wood and fibre rewards. It's such a roadblock. I had entire row of inventory of leather and bones, but barely any fibre and a lot less wood.People also mentioned bugs, but I have only had the game crash once and when I restarted the game, I only lost a round or two of combat, so it wasn't really game-breaking.
_childDocuments_.name: Goblin Stone

_childDocuments_.review: I write this review with a bit of a heavy heart.I think this game isn't worth my time now, but I'm hopeful it will get development support and fix various minor issues and add more content.Let's start with the good:- The backgrounds and art style is very charming and cohesive.- There's a solid loop here of gameplay that inches you steadily upward, but it doesn't feel exactly like a loot treadmill/- Skills are bound to weapons and jobs, which creates interesting decisions in your party composition.- The timeline turn system is excellent, it makes debuff skills interesting and valuable.- Enemies feel bigger and meaner than you, so you have to have your goblins work together to defeat them.- My initial impacts with the game did involve hitting a few wonky bugs. It looks like the developer was already getting on top of those (within release week, so good job!)Onto the not-so-good.- The narrator starts off interesting and a bit glib, but becomes fairly generic lacking personality. Overly present on nearly every interaction. Not enough dialogue variety.- The animations of the characters feels a bit stilted, especially the orcs. They lack smoothness when they're on scene.- By and large, most of the goblins don't feel like they have any personality at all. They don't have many idle animations, they all sort of do the same thing together regardless of their job, they don't banter or interact with each other. The enemy adventurers feel that way, but it's more forgivable.- There's a lot of missing UX options and polish (like smoother faster transitions between screens, support for key rebinding)- The level generation is not particularly large or impactful. A chunk of the time you'll get shops early before you've had a chance to gather money, or encounter buff effects after you've fought the combats.- The game overuses temporary upgrades that wildly swing things. You can get big buffs to Power, or resistances, or temporary weapon or skill upgrades. But they feel fleeting to the point of not feeling like a thing to build or play around with. I wish some of the upgrades gave a residual item you could apply to a future level, so there'd be more decision making in building your party.- There isn't quite enough enemy variety in the early zones, leading to gameplay feeling repetitive.- The hub area feels fairly nonperformant and feels clunky to click or move around on.- Every character of a particular class is conformed to the same skill set, meaning you can't have one crit focused character and another big chop focused characters.I really want to love this game, I didn't return it because I want to support the developer and hope this game gets worth me revisiting and updating this review!

_childDocuments_.review: The best part of this game is the graphics, unfortunately. There are a lot of design decisions in this game that summarily make it not that fun... the most fun, I guess, is the suspense that something cool might unlock. For me, 13.7 hours later, it didn't happen. I doubt I'll keep going.The story started off very interesting, but by the second map, I started to really hate it. Instead of being the underdog against the bad humans, it's all about orc supremacy and being their little errand runners non-stop, which actually started in the first map. It's not interesting enough to want to see what happens in the third map.For the design decisions that I have an issue with:The controls are annoying - finish a fight, try to loot, it talks at you like Darkest Dungeon (and repeats a lot) but removes your controls, wait, then you try to loot again and sometimes you have to do it twice to make it go. Also, clicking the mouse doesn't loot if you are too far away, it stops moving as soon as you let go of the key, but holding it down won't loot either you have to click it again. Once I found hitting the space key works, I just spam that until it does it.When completing combat, the combat loot randomly gets dumped somewhere. I especially enjoy it when it puts it behind some of the fancy shrubberies that are in front of the goblins, then I have to fight my camera or hit space a whole lot everywhere. Oh, there is also sometimes random loot that you can't see (there might be a shiny treasure pixel or something) which reinforces my space spamming.The stages have a ton of temporary buffs, most of which are weak, and the stages are short, which make most of the stage pointless.The stages are also filled with an odd walking simulator mechanic, I guess in order to see the pretty graphics somebody did, but it's annoying after a while. Maybe I'm just impatient.Ambushing (approaching an enemy from behind) is random AF. Half the time nothing happens, the other half only part of them are surprised.Why does bleed to a crapton of damage, but poison takes a very large amount of stacks in order to do anything? If anything, I would think it the other way around (small amount of poison kills, but death by 1000 cuts)The buildings are extremely uninteresting. You can dig out all this depth, but the only buildings that you can duplicate are the item holding ones and the retiree ones, which are barely helpful. Half my spaces are literally empty.I keep hoping for a way to add permanent enchantments on my weapons but I have to pray to RNGESUS for the merchant to show up with decent ones - it is rare.Soul currency is beyond weird. You do not get a soul per goblin death like you may expect, you get X amount of souls depending on if they've seem combat, how many adventures they been on, their age, and if they get to retire or not. That's right, you get more souls if they retire. No souls if they haven't seen combat. What the f...The breeding doesn't make a lot of sense beyond a basic level. The max stats seem to be tied to the story, so there is no real point to the breeding system - you just do the story then rescue a goblin or hire a squatter then breed that one.

_childDocuments_.review: I finally finished the game and I really feel like I have to share my experience.First things first: The game isn't bad. It really isn't. The main problem is, that it is totally boring.The early stages feel very refreshing. you get new goblins, make progress towards expanding your main-base, you get new ressources, get new weapons from the shop and you encounter all kind of stuff. Then it falls off. Because you do exactly this, over and over again. I finished the game in ~45h and it was a stretch, to call it the least. It gets so repetitive, that it isn't fun at all. You literally do the exact same mission in the exact same bioms over and over again, for nothing. and I mean nothing. Nothing is permanent. You find a good weapon on your adventure? Welp, only there for the current adventure, then its lost. Why? Where is the incentive to do these quests? Also: you don't gain experience. Your goblins don't grow stronger, so it is basically the best call to fight as few enemies as possible during an adventure, because it simply kills time and probably a goblin. On the other hand, when you have a branching part, you can decide if you want a buff or a fight an enemy.. what would you take? You could get money from a monster-reward to upgrade your weapons at a smith, which you may encounter during the adventure... only to have it reverted back to 0 after the mission. Also, the upgrades can fail.My whole team consists of 6 goblins, 3 raiders and 3 shamans, from the beginning up until the very last fight. Exactly this combination. The game has an "spell"-upgrade event, which gives you the option to upgrade 3 spells you currently have equipped. With only 2 types of goblins, i quite often got to upgrade a skill two times, which usually granted another beneficial aspect to the skill. If you have 4 types of goblins, the chances of getting this is way smaller.80% of the traits simply feel wasted. It was fun looking for them and completing the gene-book, only to be disappointed at the end, that even the late-game traits aren't really good. Really a missed opportunity.The narrator is very good. The sound and art-design really is astounding for a game like this. But man, does the narrator have to comment on everything I do? open a chest, landing a crit, full inventory, getting a buff, seeing a buff... That needs to be tuned down even more (they already did this after a patch).Additionally, this game - for some reason - runs like crap on my machine. As if it can't decide if it wants to show animations or skip them. It simply didn't feel fluid. And this is with 32GB RAM, a 3070 TI and a Ryzen 3900. I really don't understand how this can happen. I give the devs credit though. They listened to the community-feedback - at least in the very beginning - and addressed the problems which came around. Bugs and progressionwise. There is still a lot of QoL features which could be implemented though, for example a x2-x3 speed during combat. Its not active, so might as well speed that up.I could go on for every but I have to call it here.TL:DRI think the devs achieved the game, they wanted to create. Exactly with these "hurdles" in mind. That was their idea of a game and they did a good job in creating it. However, this doesn't really appeal many players compared to darkest dungeon for example. The gameplay loop is tedious and boring. Nothing, really NOTHING you gain from re-doing adventures. The lair (main base) simply sits there. You don't really interact with anything except breeding. Thats it. I also can't see what should give a motivation to play NG+ (and more), execpt the achivements they tied to this.In its current state, I wouldn't even buy it if its reduced by 50%, which is a shame, because art-design-wise its fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually write reviews until I am done with a game, but I want to offset some of these negative reviews. Yes, there are bugs and I have been lucky enough not to experience any game breaking ones, but this game is made by a small indie studio and they have been actively fixing issues every week.There is a lot to love about this game: the beautiful art style, the combat mechanics, and the story. There's fun in trying to breed the perfect goblin with maximum stats and ideal genetic traits. I haven't even unlocked half of the possible traits, so I know there's a lot to look forward too. The combat is unique and the bosses in later zones feel different from each other and are rewarding to beat. The merchant sells new weapons every day, so try to buy ones with high power and gems when you see them.I agree with some of the other reviews that the game can get a little grindy. It would be nice to have more variety in enemies for a particular run that usually has about 5-7 combats.  As for your goblins: you shouldn't get too attached to them because you'll be retiring them and replacing them regularly. You can keep your favourite retired goblins in your Quarters and use them for breeding. For each run, you should prioritize harvesting materials to upgrade your rooms. You should also try to rescue goblins with new traits and higher stats, so you can breed them and unlock genes. You'll also find more variety in goblin appearances as you progress through the game. Soon you will find yourself with an entire army of blue goblins!All in all, the game is fun and rewarding. I look forward to playing it more!

_childDocuments_.review: Goblin Stone invites players to embark on a heartwarming journey alongside the last surviving goblins, who are on the brink of extinction thanks to those pesky adventurers. But don't let their diminutive stature fool you—these goblins are determined to rebuild their lair and seek revenge against their oppressors, one bug-ridden step at a time.In this charming turn-based roguelite, players will navigate through a world filled with both danger and opportunity, making strategic decisions that will determine the fate of their goblin brethren. Will you prioritize resource gathering to fortify your defenses, or will you focus on training your goblin army to take the fight to the adventurers? The choice is yours, but be warned: every decision comes with its own set of challenges and consequences.However, it's not all sunshine and rainbows in Goblin Stone. Despite its endearing premise and charming art style, the game is not without its flaws. Players may encounter occasional bugs and glitches that can disrupt the flow of gameplay and lead to frustrating setbacks. Additionally, the gameplay can become repetitive over time, as players find themselves engaging in similar encounters and tasks with each playthrough.But even with its flaws, Goblin Stone manages to captivate players with its lovable characters, engaging storytelling, and satisfying gameplay mechanics. With its colorful world and whimsical atmosphere, it's a game that is sure to leave a lasting impression, bugs and all. So gather your goblin comrades, steel your resolve, and prepare for an adventure like no other in Goblin Stone!Consider checking my gameplay before making your purchase.
