_childDocuments_.review: Reading some of the reviews, just wanted to put in my .2.  About 2/3 in to the first mission, so this is more a commentary on the base mechanics rather than the game as a whole, I will update as I go as I feel it needs to. _childDocuments_.review: Really great to play a new stargate game, the controls are clunky to say the least, but once you get into the rythem of things it's actually pretty fun! Like I mentioned the movement and character selction controls kinda suck, but the variety of tools each character has to solve the situations you get into is pretty nice. I can definitely see replaying these levels a few times.Learn to save often, and keep your team separated enough to click on quickly and it'll be great!

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I have finally managed to sneak my way through the first batch of 7 missions, I can write an honest review. So here we go…Stargate: Timekeepers is a top down stealth game set in the Stargate universe. It’s a niche genre, not a bad game. Some reviews here go unfairly hard on Timekeepers, while IGN went too soft on it. When I pre-ordered this game back in October, I had an overall idea and my very own expectations of what this game is: it’s a top down stealth game set in the Stargate universe. Gameplay is OK, I had fun when I got the hang of it. I was and still am interested in the story.Make no mistake, there are stargates in Timekeepers, but the game definitely needs more stargate action! Have the players SHIFT+LMB on a DHD to dial up the damn thing! The TV episode recap-style “Currently on…” cutscenes between missions are genius!Humor was also great!Is Stargate: Timekeepers a perfect game? Nowhere near. Could Slitherine make it better? Given enough time, most certainly yes. Prove so with the second batch of missions! The respect and care is there and it’s appreciated! Peace!FEEDBACK4STORYGROUP -Elaborate more on offscreen developments. What’s up with Captain Morris and Hak’tyl Resistance post-mission 5?-The chapters and setting need more coherence: Moloc & Dolus are rivals, ok. With that in mind, how does Moloc’s prisoner from mission 6 finale end up on Dolus’ Ha’tak?-Literally all of the characters need more depth: Who is General Travis? Is he General of Lambda site?-Deepen relationships between teammates by adding dialogue that’s built upon past experiences. Even one liners can do so much for development! For example the ultimate cliché confrontation with the high priestess felt like long time coming and very-very important for A’ta. I lol’d at seeing Sam’s way of resolving the issues between the two. However funny, it had no impact whatsoever later on. I understand Timekeepers is not an RPG, but I was waiting for her to bring that up, or her expecting similar behavior from him or just simply mocking him for that treehouse incident from time-to-time.
_childDocuments_.name: Stargate: Timekeepers

_childDocuments_.review: It's a stargate stealth tactics game.  If you like stargate and stealth tactics, you'll probably enjoy this.  If you're expecting a different genre or something like an xcom clone you will be disappointed.  There's no base, research or gear to improve.  There is, on difficulty higher than story mode, things like supplies to manage.  Don't expect something it never promised to delivery and it's a solid game

_childDocuments_.review: not the full game.ok so, i love Stargate, one of my fav sci-fi series from when i was young. but what the fluff is this game? 7 stages and a "to be continued in season 2" seriously? let me guess? you're going to ask money for that?for a 30 euro pricetag it certainly not worth it.the stages are loosely connected to each other. one of the missions endings makes you do something? open a passage way? i don't know. yet the next mission acts like that was a distant past.the game is called "timekeeper" yet the game ends after you become this "timekeeper" it's absolutely terrible, it's not even explained, you just have to piece the pieces together. and only those who watched the series can think of the timeloop episode.horrendous, terrible. just don't bother. i enjoyed the concept of the game, yet the story and execution is bad. the end i feel ripped off for even playing this for free.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally that big on real time tactics, I prefer my tactics to be turn based. But given that I love the Stargate franchise I had to try this one out and have been quite happy with it.The writing could've used some work and it does expect too much knowledge of the franchise to be a good starting point for newcomers, but it definitely has that feel of a well crafted strategy game, difficult, but not overwhelmingly so. There are definitely things I would change if I was the developer, but for a franchise that has been dormant for many years it's a worthwhile experience and I'd recommend it for fans of the franchise or the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: So I looked up real time tactics games, and on the same list as StarGate Timekeepers was the Myth: The Fallen Lords series (not available on Steam) from Bungie Studios. This is NOT a real time tactics game as defined by Myth I and Myth II. From the first mission it's a top-down stealth game, starring Maximum Series 7 Finale Bolt On Our Own Story, a name which I find amusing enough that I don't refund this even though there was some misunderstanding about what type of game this is, and it is not a valid replacement for the old mods that were featuring StarGate spaceships battling each other in SW: Empire At War, Homeworld, and others. Apparently this game is developed in conjunction with the US Navy, rather than the US Air Force as per the original series. Sad as it is to say, but the days when my computer files were my computer files are gone. Recommended thus far for fans of stealth.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to write this review just because I think it's important to try and convey the badness of this game.Right I played for 10 minutes, you can say I didn't get deep enough into the game to make an educated guess.  I'd say I got deep enough in to decide it wasn't much fun and I didn't like the game.So right at the start menu, I had the option to CONTINUE, which dropped me immediately into the first mission and skipping the opening cutscene.  Interesting.  Suspicious.I restarted and chose NEW GAME.  There's a cutscene about some fighter craft fighting over a really simplistic and empty icefield.  See like, Star Wars Rogue Squadron came out in 1998.  Remember the Hoth battle in that game?  That's the kind of graphical quality for this cutscene we're talking here.  Actually Rogue Squadron was better because there was more polish and interesting features in the terrain than we see in the opening cutscene of Timekeepers.So after that it goes into a point and click adventure where you have to click on the taskbar to punch (I assume) then click the enemy to one punch him and knock him out for 10 (TEN!!!) SECONDS while you run to the next enemy and try to one punch him also and get through before the first guy or any of his mates see you.  The first guy you knocked out will wake up and either attack you or simply forget you exist.  There is definitely a spinny timer thing showing how long until he wakes up.  It's bizarre.I attempted this about 3 times and it quickly became tedious, and tiresome.It's not so much about disliking this as a stealth game, it's more about disliking this as a Stargate game and just as a game in general.  Meanwhile, it is still a bad stealth game, I've never played a game like this where the enemy is stunned for 10 seconds for some reason, and it just keeps happening.  Usually you'd be able to eliminate said enemy, hide the body in some bushes and so on?  That would be what I would expect from a stealth game.  Here they just keep stunning and reawakening infinitely.Yeah I only played for 10 minutes.  I choose to utilize my time given to other pursuits.   That's the thing, you've got to do something that's going to grab people quickly and impress them and make them say, Wow, this game is very fun, I wish I could play more!  What is this?   You've built a broken game and plastered a Stargate skin on it.  Bravo.  I think you need to take this back to the drawing board for another year and polish it up and figure out how to make it genuinely fun and interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the game, even if the lower budget is felt, especially in the cut scenes.While playing, I didn't come across many major bugs, except for one case where at the end of the mission you have to open the gate for the members of the resistance and the wheel that opens the gate didn't respond - even the saved games didn't work, so the whole mission had to be restarted.One more case that bothered me was that immediately after loading the saved position, the game does not respond to some controls for a while, which can be a problem if you save the game right before a critical moment and you need to quickly enter commands, such as finding out where the enemy is looking and you can click 4- 5 times until it displays its view coneWhat I would like to see in the next season from the view cones of the enemies will be more zones or a different size during the night or during rain/storms or some other atmospheric phenomena. In this way, new mechanics could be added, such as turning off the lights for a tactical advantageIt would also be nice to occasionally have some kind of time-limited sound barrier, for example a loud machine, when you could run or use noisy attacks without the enemy noticing.Another thing I would like would be some indirect interaction with the enemy, for example the target is located in an area where it is difficult to get to, so I would attach some device or bomb to a patrolling guard who would eventually arrive near the main target where it would explode etc.I bought the game knowing that it is a relatively low-budget game, so it met my expectations. For the first season, fine, but in the next season, it would like more varied gameplay and options, otherwise the game quickly slips into a stereotypeI'm looking forward to the next season

_childDocuments_.review: Not nearly as polished as Desperados III or Shadow Tactics Blades of the Shogun, but its still a decent stealth tactics game. I do really like the Synchronized execution option for the Tactics mode where the characters will wait to perform actions until they are all ready. I don't think I've seen that feature in other stealth tactics games.  I still like & recommend this game.Edit - With the latest Patch 1.00.34, they've added the ability to set a view marker and the characters can now move in range to complete their ability if the target was beyond it originally.

_childDocuments_.review: What I liked:- Characters and abilities. They have fun banter between them, very stargatey, abilites are lore friendly (sometimes exanding) even though the limited zat ammo is weird from a lore perspecive and you don't even use the two shots kill mode because the ammo is limited. But overall great.- How character abilities compliment each other.- Difficulty. Just hard enough to frustrate you, and not so hard it makes you want to quit.- The story is decent so far, tho it takes it's time to get to the main bad guy.- The planets feel like in the show. Just alien enough, nothing too out there, but still can't be mistaken for a Vancuver Forest. ;)What I disliked:- Linear feel to the level design- Small bugs- Not enough interactivness with the levels. Doors, Ring transports, Stargate, other props.- That I have to wait for the second part of the campaign (even though it's going to be free)What I wish they add in the second part of the season (or perhaps after that, like season 2).- A central hub area where you can talk, upgrade, etc your characters/weapons. To create a better bond between characters and the player. Perhaps let the player choose characters for the mission more often. Think Partisans 1941.- More open terrain. I know it's a stealth game and the terrain is part of the puzzle. But a lot of the lvls feel like walking down corridors. At least the forrest levels shouldn't feel like it.- More interactivity on the maps. Opening/closing doors should be a no brainer. We have a scientist and a jaffa, maybe give them the ability to open goa'uld doors. Make the ring transport or perhaps even the stargate interactive outside of cinematics. Even the "drop something on the enemy" or s"hoot something to distract" props are too few and too far inbetween on the maps.- Greater mission and enemy variety. In the first 7 missions we have different classes of Jaffa Warriors, kull warriors and sentry drones. I know the enemies are story based (meaning no sense in having replicators there if there is no story purpose for them) but the stargate lore is deep and using the Jaffa 90% of the time seems shallow. As for the missions maybe add some chalanges, like don't kill anyone, don't sound any alarms while completing x., maybe a more action packed level where stealth isn't an option for a part of the mission. etc etc. Think of the show, how often did they sneak in and had to fight their way out of a situation.- Fix the small bugs. Sometimes the characters don't do what they're ordered to. Sometimes the alerted ! or ? aren't seen on enemies. Once an enemy on the far side of the map was alerted for some reason and I couldn't save for 3min. When you throw an enemy over an ledge the body glitches weirdly. A conversation between two of my characters triggered every time I walked trough the trigger not just the first time (no reloading between the two times). Small things like that.I know this seems like a negative review, but it's not. The five things mentioned above would move Stargate Timekeepers from good to great in my book. tl;dr I liked this game.  It's a good game that rarely touches great and sometimes falls into the decent category. Just know what you're buying. It's a tactical stealth game, not something else. 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Stargate: Timekeepers

_childDocuments_.review: Some of my review is colored by my excitement of a Stargate game. I've also only completed 5/7 initial missions (and am half way through the 6th) so maybe things take a nose dive from here.Overall I think its a pretty solid stealth game with some (but imo not enough) use of the source IP. Something like 6/10 I guess. I would say unless you are either a fan of sg-1/atlantis (miss me with sg-u) or a big stealth gamer, I'd recommend waiting until the second half of the missions for this drop before pulling the trigger.For $30 price tag, only having 7 missions is a pretty rough value. If the following 7 missions in "season 2", which is included in the purchase, are of similar depth, it won't be a bad value vs $. But right now it is.For game itself, its a stealth puzzle game, similar to commandos. If that's not your cup of tea, or want a different type of game for the IP, you should steer clear. As someone who doesn't play a lot of these types of games, I will say I find it pretty challenging. Outside of the first 2 missions, I've needed a lot of reloading and saving after moving past ever small group of guards. Jaffa/enemy AI is pretty simple, which is both good for plotting your strategy to get past, but also makes the game not really feel "alive".Graphics are pretty weak and animations a bit laughable, for example the animation to kick something was... maybe the devs have never seen someone kick before?As a positive, and probably related to weaker graphics, I've run into no performance issues. CPU hovers around 40% in game and GPU never gets warmer than 70C. Sad things to note, but the state of the gaming industry, apparently releasing a game that actually runs is a challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: Stargate: Timekeepers

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, back to my original recommended review.  A month after submitting the bugs and the patch fixed them.  Thank you to the devs for listening and correcting the problems.  Now on to the good: You can save at ANY point, and it's strongly encouraged.  A lot of the characters' abilities are complementary, e.g. Max's whistle can draw in a crowd so A'ta's flash grenade can blind them all at once.  Remember, this is a stealth game, so take your time and watch the patterns.  It is winnable.  Have fun and Jaffa Kree!
_childDocuments_.name: Stargate: Timekeepers

name: Wartales
detailed_description: Join our Discord! About the Game A century has passed since the fall of the Edoran Empire at the hands of an unprecedented plague that swept the nation. Now, the land is rife with mercenary work, banditry and thievery, with honor having become an almost entirely forgotten virtue. Now, prepare to lead a group of unscrupulous characters in a massive open world where combat, death and a thirst for riches will dictate your day to day life. You are not the hero of this story, destined to usher in a new era of peace. Your goal is solely to survive and thrive in this harsh and hostile world, by any means necessary… Only the bravest and most ambitious can hope to see their story written in the Wartales! Lead a group of mercenaries on a dangerous quest for riches and recognition in a medieval world ravaged by destitution and greed, recruiting new companions with numerous unique specializations, skill sets, weapon preferences and personalities. Customize your group's skills, equipment, and appearance with an intuitive RPG progression and crafting system, while developing your camp with luxuries, tools, and equipment to help your team endure and recover from the hardships each day brings. Journey through a vast, open world in your quest for notoriety, wealth, and recognition, immersing yourself in lively villages and remnants of a bygone era. Explore abandoned mines, tombs, and camps as you piece together the history of this harsh world. Collect bounties and take on contracts. From protecting the innocent from petty thieves to defeating the land's most notorious figures, there's no such thing as a profit too small to take. Overcome your foes with a tactical turn-based combat system that rewards careful planning and strategic thinking, selecting the best combination of characters, equipment, and tactics to succeed in each unique battle. Traverse the vast open world of Wartales as a band of up to 4 players, planning tactics and devising a strategy before confronting some of the many hostile inhabitants that roam these mysterious lands and defeating them as a team. Share money, loot, resources, and end the day with a delicious meal around a roaring campfire with your loyal companions, building camaraderie and forging unbreakable bonds that will help you overcome any obstacle.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Battle Brothers except a lot more expensive, harder to find missions, a more stale combat experience, and apparently crafting if you're into that. The graphics here are better if that matters to you. Wartales also has no tutorial whatsoever and based on the threads i looked at, the community doesn't much like it when people bring that up. If you have played these kinds of games before you should be able to figure out the basics, but I'd be shocked if there aren't mechanics outside of the basics that people are struggling with.In other words relative to Battle Brothers they seem to have deemphasized the combat a little bit to add other things, and your characters are less expendable.Most reviewers seem to like it and it's alright, but I think Battle Brothers is a much better game because it focuses on the right things.The real problem for me is the price point. This is not worth anything like $35 or even the $28 that I paid for it. It's worth $10, possibly $15. If you don't have Battle Brothers, I'd buy that instead. If you do have Battle Brothers and you like these types of games, I guess it all depends on your budget.

_childDocuments_.review: So in my multiple hours of gameplay... the overall experience was marred by repeated bugs, horrible difficulty scaling and quest management, RNG quests that can ruin a run because you lack income and it rolled 4 hard quests in a row; abysmally slow resource respawn rates, merchants that DO NOT reset or clear their inventory (Meaning you are dealing with finite resources of repair kits, food and utility), a tiring and slow scaling process and the ever present artificial difficulty due to restricted income flow.So how bad is the income flow? The difference between an easy quest and a hard quest, is only 50 gold. The average quest reward is 130. Here's the kicker, on the first map there is a barony quest, that requires you to take out 2 squads of guards... they are lvl 6 and 7 respectively, rocking squads of 8 that have MULTIPLE ABILITIES including doublestrikes, ♥♥♥♥♥ DOUBLE MOVE RANGE, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stacks of bleed. The game goes full ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on you... for a quest that doesn't even give you gold.So imagine... your day to day is already a slog. The storyline quests, proceeds to slog you even farther. Im ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pissed that this ♥♥♥♥ reared its ugly head after the 2 hour mark. PLEASE DO NOT BUY THIS!I hate that this developer front-ends the good content, then turns the lategame into a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slog. For reference this is the same studio behind northgard, a decent RTS which is ruined by their lack of RTS understanding and a stagnant meta. This same lack of understanding has crossed into the development of wartales, where they cant even sustain their core gameplay loop because of finite repeat cycles and the sheer mountain of effort vs non-existent reward differences.I've spent 20 hours, grinding for gear and experience. Only to get ♥♥♥♥♥ wiped because the game decides to uber-cheat with guard squads that if given to a player, would clear any fight by turn 3. And for good measure, the average income of an 8 man squad... is 150. So you are getting into quests that cant even cover your staple pay, that is also EXCLUDING FOOD. This game is mega-scuffed in difficulty scaling. Trust me, save your money first. This game doesn't reward your time or effort... and that says something about how the developer thinks.[Edit]: I changed the review from a negative to slightly positive, as once I figured out that the game EXPECTS you to use every tool at your disposal rather than the conventional route; the game opened up itself to me. On first playthroughs, it seems insurmountable at first (especially if you play on region-locked (apart from freeroam) mode; with insane scaling jumps in between. BUT, after experimentation and hard fought victories, it begun to make more and more sense. Prioritizing status enemies, status stacking and kiting, abusing terrain and ridgelines to bypass both enemies AND tollgates... the list goes on and on. The mastery in how to play this goes WAAAAAAY deep. From optimizing runs, farming traits and materials. You hamstring yourself by refusing to interact with the game's more esoteric systems.Need stable income? Capture criminals and send them to jail for the bounty. No quests? Refresh the board by accepting and then rejecting quests, and to farm for food while waiting. Really ♥♥♥♥♥ hard enemies? Run away or die trying...Think of the game as kind of like darksouls, and it expects a mastery level from you EVEN on normal mode. Its juuuust enough that you attrition out from conventional runs and expect your mercenary band to die. So that in subsequent runs, you get just that little bit better prepared with new equipment, tactics and procedurally more in-depth mastery of its mechanics. The issue isn't that there is no way to win. The issue is that you DON'T KNOW if there's a way to win or not. A major source of income is locked behind a simple item description, barely any prompt except one that appears midway through combat as well. If it was introduced it would be better, and the longer the save goes the more your "traits spammage" begins to tilt more into your favour. The game does feel more like a roguelike in that you slowly work your way up and snowball between jumps of difficulty spikes. Its fun but only if you work out in your mind that this is like darkest dungeon where ♥♥♥♥ can go really wrong really fast.I've come to love this little jank of a game. Especially BECAUSE there are ways to break the game. Abuse janky AI pathing in a chokepoint while raining arrows/poison/fireshots/exposions, bait enemies into AoE killing their allies, stack traits on your mercenaries to become so insanely fine-tuned that you ♥♥♥♥♥ oneshot named enemies with a single spell rotation. And then master how to kill 500 hp bears in 2 turns using %hp dmg.Started this game a scrub, still a scrub. But a much better scrub that was willing to smash into the brick wall until it broke. The game definitely needs more polish. But after literally breaking it open, there's enough in there that I changed my mind from negative to positive. Hopefully they fix balancing, content and really patch it up before full release.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for version 1.0 to drop before buying this game because too many games in the last 10 years have been stuck in "early access hell" so I will go over what to expect in the first hour of the game.1. There is no hand holding tutorial or button guide to highlight UI elements. This is a sword that cuts two ways as far as I see it. First, it can take a while before you realize what button where does what and how and some important things like Path and Knowledge are hidden behind menus and given no introduction. At the same time if you feel like these hand holding tutorials are a waste of time then by all means.2. Save early and save often if you can. I save scammed my first campaign and I would do it again.3. There is no "main character" perse. The party of companions is it so there isn't really a self insert for this title.4. Some fights you should runaway from. This game can have some deadly surprises for your companions.5. Planning every last step in the overworld would probably do you a lot of good. For those older gamers out there, think of Oregon Trail level of planning and survival. But even more advanced than that.I did not encounter performance issues or stutters. No crashes to desktop or other things you get from AAA developers. This game loop feels neat and tidy. I love the quests and the spoken dialogue. Everything is absolutely well done from a technical perspective.One thing that suffers is the character models. They are of notably lower quality art/model wise but it's something so easy to overlook because this game runs well. By the same token, I think a "potato" from 2023 could run this game at 1080p without problems but please take that with a grain of salt.

_childDocuments_.review: A difficult but immensely rewarding experience. The game devs are clearly still invested in this game. Several major updates, including co-op & new regions, have released since Early Access Launch (when I first picked it up). The devs are also not shy about taking player feedback to tailor the product to their player base. Some of the most common complaints when first released was the impossible-to-meet food and krown requirements. Since then, the devs have restructured food, altered level scaling, and made troop happiness a more achievable goal for the player. I am a huge fan of the birds eye view of the world and the seamless blend of over world exploration & turn-based combat--and how your performance in turn-based combat will influence your priorities in the over world. The game feels gritty and realistic. Your mercenary group members are not overly designed, characterizations of merc troops. Instead, each character is a worn-down human barely surviving in the world they've been set in--and it's your job to help them thrive. Fantastic game, Fantastic devs, I encourage everyone to pick it up. Fair warning: the game is difficult and doesn't hold your hand, so be prepared to restart a fair number of times.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as early access goes, I'm happy to recommend this game. It's a mix of battle-brothers for the combat and party management system, and mount-and-blade for the navigation on the world map.There is a number of crafting systems implemented at this point which each feels intuitive and - more importantly - actually helpful.  (Amazing how many games exist wherein the crafting system adds zero value to your party!)Combat is turn based, with an interesting system that rewards you for playing tactically.  The hit/miss ratios seem more forgiving in this game than many in the genre which I personally prefer.  This leaves less to chance, and the outcome being decided more-so by tactics and level/gear/composition.Edit:My only gripe at this point is that I have encountered two critical crashes that have required restart within only 100 minutes of playing.  While the game may lock-up for a period of about 15-20 seconds, it seems that with some patience this rectifies itself and I can now continue playing.  Edit edit: after another 80 hours of play time (and having waited quite awhile for them to patch and develop more) I can say that this game has improved quite substantially. Since my last review the map has doubled in size, perks have been reworked, and career-paths/mercenary company paths substantially improved. Crafting has seen an immense overhaul also.  STABILITY is immaculate. Over 80 hours of playtime without a single crash or hang-up.  Big props to the development group and folks working on this game, its great.Looking forward to the further development!

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, but the balancing is horrendous. Food costs are 1:1 always. There is no opportunity to buy a more expensive food to get a greater return on your money. Seems counter-intuitive. If a chicken lag costs 1 gold, and its worth 1 food, a whole chicken will cost 3 gold and be worth 3 food. There is no point in having different food types as they all have the same value.Crafting is nearly worthless. The total cost of goods to craft a chestpiece: iron, leather, and cloth will equate to 60 gold. You craft the chestpiece and its superior quality and its worth 20 gold.If you add an animal to your party, the game will add a human NPC to enemy parties. You have a wolf with 60 health that can only use bite, no armor, that you cannot manually control and has terrible AI, while the enemy party will get an additional NPC that has a full repertoire skills and armor stacked on top of its health. This makes animals nearly worthless, outside of the horse that can wear armor, because the 0 salary cost of the animal does not nearly make up for the lack of usefulness and squishiness of any animal npc. The combat is pretty difficult at times, and I have no complaints. Its thoroughly enjoyable. I dont want the game to be easy. I want it to make a little bit of sense when it comes to balancing. Poor balancing should not be used as a pseudo-difficulty modifier though. Its lazy.Update 060722I have no clue what the developer is talking about as far was region locking. That only has to do with the scaling of enemies. Like starter region is level 1-4, region 2 is 5-9, etc... It does not affect the pricing of goods and items in anyway. Its still 2 food/3 gold for an apple, and 4 food/6 gold for a chicken. There is no reason to purchase one food item over another. There is no reason to craft items from blacksmithing to sell them because the raw materials are worth astronomically more than a crafted item. Breastplate will sell for 15 gold when all the materials to craft it can be sold for 80 gold a piece. You are punished for crafting items. You can get better items as drops or from vendors. No point in blacksmithing. I think the only craftables that are worth crafting are fishhooks. 4 gold for the materials but 5 gold for the hook. I believe medicine is also worth more than the materials, but that is a key item you need for yourself in order to survive. This balancing of the economy makes no sense to me. There is no reason to really engage in trading or level many of the professions. The game punishes you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like a Mount and Blade campaign map with XCOM-style units and battle. It's got a few bugs as you'd expect from Early Access, and there's a lot that is missing for now that's coming on the roadmap, but it's an ambitious game, and even in its current state it is quite fun for many hours. If you enjoy the battles, you won't regret buying it. But something about it is absolutely addicting. It's got fun little mini-games for crafting and a neat little camp to set up for when your dudes need to sleep each day. There's quite a bit to explore despite how unfinished the map is and while none of the classes are particularly deep yet, there is 19 subclasses that I know of already. There was 3 per class (6 classes) and I managed to unlock a fourth subclass later on for one of the classes, which sets an interesting precedent for future development. There's legendary weapons to find in a variety of ways and randomized jobs in order to keep your dudes fed and paid (most of them tracking down and killing a group like your own). There's also animals to fight to get some meat and you can run trade goods between towns. You can also knock out the animals and tame them, though it's much easier for them to die than your humans and your nightly food intake will increase drastically with a horde of animals.TL;DR: Fantastic game with a lot of fun little systems and much more promised in the roadmap. Definitely get this.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard to recommend at this stage. Should be fne for 40-50 hours, however by that point it's going to start feeling repetitive (maybe even sooner),There is none. Not really. Each region has it's own problem. For example at the starting area you have a refugee crisis. One off to the side has 2 warring lords one of which is some kind of religious fanatic etc. You do not really get engaged in the events or the people. It just sort of happens. You either spend resources to solve an issue or you bonk one of the arguing parties on the head and move on.There are essentially 3 types: Knowledge, Path and Character. There is nothing wrong with the first 2, but the character progression is a bit weird.Your character classes are per-determined once you find them. They can be Swordmaster, Warrior, Brute, Spearman, Ranger or Archer. This class will determine what perks they can pick and what weapon they can use. Swordmasters use swords, warriors use axes, brutes use blunts, archers obviously use bows and rangers use daggers. Whether it's a 2 handed or 1 handed weapon it still is restricted to the same class, so a one handed axe is only for warriors just like a 2 handed axe. If you have a 1 handed weapon you can take an offhand weapon which are not class restricted, such as shield, torch, throwing dagger, throwing axe or throwing sickle. Your weapon will decide what attack skill you use.As they level up you gain an aptitude point. You use this to level up one of the stats: strength, dexterity, constitution, willpower, critical chance or movement. You are not free to do whatever you want though, Most of the time you get 3 options with one letting you get 2 points while others are 1 point. So even if you wanted to increase the strength of your brute, you might have been given the options of dexterity, willpower and movement and there is nothing you can do about it. The only thing you can do is spend 10 influence (an unlock) to make one of the options to add 1 point to become a 2 point increase instead.The other thing you get is a perk, you get these at levels 2, 3, 5, 8, 10 and 12. These can be either passive abilities or actual skills. Your main attack skill is determined by the weapon you use. This allows for some build variety but you will quickly notice that some perks are simply never worth it and for each class there is a few obvious things to pick. The problem is that once you hit level 6 it becomes very very slow.Here I have one gripe. You can craft weapons and armor with your blacksmith. The thing is, that you will always want to use crafted armor but almost never use crafted weapons. That's because crafted armor will always have better stats than armor found in the world. The ones you find may have things like increased movement, crit etc. but crafted armor has slots (up to 3) which you can use to add the same things with add ons you craft as well.Crafted weapons, however, are only good for their stats. First of all one thing to know — skills do damage based on the sill. So for example a swords skills will use the strength stat for damage. Your sword will not have a damage range itself, instead it will have a stat boost, let's say +10 Strength. Crafted weapons will mostly have a much better stat boost. However they will always have the exact same skill. So while you may find a 2 handed sword that does single target attacks and increases damage reduction on each attack in the world, every single 2 handed sword you craft will only add strength and do a simple AOE attack in an arc. That's it.Other than that you will cook food to get more food points rather than the raw materials. However while you can find mushrooms, fish and meat in the world, for most recipes you will need salt and vegetables which you can only buy (you can earn salt passively if you have an item for it). The vegetables are annoying though, because certain regions sell certain things. So you may end up in a situation where you can't craft any of the better foods because there is no way for you to get the missing ingredients without spending a load of time traveling to the other region and back unless you get lucky with a traveling merchant.There is a lot wanting there. For one the party list and inventory list make little sense. They are locked to the top left and bottom right corners respectively and you cannot move them. Furthermore they are basically grid based icons, think like the inventory system in Diablo only that the grid is not a limited size and expands (you can't have gaps in the party list)The problem is that there is no benefit from that. In the part list moving people around has no benefit. Once you open a character sheet you can press the arrow keys to flip between them (the game never tells or shows you that) and the order determine which one is next, but that's it. There is no formation or benefit in combat.The inventory is same story. The grid just expands as you add items, you only worry about weight. Instead they could have done both with a simple table and show some stats instead. So for example you could see the level and class of a party member without hovering over them or in the inventory you could see the value of an item, an item weight and the stack weight. Instead you must hover over items for this info. Furthermore the weight is shown as per item, but when you sort by weight it sorts by stack weight.. Again, a simple table format would solve this.Finally in the combat. Only the enemy has set turns. You pick which of your companions goes next. The problem is that there is no clear indication which ones have moved and which ones have not. It's fine at first, but once your party has 20 units, most of which look more or less the same you will end up doing a lot of clicking through your units to figure out which one has not moved if you accidentally clicked off the one suggested to check on something.Tl;Dr — needs work, good for some brainless downtime, but not something I feel like returning to from this point until some serious UX and balance and changes are done.

_childDocuments_.review: Wartales is an excellent RPG that gives your band of mercenaries the freedom to explore its world any which way you choose.  There are multiple options to select the difficulty of the game and the time you will spend to complete it. I suggest you start the game with the "Save  at will" option until you know all the mechanics of the game. Your actions will have consequences on the survivability of  your party and make the world easier or harsher. You will nurture each member of your party to make them more deadly and go along together. I had a great time optimising my party as you can add or remove characters at will as long as you can afford it. Wartales world is huge. It includes 6 kingdoms which are different in fauna, culture and habitat. Each with dozens of missions to complete. You will literally walk  through this world! The speed at which your party moves on the map increase as your party grows in experience. However, I wish that that speed was twice what it is now to reduce the "walk around" time.The graphics are pleasant. The turn based combat is very good, challenging and quick. Although this will depend on how well equipped you are.There is a lot of creativity in this game and I enjoyed it for 250 out of  the 300 hours I spent in it. Perhaps 1 kingdom less and a faster on map movement would have made it 100% enjoyable.In the end, I do recommend experiencing this game wholeheartedly!

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't tried the newest co-op update yet, but if you have any interest in medieval-fantasy party management and progression, you should seriously pick this game up. In my opinion, this game is an absolute steal at full price. Shiro Games has carefully crafted party dynamics at a strategic level that set a new bar of expectation for party-based games. Visuals are great. There are definitely notable differences in region topography and vegetation. Armor/weapons all have different aesthetics to them that make you feel/see their quality before even looking at their stats. Character models and animations (both in towns/combat and on the grand map) suit the art style of the game very well.Content is where Wartales really shines however. Tavern missions become pretty copy/paste after a while, but the game offers so much to explore in each of its different zones, along with the various professions/crafting available. Stopping to collect herbs so your alchemist can outfit your assassin with poison oil for their blade is awesome. Fishing in order to feed your party just enough to make it to town to collect your bounty money establishes levels of manageable stress that make the game fun. Rooting out a group of bandits from a mine so you can supply your blacksmith with ore for new armor really pushes the risk/reward scale on the player. There's just this overall sense of necessity for every little thing one comes across in Wartales. Exploring ancient ruins and taking on difficult tasks offers some very rewarding features. Having my scholar sift through ancient rubble to discover an antiquated blade that sets my leader leagues above the opposition feels so good. And that's not even covering the party classes and relationships. Classes are pretty fleshed out. While they're incomplete, there's a level of decision-making surrounding party composition that ensures no two playthroughs are alike. Should I have my brute focus on mobility in order to min/max their usefulness? Or should I build them to draw in as many opponents as possible for combat bonuses in taking on multiple enemies? Do I craft my archer(s) for support or for damage? Choices lie around every click of the mouse when it comes to building your troop. Characters bonding and forming friendships or hateships adds another layer to it all as well. My archer sucks at aiming (for some reason) and hit my warrior in the back. Now they hate each other (imparting combat debuffs when close to one another), but the warrior has gained the eyes-in-the-back-of-their head trait so as to not take anymore friendly missile damage. I've inadvertently used my leader and lieutenant to hold a line so that my rogues can flank for kills. Now they all have this box of love for each other and gain combat bonuses when in close proximity, which, when used appropriately, really turn the tides of future battles. Possibilities are endless.The story and lore of the game go hand-in-hand. While they aren't the greatest, I really appreciate the setup that Shiro Games has established for Wartales. Each zone possesses its own "story" or theme, which is independent from the rest of the regions. And while your "decisions" don't effect some grandiose campaign that spans the continent, each area is connected to the others through the text and conversations you have. This establishes a level of connection between all of the regions. One area has you working out a refugee problem, where you discover that these refugees are the result of a war occurring in a neighboring zone. Upon travelling to that neighboring zone, you then are engaged in working on resolving the conflict that created the refugee "story" of the previous location. All the while you hear rumors of a plague-ridden area that frankly sounds terrible to explore. When you finally stumble into that very place, you realize that the rumors did the difficulty of that land little justice.The biggest issue I've had with the game is probably the difficulty scaling. The game ensures that no matter how awesome that weapon you crafted/found is, it only just measures up to your next opponent's ability to defend against it. You never feel like you've gained ground in terms of equipment or levels. I'm not asking to become some demi-god who just slashes through everything, but when you don't get to really feel the power behind the new set of gear you just made, it takes away from the rewarding aspect of putting so much effort into getting there in the first place. Granted, this forces the player to look more to party strengths and actual strategy; yet, there is still something lacking with the balance of it all. I've reached points where I made the best items the game allowed, but the enemies scaled right up to that level, often going even further. My biggest losses have always been late-game, which is not typical with how games scale. An issue that compounds this is losing a member mid and late-game almost ensures you never catch back up. Because Wartales impresses upon the player the task of progression with each character, you can't just find high-ranking mercenaries at your local tavern to replace your level 8 lieutenant. And bringing that level 3 warrior you're trying to replace your lost companion with into combat is almost a complete deathtrap. This places the player in a late-game limbo of being able to recruit people to replace your losses, but being unable to train new recruits to ACTUALLY replace your losses in order to contend with the current difficulty. All that said, I haven't tinkered with the fixed level for each region setting purely because I like adaptive games for a challenge. However, Wartales seems to reach a difficulty where instead of plateau'ing, or getting easier, it just skyrockets in term of the hardship of each confrontation. Overall, Wartales offers a fantastic array of party management and western-inspired medieval fantasy content. I will be trying the co-op with a friend to see if that's worth it and will probably edit this review to include that aspect.TL;DR: Game is great. Try it out. Or don't. The choice is yours.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so here is my review I have logged 37 hours     7/10War tales brings a beautiful genre and environment to the gaming world and although turn based games have slowly started to make a come back, this game is taken away from all the sci fi elements and modern warfare and  throws you in to the medieval timescale. The graphics are not demanding but very well done. The worlds is amazing as you venture around taking in the beauty of the land and all the items in the game are well done to not push your hardware but enough to still make it pleasant to play  7/10The sound design in the game again is not ground breaking but for a indie developer it is very much on par and does the game justice. A lovely soundtrack played in the background with various ques depending on the situation triggers the appropriate ambience for the scene. There is a sense of peace when walking around the countryside with the music to match the scene while combat brings different style of sound to match the action. All item sounds and dialogue ques are done reasonably well and just make the game what it is.    8/10The game play is the nicest part of the game offering something quite new for the saturated genre of turn based games. Yes you build up a party which can consist up to 2 dozen men where you can develop in your own way from various soldier traits and skills and the RPG generated gear and weapons to make your play through unique. It’s a wonderful game to build this small army how you want consisting of archers, sword fighters to play your way through the game along with various buffs and de buffs using items, gear , weapons and skill upgrades. The progression system in knowledge and skills is done really well where you can open up so many perks passive and non passive to help you out not just in combat but general life as well. The game encourages you to expand each party member to special skill areas like black smith, cook and so much more trades to again open up so many possibilities for crafting and developing your party. You have the manage the troops wages and food rations along with setting up interval camps to rest and take time out to arrange inventory, skills and all sorts. This breaks ups the game from travelling and fighting and really gives you a sense of adventure . The development of camp facilities also generate many options for expansion on yoru soldiers and party so there is so many ways the game evolves and makes it unique. The combat is simple but with all the right elements as you would expect with a turn based game   8/10 The controls are quite simple and all customizable. There is only really a handful of major controls needed with a few minor controls to develop your custom play. Every menu, option and action can be assigned to a key or mouse button making the game fully customized.     8/10The game has recently come out or early access to full release and in a  very quick time. The development of the game has come a long way since first release. The games works on short story missions to help people and pick sides towards a overall land divide between rulers and occupants. The rpg element effects who you stand with but nothing too dramatic like many rpg games. You are free to be good or bad and decide what do to. The story opens up across a handful or rather large lands or regions each with there own environment, set up and people. The game will keep you interested as you discover new things and take on these missions but they are mostly based on small but lots of side missions. At this stage I am not sure if a major plot line kicks in as I am only in the first region right now but the game can easily be developed in so many ways.  The game is great. Something different to play away from the shooters and stereo typed games. The world is amazing and nice to play in a non monster alien environment with real weapons. I love the divide between combat, adventure, resting and development to make the play through different and spaced out. The game has come a long way since more than other early access games and I can see and tell the developers know they had and have something special here and pushing more. 38 out of 50 A strong 38 dues to being a small development and done such wonderful things and so fast with a game that has hardly had any problems or bugs since the start. This not being your platinum AAA game with all the marketing doesn’t mean a score of 38 is low , its just the game as it is in style isn’t quite a major game but this figure will go up with content and development which I can see happening very quick

_childDocuments_.review: Wartales is a great base game that will have you hooked for a while as you figure out its mechanics and learn how to optimize the gameplay, but ultimately will disappoint the further you get through the game.Most of the flaws I see in the game are things I can imagine being solved with future DLC or expansions, but right now the flaws are as follows:- Difficulty scaling isn't good.  There are 3 modes of difficulty, and each only has a 10% difference between them.  The hard mode should be much harder than it is.- Balance isn't great.  Some unit types completely outperform others.- Unit variation is lacking.  Each area has a certain 'tribe' of unit types, which are ultimately ~5 units that are are offshoots of generic base types.  Tanky unit, archer unit, damage dealing unit.  They almost always have the same weapons, traits, etc.  There are no notable bigger threats in the way of units or roguelike elements that randomizes them in either ability or tactics.  You end up having the same fights over and over.- Lack of abilities on units.  Each unit really only ever has one or two meaningful abilities.  It doesn't feel like your units scale in complexity as you level them up, they only scale in raw passive power through items, gear and passive perks.- Lack of weapon variation in crafting.  Often the best weapons for a majority of the game will be crafted weapons, and for each crafted weapon there is only one type of attack per weapon.  In addition to having one ability, you're also going to feel locked into having one attack type a lot of the time.- Scaling in the way of party size is counter-intuitive.  If you have a big party, you will face more enemies.  This leads to longer battles that are more tedious, and notably it means that each of your units individually will have less gear, less skill book upgrades, less legendary weapon priority, will cost you more food, will cost you more in wages.  A bigger party actually makes you substantially weaker, overall.  It means your individual units are worse and you're paying more in upkeep, while the enemy scales to match your party size so there's no advantage gained.I recommend this game for fans of this genre, just know that it still feels kind of like early access in my opinion.  This is the kind of game that has a great foundation, but won't really feel finished until it gets more content.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about the game. However it was a mostly positive experience so I do recommend it especially if you like Battle Brothers. This is the same concept, but is different enough to still be fun. The graphics are obviously very nice, and the turn based combat is fun. The different character roles work well together and can create very complex battles where you really need to use your brain and think about the turn counter and how you should utilize your characters.The game is difficult on anything but easy. The easiest settings give a very relaxing experience but anything harder can be brutal. I played the bulk of my hours on the easiest settings but do plan to play again on harder difficulties. Easy can still be a challenge when you take on harder jobs however. So can only imagine how hard they are on difficult.The game, unlike battle brothers, has somewhat of a story campaign for each region you visit. You can do regular jobs, or take on these story jobs. I find the story quests to be quite fun and not a waste of time. They reward you well enough, but the stories themselves are often very interesting. And you always get to pick a side too and come out with different endings to their stories. You don't feel like the central part of these stories, but still a very influential force in the world. The world itself is not procedurally generated but is very well crafted. And I enjoyed exploring the map. Nearly all the interactions you make outside of towns and traders are interesting and leave you with a choice to handle the situation differently if you wish. Often times you can make a choice and see the effects later on at another location and face regret and sympathy which might change how you choose to play.  You might kill someone after the guards hired you to hunt and kill him, but only find from those who knew him that he was looking for materials to make clothes for his people back at camp. To help them survive the cold winter. You don't know it when you kill him, but when you find his camp later in the game you hear the truth, and they're still wondering when their friend will come home. And they doubt they'll survive if he never returns.That's just one example of an interaction you might have in this game. The world is full of places to explore. And all of this sounds great right, but why are my thoughts on this game mixed as I mentioned earlier?Well... the mechanics gets quite repetitive, stale and quickly becomes a grind. You between interactions, combat and trades, you're walking across the map and frequently have to use a rest feature to keep your camp happy. You have to feed them on each rest too. This makes travelling the vast map a chore quite quickly. You also just move across the map very slow in general so rests make it even slower and less fun. There's also a lack of people to encounter on the roads. They are either gonna be bandits, refugees, guards or traders. From my playtime that's all I've seen. Oh and wolf/ boar packs but they are just as insignificant as those you meet on the roads. So travelling between settlements is usually uneventful and pretty boring. You can attack and raid traders and any other groups you see but usually the reward doing this isn't worth it.There also isn't a huge variety in quests, outside of the story campaigns. The regular quests are usually pretty lame and consist of go here, kill these people. Done. That gets quite repetitive quite quickly. I know you're a mercenary company, but even battle brothers had a good quest variety. I think the game just needs more quest types that aren't just go here kill these people type quests.However these are really my only issues. Everything else is fairly enjoyable and the first few hours are the best. The more you play the more you realize how repetitive everything is. So yeah, just be aware of that.Solid 7.5/10 from me anyways

_childDocuments_.review: This has the potential to be a very good game, but there are some things that really need to be fixed before it is officially launched. The quests are badly written. Sorry, but my fourth grader writes more imaginative stories. Their outcomes really don't matter, and in many cases you don't have control over them even if you did: in one region there's a conflict between the locals and some refugees, and I helped them each out basically evenly, siding against whoever was being a jerk in each situation. But it left me at the end with no choice but to go and slaugher the refugees whom I'd been working with, based on some stilted and badly-explained logic within the story progression. In a well-written story system, I should have been able to put a sword through the lady asking me to do that. So, with no story to speak of, much of the rest of the game is mostly about grinding. But there isn't even that much grinding, as progression is quite quick (or capped way too low): my party got to level 5 out of the maximum of 9 before leaving the first region.I did like quite a few things: the way armor works in combat is a good idea, and avoiding the random-number generator to determine whether you hit (you and the enemy always hit) makes combat feel different and interestingly more strategic, as you are working to optimize where you're taking and giving damage instead of just hoping for good dice rolls. The equipment progression lacked diversity but overall I liked the focus on finding good materials and crafting quality equipment instead of finding whiz-bang items. Despite the game description, there are really only three classes: archer, rogue, and fighter. The differences between the fighter classes and the sub-variants of the others is minimal at best. Some of the sub-class trees, like most of the rogue/ranger ones, are worthless (at least for my playstyle), but the game allows you to respec these characters which is good. I liked the addition of "professions" to characters so they could help the party with different tasks. At one point my blacksmith died and it was a significant blow to the party, which was good immersion. Overall, the character system is good, but not great. Character advancement also needs some polish: each character really only has three stats, cleverly disguised as 6. One of them you can't even change (Dexterity for fighters and Strength for non-fighters). Willpower is basically meaningless. So you have your core attack stat, constitution, and critical hit percentage as primary stats, with combat movement speed as an awkward addition. Nevertheless, I found the combat and character management pretty fun. I wish there was more of a story to motivate it, and maybe individual personality or profession traits to inform dialog and interactions.I hope they add the ability for the community to add quests and storylines, because the ones that come with the first three regions or so are (or should be) basically throwaway content.

_childDocuments_.review: --- Early Access Review/Feedback ---7.5/10. Game would be much higher rated if it was less grindy.Here's my pros and cons:----pros----1. Neat exploration system2. Pretty good combat and some minor build variety (devs, you should really balance some of these trees)3. You can tame animals and field them, take prisoners from bandits and turn them in for bounties, there's a lot of pretty cool mechanics like this.----cons----1. Can't adjust difficulty after starting (once you learn the mechanics game gets much easier, you shouldn't have to start over in such a grindy game to have fun combat again)2. Profession exp is uh... a mess. Way too slow, way too grindy. Fishing and Mining need to give more per node, especially if you are adding a tier above journeyman in the future. You need hundreds upon hundreds of iron to level up your tinkering and blacksmithing.3. Paths are super super grindy, but you need level 4 in them for the good stuff. This is a single player game, these should not be nearly as hard to get levels in as they currently are. 4. This is a big one to me. Legendary boss drops: You should not receive items far higher than your level. I understand bosses need to scale, but why not just juice up their stats rather than giving them higher lv items that your team cannot use? This is probably my #1 complaint. It takes a long time to level in this game, I shouldn't have to wait many hours to equip cool loot an elite dropped. 5. Bears are way too OP, for both the player and fighting them. _childDocuments_.review: The resource management kills the freedom this game intends you to play with. It is visually good and overall game play is very good but after a few hours you notice the glaring problem. You go broke because you have to pay and feed your companions and a high amount too. Items are super expensive and have little resale value. Bounties change difficulties on you. You may start out with an easy bounty but it could turn into a hard bounty by the time you get there same pay though. So you will not make money on it after wages, food, medicine, and all the loot you dont get.  This game has potential, the open adventure mode is awesome, there are a lot of companions in the world. The jobs your companions have to take on is a pretty neat function. I feel like they are torn on which way to take this game. At the heart it is a open world turned based mid evil rpg. Where this game splits is between fetch quests/stuff to accomplish and an active economy based game. To me personally i would like to see this game go the economy way like Port Royale. Have some combat and a slight storyish quests and game, but add more economy at the core. Make trading an actual thing, Like being a trader yourself and having NPCs stop you for things or even open a shop or start caravans. You have all these abilities to make and craft stuff which you have to do because the economy is so broken but yet also include wages. Its so confusing when you play this game. I dont pay money on games to grind like its real life and stress over having fun or trying to pay my bills like this game does. You have to chose to grind and try to keep your original crew that you have customized and worked on or have fun but be broke and lose every battle because you have no crew and you die, game over. There is no in between. The second you start to explore or face an unnecessary battle you have started to lose the game.  Pros:Easy to figure out controlsbig world to explorechoices have consequence Fighting is fun and involves strategy (xcom like)Character roles and jobs weapon variety with craftingearly access so it may get better!Cons: Economy is badparty food consumption is too highThe world grows with you too fast (enemy stacking and difficulty)very grindy  Loot received from battle is almost noneEarly access this could be the best it gets....This barely gets a nod to recommend because i have high hopes on where this could go, its only been out a year and some change at the time of writing. This game has a lot of potential, we will see where they take it. Update: They have fixed a lot of the problems but you still have an ok game. i get making it challenging but perma death on characters you spend a lot of time upgrading and outfiting only to go into a fight you should win and get smoked because somehow reinforcements are 1 turn away and it went from 4v6 to 4v12 and you get stuck in the battle if you didnt save before so that entire game is lost because you can get locked into a battle you can not win no matter how hard you try and game over. this is one of those game it does a lot right but they just cant let go of old mechanics that are frustrating and damning more than rewarding. As it sits this is a 5.1/10 for recommend. I will give it a few more months and it may gain a little ground.

_childDocuments_.review: When the metal meets metal  in the din of combat it just feels so flat. And the combat is the bulk of your time in Wartales. Despite having to spend all your time in combat, the game's strength is its role-playing elements. Managing your party, exploring the world map, talking to people you find, taking contracts, buying/selling/crafting in town -- all fun. the combat though---Instanced battles begin with placement of your party. You are restricted to placing your troops in pre-set squares on the battlefield.You are forced to array your troops in a nonsensical and incongruous formation. There is no quick way to locate who you want other than tabbing through everybody. There is no button to easily highlight your and enemy troops.  I kept my crew to 8 men but I couldn't imagine having to manage more than that.  So by the time you manage to assemble your party, you've got to work through the battle-Its been stated elsewhere, but the best strategy is always to just DPS down the first guy to move in the opponents queue. Granted, the RPG experience always requires an element of  identifying and prioritizing enemies. But here the game punishes you for any deviation from simply banging down enemies one at a time before they take their turn, if possible. There is no push and pull in the decision on who to move or attack.You can turn off the ability to see the queue.  Since this is the only element of planning/strategy required I prefer leaving it on. Enemy fighters inexplicably go straight through fire/poison other hazards, enemies brutally slaughter their own men with arrows. Even the greenest of captains would know to position melee fighters and ranged men with some forethought, rather than subjecting them to friendly fire. I liked  idea of taming wildlife and putting them to work hauling gear or putting them in the fight. Unfortunately the enemy scales to the addition of combat bears, and the animals are no match for a man with a sword. The camera is permanently stuck at a zoomed in, low angle. This compounds the difficulty of locating your and the enemy troops. Overall it feels likes the whole thing has been designed with the console in mind (not necissarily a bad thing). After 23 hours i've learned the functions of the classes (If this is to be a proper role playing game, it would be a good idea to  present this info clearly and from the beginning). My party is slightly under level for the second zone so the main quests are a bit above my strength. I have to go grind up my men to proceed with the main quest. Unfortunately the combat is such a chore I would rather not proceed. I credit the effort made to craft a world and ask the player to plan ahead and work with interacting systems. But, rather that having to spend time thinking about the nuance and choices available, I wind up grinding through battle after battle in rudimentary boredom, frustrated with a UI that seems to also be fighting against you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was released too early. Since my original review, I've put in 15 or so hours. The scaling is omnipresent, and you'll never enjoy the fruit of your labor because of it. The challenge will always be the same. Enemies - even in the starting region - just grow with you.Further, there's no meaningful sense of choice. For example, I took a job where the client purported to require me to ransom and return his boss's daughter. I ransomed her, and she demanded I kill three squads of guards to attract the attention of a commander so she could exact her revenge. The game gives you no choice but to murder cops for her, even though the job I agreed to was only to return her to the client. There's really no excuse for this not to be a choice for the player, and this ruins any ability on your part to role play your group as you see fit.The innovative world map shows a lot of promise, but the underlying atmosphere and universe dynamics are weak at best.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not sure I have managed to come to a negative conclusion in relation to a game this quickly before.The combat in this game as it stands is irredeemably bad and makes the game entirely way too bothersome to play with.The lack of any turn markers or fixed turn order for your own troops, the need to end every single individual turn, the way of utilising skills, the energy system and combat effects are all things that in this setting just do not work well together.The way the grid system works just takes getting used so I cannot list that as a negative but there are definitely negatives arising from it, including positioning (or the lack there of) and the way ranged units behave and operate. The main problem being in all of these cases is that the game clearly is focused around engaging with the combat system itself, with everything else, travelling and interacting with the world, the profession minigames, quests, camp management and relations all falling wayside, neither being well done enough to hold the game up from a mismanaged combat system, especially with the way food management, wages and energy works.Let's be honest here, no core aspects are getting changed or modified to such an extant that would fix that feeling of incompleteness and lack of unity, so my advice is, despite the somehow overwhelmingly positive reviews that would make getting the game seem appealing, as happened to me, don't buy it, not unless there are some extreme changes done.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this as a lover of the game Battle Brothers. So in large part this review serves to help people like me that are looking for another game to love within that genre. I have played about 6 hours so far, so I don't doubt that there will be nuances to learn, so this review is very much first impressions.Wartales is primarily an RPG game, which is a major difference to Battle Brothers which is primarily turn based combat. The way that your mercenaries interact with each other is an important aspect of the game, they can upset each other / please each other etc. There is a great deal of resource collection, management and crafting to manage your squad. You also have a high degree of micromanagement opportunities for every member of your group, including traits.The story line is strong and offers a lot of genuine choices about what sort of company you want to run and which side you want to support.The strength of story line does offer some capacity for replay, where you can try to play for the other side and muck about with how guards will react to you.Graphics are easy to look at without being cartoonish.The general feel is quite chilled out, this is easily a game which you could sink several hours in to when tired or wanting to let some time pass without angst.Interesting new talent tree / build mechanics to think through.The music is pleasant, but not particularly memorable.Combat is quite basic, basically just gear checking rather than tactical. I know there are some nuances in how/when to use your points, but compared to games like Battle Brothers the combat system in this is very basic.The pathing is very poor. Your squad will regularly get stuck along tree lines / mountains forcing you to click away. Basically, you have to have line of sight to move to a space, the game will not path it for you. Some may regard this as part of the game, but for me it is a real quality of life fail on the design front.The biggest con for me, is that I don't think Wartales has the same replay value as Battle Brothers. Once you are through the story line a couple of times there won't be a great deal to aim for. That won't matter if you come back to the game every few months, and also I don't doubt that there will be DLC expansions to increase the variation and replay opportunities, but as it stands now there is an obvious 'end point' for replay value in this game.The cons aren't a big deal for a game at this price point, it is definitely worth picking up if you like RPG games with a light squad combat element.If you are looking at this purely because you want something very similar to Battle Brothers, then I would say this is NOT the game for you. It doesn't have the same tactical depth / squad building focus of BB, this is primarily a RPG game and you need to be aware of that.

_childDocuments_.review: How to describe it?  A turn-based combat, open-world exploration, small-group mercenary medieval-style RPG.  Addictive, time-sucking goodness with challenging elements both in battles and party management (especially early-game) and a load of tomb exploration, arena fights, fun mini-games and comical Easter eggs.  Don't listen to the people who are disappointed that the developers made the game more accessible.  Adding easier difficulty options was needed and they simply responded.  You can still play difficult if you like. _childDocuments_.review: Its fun for a little bit until you realize you're in a loop of doing the same ♥♥♥♥ over and over again and nothing changes, the definition of insanity. You get more party members but now you're fighting more enemies and every fight is taking forever to the point it gets very old. The game also goes by Divinity difficulty settings which means on higher difficulty the enemies will have more health and do more damage to your mercs who are literally the same level and class. But lower difficulty is so easy that its boring af and none of your people are ever at risk because you just run through every enemy you face with ease. You can still get a lot of hours in this and have fun but eventually you will hit a wall and realize you have pretty much seen all of the game play this game has to offer in terms of features. It comes off as a deep squad management open world survival rpg but really its just a barebones one that has gives you zero sentimental value towards your company members, i played 20 hours and i didnt give af about any of my people and about 10-12 died in my play through, 3/4 of my starting members died pretty quickly into the game and i literally couldn't have cared less. The game just does a really bad job in providing a narrative or just some type of crisis that makes you care for these people, they try with the campfire talks but really that's the only time you can actually see any character or life inside of your members and it still doesn't matter because the ♥♥♥♥ they say isn't well written in the sense that "oh ♥♥♥♥ that was deep" or "i really like this guy". The members usually just say the stupidest ♥♥♥♥ that has nothing to do with anything and than the game gives you dialogue options that have little to zero effect on the party or character. I want to recommend Wartales but its just boring, period I regret buying it even though i had fun for a little bit. Im just upset because i was hype for a good alternative to battle brothers with the same amount of depth and sentimental value in terms of squad members . Battle Brothers is way better and BB did a phenomenal job of making you care about your company members and not too mention Battle Brothers is one of the most goated games of all time when it comes to replay ability. Sure Battle brothers game play loop is similar in terms of your literally just feeding and paying your members until you get wiped but battle brothers is always interrupting you with narratives that involves your company members and you get very immersed in your members this way by reading all the absolutley well written random narratives(dont know what else to call it, anyone who has played BB knows what im talking about) It brings life and personality to your characters you begin to care about them to the point that if a certain 1-2 of them die than its game over or you will want it to be game over. _childDocuments_.review: + combat system+ complex management of resources and people+ decision making in maps+ difficulty- very lengthy- boring mini-games with professionsIn Wartales, the player controls a group of soldiers who can perform various tasks on a large world map or just rob, kill and even eat their opponents. It depends only on the player how he decides. Individual members of the group have their own classes, mainly weapons and equipment depending on what attacks they have available, and their development also depends on the game. However, the game drags on a lot, and it takes a long time to level up or to solve the entire map area, and it involves a lot of well-mastered, turn-based battles, which at times are very similar. The group must not only have human members but also various domesticated animals.Each character can have their own profession, the use of which is connected with an annoying QTE, which unfortunately affects the result. And so when forging armor, mining materials, fishing, the player must be bored during QTE.In addition to battles, the player is in charge of managing the camp, which gradually improves the management of resources such as food and healing.Areas have their own main story, the course of which is influenced by the behavior of the group, and often offer different solutions to the quest or the main problem.The game also includes a relatively unsuccessful exploration of old ruins, which offer part of the story and relatively uninteresting puzzles.Wartales is a good game, but a bit too slow to finish, especially if one chooses a higher difficulty in combination with a fixed level cap of individual areas, which then requires a lot of grinding.6,9/10
