_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game.The good:- Great variety in play style and class builds allows for varied replayability.- The story is decent and takes a back seat, allowing the player to pave their own way without being locked into some alignment or another.- Your party members are a bit bland personality-wise, but every one of them will prove themselves vitally important, making your team feel like a true squad of bros that you care about.- The danger of permadeath means that even on lower difficulties you can't simply faceroll everything.My gripes:- Game was clearly made for console. PC controls got a back seat. The world map is meant to be analog-sticked around. PC has some wonky pathfinding that was clearly tacked on without much consideration. Pathfinding is not smart enough to get around objects. That goes for climbing a mountain as well as walking around a broken down wagon.- The camera during fights is annoying. It's got the Larian whiplash issue (jumping from character to character at light-speed as turns change). There's some issue with looking around the battlefield. I assume it's a bug, but the camera doesn't like to pan far from the character you selected until you click around a few times and then it suddenly loosens. Probably my biggest gripe with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic!(No spoilers ahead, just our first experience)Four friends set out to become adventurers and make a name for themselves.  The first 3 weeks went well, but on day 23, things took a turn for the worse.  It was a chilly winter's evening in the Tiltren County mountains, when the party was ambushed by a pack of wolves.Renn was the first to fall.  The ranger did all she could to keep her friends safe, and threw out one final poison vial before she was torn apart.Belmont, the brute, watched in horror as Renn was swarmed by the beasts.  He lashed out in a furious rage and killed as many as he could before finally bleeding to death.Omen, the swordsman, stood strong and kept the remaining creatures at bay while the archer fired her bow as fast and as hard as she could.  He eventually succumbed to his wounds, leaving one final wolf to deal with.Exhausted, terrified, and devastated by the loss of her companions, Fletch fired her final three arrows, while running for her life.  The last one landed right between the eyes. It was over... She was the only one left, aside from their pack mule, Darlin...Fletch buried her fallen party in the snowy mountains and took the mule, now over-encumbered with the belongings of her closest friends, and made the three-day journey back to town in silence...

_childDocuments_.review: Edit:Each time I go back to this the less I like it. It feels like they've looked closely at Battle Brothers and tried to replicate the basic features.However, it doesn't play like BB at all. The battles in BB are far more nuanced than Wartales. * In WT, suppose you have X armor and Y health, and someone hits you for Z hit-points.** If Z > (X+Y) then you are toast.* Hits always hit, never miss.In BB, troop formations matter hugely, having your shield-bros backing you up gives you extra protection, but  being surrounded is a nightmare. You get back-line bros who can pole-arm, you get duellists, swordmasters, cleavers. Sometimes your guys miss.In Wartales, you start battles in one of several predefined positions. Your guys are solo fighters, formation doesn't matter much.I feel the Wartales economy is entirely frustrating, with a constant grind for food and gold which you then immediately pay-out. The need to heal / repair after battles is fine, but it's really damn expensive, again leaving a constant grind for resource.I'll leave this as "recommended" for the time being, but in my opinion BB is the better game and the extra polish on Wartales graphics doesn't quite cover the gaps I've begun to notice.===For an early access game, I'm reasonably impressed. The core mechanics are fairly solid already, although there are one or two character buffs I can't figure out how to use properly. The battles play nicely and have some novel elements, such as spears you can pick up and throw for zero AP. The main limitation at the moment is the map area and the cap at level 5, but despite this I've had a fair amount of fun already. The UI took me a little time to get used to.It seems to me that Battle Brothers is one of the influences they're drawing upon, and I think they may get close to achieving this.I did receive this product for free, but this was via a gaming site membership, not specifically from the publisher.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is in my self-interest that I'm hoping more positive reviews will bring more players and help the devs to further build better and more complete game. This is going to be very long post because I don't know how to write reviews and this is my first time posting something on Steam.In summary, I recommend this game.Pros:1. Many build options. There are six basic types (Sword, Mace, Polearm, Bow, Dagger, Axe).And Sword, Mace, and Axe could split into 2-h and 1-h with a Shield.So I would say there are 9 basic types.Each basic types have five layers of 3 skills. (one of which is class, and I'm not counting level 12 skills since it's not unlocked yet).That's 15 skills per type.With 15 skills, you can have 243 permutaitons.243 times 9 = 2,187 different characters you can build.And that's not including two additional classes I unlocked with their additional skills.And then there are 7 (it shows 8 but I haven't unlocked the 8th job) jobs.Of course, not all permutaitons would be optimal and I see posts about certain builds being OP etc. etc. My point is that there are many options to build your character and your band of mercenaries. I would say that it's a good replayability.2. Many crafting options.Food, offhand weapons, primary weapons/armors (though weaker compared to your loots), oils, camping gears, etc. I'm still unlocking them and learning them after 190 hours of play.3. Different options to resolve quests.Though there are some quests that broke immersion by first asking me to kill everyone to reach the point where I get an option to save people. I still like the fact that I do get an option to pick a side (at least at the end, most of the times) for story quests and get an option to avoid violence using food, items, or influence points.4. Wanted LevelSo not everything is for you to pick up freely. You steal something and you are not skilled enough, Guard may chase you. Makes things more interesting and challenging. You can't (or you could if you are strong enough) just walk around killing everyone either. (that stupid merchant...).5. Different region with different challengesI got pretty comfortable with Tiltren, Arthes, and Vertruse, then I got to Ludern.Those mosquitos, crocswine, and poison puddles... I loved them!I thought I figured it all out, and the game threw a new challenge at me.6. Food/Wage SystemI just like the consequences of having a bigger group. More things to manage, more things to think about, more challenge.Cons:1. I like the crafting system, but the crafted weapons and armors's usefulness become obsolete rather quickly. Not a huge con.2. Lack of log screen with details. It's hard to know exactly how damages are calculated and how certain probabilities are playing out.3. There are bugs. Well, this is an early-access game. One bug that got me good was Paused battle. If I hit pause while getting ambushed by an enemy, the battle screen starts with pause, but it cannot be unpaused. Only solution for this problem is to re-load. I had to re-load twice for this problem. Both cases were after a long battle. Another bug is the Arthes region cannot be completed (I was able to "Finish" the story quest, but I couldn't get the region completion) if you take a certain action. Not a game-breaking, but I'm missing that region completion flag for Arthes. And the last bug I've seen is the tile-overlapping-preving-your-unit-from-moving-bug. If you have an animal unit next to a person unit in certain way, your person unit won't be able to move. I ran into this bug twice so far. Both times, all I had to was moving the animal unit out of the way.4. Battle could get very long. I selected "Free" Exploration mode, so the game's level-scaling. Level-scaling itself is not really a problem for me. I know there's Region-locked Exploration mode which doesn't level-scale. But some easy battles (like lower level Boars attacking you in forest) could get tedious sometimes. Especially, when you have 20-member band ;)5. How do I get wheats consistently???For me, it's not iron, wood, or any other components, but wheats I can't get enough.Not a huge problem. I'm just ranting and wanted to write five cons.I wish:1. There's a toggled feature of turning the economic system more organic.The trade routes are fixed that I can always expect to gain krowns between certain cities and the buying price of trade goods never change. The selling price does change based on the perks unlocked which is a good incentive to trade continuously.Once you figure out the trade routes (either by reading something on the net or write up yourself with a google sheet), making money becomes really easy. Not that I'm complaining, but maybe we can have a system where selling/buying a good could decrease/increase the price with increased the maximum number of trade goods (intead of 5). But agian, this may make the game too convoluted, thus a toggled feature.2. There's a auto-battle option. When a group of boars attack my band and I know I can beat them easily (well, I could out-run them, but I kinda want those porks, too). Instead of spending a tedious 20-min battle with them, I could just win the battle (or lose??) with a simulation. (maybe a secondary option to wipe them out vs win when the moral reaches high enough?)3. Wolf's guarding skill(?) (forgot the exact name. there's a skill for a wolf that can prevent it from being surprised when ambushed during a rest) is applied to the whole group. The skill's benefit is only applied to the wolf unit, but it would make the skill whole lot more useful if the benefit for not being surprised applied to the entire band.That would make taming a wolf (or an Alpha) a lot more sense.4. Boars (and/or Crocswines) were immune to mud terrain. Or similar passive to animal units. For example, mole rats in the ruins get a benefit for being in the dark and negatively affect by being in the light. It would certainly make them more challenging. Maybe a toggled feature? i.e. Allow Animal Units' Terrain Passive []5. There was a log I can see in the game. There is a lot of things happening in the game with probability including crits, sussccful negotation, tackle at a ball game, capturing a person/animal, mining a precious stone, etc. And then there are things happneing with percentage including the amount of damage blocked by Guard, Protection, Deflection, etc.The problem I'm having is that it's hard to know how effective certain buffs are without a log being printed out. For example (made up numbers and not actual numbers), my Cutthroat has 56% Crit chance with 40-50 dmg and 50% Guard-ignoring oil applied. Now he hits a Wrongdoer from behind (Ambush as it's called) and makes 40 dmg with yellow letter, meaning a Crit. Now, I do not know how much damage was blocked by the Guard, how much the original damage, how much increase was made by the Crit, and how much was actually blocked by Guard. I keep blindingly stacking things up and hoping he will deal more. If there was a log I can see in the game with some calculation details, it would make building and optimizing a lot easier.6. There was a passive income. Maybe an option to buy a mine or a sawmil or a shop to generate a passive income of krown or ingredients?My Play Summary:I'm still on my first play through and have played about 190 hours so far.Starting Region: TiltrenBattle Difficulty: NormalSimulation Difficulty: NormalSave Mode: NormalExploration: FreeRegions Completed: Tiltren, Arthes, VertruseRegions In Progress: Grinmeer, LudernCurrent Party Size: 25 (mostly lvl 10 except some work ponies lvl 8-10)* 17 battle members (14 human, 2 bears, 1 war pony)* 8 work ponies

_childDocuments_.review: Game scratches a very niche fantasy itch for me, so I keep returning to it from time to time. Forming a mercanary group, taking on bounties and missions, traveling around an open-world map and even going against law sounds very interesting to me and you can sometimes feel the thrill and hardships of such an endeavor in this game. However, it also feels extremely grindy especially if you are playing adaptive difficulty mode.    What it means is that every single fight you do at any point in the game no matter where, scales up to your party size and level. This sadly means you are losing power as you progress, more so if you are running a relatively crowded party of 8+ size. All enemies in the fight are scaled and they get bonus abilities passives etc similar to your guys leveling up, but their stats also get massively increased while you struggle to find/craft adequate gear for your mercs. I play on expert difficulty mode on both combat and exploration, with a party size of 12 mercs (one for each weapon type and profession) and every single fight takes at least 30mins I'm not joking. And believe me, you fight A LOT in this game and there are many regions with their own plot lines. So every fight becomes a slog where you do mostly the same things. Boss fights and some other structured fights like pit etc might be outside this rule but by the time I get to that content I am already bored and tired.   There are DLCs that add some content OUTSIDE the usual gameplay. One where you manage a tavern similar to dungeon master games with it's own resources, one adds a completely new zone with it's own enemy types and mechanics and one with structured endgame arena fights. While I don't have a strong opinion on these DLCs, I would like to see something that adds to the core gameplay loop instead. I think with a mercanary management/ tactical tbs game like this you can do much more and the setting has so much potential. If you wanna give this a go, I strongly suggest only buying the base version on discount, as DLCs don't add anything to your main experience, and then buy the DLCs if you like the game. Oh and play on region locked difficulty where you can at least feel meaningful progression.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game. I don't get why people are complaining about enemy scaling since you... can just turn it off. The only reasonable complaint there is why the devs made it the default optionAnd anyone complaining about food/money being hard to get, they aren't aware of or aren't using the many game mechanics to scavenge and manipulate your consumption. You can make a days worth of food last two if you know how to use the game mechanics to not receive any penaltySome tips:Stealing is literally free. Easy to get 3-4 days of food stealing one stack. Just don't surpass 100 and become wanted. If an object is in your range to not go above 100, just click on it and if the popup comes up, click cancel and click on it again until you successfully steal it. Stealing RNG is calculated per-click not just once total, so you can just keep re-rolling to stay under 100 since it warns you if you'll go overGood vibes is just as life-sustaining as food. For each person around the campfire, you can take -1 happiness from lack of food without any malus. And if you throw in one alcohol, you can receive -5 happiness total from lack of food- which in my current case is like 14 food a day we don't have to feed my troopThere's gems in the salt. Have a dedicated miner. After the first level, which you can clear after doing the first two mines once, you find gems all the time mining which is just free cashCraft your own damn gear. Rush the armor crafting perks from the start and you can have +30 armor immediately at the start of the game if you visit the mines. Unless you're a bozo, then go ahead and keep fighting those bandits for their ♥♥♥♥♥ armorMoney isn't a problem. Only thing you should really spend money on is salary. Always have enough for one salary's pay on you. But if you have extra and a source for your next paycheck coming, it can be useful to buy a good weapon from a trader very early in the game before you have all the crafting recipes unlocked. Or maybe you need 3 quick leather to make that good armor of yours. Otherwise, there's never a need to spend moneyPlaying Co-op, have the host manage armor repairs/healing. _childDocuments_.review: This is like a collection of my favorite games combined forces into a lean and mean fighting machine!There's overland travel and independent warbands wandering around like in Mount and Blade, there's a mercenary brotherhood to manage from Battle Brothers, there's resource gathering and experience earned through building and discovery like Kenshi, and there's individual development of skills and combat techniques for each soldier similar to classic RPGs like Star Ocean where in addition to learning a new way to fight your units also learn a trade, train with without weapons you can scrounge, and learn new trade options whenever you volunteer to try out a job. Basically you are traveling about with a group of destitute warriors in a wartorn land with a sandbox approach to the adventure to come. Want to earn more Krowns? Find someone who needs something done and collect the reward or loot a passing warband (or caravan if you're bold and ruthless) and sell it to the proper people to gather your money and buy better gear. During downtime at camp you can build niceties to make travel and roughing it easier. Your blacksmith can build a cooking pot for instance and you can learn additional skills to improve the warband as a whole like improved carrying capacity and gaining Valor for skills by either standing courageously beside a foe without attacking, finding an ally to bolster, or slaying the foe. There's moral choices that are not all black and white too. See what happens when someone you tried to care for takes advantage of you, or when the easy way is also the most profitable! It's a slow burn and it may take several tries because you learn by doing, but the interface is so friendly, all the parts are voice acted, there's fatalities and location specific traps to keep combat fresh, the music and sound is on point...it's just a very accessible, deep, and entertaining roleplaying/management sim!

_childDocuments_.review: An immersive an unique - though buggy and repetitive - tactical adventure.Wartales is a low-fantasy turn-based tactical RPG with open-world exploration and light survival elements. The player manages a mercenary band and adventures across the various regions of a war-torn continent, finding fame and fortune along the way. Between small skirmishes and larger battles, the player will need to make sure the band earns enough food, wages, and resources to keep its fighters healthy, paid, and safe.Combat in Wartales is deep and satisfying. There are a handful of different classes available to your adventurers, with each class having multiple specializations to further customize them. The unique skills and strengths of each unit create meaningful decisions when moving them on the battefield and engaging with enemies, whether that be through control-heavy melee attacks, powerful ranged attacks, or various support abilities. Although Wartales is relatively light when it comes to active abilities in combat, a unit's basic attack skill changes depending on what type of weapon they have equipped, leading to a large variety in tactical playstyles between even units of the same class. There is a moderate amount of enemy variety to keep things interesting for several hours of play between humans, animals, undead, and beastly monsters, though the variety does start to stagnate after completing a few regions in the game.Speaking of regions, each of the seven regions in Wartales boast their own self-contained narratives that piece into the conflicts of the larger continent. Although these narratives are not particularly inspired, and there are very few interesting NPCs that stick around for longer than a few conversations, they provide enough variety from one another to keep things feeling different from region to region. For example, one region tasks your band with assisting in the solution of a refugee crisis, while another region recruits your adventurers to investigate an important political assassination. In all these narratives, players have the ability to make decisions that impact their outcomes, though these can feel somewhat hollow or unfulfilling since they don't impact the narratives of the other regions.The light survival mechanics of Wartales are quite enjoyable, and add a lot of immersion to the experience of managing a mercenary band. Units can specialize professions such as blacksmithing, cooking, or mining to generate important resources for the squad outside of combat. Prioritizing basic necessities or equipment improvements, spending additional time to gather materials as the deadline for a quest approaches, or deciding which injured unit should get the last bottle of medicine that the party can afford are just a few of the important and meaningful decisions players will need to make as they travel the continent.Although the core gameplay loop of Wartales is gripping enough to entertain for tens of hours, Wartales is at its best when it's introducing new locations or customization options to discover, such as the ancient ruins dungeons or quests that unlock rare weapons or new specializations. However, these eventually dry up before the game's narrative content, which can make finishing the last region or two feel like a chore. Additionally, it is not uncommon to encounter occasional frustrating bugs that may require the player to restart the game. In particular, in October 2023, I encountered (and reported) a bug that softlocked my game unless I reloaded a much earlier save, and at the time of writing this review, this bug unfortunately has not been fixed.Despite its content that eventually overstays its welcome and occasional bugs, Wartales is a fantastic adventure that I would recommend to lovers of tactical RPGs - especially those that would rather flex their agency with meaningful choices instead of be beholden to some kind of sophomoric narrative.

_childDocuments_.review: Your first impression will be that this is a very basic, relatively uninspired low fantasy medieval mudcore slog, but you will quickly fall in love with the sheer amount of depth this game has to offer.The class system is amazing, the combat is really fun and actually kind of innovative for a turn based strategy game and is at the same time beautifully simple to get ahold of. There's so much story that you can find by just looking around, talking to people, reading books like an old classic RPG instead of the modern RPG storytelling meta where its shoved in your face via a cutscene. You could be just killing bandits and find a body, and then the game will inform you that that dude you picked up at the sawmill 20 hours ago recognises one of the corpses. You could do a whole zone, move to the next, and find out that one of the NPCs you met has something to do with one of these people, and you'd never have thought. _childDocuments_.review: I came to this one after bouncing off Band of Brothers, and this game definitely has some of the same similarities - managing a mercenary company that needs to be constantly fed and paid and dealing with the pressure to push forward against the risk of permanent loss.  It's an ironman-lovers formula, where stories told are largely generated by your decisions and the rolls of the dice. Wartales is much more personal, however, with your initial starting band sharing a small history you decide, and each character having particular jobs and roles in your found family of bandits, heroes, or mercenaries.  The death tolls aren't quite as high (although it's possible I'm just bad at Band of Brothers), and the personal growth of each character feels nicely paced and carefully managed.  There are all these little, simple systems that categorize how you are progressing, from your knowledge of the world leading to general party perks to each characters individual relationship.  The best example of what Wartales is, I think, comes from a simple thing I found in the first few hours. in firing a shot from an arrow into a crowded fight, I hit an unlucky 20% and accidentally shot a companion.  This wasn't a fight ender, but it had two specific mechanical consequences: one, the two party members relationship deteriorated, and two, the wounded member developed a new perk called Eyes in the Back Of Your Head, to prevent such occurences from happening in the feature.  That's the core of it - tight mechanical tactical combat coupled with consequences that are narrative on a personal level. I could speak a lot to the games seemingly open nature and the really elegant nature of its combat and experience systems, but its whats in between them that most fascinates me.  This game uses its quiet preparation time really well - despite fairly light procedural dialog, the small systems interlock in a way to create a sense of family and camraderie in your little band that feels meaningful.  Because of the non combat class system the characters you're risking aren't fully featureless fighters - they're also the ones that cook your meals, or smith your weapons, or do your laundering.  They're people that  you care about.  That's a hard trick to pull in a game of this style, and its definitely worth price of purchase even if you're only in for a few runs.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by stating that this is not a bad game. On the contrary it is a stupendous game, however, the developers have severe oversights and failed to uphold some people's expectations when it comes to certain things. I shall elaborate on these things in my review. If you do not wish to read a long review then you can read the "TLDR" at the bottom of this review.It is very fun and sort of a more simple Bannerlord style type game. You traverse regions and accomplish tasks to proceed farther throughout the story. There are many side quests to do. You can compose a group of adventurers from many different classes that each may be built in different ways. It has a lot going for it in that aspect.You can choose how difficult you wish your adventure to be. You can play it on an easy setting that a young adolescent could do or you can play the iron man mode that will make you flip your desk. Each setting is true to what it says but not being able to reload may prove troublesome when it comes to some of the issues, which I will discuss soon.The graphics are of enjoyable quality and even on lower settings it does not look like a hand drawn paint job by a squirrel on methamphetamine. The music and sound effects are of illustrious quality and you can relish in the bloody sport of war as you hear an ax crunch into the sternum of your foes severing their chest in twain. The music is soothing in so much the main menu orchestrates a simple reminiscence of medieval times in a tavern so much you could sit back with a tankard of ale and immerse yourself.Be forewarned there are spoilers ahead for the game so if you don't wish to have them please do not read farther. I will merely state that some of the features of the game need to be polished, adjusted and fixed for a more pleasurable experience. The developers should listen to the feedback of the players and adjust things as needed. Time will tell if they listen to their fanbase.The criminal thief system is quite a jest if I may say so. You are given a suspicion level in increments of 100 points. The 100 points seems like an interesting way of handling things until you realize it compares itself to Grand Theft Auto in a wanted style feature that I find to be quite extravagantly droll and rubbish.What also makes this feature rubbish is that there is an issue in the way the system relays information. If you desire to steal something it will forewarn you if you will earn a wanted level. The only catch, however, is that guards will still randomly stop to frisk you if you are over a certain suspicion level. There is a camp chest where your thief may launder items to make them legitimate however the game does not warn you if you were observed stealing which prompts guards to frisk you if you come near them.The issue with this is that if I steal from a merchant and the merchant heads east I could be stopped by guards to the west. The guards to the west were given a report of my theft and they search me. Well my good guards how could someone report it to you if they headed the opposite direction I did? If I was seen why did they not stop me if they have caravan guards themselves? Why didn't they attempt to apprehend me, warn me or confiscate my gold?So once these guards stop me I am limited on my responses. My options are to decide to fight, pay taxes on my stolen goods or to forfeit them. When I forfeit them I receive no punishment. I am let go. The system lacks immersion and also exposes guards corruption to certain events that happen in the regions as well. What motivation do I not have to not steal?To add to the matter of immersion there are many stories that do not make logical sense or cohere together well in the slightest. One such example is a woman is crying at her home. "Well my lady what is the matter?" She tells you that her poor old husband has been bitten by a plague rat and is now infested with the plague. You speak to the man and hire him into your group of merry adventurers. You take him to a doctor and he is cured. You return to the home and I thought mayhaps the wife would be exuberantly ecstatic to see her beloved again. I walk in and she is still crying. "Oh my poor husband, gods help me live on without him..." Well my good man it appears she is so overwhelmed with melancholy that she has kept the home, not divorced you and you are now deceased to her. It appears you're staying with us.There are many stories, quests, missions and dare I say plots that have this issue. It breaks the immersion of the role play of this role playing style game. Normally I could overlook some of these issues but it is a common occurrence and ruins the very theme of the game. It does not make the game itself a bad game, however, it does take away from part of the core of the game itself which is the story telling aspect of the regions and the situations going on in the game. The game itself is called "WarTales". How can we tell a tale if the tales make no sense? It can't be a fairy tale for there is no magic in this game either.There are other issues with the game of slight annoyance. When you go to a city or town you may not proceed through it. You must march around it. The pathfinding in this game is most wretchedly foul and about as reliable as a Swiss cheese boat or a lead balloon.The crafting and knowledge point system can ruin your first game if you are not careful since your knowledge point earnings are limited per region based on places you find, items you make and certain other events that give you the knowledge points. This may result in you not being able to make good food, decent early weapons or other items you may need. That being said the crafting system is severely weaker than items you will just find off of brigands and vagabonds. It almost makes blacksmithing pointless in my humble opinion.The sheer amounts of food necessary for feeding troops make you take every point you can in food reduction usage. You'll be scrounging for iron early as soon as you are able to make a cooking pot too to reduce food usage. You would think for a group of 14 adventurers 4 whole chickens, 4 giant loaves of bread, bushel of fruit and a wheel of cheese it would be enough. No my dear fellows it would seem that you will need 6 chickens, 6 breads, 2 wheels of cheese, 2 bushels of fruits, 6 bundles of jerky and some fish or mushrooms. It appears that I have an army to feed and I do not get the said benefits of an army.The game needs some polish. They even have "titles" that you can earn, but yet they are of no use. It is remnants of a system they apparently abolished in development and merely were lazy and left it in there. These signs of laziness are quite apparent in this game. As I stated before the game itself is not bad per say, but it is not quite as good as it should be.I feel as if the developer were lazy and left out the most important aspect of the "Tales" part of the game. It can not be WarTales if there are no Tales that mesh together accordingly. You can not create immersion if things are not blended together as it should be. Your core aspects of the game must make sense in order for it to be wholesome and have meaning.The game is worth barely what the price may be. I would suggest getting it on a sale, if or when there is one. If you do not care about stories, immersion or aspects making sense then perhaps this is a simpler version of Bannerlord you might enjoy. I have spent a deal of time on it and while enjoyable it has left some sand rubbing in places I don't enjoy so much. The primary place it rubbed me wrong is the immersion lack of Tales in the WarTales.I bid you good day. Safe journey and travels to you stranger. Until we meet again some other time and place.

_childDocuments_.review: After a mere 7 hrs of play it might seem a bit early to be talking superlative or sensational or whatever. What I can say as an octogenarian still  searching for the perfect game is that War Tales , for me at least is a fairly special kind of RPG experience.  For me the ability to name  your band of warriors has always been key to the successful start of any adventure or journey and War Tales lets you own your characters right from the word go.  The learning curve is manageable and even when it involves failure you wont need exhaustive tutorials to get you back on track. The graphics might not be spectacular but even the drab interiors help to set the mood of a dark and brutal world . There is a sense of ever impending doom and danger as you move through the well drawn  landscapes  and your imagination is allowed full rein.  The turn based combat and levelling up is spot on. i'm hoping I can continue to keep my band happy well fed and most of all alive.   A promising game  unfortunately let down by janky movement and directional difficulties.

_childDocuments_.review: UPD: my main point about party numbers may be wrong as of current version, as several other players have pointed out.I want to make this clear from the start: I don't think it's a bad game. I think it's maybe somewhat above average, and has some fresh, interesting ideas. Also, I would totally recommend it if you want to just chill out and do some sword-swinging.__TL:DR: the earliest versions were a masterpiece, even with missing features and full-on autoleveling. Then they have made some tweaks that destroyed a lot of tactical/strategic variety, as well as atmosphere. Now, however, my main issue is that everything in the world depends on the player's party, from enemy's numbers to contract rewards to costs of hiring additional people. But, the core features are quite good and "region-locked exploration" is a promising step.__When I got Wartales as the very early and incomplete version, it was awesome, arguably the best "tactical RPG" I know, even devoid of many features. But, as the versions progressed and the changes were made, it became worse. Today, it's... just another tRPG, I guess. With a couple interesting ideas and a number of annoying problems, just like most games.The changes themselves are quite subtle. (sorry for long explanations, it's fairly intuitive when you play).As an example, there is a very nice implementation of turn order: both your and your opponents' men are "distributed evenly" in the turn order for the round, so if the number of combatants is equal, you and enemy take turns acting with a single fighter, until all fighters act. However, for the AI, the order of its units acting is fixed, while you can act with any of your guys (who didn't act in this turn yet). While "unfair" towards the AI, it provides many interesting choices and tactics.Now, if the enemy has twice as many people as you do, for each of your actions, they make two. So, even if you kill (or otherwise deal with) the guy who acts next, another enemy will act after that and probably you'll be in some trouble. So, the difference in numbers turns out to be very, very important.What did they change? Now, the number of your enemies is always quite close to yours, and in cases it somehow isn't, the extra units will arrive later (when you already killed many enemies) as reinforcements. So, the (rightfully dreaded) experience of being outnumbered is cut from the game. Now, a lot of battles follow the same pattern: you neutralize the enemy who acts next, then he doesn't do much (or anything at all, if killed), rinse, repeat. A hundred of perfectly forgettable battles. See comments/other reviews for more examples. The early versions did convey the right experiences: you struggled to stay afloat with money, thoughtfully picked your contracts, took care of your men. But the updates made the game progressively worse. My best guess is, the game designers knew what they are doing and made bold (and really good!) decisions, but then some salespeople took over the game and made it "accessible for wider audience" or something - just another game.UPD. A list of more concrete thoughts, as brief as possible.1. The battles are similar to each other, despite good core mechanics that could allow much more variety.2. Many units from other factions that you can imprison and then recruit (unlike Battle Brothers). Sadly, with auto-adjusting enemy numbers to your party size, the game punishes you for such experimenting. 2a. Also, battles with larger parties take forever to play. I'm not saying it's wrong, just... a consideration.3. The troop deployment is atrociously illogical (many "islands" distributed evenly along the map). It speeds up the battles though.4. You're not burdened with strategy (thinking, planning, resource management), especially compared to the early versions. On strategy map, you only need to sometimes take a contract or two between free, sandbox-like exploration. On tactical map, the most dangerous enemy is the one who acts next.4a. This means that I actually recommend the easy difficulty - it's the same experience, just less grinding. 5. There is a camp management layer. I believe it was originally aimed at giving you the experience of caring for your fighters (make them a mutton stew, share a drink, and they become happier). With updates, the camp became cluttered with buildings (seriously, beehive?), and now feels like a pixel-hunting mouse-clicking chore.6. The plot is good in the first region (Tiltren), and very mercenary-appropriate in the Arthes County. Some argument can be made for Vertruse. The rest... belong in a bad Warhammer game. (for Alazar, I made this conclusion by reading the release announcement).7. Level requirements for weapons - is an artificial and counter-productive mechanic (and  also smells of MMORPG influence). Hiring a low-level character and equipping them with a nice weapon is definitely a choice, and it actually sometimes makes sense within the game's framework.7a. Considering that looting weapons from battle is randomized, I'd prefer they didn't have any level (as in, quality tier) at all. Getting the fire bow requires enough grinding/luck as it is, and repeating it for a higher level bow... is annoying. (as an exception, low level fire bow is still good). Or, make all weapons upgradable.8. Happiness mechanic is now an influence generation mechanic only.9. Paying money by rests, rather that by hours, makes food and money basically the same resource. Also, you can march your companions to near death, so that they get less money for their time...10. Plague ravages the lands, infectious are killed on sight!.. Also, you can buy a cure from most healers for a price of, say, an axe. Or, you can just eat meat and be fine. Common medicine made from two common flowers also helps.10a. Random people from tavern are better fighters than the Legion, Guard, Inquisition.UPD. The release actually happened while I was writing this. Congratulations! Despite all I wrote above, kudos for actually going all the way to the finished game, I know it's hard work.- Leave autoscaling option as is; the following applies only to region-locked mode. Maybe add an option to switch between the two, re-spawning everyone (maybe on rest) according to the new setting. (to be honest, I just want to make my old save region-locked).- On region-locked exploration, make the number of enemies fixed (maybe with random +-N%) for every entity spawning on the map. - Of course, the numbers in the later provinces should be higher. Use reasonable assumptions about the party's changes in numbers along with levelups, and grow the numbers a bit faster than that (this will make obtaining "temporary companions" a viable idea)- Make the number of deployment slots proportional to the number of enemies, and independent of the party. This way, if you're badly outnumbered, you will be able to gather everyone in one or two corners and hold the line, while the "reinforcements" will happen more naturally, starting on the same map but taking time to arrive. (obviously no artificial "reinforcements" mechanic)- Make the contract rewards dependent on the number and level of enemies, not on the player's party. This will disable the obvious exploit of the first region, and also makes more sense.- Overall, . Maybe with exceptions, when someone gathers people specifically to attack the player. The game has enough instruments to prepare and deal with fights that are hard with current party.

_childDocuments_.review: The charm and adventure of an old-school fantasy RPG intertwined with team tactics combat that feels like a Venn Diagram of XCOM and Divinity: Orginal Sin 2 that removes almost all of the RNG elements that could make it so frustrating, instead relying on genuine strategy, troop placement, and teamwork.  While it may not seem like it in the initial stages of your journey, this game has (almost) more layers than Shrek. 60+ hours in and I'm still having plenty of "oo, what's that?!" moments.  The story isn't going to be anything you haven't seen before in standard fantasy fare, but, coupled with a rich, detailed world that feels like you're walking through a renaissance painting makes for an experience that's hard to walk away from for extended periods of time. The few drawbacks I've found are that the pathing could still use a little smoothing out when it comes to the rockier terrain, and that the difficulty balance of the encounters can sometimes vary wildly within a zone regardless of difficulty settings.  Finally, I think the food consumption rate for animals needs a bit of tuning, especially since there are build options that support having a larger animal presence in your troop.  I think if you enjoy strategy games, the fantasy genre, team tactics combat, or all of the above, this is a must play.  The devs care about their game and their community, and there is so, so much to experience in the world.  It can easily be tailored for as chill or as anxiety-inducing as you want based on the encounters you seek out.  Wartales can also be played co-op, though single-player is equally as fun.  Definitely give this one a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing for over 24 hours of this game, I would say that I am quite impressed with the lore of the game and the combat system. However it is quite buggy.Lore - although I have not completed the game, I have finished the first area and helped the refugees which was cool once you finish the last battle at Stromkamp. All the characters connect well and I think there is alot of potential for the game to expand its content with even more charcters/perks/easter eggs that enriches the overall player experience in each Kingdom.Combat - I like the concept of the combat system and it is very similar to other games, however I think War Tales can improve in this regard by adding more weapons/armour types in each unit category. Even though I have been playing for only 24 hours and have not explored other parts of the map, I think that there needs to be more variety in order to balance the combat system as I found myself using the same wepons in each battle because they were just too good! For example I used the justice axe for my bersker which allowed him to double hit the enemy and kill them in one turn. A bit too op if you ask me. (More Variety and perks with units would solve this.)Bugs in the game - I found very little bugs although I got really annoyed whenever I attempted to enter into the three hares market or any other market for that fact. My game would always crash 90% of the time which is annoying since I had to buy a lot of food to maintain my band of mercenaries. So I tried avoiding entering a market for most of the game. Also some caravans would get stuck running into a town and would just bug there and not move at all. (Please fix the market glitch, very annoying.)Overall - I love the game and would recommend anyone interested in strategy/medieval Fantasy to buy this game. However I do think there needs to be more styles of weapons/perks/gear for each companion type and also more content to be explored in each kingdom which would give more bang for your buck in purchasing this game. Please also fix the bugs mentioned above. Keep up the good work Shiro Games!

_childDocuments_.review: Wartales can loosely be described as mesh of CRPG and TRPG with a heavy dose of exploration. For this reviewer, it scratches that CRPG inch for me without needing to memorise and understand a list of mechanics or skill tree(s). You are the puppet-master of a band of mercenaries who are just trying to survive in a war torn, plague beaten world. Survive is the key word in the previous sentence, no magic superpowers are around to save you. Your band of mercs are faced with a world divided into separate regions, each with there own "stories" to solve. When the compared to other CRPGs', the levelling system is basic, but fits the atmosphere of the game's world. There is a crafting system, a combat system, a "job" system, hunting and dungeons. The real highlight is exploring the world. There is just so much to do and see. Tons of mini-side quests exist to keep it fresh. Needing supplies to survive keep you moving and exploring. On harder difficulties, the combat (for me) is challenging and you can lose comrades if you don't properly prepare.Wartales is a win in my books. I don't feel the need to dedicate hours to understand and enjoy this game. I can take a break for a couple of days and jump back in and enjoy the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good surprise!I’ve been playing the game for a dozen hours and I’m still hooked.+ A refreshing experience mixing genre: tactical rpg, survival, crafting, trade, exploration etc.+ Very nice graphics (I love the bird’s view angle)+ The map seems very large and is quite busy (merchants, guards, animals walking around and sometime fighting among each other, giving you the opportunity to join)+ Plenty of things to do: missions (relatively varied), crafting (progress system very well thought), trade between villages (cash is important and not so easy to come by), camp management etc., choices to make (which faction to help etc.), new locations to discover+ The loot is well balanced (not overwhelming  like in too many games)+ Nice combat (while it may look very simple at first, improves a lot over time with a lot of different skills and more ennemies/weapons)+ How skills (including for the world map) and craft receipes are unlocked+ Mini games (and job progression) are a nice little touch, even if not much of a challenge (at least till now for me)- The atmosphere should be improved: more ambiant sounds, more music and voice acting (a least a bit) would help a lot to make the world come to live a bit more- The scenario could be more engaging, with some cutscenes and more lore- A tutorial: I like to discover things on my own but some mechanisms should be explained (capturing animals and prisoners etc.)- Combats could be more dynamic (faster pace, more special effects, close ups etc.)I noticed that people were complaining about a high difficulty.I’m playing normal and I’m enjoying it (and will certainly try the future Ironman mode in high difficulty later one when it comes out).I think the game is well balancedas it is. Some skills might be a bit too powerful, and once you have good armor (and plenty of supplies to fix broken gear after battle) it gets much easier.The studio already announce a nice dev roadmap so no doubt the game will keep improving.There would be much more to say and I think I still have much to discover but so far it has been already a very pleasant journey!I highly recommend this game, even in its early access state.PS: after the recent patch, it's getting even better (happiness, tutorial etc.) I'm now restarting the game in hard mode ironman ;-)

_childDocuments_.review: Game is great and the early access phase has been awesome. It's always nice to see when an early access game actually gets delivered in a timely manner. Not only has the price not been increased but they are launching with a 25% discount, meaning people who bought it during early access paid more for the game than people who bought it on release. _childDocuments_.review: Good groundwork, lots of continuing work to be done. Not a diamond yet, but with polish it could be. 6.5/10 with 9/10 potential. The first 15 or so hours in this game are amazing, they built a cool world for you to explore. Great mini-games, great XCOM like combat, mid tier RPG system, cool art style, wonderful blending of Mount and Blade with XCOM with multiple other influences sprinkled in.Then you get to the 20-25 hour mark and realize that the game just becomes an incredible grind to get better gear. Your character levels don't really matter, your character abilities don't really matter without great gear, and your party size is almost more a hindrance than a help as enemy groups will ALWAYS scale with you. If you are super lucky you might get a single group of enemies that have the same unit amount as you. While this is usually isn't an issue as your characters are more powerful then the enemy, it makes you feel like you NEVER get ahead. You will NEVER have an advantage over the enemy due to numbers, which makes having a large company feel worthless. In cases like the rat hives, and in wolf packs great! In cases of bandits and high level opponents this is so painful.(Note that the enemies will not scale with the total level of your characters, they will scale with the highest level character. Having a group of 6 with 1 lvl 7, and 5 lvl 5s will get you an enemy group of lvl 7s.) To the devs credit, the enemies do NOT scale their abilities, they will always remain the same(exception for faction abilities that show with certain groups later on) making certain enemy groups easy to defeat at nearly any level.Here are a few more notes:-If you don't have the materials to create better gear, you will find yourself traveling vast portions of the map wasting your food and money, clicking on farmable resources that you wish you could buy in excess(wood, leather, ghost hides), only to get trapped in the gameplay loop of, mission->money->resources->crafting with looting speeding the process along. -Heal system makes sense, and is well thought out. -Armor system is painful and makes you want to pull your teeth out. Having to pay to consistently repair the armor on ALL my characters felt like an intentional method to slow the game down in order to stretch game time. Having an armor durability system allowing the armor to break, offering less protection at lower condition makes more sense, this system seriously sucks.-Food is a cool system and does a good job of putting a survival element feeling into the game. You will rarely go hungry, and food sources are easy to come across, or buy. No issues to speak of with this.-The amount of resources around the map is pitiful given how often you are expected to have them.(Purely map collected resource points: wood, flowers, iron, mushrooms, etc.)-Many resources can only be acquired from certain mobs, makes perfect sense, but the amount you receive is hardly worth the effort. Killing an entire pack of 8-10 wolves can reward you with 3-5 leather. An incredible waste of time that again serves to lengthen the game as this resource is fairly difficult to buy but incredibly important.-Crime and stealing is a very odd mechanic. It just makes no sense. The patrols are incredibly easy to dodge, the detriments are nearly nonexistent as your crime only lasts for as long as you can. Just makes no sense to me at all. That being said, its super useful and can help you avoid a lot of costs.-World map items are genius. The pinion mechanic is brilliant and more mechanics similar to this would really make the game shine.-Combat is easy to grasp and presents similar to XCOM. It is very odd that status effects never appear to end without player intervention. Poisoning and Burning can quickly become very dangerous for the unprepared player. Burning patches of ground continuing to burn during rainstorms, and poison clouds that never dissipate is another oddity. -Character RPG elements are mid-tier to lacking. While you do have the ability to customize your characters, many of the abilities that you get(whether active or passive) feel very similar and offers limited amount of playstyles with certain characters. Your characters stats do effect the gameplay, but only slightly, as the largest bonuses are gained through equipment bonuses and not necessarily through experience. Late game a high level character with many aptitude points will be better than a low level character, but a low level character with the best gear in the game vs a high level character with lvl 1 gear is no contest, The gear level makes a MUUUUCH bigger difference than the character stats. This is my biggest issue with the game as it feels that there is no point to developing your characters as the gear means much more than their stats.The exception to this is character professions-Character professions are a very cool element added to the game, HOWEVER characters being locked to one profession really sucks. If characters were able to still reach level 2-3 in other professions while specializing to reach level 5 in one main would make much more sense, and would offer much more options in team composition. The game uses this system to inflate the amount of characters you need in your party as you need more characters to fill all the professions.  Additionally, you gain profession experience at painful rates. Thieves gain experience at a very fast rate, while anglers and cooks xp bars move like molasses. Regularly this would be no issue as character professions would be an afterthought and could be put to the side, however in this game many important recipes and buildings that offer numerous buffs are hidden behind character professions that much be individually developed. Don't like smithing? Too bad its really important or you are going to spend a ton of time farming. Don't like crafting your own medicine? Pay the price in time spent in the town at the apothecary and you will never be able to get too far from town. Don't care for the camp layout system? Too bad, it matters where your characters go and that you cook better food and create useful tools. My point is that the game gets so micromanaged at times that you feel as though you cannot even accomplish some of the simplest tasks without needing to make a mission out of it.-Capturing injured enemies and animals is a wonderful mechanic but its incredibly underpowered and should be avoided unless attempting to capture a powerful animal. The animal that you capture will be considered a new company member and will artificially inflate your company numbers against the next enemies you encounter. Perfectly fine if you have captured or bought a bear, but a wolf, or a boar? They are nothing but fodder and will get you killed against enemies more powerful than them. This title has so much potential and I can see a truly awesome game that just needs some polish.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I like this game, in its current state I can't recommend it.Pros:- Well designed combat mechanics- Great concept, feels like a mix between Mount and Blade and some of the Fire Emblem games- World design is also well writtenCons:- Traversing the map can be a nightmare as you have to figure out routes to get to certain spots, which sounds like an interesting design, but you may be forced to save scum just so you can get a route that doesn't end with your party's immediate demise, it's also glitchy, as whenever you click on a location to enter, sometimes your party doesn't even go there and just stands in place like a bunch of tards, which could make life or death scenarios go completely against your favor, especially when you're getting chased by a party significantly stronger than yours.- Your party can get exhausted from travelling, which isn't so bad at first, but it just gets tedious after a while, the only redeeming factor is the camp system which is "OK" but in the early game can get pretty boring- Combat can become completely unfair, sure the game tells you when each enemy is going to attack so you can plan accordingly, but sometimes you are forced to split your party in the most inconvenient way possible, as at the start of each encounter you must place your mercenaries in predetermined spots, but more often than not the spots are placed in the worst areas possible, meanwhile the AI is able to consistently flank you at the start of the match because they almost always get the best starting spots. Not to mention the random bits of terrain that keep you from moving to vital positions in the worst, most unfun ways possible.- Finding resources to make decent equipment is really hard to come by, and the weapons/armor to do so are way too demanding.- UI desperately needs improvement, and due to the lack of a tutorial I was left confused wondering how to access certain things or what certain icons even meant.- Enemy AI can be dumber than a bag of hammers. I have, on numerous occasions, seen the AI outright skip its turns on normal difficulty.- Game needs to tweak the difficulty of early game enemies, or at least give the player some way of reading how difficult an area is without shoving enemy parties twice their size with no warning.

_childDocuments_.review: Wartales is a game that has truly exceeded my expectations. This PC game from Shiro Games is a perfect blend of RPG and strategy elements, and it provides players with an immersive and engaging experience that is truly hard to find in today's gaming world.First of all, the game's graphics are absolutely stunning. The attention to detail in the characters, the environments, and the animations is remarkable. Whether you're exploring the game's beautiful landscapes or engaging in epic battles, you'll be amazed by the level of detail and care that has been put into the game's world.Juggling wages and keeping your band of mercs and possibly some captured prisoners fed, can prove to be challenging at first but plays a keep part of the immersion simulation, and does tend to feel easier to grasp the more you play.What really sets Wartales apart from other games in its genre is its deep and intricate gameplay. The game allows players to control a small group of characters and engage in a variety of quests and battles across a vast, open-world map. There are countless ways to approach battles, exploration feels truly rewarding and the game's non-linear design means that players are free to explore and experiment as much as they like.One thing that I particularly love about Wartales is its emphasis on strategy. Battles are challenging and require careful planning and execution, but the game's mechanics are easy enough to understand that even novice players can jump right in and start having fun. And with the ability to customise and level up your characters, trying out different builds and specialising their skills, you'll always feel like you're making progress and growing stronger as you progress through the game's various challenges.Overall, I highly recommend Wartales to anyone who loves RPGs, strategy games, or just great video games in general. Its beautiful graphics, deep gameplay, and emphasis on strategy make it one of the best games I've played in recent years. If you're looking for a game that will keep you engaged for hours on end, Wartales is definitely worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Wartales

_childDocuments_.review: So, I'm in over a 160 hours. You're paying for an early access game (which i do feel like is pretty high for an EA) so it isn't completely flushed out as far as content goes. From the road map they have laid out - It looks like that will eventually come. So there is ZERO hate towards to current available content. It is what it is. It is EA. This isn't an RPG as i think most people had hoped for. I'm not even entirely sure why they labelled it as such. There is very little character or "troop" development passed the rudimentary skills applying to each member of your band. You aren't getting yourself a true RPG game. More so .. maybe troop management, none of your characters have a backstory and none of them have any ties to the world they now reside in.. There is very little for the player to connect with their characters. They are easily disposable and replaceable. So there is no player emotional connection. Your troop are nothing more than just fodder for you to get to the next area or contract. I think if the dev's place some importance on character to player connection. That would help this game some. The base of this game, so far, is to roam back and forth between the available map areas, pick on contracts and collect money to pay and feed your men. There is no other reason or goal, other than this. If you don't pay them or feed them. They get upset and leave your troop. Which, has no real penalty because the game scales its' difficulty to the size/level of your troop.  In fact, there really isn't even much incentive to hire new mercs'... because the larger your team, the large to enemy team will be. The majority of your time in this game, is spent doing the old rinse and repeat. This is where the game loses its' immersive environment.  After over a hundred and sixty hours, I feel like I can put this game down and i have seen all it has to offer. With that being said, the last 20 or so hours where very much forced to sit and continue to do the same mundane tasks over and over again. There is a story line for each area of the map- i feel like it isn't fully developed, hopefully that comes soon.. Again, no hate towards the current content, and I'm sure they are working to make it more immersive. I hope.I give it a thumbs up on the battle mechanics. I'm not a fan of turned based combat, but these guys seemed to have figured it out pretty well, and the more you progress, with the game scaling, the battles do maintain a certain level of difficulty. A couple of simple mistakes can cost you the lives of one or more of your troops.  So kudos. I still recommend this game- but only lightly, you'll enjoy it, for sure, but i'll almost guarantee it is not the game you hoped it to be. yet.

_childDocuments_.review: It is very difficult for me to not recommend this game currently, as many systems in the game are very well done and overall it is a nearly finished product as is. If you like tactical combat games with grid movement and turn orders, you will love the combat in this game. You must also enjoy games that involve crafting systems (which this game does well) and management systems, such as hunger, armor maintenance, happiness, and wages.This game checks all of the boxes I enjoy, adventure, simulation, tactical combat, RPG progression, etc. However, I cannot currently recommend it because the economy is severely unbalanced imo. Repairing your armor (which needs to happen in almost every combat early game) costs gold at the blacksmith, or it requires expensive repair kits, which do not even fully repair higher tier armors. So far it seems to me there is no way to circumvent repairing with your blacksmith or your tinkerer. This is only the beginning of your financial headaches.If your unit loses its armor and becomes injured (takes 50% HP damage or below) they will get a very negative debuff until you heal them with a healing potion. You can acquire more than one injury per person, which increases the cost to heal them and makes them nearly useless in combat. You can make your own health potions, but the problem with this is that the ingredients are not close to each other, and you will have to pay your troops wages to spend the time to gather the herbs, with basically counteracts the savings you get from making your own potions.  This is still not the end of your financial headaches.The upkeep cost of troops is entirely too high in my opinion. If I go out to do a quest with 5 people to make 120 gold, I might get 100 gold from loot drops in the battle. The time spent on this quest will incur 70-90 gold in wages, 20-50 gold in repairs, and 30-60 gold in healing roughly. Do the math here, you're lucky to make any money early game at all, and late game the expenses and the difficulty scale, the only thing that saves you money late game is that your tanks become strong enough to become the only ones needing armor repairs and healing.Another issue I have with this game that makes literally no sense to me thematically or mechanically is the happiness system. I refer specifically to the massive debuff to happiness for having.. well.. soldiers in your mercenary company. Seriously, I had 6 people in my company and that gave me a -6 debuff to happiness or something for "company size. 6 PEOPLE?! If being a mercenary makes you unhappy, go do a different job!! This will REQUIRE you to get a cook and learn recipes which will take components to cook to make your people more happy. If you want to give me a fat debuff for party size to happiness, make it so my party is happy if we win battles and complete quests, which makes more sense to me than a party size debuff.Solutions: There are many, but I doubt the company would take my advice. This game needs to seriously reduce the input costs of being a mercenary company, or it needs to make the repair kit and the healing potion have "durability" or "charges" so one repair kit can be used multiple times. It makes 0 sense that I flatten a dent in my armor and now I have consumed all of my repair supplies and cannot use it on someone else's armor. Also: Add a tinkerer ability to repair things without a repair kit at reduced cost or something. If you want the bandit route to be viable at all, I need to be able to live completely on my own without having to go to town for repairs, you should be able to be a self-sustaining company in this game, but you are handicapped by early game costs of.. well.. everything.7/10, a good mercenary management and combat game, but needs economy balance if they want me to keep playing.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR It looks good, but it isn't. Fundamental problems exist within the combat system and gameplay which force you to play a differently than you'd like.I'm posting this from a J-tactics game perspective. In short, what I dig: 1) Every member of my party is "my guy;" there is no named character nonsense that I was forced with in my ten hours of play. This is the cardinal sin of japanese games, even ones that let you create infinite soldiers for your army like Disgaea.2) Animations look nice and graphics are serviceable. Sync kills are EXTREMELY satisfying even if they are actually just basic swings. For example, when a swordsman finishes an enemy off, the camera zooms in on them stabbing them in the gut. When a backstabber-type character comes up to finish a character off from behind, you see them slit their throat. Great stuff and A+3) Speaking of animations, when you 'engage' an enemy, it shows the two characters trading blows throughout the combat. Great stuff and more games should copy that. The last time I saw something similar was Xenosaga 3 with the mech combat or Skies of Arcadia. Games which don't do this should be shamed.4)  The premise of going around growing a merc group in a crafted world is pretty cool.5)  You can apparently be a bandit: always great to have.6) Combat is ok at first, but problems arise as soon as you level up.Problems:1) Deployment is weird. You can sneak up on a large group, but for some reason it will split your party up with the enemy so that the enemy surrounds you. Weirder still is that there are a limited number of deployment slots.2) Initiative is asynchronous: the enemy has strict initiative rules (unit a will go then unit b) while you can choose any of your units when your turn comes up. Moreover, it isn't clear why some enemies go faster than others. This becomes extremely annoying during 'boss' fights.3) Boss fights might as well be an entirely different game. I was playing in a fixed world (you can choose to have the world autolevel with you for some reason; do people enjoy such 'gamey' worlds?) and encountered a boss at level 4 with 10 of my men: the boss is by itself, has 4x hp and armor and can one shot every character I have, including the one armored in "plate." In and of itself, not a problem, but the boss can go multiple times. The conceit is that it "marks" an enemy, then walks up to it and readies an attack in one turn. The second time it goes, it carries through on the attack. The big issue with this is that, since the boss will do this three of four times a turn and you can only move your guys once, it will catch up and kill whatever it sights. More annoying, it often would often get two moves in the turn order right next to each other. This means that itw ould ready an attack and then immediately carry it out. The game needs some sort of time unit system like Final Fantasy Tactics had with magic, large abilities, .etc. Moreover, as bosses appear to be normal humans with lots of hp and do not obey the 'engagement' rules of the game whereupon you can 'engage' an enemy and lock them down in combat with someone. Thus, whenever bosses show up, you play a different game.4) Non human enemies in general break the rules. Rats, ghosts, .etc all populate the starting area and have annoying fight mechanics. You are never fighting "Nightmare ghost" or "plauge rat" you are playing the "Nightmare ghost stage" or "plague rat event." 5) Combat is broken in general: you get valor or morale or whatever to power special abilities. That's great, but it's shared across the team and allows you to channel them all through one guy so that they can do multiple actions whereas everyone else has one. For example, I had a swordsman with a two hander powered up do his normal sweep attack, a special 'rage' attack for one morale, and a "destabilize" attack for another. This allows you to alpha strike enemies with one guy, and, it doesn't feel saitsfying. You find yourself not using the abilities for their unique usefulness "50% snare! 50% weaken! 50% rage on hit!" but instead because they're just more damage to alpha strike an enemy. Morale is cheap and plentiful even though it's a shared resource which can get regenerated from actions as simple as moving one of your party next to someone else.6) the music: just because they're in some medieval type setting doesn't mean the music has to be bland and terrible. I'm sure the music is an amazing example of the period, but it's bad, not catchy, and depressing. What's more, you sometimes forget the game even has music since it randomly shuts off or sweeps up depending on conditions in the game. Battle music tends to be the most consistent, but you'll quickly just turn it off and replace with <insert japanese tactics game here>'s score.I would hard pass on this. The concept is great and I hope they turn things around, but it will require a huge reworking of the combat system to make this fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Wartales

_childDocuments_.review: The game's economy is too harsh.You need to pay gold to do all the things and it's just too much.Here's all the things that cost gold...--Armor kits to restore armor, even trash fights deplete it.--Health items to restore health.--Healing your units of debilitating effects--All the other things you might want to explore/purchase in the game--Food for camping (some of which you can farm from trash fights vs boars and such)Recruiting new party members costs big moneyGetting a new pony to help you carry all the things so you can try to eek a living out costs big money.And then, here's the kicker, you have to pay all your party members a wage or they get unhappy. And that's like on the daily. It's super hard to keep up with. I can't progress. I can't complete quests to make money. Getting to a quest costs me a couple days of food and wages. There is WAY TOO MUCH real world money management in this fantasy RPG. It's totally stopping my progress and making every aspect of the game stressful and unfun. DEVS! Do away with wages. I think that's the straw that's breaking everything. Pay to recruit? Fine. Pay for all the parties needs? Fine. But I can't set goals and explore your world. I'm just worried about where the next payroll is coming from. Is that the game experience you wanted to design?

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a party based, turned based, RPG. It's got good graphics, it's got inconsistent storytelling ideas that are borderline idiotic, but it's got a lot of spirit. You can probably marry your horse, though I haven't tried that. Why not recommended? The level of frustration vs fun is not good. The game has a lot of dice rolls and IF that is your thing, then absolutely go for it, enjoy your luck. Otherwise, there are unnecessary frustrations to be had along the way - some of which have been there since EA release. As an example, having 90^% to hit leading to hitting teammates: only frustrating, nothing fun about it (again, if you enjoy that sort of thing, you're good to go). I think, if you are a casual player who picks normal difficulty in their games, you will get a bit bored by midgame. In some cases you will encounter a bug that prevents you from completing a quest. This is what I find unacceptable in a finished product and I don't care if that's the standard nowadays. The idea here is that, if you enjoy potentially getting frustrated and love save scumming, then this game is for you. Otherwise it's got some serious issues with gameplay design so don't bother.
