_childDocuments_.review: Wartales is a turn-based strategy game that has heavy elements of troop and inventory management. You pick a story for your starting 4 troops and that determines their class and the items you start with or don't start with. I thoroughly enjoyed this game, I got caught in a deep rabbit hole where all I thought about was Wartales, what I could do while I wasn't playing, watching Youtube videos to plan things, all day I would play the game and I didn't get burnt out until now, around 160 hours. The story. It's honestly not that good, and it's presented in a unique way that you don't expect. There are many regions and each region has their own "story", or rather, a conflict, that is taking place. Your job basically falls to discover what is happening in the region and then be involved in 5-8 scenarios where you have to make a decision about what to do, and what you pick determines your rewards (you might miss out on something really good if you pick the wrong decision) and the "fate" of the region. But there is no overall story, it suffers a lack of direction, you really are just mercenaries that just travel region to region doing jobs.  There's also dungeons to explore but I'll be honest and say that I'm not going to talk about those, they honestly weren't that exciting and the fights in the dungeons are in darkness, you clear a dungeon once and then never revisit it. And to get meaningful backstory and rewards from the dungeons, you have to clear almost the dungeons in the game and by then the lore doesn't matter to me because I cleared that dungeon 80-100 hours ago.The combat.At first, it's one of the stronger aspects of the game, the thing that pulls you in. I recommend playing on Adaptive, all the gear scales to you and it is better rather than playing Region Locked, clearing a region only to get gear that's 5-6 levels below you. You can basically never catch up and get stronger if you play on Region Locked. You'd have to rely on crafted gear which is good but could be better. The combat is fun but the more you grow your company, the longer you play, the more time you invest into Wartales, it feels more and more like a slog. Your company grows, your battles also get longer, your fights go from 4 vs 4-6 or to 12 vs 12-18, they go from 10 minutes to 30 minutes, even longer if you have a big company. it just doesn't feel good when you spend so much time and get little reward. Some people have companies of +40 and the battlefield is littered with units and each fight takes an hour. In a game where you're gonna fight hundreds of battles, the idea of going through that is an absolute turn off for me, but maybe it isn't for you.The Balance.At the moment, in this current build of the game, once you hit level 7, (max level is 12) levelling becomes near impossible. One region will get you 1 level up and you will feel like you haven't really progressed. There is a balance issue where the xp earned is just too damn low. You can fight 10 boars and it will still give you the same experience as killing 20 strong humans. It doesn't make sense, the level cap was raised to 12 at launch but they haven't done any balancing for it. You can get the dummy which gives really good exp every rest that you do, but it's tucked away in a certain region, and if you leave that region to last, then you got it far too late.Classes are good, but some shine more than others. Tanks are ironically better damage dealers than the damage dealer classes, and you never really have to worry about them. Archers are meh and their skills are underwhelming, utility is great but their damage is so bad compared to the others because they only normal attack and use 1 ability. Other classes can spam 1-5 abilites in one turn and do so much more. There's also the issue of just travelling everywhere, there are travel posts that enable fast travel that you can get later on, but you still have to walk so damn much, effectively walking around the entire map, no places missed, fights along the way, that's what burnt me out.The Minigames are timed mouse clicks that are fun and innovative but they all suffer from frame stuttering/freezing where it freezes for a second and it's 100% guaranteed to happen -only happens once per minigame but it's frustrating.The one thing that remained fun for me throughout the 160 hours that I played was the aspect of troop management. I was always excited to gear up my troops and see what better gear I could find them. It was also fun to see my troops slowly develop a build that I had envisioned for them. Loot and gear that you find is satisfactory though I wished there was more variety, the main loot that you find is stuff like cards, dice, figurines, sapphire or rubies (there's only two gems for some reason, why not add more?). Overall, you will enjoy Wartales if you enjoy managing a battalion of troops, doing quests and fighting (to a degree). Despite the negatives I listed above, I still recommend Wartales as it is a genre and style that you don't really see nowadays, Battle Brothers is the only thing I can compare it to. I just want you to be aware of why I stopped playing and what things ended up discouraging me from playing further. I stopped but I still think I got my moneys worth and I had a blast. Maybe in the future when more content comes out, I will revisit Wartales and play it again differently. I have a habit of writing too much so I'll stop here.

_childDocuments_.review: Wartales is a quirky game. It's different than the usual schlop that is churned out by the gaming industry. Here's the thing: At it's heart, Wartales is an open ended sandbox experience. There are certain expectations of the player. If you need hand-holding by the devs, if you want something on-rails, then Wartales is not for you. But if you enjoy simple roleplaying for the sake of it, then Wartales might be for you, if you can look past some serious flaws.You control a group of individuals as they traverse the land doing mercenary work. This includes a scripted "region scenario" for each region that you're in. This is a mini-story within the grander scheme of things, and you can choose how this story pans out by the choices presented to you. The scenario really just serves as a backdrop to what you'll be doing; mostly procedurally generated missions from the job board, and wandering around the game world. These missions are usually hunting down bandits, and the occasional trade or message mission. Each region also has a Tomb which you can explore like Indiana Jones, for treasure. Battles are done XCOM style, a focus on abilities and tactics. Progression is your typical level up, but you also get "Knowledge" which you may research new abilities and new things to craft, and "Paths" which reward the player for doing certain actions, with new abilities and buffs on top of Knowledge. Crafting is a big thing in Wartales. Professions, which are your crafting levels, matter. You'll go around mining ore, fishing, chopping wood, etc.There are 2 currencies: Gold and Influence. Gold sounds like what it is. Influence on the other hand, represents your parties' prestige and can be used in certain actions. As you wander around, the relationships of your characters might change, from love to hate. These include "thought messages" after you rest, in which you must make a decision out of the three options presented to you after you camp.All of these systems are supposed to come together to create an open-ended, sandboxy system that you can use to satisfy your urge for adventure as you sit in front of your computer. They're SUPPOSED to, but unfortunately, there are major flaws.The biggest thing about Wartales is that it's just not ready for release. This game feels like it belongs in beta or even alpha and it shows. There's just not enough to do and there's not enough going on. The choices you make are ultimately extremely shallow in the scenarios; there's barely a story there to begin with, you're not invested in what's going on, and the choices boil down to A or B. There's hardly any actual writing; you simply complete the missions and move on. There are no after-effects to your choices; once the scenario is complete, that's it. The relationship dynamics and thought bubbles are ultimately very shallow. After my time playing the game, I believe I've seen 90% of all thought prompts for your characters. These psuedo-random thought bubbles get very repetitive. Use 30 influence, get a small buff, or use none and get a small debuff. Eh. Whatever. All companions are Bi-sexual. They will get a random relationship/love prompt if they have a +3 relationship score. Really? Really devs?There's nothing else going on then ultimately assassination missions and trade, and trade is already extremely shallow with just a few items to trade between settlements. The devs really could've expanded this but this is what we get.Battles are somewhat enjoyable, but they become a real slog as time goes on in the game. Battles are a little too frequent and they give too little rewards. There is a grind and this grind is just too much.Weapons and armor grant unique abilities which you may use in combat. Each weapon has it's own unique attack ability. On top of that, you can find unique "rare" weapons, or legendary weapons, and you can upgrade them. Or you can craft them. However, the player is restricted to the ability attached to the weapon itself. This makes weapon crafting redundant and pointless as once you find a legendary weapon, your crafted weapons go out the window. Unique abilities to each weapon is cool, but what's the point? Why cant you extract the ability from the weapon and attach it to a crafted item? Let's go devs. Wartales is in DESPERATE need of an antagonist, a villain, something for the player to motivate themselves to destroy once they hit max level. Some kind of over-arching storyline. Because this just isn't cutting it. The systems are in place, but they need serious tuning and more fleshing out.The DLC expands the world, but it feels incomplete. Ship mechanics are wonky. The Devs should be focusing on completing their game, not releasing new content, because the game just feels incomplete.Overall, Wartales has the potential for greatness, but it needs alot of work. I can applaud the devs for their ambitiousness, but the game feels incomplete and it needs alot more work.

_childDocuments_.review: This is how games used to be developed, back in the day when people cared about what they were doing, when games were design with a longevity in mind far beyond the week after purchase. Wartales has a game mechanic that is rich, that allows the player to create his or her own path with numerous options and bifurcations within the story line. In a way, there is a game within the game, the story of the companions that you have put together at times, completely overshadows the actual story-line of the game. You end-up connecting with your characters and caring about their fate. Unfortunately the same thing cannot be said for the story lines of the regions of the game. These feel very task driven an there isn't an overarching theme that keeps the plot together. This game was no doubt inspired by the Divinity series, the mechanics are very similar, but on that game the story is consistent and it really binds the player to a plot that makes you want to finish the story. Wartales is a rarity in today's gaming industry, it lacks a strong underlying story, but its worth every minute you invest in it.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy mostly grande strategy turn based games but also enjoy the odd foray into TRPG games. I have recently played several TRPG’s: Pathfinder, Solasta, etc.. While the genre features some good games mechanically, I have grown so tired of the high fantasy settings and incredulous magic systems with 10,000 spell buttons. If I have to slay one more demon or read one more cut scene about the God’s interfering with this, that or the other, I think I may be sick. Enter Wartales. Finally a low fantasy setting that has reasonable combat and crafting mechanics all set in a nice, neat sandbox world where I can make my own story as I go. I have enjoyed the immersive setting with concise missions that spare me the poorly written 10 pages of dialogue that drone on and on.Here is my take on the pro’s and cons of WartalesPros•	Low Fantasy, gritty, medieval setting that is believable•	Immersive and reasonable Combat system•	Interesting, Immersive Crafting system that matters•	Interesting and Immersive missions that have concise dialogue but engage you in the setting without         reading 10 pages of text•	Tired of being limited to 4-6 characters in your party? How about having 8, 10, 12 or more in you party         that becomes a believable warband.•	Varied difficulty levels and options•	Rogue like element that fits with the setting•	Interesting and reasonable Progression systemCons•	Gritty and mildly depressing setting might not be for everyone. The Middle Ages weren’t always colorful         and bright after all!•	Turn Based Combat is slow and methodical. Some will find it tedious after awhile but Im liking the pace         for us older gamers that are slow on the button mashing.•	Graphics are decent but not anything special.•	Limited customization choices•	No tutorial

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to start off that I RARELY write a review on a game, out of the almost 300 games I have on steam. I have maybe actually written one legit review.Here is my take on the current game as of July 31, 2022.The game is HARD! I don't mean the combat or exploration. It's the balance of the game, when it comes to having enough money to pay for your companions. In this game, you have a limited time to get the resources you need before you have to rest your troops and pay them their wages and feed them. Yes, you have quests that you can do for making a bit of money. But, the time it takes to travel between those quests and the time you have until you have to rest. Just doesn't seem to add up. You'll be spending a lot of time just trying to figure out a way to resolve this issue by restarting your game at least a dozen times before being able to understand "somewhat". It's a fine line of using the right knowledge points and focusing on the right professions. Example (cooking and fishing) I just want anyone that is reading this to understand that this isn't going to be a jump in and go all out right off the bat. You really have to take your time figuring out the best way to just survive the management of your troops.With that being said, this game is really good. The combat is fun and you really need to use your head. The exploration is rather entertaining because you are always looking for something to find when it comes to resources or buildings etc. Because finding buildings or other unique places gives you points towards knowledge. Which helps you unlock more skills. Also, crafting in this game isn't overly redundant like it most games. You can make decent stuff with rather small amounts of Iron, wood etc.Keep in mind, I hope the devs look into a bit of a balance when it comes to the troop management side of the game. I'd also suggest more armor and weapons for crafting because as of time now. You can craft the best armor at level 5.I will edit this more as I play...

_childDocuments_.review: Shockingly refreshing game setting new standards and a new direction for a mix and match of game genres. It is rpg and survival and strategy on a map that plays like HOMM. There's crafting, quests, cooking and a lot of exploration to do. My main problem with the game is the way the difficulty scales. You start up with 4 people vs 4 bandits and it's awesome. But later on as you progress into the game you get pitted against 10 enemy soldiers, so you are forced to recruit more people which is fun. Now imagine you command 10-12 individual soldiers, each with a class and full gear vs 26 (!!!!) enemy soldiers. It gets tedious to say the least. And mind you there are no spells AOE damage to get rid of the cannon fodder, every soldier counts. So it;s a nightmare having to go through 36 units each round, reminds me of really difficult fights in D&D that you need a whole session for an encounter. It's fun but draining and in D&D it's once in a while, but in this game it's the norm the further you progress in the game. Even random encounters as you go it's 10 v 10 or 10 v 15 and you have to watch every single enemy unit take it's turn and guess what one of yours died so you have to redo the battle, so you wasted 20 minutes.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game. There will be some spoilers in this review.I like games where you are controlling tiny guys on the screen and part of this game has that. It wasn't particularly compelling, but good enough. I also like turn based combat- again this game wasn't particularly compelling but good enough. There is some resource management- your soldiers can be miners, scholars, tinkers, etc. and there is some mini-game like features associated with crafting... that isn't particularly compelling but good enough. Just about the whole game is good enough but nothing special.Then, for some reason, when you get to the fifth zone this very, very low magic world introduces zombies.It calls them plague victims, but they're really zombies. I could deal with that, but it also introduces new game play features which amounts to being good at running away. There are encounters where your job is to run away because the zomb... plague victims will spawn endlessly. If your guys, which you've spent hours developing as tough, stout fighters aren't fast enough they will die. I couldn't stand it.I'm sure some people will like this game, it's gotten very good reviews. If not for the run away encounters it's very likely I would've finished this game because it was a competent game that was good enough, but mainly because I don't have anything else to play. I'm not going to ask for a refund or anything. Up until Luden I was happy to keep playing. As I said there's plenty of OK gaming here but, at least for me, there's not enough to justify having endure encounter styles that I absolutely loathe.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent and beautiful game.Graphics are good and the small little execution cuts in combat are beautifully done and seem very realistic.  Combat is challenging even on normal and I love the difficultly level so far, anyone else saying it is too hard really needs to try and work on their skill a bit.  Definitely needs polish overall for quests and NPC interactions.  There really is no different feeling talking to the Village leader vs. talking to a trader or refugee.  The factions need more depth overall as they seem like a shell but probably that way as placeholders till they write up all the story details and such.The only real way to earn money is to capture enemies with chains from the jail but there is not a lot of information that points you that way and I had to look online at a guide to it all, after that it was smooth sailing but before I knew to do that I spent a lot of times going immediately back to the town for repairs and medicine.One of the first quests has you try to kill the Lund farmer guy and there is not much warning to let you know not to ♥♥♥♥ with him for a while.There doesnt seem to  be a good quest tab to keep tabs on quests that highlight regions or goals well enough.The game seems pretty early access and not fleshed out story wise , it seems they were concentrating on mechanics and all that first.  As far as the mechanics go the combat feels fresh even though it is turn based , the difficulty is good and the 'skills' for points you have to earn in combat can be a nice mix and fun.  The camp has a lot of potential but currently it doesnt do much to tell you why and how it is important (mainly talking about the camp equipment such as tents) , I look forward to see these things develop.Currently I have played enough to get out of the first starting area by doing 'quests', I did not feel the heavy need to really continue on but I intend to once the next update comes out.  I do recommend this game but I do not feel it is completely ready to spend hours upon hours playing just yet.  I would recommend getting it at the early access price and keeping up with it as it is a very exciting game with a lot of potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Man this game is hella fun, but flawed.First of all, while the game technically has no end, each province in the map has their own little campaign followed by side quests spread across it. Quests are usually pretty dumb and offer poor rewards most of the time - it's basically go there, kill enemy, come back, or even go there, talk to someone and come back, and then you get a meager reward. Whatever choice you make in the province stories bares no consequence anywhere, not visually nor gameplaywiseProgressing your gear is fun, gathering resources and knowledge to craft better gear is really cool and is the top-most reason I like this game, having to wear poor rags and upgrade to a plate armour or brigandine is really satisfying, although I do wish this game had more variety of armor to craft and find. Travelling on the map is really slow and takes most of the time of the gameplay and combat, although tactical and fun, gets really repetitive really fast.Each companion has a profession that gives you different resources, like a woodcutter to get wood or a miner to get ores, an angler to fish and a cook to prepare meals, you have the alchemist who makes potions and refine ores or the scholar who studies and unlock new recipes, you also have the blacksmith who makes the armor and weapons and also the thief who lockpicks and steal.You have a camp that is customizable on the layout that you want with the different assets and companions that you own - you have the tent who gives special combat points to whomever sleeps there, you have the workshop to make tools and upgrade your camp assets, you have the strategy table that gives combat bonuses, the hitching post for your ponies or a campfire that gives happiness.I guess the only thing that saddens me is that the world is quite static, there isn't anything dynamic aside from random spawns to fight on the map. I figure once I beat the game and the DLC, there won't be any reason to return to it at all

_childDocuments_.review: I would not post this review if they had refunded my purchase. So here we go. In general I was looking for 3D alternative to Battle Brothers which I really enjoyed and spend hours playing it. These games have common ideas but this one is way more superficial. Survival system is a bit more advanced because of different specialties for you mercenaries which is fun. I don't quite understand why a blacksmith can't just cook food for your band, but maybe that is something I hadn't reached during my 5 hours of gameplay. The most off putting thing in this game as for me is the terribly awful battle system and here's what I mean by that. I went on a mission with a bigger map than usual where a single archer could simply kite all my team being able to run and shoot after while I could only run the same distance with my melee guys and do nothing else. At the same time my AI controlled dumb ally whom you should protect runs after that archer taking damage every turn and eventually dies which is where I failed the mission. What is even worse there's no such thing as ammunition limit concept where an archer could only bring a certain amount of arrows to a battle and eventually run out of them, which is kind of strange for a game with one of key aspects - survival and caravan management. So anyway this single guy could have shot most of my gang as well with such a trick. Other games with similar mechanics like XCOM or even Banner Saga would not allow such madness because each action you take costs abstract action points, not just run and hit. I had doubts about this game from the very first fight with bandits so I gave it a chance but unfortunately that was not worth my time. If I were you I would seek for some other representative of this genre where most of these game mechanics were taken from because there are plenty of them. This studio has some really awesome games and that's a shame this is not one of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I told myself that I would finish the game before I posted a review, but since I really can't see that happening, I'll go ahead and post some insights for people making the consideration.I played in Hard mode, and had my main session in the Region-locked progression mode. (I found out that adaptive progression is a MAJOR time-sync very quickly)- Unique style of combat with a twist on traditional squad based tactic sims, reminiscent of X-COM- Beautiful graphics and impressively detailed world environment, filled with secrets and new areas with a broad array of seasonal effects.- Has special nuances that add to the charm of the game; burying fallen companions, the campsite being customizable, trade routes, arena modes and other one-of-a-kind elements that I have seldom seen implemented in games of this nature.- After nearly 80 hours in a play-through, I am not exactly motivated to complete the campaign, mainly because of the massive time-sink that is involved with that.- The fights take increasingly longer as the campaign goes on, and meaningful progress becomes much more difficult to achieve.- Watch as your level 7 and higher characters now take more than 10-20 fights in order to level up, at which point you will have made it into the next area and are now facing enemies 2-3 levels higher than where you just progressed from.- "Grinding" is my least favorite part of playing an immersive RPG, and yet we are forced to in Wartales. Don't think you can get around this by playing the adaptive difficulty either- it is absolutely that much more of a time sink.- The DLC options look... Silly, I guess. I would never have thought that pirates or sailing really would have much of a focus in a game like this. The new DLC looks like more of what we already have in the game, which waits behind a large wall of time you need to be willing to invest in order to make it through the slog of battles.The slog of combat turns a beautiful and uniquely immersive RPG into a massive time-sink with an awkward feeling when it comes to progressing the campaign, and increasingly less reward-to-time ratio as the game continues. I'm really hoping we see a Wartales 2, for all intents and purposes.

_childDocuments_.review: Mildly addictive.  Has a lot going for it, and the biggest issues are QoL.Guide your band of medieval mercenaries as they seek fame and fortune in a fictional setting with low/no magic.  Keep them paid and fed, recruit new mercs, and build their skills so they can win fame and glory (and money!) through tactical, turn-based combat.The combat is good.  There's a good amount of variety in the class choices.  The tactical fights have sufficient depth to keep me interested, and are challenging enough that triumph is satisfying.  They  take a while to finish in the later levels when there are two or three dozen combatants on the board, but the enemies will often give up once it's down to the last one or two.  There are animals, men, champions, arenas, friendships, and a lot of little systems that interact well together.When not being murder-hobos your mercs can learn useful professions like fishing.  Many of these have minigames so they're more than just 'press F to acquire fish.'  When you visit a new area you're greeted with a static screen where you can interact with people and objects.  What may not be initially obvious is that these are basically hidden object puzzles where you can find some bonus loot if you mouse around thoroughly.  There are all sorts of reward tracks to follow.  Each one offers new abilities or stuff to learn how to make.  The early part of the game is fantastic because there's so much to see and do.The sound is good, and the music is decent.  It's not amazing, but I do get the battle song stuck in my head every now and again.  If anything it could use more variety since the first 50 - 60 hrs of the game has the same town music.The art direction is good.  It tends more towards photo-realism than something like Battle Brothers, with its minimalist icons.  The animations are solid, and the kill shots are cool the first few times you see them.The power levels are jagged and inconsistent.  You're continuously collecting gear from defeated opponents, but this is pretty inconsistent.  You'll want to have a merc learn to blacksmith to make you gear, and when you do that you notice that as soon as you hit a new tier of gear (5, 8 & 11) you're unstoppable, but when you're a level shy of that new tier you feel underpowered with your old, sad gear.It feels kinda grindy.  I've been taking longer and longer breaks because I've maxed several different reward tracks by lv8, my troupe takes dozens of battles to level, and the Ludern swamp is difficult and boring to navigate.The item management is just bad.  The UI in general has enough irritations that I don't think anyone on their team has any UX experience or talent.  You can only interact with the item screens through small windows that can't be resized.  For a game with a large collection of crafting materials for your three crafting professions, this is painful.The worst part, is the hitching and stuttering.  It feels like the graphics stop responding for half a second every 30 - 60 secs or so.  This isn't much of an action game, so it could be worse, but if you accidentally give a move order that you didn't mean to, or miss a note in the Guitar Hero minigame for no other reason than a bug, it feels bad.  This is a known issue, so I expect it's being worked on.I do recommend if you like this sort of thing, but I feel it falls short of greatness.

_childDocuments_.review: For the first 100 hours of gameplay, I recommended this game.  After 100 hours, however, I have encountered too many frustrating and tedious battles, I have changed my opinion to not recommend the game.  This game is like a simplified version of mount and blade with turn based fights instead of fps, and the result is just too much work.Pros: This game is a fun medieval simulator.. build a troop, including wolves, bears, boar, rats, etc., and then control them in battle.  Travel to other lands and trade goods for profit, or run missions to earn some cash first.  Cons:The number one failing of this game is that each character can only have 1 profession, and humans can't carry much weight, meaning that you must have a troop of at least 20 or so in order to meet the various challenges in the game.  The size of your troop, however, determines the size of enemy troops, which means that you end up in battles of 15-20 vs 15-20, and this leads to some tedious battles.. especially if your trying hard not to lose any of your characters which you've trained up.  First, you must place your characters in any of the allied squares (grouped around the battlefield with, as enemy troups are also grouped around the battlefield), which takes quite some time as you must choose tanks, dps, and maybe crowd control according to the enemies placement, and the allied squares available, in order to maximize your chances of success.  Some enemies are just lousy to fight.. one enemy, for example, lights his opponent on fire, which means that character will spread fire to any adjacent units, and take damage each round.  As this character has very high defense and defensive abilities, as well as being a leader giving a huge bonus to the rest of their troop, it means you pretty much have to dedicate a few units to going in and killing them early in the fight.. and there's a good chance the fire will lead to those units death before the fight is over.  You can put fights out by using ability points, either by using a movement skill if that character has one, or by another character who has first aid walking up and using that ability.  In either case, ability points are precious, as are the actions each character takes during a round, so putting out several fires is rarely practical to do, and you instead aim to win the battle soon enough that your characters survive.. but this means they end the battle with no armor, and in need of healing, both of which require carrying heavy resources, and cut into profits.This is another issue I dislike about the game.. While the size of your enemies troop scales to your troop size, the size of the rewards does not seem to.  If you encounter a random enemy which is not quest associated, but it's a difficult fight, the profit for the fight vs the heavy time investment that fights take (I often take over an hour for a fight I'd say) does not feel at all satisfying.  You will get 1-3 weapons, and 1-3 sets of armor, and less than 50 gold in a fight.. a healing potion used to cure acquired afflictions after battle cost 35 gold, and you'll need 2-6 each fight to stay healthy.  (You can make them for cheaper, but finding materials is tricky early game)  You'll also need to use several "raw materials" for armor repair, generally about 10 or so of these each battle, at around 5g each, I believe.    Each weapon will probably sell for 20-40, and armor for 40-80 (or more for a very rare item), so I doubt you lose money (unless someone dies, then you definitely do), but it makes big battles against ambushing foes just tedious and pointless.  You may make 100 gold off the battle, but you would have made 1500 gold in that time if you were just doing trade runs.   All in all, it's a lot of fun.. I just find myself alt-F4ing a lot if I get ambushed by a foe who I know it's going to be a long and expensive battle against.. then I'll wander off for a few hours, and when I come back, I'll decide whether to load the battle for a tedious and unrewarding hour, or if I'll load the last save (each time I enter town), and trade that lost progress for saving the time of the fight.  It's probably always worth loading the town in that case unless you have completed quests in the mean time, but I'll sometimes follow through on the fight in the hopes of getting a useful item.

_childDocuments_.review: Closed Beta tester here recommendation based on ~130 hrs of play since closed beta (plus another huge chunk of time in the demo) at time of writing.Overall - this game is just exactly what I'd been looking for for some time. It combines a turn-based system of combat (more on that later) with overland exploration in a low-fantasy world that just really hits the mark.My favourite parts of the game:- The squad based system is very flexible - there are so many possible party combinations that you really do get to choose how you want to play the game 4 or 10 companions, or what about some wolf 'pets' (just make sure you have spare meat on hand!) - melee focus or a ranged focus - do you spec for single target damage or go for some huge AoE. While some fights are easier and some harder depending on what you choose,  you get a choice!- The camp is another 'party member', building and growing the campsite is really fun and gives some nice bonuses. It really comes alive toward the later parts of the game.- Combat - I love the way the turn-based system has been implemented, being able to mix and match turn-order allows for much more flexibility and leads to some really intense fights where your otherwise outnumbered and over-matched squad can pull through.- Combat skills - the way skills have been implemented allows for much more free flowing combat than in the demo version - giving you the chance to build 'valour points' and therefore use skills more during combat, again promoting conscious choices of squad mate turn order and positioning.- The map and land is just gorgeous, I particularly love the weather effects- Professions, simple little mini-games that I really enjoy, crafting things that feel useful (but not over-abundant), they also complement the class system.- It is fairly free-roaming, you don't HAVE to do the main storylines, but at this stage with only a couple of regions released you likely will.- 20-30 hours of gameplay per run depending on difficulty and how much of the game you want to complete (three regions accessible at the time of review).- 'Paths', a way to progress just by doing... well anything - stealing, killing, trading - etc. These also unlock new quests options as well.- Secrets, there are a bunch of hidden secrets (some you find through treasure maps!) around the place. Some are tricky to get to but it a satisfying little feeling to figure it out!Cons:- It is still Early Access, there are some bugs - the Devs are working on these though and will hopefully pick more up. If you want a smooth bug-free game - hold off on the purchase for now. (e.g. a save file might corrupt or a party member need to be booted from the squad to continue).- If you are musically inclined, there has been feedback that more might be needed on that front (I quite like the music but also don't really pick up on music loops >_>). Note: there have been some upgrades made to the music over the closed beta - so it is something I expect to see more of.- more regions aren't accessible yet! This will change over the course of early access, I will update this review as the game receives updates as well.Always happy to answer things on discord and grow the community :)

_childDocuments_.review: A century has passed since the fall of the Edoran Empire at the hands of an unprecedented plague that swept the nation. Now, the land is rife with mercenary work, banditry and thievery, with honor having become an almost entirely forgotten virtue. Prepare to lead a group of unscrupulous characters in a massive open world where combat, death and a thirst for riches will dictate your day to day life. You are not the hero of this story, destined to usher in a new era of peace. Your goal is solely to survive and thrive in this harsh and hostile world, by any means necessary…

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great! The story isn't the main focus so if you are coming for a super rich story that rivals the likes of even Mount and Blade 2 then i do not think you will be satisfied with it. That being said what this game is isn't a story based game it is a management game. You will gather a party of people diverse in traits and methods of fighting and develop their skills though out a very long journey, and in that this game does a fantastic job and is still being added to and expended by the devs. The reason I leave a negative review is because there are so many completely game breaking bugs that can force you to reset an entire fight you may have just spent 30 minuets planning it out just for the game to get stuck right at the end leaving you with the chore of going through it all again and hoping the rng remains the same as with variable damage the same strat may not work twice and work perfectly. The one and only part of this game where I have never encountered bugs however. is the tavern management in the dlc which works amazing and i absolutely adore it. If you want to buy this game and have the buggy merc experience be prepared to have to reset and relaunch your multiplayer lobbies repeatedly, but if you want to play a tavern management simulator and walk around a pretty environment with ruins to explore and missions to do for the people (that do involve the fights I've mentioned above) then go for it!

_childDocuments_.review: In the sea of games, this one piqued my interest with its style and no-nonsense approach about the setting.I'm having much more fun than I expected to have, playing around with the game's systems, which I think are incredibly done. Why is that?Well the game has already seen systems such as crafting, leveling, etc. However the way they're intertwined is very entertaining, and the game doesn't try to handicap your character/party development with making it difficult to do, rather it welcomes you to try out professions. (Losing progress by swapping professions can be seen as a handicap, but I didn't find it problematic personally)Professions give your characters extra stats, and allow you to craft items that make your warband more OP.I love that, how I can choose to minmax my characters if I want to, or just slap a higher level item on them and not worry about it too much.The difficulty is much better now than it was on release, having introduced a "fixed level" per each zone by choosing "Region locked". I found this much more rewarding than "Free Roam" just because I felt like my work and playtime meant that my characters are way more powerful than the initial zone they started in.The classes are cool, with a lot of variety in how to play and compose your party.I would love to see some more choices in the build tree, but not TOO many more, as this could get very micro managy and overwhelming quite easily. Also I would like to see more information on build limitations, such as only certain classes being able to wield maces/axes/swords. In my first playthrough I built a party without a warrior, having never encountered one in the tavern, so I didn't have anyone to wield axes, and couldn't cut wood due to that "handicap"Overall, I will wholeheartedly recommend this game. The devs put out roadmaps and update the game regularly. I'm enjoying it a lot, and it seems to make time fly when I'm playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic so far. I've just conquered Calradia in Bannerlords for the first time so I am still very much in the mood for something Medieval. Unfortunately Manor Lords seems to be quite unfinished (it is early access after all) so I chose this game. Have to say I'm not disappointed. I've just cleared the first area and have a pretty neat little troop going now.Combat is your average turn-based system which isn't too taxing or convoluted and is quite satisfying. You can build up valour points by being in certain circumstances (such as killing someone, being next to an enemy/ally at the end of the turn etc.)  for all your special skills which are vital to winning the battle. The world map so far seems quite huge, I've only done the first Kingdom and it's taken me around 20 hours as I like to 100% explore as much as I can before moving on.  Questwise there's plenty to do and as you're a group of mercenaries you probably get the idea. Go and kill stuff, help people, escort people etc. Each area has it's own main questline to complete as well.One thing I like the most about the game is the amount of skills/knowledge/professions etc. the game has to offer. Not only do your characters have their main skill like a fighter or archer but they also have their own professions. You can make someone a miner, fisherman or woodcutter just to name  a few.  As well as all this there are loads of things you can learn, like recipes for food, weapon/armour blueprints, camp equipment and much more. All of which aids in keeping your party alive, equipped, fed and happy. Overall I think the game is great and well rounded and I am glad i purchased it.

_childDocuments_.review: Think of this as more of a neutral recommendationThe game itself is fun, I might be a bit biased because i enjoy turn-based strategy games and i think the combat itself is done quite well. The game is very fun to play with friends, wandering around and exploring new things, getting stronger. The game does have a few issues thoughIssues:1. The game itself is super buggy right now, I've experienced stuff such as items being vaporized when trying to equip it or being unable to select and use abilities during combat among other bugs, nothing super impactful except for the item deleting thing but still annoying.2. The pathfinding is horrendous, your character often gets stuck trying to climb a small hill or something similar.3. The different regions don't really feel super different from each other right now, it's kind of like you got to a new region and you repeat the same tasks until you go to the next one, it gets quite repetitive.4. I don't think there are enough skills in the skill tree at the moment, the current amount of skills feel quite restrictive in how you build a character. There isn't a lot of skills later in the skill tree that really compliments the earlier abilities. There are also some skills that are just way better than other that kind of forces you to pick it which just ends up with you practically creating a clone of another.5. I feel like a lot of the melee classes don't have a distinct style. Some of the classes are fine, the archer shoots from a distance, the Ranger is like an assassin, squishy with high burst damage, the spearman is kind of like a support-type class with area denial and buffs.The issue is the swordsman, brute and warrior. You might think "brute = AOE, warrior = tank, swordsman = dueling" but the thing is, they all pretty much do the same thing. All three of those classes can do AOE, they could all become a tank, they could all be single target if you want. They don't have their own unique identity, it seems kind of pointless that all 3 of those classes can do basically the same thing with a small tweak in gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember I had a few nights of really fun time in beta, but can't make myself to play it after release. Dunno, it's like I was hoping for something different, not THAT many fights on every step maybe? Or that combat would imporve (and it did at some point, just not the things I hoped for), I feel that some mechanics became worse, like spawning militia on your head (and going straight to you, no matter if you hiding or not), pursuing you to the end of the map, if necessary, and then unwinnable fight with reinforcements on their side (you was running after me all the way to the border, haven't seen any reinforcements running along my dudes, ffs).Mechanics like size of foes depends on your squad (it won't fun, I assure you. The whole party management become almost, useless OR your battles would be super lenghty, like 1 hour long at some scenarios), adaptible level - maaaybe.... but it's always a design flaw, not fun aspect, but it's ok, I admire devs effort, persistence and support for game even after release. They were really adding things that community was asking for (maybe not ended well for the game. Like, I think that coop wasn't worth the effort at all. Steam Play Together - best coop for this game lol), and overall idea was great. It's still great. Just... after some (not distant at all) point game fails to be fun with it's core mechanics (and other things doesn't matter really).That said, I haven't tried to play with mods, mayb that is were game shines.I will try to play in the future, but for now I just can't make myself.

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:Engaging story and characters: Wartales features an engaging story and well-developed characters that players can become invested in. This creates a narrative-driven experience that is both satisfying and rewarding.Unique gameplay mechanics: The game features unique gameplay mechanics that combine elements of strategy, RPG, and survival genres. This creates a gameplay experience that is both challenging and immersive.Beautiful visuals: Wartales features beautiful hand-drawn visuals that bring the game's world to life. The attention to detail and art style make the game a joy to look at and play.Meaningful choices: The game features meaningful choices that can impact the game's story and world. This creates a sense of agency and ownership for players, which can be satisfying and rewarding.CONS:Steep learning curve: Wartales can be a challenging game to master, especially when it comes to the game's mechanics and strategy. This might be off-putting for some players who are looking for a more casual experience.Limited replayability: While the game's story is engaging and well-written, there is limited replayability once the story has been completed. This might be disappointing for players who are looking for a game that they can play over and over again.Slow-paced gameplay: The game's gameplay can be slow-paced at times, which might not be engaging for some players. _childDocuments_.review: Battle Brothers meets Destinies: the board game.Slow pacing which is a plus for me, the game rewards smart strategic decisions and planning. Battles are very enjoyable (and sometimes annoying, but rarely due to rng). Has that HoMM3 feel of "just one more round/battle".Unlike Battle Brothers however, it's less of a sandbox and more of a pre-made campaign with some backstory that in itself adds some depth to the game but isn't crucial and can easily be ignored.The sound and music is decent enough, nothing to write home about though, graphics are ok, but not jaw-dropping.Can't say much about the coop but I like the idea, as it actually may work pretty well in this type of game.EDIT: A thing that I noticed after a couple of hours playing, the game seems to be very taxing on the CPU/GPU - 3 hours into the session and the pc fans are spinning very fast. The game may need some optimization in that regard.Overall a very solid game, I'd say addictive even, an 8,5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING-this game runs scripts outside of the game itself.  Starting off, this game reminded me of Gladius (ps2) and of course Xcom (pc), which are two of my all-time favorite games.  However, it didn't take long before I started getting the 'black screen of death' and I'd have to restart the game.  This started happening about once an hour.  But I really wanted to keep playing, so I started saving after every little event and team micromanagement.  Having to replay battles and re-micro-manage was wasting hours and hours of my time and I was starting to hate the game.    Yet, despite these constant crashes, I kept going because there just aren't that many games like this and I almost always finish games.  But then today, the game crashed again and suddenly, BOTH of my computer screens go black.  One of my monitors appears turned off.   I check settings and my computer isn't recognizing my second monitor.  I thought maybe it was just a coincidence that this happened during the exact same half-second the game crashed.   So I ctrl+alt+del the game to shut it down and then reloaded it.  As the game loads up, a static-colored block appears in the middle of my screen.  Something's not right.So, I closed out the game again, thinking maybe they are patching it right this second.  I'll come back later. But after I shut down the game, the weird block of color is STILL ON MY SCREEN.  I waited a few more minutes thinking it was still trying to shut down, but it never went away.  So, I shut down Steam.  That'll fix it.  Nope.  The weird colored block is STILL THERE.  At this point, it became clear to me, that the game is running something outside of steam, that can affect your computer's ability to detect your monitor.   Personally, I find this behavior creepy and will be avoiding this developer from now on.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot to like. Good combat, Good mechanics, good crafting systems, lots of things to do, lots of content for early access. Excited to see the final game! Its like battle brothers but with a story and clear objectives. The atmosphere is strong and sets the tone. My only complaint is that some of the quests and the story is kind of weak. As someone who likes to roleplay int these types of games the quests and choices leave something to be desired. Here is a quest that exemplifies what I mean. A bunch of peasants get angry at plague victims and want to kill them, they hire you there are guards outside the Abby that the plague victims are in, there is no option to change sides here you have to fight and kill them THEN after that you get the  chance to protect the plague victims and kill the peasants that hired you. So you killed the guards for nothing basically. This happens multiple times where you can do a 180 after horrifically murdering people. Its more like a murder hobo situation than a professional merc company but that's my only complaint about the game Highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: War Tales is a great game already in early access.The mix of Party Management, Crafting and doing missions while experiencing the story of war in a low-magic fantasy world is a great combination.The making of real gem is already there in early access.I have played until the current max. level 5.It took a while and was very fun and engaging.If you like a sandbox game which gives you a story to go for at your own pace this is for you.Just mind it is currently early access.But it is very stable and has quite some content already as well as showing the love the devs poured into it.Pro:- Fresh new world with it's own feel and conflicts, legends and beauty- Mix of Party Management, Crafting and Missions (generic and story) work very well.- Party Camp developing with your crafting of it is very fun and engaging! Build your own camp and use the meaningful options it provides for your party!- Combat is easy to get into yet challenging the more you get into it- Crafting and professions for your characters are a meaningful and fun addition Cons:- Level scaling at the moment is pretty harsh unless you play on easy/easy for the World/combat   As for me "normal" was too much feel of no progress due to level scaling. - Quite some price for a early access game but seeing how stable it is and how much content you get already it is fair. Still it is quite some money to pay for.- Much content is already in place but only basic. Like the "Ponies" (more like Pack Horses) which already have some character stats and later are planned to also "level up" and develop as semi-characters but are nothing more than additional carriers for the loot and gear at the moment.  Also character level so far will be 9 and you can only proceed to 5 as for now.- Many mechanics ("Happiness" party mechanic, mini-games, camp system etc.)really need a tutorial else they are very frustrating until you learn them or find a video on youtube to explain.Many of the cons are actively worked on by the devs. Their roadmap shows they are listening to players and try to implent feedback. I am optimistic this game will be a real gem when it is finished!

_childDocuments_.review:
It has been a hundred years since the world saw the fall of the once great Edoran Empire at the hands of an unprecedented plague that swept the nation. In the turmoil and uncertainty that has followed, mercenary work, banditry and thievery across the land is abundant, as honor has long since become an almost entirely forgotten virtue.

Now, prepare to lead a group of unscrupulous characters who revel in such activity in a massive open world where combat, death and a thirst for riches will shape and define your day to day life. You are not special, the chosen one or a once in a millennia hero ushering in a new era of peace. Your goal is solely to survive and thrive in this harsh and hostile world.

Only the bravest and most ambitious can hope to see their story written in the Wartales!

name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs
detailed_description: The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a first-person, metal-detecting narrative game designed to be played in a single evening. You play as Adam, a sharp-witted but compassionate man returning to his childhood village of Stanning. There he'll help a woman named Beth on her mission to unearth a local treasure. As cracks begin to appear in Beth’s fairy tale plan for everything, you’ll delve into her history and discover all may not be as it seems. And you’ll have to choose how Adam responds to Beth as she faces her demons. Gameplay combines laid-back metal detecting and exploration with a strong interpersonal narrative, all set in a beautiful English countryside. The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a game about trying to find something, and the tone it sets is like a typical English summer: mostly pleasant, but with stormy moments that threaten to ruin everything . Features: Metal detecting! Meditatively exploring a peaceful English farm Finding “treasures” (mostly rubbish) with your detector Digging them up with a large shovel and a small trowel Sharing photos of your finds with Beth Relationship building! Chatting with Beth via walkie-talkie and instant message Unravelling a mystery through interesting narrative choices Learning about Beth’s hopes and fears Directing the conversation to root out the truth Starring: Arthur Darvill ( Doctor Who , DC’s Legends of Tomorrow ) as Adam Luci Fish ( Safe House , Another Eden ) as Beth From the lead designer of Everybody’s Gone To The Rapture , AMC Games, and SundanceTV: The Magnificent Trufflepigs . Story: It’s summer in the idyllic northern English village of Stanning. Beth is a successful twenty-something who’s poised to become the CEO of the biggest company in the valley, on the cusp of settling down, maybe having a couple kids. Life seems so straight-forward, but something’s missing… Many years ago, Beth found an earring while metal detecting on a local farm. It brought her brief fame (and a modest sum of cash for a pre-teen), but—most importantly—it made her feel special. But she never found the earring’s match. Now, the old farm is only a week away from being demolished so an energy company can turn it into a solar farm. Beth decides this is her last chance to rekindle that childhood sense of adventure. There’s too much ground to cover by herself, so (despite warnings from her friends) she’s hatched a plan to invite Adam back into her life. Beth’s search for the long-lost earring will unearth much more than she's bargained for.

Beth is a successful twenty-something who’s poised to become the CEO of the biggest company in the valley, on the cusp of settling down, maybe having a couple kids. Life seems so straight-forward, but something’s missing… Many years ago, Beth found an earring while metal detecting on a local farm. It brought her brief fame (and a modest sum of cash for a pre-teen), but—most importantly—it made her feel special. But she never found the earring’s match. Now, the old farm is only a week away from being demolished so an energy company can turn it into a solar farm. Beth decides this is her last chance to rekindle that childhood sense of adventure. There’s too much ground to cover by herself, so (despite warnings from her friends) she’s hatched a plan to invite Adam back into her life. Beth’s search for the long-lost earring will unearth much more than she's bargained for.
short_description: The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a first-person, metal-detecting narrative game. It combines laid-back detecting and exploration with a dramatic story, all set in a beautiful English countryside. It’s a game about trying to find something.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever been stuck in a rut, afraid of being an adult, maybe even ridiculed for it, called out for not having plans or having too many, The Magnificent Trufflepigs might resonate with you like it did with me, even though its story suffers a bit and is not as nuanced to make it really great.Set in a lush, quaint English countryside, or a utopian vision of what said countryside looks like, in a small town called Stanning, the game's visuals are superb. Cut down on details, but still gorgeous, vibrant, nailed in proportions, with mountains touching the horizon and framing the scenes, clouds creating shadows, crumbling stone walls splitting the fields and verdant green grass hiding secrets. There's even a sad, smiling scarecrow in need of a hug and a happy sounding dog bark wafting through the air, both just out of your reach, behind old wooden fences, hidden in fields of wheat.The soundtrack is melodious, sometimes joyful, sometimes sombre, filling out and deepening or lifting the mood of the character's conversations. Ambient sound design is also wonderful, melding all the expected countryside noises seamlessly. From insects and rustling trees to the whistling of the wind and the occasional man made sounds from a passing balloon or a hang glider. Voice performances are a real stand out, both characters and their relationship brought to life through their banter.You walk in the shoes of Adam, an old childhood friend of Beth, helping her find a missing earring, second of a pair. Beth found the first one as a child in these same fields you're sauntering through today. Your only simple gameplay mechanic is an old metal detector, a hand-me-down from Beth, which you use to find, and in combination with a shovel and a trowel, dig up rusted, old items that trigger memories, conversations and move the story forward.Whenever you find an item, Adam takes a photo of it, sends it to Beth and she either responds with a message or calls him on the small, plastic, toy walkie-talkies they're using to communicate. If you pay a bit more attention, look around and explore the boundaries, you'll find a few more things you can photograph that will trigger additional conversations and reveal more of the story.It might not be immediately obvious who the main character is, but when the story starts unravelling, along with Beth, it becomes clear she's the main character. She comes off as somewhat spoiled, self-centered and always in a rush, a stark contrast to a more slow, laid-back and carefree Adam. But the more lunch breaks you take and the more you talk to her, the more the conversations veer off to differing measures of value in life, societal judgments and expectations, dreams and wrongly perceived ambitions. A reminder that life is what happens when you're making plans, that it can go in so many directions and that it's never too late to initiate a change.With a lack of gameplay, so much rests on the conversations between the characters. It's unfortunate then that when a conversation starts, you can't do anything but plod along at a snails pace until the conversation's over, which makes sense since that's how the story moves forward, but it does derail the pacing a bit. And it occasionally feels too blunt and on the nose with some of its remarks. The ending deserves a special mention, seeming somewhat rushed, confusing and jumbled, and according to other Steam reviews, left a lot of people unsatisfied. It's telling about a "faulty" script that so many people missed what might be the main point. Slightly cleverly hidden, but very discernible if you pay close attention to the conversations, read between the lines and don't take everything literally, even though the game is guilty of being blunt.That's where the nuances fail a bit, but I still think the story is solid, competently written and deserving of your time. It's still an interesting take on the choices in life, society's dictation on what you should acquire and accomplish to be "happy", and the metal detecting, as simplistic as it is, makes for a relaxing afternoon exploring the fields of a quaint English countryside.PC specs for review purposes: i7-7700, RTX2070, 32GB of RAM, SSD. No noticeable issues.: Story achievements and a few missable ones. Story+ mode and chapter select are available and there’s a good guide on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: The entire game is about the story so that's what I'm going to focus on for my review. You'll understand why I think the story is the only real subject of the game later on. The fact that there is no gameplay or real treasure finding is kind of the point of the story.A lot of people are kind of confused about the ending. I think that it's a symptom of bad storytelling. It has an interesting idea but it doesn't execute it properly. Before I go into spoilers I'll go ahead and mark a grade for the main elements of the game.This game is a linear storytelling script where you can walk around and observe your environment. The premise is that you are helping Beth find an earring on a farm about to be paved over by a real estate company. You playing Adam, a childhood friend, helping Beth work past her domestic troubles while metal detecting out on a farm.Graphics: 6/10 Story: 6/10Gameplay: 1/10 (I'll get into more later in spoilers)Voice acting: 9/10 Overall a very short walking simulator once you understand what is actually going on. I would say wait until this game is under $5 if you want to explore it for yourself, but if you do want to play it don't read these spoilers. Once you understand the story there is nothing else there for you, unless you really think you're going to be impressed by the graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a first person narrative based game surrounding two characters, Beth and Adam. Beth has not seen Adam for years; Not since she became famous for finding a precious earring on the local farm. They shared a relationship but it came to a grinding halt after this incident. Beth invites Adam to spend the week with her metal detecting on the same farm. Her life has begun to unravel and she wants to revisit the glory days by finding the illusive second earring.Adam has a lot of questions to ask Beth, especially as things never quite got resolved between them. They discuss various issues whilst trying to find that second illusive earring. Firewatch is one of my most favourite games and left a long and lasting impression on me. The Magnificent Trufflepigs (TMT) promised to be a kindred spirit, but it pales in comparison and left me discontented.There are many similarities between the games; they are both narrative games with two main characters and the stories are both told whilst communicating through walkie talkies. It is obviously a Firewatch clone.TMT has a detestable main character in Beth. What an egotistic, spoilt and ungrateful woman. Throughout the two and a half hours I played this game she shocked me on several occasions with her unbelievably selfish comments. The whole story is based around what she wants and it feels terribly unbalanced.There are many villains in games and I don’t often dislike games because of a despicable character but she annoyed me intensely. The voice acting of the character is also aggravating with her fiercely exaggerated mannerisms and fake demeanor. The problem is that I don’t think she was intentionally meant to be portrayed like this, and I can only put it down to poor storytelling.From the initial scenes I was asking myself questions about the story. I couldn’t understand why she was inviting him, knowing she jolted him years ago, and she showed no remorse or was apologetic in any way. This set alarm bells ringing and this flagrant disregard for Adam’s feelings continued throughout. It was painful to watch and made the whole game very unenjoyable for me. I think this was just lazy character development.Every conversation seemed contrived and over exuberant. It just didn’t feel believable and the discussions they had seemed boring and didn’t offer much emotional content at all.There is a frustrating conversation skip mechanic where the skip button is displayed on screen with a timer after every dialogue. It is too quick to use and just becomes annoying to look at. Even with the subtitles off it still appears.Occasionally, there is an option to choose between a couple of replies and this often causes chaos with that. What is wrong with just pausing the conversation after every dialogue and pressing a button to continue. A skip button is not needed. The conversations are always short and text appears quickly. It is an absolutely bizarre mechanic to include.In-between conversations we can do a bit of metal detecting. I was interested to see how this would materialize but it proved to be disappointing also. The detector was cleverly designed which made it easy to find items but there is no enjoyment in locating buried treasure. It became quite obvious that these items were meant to be discovered to drive the story. There is no real challenge, although I didn’t find all the items so I was either too slow or it’s designed to find more on subsequent playthroughs. There is a frustrating element where you can easily leave your metal detector lying around in another field only to realise it’s missing when you go to use it. Although it is easy to find, it is just disheartening to go looking for it when it could just be there for you to use.The game looks nice and there is a pleasant enough generic soundtrack playing in the background but that is about the only positives I can think of.Beth and Adam communicate through their walkie talkies, discussing life issues and commenting on the objects they find whilst metal detecting.They also communicate through their mobile phones, taking photos of the objects they find and conversing through text messages. Occasionally, the item will invoke a conversation over the walkie talkie and Beth will talk to you about the item, either explaining its historical value or reminiscing, if it is a familiar object.The metal detecting scenes seem quite linear even though you do have free range of the field. There is by no means a large area to explore but there is enough room for you to feel like you are trying.The detecting mechanism is done very well. It acts like a traffic light system. Green is warm, amber is closer and red means you are on top of the item. An audible sound of beeping directs you to the goal and it feels quite satisfying the first time you strike gold. You soon realise that items are found regardless of where you search and this takes away the enjoyment a little. Also, Beth does hardly any metal detecting at all. I’m not sure what she is doing but she isn’t metal detecting! There are five days of metal detecting to perform and the story revolves around these activities.Occasionally, you can take pictures of unusual items (usually achievement based) and Beth or Adam will comment on them. A camera icon will appear and you’ll be able to take a snap.There are fifteen relatively easy achievements to chase.Visuals are very pleasant and the art direction is sometimes beautiful and imaginative. There is a nice atmosphere in the game. It invokes summer days and wide-open spaces which is perfect for a farm location. Landmarks are rendered nicely and fit into the story well. For example, we can see Beth’s place of work in the distance which is a place providing much angst for her, and through her dialogues we get a good feeling about the small-town mentality she experiences.The text boxes and the font of the subtitles seemed a bit amateurish to me. They just seemed too basic.The voice acting is clear and crisp but they have regional dialects which I didn’t enjoy. Although it may represent a northern accent, people do not speak with so much expression and vigor all the time. It just felt like Beth was over-acting constantly and there weren’t any poignant or sad moments in the story because she was always way too jovial. Adam was much better. He wasn’t so hectic in his approach, but even his dialogues didn’t seem very plausible. I felt like they were both trying to over compensate for the bad script. There are different music tracks playing in the background. They are gentle and relaxing and sound quite charming.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: A nice idea, overshadowed by several glaring issues.- The story is... not good, and it is constantly thrown in your face. You get maybe 1 minute of metal detecting, followed by at least an equal amount of time of listening to quite badly written dialogue, as you stand still doing nothing (the only option during these sections). These interruptions are constant.- It seems (at least to me) that where you dig doesn't actually matter. It just produces the next item off a predetermined list, so the characters can talk about it (and as mentioned previously, they'll talk about anything).- The "moral" of the story, which I won't spoil, is the most insulting thing I've encountered in a game for ages. It seems to think it's saying something profound, when it's actually about a very privileged person having a minor crisis about which extremely fortunate opportunity they should pursue.It's a shame because the core idea is nice. Give me a metal detector, some items to find, and a big field and I'd be happy. The story could be delivered mostly by text and not lose anything, allowing me to read it at my leisure.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: A well-written narrative game which tackles questions about happiness, meaning, privilege, and confronting the truth about ourselves and our memories. It's not quite a walking simulator, but it's not far off from one, so only get it if you're interested in a well-written and beautifully voice-acted interactive story, not a mechanics-intensive game.Full Review: I Enjoyed:+Good writing+Great voice acting+Beautiful scenery and music+It's quite relaxing to wander around looking for treasures+Good accessibility optionsCould Use Improvement:-Impossible to skip the dialogue until the voice acting is complete (annoying for deaf players, fast readers, or those replaying for achievements)-The controls are slowed quite a bit during dialogue even though you can still walk and look around; would have preferred if you could just walk normal speed the whole timeOverall, I recommend The Magnificent Trufflepigs to anyone who might enjoy a compelling interactive indie film rather than someone looking for in-depth gameplay.

I put it on , just to see how nice it looked and, before I knew it,  3 hours have gone by and I hit the credit screen.Only problem I had was I missed the graveyard in my first play. when I went back to see if I could find the achievement. _childDocuments_.review: Hello everyone!  I just wanted to say that I really enjoyed this game!  It was mostly peaceful and relaxing throughout the entire experience and the game is very beautiful.Unfortunately since most of your time is spent looking at the ground some of that beauty feels a little wasted.  The game is also incredibly short and does not offer much time to actually just use the metal-detector and it often felt like the story/commentary was the main focus of the entire experience.  I really think that this game could benefit from just having more time to use the metal detector and find stuff and also having a mode that's driven towards using the metal-detector.As far as the story went, I wasn't terribly interested in the whole ordeal.  I did enjoy a few of the witty quips between the characters, but the overall story just felt really inconsequential.  The ending to the game particularly threw me off, but maybe this type of story just isn't for someone like me.Overall I had a pretty enjoyable experience and I'd definitely recommend getting this game especially if they end up doing something more with the metal-detecting side of the game.  Just remember that the game is incredibly short (I played it all the way through and only played for 2 hours) but does strangely seem to offer a New Game Plus experience which I didn't really delve into at all.
