_childDocuments_.review: Alright so this is a "I don't recommend, BUT..." The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a narrative heavy game (NOT a simulation game...not really anyways) but there were several little moments where the game could've made just a smidge of a change and made it just a bit more interactive and maybe a bit more engaging. Which just puts a damper on the situation a bit. The writing for the story is at times a little confusing and really I didn't like either character. I'll try to go in depth with as few spoilers as possible. Pros: - Visually, the game looks great! It's stylized views of the grassy fields overlooking the village are nice and relaxing. I also find the wind farm relaxing. Is that weird? - The voice acting is pretty solid! Both characters have some banter which is worth a chuckle, but really they have charisma and feel like people you know...unfortunately as an introvert neither of these are people I'd like (jk, well sorta)Cons:- So right off the bat, the game lets you click to skip dialogue, but only like the last literal half second of each line...and it's got a quick time event style timer that when it drains, it just advances the dialogue anyways...Either make the lines skippable completely or make it unskippable. - First thing I did was look at a windmill. My character (without me doing anything) pulls out his phone, takes a photo, and sends it to Beth to start a dialogue. Just a small touch, but if you let me click a button or two to pull out my phone and decide to bring it up to Beth or not, it would've been just a little bit more interactive and given me more control over the story. Or at least the illusion of control. Looking at you Mass Effect 3. - The metal detecting was relaxing at first, but dear lord. You will literally photograph every piece of scrap metal and text it to Beth. I think I found a screw or tent pole, something whatever and I thought "There's no way we call Beth to have a conversation about this..." behold, we whip out the ol' phone to send Beth a photo and the game feels like we've gotta start a dialogue about it. - Also every time you find an object, the time it takes to put away the detector, pull out your phone, photograph the item, text it to Beth, and then pull out the radio and wait a bit to start a conversation about nothing is really noticeable after awhile. I'm not asking for break neck action or anything, I love simulation, narrative games that just have some charm, but the actions are sometimes a bit drawn out. - There's a hint of a twist that's possibly here, but the game doesn't really do anything to flesh it out. It also doesn't really affect much? Like I don't think "Oh woooow that's so cool" I just kinda go "huh" as it seems odd and there's other points in the game that kind of contradict it? Whatever, I just thought it was worth mentioning. - Lastly, the characters are suuuuuper unlikable. Maybe it's because I'm annoyed by these types of people. I won't say much beyond that in case you want to experience this for yourself. All I'll say is at first I was in disbelief at how one character was treating someone, then the other was also being rude. I just rolled my eyes and am reminded that I'm an introverted hermit for a reason probably. TLDR; Okayish story, good voice acting, has opportunity to make it a little more gamelike or control the narrative a touch more, and both of the characters are kind of trash people. But this game does hit some high notes, just wasn't thrilled with it overall.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Intriguing concept poor executionAt first glance, the concept seems to fit perfectly as a walking simulator, with apparently enjoyable gameplay, decent voice acting, lovely scenery and a great soundtrack. The problem is that the game does not know how to proceed with the ideas.Gameplay is half-baked. Instead of letting the player decide which tools to use for the job the game does it for you by showing some button prompts. You cant even interact with your equipment when they are not needed. The problem with this decision is that the game is limiting an already shallow gameplay mechanic. The pacing is the worst I have seen in a long time. Every story prompt or dialog sequence forces the player to stop playing the game. You end up standing in one space for what feels like minutes without anything to interact with. This decision makes a slow game unnecessarily tedious. Arguably one of the most important elements of a walking simulator is its story. But this story is not capable of carrying the game on its back even if the previous problems were solved. The story felt shallow and uninspired. The dialog was a bit unnatural, and the main character was unlikeable (maybe intentional?).  Despite all my issues whit the game, it has some qualities. If you want to relax in the countryside of England with a great soundtrack charming environment, and great ambiance I would recommend it if that's what you're looking for. I wanted to like this game so much, hoping that I had found a hidden gem, but ultimately the game was not meant for me to enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a first-person, metal-detecting narrative game. You play as Adam, a sharp-witted but compassionate man returning to his childhood village of Stanning. There he'll help a woman named Beth on her mission to unearth a local treasure.The game has amazing visuals, with stylized graphics and a bright color scheme, that makes you wonder how accurately they actually wanted to picture quaint English countryside, since it looks more like a fantasy than reality. I kinda wish they would have worked more with this game, because as it is now, it feels like something that was not finished properly. There is interesting slice-of-life type of story unfolding as you play, about Beth and her day to day life, but we learn next to nothing about the main protagonist, who was more interesting to me and the actual gameplay of searching for treasure with the metal detector is very very slow, to the point of being annoying.If you are a gamer who strives to 100% games, this game might be a pain, as skipping dialogue is not possible and even in new game+ finding the remaining treasures you need for one of the achievements gets a little annoying. Atleast they have chapter select, which works as intended, but sadly you can't use that to find the treasures you are missing after completing the game for the first time, that's what new game+ is for.The ending of the story was quite predictable even at the start, and sadly it left a sour taste in the mouth, even though it was enjoyable for the first time playing. It felt like the short time of 7 days metal detecting was not enough to uncover the whole backstory and story fully and interestingly as possible.In the end however, I did enjoy playing the game, mostly because I enjoy walking simulators and I find metal detecting to be actually quite interesting. Sadly I don't think this is a good game for anyone else who isn't interested in those very specific topics/genres. I also think the price of it is a little bit too steep for the amount of content there is. Otherwise, I do recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much going for it but gave very little thought to the plot as it is half thought out and just seems to end suddenly. i thought collecting everything might change this but this adds nothing to the final result  it is a very good looking game but either the detector mechanic nor the story get anyway close to this unfortunately, with more time and a better plot this could have been amazing

_childDocuments_.review: TLDRPros: - Beautiful, calming, English countryside scenery/atmosphere- Lovely soundtrack- Great voice acting- Fun detecting game playCons:- Unlikable main character who keeps interrupting your sweet sweet detecting time- Inability to multi-task (ie walk and talk / detect and talk)- Predictable plot twist- Shallow, rushed story line- No replay valueOverall rating: 6/10 - but that is largely because it fits two of my specific interests - metal detecting and walking simulators. Actual Review:I love metal detecting and am always excited to find a new metal detecting video game. This game has beautiful scenery, great voice acting, enjoyable metal detecting game play. It is a bit short and I feel like this left the story aspect feeling very surface level. The main character, Beth, was not very likeable as a character but I don't think she was supposed to be. There were quite a few times where I got annoyed at her for interrupting my metal detecting with her narcissistic childhood memories. I was like "girl just shut up and let me find the bloody earring!" I don't think I would have minded so much if the game let you continue detecting while you listen to her but for some reason you have to stop everything you're doing whenever she talks to you over the walkie talkie - it even makes you walk painfully slow for some reason as if you can't walk and talk at the same time. I saw the twist at the end coming and it wasn't particularly satisfying. I dunno felt like maybe the story was a bit rushed as it all had to fit into 7 days. I had fun time playing it but it wasn't anything to write home about which was a bit disappointing as I was really looking forward to playing this. I'd give it maybe a 6/10 but it did fit into my very specific niches of both metal detecting and walking simulators so I probably wouldn't recommend it to any of my friends.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: So many ways to do a story exploration game. Yet The Magnificent Trufflepigs chose the most insufferable one. I rarely write opinions on games I do not finish, but getting to day 2 (out of 5, apparently), has been such a painful experience that I can't even believe.Bits with metal detecting exist to "add gameplay", but there's no sense of exploration or discovery and every couple of steps or actions you're bound to be abruptly forced into a "conversation" between two unlikable characters with no skip line button (there's a "skip pause between lines" button which is the most useless idea I've ever seen). I've seen lots of games of this type accused of "better being just stories/films", yet this is the first time in my experience I see a title designed with so little understanding of how a GAME works, that it might've indeed been better off as a story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: I was really excited for this game when I saw the trailer. The visuals are absolutely gorgeous, and it has a very peaceful atmosphere. But this isn't what I expected from this game at all. Based on the trailer, I expected it to turn into a serious game full of mystery, similar to Firewatch. I do feel the trailer was intentionally misleading with all of the little lines they through in there. "You're not going to believe this," "Did you find something else?" "The police have taken an interest in what we're doing," "Are you going to pretend nothing's happened?" and so on. As well as the sudden shot of the helicopter flying overhead right after the mention of the police with that "ominous" sound effect. And the music in the trailer had a bit of a serious vibe, like there was going to be some big twist, like discovering a hidden conspiracy or something along those lines.Now, I wouldn't really mind playing a metal detector simulator. I'm definitely a big fan of sim games. But this doesn't even really succeed at making that fun. One good thing other than the beautiful graphics is the voice acting. Although the characters, especially Beth, are another story.All in all, I went into the game expecting a mystery set in a game with beautiful graphics. But I was left feeling disappointed. Looking at the reviews, I know there are people who DID like the game, so maybe you will, too.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: At its best, The Magnificent Trufflepigs feels similar to Firewatch, transporting you to a relaxing, scenic location to lose yourself in for a few hours, far away from the hustle and bustle of city life. It’s also supported by some great acting between the two unseen protagonists, but here the drama never really amounts to anything and even the ending just doesn't quite hit home. Unlike the abnormally perpetual sunny skies of the game itself, the experience here ends up feeling much more like the weather we Brits often bemoan, tempting players with the odd ray of graphical and conceptual sunshine here and there but ultimately clouding over and dampening any promise with its confusing narrative and unlikeable leads.Good:    Stunning English landscapes to explore    Strong voice acting, especially from Doctor Who’s Arthur DarvillBad:    Characters are hard to relate to and unlikeable    Whilst fun at first, metal detecting gets repetitive    Story peters out to an abrupt ending
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the writing in this game, the superb voice acting, and the very English conversations (I'm overseas and it's a nice reminder). Was honestly really impressed with the tone and pacing and thoughtfulness of everything.  The character and story development never felt boring or too hackneyed, and part of the ending was a bit of a surprise!
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely little tale. A quaint stroll through English, farming fields, with beautiful melodies and scenery to keep one company. Beth and Adam are great characters to listen to and their dialogue, for the most part, seems magically authentic - even with the psychological leitmotifs and... litotes laced beneath. There is a wonderful connect and concurrent disconnect between the finds in the field, sparking this way or falling away like the transient butterfly with the other. It's a beautiful story that requires investment from the listener; as much as the game might be passive, one's cognisance of character congruence is certainly most active. While I do wish there had been a bit more length to the title and a bit better use of the narrative-detector-unearth gameplay, 'The Magnificent Trufflepigs' remains a short, heartwarming experience I'm glad for having had. Thank you for making this, and thank you to the voice actress and actor for rendering this to a stirring life.As far as gameplay goes, just one annoyance and one minor bug I came across and hopefully these can be patched out:Annoyance: The press 'A' or 'lmouse' to continue after every line of dialogue is rather annoying, both aurally and visually and I don't see any need for it to be there - the dialogue should just flow without impediment.Bug: I had two crashes when the game was paused and I unpaused it to continue, the game would lockup.P.S.I now know the name of my star ship in Star Citizen: The Magnificent Trufflepig - thank you ;D
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to like Magnificent Trufflepigs, a story of metal detectorists in the manner of Everybody's Gone To The Rapture (i.e. more of a choose-your-own-adventure audio play than a game) with the graphical style of Firewatch (i.e. cartoony but sufficiently representative of the countryside to be convincingly immersive). However, it's just too darned slow, even by walking simulator standards. The total play time is rumoured to be no more than 2-4 hours, but even I struggled to maintain interest past half an hour. The main problem, I think, is that the plot revolves around the relationship between the protagonist and the off-screen antagonist and, frankly, it's too insipid for anyone to care about. Furthermore, not only is movement frustratingly slow, but the player is also constrained to one field at a time - you can't explore, or at least, you can't explore for the first 30-40 minutes that it managed to cling on to my attention. The well-acted dialogue is ruined by poorly timed, lengthy gaps between responses, which soon becomes frustrating. It's a huge shame, as it was developed by former Chinese Room folk (the software house behind Rapture) and the player is voiced by Arthur Darvil (Amy's husband from Doctor Who). It deserved to be better. Still, I paid less than a tenner for it, so technically it's not bad value.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: I sadly cannot really recommend this one. As much as I love laid back walking simulators and story drive games, the bar with this one was set too low.Firts of all: the whole Beth - Adam relationship is annoying at best. She is there to help as last resource only because nobody else could/would help Beth. I don't need to tell you what happens to Adam when the story finished, what do you think? Beth is really an unlikeable person. Why would you put button prompts to CONTINUE a conversation? The conversation does continue without pressing the button, but there is a weird timer between EVERY sentence, which is a pause. You can skip the pause by pressing the button, but why? Just let the conversation go on with the normal pauses between sentences. A "dialogue skip" button would have made much more sense. Can it even be a game developing mistake? Maybe they were meaning to put a skip button, not a useless rest between sentences.Second: the game technically is just not well executed to justify the close-to-none mechanics. You just have to scan the floor with the metal detector, nothing else. Means, looking around should be entertaining to balance the fact that you are doing absolutely nothing in the game. Instead:- graphics are bare to a minimum. The lighting system is fake = shadows do move in real time, but sadly doesn't correspond to the sky. Means: if it turns shadowy for a second, you expect a cloud to have come in front of the sun....well it's not. This totally breaks immersion if you are supposed to enjoy the scenery and the looks of the farmfield. If a cloud is indeed in front of the sun, the grass shines just as bright....doesn't make sense.- there are no interactions: the objects you find will float in the air, just like the walkie talkie. Why not render a simple hand holding the objects and the walkie talkie? I mean since the game is stripped to a minimum, some simple details WILL make a difference. Don't get me started on the animation of the van at the end...seriously.It is in a way still entertaining but not memorable. Also, you will enjoy the story (personal opinion) only if you are of a certain age, where you personally thought or lived a wedding or a long lost friendship, some things where you can actually mirror yourself into.Voice acting is good.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing narrative game which feels very badly written and with underdeveloped characters - but mostly this is due to the story having to hide the ending "twist".  If you replay the game (even just the start) suddenly a lot of the dialogue makes a lot more sense.  The visuals and music are both beautiful (though environments are limited to a small area at a time).  The mechanics for metal detecting are well done, but sadly this is only a cursory part of the game which is mostly about pausing for the unsatisfying narrative.  Fans of the characterisation of "Firewatch" or the esoteric style of "Everyone's Gone to the Rapture" should look elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Again, I wish that Steam had a thumbs-middle option.An hour or two into this game it was a firm thumbs-down; too many things didn't work or grated slightly.  When the credits rolled and I went back for a "new game+" (a slight misnomer perhaps), it was a thumbs up.  Now the sun has set it's a thumbs-middle.Let me explain.Firstly, one thing I wish I'd known is that reportedly TIME ONLY ADVANCES WHEN PICKING ITEMS.  This I didn't know and it made me a little anxious about missing things, which is not what one wants from a fairly chilled walking sim with a story to tell.  Maybe it put some pressure on a personality-nerve, but I found myself rushing from place to place within the fields, worrying that the lunch bell would ring and I'd miss something.Secondly, and maybe related to the first (in that I wasn't idly swinging my detector, drinking in the bucolic countryside), it seemed a near constant flow of radio chatter without much space in between, nowhere Kojima-level, but I did notice it.Thirdly the Firewatch comparison.  Yes, the other spoken-narrative game where one wanders with a walkie-talkie a lot.  In that game one could chatter back and forth *while moving* at a pace and getting from wherever you were to wherever you were going.  In "Trufflepigs" every call from your companion stops you walking more than a snail pace and, frankly, there isn't anything more to do while you listen to the story unfold, for example you can't go and detect the next item.The story is good and that's not the problem at all, but it did feel a bit like "walk ten yards, listen to two minutes of story, walk six yards, listen to one minute of story".I know, it's a game about looking for things in the ground and answers in the air, but essentially pausing the game quite often did take the wind out of the sails.  If I was walking slowly, waiting the beep instead of hunting it I think my take would have been different.The good then; it's a beautiful game no doubt.  Capturing the summer in this grean and pleasant land of England perfectly.  The scenery and setting is lovely and I could nearly smell the grass.  The mechanics are good and finding all 50 items was never a chore as the beeps were very satisfying.  The music and general soundscape complimented the visuals just right and plucked me from these frigid January days in a most welcome manner.The voice acting is of a high quality by professionals with nice voices to listen to, though the characters never quite "drew" in my minds eye like I thought they would.  The story is good and gave a surprise or two which, after mulling on for a while, is far smarter and deeper than I thought at the time.  It did open up the opening monologue in an unexpected way the second time around, which is always nice.So yes, there it is.  At the end of this review I'd probably still give it a thumbs-middle but will give it a thumbs-up, this is because the game was obviously made with a lot of love, commitment and belief and I appreciate that.  If someone is making a walking sim about metal detecting in the English countryside, I'm keeping an eye on them and look forward to what else appears.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game. I absolutely loved Firewatch for its dialog, exploration and mystery. I did not find any of that in Trufflepigs. Granted I only played for a short time, but did not enjoy the dialog and felt absolutely zero connection to the characters. I did enjoy the setting and the simple metal detecting gameplay, but it was interrupted far too often by the dialog. Maybe I didn't give it enough time, but definitely gave a poor first impression.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: I am a simple man. Give me a metal detector and a field and I will be happy. Interrupt me every minute with forced dialog that I somehow can't continue to detect during and I am sad. A metal detecting game should contain at least some mindless fun, but it feels like I am punished for succeeding because if I find even the most boring rusty screw, I know I will be forced to stop playing and glaze over slow dialog about how rusty screws are like life or a metaphor for love or growing up in a small town. Just let me find junk in a field, dude.

_childDocuments_.review: A compact title that delivers on it's goal to give players a narrative game that can be consumed in an evening.A bit shorter than say Firewatch or Sunset but I feel the price reflects this and is well worth the cost.The voice acting is wonderful, detailing the existing relationship between characters and setting the scene for the current day events and dialogue.Holding out for that TrufflePig Battle Royale mod, 99 Detectorists, 1 Field, 1 Treasure. :D

_childDocuments_.review: About 2-2.5 hours long walking sim with treasure collecting that is imo way better than the overall review score might imply.The game looks nice, it's story focused, writing and voice acting is pretty good. Very enjoyable and relaxing game. Only thing I wasn't really liking was the ending. (like in most video games lol)
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Short but sweet. A human, emotional story interwoven through a genuinely fun in its own right detecting mechanic. Seriously, I would play the heck out of a longer dedicated metal-detecting game. Finding the items was a lot of fun, and having them either prompt conversation between the two characters or reveal something about the history of the place was a very nice touch. The story itself if quite low stakes but full of heart. It's more about the characters' internal emotional journey than any great occurrence, the final revelations more like natural turning points for people thinking a lot about where they want to be. I half expected some greater mystery to be revealed, but that's not what this game is about. Like the characters, you're just exploring and enjoying the scenery while working out where you fit into it all. Some might find the ending unsatisfying, but for me it felt very honest and natural.I'd have liked more time for exploring and finding items. I felt like the breaks in detecting came a bit too soon for me, and I left each day feeling a little dissatisfied that I hadn't gotten to fully sweep each section, but other than that I very much enjoyed the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: 4-5h 1/10 1,5 No I wrote  to tell you the items/landmarks you need to photograph for some achievements. Those achievements are missable. 1 on Astats No Yes, the things you need to photograph and you need to choose to detect a little longer on each day.  No No No No No difficulty option NoThis is a very relaxing narrative game with excellent voice acting. You will go metal detecting while chatting with Beth by Walki-Talki or during breaks in her car. You'll talk about items you find but also about life and the choices we make. Don't expect to go fast through this game, walking with a metal detector is a slow progress, but the game isn't that long. The story takes around 3 to 4 hours. The game has some missable achievements like choosing to keep metal detecting each day when Beth tells you it is time for Lunch. And you have to photograph some landmarks and other things, see the link to my guide above to know where they are and not miss out on them. You have to play through the game a little bit more than 1 playthrough to find all the items. The game has some story-related items you will find, but also random items. In the new game + the random items you haven't found will come up first when you find a random item. I got the idea that whenever you choose to go on metal detecting after Beth calls for a break, you for sure find a random item, but this is just the idea I got. Things the game can improve, the devs seem to think about those, so there is hope they will implement them:1. I wish there was an option to select a day after finishing your first playthrough. That would make that none of the achievements would be missable anymore. 2. I wish there was an option to skip dialog, especially in the new game + since you already know what the conversation will be and it can give a new perspective to hear it after you know how the story ends but still, it felt tedious the second time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Does walking around slowly staring at virtual grass, while a woman speaks in cockney accent about her extremely boring life sound like a fun time? If not the you may want to skip this.... I am sure this will appeal to some people, its meant to just be a chill game about finding metal, and don't get me wrong I am a big fan of so called "walking sims", but I felt like I got nothing out of this, and the one "plot twist" was so dumb and nonsensical.At least the devs were kind enough to let you replay "chapters" if you want to go back for achievements, but as of this review you cant skip the mind-numbingly boring dialogue... so really you should consider going outside and stare at the grass for 2.5 hours (the length of the game roughly), I can promise you that you will be more entertained than playing this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very clever and nicely manipulative game that is a pure joy to play.It doesn't overstay its welcome. stays fresh and intriguing pretty much all the way through.The most important thing about it is how it's creating and reacting to your expectations - you're never quite sure what's going on, and the game often chuckles at your assumptions, but weird bits keep being casually dropped in the middle of dialogues, making you want to learn more.Also, for a game where essentially two friends are casually chatting, it has really good writing and a very refreshing depth to the dialogues - I was always annoyed at games like RDR2, where you have a bunch of people who know each other for ages, yet when it comes to casual chat, there's just one or two inconsequential lines, failing to show any kind of closeness. Not here, this is real stuff. I think it creates the best feeling of hanging out with a friend than anything else I've played. Also, as a waking sim and as a story-driven game, I think it's one of the best out there, definitely top tier as an emotional experience. Recommend even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a very touchy story in my opinion, it takes one thru ups and downs and unlike other games, it has a kind of sad ending for the palyer, atleast in my eyes. _childDocuments_.review: This game is many things, perhabs to much things at the same time. Some kind of Jack of all Trades and a master of none. It comes with flaw and problems in any form and shape, but surprisingly managed to leave behind a meaningfull lection to be learned by the player. When it comes to other review it seems that one half expierenced an amazing revelation while the other half got turned away missing the twist of the story and therefor the lesson.I wanna write this review a spoilerfree as possible so there is some stuff I cant talk about. I am going to adress some issues that would be part of big spoiler and I am going to vaguely speak about a few things. Please mind that.You are Adam and you are called by Beth an old friend to help and search for an earring on an old soon to be demolished farm. The game takes place across 5 days. Your tools to find the earing are a metaldetector, a shovel and a trovel. At first running arround the really beautifull scenery on this old farm and try finding and digging up mostly metal trash while being on the hunt for the big treasure sounds exiting. Sadly its not. Detecting mostly consist about walking really slow with a big metal detector arround and wait for the game to spawn something in front of you. You heard right. The game doesnt hide stuff arround for you to sweap for. It has an internal timer spawning items everyonce in awhile. A quick test to try this is to not actively search and run arround without detecting. Once you start the detector it goes of imidiatily. While some story items are fixed the game spawns random stuff for you to find. You cannot find everything within the first time you need to replay the game on new game + to find the last and missing items for the final achievement. Just a side note. This choice in gameplay is boring. Active the detector and press your forward button until the game spawn an item then one button for the shovel and 3 to 4 for the trovel till you have your item in your hands. There is no thrill of the hunt about it. Just a waiting game. This mechanic exist for one reason. To advance in time. Each time you pick up an item you take a picture and send to Beth. Depending on the item found you either get small talk on your smartphone or a full blown conversation on the walkie talkie. Each time slowing you down forcing you to listen. Just because this game is about a story. The story of Beth having trouble in her life growing up. The problem I have with this progession method is that is a way to complex system that could have been a simple walking simulutor. Instead I am forced either to the gameplay interrupting the storytelling or the storytelling interrupting the gameplay. The majorty looks like this. You spend a minute sweaping to be interrupted to talk for 3 minutes. Depending on what you enjoy at the beginning the other is interrupting therefor creating an inbalance of gameplay and story. Of course it may be you like both so the problem doesnt apply but i my case I didnt enjoy either. The first two days storywise are painfull to listen. As the player I felt like the third wheel stuck inbetween to friends on a long flight across the globe talking to each other about anything and everything. I had trouble finding anything to bond with either Beth or the character we play Adam. While some background story is dropped pretty early on about Beth. Adam seem to just exist. It give the vibe that Adam is no stranger to the player and we are supposed to know him very well. In reality we dont. We control a shallow shadow of a figure I couldnt care less about. Beth isnt better here. My dislike in her grew and grew early on. She is this type of workaholic that feels entitled and selfish about herself and we played the role of the mechanic fixing her after some stuff went wrong. Adam gets treated like ♥♥♥♥ by Beth. So I felt stuck inbetween boring conversations and boring gameplay. But I went on torward the end. The later half of the game got better for me. Obviously only the story started to get more serious and the greater picture gets more and more shown. The highlight are two twist the story has. One being kinda obivous and figurable pretty early on and the other is the one a lot of players miss. I liked the last twist. It made a lot more sense and gave away a great lection a lot of people should learn in life. However the first half ruined the game for me and the later could save it entirly. It just made the time not feeling like wasted fully. More or less like a little reward earned at the end. The story itself is more suitable for young adults struggling with the shift from being young to getting older. Specifficly arround the age of thirty. Its about dreams and purpose and understanding the meaing of life. Itself that would be a nice story listen to and with Darvill voicing adam I got one of my favorite Doctor Who companions Rory Williams talking. Which is really nice. However the game misses of balancing the story. One big mistake is not proper introducing the characters.A similar game, Firewatch, which is build almost the same way. A game hiding a story based walking sim within some gamplay, in this case exploration and observation. Firewatch has an introduction build arround giving us a brief choice of action while exploring the past years of the main character. He starts with broken feelings and we understand why and can feel themself. Trufflepigs doesnt do this. Adam exist without anything in background at the beginning. The only thing we know about him that nobody except Beth likes him. Which as part of the biggest reveal remains a mystery for the long time. The game tries to gain sympathy for Beth but fails to give a proper picture and paints only the bad things about her.The wonderfull Emily is away is game about to characters having conversations every once in awhile over a messager. Its only pressing one button for the text to appear and sometime making a choice but it does this whole social drama better. It has the same nonesense and meaningfull stuff at the same time. Eventhough Emily is away has a more romantical plot while this game is not a romance. It may come of here and there but trust me the twist shows my some stuff seemed like this.For me the game has a good idea making the wrong design and writing choices. Leaving it in the vast ocean of mediocre titles rarely remember in the future. I fait I wish no game.

_childDocuments_.review: Do I recommend The Magnificent Trufflepigs? Well, no. And not necessarily because the experience was wholly abysmal (there are brief glimpses of heart here and there), but because it’s the video game equivalent of a disinterested shrug, and I’m genuinely not sure what it can offer to audiences that hasn’t been done better elsewhere. Gameplay-wise, it’s repetitive and monotonous, even by “walking sim” standards. There’s nothing fun about the metal detecting mechanic since it literally consists of pressing the same buttons over and over again, which causes it to wear out its welcome within minutes of starting the adventure. Things don’t look particularly great on the narrative front, either: I had hoped the storyline would help make up for the lackluster metal-detecting mechanics, but that never quite happened. Instead, what we get is a well-intentioned but woefully unremarkable tale that I'll probably forget about in a matter of weeks, if not days.Gameplay footage with Hungarian commentary: For more honest indie game reviews, check out our Curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended...with some caveats. I like walking simulators - if you don't, stay away, there is nothing for you here. The metal detecting I think should have been made a little mini-game rather than a simple Quicktime event (single press of E followed by three presses of Q, that's it). I think there are a little too many interruptions - especially in the beginning where you seem to move 3 feet, then get interrupted by a little cut-scene (where you hold the walky talkie in your hand and listen to dialog), it gets quite frustrating. And it is a little short (2 hours for me, and I was not rushing it).
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Well, well, well! It's time to write a review for Trufflepigs! Trufflepigs gives you a break from the world much like the main character Beth needs. In this short but sweet story about "finding oneself" you find yourself digging up the past, be it metaphorically through a walkie talkie, or physically via a shovel. At times, Trufflepigs can get tedious and slow - It, like all games in this genre, relies on storytelling and heavy dialogue. There were moments where I felt like Beth could maybe not get involved in absolutely everything and leave me be, but it didn't ever feel like I wanted to disconnect the battery from the walkie talkie.The scenery can get a little boring, too. I spent 2 hours walking around fields that looked identical to be rewarded with (another) plastic earring OR some odd piece of metal.For everything it isn't, Trufflepigs is lovely. It's playful, full of dad-humour and takes you back to the same mistakes you once made. It's coming of age, in the middle of life, but it does make you think afterwards that maybe, just maybe, life will be OK.A solid 7/10.

Its one of those just okay games, nothing amazing but not terrible either. Keep in mind this is first impressions not an actual full review. So take that with a grain of salt. _childDocuments_.review: Kind of short overall but I'm glad I picked it up - I don't usually go for anything on release date, but it looked like something I'd enjoy - probably much closer to a slow-motion version of Rapture than Firewatch though. A similar situation recently happened to someone I know (finding something lost with a metal detector) that resonated with me a bit, which probably helped with the positive review.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: I was disappointed by this game. I don't want to compare it to Firewatch & Rapture unfairly but given that this game used those titles in the advertising I do feel it's fair to do so. The story seems as though it's going somewhere, and then never does. Nothing you actually dig up has any relevance to the story at all - which seems like a massive oversight, frankly. Why not incorporate a subplot through found items that's actually interesting? The trailer suggests some kind of mystery, but all we end up learning about is some woman's personal crisis about a marriage gone wrong and a job she doesn't want. That's not interesting in the slightest.  I - and the two other people I played this with - could see the Adam reveal coming a mile off. Why do we have to walk so SLOWLY when we're detecting? Why do we have to send Beth a photo of every single item we find - nails, coins, pins? Only for some shoehorned in exposition about Beth's life? NahhhhThe graphics are beautiful, but the English village setting is - well, almost entirely irrelevant, given that we're in fields the entire time that all broadly look the same. Compared to Rapture, where the village is stunningly realised, with an enormous depth of environmental storytelling, this is just... not even close. It's a shame. I really wanted to love this - have been looking forward to it coming out as I'm actually a big fan of walking sims, but this was just really boring. Could have been amazing, but wasn't
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Having loved Everybody's Gone To The Rapture, I was buzzing about playing this. Unfortunately, it's difficult to pinpoint exactly but theres just something missing here.It may be the gameplay, which never changes or progresses from the first minute, or the fact that it frustratingly holds you back from fully exploring each location for buried items.Or it may be the story, which promises so much but ends so abruptly and awkwardly that it feels rushed. There is the hint of a really interesting imaginary twist near the end but that doesn't come to fruition either, leaving you distinctly underwhelmed.What we do have here is a really relaxing, somewhat beautiful game that tells an average story with disappointing gameplay. I'll certainly be playing it through more times, but it does feel like a missed opportunity for many reasons.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Graphically and audially, the game is absolutely gorgeous. The environment is incredible, the voice acting and overall charisma of interactions both Beth and Adam on the radio and by text are fantastically well written and well delivered; albeit occasionally there's a little overload on the radio conversations where it may have been nicer to break it up with a couple more text-message only interactions so it didn't feel quite so much like the radio was preventing you from getting on with detecting.It's not a lengthy game (2.5 - 3 hrs in my end-to-end playthrough), but it's just the right length to tell the story the game wanted to tell. Artificially extending it would probably have made it drag, so kudos to the developer for avoiding that particular temptation.As a prior fan of Firewatch, Eastshade and What Remains, this is a really solid piece of interactive storytelling and if you enjoyed games like those, it's definitely worth giving Magnificent Trufflepigs a try.I wanted to say all of that before turning to address the slight elephant in the room which is the story itself. While I won't directly spoil anything, and if you've not played the game, definitely don't mouse over any spoilers in other reviews here, I think conceptually the main story twists ideas are interesting, but as another reviewer commented, I think they may have worked slightly better on paper than in practice. The mechanics of the game are well set-up for emergent storytelling by discovering things, and the sense that you're about to uncover something other than the mystery you set out to solve is present throughout. And technically you do, but I think the actual story that unfolds, while very clever, risks being unsatisfying for some - particularly in how story beats that had been building up from previous days were resolved, and the pacing of the final day where all of the bombshells have dropped and to an extent you're waiting around for a bit wondering what, exactly, you're still doing out in the fields with a metal detector. Will definitely be keeping an eye on Thunkd for the future.
_childDocuments_.name: The Magnificent Trufflepigs

_childDocuments_.review: Video Review:  7/10 You play as Adam who is called by his old childhood friend Beth, back to the farm she once found an ear ring. In search for the missing one, along the way conversation ensues over text and walkie talkie as you meander the beautiful land scape, soon understanding the reason for the search. The Magnificent Trufflepigs visually is stunning with wide landscapes of rolling hills, wind turbines, and fields of green, even though you are sanctioned to a small area of the map it truly brings the world alive and begs to be explored if you weren't so damn vertically challenged. But Luckly it's not the same area each day, with 5 days on different parts of the landscape to soak in and absorb its beauty. Even though you might be looking at dirt for the majority of the game. Because in this story, metal-detecting is the game. With you slowly scanning for any registers and digging up the treasure. Showing pictures to Beth, and her either responding via text or hitting you up on your old kid toy walkie talkies. Either commenting on the item you have just found or bring up past memories or issues she is having in her current life. Allowing you to choose at times what to say to advance the narrative.  It Reminds me of Firewatch in gameplay and storytelling. It’s a slow-moving story at times even though the game is only about 2 hours long, with sections of conversation that makes you wonder was this screw truly necessary to stop searching and talk about. But it builds on the relationship of the two characters giving them personality and grounding them in reality even though you never see them at all.  The magnificent trufflepigs is a relaxing story-based game lead designed by Andrew Crawshaw the person behind Everybody’s gone to the rapture, so you know the conversations and themes will hit in type of way. This is a game when you want relaxing gameplay a beautiful landscape with soothing music, Its relaxing and oddly satisfying digging up not just the treasure of the past but the memories as well, and the reconnecting of childhood friends,

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could have played this game without any of the story to be honest. The main characters are so bad and annoying. Beth is annoying, Adam is a knob. I might even be more forgiving if you were able to keep detecting as she prattled on about her insipid midlife crisis, but this was painful at times.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite obviously, this game must have started off from one simple idea - metal detecting, but an idea is definitely not enough to make a game good. This game turned out to be an example of a seemingly interesting concept that went terribly wrong. What a missed opportunity.It can be somehow felt that this game was trying to learn from or imitate some of the more successful “walking simulator” games, such as  or . It has a beautiful landscape, an explicit narrative, a couple of playful gadgets or Easter eggs. However, unlike other games which take players on a journey, in this game, you, well, just detect metal and find literally piles of junk. Maybe the game could give a backstory to every “crap” found to develop further on its narrative? IDK.To be honest, metal detecting IS a unique idea that has not been done often enough, and we can see the possibility of developing it into an enjoyable game mechanic or using it as an interesting story telling tool. However, this game dedicated the majority of its effort to a bland, predictable and shallow story; and the characters are under-developed and not even half likable. This is such a huge let-down that with or without the metal detecting element, the game feels boring and uninteresting.

_childDocuments_.review: Look for treasure that might bring two people closer than ever before.It should be noted right away that this is a story-first type of game. Saying anything about it would lessen the overall experience. All you need to know is that Beth and Adam, two pals, go to search for an earring in fields near a farm. Beth discovered one earring when she was a child, but she couldn't find the other for years because the farm owner wouldn't allow it. Now that he has died and the farm is being sold, Beth and Adam have one week to find it before the place is sealed off. But while Beth is obsessed with finding the earring, Adam is there for another reason.You play Adam, and Beth communicates with you via walkie-talkie. Because you don't hear or meet any other characters, the story concentrates entirely around these two. You can sometimes choose between two responses, but they don't lead to any unexpected routes or conclusions. This is a game with a predetermined plot. But don't expect any twists or surprising themes; it's quite bland.Accents in voices actors are extremely evident and have a British undertone. If you can look past that and certain stereotypes, you'll discover some excellent voice acting. Both personalities are believable and do not simply read the lines. There are lovely tiny additions like sighs and laughs sprinkled throughout. There's one thing I didn't like the closer I got to the end: the female is selfish and entitled. The relationship between the two characters gets dangerously close to toxic.If you think you'll struggle to follow the plot, you can turn on subtitles. Text and voices cannot be skipped. Well, not straight away. There is an odd feature that is actually meaningless, especially if the subtitles are turned off: you can only skip when the voice is nearing the end of a sentence. The chance to skip lasts for a second or two before the story continues on its own, so the feature is clearly unnecessary.   Although interaction with game’s world is present in a form of metal detecting activity, it’s not exactly exciting or groundbreaking. The idea is to sweep a field with a metal detector and collect whatever you find. Graphics are decent, but not remarkable. You only walk across empty fields so there’s not much to see. The countryside is nice with houses and wind turbines on the hill, but there’s nothing that would stand out.The detectors' pinging sound and visual aids alert you when you're approaching something interesting. Most objects are random and might be found anywhere on the field. The discovered object is then photographed and sent to Beth. She shares her thoughts, and you begin searching for another object.However, finding stuff isn’t that important. It's really just something to do while you wait for Beth to call with new story bits. You don’t even have to find everything. You have a map of the area, but it is only handy if you neglect to pick up your equipment near the digging site. Aside from the achievement of locating everything, there is no idea how many objects are hidden in a field for a single day. Once completed, you proceed to the next day and field, and so on until the end. If you missed anything, you can always go with new game plus or select a day.

_childDocuments_.review: Take my yes with strong reservations and some fine print.The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a game of strong potential that doesn't deliver on most its aspects.The environment is beautiful and the sound design is excellent. Unfortunately the gameplay doesn't really reward exploration because the "levels" are so tiny and each day is so short. On top of that, the gameplay loop is so unsatisfying that it impedes getting lost in the game's atmosphere. You spend much of the game staring at a meter waiting for it to turn red so you're not really looking at the environment. Because the point of the game is metal detecting and trying to find stuff you essentially get punished for taking your time and being lackadaisical. I feel like there was a missed opportunity to making this truly a "metal detecting sim" and instead the metal detecting aspect is a shallow excuse to push a story forward. Starring at a meter listening to beeps can only go so far. The designers could have implemented real aspects of metal detecting. There could have been different types of sound cues depending on the type of metal, or there could have been ui indicating how deep the metal is. This could have made the gameplay loop a little bit more engaging. The area of detection could have been more broad depending on the size of the object, forcing you to spend more of your precious time digging. You could spend a large portion of your limited time digging only to find  that you've spent a bunch of time digging up an old feeding trough or a water main.The gameplay I could leave or take. This is a walking simulator after all, and one of my favorite """games""" is To the Moon, something that just barely skirts the definition of a video game and is truly just an interactive experience that tells a story. It's very clear that this was strongly inspired by Firewatch. It's a beautiful walking sim where a disembodied cheeky woman talks to you over a radio giving you instructions and helping you unravel the story. The differences are startling where Firewatch hit the target and The Magnificent Trufflepigs completely whiffs. While the voice-acting is excellent and the dialogue can be pretty well-written, the overall story is messy, poorly told, extremely rushed, and ends abruptly with an unsatisfying resolution. I feel like the writers and designers could have taken a cue and made the story unfold over the course of a whole season or several weeks rather than trying to fit a convincing story arc in five days. This would have made the character changes less jarring and sudden. There are some very unclear aspects of the story as well because of how crammed the story feels in the short time span. AMC Games describes this as a "first-person, romantic, metal-detecting game." My question is: Is it though? The relationship between Adam and Beth comes off as two old friends that reconnect, but I get zero romantic tension between the two. I feel like the writers were trying to imply past romance between them, but it's unclear when the last time the two saw each other. Based on the dialogue, sometimes it seems like it could have been when they were children, but other times it could have been when they were older? Were they previously in a relationship? We don't know and it's not a story that makes asking that question exciting and engaging the way you wonder what happened to Henry after the end of Firewatch. The banter make me feel really uncomfortable for Beth, Adam's dialogue makes him extremely unlikable, like a toxic smarmy know-it-all with a chip on his shoulder that he was possibly friend-zoned by Beth. Beth isn't a particularly likable character either, but at least she has an interesting arc even if it's rushed and unsatisfying. By the end, the game wants you to think that the characters could have developed some sort of relationship, but I don't get that because Adam spends the whole time either whining that Beth disconnected with him or lecturing Beth like a child about her life choices. Furthermore, Adam doesn't have his own arc and when the resolution happens, it totally makes sense based on how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ he has talked to her the whole game. Maybe that was the writers' intentions? Who knows because it's really unclear. The game could have really used more space between character interactions and made the experience much longer so the characters could have more time to develop a rapport. Instead, something drastic happens in Beth's life literally every gameplay day, and they should be the story beats that happen over the course of weeks or months to be believable. In Firewatch, the game takes place over the course of a whole summer with large chunks of time between gameplay which makes the Henry and Delilah's relationship totally believable and honest.My biggest gripe with the game truly is the story that is too rushed and is constantly throwing new story beats at you taking away from being able to get lost in the world. Each "level" is so small that you're constantly listening to Beth blabber on on the walkie talkie with few moments of serenity to take things in. The only way you activate new story moments is by digging up a new item and there is stuff scattered seemingly every few steps in the fields. It would have been much more interesting if the fields were much bigger with cool set pieces that could have activated new moments in addition to digging up interesting items. Maybe you talk to Beth when you see a huge tree or an old rusted tractor that triggers a memory of the two characters in their youth. There's nothing to interact with in the environment, Instead the game attaches story beats to arbitrary things that you dig up. It's all "look I found a screw. Why are you marrying this jerk?!"All that said, if you like Walking Sims, you will probably find some enjoyment from this game but otherwise I would pass on this.

_childDocuments_.review: For fans of Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, Dear Esther and Gone Home.TL:DRI SO wish there was an in-between rating for this one, as I enjoyed the game but wouldn't recommend it.Trufflepigs is a beautiful game that warrants a few hours of escapism. Once you give it a chance getting through the first few days, it becomes a little addictive trying to find the hidden items. I'll potentially replay to get the achievements I've missed. However, it becomes irritating as the game's shortcomings emerge. Not sure I would recommend it to anyone based on my experience. Great to see UKGF recipients making good use of funding <3TOPS:- Score is great, and definitely highlights the setting and desired moods.- Loved the scenery, the art design and the added details of extra items to photograph if you pay attention.- The weather and lighting *chef's kiss* perfectly sets the tone for the conversations in each scene, and suits the narrative well. BOTTOMS:- Lack of multi-tasking; I wanted to detect while listening to the dialogue, rather than being forced to focus on one. - Sometimes it feels like the time for each day is super short., If I found a few items in a row, even though it'd been a few minutes for me, it's been hours for the protagonists. Ripped me out of the fantasy.- So many directions the plot could have gone; I was left feeling cheated out of a super impactful ending and the red herrings didn't satisfy me like with other games in the genre. - being unable to skip dialogue on repeat play is really frustrating and time consuming in a bad way. - Some small inconsistencies that I couldn't ignore (battery level on the walkie isn't always consistent through the day depending on the conversation; crosshair appearing in cutscenes, game crashes when I paused/tried to open Steam overlay)

_childDocuments_.review: In terms of gameplay, I actually quite enjoyed it, methodically making my way through each field in search of buried treasure, though I do wish the game would let you finish a field before ending the day.However, when it comes to story, I have to ask, am I meant to be rooting for Beth? Because if I had a 'friend' treat me the way Beth treats Adam, I certainly wouldn't be dropping anything to help them out again any time soon. Beth tries to get help from other friends first, before finally feeling like she has to resort to Adam, because no one else she went to actually came through for her. It's these people that should probably feel the brunt of her ire. But no, it's ol' dependable Adam who comes through for her in her time of need. And then he gets to hear about how her family and friends all don't like him, he gets Beth talking non-stop about her fiancé when he clearly has some kind of unresolved romantic feelings for her, then at the end of the week, a week which Adam has reliably and consistently arrived to help her and be a sounding board for the issues she's working through, here comes the kicker - she tells Adam he's no good for her, to go away, and then she runs back off to the friends who had no time for her at the start of the week.Beth completely takes advantage of Adam's unresolved romantic feelings for her to get him to come running like a lost puppy to her, and then as soon as she's gotten what she's wanted out of it, he's kicked to the curb again. Adam's a bit of a doormat, but he doesn't deserve to be treated like that. Beth just seems like such a shallow person, I can't imagine what Adam sees in her.The game tries to present Beth as the protagonist that you (Adam) are helping to achieve a long held ambition, but the way I interpreted this, you (Adam) are the protagonist and Beth is the antagonist, the fair-weather 'friend' who is ready to chuck you aside once she's gotten what she wants.On the whole, really good story and game, as it really made me think about whether this is something I could let happen, either to myself or to a friend. A thought-provoking experience with a nice bit of treasure-hunting too.Good job.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this review by saying I played this on a friend's account and it had such a profound effect on me, I felt the need to re-buy it on my account and post this. Firstly, if you are reading this review, there is a very good chance that you know what type of game this is. It's a game created by the developers of Everybody's Gone To The Rapture, a spiritual successor and one that I think does hit the spot if you are willing to take a chance on it. The game play is admittedly the weakest part of this game, if you choose to view it traditionally. If you accept that the metal detecting is a vehicle for the story (which it truly is in my opinion) you will let it wash over you and settle down into the game.Visually, it is a beautiful game. It isn't photo-realistic so don't expect that, but it is peaceful and serene. The verdant hills of Northern England are lush and green, the sky is atmospheric and mirrors the twists and turns in the story. From clear blue skies to a roiling grey clouds. The setting - a farm in a village called Stanning - is captured perfectly and in my experience of growing up in small village England, it is like so many places I explored as a child.The score is fantastic and really helps the story deliver it's punchy narrative. From uplifting tones to mournful melancholia. In game a such as this, you need a strong score and this is just perfect. I would be remiss without mentioning the extraordinary voice work of Luci Fish and Arthur Darvill (Beth and Adam respectively). It is some of the finest voice acting I have heard for a long time and Luci in particular really stands out. I could feel the passion, the frustration and even their history together, in the words spoken.My final point, is the reason I am writing this review. The story. I played this game when it first came out in the Summer of 2021. I was 29 and the big 3-0 was coming up real fast. I was in a weird head space, a sort of aching nostalgia that I didn't quite understand. With the stresses and pressure of being an adult, perhaps I just longed to return to a time where the only thing I had to worry about, was what cartoon to watch next. A time where the smallest things excited me, and the world was a bright and captivating place. Before the drudgery of an office job and taxes. That is possibly the reason this game resonated so hard for me.The story is about dealing with the fleeting nature of youth. It's about learning to keep dear your memories and past but also grow and evolve into your future. It's about not being afraid to move on to the next chapter of your life - No matter how much it hurts you.I feel as though this game perfectly captures my essence, from the small slice of rural England that I remember fondly as a child, to the uncertainty and the melancholic nostalgia I feel as an adult.The fact that this game has a mixed review (at the time of writing) is a travesty in my humble opinion. I understand that some games are not for everyone, but if you've made it this far into my monologue, I hope you will give this game the same courtesy and time. I love this game, and like it's older brother Everybody's Gone To The Rapture, it will always hold a special place in my heart.Thank you Thunk'd for this game. I eagerly await the next masterpiece you create.

_childDocuments_.review:
The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a first-person, romantic, metal-detecting game. You play as Adam, a sharp-witted but compassionate man returning to his childhood village of Stanning. There he'll help a woman named Beth on her mission to unearth a local treasure. As cracks begin to appear in Beth's fairy tale plan for everything, you'll delve into her history and discover all may not be as it seems. And you'll have to choose how Adam responds to Beth as she faces her demons.

Gameplay combines laid-back metal detecting and exploration with a strong interpersonal narrative, all set in a beautiful English countryside. The Magnificent Trufflepigs is a game about trying to find something, and the tone it sets is like a typical English summer: mostly pleasant, but with stormy moments that threaten to ruin everything.

_childDocuments_.review: This is Digimon World 1 expanded edition with reused models from Cyber Sleuth. Story is pure nonsense but game mechanics are what kept me here. For some reason game was constantly crashing back to desktop but that didn't stop me from continuing to play. Here you have some tips based on my own experience, because the game won't tell you much:- No autosaves, save manually-- save often! - Getting your team wiped out is better than running from battle- You see a digimon with their name in red? It's surely going to destroy your team- When training your team, don't let the tiredness reach half the bar- Eating at the restaurant can help a lot to increase/decrease weight or stats- Get the tamer perk that increases longevity asap. Longer life = almost guaranteed you'll get a mega- Find Birdramon in Logic Volcano asap, so you can fast travel around places you've already discovered- As soon as you hit chapter 2, find GrapLeomon in Server Desert so you can stop unwanted evolutions- Having stats around ~4500 and over 20k HP/MP will get you far in the game, it's quite decent until mid chapter 4- Bring a plant digimon to Mod Cape and have it fight against Taomon so it can learn the two best plant moves in the game- Have at least 1 digimon use support moves that increase attack, *it does* help- Is your team getting wiped out easily? Increase STA by 1000 points and next time you should be able to survive.

_childDocuments_.review: If, like me, you enjoyed Digimon World for the PS1, you'll like this game for sure. If you haven't played it, but you generally like Digimon, this may be worth checking out.Ignore the 17.8 hours on my record, I already borderline 100%'d the PS4 version.However, there is something I must clarify. This game is  like Cyber Sleuth. That game is a Digimon  game whereas this one is a Digimon  game (Yes, I know that might get confusing with DS and Dawn/Dusk, but those being called Digimon World was a mistranslation, their original names were Digimon Story and Digimon Story Sunburst/Moonlight). This is a monster-raising action adventure game with RPG elements attached to it. Your two Digimon partners will eat, sleep, poop, evolve, and eventually die, ad infinitum.With that in mind, the game becomes one of time management. Your Digimon have a limited lifespan that, up until the super lategame, can only be extended by a limited number of evolutions. Raising your Digimon well will be the key to success.There are various guides online you can look up to get a better understanding of the game and I highly recommend anybody who is struggling does so- this game is a lot more fun when you understand what you're supposed to do.I cannot offer a full guide, but I can offer a few tips to help smooth things along.First off: If your Digimon starts showing signs of fatigue when their stats show they are otherwise healthy, that means their lifespan is about to run out (read: they're about to die). This was in the original Digimon World as well, but it's more pronounced here because your Digimon make noises when they show fatigue. Understanding this fact can help you avoid being blindsided by your partners' deaths: There is a clear sign it's coming (it still hurts, though).Secondly: While the specifics I've forgotten, battling is generally a better way to train any Digimon of the Rookie level or above than spending time at the Gym, because it accumulates less fatigue and passes time far slower than Gym training does, for greater gains, if you're fighting in an appropriate area for your stats, though if you're passing time to wait for an evolution (or for your partners to die so you can start training the next generation) Gym Training is good for that role.Third: For battling purposes, unlocking the Defend command early can help a skilled tamer mitigate the damage dealt to their Digimon to an extreme degree. At a baseline it cuts damage by 95%, and once upgraded makes any attack that hits a guarding Digimon only do the minimum of 10 damage. It can go a long way into making your partners tougher to bring down.Fourth: Try not to overtrain your Digimon. If you see the sweatdrop icon which appears around 50% fatigue, your Digimon will lose a bit of their lifespan. Regular resting is important for good health. Fatigue also reduces your stat gains!Fifth: Don't feel bad if you don't get the Digimon you want on your first try. The game opens up tremendously as you progress through the story and recruit more Digimon to your city, providing far more flexibility in how you raise your Digimon. Later in the game you even essentially gain the ability to choose their evolutionary paths!Sixth and last: If you lose a battle, one of your Digimon is a Mega, and you have 100 Bond with both partners, listen for a heartbeat. If there is one, something special will happen.Happy hunting, Tamers.

_childDocuments_.review: Shares many similarities to Digimon World 1 for Playstation 1 with modernised mechanics such as unlockable digivolution info, more Digimon to raise and a story that follows continuity from the PS1 game. Those of you unsure about raising two partners i'd highly suggest giving this a try as I was also unsure about the concept. Bear in mind this is a much longer game, you can sink many hours into this especially if going for the achievements.The gameplay is similar - Raise Digimon by feeding them, going to the toilet (yes the poop from the 1st game is here) and train them to get stronger as you recruit new Digimon to the city to progress the story. It follows the tamagotchi style v-pet system where your partners eventually turn back into digi-eggs, getting stronger each generation. An issue I see people raise is both partner lifespans not syncing, as long as you treat them both equally well this usually isn't a big issue, there are benefits to having different stage partners like a Rookie and a Champion such as boosted stat gains from Gym/Fights.Another issue is getting certain digivolutions early-game, this is either extremely difficult due to very high requirements, a small few are locked until later in the game or Digimon meet criteria for multiple digivolutions and becomes something you weren't expecting. You do unlock the ability to block off undesired digivolution paths which helps with this problem and you gradually obtain info on requirements as you raise Digimon which gradually helps you to train towards the one you want. As you play your Tamer level will go up, giving you Tamer Points that can be used on traits that can help out significantly. These range from boosting training stats, digivolution stats, increasing lifespan, boosting base stats more every new digiegg, additional battle commands, etc. As such you make progress even if you are stuck at a part of the story.Fair warning but early-game is a bit slow and you will most likely grind especially on the higher difficulties. I recommend playing on Beginner as the harder difficulties just make farming bits and stat gains from gym smaller. The game is already really long as is and you will still be presented with a challenge, plus you can change the difficulty at any time.As you gradually obtain bits, get Tamer Levels, recruit more Digimon to the city and unlock more facilities it makes raising Digimon easier which opens the game up. On that note the more progress you make the more fun the game becomes when you can consistently get Mega digivolutions.Overall I would strongly recommend this to Digimon fans, people who played Digimon World 1 for PS1, those that like the tamagotchi-style gameplay and the satisfaction of gradual progression.
