_childDocuments_.review: Full gameplay: I really enjoyed this game, to be honest didn't expect it. Not saying it's perfect since it has some issues but overall I had a good and fun time with this game. I haven't played previous game so this one was a complete fresh experience for me. The game has lots of elements of RE games so if you are fan of those I am sure you can enjoy this one too. It has beautiful visuals, great sound effects, challenging combats with OK story for about 7-8 hours to play.Graphics and Visuals (4/5):Game graphic and visuals are really good, honestly didn't expect it. Everything is well detailed and designed. The animations are good, some character designs and their facial animations are not great which is OK I think since it's from a small studio.Gameplay and Mechanics (3/5):As I said this is same as RE gameplay, you have limited inventory and ammo and need to survive. One of my main issues with this game was limited gun availability, just two guns, a shotgun and SMG. Although you get a frost grip in the game that you have to use to kill enemies and it improves the combat a little bit. The combat can be challenging sometimes depending on how you manage your ammo but if you learn to use the frost grip usually you can manage most of enemies easily.The other downside for me was the enemy variety, there aren't many of them maybe 3 or 4 overall? Also the ending fight in my opinion was really bad and annoying and somehow anti climactic, I was expecting a big/epic boss fight but it was very underwhelming for me.Storyline and Immersion (3/5): Story is ok and fits this game, although I wasn't able to connect or care about any of the characters but it gets the job done. There are lots of texts and audio books that you find through your gameplay that uncovers more details about story and game has lots of cutscenes which mostly are conversations, so if you are not a fan of them be aware. I can't say this game is horror, it has mostly jump scares which are achieved by hiding some enemies behind corner which they jump at you. Other than those I haven't got scared at all during my gameplay. Mostly there was tension of fighting the enemies and not running out of ammo. Sound and Music (3/5): Overall sound and music of the game is really good, music mutes and resumes at right times to add to the tension of the game. Sound effects are really well designed too. Voice acting on other hand was average in my opinion through the whole game. Performance and Bugs (5/5):Performance is really smooth with 3090 and 12900K at 1440p resolution, got an average 100+ fps on highest settings. _childDocuments_.review: I literally loved the first game, Daymare: 1998, but sadly, this game is just nothing but frustrating. If Daymare 1998 was the 'RE2 remake' then this is the disappointment that was the 'RE3 remake'.I'm over two hours into the game, and I've only seen two enemy types (plus one boss) - TWO. Much of the combat revolves around very fast-paced use of your frost grip, a unique gadget that allows you to either shoot frost bolts, do a freeze spray in a cone, or slam the ground in a burst. It's an interesting addition to the survival horror genre, and even satisfying at first once you get the hang of it, but then after awhile when wave after wave of enemies (the second type being invulnerable unless you freeze it first) pours in faster than you can recharge your frost grip so you end up being overwhelmed and it becomes a button-mashing frenzy to get the enemies off you. But then as you ready your weapon, the next one grabs you into a sort of stun-lock and you die a cheap, frustrating death. The freeze spray just takes so long to turn the enemies to ice, that the ones behind you grab you, or you don't have enough frost left to do a 'finisher'.I appreciate that possibly makes no sense if you haven't played the game, but the take-away here is that there is an interesting frost mechanic that just makes combat not fun.The environment isn't interact-able either, unless it's for the story, like a computer you need to use, or a switch you need to press - but there's nothing that says something like 'there's nothing here but a bunch of old files' when you check the scenery, when this is supposed to pay homage to the old 90s games. Even if it's pointless, that old-school interaction is missing, which means there's just a lot of running about through corridors and empty rooms.I will say the environment is pretty, and animations are impressive, but my gosh, the gameplay is so horrendously frustrating I don't know if I'll even see this through. I can't even refund this as I'm past the two-hour mark.How can Invader Studios do so well on a debut and fall so short on the follow-up? I should have listened to the reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: If this game wanted to win an award for being annoying, it sure did a good job at that.Where do I begin? Personally, I wanted to give this game a good review but I just couldn't bring myself to do it. I liked the previous Daymare 1998. I get this game is supposed to be a prequel or whatever but I can't even have that as an excuse here.So here goes my list of issues.The unnecessary quickness to the enemies isn't really fun nor is it difficult, considering I have a freeze weapon to slow them down, that's the whole gimmick of this game. Check me out guys I am Mr. Freeze, look at me freeze all the enemies, only for me to get the best of its upgrade late game to where I can really have fun with it.The weapons, where do I begin? Why is it that if I am a military organization named Hades can only go into my secret missions with a Shotgun and just an MP5, are you serious? You think after the first game you would have thought, hmm maybe we can add more guns to the game or at least a new pistol or assault rifle or even a new shotgun. I opened one locker and saw a shotgun that was a different color and was like no way and long behold it's a shotgun skin for the shotgun I used in the last game which was the same weapon layout. If you can add a frost weapon why can't you add more automatic weapons or at least newer variants of said weapons maybe?I gotta say, the enemies in certain areas made zero sense spawning here or there, they just zapped in with sometimes no real reason to me, and not only that, in certain rooms I traveled to, there was one random enemy to jump out at you or if you moved near the room just close enough it will activate and attack you with the command prompt to do so. I mean I get it but I mean it's kind of daunting after a while. Also, why couldn't they add music or some upbeat elevator music as I am walking around the area, instead of just hearing the character's heavy breathing the entire time or the footsteps, that made the game kind of drag on. I also wish there was a map, is it really that big of a deal to have some sort of mini-map so I can maybe kind of recheck what room I might have went in already.I have to say this when I got to the last boss in the game, it was literally so annoying for no reason. I really don't understand why you would intentionally go out of the way to add a boss that grabs you and teleports you back at the start and you have to dodge the boss the entire time as you go through doors you have to wait to open. Once you get the trick down pack it's not so bad but the boss seemed bugged, for example, I would dodge her grab animation and as her arms were folded back in after she did the grab and let's say I was stuck and had to slide through her to get out, she would automatically grab me without doing the animation, she wouldn't even open her arms, the animation would just trigger if I touch her after dodging her grab. The people who made the game knew this considering they would constantly spawn in the health items you already picked up so you can keep on retrying.I just feel like they should have waited, the game still seems buggy in certain aspects at least when it comes to the enemies and sometimes whenever I used the MP5 if I held down the trigger the gun would go up and shoot at the ceiling and the screen would start to shake some, maybe the shaking could have been on my end. I mean I get being realistic with the MP5 shooting but come on, many guns like that nowadays you can hold down the trigger at close range with some force and it wouldn't just launch up to the stars, it's a MP5. It's not like an AK-47 OR M16.Personally if you are a fan of the serious, wait for a sale and if you do play it just play it on normal, save yourself the headache and the waste of time. Once I got through the game on hardcore I uninstalled it within seconds. It wasn't even the full game itself, really only the med bay room and the boss fight at the end left a bad taste in my mouth. I just wish the last boss fight could have been a fight and not some oh you have to retry again you didn't make the run, oh no let's start from the beginning. I liked the story, just not the core gameplay itself. I hope if they do make a new game they really take their time on it or at least let maybe a fan or two try it out for free, not just some friend you know, an actual person who is a stranger to get better feedback or at least triple, quadruple check the game multiple times. I am sure once they work out all the bugs the game will be some what decent to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle, a prequel to Daymare: 1998, is a third-person survival horror game that immerses players in a world of conspiracies and terror. Playing as Special Agent Dalila, you'll navigate a sinister research facility.The game's gripping narrative follows Reyes as she unravels a web of mysteries. The setting is haunting, creating an atmosphere brimming with dread and tension.Daymare excels at merging classic survival horror elements with modern gameplay. Combat is intense, and innovative weapons like the Frost Grip add depth. Smart and relentless enemies keep you on your toes, with various difficulty levels catering to different players.The game offers exploration. Reyes's scanner adds depth to exploration, revealing clues and hidden items. Environmental puzzles keep the gameplay engaging.Conclusion:Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle is a must-play for survival horror fans. With its compelling story, intense combat, intricate puzzles, and richly detailed world, it offers a genuinely terrifying and engaging gaming experience. Its mix of modern and nostalgic elements sets it apart in the genre. _childDocuments_.review: This game is Ok, but not really better than the first game. I'll start off with the positives, the graphics looks somewhat better, the ice power gadget is a pretty unique mechanic to kill the tougher zombies, and the zombies new abilities makes the game a little more dynamic to keep you on your toes. The puzzles are well made and fun to solve, except for one that took place at a hotel which I couldn't figure it out on how to solve it, so I had to find the code on google.Now for the negatives, the animations in the cut-scenes and the main character looks off, it looks like the developers didn't really improve that much from the first game, and that's the problem with a lot a modern video games. Most developers think they can make a great game by adding a lot of cut-scenes and focus more on story, but in reality it makes the game boring or nobody cares about the story because the pacing is too slow or some cut-scenes in the game drag way too long.Now for the game-play, I was so mad at the game because you can only carry 2 guns for the entire game, which is the shotgun & the SMG, and you can't switch them either. In the game I can see dead HADES soldiers on the floor with guns next to them and the game doesn't let you pick it up. Also the developers removed some game-play features from the first game like the sprint, weapon variety, drugs and secondary ammunition. Most of the common zombies only attack is to run up the player, grab you and drain your health, this was disappointing and annoying because they are suppose to be enhanced versions of regular zombies and they don't really do anything special. I know they can teleport and dodge but i'm playing a zombie game, not a doom game. The game reuses the same mini boss for the entire game and the final boss is basically the mini boss but bigger and it has a little bit more abilities, at least the first game had a Little more boss variety.Overall I give this game a 5.5 out of 10, This game could have been better if it wasn't a console game, instead of a game that is meant for both PC and console, bring back some of the game-play mechanics from the first game, and not make the ending plot a sad lesbian love story.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm happy to say that Daymare 1994 Sandcastle exceeded my initial expectations. While I enjoyed Daymare 1998, it was pretty rough around the edges. In comparison, this prequel feels more like a survival horror experience closer to Resident Evil 2/3/4 Remakes. I thought the story/lore was pretty interesting, and they expanded upon some of the events that occur in Daymare 1998 a little. I'm glad that they were bold enough to turn this game away from the typical virus/zombie scenario so that they can craft their own survival horror experience and do their own thing. With this game, I think they've laid out a blueprint for a series that can stand on its own while staying true to the survival horror games that it's inspired by. Looking forward to another Daymare sequel in the near future.
_childDocuments_.name: Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle

_childDocuments_.review: I gave up completing this game for three main reasons.  First, the final boss is barely even a boss.  Its just a time consuming tease that is not enjoyable or worth beating with how tedious it is.  Second, the entirety of the castle level ran on an almost unbearably low frame rate barely touching 30 and dropping as low as 24 even with the graphics turned way down (which makes it look like windows 95 game). Lastly, the story which I enjoyed at first, but became thoroughly disinterested.  If the story was better I could probably force myself to just keep trying but I have lost all motivation.  I wanted to like this game and I really did for the first half.  But the jumpscares around corners became too common, the monsters were not varied (which I felt was a waste since you have electric eldritch monsters, you can do so much with that.  Maybe should have stuck to zombies), monsters were way too fast for how slow the player moves, the weapons were not very good either (the smg was a terrible choice for encounters and I found myself using the shotgun in almost every fight unless I was out of ammo, plus the abilities for the ice pack were just not well done with the grenade and shield being useless, there needs to be rebalancing and more weapons to make the game interesting).  The scanner item was pointless as it is basically only used to read documents from electronics but that could have easily been delegated to pressing E or something.  It was a bit tedious to switch to it like a weapon, especially since it doesn't add anything to gameplay or story.  I did not find the protagonist or the other characters to be interesting but that's a more personal gripe.  I really liked that first game but this one felt less like an entry and more like a poorly made spinoff.  I wanted to like this game but unless you buy this game at a discount I feel it just isn't worth the thirty dollar price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the previous game Daymare 1998, which is a classic survival horror game in style of the 90's RE games -- or their modern remakes, to be more precise. This game, however, is not a survival horror game -- it's a third-person action shooter,  which by itself is not a bad thing, because I actually like action-packed third-person shooters, but unfortunately, this game is a pretty poor example of this genre -- and I'm not talking about graphics or voice acting or any other of that AAA-stuff.As some other reviewers have pointed out, you're not dealing with slowly moving zombies in this game, but with pretty fast moving electro-mutants that frequently teleport around you during battles, which (ignoring the teleportation) seem to be inspired by the husks from the Mass Effect games. The only times that I have died was when one of those flying mutants teleported behind my back and insta-killed me while I was busy fighting some other mutants -- and in this case, none of the eight medkits that I have been carrying around in my backpack could've helped me.The sheer flood of medkits is compensated by a lack of ammunition -- I consider myself a fairly skilled player, but I had the feeling that I really have to make every shot count to avoid running out of ammo -- which is especially tricky since the hit feedback is pretty nonexistent (unless you disintegrate an enemy). Also, on several occasions (usually after jumpscares) I have tried to kill an enemy by shooting it with a shotgun at point blank, in which case the game decided that this was too close and instead fired right "through" the enemy without hittin it... Changing or reloading weapons during a fight is a real pain in the bum, because miss sunshine is taking her sweet time.I believe that the lack of ammunition is intended by the developers to motivate you to spend more time with their new favorite toy: the frost grip, which also seems to be inspired some Mass Effect power. This toy lets you freeze enemies, so that you can shatter them, which is not half as much fun as just blowing them into shreds using the trusty old shotgun... Also, this freezing toy feels completely misplaced in a game that considers itself to be a survival horror game...This really reminds me of how EA ruined Dead Space 3 by turning a survival horror game into a shooter: there's too much action for anyone who is looking for a survival horror game, and there's too little ammo, guns and enemy variations for anyone who is looking for an action shooter -- it's kind of the worst-of-the-two-mix that will make neither side happy. The only thing that really keeps me playing this game is the fact that I really like playing games with tough-girl protagonists...-- Edit --I have stopped playing this game at a point where I have run out of charges for that frost toy and I have to pass through a narrow passage with two red enemies, which can only  be killed by freezing them... what a brilliant game design choice...
_childDocuments_.name: Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game but with reservations. - This is no longer a horror survival, now its a horror action- Compared to prior work (Daymare 1998) this actually felt like a step backwards   - Horror survival has been replaced with action (akin to RE4 transition)   - Limited weapon choices and inventory management was simplified which removed some of depth   - Ammo management went from rationing and being carefuil with every bullet to "spray and pray" mode   - Even on harcode the items were ridiculously plentiful- Story was all over the place, i read every document and hear all audio and im still confused- Went from zombie franchise to.... running alien mutant?    - I'm happy to have a franchise where the games have different enemy/storylines but the feel has to remain    - Between 1998 and Sandcastle they feel like they are not even vaguely related to each other- A lot of he game, especially the later parts, is walking from one place to another, no enemies, no risk, nothing of interest. Just a time sinkThat being said:- The new battle system was engaging and innovative. Similar mechanics with more variety and polish I think will work well in future games- Some of the enemy design (floating ones) was very lovercrafct which was actually creepy- Animation of cut scenes has improved as has the voice acting, however relative to other games it is mediocre at best. Still important to note the improvements- Collectables are always a good thing to have and it was not overdone. However, a better rewards system may improve that (cosmetic or gameplay enhancement as you find more e.g)Overall I really like this studio and the work they are doing, but this game felt like a step in the wrong direction. It is still an enjoyable game, but no where near as enjoyable or in depth as their previous work. Everyone makes mistakes, I just hope this was a misstep on their part and they refine the "survival" element of their games rather than going for fast paced battle action, as it near impossible to do the latter with a horror game that is, y'know, actually scary.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually went into this with very little information and I gotta say its a pleasant surprise of an actually decent game. Its literally Resident evil 2 remake game play with its own little twists in mechanics and the enemy types are pretty cool to go up against. The story so far is actually very interesting as well. _childDocuments_.review: If i  had to give Daymare 1994 SandCastle a review note  it would be a 7/10. The biggest issue with the game is the combat. It is really clunky with enemies that will one shot you and attack you were you can't see them. This is my biggest gripe. Also the overuse of the Cryo Gauntlet to finish enemies. If the dev would get rid of the oneshot enemies and Cryogauntlet overuse, the score would go up to a 9. Visually its years better than Daymare 1998 (the first one). The story is pretty good and the acting is good as well. For an indies studios i would like to see more maybe a XPAC or a sequel. Now that they got the visual right if they couls balance the combat and make it less clunky have better and more enemies type i would say weapons too while at it i think they could slowly rivalise with capcom.
_childDocuments_.name: Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed feelings about this game. The action is good, the sets are beautiful, the pacing is good. The animation is not great, but I can forgive it. My main gripe with the animation is actually Reyes' walking and running. She jitters all over the place. The creatures are better animated than the first game, so even though it isn't amazing, its a big leap forward and I'm happy to see it get better.My most frustrating problem is the hack puzzles. It feels like a classic case of: the developers already know the strategy and think its easy, so they add more elements to make it harder, alienating people who don't know (or are not good at) solving that kind of puzzle. Even thought it took me 20 minute to learn how to solve those puzzles from the tutorial, I still can't get even one of those locked cabinets open. Get rid of the "X amount of tries left" counter, please. Just let us ♥♥♥♥♥ keep trying until we get it. What do you have to lose by letting us win?And my final gripe, but this is completely ignorable... the writing is terrible. The dialogue is terrible and the acting is kinda bad. You can tell they're just reading from a paper into a microphone. The direction should have done a better job of making sure the emotions fit the scene. There are moments when it seems like  Reyes goes from screaming in terror to making a snarky comment in the blink of an eye. This holds especially true when you're exploring. She'll be attacked by a band of monsters, and immediately after the battle, she'll make some goofy comment about a clue to solve the next environmental puzzle.Most of these concerns can be ignored, as I said. Just fix the mini hack game. Please. I can't imagine if the electronic jail door puzzle from RE2R had a timer and a limited amount of times that we could attempt to solve it. I think I stared at that thing for an hour before I made any progress.
_childDocuments_.name: Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle

_childDocuments_.review: Daymare 1994 is at its best when its delivering environmental scares mixed with an even flow of fresh puzzles. The tension and horror elements within its combat are extremely well done, even when the enemy variety feels less than amazing. The plot is straight forward and i think it fits this 90's story telling method. The camera view is "perfect" imo and the game looks great. At its worse, its brought down by choppy voice acting and lack luster enemy design. Overall Daymare is a great game i'd recommend to any third person horror fan.
_childDocuments_.name: Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle

_childDocuments_.review:
Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle is a third-person story-driven survival horror game prequel to the critically acclaimed Daymare: 1998.

Step into the shoes of special agent Dalila Reyes, a former government spy now in the service of a unit called H.A.D.E.S. (Hexacore Advanced Division for Extraction and Search), and get ready to enter the most advanced experimental research center in the United States of America. 

A perfect mix of fierce and deadly enemies, hardcore action game mechanics, environmental puzzles, a chilling soundtrack, plenty of exploration and massive doses of concentrated horror wait for you in Daymare: 1994 Sandcastle. No place is safe, especially when you're being hunted by your nightmares.

name: Distant Worlds 2
detailed_description: Distant Worlds Returns! Distant Worlds, the critically acclaimed 4X space strategy game is back with a brand new 64-bit engine, 3D graphics and a polished interface to begin an epic new Distant Worlds series with Distant Worlds 2. Distant Worlds 2 is a vast, pausable real-time 4X space strategy game. Experience the full depth and detail of turn-based strategy, but with the simplicity and ease of real-time, and on the scale of a massively-multiplayer online game. The Universe is Yours! Huge Galaxies with up to 2,000 star systems and tens of thousands of planets, moons and asteroids are yours to explore and exploit, whether peacefully through mining and diplomacy or by conquest! The complex process of generating a galaxy ensures that every new game will be different and the many galaxy setup options ensure incredible replayability as well as the ability to have your game be just the way you like it. Galaxies are so deep, fun and immersive that you won’t want to finish the game. Choose from seven playable base game factions which cover a wide variety of playstyles. Build, expand and improve your empire while playing through the storylines, with victory conditions or in an open-ended sandbox mode. Each galaxy is packed with life and activity. Encounter other empires, independent alien colonies, traders, pirates and space monsters. Explore star systems, asteroid fields, galactic storms and black holes. Discover evidence of civilizations long since past, uncovering secrets about the galaxy's troubled history... Intelligent automation allows you to tailor the game to your preferred playstyle and scale. Decide how much you want to control and which gameplay areas suit you best. You can limit your focus to just one ship or expand it all the way up to everything in a vast galactic empire. Let your advisors and the intelligent automation handle the rest! A Built-in Game Editor allows you to fine-tune your own galaxy, adding or removing star systems, planets, asteroids, ships, star bases, space monsters or anything else. Modify the attributes of any empire in your game for the ultimate custom experience. Extensive In-Game Help is included. Exhaustive, built-in, context-sensitive help is always only a single key-press away. Press F1 at any time for a detailed explanation of the current game screen, your currently selected item, and so on, or just browse the complete “Galactopedia” Tutorials are included to quickly familiarize you with all of the game elements and tools. Best of all, these all combine to let you play the game your way: enjoy a quick, intense game in a crowded sector of space or take your time in an epic game spread across a vast galaxy!

_childDocuments_.review: Sequel to the best 4x space empire game ever it really just builds on the old game. In a harsh and unforgiving universe take the reins of your civilization as it crawls out of the gravity well that has sheltered your forefathers and take to the stars where you will face space monsters, pirates and aliens galore!On release though the game is super janky. I've experienced numerous crashes. The interface is lightyears ahead of the old one, but still manages to be clunky and unresponsive -- it also still makes it difficult to find information, there is no search function at all. Sometimes the AI pathing is INSANE ignoring fuel ranges or sanity. Still I've been having alot of fun fighting off alien pirates and even more alien monsters. Once the interface issues have been ironed out and the AI tweaked so as to NOT decide to scout planets on the other side of the galaxy I think this will be the best 4x space game ever!Really looking forward to the missing content from the previous title (more races, actually being able to play the pirates!) and hoping for some more robust diplomacy/espionage options (the whole system seems ported over from the old game and not polished or updated at all) and perhaps a GalCiv ship editor (as the ship assets are obviously modular and slapped together) this game is truly epic in scope if not currently in control.But beware of the janky release.....

_childDocuments_.review: I have played Distant Worlds: Universe for quite a while, and it is to date my favorite 4x sci-fi of all time, so I really looked forward to the sequel. Well, now it's here, so I want to share my thoughts on it.First of all, I want to mention that there were a few bugs on release. At the time of writing, the game is barely a day old, and I imagine that most bugs will be fixed soon, but unfortunately, they have really detracted from my current experience with DW2. I'll probably update this review when the game is a bit more mature.Disregarding the bugs, there are quite a few things I like about the game. The graphics are crisp and don't feel like they were made by such a small development studio. Every part of the visual experience, from the look of the ships and planets to the menus and statistics screens look nice and smooth and sci-fi-y. Well done :D   I also really like exploration, which was a rather underwhelming experience in the predecessor, because I explored even the largest galaxy in a few years. Now, it takes decades just to discover your surrounding solar systems, and the multi-tiered exploration mechanics mean that your ships spend a long time at each new place.Unfortunately, other than those aspects, I cannot really name any part of the game that I think is better compared to DW:U. Mechanically DW2 feels very similar to the first game, which is not a bad thing at all. But there are also a few systems that I think are worse than they were in DW:U.   Surprisingly, the thing that annoys me the most is the new UI. I probably just have to get used to it, but it honestly feels even clunkier and less intuitive than the old one. I hope the developer will give it some more love <3. The thing I fight with the most is the UI's reactions to my mouse, both when I hover and click on the bottons. There are often these weird delays when I interact with the elements on the screen, and also, sometimes, the whole map moves when I click on buttons which I don't feel like should make the map move. There is also an eternal stream of blaring pop-up alerts that are weirdly difficult to remove. I'm also a bit sceptical about the new ship design system, but hopefully I'll warm up to it over time. It feels pretty limiting compared to the old one, especially early in the game, like there's only really one good way to design each type of ship. The socket system is pretty cool though, so it's not all bad.Finally, I am not a fan of the new randomized research system. You can play without it, so it's all fine in the end, but the way they have implemented randomized research is that they remove some random options for each player. Maybe that doesn't sound too bad, but it can lead to some serious setbacks. For example, in my first playthrough, I had a rampant corruption problem, and about half of my economy disappeared into nowhere. The main way of combating this is to make a building that lowers corruption. This building has several tiers, where each gets successively better, but because of randomized research, I was locked to the first tier, and this by itself means that my economy is in tatters, and probably will continue to be so for the rest of my playthrough. Overall, I did not have the time of my life. Still, it's a good game, especially if you don't compare it to DW:U which had years of active development post-release. It has a few kinks, but give it a few months, and we'll probably have a new contender for best sci-fi 4x game :D
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game felt like I was wrestling with the UI instead of playing the game. It's pretty, but ultimately a huge pain in the ass to navigate and use. It really doesn't help when I felt forced to sort through the menus for every single action I wanted to take. So many odd choices were made for these menus that it turned me off the game entirely.In comparison, DW:U had some aesthetic issues with the buttons, but was actually playable.1 year later edit for the Hyperspace update:The UI still sucks. Some more thoughts. Upgrading ship designs is a massive pain in the ass. If you automate it, the AI will refit the designs into unusable crap. Manual upgrades are a must, BUT it will require you to go through the upgrade screen for EVERY SINGLE DESIGN.Consider this situation: you research a new fuel tank component that's marginally better than your previous fuel tank. Every design in the game uses a fuel tank. If you have a specific design you want to keep using throughout the game (for example, a large mining station with a bunch of small mining engines installed for higher extraction rate), then you'll have to manually upgrade the design, as automated design upgrades will default back to generic (hardcoded) AI design without your changes. So you click the upgrade button - the game takes you to the design screen. You don't need to review the changes, because you know the only difference is that the 2 or 3 fuel tanks are now the somewhat better fuel tank. Click confirm. Not too bad. Now do it 25 more times for every manual design your empire owns. And do it every 7 or so minutes each time you research a new component.Original DW:U had a single button that allowed you to select multiple designs and simply upgrade components to latest tech WITHOUT having to individually go through every design screen of every ship and base.In 2016, DW:U let me do this in 2 seconds. In 2023, DW 2 forces me to do it in 2 minutes or else surrender to the incompetent automation.This issue is characteristic of the entire game. A lot of missing features that make manual micromanagement a complete nightmare - meanwhile, automation isn't just inefficient, it's an actively dangerous choice for the survival of your empire.

_childDocuments_.review: Performance of the game was mostly okay, although I had a 3-4 random crashes in 40 hours. Not really frequent enough to be a significant annoyance, and I expect stability will improve. The UI is not very intuitive and is missing some basic quality of life features (or the options are embedded horribly deeply in somwhere.) For example, why can't I see Empire names on their sphere of influence and easily identify their colonies. I find myself having to zoom all the way and whoops that's a mining station or independent instead! It makes it difficult to tell who I am even at war with in large 2000 star galaxies with 20 empires. Why can I not scroll through ships in a selected fleet with arrows rather than going back to the fleet menu and clicking on the next ship - I understand we have the filter screen but this is basic UI design we are talking about. 3x the clicks and even more time compared to just a single button.The default AI settings are pretty bad - fleets will suicide themselves into enemies and you'll be left with nothing if you dont keep your eye on them early to mid game. Manual fleets also react automatically in the same system (which screwed me over when a fleet defending my main fueling station reacted into a huge crowd of space monsters and got wiped out right before an enemy invasion.) While you can minimize all this with proper policy settings, this is not at all obvious and was a great source of frustration for me early on.Resources should matter more than they do - why is a single node I've mined since early game able to supply an empire of 100s of billions and a massive space fleet? There is basically no depth here, despite the huge amount of resources. Nodes should either have depletion, or colonies should consume large amounts for development. We are talking scifi tier planet spanning developments here - resources to build and maintain these SHOULD be an issue, or at least more of an issue than it is in this game. Imagine a world like Trantor from the Dynasty - building a massive developed world like that should require resources for all over the galaxy and they should absolutely be more than the afterthought they currently are.The combat/ship design and research were much more engaging than nearly any other game I've played, so I had quite a bit of fun with that. I opted to just go for a scorched earth approach and loaded my battleships with planet destroying nukes and railguns and basically turned planet after planet into cinders since they kept annoying me every 10 seconds by declaring war early game. Much easier to do that here than in many games :)Overall, a slight recommend. I had fun with it, but probably will be waiting for more content/expansions before really diving in again. The state of the game seems improved from launch, so the developer is at least continuing to work on the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Although on paper this seems like the kind of game I'd really enjoy, there are a few problems with it:1. Performance. I haven't had the crashes that have plagued other people, but the performance of this game is quite bad. During the game, I'm constantly zooming the main view in to look at a planet, then zooming out to look at the galaxy map. Each time you zoom far enough to switch from galaxy view to sector view or vice versa, there's a pause for a second or two. There are pauses at other times too; whenever I kill a space creature, the game pauses for at least a second or two before it explodes. I'm not sure what the game is doing during that time, or why the developer couldn't optimize for these extremely common use cases.2. Automation. The automation in this game is supposed to be one of its big selling points. Don't care about some aspect, or has it gotten too tedious? Let the AI automate it! Unfortunately, I think some of the systems have been designed *around* being automatable. For example, I find the resource gathering aspect of the game naturally interesting. I could imagine a game where you're making interesting cost / benefit tradeoffs around individual resource nodes, setting up logistics networks, etc. Unfortunately, here it's pretty shallow. The game gives you a list of potential resource locations, with the highest "priority" ones (I guess the ones the AI would have chosen?) first. It tells you which ones have resources that you're currently underproducing, and what kind of a deficit you have. And you click a button, and a mining base gets created. That's it. It's easy to automate, and I almost don't feel like doing it manually because I'm not sure any strategy other than the obvious one the AI picks would be an improvement. The issue isn't the way the game presents information; the issue is that the "problem" the designers want the players to solve has more or less one clear best answer.This seems to affect other areas of the game as well. Do you want to become friendly with another race? Give them money so they like you, then open free trade so they like you more. Repeat until you're best friends. Again, easy to automate, but as a human there's really nothing interesting for me to do or improve upon.The game has a lot of moving parts, each of which the player has to take time to understand. But each part is so mechanically simple, I often feel like I'm just watching the game play itself, making the obvious decisions as I go, rather than coming up with clever solutions to problems.The criticism above doesn't apply to fleet automation, which I find confusing. If I add a ship to a fleet that's not at the same location, will it join the fleet? If I order a fleet to go to a system, will it refuel along the way, or will it arrive with very little fuel? Will ships in a fleet auto-refit? Will ships in a fleet auto-repair? Will ships in a fleet auto-refuel? Will a fleet automatically build ships to restore lost ones? I don't know, and the fact that there seems to be a delay between when a fleet is automated and when it actually takes some action makes it hard to experiment.Admittedly I haven't played long, but if the early part of the game is like this, I'm worried the later parts of the game will be more of the same.

_childDocuments_.review: I can finally say it: This game is a true master piece and in my opinion the ultimate 4X experience at this point of time!What really ads to the experience is the developer, that solved basically all issues, the tile had at launch and is still supplying the game with constant (free) content updates, as well as reasonably priced dlcs, that are REAL addons and not something that should have been in the game in the first place.What amazes me the most, is the level of automation you can play your game with, the level of adjustability and the level of detail.This is the most accurate and belivable depiction of a living and breathing universe, that constantly changes and evolves, it simply is amazing!Fleet management is amazing and very comfortable, as is colony management, the space battles are absolutely breathtaking and the story events are really engaging and interesting.Give this a try, if you are in doubt! You just have to give it some time to grow on you, be prepared on that, but after you have understood how the game works and more importantly how you can make it work for you, there is absolutely nothing comparable to it!
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game has serious interface issues. For example, I built a small invasion fleet and ordered it to invade a planet, but they won't. They just sit here and tell me there aren't enough troops to invade, without telling me how many I need and no way I could see to find this important bit of info. After spamming more units until I had enough for the AI to let me "Attack" they raided instead of invading. Post raid, they went back to sitting in orbit.Another painful issue - lack of resources at a planet I want to build a ship, even though I've got tons of it in stock. Dev's answer was the planet has requested the resources, you just have to wait for the AI to move them there. Three game years later, still short, had to take manual control to tell the planet to stock up. For a game that supposedly so highly automated - to the point where I often wonder why it needs a player, as it just seems to play itself - it falls down hard in some areas, often.Most frustratingly, the game punishes expansion by saddling you with colonies that are a drain on your economy for a very, very, very long time. Decades later with a population a third the size of my homeworld, and almost as large as my homeworld was at start, my first colony is still a net negative income. While this may all be very "realistic" - and I would debate hard against that using European settlements in the New World as an example - it is not fun gaming. Let me repeat that: It is not fun gaming. The Devs and the die hard fans need to remember that this a game, to be played for enjoyment, not a master's class project on logistics or a training program for actual space colonization.With dozens and dozens of 4X games under my belt, including over 1000 hours of Stellaris, this game is a huge let down and in no way a contender. While it has some interesting features, it pales in comparison to the current leader. Gameplay, interface, graphics, soundtrack, etc. are all far inferior. If you have to choose one or the other, go with Stellaris.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Edited to a positive reviewA lot of bug fixes and stability and gameplay improvements have allowed me to enjoy this game further. There are still things I want. I want to be able to edit an automatic design, maybe add assault pods or change weapon loadout. Maybe go for more efficient engines on some instead of powerful thrust. And not have the AI design over it because I don't want to design the myriad civilian ships. Not a dealbreaker, but I want to influence loadouts on a doctrine scale, but not have to babysit every design for every ship.There is not a lot of difference between alien races, that is fine. But why are a lot of the previous races only available as isolated minor colonies instead of a starting race?But I totally recommend this game for 4X in space with a wonderful level of automation available for most things.-------Give it a year for them to work on stability and bugs. I can get a good game going, and then get CTD. Sometimes, launcher will fail to launch game until I verify game files. This is after a successful play the day before.I wish I could set an order for a fleet to synchronize their jumps. I wish I could tell a ship to load it's fighters BEFORE engaging jump. This doesn't cause the fighters to be left behind, this causes the ship in question to literally crawl behind the jumping fleet with the fighters chasing it in a futile attempt to recover. I'd prefer the fighters lost than the force split.I wish a fleet could refuel at a station without model collision preventing the refueling from the station.I love the scope, I love how the game is built on the previous.But it certainly comes off as undercooked.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game should still be EA in my experience so far.  There are just simple raw performance issues that are inexcusable for a title that has been released.  The research screen (Tech Tree), for some odd reason, causes massive visual lag.  There are memory leaks and other glitches all over the place.  The team needed to handle performance issues before planning paid DLCs.  The AI, also, is hot garbage in so many scenarios.  I've seen 40 construction ships face plant into space monsters before.  It's just a silly, silly game.  Demand more, don't spend your money here.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I loved DW:U and wish I could recommend this game but I can't.  The key difference between DW:U and DW2 is that DW:U was made to be played and has great automation options to help you out, while DW2 was meant to be automated but you can play it if you want.  Almost every system seems like it was almost intentionally designed to be frustrating to use manually.  Examples include:-No order queuing.-No sector grid, even though multiple important things are measured by sector size there is no way to tell how big that actually is. -If you want to upgrade your ship designs with newer modules you basically have to save your ship design as a new design and then go into the designer, find the old one, and manually mark it as obsolete.  There is a button to just upgrade the design with the latest tech except that button will happily replace your modules with other types of modules if it thinks those are better.These are just a few examples but the general feel is that the game just doesn't want you to actually play it.  No reason for order queues because the player shouldn't be giving orders. Which I think is literally what the devs said about that one. Once you know that's how they were thinking you can see how that design philosophy as seeped into virtually every aspect of the game.  The end result is a game that ultimately feels unsatisfying and even frustrating to play.  The fair few hours I've put in is honestly more a testament to this games predecessor than this game itself.  I really really wanted to like it and I tried hard to do so.1 other big issue I'd like to note- The pirates don't really play the game like they did in DW:U. These guys have more in common with Civilizations barbarians than they do with the DW:U pirates.  One weird thing I've noticed about them is that they will never stop invading a planet until they are chased off. It doesn't matter how good your ground defenses are their ships will drop and endless stream of units until they've been chased off or they succeed. One time I cheated and spawned a bunch of titans on my starter world just to test this and eventually the pirates overcame 100 titans.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a bit slow, the worst feature I found is that you can only push time forward to 4x. But the game is very interesting, and I am enjoying it. When it says I played 21 hours that isn't quite correct, but I leave games running on my computer all the time. But I have played several hours and I'm finding the graphics to be acceptable, the game to be bug free, and the game mechanics to be excellent.  I like it better than Stellaris.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from someone who remembers buying Distant Worlds and it's DLC's on the Matrix Store, downloading installers and installing old school. Remembering when it was packaged as Distant World's Universe on Steam years later. I have to say. I'm not impressed. There's a few features and content missing from the last game. And while the shift to 3D graphics is nice, it's not nearly as nice as I'd hoped. The biggest issues are lag, stuttering, hitching, slow down in the simulation etc. I get I'm doing a 10x10 galaxy size with 2000 stars but I'm not even out of my own solar system yet and it has these subtle hitches all over. But I'm also disappointed in the fact there's literally.... nothing new here. The ship designer is tweaked... arguably for the worse. No new changes really, no new mechanics or features of note. I'd say give it a while or buy on sale if you're really into these games but honestly, probably not worth it for now.EDIT: After 15 hours or so now, my opinion still holds. The game is a little more stable now but it's a step back from Distant World's Universe. The UI and graphics are better but never really minded the old ones. But there's many missing features and content. And most importantly/annoyingly... there's features/mechanics here but as implemented are buggy and/or non-functional. Short of that, in a few years I see this being a gold standard of space 4x games. Like the prior entry. Just so disappointed it was released in this state. It really should be in early access. It's still a very deep and involved game. You can definitely enjoy yourself here, if this is your niche. But, it's just unready for release really. I haven't crashed in 15 hours or so. And my empire is humming along (though can't figure out why I'm so in debt) but it's just really hard for me to recommend spending the money when DWU is the same game but more feature rich and bug free. This is solid though, in a manner of speaking.EDIT 2: I've changed my recommendation to a thumbs up. The game has been fixed for the most part. As comparable content to Distant Worlds Universe. And is a step forward in a few ways. Especially in scale. It's a solid 4x game. A couple DLC's/expansions later, just like Distant Worlds 1, it will become the best space 4x out there. Arguably it already is.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a damn fine 4x strategy game and it addresses a lot of the gripes i have with others like Stellaris. a lot of the complaints on here seem to stem from people not reading/learning/understanding this game. it is way less limiting than one may think. this is my new favorite space empire sim now. looking forward to maybe more races and updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Update: The second and third issues seem to have been resolved in updates and automation has been improved, if they keep good updates like that going I might swap this to recommended. Some good updates from the devs!I really, really wanted to like this game. I really did. It has tons of things I like about it over stellaris.Problem is I simply can't play more than 10 minutes without finding a new problem.First problem I encountered, on the first day. I had set fleet top up to automated. It's supposed to keep fleets full with ships, right? No issues with it, until I updated a ship. The ships retrofitted.... then left the fleet. If I manually added them back to the fleet, they would immediately leave it. If I manually clicked top up, the game would build NEW ships for the fleet, who would leave the fleet as soon as they were finished being constructed. So I had to turn off automated top up to fix the problem.Second problem, Fuel tankers would not refuel ships even after receiving manual orders. I don't know exactly what caused this, and it has not happened again after starting the game up again the next day but it caused me to nope out after it happened. I took a video of it: Third problem I hit, Gravilex space creature spawned inside a star and would not leave it. My ships would not go into the star to attack it, but they happily flew around in circles doing nothing until I manually called them away. If I set  assault fleets back to automated,  they will fly right back to that star and waste more time. I had to lure it out of the star with a fuel transport to finally kill the darn thing. Fourth problem....  Another issue with automation. Facility construction was set to Advisor suggest, meaning advisor is supposed to say "hey guy you should build an admin facility here!" and I am supposed to say yes or no to it. The advisor suggested exactly such a thing, and I said no because I don't have the funds for it right now. The advisor did it anyway. On every colony. I lost all of the money I had been saving for a new fleet. This happened with multiple buildings until I finally set facility building to manual only and it stopped.Fifth problem. A war with an enemy AI empire. I have a colony that is poorly defended. Enemy AI sends an invasion fleet. "Oh no!" I thought, and sent one of my dedicated defense fleets to defend it. That invasion fleet never arrived. I assumed they had decided not to attack because my defense fleet was there. Fast forward 30 minutes and I get the same notification, invasion fleet inbound. I send my defense force back. Again the invasion fleet never arrives. Another hour later and I get yet another notification, at this point I have built a few star ports and monitoring stations in the area because the ai has kept trying to attack it. So I looked to see what was happening.I found that invasion fleet, along with the 2 previous invasion fleets... stuck in a nebula because the AI is too stupid to avoid it and sent THREE FLEETS through the same path. Why even have nebulas if you can't figure out how to get the AI to play around them?!6th problem is performance. This is maybe mid game, and it is a slog. After having multiple nation maps revealed through diplomacy the fps slows to a crawl. It's like a slideshow. People complain about stellaris' endgame performance, but this is MUCH worse. I dread to think what it would be like at end game....And the final one, the final straw.... You apparently can't have more than one role for each ship type. I built a combat destroyer and put it in all my fleets. Later I designed a bombardment destroyer. I set the combat fleets to specifically keep the combat destroyer, but they retrofit to the bombardment one anyway. WHY even have the option to specify a type of ship for a fleet if the fleet doesn't use it?I wanted to like this game, I just can't. There are too many problems. There is definitely a good framework here, and it might be fun eventually, but it just isn't done yet.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not quite sure why the game has such low score here. It IS good! Yes, it requires patience to learn, and it is more like a world/universe simulator than a "game" like Stellaris, but I found myself more often to play this game, and not Stellaris "abstraction". This game just feels more real.The game improved since the launch in terms of better automation. It will for sure still improve more, because the development is active. The races are quite different from each other. The diplomacy/interaction is understandable and also has more realistic feel than in most of the games. Being able to automate any part of the game is just fantastic. It is also a heaven for those who want to micro-optimize things better than automation will do for you.One thing about the game that it will take loooong time to learn the game, yet you will be able to play it and continue learning, because of automation. I am usually become bored with games quite fast once I learn it, but not here. There is just a lot of complexity to continue learning, yet, automation helps if you do not understand something or do not want to be bothered by.While I admit that this game is not for everyone (I mean the whole genre is not for everyone). If you are into 4X, and Sci-Fi/space games, this one is absolutely a must.

If I click a button, and it registers that I've clicked it, but I have absolutely no idea what happened because nothing on the UI changes, then it has issues. _childDocuments_.review: Quick review, I'm not going to summarize the whole game here. It's essentially an upgraded version of Distant Worlds 1, so look up the reviews there to see if it's the right kind of game for you. This is just to give a overview of that I found the state of the game to be at release.It's stable and feels very much feature complete. There are a few bugs here and there. Most annoying being that the AI will ask you to do stupid stuff like constructing a mining base in a place with very low yields over and over even though you said no to that location multiple times. I've also had civilian ships happily waltz half the map away after getting star charts from a pirate which revealed both mining locations there and a friendly indy colony which would provide fuel, problem is there is no way the civilian ships would make it there before running out of fuel which makes them move at a snail pace essentially trapping them in the middle of nowhere. Another bug I had was a few military ships teleporting across the map which also made them essentially stuck there since the return trip would take forever. Luckily I had a small horde of military ships by that time, so a few being AWOL didn't matter that much.These are the extent of my issues on launch day after half a dozen hours played late into the night. I personally think that these issues weren't particularly severe and very much still enjoyed my time with the game. I'll leave it up to you if you would think the same. If you're reading this later, then I assume these issues should be mostly fixed by patches.

_childDocuments_.review: Space sim/4X fans, this one has the goods!So I've finally gotten some time to sink my teeth into this game and it's pretty impressive.  In my opinion it it is best described as a space sim/4x game that leans heavily on the sim side.  The first time I tried the game I didn't quite get it.  Essentially the game seemed to be playing itself.  After some experimenting and a little research, I discovered that almost every aspect of the game can be automated.  As you learn more about the various mechanics, this automation can be tailored to your exact preference.  I can't emphasis enough the level of customization you have in terms of gameplay.  This extends to not only automation but also setting up the game itself.Most players will likely try to compare this game to Stellaris.  While this is fair, there are some major differences between the two.  DW2 provides a deeper level of automation/control/setup.  Stellaris provides a more polished product and requires (by default) more direct interaction from the user.  Also, Stellaris has a longer development history and an impressive array of DLC that help round out gameplay in a way that DW2 can't (at least not yet).  I won't say one is better than the other as I am enjoying both.  Things to consider before buying:	-Price:  At around $50USD, this is not a game I would purchase unless you understand what a space sim and 4X game is.  Watch some videos so you don't end up with another un-played title in your library.  If you like what you see, or you are a fan of games like Stellaris then it's a solid buy (especially if you can get it on sale). 	-Camera:  One aspect of DW2 that initially bothered me was the lack of complete camera control.  While the game is 3D you cannot lock onto a ship or object and rotate your view around it at any angel.  The default view is a tactical style view that allows you to zoom all the way from a galaxy view down to any local system.  This is functional and doesn't impact gameplay but, it does reduce immersion (and seems like a big miss IMO).  With many slow paced games like this, I like to lock onto a ship, find a good camera angle, crank some tunes and zone out on the journey's visuals. 	-Learning Curve:  There are a lot of menus and aspects to the game.  Complete understanding of all the mechanics will take a long time (but for me, the journey is part of the fun).  Fortunately, the game is defaulted to where many aspects are automated.  As you learn more, you can reduce (or increase) this automation. 	-Single Player. 	-Expect to watch at least some videos on how to play. Recommended for Fans of the following:-Stellaris-Avorion-Sins of a Solar Empire-X3/X4-Star Point Gemini Series

_childDocuments_.review: While not as developed as Stellaris I fully believe this will be a much better game in time. The more in-depth economy and logistics mechanics alone are very enjoyable and I really like how my empire feels alive with private transport ships taking resources from mines to colonies. There isn't as much flavor or event chains like Stellaris but ship design is intuitive and it is very fun using your starting system as a kind of traning wheels for your empire.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is the 4X game for wargamers. It includes all the fiddly bits that wargamers  like. War, Logistics, Diplomacy, Maps - this list goes on. DW2 allows the player to focus exactly on what you want - some, all or none, thanks to  the management AI. Pick and choose what you like and leave the rest to your AI admins.  Distant Worlds 2 can have a large learning curve or not - because you can choose how much gaming goodness to pile on. A good first game is to sit back in the comfort of your gaming chair with an adult beverage of your choice... and watch the narrative unfold for good or ill. Just let the computer take care of it all for you. Then after a time start making decisions you want to dabble in. Sit back, rinse and repeat. Take it slow, savor and enjoy the ride.  Eventually you'll learn the game before you realize it,  Emperor.

_childDocuments_.review: Do Not buy this game,  it isn't even a game.  It's more like a simulation that you watch as it plays the game.  it's stupid as hell.   STELLARIS is FAR SUPERIOR in every way.Any other game in the same genre you can think of is better than this game,  even the free ones like Dominus Galaxia and that isn't even finished.   Probably never will be.Terra Invicta makes more sense than this game does,  TERRA INVICTA is EASY to learn compared to this game.  EASY.   Doing anything in this game is a struggle and it's all about INDIRECT INFLUENCE,  that is the core 'mechanical' concept of this game.  AUTOMATION AND INDIRECT INFLUENCE. The developers do not care if you play it or not or even know how to play it,  that's your problem once you give them your money.  They don't care if you can easily keep track of every ship in the game or what it's doing or where it's going because the game will take care of everything for you anyway.  Figure it out or don't,  you can always AUTOMATE the living hell out of it and watch the game play without your input at all. It's a ridiculous game 'concept' and it's not much different than the first one.   It's a very niche sort of 'product' for lack of a better more descriptive term.  I just consider it lame old reskinned crap.   It's a cash grab with a new look but it's the same old game.  There are no real innovations, there is no refinement,  there is no clarity. _childDocuments_.review: Damn good 4X. One of my favourite parts is when I managed to destroy a wandering evil spacehulk-like danger from the galaxy's past with my fleet:I had been called by the biggest pirate faction in the known universe to date. A bunch of pricks that liked to harass my fringe mining outposts between my space and another major civilisation that was one of two that were major competitors. I never liked them. Then all of a sudden they are calling me for help against a great evil that has awakened from the shadows of the past. They spin me this tale that their ancestors had passed on from before the age of shadows and told me that this thing was after them and all other life in the known galaxy. I agreed to help them out and sent out an expeditionary fleet immediately for time, unsure if it would be enough, but surely capable of at least investigating the danger. Now I've been hearing rumours of this dark threat from the past from independent traders for some time, as signs of it moving about in the dark places of undeveloped space were only seen by space captains that traversed them.Now two thirds into the journey, the pirate faction calls and tells me that things aren't going well for them and feel that in the event of their death, they must tell me what their ancestors had passed on so that I could effectively fight it before it becomes too much of a threat to the rest of the galaxy. Then some time later, they go dark and cease to exist. They were pains in the ass, but I kind of felt bad. Shortly before my fleet arrived, my first sighting was by one of my mining outposts. They didn't last long as this massive space-hulk-like horror descended upon them with the converted survivor ships of both pirates and at least two other faction ships and some independent vessels. I found out that my fleet, although bad-ass, only matched the entire lot in potential firepower. So it was an unsure battle. I knew this thing was only going to grow as a threat as it moved from system to system, so I jumped into location and ambushed it before it could leave.It spewed swarms of missiles for cover as boarding vessels closed in and as my crews fought off the horrors on board, system after system going down as the boarders progressed, outside was a desperate exchange of firepower. This thing, despite it's size was fast enough to keep distance from my two battleships and held the closest at bay with a very large tractor beam. My destroyers and frigates flanked and dumped pulse cannons into it's fortress shields and regenerating armour. Any ship that did get the focused ire of the space-hulk would pull off to draw fire and hopefully retreat to come back when it's shields recharged enough to come back into the fight, but some were outright destroyed by those swarms before jumping and others were disabled and left adrift, hopefully salvageable under their own power. But finally I managed to destroy it and it's entourage and saved the game immediately.Surprisingly, I still had most of my fleet, although much of it was disabled and making repairs. Now I had to hold position and guard the wounded against poachers as they restored their systems over time. I was a long way from home and near the edges of another civilisation that hated my technologically superior ways. Problem was, some of these ships suffered all module losses that provided repair capabilities, so they sat adrift in space unable to repair without outside help. On top of this, some had their fuel tanks ruptured during the battle and lost all fuel, so they couldn't easily hyperspace to the nearest fuelling point either. So they had to sit and wait for a deep space fuel tanker and a construction vessel to come along and save the rest.Now as great as all that was. My favourite part was this: As I waited and the other civilisation, an ornery bunch of space toads that coveted my sweet tech, came along with a numerically inferior fleet that hung around and hummed and hawed for a while on the fringes of the solar system before jumping around my fleet and bee-lined for my salvage. Big note: anything that is destroyed, leaves limited time salvage. Anything can pick it up and all salvage, as far as I know, provides a little bit towards technological progress when recovered, and has a small chance to do a lot more, especially computer cores. Now I wasn't going to stand for it. My secretes were my own and so I ordered them to attack the nearest ship, a frigate and added it to the floating wreckage.The fleet immediately turned around and bailed.No "diplomatic incident"No war declared.They just got the message and stayed the hell away until I could salvage it all and get everyone back home.Sure there was a hit to my rep with them, but it was understood. Back off.A little thing that just stood out on top of a lot of other awesome stuff.Recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's just too boring. There's no core gameplay loops here that I find enjoyable, or can even find. I challenge anyone to identify what the gameplay loops are, because I can't find any. The game isn't really a 4X strategy game, it's a 4X galactic expansion simulator, and there's not enough meat in the game to keep one interested. Let's start with the economy. It's very trivial. There are many resources in the game, but you are unlikely to have any shortfalls in one. Money is the only thing that actually influences your ability to grow and/or project military power. Money is derived from the development of your colonies, and in turn development is just some formula of population plus luxury goods. Unlike say, Endless Space/Legend, luxury goods are very boring. They don't provide any empire-wide bonuses, rather they provide mostly development, and rarely tiny bonuses to population growth and colony income. There are a few 'super-rare' luxury goods, which provide even bigger bonuses to development, but are otherwise completely vanilla. So the devs have spent a ton of time on optimizing the mining and transport AI so you don't have shortages, and the result is the economy part of the game is trivialized for the player, as you don't have to make any decisions.Warfare is basically blob-ology. Throw a bigger bunch of ships with a higher ComPot (combat potential) at a smaller group of ships and you win the attrition war! Yeah that's about it. Ground warfare is even more boring, it's just attack strength versus defence strength.Then we get to balance. Some content creators (DasTactic) have claimed this game is intentionally unbalanced. I will say that democratic/diplomatic gambit absolutely crushes the militaristic/feudalism. But it's even worse because the diplomatic playstyle involves a handful of clicks whereas if you are a militaristic power you have to constantly micro ground forces to counter the silly rebellion mechanics.Then onto the UI. It's so much better than Universe, but it's still so inadequate. If I want to add a specific class to a fleet, what do you think I have to do? I have to click on the appropriate construction tab, build the ship, then navigate to the all ships tag, find the ship in the giant list of ships, and then use the menu to attach it to one of a myriad number of ships. You would think I would be able to build a ship from the fleet interface, but no. Similarly, building and loading troops for invasion armies involves a huge number clicks to accomplish what should be very simple. The game seems to try and force you to use templates for every  fleet and army, and that's just not realistic until you're in the end game and such small inefficiencies can be safely ignored.Overall, the game doesn't expect the player to make any decisions, and as a result it is not engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is build around idea of automation so player would take control over most interesting mechanics and leave everything else to AI. Intriguing idea on paper but in reality - everything is bugged or contain WIP elements despite of how many years game'd being released.Basically whole gameplay is screwed as you need to constantly dodge existing bugs and AI automation "features".Some examples:a) You have a special option to allow AI to maintain your existing fleets automatically according to fleet template. Great? Except it don't work correctly and massively overbuild excess ships.b) You want to maintain your fleets manually? Great, but game "forget" to warn you that you can't scroll in "pick a fleet" menu. For me, with 1920*1080 display it mean I can't maintain more then ~36 fleets.c) You want to move your Admiral into biggest battleship in your fleet? Forget about it, it will require fighting with UI (first at fleet window, then at officers window).d) Game spam you with info messages but guess what's happening when you rolled a Demoralizing officer? Nothing happens, no warning at all.e) Guess what's happening when while your agent doing mission against a faction - you'd destroyed this faction (or already received that tech from salvage/event)? No, mission is not canceled, instead it leading to auto-fail and death or capture of your agent.f) We have tons of racial unique techs but auto-designer do not understand them and in most cases think they're inferior to "normal" one. What's better : a cheap 150 fuel storage or newest & super expensive 150 fuel storage? For DW2 is the last one.

_childDocuments_.review: Until now, very positive experience! I've been having fun.As far as features go, it has quite a solid base. AI assistance can be a little extreme and inconsistent sometimes, but this is compensated by being able to customise and disable it altogether, so it's not all that bad. Personally I could solve mine and have not experienced crashes ever since, but subsequent hotfixes *should* improve things, hopefully.Overall, it is quite a good game with a lot of potential, I'm definitely excited to see how it develops in terms of future content.If you enjoy Stellaris, you may also enjoy this. It is similar enough as a whole with quite a fair share of differences in its core features and gameplay that keep the experience fresh and unique (they're both great games!)Also the soundtrack surprised me a bit. _childDocuments_.review: I'm in a very tricky situation here, like many others. The idea, the mechanics, the whole game concept is great. The execution of it all, not so much. Crashes are common along with performance problems. Advisers asking you to build the same building over and over again no matter how many times you've refused before. Ships/fleets taking on long trips without the sufficient amount of fuel or even stopping at a nearby station to refuel before they start their journey or when about to run out of fuel. Automated constructor/surveyor ships going back to systems where there's aggressive creatures/enemy ships are waiting the blow them up, just like the 5 automated constructors before them.. (you have no option to tell your ships/fleets to avoid a system, you can only set them up to flee when there's enemies in a system they're in, and by that time it's too late to run away in many cases). This is not a full list of issues I have with the game, these are just the ones from the top of my head. The game would be the best space 4x without these issues and I hope with time it will reach it's full potential. Until then I can't recommend it. :(Edit#1: So Aurora update just came out so I thought I jump back in and see how's the game after a year. Well. there seems to be improvements and I started to enjoy it just when a newly built fleet of mine for whatever reason chose to go into the nearby Nebulae and every single one of them get completely disabled and stuck there.  I did not send them there, there's literally nothing in that nebulae apart from a single unexplored system. I gave them the order to get to the nearest spaceport about 20 times. What happens is they sort of try to go, but since they can't, the order simply gets cancelled and the fleet has no mission again. So they just keep sitting in a nebulae. Then I found a button when I selected individual ships within the fleet that said "escape from here". I thought....oh, this is how I can get them out of here then, one by one.... Well.... pressed the button, gave the order to escape just to see the ship just start going in the direction it was facing.... which was the wrong direction obviously, deeper into the nebulae.....That was the point when I just closed the game and came here to tell you guys, the game is still not ready and at this point I'm not sure it ever will be. After a year of development AFTER release and just before a DLC comes out ships/fleets still go to places automatically where they shouldn't, still no way to blacklist star systems/areas for them so they could avoid them and in a game in which every single unit can be automated it's just unacceptable. For those of you who never played this game: A nebulae in this game is sort of like mountains is other game. They are used as an obstacle to separate areas in space. They are traversable but most of them should be avoided as they would ruin your ships.The game is still not : After the incident with the fleet in the nebula (I sorted the situation using the Game Editor) I started a new game to see if something like that happens again. It didn't. The whole game so far (I'm in late game now with 40+ colonies) went mostly flawlessly. There are some annoying stuff and room for improvement still but the game is very enjoyable. I started with a lot of stuff set to manual control and slowly started to automate things as the empire got bigger. Scouts, tankers, builders, combat ships... all worked just fine.Lastly I automated all my fleets. Attack, defence, raid, invasion, it all works. My fleets went to clear out defenders then invaded, destroyed mining bases of the enemy...etc.I'l; start a new game after finishing this but apart from a few things the game is actually a lot of fun now so I change my review to recommended. :)
