_childDocuments_.review: This is really a sideways thumb rating -- thumbs up because I am really glad games like this exist, and I'm happy to have bought it and supported the devs.The game is not really for me long term - but I think there are people who would really enjoy this.    This game is in sort of a weird position -- it's not a "Casual" space opera like Stellaris, but it's also not a wargame or turn based like Shadow Empire or MOO2.   If you want to spend a LOT of time building an empire, doing diplomacy, managing resources, etc. with a somewhat clunky (but 'ok" once you get to know it) interface - you might really enjoy this game.  The detail for ship building and related tech is AWESOME. However, I just found the game a bit to dreary/sleepy to play (I have better things to do with my time).  The music is also bad - so shut it off and put something else on in the background.    I can't vote this game down though because it's clear the devs and engineers put a lot of work into this game, and there are some really cool side missions and storylines that pop up occasionally.  I also liked the variety of races and sub-species.  It's almost great but not good enough at the same time if that makes sense.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an updated Distant Worlds: Universe with a few minor changes.Get it if you really like DW and you want it to run better, or at least with new problems in place of the old.Get it if you've never played DW and you want to play a 4X in which you can automate everything you don't want to do manually.Don't get it if you didn't like DW.Don't get it if you expect more content than in DW.Don't get it if you expect a streamlined user experience.Don't get it if you expect a finished product.It's still fairly rough around the corners in terms of stability, performance, game balance, AI and information presentation. Some of those faults were inherited from DW:U, some must've come about due to the new engine. Overall I'd call it an early-access level of quality. Playable, enjoyable even, but also disappointing and frustrating at every turn. Sooner or later during a campaign you will encounter something that will ruin your enjoyment - unbeatable self-replicating enemies, performance degradation, AI SNAFUs, or just plain crashes for example. And there are design problems - many parts of the game that you will want to turn over to the AI for automation because they end up being repetitive busywork, while also being horrified by how glaringly inefficient the AI can be at times, and how little it cares for your plans - sooner or later you choose between letting the game play itself or micromanaging absolutely everything, because the selective automation fails to have a good cooperation between manual and automatic components.In my opinion the move from 2D to 3D did not do the game any favors, since the 3D models almost universally look like ass. Sorry to whoever made them, it must've been hard work, but I don't like them. Some of them are just random fantasy shapes. Many are clearly backwards. Almost all of them have glaring structural weaknesses for no reason. I know DW isn't hard sci-fi by any means, but having spaceships shaped like pretzels isn't good for immersion. The textures and shading are also extremely slipshod. This is in contrast to some things like planetary facility images and 3D planets, which are very evocative. The tech tree is 100% technobabble, the races are warmed-up clichés, events and stories are forgettable, you will switch off the music, diplomatic interactions are extremely predictable and repetitive, your leaders are one-dimensional vehicles for passive stat boosts, and there's generally not much of a setting here. For all that you're supposed to be building an empire, witnessing technological revolutions, population booms and great economic developments, you'll never see anything other than unchanging planets and a few spaceships. In the end you leave the universe much like you found it, except with some numbers having gone up and a few more spaceships sailing around. In general, Distant Worlds doesn't even try to present itself as having character, or to immerse the player, or to create a believable world or worlds. The relationship between game world and player will always be a distant one.There is a noticeable lack of things happening in the endgame. Once pirates are no longer a threat to you, there's a brief phase in which you and your neighbors jockey for who's on top, and if that ends up being you then everyone who is not already effectively allied to you will hate your guts out of fear or jealousy and refuse to do business with you, leaving you to either sit in your corner of space and watch the credits trickle in or to declare wars of aggression in order to shake things up. There is no political dynamism, no initiative on the part of the AIs to dislodge or undermine you, they just sit there and wait for you to mop them up one by one. And it's not like the AI can actually win; they're extremely passive and inefficient regardless of game settings. This takes a lot of meaning out of many game systems - there's no need to do a lot of tinkering with the economy, with ship designs, or with...well, those really are the two deepest systems in the game and the rest is mostly obvious and straightforward. And even in economy and shipbuilding you don't really have many interesting options. The game generally has many systems, but most of them are either shallow and straightforward or they do offer some degrees of freedom but it doesn't matter because the AI can't compete anyways. You can choose to build tall-then-wide or wide-then-tall, maybe invest a little in tourism, choose whether to emphasize research or growth, and taxes or growth, and maybe prioritize certain mining sites. You can create this or that fleet doctrine and ship designs. You can use these or those technologies. You can make lots of choices, but ultimately some things are always obviously smart and you'll end up doing those a lot - colonize good planets, tax densely populated worlds, befriend everyone except for whom you intend to conquer, integrate many races so you can colonize different planet types, research as much as possible, build administration buildings everywhere, and if you do all that then you're probably already winning on any difficulty level and no need to fiddle with the details.The difference between a well-managed empire and one on autopilot isn't really significant enough to make or break a game because the AI isn't much competition no matter what course you take. Performance is also a problem. If the simulation just slowed down, that'd be fine, but instead ships suddenly stop moving for a few minutes, presumably when the game thinks you aren't looking at them. The UI stops updating for a while, only to suddenly shuffle in new items under your cursor just when you were about to click a button. UI animations get entirely out of whack and display messages that you already closed seconds ago. You can get around these issues by pausing the game whenever you want to do anything, but it still feels bad.The manual and in-game galactopaedia and the UI all try to tell you how the game works and what's going on at any given time, but they're also all fairly bad it. Various mechanics remain unexplained, many in-game items have no description to speak of, the sci-fi universe of the game completely fails to paint a picture of itself, and the game notifies you of many utterly irrelevant events (like ten separate messages for a freighter being attacked by ten space fishes before it escaped unharmed), while failing to draw your attention to highly critical ones (your fleet and the entire orbital infrastructure of a planet were just wiped out). You also can't really rely on the automation AI in anything, because the game doesn't document or display what it actually does or does not take responsibility for, leaving you with a lot of manual busywork even when you ostensibly choose hands-off settings.Then there are features that just plain don't work. At all. Things that are described as doing something but that do nothing. Or that cost resources but do nothing. This includes key game mechanics like fuel tankers, planetary defenses, and repeatable technologies. And the game gives you barely any tools to actually check up on its inner workings; it takes a lot of observation and manual experimentation to gain any insight into what works and what does not. This is alpha test territory, a very bad state for a game to be in. Doubly so over a year after release.It's still a unique game well worth playing, if only to see the private economy do its thing and to enjoy selective automation, but temper your expectations. This was never ready for release. It needs more work. It's as unfinished as they come. There are post-launch patches coming, but there's still much more to be fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, any singleplayer strategy game lives and dies by its AI. Doubly so for a game that has a lot of built in automation.And quite frankly, the AI in this game, both friendly and enemy, is atrocious. Well its not really that bad, but it leaves a spoiled taste in your mouth. And then just as bad is the diplomacy screen. Your AI advisors will recommend peace deals with tons of options from demanding tech, mining stations, resources and money, etc. etc. But when you try to craft a peace deal? You get none of those options. And you can have every single enemy world blockaded. You can destroy every single mining station they own on the map. You can destroy every single space faring ship they own. But for some reason, the enemy AI will not give you a mildly decent peace deal. Oh and 2 other AIs that will never attack you and can't even reach your sector of space will declare war on you while you're trying to end the previous war. Also orbital bombardment does not seem to affect the AI's willingness to peace you out.

_childDocuments_.review: Warning:   This review is identical to 50% of the other reviews on here!Gameplay is great.   It feels like a big, deep galaxy.   The vast numbers of stars, planets, asteroids, ships, events... everything feels as epic as an interstellar empire should be.I just wish I could finish a game.   The further into the game, the more frequent the crashes - but they can happen any time.There's also an... unpolished... feel to it.   20-ish digit galactic references are silly.   Map pinging for events is good - but when there's two locations (enemy fleet xyz in enroute to your colony abc), only one gets pinged.  And half the time that ping is under a message box, and I always need to scroll way, way out from what I'm doing to find it.   Links and references aren't quite all there, information is hard to find, sometimes. (why, when I've just completed research into basic colonisation, can't I build a colony ship?).   It's not bad, but neither is it great.Current verdict:  Incomplete - it feel like a beta.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not the type of person that min and maxes things all the time. Which might be why I enjoy games such as distant worlds 2 and Hoi4. This is the type of game that I get an itch to play for weeks at a time before putting it down for a few months and coming back feeling like I learn a little more every time I play. The automation may not be the best (going back to what I said about Hoi4) as many people complain it does wonky things, and there has been a few times in game I get slightly annoyed to find a ship slowly going through space without fuel. Overall though, the AI is good enough for me to let it run most things while I just jump in and out of areas that draw my interest. An example of this is the spy mechanic, overall I just leave most of the spies on auto to let them do what ever they feel like. I only jump in when one empire decides to get hostile enough that I can have a hand full of spies that I jump in and out to have my spies focus on objectives that I would like done. There has even been one time I was just too tied to really play the game, but I felt like wanting to watch a game play out. This is were the full automation was fun just how the game played out.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is fun to an extent, performance is where it hits you. The game is good for the first hour or two, but once mid game hits, say goodbye to a playable game. By no means do i own a high end comp but i am rocking a i7 with a RTX 2080Ti and have this game on a M2 drive, while having 32g or ram. (of course, both cpu and ram are OC). Only reason i have added this is for others to compare your system to mine when deciding on getting the game due to performance issues. ==========For those wondering, Diplomacy options are neat (lots of options)Virtually no cap on ships (this is where performance kicks in mid game)Learning curve is quite high (compared to other games and first timers)LOTS of automation (turn a movie on and let the game do its thing)You can edit the entire map ingame (add more planets, moons, ships, money, ect. you can make a opposing player go bankrupt if your tired of constant wars with them lol)Hours of play time per map==========Some cons:There are some menus "areas" that will bug out and vanish, forcing you to reload your game for it to appear.Mid game performance issues will cause a CTD (use care, safe often)Pirates can be quite a problem if you refuse to pay them "protection" (fairy easy to deal with, just annoying when there are lots of em)OPTIONS OPTIONS OPTIONSThis is a biggy, at least for me. Graphic options are virtually none existent. There are some areas you can tweak ingame. such as the UI interface (small-ultra large, super important for 4k gamers). But with that said, if your a computer savy person, you could always go into the game files and tweak even more options there using notepad or something equal to it. ==========OVERALLThis is a fun game if you dont mind freezes and such. I think its safe to say, once they release a update to tweak the ingame graphic settings (meaning adding lots of graphic options), the performance issue should go away. Is it worth the 49.99? possibly not. The game feels like a early access, uncompleted game. Give it time. In my eyes, this game has lots of potential, and im waiting eagerly for future updates.

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't perfect, won't even try to defend the performance issues.However, it offers one of the deepest 4X experiences that I've ever had, the most complex and interesting, but, it also is (relatively) easy to get into. The automation options are substantial, you can actually have the game play itself, or do everything manual, or a mix of the two.Default (normal) settings have you starting off pre-FTL, so going from your planet to a nearby planet will take a LONG time. You should start researching the first Warp Drive, and bam, stuff that took forever to do, is now (nearly) instant. Going to nearby stars takes forever however, until you get further techs.You can research tech to get boarding parties, seize enemy ships that have technology you don't have (which is basically the entire ship early game), scrap it, gaining a ton of technology super fast. Alternatively, enlist it into service, add it to your own fleet and use it to help capture even more ships.You balance exploration, expansion, exploitation, and probably a fair bit of extermination. Worth a pick up.

_childDocuments_.review: Buying a game today and down voting it because it has bugs at launch, shows peoples ignorance, please tell me of ANY game that has no bugs at launch. So back to this review. I am a super fan of DW1. I had DW1 + all the expansions and ended up buying DW:U on Steam just to support the developers, and modded the game as well for years and years and years. Distant Worlds 2 brings a interesting new twitch to this game that I really like. The 3D engine and all the 64-bit engine needs a bit of a tweak but I guess the developers will iron this out. I love that you can choose to set research to random and one has to explore a tech before getting a new one. Also on a sidenote, I find it awesome that one can design fighters and bombers. While also ships has hard points, so one can't just make a 2000-size frigate, with Doomsday weapons, Fighter bays and a shield of the gods like in DW:U. _childDocuments_.review: In theory one of the best space strategy games out there. In practice a broken, barely playable piece of garbage even after patches. There's tons of other stuff like this that happens all the time (set land units to garrison planets, they automatically leave garrison despite manual army management, exploration ships miscalculate fuel reserves all the time when set to automatic exploration and then limp back on their minimum speed, severely reducing scouting effectivity. they also do not jump to system, scout system, then move to next system - instead they randomly jump between systems, scout one planet, then jump to another system, and so on).The complexity of the game is its greatest asset, but also its greatest bane, and at the pace the patches are happening, it'll need at least 2-3 more years before most of the issues are fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing almost 10 hours i quickly lost my interest in the game. Even if most features from the previous games are still there it somehow feels empty and dull and also seems to lack atmosphere. I'm not sure i can put my finger on what happened, though. But my guess is that the problem for me might be the general art design and the quickly fading interest in exploration.Exploration felt so special in the first part. It just felt more meaningful to find a derelict ship, to repair it and add it to your fleet. Even coolar was to find some long lost tech. All i seem to get are boosts to techs you can research anyway and nothing that makes every run feel a bit more unique. And the ships are never that special, that finding them makes my day. It feels to me that someone hit the exploration game with the balance bat and knocked the fun unconcious. The new interface is pretty ok. It's usable and better then the old one. But it looks not really like professional design, but made by a programmer, who has no sense of aesthetics and symmetry.I also dislike the general atmosphere of the new 3D graphics. They are ugly and lack a unique flair. This makes me care much less for my ships. They somehow became numbers to me, while in the previous game i loved to follow everything around to see what they do/explore or how they fight. It also feels a bit like a game with the Stellaris DLC mindset. Paradox delivered a relatively shallow game at release when it comes to basic mechanics. And Distant Worlds 2 feels the same. It has more options as Stellaris at release - for example it has simple espionage - but most feel basic. My guess is that we can expect a lot of DLCs to flesh out this game. Maybe i'll give it another try, especially if they are able to enhance the atmosphere. But for sure not at the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I, like many, was hyped for DW2 when it was announced but let down by the state of the game at release. Countless bugs, dumb ship AI and unfinished mechanics rendered the game pretty much unplayable. Now, a year later, much has changed. The devs improved the game in every regard, listened to the community and finally realized (much of) its potential. DW2 is a great game now with deep, unique mechanics and lots of potential for future development. The simulation aspects of the game make the galaxy feel alive and force you to think strategically in a way lots of 4X games aim but only few manage to. Blindly colonizing a planet in the outer rims of the galaxy, far away from the rest of your empire, has inherent economic implications like thinning out the availability of private sector freighters since they now have to ship goods to a far away world, increasing fuel expenditure and preventing them from investing in more profitable projects. The distance to your capital also increases corruption and political deviancy. Of course this new colony is also susceptible to outside threats as your fleets will take a long time to arrive there, making it a particularly attractive target for foreign empires. This is just one example for how the games' mechanics make you evaluate every decision with much more becoming apparent the more you play. There's a lot to learn and uncover here.There's still some problems with the game (looking at you, fuel tankers not refueling fleets that are in transit), but the overall feel of the game is amazing and if the devs keep up the work they've been doing this past year it's only going to get better. At this stage it's definitely worth playing, especially if you're an avid 4X enjoyer.

_childDocuments_.review: After putting nearly 200 hours into this Gem i think i can finally write a worthy review, I was a big fan of DWU and when this game first dropped it was a mess, so many problems for people unable to launch and many crashes for others, the optimisation was poor and honestly it should of been an Early Access release.However the small Dev team have committed to game and have expressed that there will be many more updates and improvements for years to come,  and so far they have been following through with that promise, the optimisation has come on leaps and bounds from before, game play is extremely smooth, the AI has been improved and we have had new Factions along with improvements to base faction Races.That's not to say there isn't room for improvement, the biggest floor for this game is its entry level to new players, this game can be a HUGE learning curve and new players to this game better be committed to learning all automation settings and what they do otherwise there gonna be wondering why the AI has chosen to completely ignore what you THINK you have told it to do. This is a simulation game you can control as much or as little as you want to, and until the game has a better tutorial i would highly recommend the Youtube content on DW2 by DasTactic he explains the automation pretty good. Overall i'd say i haven't really ever come across another game like this, many compare this to Stellaris but in my opinion they aren't even close, not to say theres anything wrong with Stellaris i just dont think they are a good comparison.I would highly recommend if your coming back to this game or checking it out for the 1st time opt into the beta branch that's where all the latest and greatest new UI and game play improvements are and right now the game is in a REALLY good play and i look forward to what the Devs are gonna add in future.Good luck Uniting/Conquering the galaxy!

_childDocuments_.review: I played another 8hrs and it's simply not fun. I want to like it, enough that I dumped 12hrs into this unfun thing that should be fun just trying to find the fun that should exist here. It's Master of Orion 3 all over again. Slow as possible to get anything done. Too many nuanced systems to the point that automation is pretty much required on some of them to make any progress, plus the automation is simply better in many cases. Combat is lame. Ship design seems cool, until you realize all you're really doing is picking your weapon type so it's just a far more complicated version of stellaris ship design. "Colonizable" worlds are a trap, 95%+ of them will doom your economy for the rest of the game, and taking over the independants is usually the only way to make taking new planets not the stupidest move you've done in your playthrough.All that said I'll probably try another run or two, because I want to like it and even after my initial feelings on the game it was far too late to hit refund.Original review after 4.7hrs played is below:it's a janky mess. The closest comparison is Stellaris and that feels and plays way better.Major turnoffs include:-Message spam, constantly, endlessly, and growing in frequency. Apparently you can disable them, but it clearly isn't easy to fine. Take a page from your closest competitor and let us right click a message to get the popup options for it.-Almost everything is default automated. At first it made sense, there's a lot going on and I get to pick what I want to do. Then I realised it was Master of Orion 3 style where I'm just there for the ride. Attempting to take control of stuff makes it significantly worse. Automated fleets are stupid and terrible, they're half automated and badger you with popups (see issue 1)  for what they should just do while automated.-Slow. Sooo slow. 4x speed (the max) is what normal should be. Not only are you mostly just there for the ride, but it'd be faster to walk.-Lack of map clarity for war. Eventually you'll get tired of paying tribute to some random pirates that demanded tribute really early on that you couldn't kill at the time. So you'll break that tribute treaty...and then scratch your head as to where they are so you can go gt them. Actual war with another empire is far worse, warning spam (see issue 1) that's mostly useless or irrelevant, and then a warning buried in the middle of them where an invasion fleet is on their way. If you catch it you'll pause and try to find it so you can go defend yourself, eventually you might even make sense of the mess and get your fleet on it's way to defend. However a few short moments after you unpause you get another warning that your planet is now invaded.-Income makes no sense. I can have +5,000 income, but watch my money slowly drain. I can have -5000 income, and watch my reserves slowly grow. I check my treasury income screen, and it says I should be losing or gaining that same amount, yet my reserves clearly have a mind of their own for both positive and negative.-Research doesn't tell you what it actually does. Some tell you that you get a new ship, or a new mining station, or whatever weapons, but there's no stats so it's just a differently named thing where I can't tell if it is or was worth getting. There's 4 or 5 sensor researches in the second column, what's each one do? Not a clue so I got them all. What did I gain for that? Not a clue, I couldn't tell any difference on my ships scanning range or speed.

_childDocuments_.review: This represents the progression and next gen concept of 4x games. Stellaris successfully pulled off real time 4x. Distant Worlds has successfully pulled off a "living galaxy" of industry, supply, trade, and military ships. You don't have simple magic interconnectivity of resources once you settle a planet or build a space station. You now have actual supply and trade vessels traveling automatically between destinations to maintain your supply chain. As is practical, these supply chains need to be defended and can be disrupted as part of your strategy. Think this sounds too complex and involved? You can automate almost every gameplay element of the game: resource management, station building, world settling, population balancing, ship building, combat missions, fleets, war, invasions....everything. As far as I can tell, you can largely set the entirety of the game to play automatically as a simulation if you'd like.Warning: There is a steep learning curve to get your hands around all this. So don't expect the first play to be easy to pick up as your 5th play.There is still room for growth in the 4X genre:The only main drawback is the lack of customization of races/civilizations and everything plays out to "good guys are liberal egalitarians and bad guys are the opposite. Races are pretty fixed to either good guys or bad guys for species relations. While that might be practical and realistic....it means you can't play as the Warhammer 40,000 Empire of Man without SIGNIFICANTLY hamstringing yourself as the gameplay mechanics makes racial diversity of your empire crucial (no humans on ocean or lava worlds).

_childDocuments_.review: More modern take on the classic Distant Worlds: Universe. Had a bit of a troubled release on some hardware configurations  that was missed during testing, resulting in negative reviews, but the developer has been burning the midnight oil releasing fixes resolving said issues. The roadmap going forward is also looking great with two more playable races being added soon. There has also been more developers assigned to the project to squeeze even more performance out of the engine.The game is a great addition to the "Easy to learn, hard to master" category of 4X games. It is very deep but offers significant configurable automation that lets the player decide what parts of the empire they want to control more directly. Or they can decide to get prompts on important decisions from their advisors to either greenlight their plan or deny it. Recommended for any fan of 4X strategy in space.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Oh my god, this is a complex title. This is probably the first thing you think when you start playing this behemoth of options. Reading the +100 page manual helps to understand the game mechanics, at least the key game concepts. Build a space empire, expand, improve the economy, crush other empires in military conflict or use your diplomacy to make them your allies. Sounds easy, but it isn't.Your empire will become large, and you can micromanage many things, from taxes to research. You can also give up on micromanagement, and just let the computer do it for you. That's what I did, and to be honest I think you have to do that as soon as your empire has grown a bit. The game is kind of a logistical simulation - build a stable economy to expand your influence. There are so many creatures, places, research, spaceships and other things that happen that you would actually really need real-life advisors to keep track of the universe. I just turned off the notifications most of the time, because my brain is too small to keep track of all this. The in-game advisors are kind of idiots sometimes, btw. Is the game better than Stellaris? Hm... no. Stellaris is far more streamlined, far more... casual? Ok, of course Stellaris is no casual game, but Distant Worlds 2 is a real hard-core strategy title. So, is it a masterpiece? Hm, no, it is too complicated, there are things later in the game that I am not sure they actually work, and most of all - sometimes you simply do not understand what happens and why. I would say that the game design is not perfect, but maybe I am just too intellectually challenged.A highly complex 4X trategy title with tons of options, looking (but certainly not sounding) better than the first part (but not much). Epic in scope, offers plenty to get stuck into, but requires a lot of time.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a solid competitor to Stellaris, it has much more interesting combat and ship design. You do get the feeling that every single ship matters. A big improvement over Stellaris is also the Damage propagation to internal components and the simulation of the damage of every single shot (Stellaris only throws out a bunch of stats per battle).Logistic is also much better then stellaris, you do get the feeling that the flow of resources,migrants and population is happening in real time and blockades play a major impact (come on, you have energy production simulated from the actual fuel in the cells of the ships and you have to  bring fuel tanker with the fleets while traveling!).Ground combat on the planets is simple but effective. Modifier and troops used add a lot to the gameplay.The only down side of the game is the user interface. Or actually to be more precise is the way you select things. It is playable if you understand that holding left and right mouse buttons you get selection details or target choices. But the implementation is very bad. I still believe the game is so good that it is worth learning the work arounds (maybe filtering for manually controlled fleets?).Also they should allow filtering for the popups on the right, they get overwhelming and there is no way to shut down part of them, sometime you loose an important one in the middle of crap.The storyline is there and it is interesting and not as intrusive as Stellaris, but the latter one has much more in this sense (kind of boring for my playstile).So, get the game and hope that after 2 years the devs understood  they should allow you to left select everything and re/automate multiple ships at once. If this ever gets solved the game is fantastic and the automation system very helpful (you can automate 3-4 fleets defending, while you have fun controlling manually the ones doing the conquering).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a flawed masterpiece. Great but very uneven,Often it feels like the best 4x space game, other times it seems unbelievably amateurish.You can scroll from single ships to the whole galaxy, it works very well, although when it sometimes crashes it is in the transition from planetary to single ship scale.You can micro single ship/group battles with ships you researched and designed yourself. It works very well. But the game doesn't want you to.The game is about automation. Everything can be automated. Well yes and no. The automated economy works well. This is a great achievement. The civ ships distribute mined resources from colonies to shipyards and navies can be built. Very good. But using the navies? Don't ever put military ships under automation. Even if they don't immediately suicide they will take the most inefficient approach to everything. They are happy to fly around with no fuel.Civ ships also, and when they do refuel or pick up resources, they are happy to fly right across the galaxy to do so. Which takes ingame years. Most guides recommend large swarms of explorer ships cos they are so inefficient. If you micro them you can use half as many. But there isn't even a way to queue orders!AI combat is ok on a small tactical scale, but above this it is hopeless. They happily send in single ships to die, one after the other. They happily build massive numbers of troop transports, with zero attack strength, and send fleets of them to "attack" and die.If you play on normal difficulty and don't really zoom in, you could have fun watching your side slowly take over, I guess. But if you want some challenge, where you need to optimize things, you eventually realize the game isn't up to it. It's designed to work on a large scale, things averaging out so nonfunctional details don't matter. If your economy is big enough (which means more planets) you will overwhelm.Anyway, I played a bunch and got my money's worth. That's why I recommend it. But it could have been No. 1.

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is a bit of a mixed bag. With some elbow grease from the devs it has the ability to become a great game, but as of now it's hard to say. I'm enjoying it personally, but there are some issues I have noticed.Pros : Customize the Galaxy how you like. Decide it's shape, size, difficulty, pirates, space monsters, independent colonies, number of other empires, starting tech level, storyline events, race specific events, use the ingame editor to recreate the Sol system and become the IMPERIUM OF MAN, amazing indepth personal control *or* automated control for things you don't feel like micromanaging. Also design the ships somewhat how you prefer.Cons: Well, it's mostly UI issues I've been having. The game doesn't like saving my preferred UI text and box sizes, as well as the coloration. Sometimes it can be difficult to find what you need in all the different options for your empire, and I have a hard time selecting troops to choose if they should be garrisoned or ungarrisoned at a colony, as when you recruit a ton of troops, the icons start to occupy the same location and it doesn't help your leaders also occupy the same space in the colony screen.Another thing: All my generals very rapidly end up with the drunk trait (happens from them sitting around in a colony doing nothing - Admirals do this too amongst others) and I'm constantly dismissing them.Also my colonies keep rebelling the moment I colonize a planet because my empire had *some* of my spies get detected during missions (not captured) which lowered my Empire rating a bit much - which was made worse by starting out as a Military Dictatorship. Which meant I had to send in the troops, which lowered my rating even more. Right now things are stable with five divisions per colony of 30-100m but it's a bit frustrating. Even more when other dictatorships look at your rating when theirs are already terrible and go "I can't/won't talk to that guy."Ships aren't as customizable as they used to be from the first Distant worlds as the hulls only allow for so many components as well as size. In the older DW it was just "how much can this hull hold?" So you can't really make a barebones frigate anymore covered in lasers, or a super battleship able to wipe out an entire fleet on it's own.Fun thing: Discovered you can rename prisoners. Had an enemy spy get captured who had nothing but negative values for everything so I renamed him Dhip Schit and sent him back home. I wonder if I'll ever see him again...Anyways. Yeah, the game still needs a fair bit of work, but with some TLC it definitely has the ability to be one of the greats like the original was. Now then, back to running INGSOC and kicking the little three-eyed rat people around...

_childDocuments_.review: This game is strange.On one hand, it is perhaps the most in-depth sci-fi 4X game I have ever played.  The intricacies in the economy alone are something that I hope other games can aspire to contain.But... on the other hand, it's also the most... under-achieving 4X game I've played.  The game's loop is... fine, but there's literally an option to have the empire run itself.  Player input is optional, at best, and unideal, at worst, as the AI can manage literally any, and every, part of your empire, which sounds like it'd be good, but it ruins much of the agency that I've felt in games like Stellaris.In a game like Stellaris, I love crafting my own empire to my own specific tastes; giving it ethics and governments that suit what I envision my species to have.  This game has... about 8 pre-made species, with set-in-stone playstyles that don't seem very different from eachother.  To say it's a downgrade is to state the obvious.If the game is cheap, give it a go, and I think you can find a few hours of enjoyment, however, at this asking price... just go buy Stellaris, or Sins of a Solar Empire, you'll get much and more from those than this.  At least, in it's current state.  If they add more species, or make a species customizer, or even just give us the option to choose our shipsets... hell, even just giving the option for mods... maybe it'd be worth your time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I like Distant Worlds 2 more than I don't like it. Game seems to be pacing relatively well but I'm not sure how interesting things will be for replayability for me though. (Tech trees, random events, victory conditions too vanilla?).  I'm hoping DW2 keeps evolving and keeps things interesting. For all the automation going on, some strategic road maps for commerce, mining, and war would be nice--to show you what the AI is attempting to accomplish where and why. And, for the things you do control--like colony upgrades--it's a click fest. It'd be nice to have a colony doctrine to allow you to cookie cut upgrades for new colonies. For those who don't know, everything is running in a simulation--you decide what the manual changes will be or how to augment current automation. Am I being picky? We'll years ago there would have been next to nothing like DW2, but now 4x games are catching up. So there's that.And there's the problematic end game. For example, I built a gigantic galaxy with only six additional races. Even so, the game is slowing down to a crawl or crashing during epic space battles. I'm running an Nvidia 3090 with AMD 5950 and 128 GB of Ram--I even reduced window sizes to try to increase performance (Remember to verify file integrity in Steam which will help if there's some file corruption AND I switched to Vulcan 2.0 driver which helped as well).  So this is bitter sweet. I bought the first DW with all the packs and paid a small fortune just to find it too clunky and tiny to play. Now, I've got DW2 and things run most of the time, but don't seem to run that well which really sucks the life out of immersion. And yes, I started playing again just after the Aurora update.The newly released DLC--for me--seems ill advised because I don't want to add more races to a game that bogs down with only six selected in one galaxy. I really think DW2 could use more quality of life/performance enhancements. I think the DW2 developers should get together with the X4 developers because I think X4 has figured more out about how to run simulators more effectively especially with Vulcan.Anyways thanks for DW2--I hope it keeps on getting even better. Adding QoL and increasing performance will keep me coming back to game in the short term. I'm hoping for some more innovation in the long term.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very niche game but I recommend it for someone who wants to try a bit of a different take on 4x.  Every ship is modeled, every transport, every tanker, etc.  Resources aren't abstracted, they are mined and have to get transported where they are needed.  It's wonderfully detailed and your empire feels alive more than any other game of this type.  However, the problem is managing it all without feeling like you're just rubber stamping everything the advisor wants you to do.  While you can turn it off, the automation is so excessive that it feels like the game is just playing without you.  Because it largely is!    When you DO try to manually do a few things - say manage a fleet - things still behave wonky and can be frustrating.  Why did all but one of my ships refuel?  When I hit refuel, why did they choose THAT starbase that's far away instead of the one in system?  Why aren't the ships of the fleet staying together?  Why are ships falling out of the fleet?  (This is all happening while you're constantly approving the advisor suggestions for other matters by the way).  So be aware this is a bit of a frustrating though very unique 4x game.  If you're burnt out on Stellaris, this can be worth a look though it actually makes me appreciate some of the QoL things in Stellaris a lot more!
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I loved its predecessor and I can see that this one is headed in the right direction. I'll go ahead and drop my cons here:- I hate when I click on a ship to take me to it, I always end up in blank space (and can never find the ship I am looking for).- Seemingly no way to queue orders for scouts- In Universe I was able to right-click systems for exploration but that is gone- Where are all the races? 20 to 7 is a huge drop.There are more but I can think of them all right now. I see the game is sitting at "Mixed" right now and if things do not keep improving, I guess I will eventually join the negs. As it is, I know CodeForce will bring it around.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: There is a really cool and engaging game here but it feels like it's in early access with another 2 years before it's playableThe UI and UX frankly sucks, I can't simply right click a planet and choose what to do, the game assumes it knows what I want it to do. Example: I select a constructor with no easy way to build a research station vs mining station so I right click the planet and it just starts building a mining station with no clear way to select a research station. So instead I left click the planet and select build research station. But for a constructor ship to go and build this you have to select the constructor ship and set it to fully automate or automate research buildings, It's very backwards thinking. Sadly this isn't one case, but constantly happens with every simple thing you want to do.Disabling the Automation punishes you and the automation constantly fights you if you have it turned on.I turned it off because it felt like I wasn't making any choices and I was just allowing the game to play itself.Also the fact that when selecting a ship theres no clear detailed info on what they are doing is really bad, not sure why selecting them doesn't show their progress on constructing something or show how far they are from something and how long it will take to get there but then highlighting over them does?What led me to quit was uncovering mysterious alien ruins I then investigated that spawned 5+ pirate ships with a strength 4x greater than my ships, and my ships kept warping off to 1v1 their ships instead of using their numbers to take them out. I only had 4 military ships of a str of 30. So the only way for them to kill 1 was to attack in numbers. I immediately started building more, but each new one would immediately teleport and solo attack an enemy ship that again is 4x stronger, then get disabled. So I then disable the automation and change some settings in the policy to prevent them from 1v1, and now I can't manually select them and attack their targets? Again some very backwards thinking went into the logic of these systems.Sadly, this game isn't early access, and only time will tell if they will improve this, but I have a feeling it won't happen with how complex and deep this game is, and how huge these problems are, since they tie into the core systems of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: My pros and cons.Pros - I like the game and this is the first space oriented game I've ever played.Cons - Game freezes about 80% of the time when I mouse over a message and practically anything else. This last for up to 5 seconds. Simply a pain and all that time adds up over a long session.I may be doing something wrong but, no matter what combo I try either manual or automated; the fleet pretty much does what it wants to do. On auto it scatters itself over the system thereby leading to piecemeal attacks. On auto or manual fleet formation settings very tight and tight the piecemeal attacks continue.We have a new motto for the fleet: "Tankers Lead the Way!" Depending on ship positioning (due to scattering) if the tankers are closer to the target, they head right into the battle. This is after the last patch.Please colonize my planet. (20 requests later) If I could while on manual or auto. Even when chance is 100% it doesn't seem to matter. I had one success with manual colonization. Hit or miss while set to auto.When I hit the settings button the game flat out crashes. This is a new issue that cropped up after the last update.While I'm sure these issues will be addressed in due time, the fleet operations at this point are simply killing the game for me. If the issues are baked into the cake and I'm making wrong choices with the settings then what can I say except I'm dumb? It's my opinion that fleet ops don't work as intended. I will still give the game a thumbs up as I'm sure these items will be sorted out. Give me a shout if you have some answers but remember what The Duke said, “Life it tough, but it's tougher if you're stupid.”

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice game with a living, detailed, customizable universe. Responsive developers with proven track record of improving things and adding features, as can be seen from the patch notes.It is a game so abstraction obviously exists BUT resource flow is less abstracted than most games all cargo need to physically travel which means it can get destroyed on the road. For example steel that has been just mined from an asteroid has to actually travel in miner ship to the space station and you can see the ship travelling in the map! If you want that steel on a nearby planet, it needs to be transferred from the space station to the planet. You do not HAVE TO worry about it though, game has a very customizable automation feature so it gets as detailed and low level as you want OR if you prefer not to deal with chores you can automate them. Resource auto-transfer and auto-stock levels work great by default.Basic diplomacy exist, so does intelligence/counter-intelligence.Ship design feature exist, not as detailed as block-based games (Empyrion) but a good developer-made-component-based approach so you pick devices/components from the menu of hundreds of items, unlocked via tier 1-10 tech tree.Game universe / difficulty setup is extensively customizable to allow a customizable & re-enjoyable experience.On the point of automation: you can also have mixed bag, for example on the military side, give the AI 5 fleets to defend your empire, then with your 2-3 other fleets you run your own war campaign.While I love this game, I admit it definitely is not for everyone because even understanding and correctly setting up automation exactly the way you want can take some time. Trial and error (e.g. fuel tanker automation) needed, you also need to figure out what you like/dislike again takes time. All this is not hard but it does take time. If you demand instant smooth sailing you probably would rate this game low.If you are up for learning, enjoying the process, then customizing your game experience via various Automation Toggles then this game is for you.I think it is worth the full price but do check the PDF game manual for free before you buy, also check out a few YouTube videos.Overall, I think it is a great, detailed, customizable, actively developed high and low level space grand strategy - tactical empire management game, and I recommended it.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor to my favourite 4x game...But it needs some serious refinements. Thankfully it seems like Codefore is on the right track, but if you're not going to tolerate the instability, lack of fluidity in some aspects and general roughness then feel free to wait and get back to it in a year or two. Personally, I enjoy it nonetheless, because there's nothing quite like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is the sequel to my favorite space 4X game. It improves in many important areas, specifically the UI and the combat mechanics, though in the first release there are some areas where it falls short of its predecessor. With this I refer to pirates, mostly. Distant Worlds Univers has very active pirates who can corrupt and take over your colonies. The pirates in DW2 are more on the level of the original DW1 release. I don't know what the future holds for them, but I find them less interesting in this game.However, it should be noted that DW2 is a completely new game, whereas Distant Worlds Universe is the culmination of years of work. There is no doubt in my mind that DW2 will eventually stand head and shoulders above DWU.Having been a beta tester, I've put hundreds of hours into this game. This did not feel like work or an obligation to CodeForce in any way. I had a lot of fun.Yes, I recommend this game to everyone who is interested in space games or 4X games.

_childDocuments_.review: 6 hours in and this is just such a joy to play. There are some quality of life issues, just like with Distant Worlds: Universe, but it's such a improvement on the first one. In fact, it is almost exactly what Universe was but with 3D graphics, a cleaned up UI, and some other neat story related additions. I absolutely love it, and while some people don't seem to like it, I think the UI is pretty easy to navigate. I didn't find the last games UI that bad either though.Honestly, Distant Worlds is one of my favorite games of all time, and now we have a more modernized version of it. If you're a 4x fan this is a must have.Also, how is this game not bigger? It deserves a massive community IMO.My only complaints so far are that...-Fleets don't seem to stick together or even get built like they should. Not sure if I'm missing something here.-The UI needs to do a better job identifying threats. Whether it's enemy ships, monsters, or even a plague I seem to have no way to identify where this stuff is happening other than just going back through my messages.Update:After playing this for a while on and off, I really feel like I need to add to the review. The new quality of life and AI changes can't be overlooked. The game looks average... Pretty to me but it's not stellaris quality or anything but does that really matter? The game looks great in action and it does so much more than any other 4x.The UI does a better job with shortages around materials and other empires territory but I still wish I could identify monsters easier or pirates/etc within certain systems. It's often up to me to find them in the menus and figure out who is doing what. This is clearly a work in progress with the UI.That said, the new races, the new events, the optimization, and the living economy can't be overlooked! The game just WORKS so much better now and my fuel tankers are carrying so much of the work.This is hands down my favorite 4x game. Old World was up there but as a sucker for space and the "simulation" of the world this can't be beat. Civ, dwarf fortress, and star trek had a baby and I'm in love with this damn game dude. Distant Worlds Universe was perfect at what it did. This is fantastic and 3d, offering new options, details, and races, and special events. It still has places to improve and I welcome the DLC but after a year I can't wait to play more Distant Worlds 2. An indie team has made not only the best 4x game but the best strategy space sim on the market imo.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game that will fulfill it's great potential after the bugs are fixed and more features are added in future patches which might not sound reassuring to most people but it was the same scenario with the original Distant Worlds. When it first released it was a decent game with great potential and after it had been improved with patches and expansions it became an amazing game one of my favorites and one of the best space games ever made so I have faith the same will happen with this one. In fact I liked the original so much after the expansions I used the ingame editor to handcraft a 1400 star 15x15 sector galaxy and when I say handcraft I do mean it as I looked at every single star, planet and moon and altered them all to my preference anything I didn't like I changed or removed even made the Sol system as accurate to reality as possible including every planet and the major moons of the gas giants and the asteroid belt and Kuiper belt. If someone likes a game enough to spend the time necessary to handcraft such a map it has to be pretty good.So my recommendation is buy the game now and you will see how it goes from just good to amazing.Most the complaints on my rather short list of issues are all things I know for certain will be dealt with.The old fun of playing as a pirate faction? It will get added in sooner or later.Some of the races aren't playable yet but they already stated they will get all of them finished and maybe even add new ones.Ingame editor not having some of the abilities that it had in DW? That will be fixed as I think the original editor when the first DW was released had even fewer abilities then the one in DW2 currently has and after all the patches and expansions the DW editor turned into the most amazing ingame editor I have ever seen.The only single problem I have is the lower customizability of stations as I miss making the super mining and research stations of DW1. So devs if you see this do me a solid and add 1 or 2 more station hulls that can be used in multiple roles and have more hard points for customization as I loved making mining stations with 4 times the number of mining engines+docks and with enough armor and guns even fleets would generally leave them alone or die trying to kill them which might sound too expensive to be useful but was a tactic I found useful for my primary fuel production systems or resources that I had only 1 or 2 sources of in my empire.

_childDocuments_.review: A decade ago, I wrote a review for a game called 'Distant Worlds'.I opened that review with the bold claim that it was "The best 4x money could buy".If you asked me today what's the best space 4x money can buy, I'd be tempted to say Stellaris, along with all it's DLC and a few dozen mods to make it really interesting.However, the other title that would come to mind would be this one, Distant Worlds 2.Yes, Stellaris is brilliant, if you're willing to spend your hard earned cash on a plethora of DLC and a chunk of time playing 'compatibility roulette' with more mods than you can shake a stick at.But Distant Worlds two is brilliant too, in a different, less obvious kind of way.All the standard 4x bits and pieces are here.You'll design and build ships and stations, you'll colonise and develop planets, you'll research tech to build fancier ships and better colonies.You'll meet the neighbours and try to kill them. It's all good space strategy fun. But where this game sets itself apart is with the sheer volume of resources to discover and exploit.Every ship you design is going need different 'stuff' to construct it. You might have researched a fancy doodad which you've incorporated into your new ship design, but do you have a supply of the thingamajigs and whatchamacallits to manufacture it?Even if you are mining the resources you need, they're no use to you stuck in some far off storage facility on the other side of the galaxy.If they're not at the construction site where the ship is being built then they'll need to be hauled there.That's where the civilian sector comes into play, and that's what makes Distant Worlds 2 really special.At first your civilian sector is going to be buying a lot of resources to build the components you'll need for your ships and stations, but before long, you'll have a fleet of civilian ships (all AI controlled) flying around mining asteroids for minerals and mining Gas Giants for the much needed fuel you're going to need to expand further.Unlike most other 4x games, Distant Worlds has a fully featured Civilian economy which works independently to you. You can influence it with your actions but you can't control it directly.You can design civilian ships, freighters, passenger shuttles etc. and then the civilian economy will buy them from you and use them move goods around to complete the building contracts or colony requirements within your empire. This happens automatically, and you can actually see every single civilian ship flying around, check it's cargo, see what it's carrying and where it's carrying it to.Place a large military ship build order at a space port and watch all the little civilian ships scuttle around sourcing the resources for the project and ferrying them to the construction site.Of course the civilian ships can be easy prey for pirates, so you might want to protect them with a military escort.The scope and depth of this game is amazing. It always feels like you're playing in a "real" universe. Of course this depth comes with a learning curve which can be punishing at first.This is a game you're going to want to watch a lets play or two on before you take the plunge.You can also automate almost everything, so if you ever feel overwhelmed you could hand the reigns to the AI, sit back with a coffee and watch how your growing empire gets on without you.I started this by referring to my original DW1 review from 2014, A review which I ended with the line "Now if the developer could just make a prettier sequel..."10 years later and that's exactly what they've done.I gave up writing game reviews a long time ago, but I've come out of retirement to key one last review, that's how special I think this game is.Distant Worlds 2 is amazing as long as you're willing to take the time to get to know it.What's even better is that as I write this, a new DLC is about to be released!I've waited a decade to write this review, now all I need to do is wait until payday to buy the DLC. Now I'm here, I know which wait will seem longer...Seriously folks, if you're looking for some space opera feels and like 4x games then you can't go wrong with Distant Worlds 2.Thanks for reading and If you do take the plunge, I hope you love it as much as I do!

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is essentially a 3D conversion of Distant Worlds Universe. Along with the jump to 3D graphics comes an updated (and readable) UI. If you liked DW:U, then you will like Distant Worlds 2.  DW2 does not have all the races from DW:U yet or the ability to play as a pirate faction, but the core/main game play is there. _childDocuments_.review: It's probably a stale meme at this point but I'll just put this out there as a warning anyways: Not having a order queue function is silly in a 4x game. *Removing* this function when "modernising" into a new engine(?) and a brand spanking new title with your usual package of mod--I mean DLC's is borderline something (not exactly sure of what). I'd stake my savings on it has everything to do with "streamlining" automation, and being able to crown oneself King of "it". Sell titles because of "it".I'm left wondering whether or not CodeForce were ever really aware that the mightiest feature of the order queue is not to queue anything at all, really - except time. Skilled players have internalised distance on the map in relation to tech (jump trigger range, acceleration etc) to such an extent that they can insert precise ad hoc timers for individual fleets up to several minutes -- just by holding shift and painting a few lines ... And I don't even think they are particularly aware themselves. It just feels fundamentally wrong when that tool is gone.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid game from an indie developer that is very much worth your time if you like the 4x genre. It offers middling complexity in strategic, economic and diplomatic layers which combine satisfactorily to create something greater than the sum of its parts. It has elements of stellaris and galactic civilisations, with an economic layer similar to (but better than) the supreme ruler series.Given the mixed reviews, should you buy it? Personally, my answer is yes.A lot of us were disappointed when this first launched as we had hoped for something that turned the unrealised potential of Distant Worlds: Universe into reality. It was also buggy and unpolished and in that respect, the game failed at launch. I bought it at launch and found I couldn't play it, both literally (it kept crashing out) and I found it a disappointment compared to how much I loved DW:U.Now the game has had time to mature, it is coming much closer to realising those initial hopes. Playing is now an enjoyable experience (I am clocking up the hours!) and the forthcoming Shakturi expansion looks interesting and will add a lot of flavour to the game.There is still much to do before a good game becomes a great game. My personal wishlist would be:- Comprehensive modding support - unleash the creativity of the community and the game could be amazing. I lack the skills to do anything other than rudimentary modding myself, so proper tools would be a godsend.- More control and granularity for galaxy and empire setup in the game settings, along with an expanded in-game editor (the current one lacks the functionality of DW:U), to enable us to tell the stories we want to tell.- Continue the expansion of various mechanics to make races and gameplay more interesting. As mentioned above the Shakturi expansion looks like a solid step in the right direction.

The selection of ships with which fleets are comprised is automated.  Finally, combat is highly simplified and is not viewable. If your are detail oriented commander, this game would not be a good fit. If, on the other hand you are a highly strategic commander and the details are not as important, then this game would be a good fit.

_childDocuments_.review: It is basically "Distant Worlds Universe REMASTERED"And that's not a bad thing in an age where seemingly every sequel to beloved games try to change so much of the core formula that they are no longer succeeding in what made fans love the first game. (Command and Conquer, Dawn of War 3, etc etc).Yes, one might have wished for more substancial mechanics or gameplay changes in DW2.But again, you have to realize, DW2 is DW1 with ALL expansions and mechanics included.You're not gonna pay a second time to get spy mechanic DLC.Future updates will bring new stuff, and new (and old) races.That's what makes this better than the old game, in the long run.The old engine simply couldnt handle even opening a UI screen, this engine can be expanded upon.Yes, there are weird issues, such as me actually getting worse "zoom-in" preformance after the most recent "preformance patch", and many changes are now added to a .ini file you have to manually edit regarding memory limit values and such, that most users will have no clue about.This should be unified in the ingame menu (even if it asks for reboot), and be complemented by detailed tooltips giving examples (such as, "if you have a 6gb vram gpu, we suggest this value".But other than that, it absolutely without question runs far better than the previous game.Which isnt really a huge feat, because DW1 runs terribly. 5 second pauses on opening a colony list etc.That doesnt happen in DW2, thankfully. And its in 3d.The planets look either absolutely jawdropping (ocean, continental or otherwise oxygen-rich planets with their dynamic moving clouds along with cloud shadows, and terrain detail that is practically infinite zoom), or absolutely dreadful due to a seemingly complete RGB random value assigned to all gas giants.You'll see gorgeous cream colored gas giants with brown rings, and when zoomed in at 4x speed, you see each individual band of gas in the planet morph and move as the shader animates.But you'll also, more frequently, due to afformentioned seemingly totally random RGB color assignment, see literally neon green or pure pink gas giants, stand out like a sore thumb to the rest of the games aesthetic.I love color in games, i usually apply my own Reshade to most games to enhance saturation, to put perspective on my opinions here.. And i love the idea of pink or green gas giants. More color variation is GOOD, it doesnt have to be entirely based on hardcore scientific plausibility.But what i'm talking about here are, literally, bright pink as if you loaded up MS paint and selected the brightest default pink color from the color picker, same with neon green.I'm talking 0,255,0 RGB values for some of the green gas giants.Not even 20,189,5 or something to give SOME minor natural shade.I'm talking pure undadulterated 0,255,0 as bright green as a computer monitor can possibly render.That has to change, it destroys the otherwise gorgeous plane shaders.It feels like the game engine itself COULD (and shows this, by the continental planets) render absolutely almost Star Citizen level quality of visuals, but it is the artists choice of values and color hues that prevent certain planet types from looking as good as they could.I hate hammering on artists, but its also a compliment to the tech programmers instead.Imagine seeing a gorgeous ocean planet with beautiful realistic atmosphere colors and animated clouds moving across the surface, crisp and bright in the sunlight.Then half a screen away a huge neon green gas giant looms like something straight out of MS Paint.Not even No Mans Sky have planets that vibrant, that ought to give some perspective.So what about gameplay?I dont know what to say really.It's Distant Worlds 1, but in a modern layout and engine.Just the revised UI alone is enough to be worth buying.But this isnt just a review of what it is today, its a review of what i know it will become in some months time.Just as Distant Worlds became Distant Worlds Universe.Distant Worlds 2 will become something greater than it is today.What it is today, is a great framework for continuing the unique game mechanics. It is up to the developers to make of it what it has the potential to be. In some respects, perhaps this should be sold as "early access".

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is a really nice space 4x game and some great ideas that help make it feel a lot more unique than other games in it's class, however the game does have some rough edges I will explain below.The space battles in DW2 are for me some of the best in modern times for its scale with a good amount of weapon types and modules that you can fit your ships with manually or allow the AI to fit and I often enjoy seeing them play out. One of the problems though is that especially in the mid-late game they can stutter and by the time you have end game ships you probably won't have smooth battles anymore. Hiding the UI can help and it should go without saying but also by keeping the game on a standard speed (slower didn't change anything). When that's not an issue the customisation is great for anyone who really wants to tailor ships to do what they want and the battles feel quite satisfying.One of the greatest strengths of this game is the ability to automate areas you don't want to manage and the policy settings to control that with finer detail. While you can manually do everything if you really want to, it's probably better to at least automate some things or you might find yourself overwhelmed or taking a long time to get anywhere. The core game mechanics are good and I love the various diplomacy options as well as the fairly extensive espionage options without having to buy it as a DLC like a few other strategy games these days. One downside to the diplomacy and the game as a whole is that not all races are present so diplomacy I find is wildly mixed. Some games I play races will be quite friendly with me and others will be very hostile and usually I find the latter to be the most common which means I don't get to use diplomacy as much as I would like and get somewhat forced into bashing down my neighbours. I think this might be because not all races are in the game yet and most that are already in are either Evil or Neutral Evil aligned which makes being a more peaceful/passive race quite difficult (Ikkuro and Teekan for example).Things I think the game would be benefit from are:*More options for policy control, in particular being able to set a focus on what parts the AI uses in ship designs (E.G. Use stealth components) and a similar focus for research like in DW1*Smoother FPS late game but also for mid game as often the research screen lags unless you zoom slightly into a system*Change diplomacy positive and negative values to encourage "good" races being more friendly if you are more peaceful and aggressive races being impressed with other aggressive races as long as you haven't attacked them. *Bolder differences between weapons and tech as often I don't feel like there is much difference in what I take because most things fall into the category of good or completely useless. For example, blasters pretty good and area weapons kinda awkward due to friendly fire. Another example is unique faction techs, like the new Ikkuro boarding pods are hardly much better than the standard ones.*This is probably just me but more ways to tackle corruption as the planetary admin never feels like enough and seeing the amount of money lost from corruption is painful

_childDocuments_.review: This did have a rocky launch and took quite a while after release to get fixed up and working. Those of us who played the original Distant Worlds from early in development knew how developmenton this progresses. It's basically just one guy with a real passion and it's now finally at a point where it deserves everbody's attention.I've played quite a few space 4X games and this is the king of them all. For sure, Stellaris is more popular and is equally complex but it never has had what this 'simulation' has in spades - a living universe and a private sector economy.There are a good number of unique factions in the base game, each with their own quest lines and more importantly, ship hull configurations. These hulls matter a lot and make each class play differently from another factions.Combat is very detailed in this sim too. you have a range of weapon types including blasters beams, missiles, kinetic weapons, gravitic and area weapons as well as torpedoes of different types. races often have their own unique weapons or defences which keep it interesting.the ship designer is better than DW1's but still  requires some time for the player to work with. Adding and upgradinbg components is not hard but on the right side of the screen, you can see how much energy generation you need to allow everything to function in combat. Don't pay attention to that and you might find your ships not attacking duriong combate because they just don't have the ebnergy to do much besides move.There are a very wide range of ship components and they all have their own tech lines - engines, reactors, hyperdrives, shields, weapons, crew quarters, docking and refueling points, fuel tanks, cargo storage, etc. It's all there. But what happens if you don't want to manage all of that?The automation is also incredible in this massive simulation - I've read some folks complain that the game canb play itself and that's true that you can do that but that's your CHOICE. You can turn off all the automation and manage everything, and I do mean everything, by yourself as well. It's easy enough to manage in the early game but by mid-game, you're going to want to automate more and more of the less interesting features to concentrate on what is important to you. I tend to go with a fair mix of both, prefering to design my own ships, bases and fleets as well as manage my spys but I tend to automate fleet operations as the maps can be vast and I want the AI to manage much of the effort.The tech tree is massive and progressing through it is dependent on how high your bonuses in each area are. If you don't have 20% or better (a number pulled from my head) in a particular area, you may not be able to research beyond level 3 or 4 on that branch of the tech tree.The DLC has added some new factions which are another matter but the eight than come with the game all have their own unique victory conditions and some unique form of government wehich matters. Declaring war when you don't have support can mean parts of your empire will break away and rebel so you can't just steamroll the entire galaxy unless you have a faction that loves war. You need to play towards your race's strengths so you can't really play a peaceful, trading game as the Boskarans as everybody hates you and you them so find a race that matches your playstyle and have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The most realistic space faring 4X game out there. I love how the private economy basically manages itself and you have the option of automating the entire game, essentially making it an auto4X game if you want. But you can turn all that off and micromanage every aspect of the game as you see fit (outside of the private economy). You can, however, greatly influence the private economy through how you setup your form of government at the start of the game and through various tech paths (which there are tons of) as you play. The game is also extremely well optimized, I had an empire with over 250 planets, a population of 2.5 trillion, and over 2000 warships which made up over 200 fleets and was still getting 70+ FPS in massive fleet battle scenes. You can customize your ship load outs how ever you want, and tweak your fleet and individual ship behavior to your liking, tons of possibilities and replay-ability. Each race also have story lines that play out if you choose to turn them on. It's not as deep and rich as something in Stellaris but it's good enough. The scope is far more massive than any other space 4X out there, highly recommended if you want to sink hundreds of hours and fulfill your empire ruling fantasies.
