_childDocuments_.review: Incredible indirect gameplay, that's my main view on Distant Worlds 2 after a few hours playing. Well, that might not be a bad ingridient for a lot of players, but for me it is like I don't have full authority over the empire that I'm supposed to lead. The game, the mechanics are well done and work as intended. With the new 1.0.5. BETA patch the game even runs on Linux with Proton support without any major issue. I got some typing issues playing with mod-driven localisation, where my keys on the computer are local, while in-game it's plain EN style. So far stable and smooth. You start your career on a planet that just manages to start research on warp-drive engines, while your STL-ships start exploring and exploiting your systems other planets. You better start your game with full automatisation for every task activated, otherwise it is way too overwhelming for a beginner. I'm an old fox when it comes to 4X games, but my first tasks where to alter given ship designs myself with every new tech my scientists researched. All other aspects like taxing, ressource management, build queues and others need you to understand the mechanics and circumstances to avoid wrecking your empire deeply. With new warp-drives in place. your scouts immediately start exploring every other system in reach and your civil ships try to exploit ressources. Your advisors give you the impulses to build the needed infrastructure, like stations, to back your expansion plans. Frankly spoken, that is all not a new approach and it is working as intended, but there is no fresh new idea coming with this game. DW-2 is like a growing-up of DW-1, while the devs seemed to cut off parts to go more mainstream. That's ok, but then you don't build an interesting fresh new game but only a iteration of what is already on the market. It is a risk-free development, I guess. Probably the glasses I'm wearing while studying DW-2 are too much influenced by other grand strategy 4X games, but I'm missing some inspirations, some fresh new ideas, something that makes this game unique over the others, so I would have reasons to prefer to play it. So far I didn't reach that point or didn't get how to step into the position of the real space emporer that controls every single aspect and decission for his very own empire. Most of the time I'm just searching for informations, that are not provided on a single screen, but hidden behind several masks and sheets. Every single object you can click on could hold a button how to inflict it...or not. For me it is like the game UI didn't follow a strict design pattern and different devs simply put informations or controls where they thought they might be usefull. In fact they spread out the controls widely over a load of different sheets, so you don't have a central where you could do your changes. So there is micromanagement, but more the negative aspect, where you have to search for the buttons and informations to control your expanding empire.Recommended? Well, that depends hardly on how you like to play 4X games. If you like automatication and only have to care on aspects you really like to control, then Distant Worlds 2 would be exactly what you are searching for. If you like to have micromanagement lead toward an optimized outcome, you might better search for games like Stellaris, Endless Space, Master of Orion and others. As the game mechanics are quite good and working without issues, I still rate the game positive and hope to come to the point where I start to like it...UPDATE 2023:After waiting for several months after that patch that destroyed Linux compatibility, I switch my recommendation to not recommanded for Linux and in specific for AMD players.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I came back to this game and played the heck out of it for a few days, and I think I'm changing my mind about it. The devs have clearly done a lot of work on the game, including two major patches to correct gameplay issues. It's enough to change my mind from "steer clear unless it's on a big sale" to "okay, yes, but..."Like it doesn't seem to crash anymore. Admittedly, I have a more powerful CPU and GPU now, but I've run this game for days now, and played well into it, in a somewhat large galaxy, and it's yet to just crap out on me the way it used to do all of the time. Given how frequent crashes USED to be (and the contents of some of the changelogs), at least part of this has to be due to the dev doing some serious bug-squishing.The AI is also more functional. You can delegate control of some of your fleets to it without it promptly throwing your ships into a cosmic wood chipper. And you can actually start a pre-warp game without a hyper-advanced bunch of pirates spawning in your system to use your fledgling returned to the stars civilization as a loot pinata.My "but" is that this is a game that is definitely a beast that can absolutely devour computational power. If you have a lower powered/older CPU, you might be stuck with smaller games. There isn't really a way around this, because there's a lot of simulation going on, and the bigger the galaxy the more ships, admirals, diplomats, spies and teacup chihuahuas it's tracking, the more economies it's modelling, but if you have the power to run it, it does give you that high level ruler feel.My original review:It bills itself as a space grand strategy game but in practice it's about herding a bunch of terminally stupid space numpties about and watch them explode, but without the cute charm of Kerbal Space Program. You can either endure them in auto-stupid mode or micro-manage them, which will prompt them to find the most stupid way to execute any given order. Many systems within the game seem to be extremely broken. The mechanics associated with pirates seem particularly suspect, and they're prone to these weird feedback loops where they undergo extremely rapid technological acceleration and are suddenly throwing fleets of hyper-advanced vessels at you, which seems to advance their technology even more rapidly. The game is a pig, even on a reasonably powerful machine. It does caution that larger maps require more and faster cores, but any game bogs down the later it gets. And of course crashes abound, which stack up to intolerable levels once you're out of the early game. But that doesn't mean it won't crash on you right at the start because it's literally done that right out of the gate just now. Up until that point, I thought it must be some kind of horrific memory leak, but it really seems much more poorly made than something that mundane.There do seem to be regular updates, but it really reads like the game is actually in secret early access. If you do buy it, wait for a hefty sale. Like a 70+% one, because it definitely isn't in a state where it's worth $57 Canadian.

_childDocuments_.review: Did not play such much at release, Distant Worlds 2 was buggy and crashed at times. I gave it another chance after some updates. I have to say. It´s great. They have from what I have seen, made the game stable. I am having a blast, just like I did with the first game. Distant Worlds 2 occupies a unique niche in 4x space games, real time empire management on a grand scale. Distant Worlds 2 is somewhat of a sandbox, you can choose to manage many different aspects of your space empire, like spying, diplomacy, colony and fleet management, research and more. Or you can choose to let the AI run parts of your empire and you focus on the bigger picture, or just sit back and watch the journey of one of the many ships in the galaxy. The game features a fully fledged private economy. In addition to the ships you build and can directly control, there is an entirely separate part of your empire which is private, that you operates independently of the player (and all other computer/human players as well). Additional gameplay mechanics include: Tourism and migration inside and between empires, exploration of an unknown galaxy with long lost fleets and ancient dangers that might want to murder you, different races and government types,  individual characters that develop personality and skill over time like captains, spies and governors. The game also features independent colonies and pirates that you can choose to interact with in various ways.Distant Worlds 2 is a game that exists in its own genre. Very well detailed galaxy with many moving parts, runs well and keeps on being interesting in many unexpected ways. A definite experience that will only improve with time and future expansions.

It is best to set zoom in and out on Q & E, which saves you tendonitis in the long run.  ..Most of the time you have the feeling that you are only a passenger of the AI, which expands every small mine and constantly begs for permission. While annoying news pops up and AI rich beg for money. Pirates are constantly annoying (don't understand why these should be a great feature, they should only appear in the midgame, that makes sense). That brings me to the second point, mining stations are unarmed, why? They are constantly attacked by pirates while the fleets are light years away. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This game is really fun, but its not for everyone!There are few games I've played that truly commit to their vision as much as this game does. While this adds clumsiness and complexity to be sure, its really cool to inhabit the developer's creative endeavor. I think the developer has a good sense of how to add good complexity and emergent game-play for the amount bad complexity; Distant Worlds has a good crunch to clunk ratio.This game is clearly loved by its creator. To be honest this is quite significant. Almost all of my favorite creative works are products of love (though certainly not exclusively). My principle example would be contrasting the Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit Trilogy. Even The Room, which is about as close to being an *objectively* awful movie as is possible is enjoyed by many due to the strange endearing quality brought about by earnest misguided passion of its creator. I fully expect this game to have a timeless quality that continues to drive a cult following in various games of yesterday. (e.g. Quake, Homeworld, Age of Empires, Mario)The game has its failings: it does still crash once every few sessions (EDIT: NOT ANYMORE!), there are minor UI bugs, the music needs work and the game can be quite oblique whist making you feel like you are supposed to understand everything. Other comments enumerate other problems the game has, and I think a lot of them have good points.The emergent game-play is a strong suit here. Its story time!During one game an otherwise weaker enemy empire had found a very powerful ship that made it exceedingly difficult to win battles. One issue was I simply could not fight it: it had much longer range than my ships and was significantly faster to boot. This meant every battle I lost a significant portion of my forces without having a chance to deal with the most important threat. I had a problem: if I stripped my ships down to put make them faster, there would be no way I could win the battle as they would be too weak. On the other hand, I couldn't win as is anyways. So I hatched a plan: I refitted my ships, stripping thier engines and making them even slower to make room for larger and more powerful weapons. Simultaneously, I made a swarm of very small ships with tractor beams. My idea was to drag the unstoppable flagship into my pondering brawlers next time the opponent attacked one of my worlds. AND IT WORKED FLAWLESSLY. The enemy was pounced upon, dragged down and ripped apart as if by a pack of rabid hyenas. After the flagship was destroyed, the enemy cleaned up my tractor ships, rendering my super slow, low range brutes useless. Much of my fleet was lost, and the world that I was defending fell. But, since I had a stronger economy, I rebuilt and eventually won the war now that I was free of his strongest vessel!Its hard to impress just how satisfying this event was. Often times we hear stories of video games that sound amazing, only to learn that they aren't *that* cool. Don't get me wrong, they are still fun and often even fulfilling, but how many times has being named Archmage meant 2 changed lines of dialog, or your fantastic sounding weapon gifted from a god simply felt like +numbers? What impressed me here is it didn't feel like numbers. It didn't feel like an optimal general solution to all problems (remember, I lost the battle because I could not fight back). It felt like I had to make a hard choice based on non-linear, asymmetric game mechanics with no obvious best choice. Honestly, it made me feel clever, and that's a warm fuzzy feeling that we can all enjoy from time to time :)This game reminds me of Twilight Imperium in some ways, I think it scratches a similar itch, and darn it I would be so, so happy if it had multiplayer. I recommend this game wholeheartedly to the right kind of person, and you probably know who you are!p.s. I should also note the game receives patches regularly that significantly improve the quality of the game

It fixes a lot of the problems I had with the original DW:U, namely too many asteroids, separation of gas and material mining, and an extremely poor UI. I expect this to be the premier space strategy game after a month or two of fixing bugs and optimizing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a challenging game.  It simulates the time it takes to get from one part of a galaxy to another so.  So foresight is necessary.  When things go right it's great when plans don't work out it can be frustrating.  That is the challenge.  This game demands concentration particularly at the harder levels.  So you have to be up for that if you want to do well.  I have enjoyed the complexity.  So I look forward to additional future sophistication particularly in diplomacy.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I had quite a few problems early on with this game with the crashing bug happening over and over again.  Then, I got the latest update and followed the instructions and deleted some old files and it seems to work fairly well.  There have been a few crashes, but not often and with autosave, not really game breaking.  This game is AMBITIOUS to say the least.  hundreds of detailed ships doing various tasks ...Ship Tasks- Mining- Exploring- Fighting- Construction- Private ships doing various things including passengers travelling around doing sightseeing at resortsAll in all a very cool assortment and I'm sure that is scratching the surface with much more actually going on.The amount of information available is astounding and the layout makes it easy to use.  On the left you can look at construction yards, research, colonies and other information.  Each has a detailed set of sub tabs.  So, I can be looking at information while looking at the main map at the same time.  With my widescreen monitor, this makes it really nice to have the main map and whatever info I want to be looking at going at the same time.  My only complaint is that the squares with info about colonies are too big on the map for some reason.  They can cover things up and can make it difficult to see important events happening on the main map.Probably the best thing about the game is that it does handle fairly well all of the mundane activities.  This is nice as it allows me to focus on what is important to me.  I tend to pay attention mostly to research, ship design, and combat.  I really have enjoyed this game immensely.  The final hook was when the game asked me to look in on a destroyer fighting a space creature.  I clicked to see the action and was rewarded with gaseous clouds with lightning flashing while my ship killed the space creature.  As the creature died, it made a great noise as it breathed it's last.  Then the model slowly died.  (The model was amazing and it looked very real and immersive.)  I LOVED IT!  I really felt like I was watching a real battle.  Thank you for creating such an amazing game.  I know that there is more work to do, but am grateful even to have played the few hours that I have.  Probably the best space 4x game ever made.

_childDocuments_.review: Just getting my feet wet in this amazing game. It's a game that really improved upon DWU and still maintained the sandbox, do it your way, mechanics of the series. Through automation you can turn the game into whatever you want to play. Automate what you don't want right now and focus on what you like. Right now I'm focusing on colony administration and letting the game handle ships, research, and diplomacy. Tomorrow I may just try building my own escorts and make a fleet of raiders, who knows. It's all up to you the player, I can see many many hours going into this basic game even before modders get their arms around it.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played previous Distant Worlds game, so I'm coming at this from having played Stellaris and older space 4X games like Imperium Galactica.I find the interface thoroughly frustrating. Something as simple as moving ships around is difficult. For example, ships under construction show up in lists like normal ships--except you can't move them. There's a tiny list of ships at the bottom of the screen, but you end up with so many tiny icons it's useless. If you want an explorer to scan a particular location it disables automation...but you also don't see an arrow telling you where it's going.Interacting with things--like colonies and shipyards--is mostly done through lists in menus since doing it through the map provides so little feedback. Clicking "send a ship to build this" button in various lists is not interesting for me.The game feels like there's a lot underneath, but I haven't gotten to the point where that's worth fighting such a useless interface.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, It is hard to learn, but it is easy to master.You actually get to  planets. As in, theres something you dont like about a planet for no particular reason and it irks your ire to see it each time you pass it by? Then literally, exterminate it from existence and feast on its corpse for resources.Yes, you read that right, you not only get to completely and utterly destroy a planet thus wiping an entire race off the face of the universe, you get to  resources from it afterwards. A:10/10V:10/10There is no real "campaign" but when you play a game to find out if you can send a planet to its doom in a spectacular show of force and dominate the entire galaxy with your might, a campaign would only restrict you. A little tip for newcomers, spend most of your time in the Automation section of the menu, thats where you adjust the way you want to play the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fairly cleaned up now, so good on the devs. As for it's ability to automate literally everything, that's true. It was true of Distant Worlds as well. This is a strength and a great feature. If you want, you could spend the entire game observing the activity of a single civilian trader as it plies space over the years. Or you can turn all automation off and go raving mad micromanaging every aspect of the game. For most of us, the level of automation is somewhere in between. What's the benefit? It allows you to PLAY the game rather than being buried at a level of game management where the game becomes an out and out chore. You want to play as a high level leader? Set it so you actions are only needed at that level. You want to grunt it out and tinker with everything under the hood? Turn it all off and enjoy all the complexity DW2 has to offer. The best thing is you get to choose. How many games give you that option?
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best 4X games I've played recently. Despite the visible budget, you can see what the creators wanted to achieve and they achieved it very well. Probably the only one that is currently worthy of competition with Stelaris, which makes up for the shortcomings with its unique solutions. Of course, artificial intelligence often limps, which makes managing fleets difficult. For example, I miss the possibility of flooding ships with fuel if we have a tanker in our fleet. Sometimes it happens that some of the ships in the fleet are left behind because they have not refueled, some are refueled or full, and the tankers still have plenty of fuel to refuel all the ships in the fleet. This can kill a quick military operation. The game requires patience. A very nice way to break away from the "you found a planet, colonize it first." You have to get used to the whole thing because it is unusual. Unfortunately, the entire game is set to "automatic" at the beginning and it is worth looking for tutorials that will explain which options are better set to manual. At least after half an hour you can learn how to play the game... and the rest is just great fun for fans of grant strategy.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun, but feels unfinished. The tactical combat is something that was always missing from Stellaris. I get that they're creating a similar game, but they copied some of the stuff that makes Stellaris tedious and boring at times. This game needs cutscenes, not just boxes with paragraphs of text to read. Every ruin explored doesn't need a scene, but all of the reading seems like work and definitely takes some fun out of the game. I hope they continue to fix the bugs (there are a lot but none game-breaking for me yet) and expand on what could be a really good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent. The technical achievement of moving to a 3D engine cannot be understated - it adds a whole new level of immersion to proceedings. With time, the performance will be improved (though it is serviceable on my pretty moderate PC) and more importantly the rest of the factions that are not playable yet. This is an excellent starting point to the second edition of the best 4x Space Strategy series. Returning players will feel pretty much at home straight away. New players can go with automation on high and gradually turn it off as they grow more comfortable. Good luck to Codeforce in the continuing development of this game - I look forward to putting many, many hours into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, I really do. I enjoy 4x games, especially science fiction ones, and a real time one, like this one, should be a refreshing treat. But, it isn't. It just feels flat. Then there are all the little quality of life things it doesn't have. From the constant spam of messages for things you may not want to do, to the deep menus you have to dig through to find a specific setting. For example, if you want your fleets to defend your assets, or attack targets, you have to set every single fleet manually. There might be an empire wide setting, but I've not found it yet. There are DLCs, but what do they add to the base game? Each DLC adds two new factions to the game. That is it. This is like a college level project competing in the professional market. It has some good things it is a solid meh. There are a lot of customization options in the minus, but digging through menu layers to adjust one setting every time I play the game is a waste of my time. And while you can automate a lot of stuff in the game, you still have to micro manage a lot of things. Distant Worlds 2 is a buy on sale game at best, and I mean at least a 50% off sale, as it is not a 50USD valued game, 30 maybe. I'm sure there are people who like this game, but I'm not one of them.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: As you can see from my playtime, my review is from a very bare bones experience. However, my review I feel is valid regardless.First: The Polish. In my humble opinion, one of the first things many people do when they launch a new game is go straight to the volume mixer to turn it down. This game currently has a bug where if you try to do that, it reverts to max volume instantly. You cannot move the slider. A bug like this, is in my opinion, unacceptable. The game has been out long enough for a day one patch to fix this. I do not understand how you can still have a bug like this in the game. The first impression tons of people will have is "This game is so poorly crafted I cannot even turn down the volume THROUGH MY OPERATING SYSTEM."Then there's the ABSOLUTELY INANE noise that plays whenever you click something. A high pitched ticking noise. It is NOT affected by the IN GAME volume settings. You can have Music and Effect sounds set to ZERO and it will still happen on every click at max volume. This coupled with the inability to use the volume mixer to turn the game down only doubles down on the bad first impression from the volume mixer.Your planets don't look lived on. There is no indication "I live here" on my starting planet. It's just a blank looking planet. No cities, nothing. The game immediately zooms you in to your planet at the start of your game to showcase that your planet does not look lived on too. A space age civilization with 2000 Million people would probably have idk at least ONE city visible from space.Second: A little inconsistency. Everything is decently in depth. There's the whole Private economy mechanic, the ship designer is... interesting, and I like the idea of all that stuff, but I can't make my own species? Don't expect to do any sort of reasonable RP here if you player with more than 8 total civs, or even if you use the random civs. Because you WILL have two humans. you WILL have two rat people. Their species WILL be the same. I can understand maybe finding aliens that are very human-like, but to find two identical forms of human on different planets unaware of each other? That's getting into unreasonable odds territory. I'm fine with the government types, but the species thing really doesn't make me feel invested in my Civ because it's more like picking England in another Civ game than anything else. This game doesn't have to be stellaris. But this game is currently presenting like half stellaris, half generic 4x game, with a sprinkle of in depth economics and AI automation.Ultimately: You may enjoy the game, but don't expect to feel very unique. Don't expect the volume mixer to work, and don't expect the options menu to have tabs. Don't expect the volume options to fix the clicking noise, and do expect to feel like everything seems very empty.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I am writing a review. I think it is important to provide perspective for people with a certain playstyle.To give you an idea of what I mean let me start by stating that I love .. neh ... adore DW:U!I have possibly played it over thousand hours (not on Steam) and know all its imperfections and strongpoints.DW:U shines when it comes to the military aspect: Its mechanics and realtime nature combined with the very liberal ship design possibilities present tactical and especially strategic depth like any other space4X game can provide.Unrestricted micromanagement on top of that and the deal was sealed many years ago. I found a game I could imerse into when feeling the urge to build a galactic empire.Ofcourse its let's say ... rudimentary UI dampened the experience but in its final state it was tolerable for me.When DW2 was released it was obvious that this is one of those cases where a game has been declared ready for release when it's actually clearly only an early access product, so I waited. The Devs November announcment/roadmap and then the December patch convinced me to give it a go and support it with a purchase.Here goes:TL:DR To say it up front, DW2 is far from ready and really disapopinting to me; therefore in its current state I do not recommend a purchase. IMO you will still get an unfinished game.I think from what I read, people share my views on certain issues, which are:- The change from 2D to 3D causes many problems, yields little to none benefits. I can see the appeal of it but it is obvious that porting a perfectly functioning 2D game to 3D is going to create some kind of strain. And it still does: Ships bump into planets instead of going around, time is wasted, orders not carried out. It's a micromanagers nightmare.Also very important to underastand is they decided to go for one of these fake 3D engines wherein, yes all entities are now presented with 3D models, but the whole game is still nailed to a 2D board. You can't move fleets above or below the plane to move more freely around or gain tactical advantage. Can't build stations on the poles of planets, say goodbey to all that. This happened to many games and it always makes me suspicious. It's hinting that a port from 2D to 3D is mostly a marketing decision and not done to truly enhance the game.Additional the camera options are too restricted. You have 4 angled views available: from top down to low angle across the plane, can zoom in and out cursor sensitive (not optional!) and rotate sideways around the center of the screen, thats it. I can imagine it must be nice beeing zoomed in to manage your fleet orbiting your homeplanet and then the sun comes up in the background from behind the planet and flares nicely over its oceans, illuminating your ships; that's a hard to come by screenshoot in this game. Besides, haven't seen much dynamic lighting anyway, it's a very basic 3D engine.Its my view that if you go 3D and restrict the camera too much you shoot yourself in the foot. Always make some kind of free camera mode available, give the community the means to create nice content and micro.Oh jea, really worth mentioning in that context is something that completely struck me when I realized it: There are no more orbital mechanichs, planets and moons don't orbit anymore, they stand still (almost kills more imersion than 3D provides). To me yet another suspicion that there are technical strains not yet overcome with the 3D engine. Why else would you just get rid of such a nice feature ... in a SPACE game?)They decided to go for a 3D approach and in every respect made the wrong decision, thats my conclusion on the 3D controversy.- Next up is queueing orders: It's gone. not just for certain units, they have taken the whole concept out of the game. I can't imagine anything that would lead to such a decision. You still can set construction orders at planets to queue mining stations for example but it isn't really a queue order but a signal that will be picked up by the next and nearest construction-ship as soon as it's idle. This doesn't even closely compensate for the removal of this so very important function and also has on some occasions lead to two ships picking up such an order and basicly competing to get there. I dont know how people who like to micro everything will be able to cope ... large empires ...   ... late game...- Jea, the weapon hardpoints and the hulls... not a fan obviously. Not so much the models of the ships, can live with that, its just too restrictive. This point has been made many times already but I can only agree. It was one of DW:U strenghts that made it stand out to me. The reason is simple: I believe there shouldn't be arbitrary restrictions in space ship design, due to the properties of space. In principle you can clump any number of systems, as long as you can afford to build and maintain it and it works as intended, you have a station or a ship. The only restriction should be the bigger the design the more of everything u need: power, thrust, life support, funds and so on. DW:U did it so well. It was a perfect base to build and enhace upon but they changed it completely. The current system is bland and generic. Just more of the same like in so many other games. I was aware of that change before the purchase BTW, it's not a dealbreaker per se. In the end it's all a question of how things are balanced but it appears to be too narrowed for my taste.There is more (especially UI and fleet management) but those are the most important points I'd like to make and I believe these are also among the most discussed in the community.There are positive things to mention, too:Most notably diplomacy and reputation have been improved, though I believe bad reputation decays way to fast still. Stockpile limits can now be managed, more options for galaxy creation, more options for message handling, and some menus have been improved.In general the game has the look and feel of Distant Worlds, many things stay exactly the same and that is a good thingSo, I think not all is lost, you will find people who like DW2 and play it actively. Its fair to say it's playable but people draw different lines I guess. This game is right on the edge and still has the potential to turn into something great, just like its predecessor is, but this I can not play and I wish I hadn't spent money on it.Go to Steam Statistics and look at certain space4x games, might give you more clues about whats going on here...Greetings

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay look nice, but after paying $50 and waiting little over a month the game still crashes to desktop and sometimes crashes my entire display driver every time a space battle is viewed. My entire playtime of 6 hours has been attempt after attempt of crashing, retrieving crash logs, and sending them to the developers. To their credit, they have been responsive in their attempts to fix my and many other's issue with space battles, however they seem to been completely unable to solve this issue despite this.I shouldn't have to check in every week, put an hour or two into gathering files and formatting forums posts just to play a game I paid for. _childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like it. I really did. We could all use a 4Xish title worth playing.The way the game stands now, you have two options for gameplay: 1. Go with the automation, then try to troubleshoot the silly things it does. As one example: I had an enemy fleet passing by my system with a defense fleet. The defense fleet had one ship with low fuel but plenty to intercept. Instead, it waited to top up the one ship, at which point the fleet had passed and couldn't be caught. 2. Undo the automation and descend into a world of very tedious micro. And it can be very tedious.With a little smarter AI and some better direction options for the AI, it would be fun to play. I found the first option frustrating, and the second one excruciating.

_childDocuments_.review: I really didn't want to leave a bad review for this, but I can't even finish my first campaign because of constant crashing.  Once I reached mid game the lag increased, and now anytime my camera zooms in on something I crash to desktop. 32gb of RAM 8 cores processor RTX Card. _childDocuments_.review: This game isn't ready for release and probably will not be for a year minimum.There are multiple issues with this game, and currently some are back-breaking:• CrashingCrashes are regular and to be expected while playing, every hour or so. It makes trying to play the game tedious, but it is not a back-breaking issue.• UIThe UI is ugly but semi-functional at best of times, ugly and unuseable at others. Manually managing a War is next to impossible, even with a small empire at the start of the game. Its a chore to figure out empire borders, what belongs to whom and those things should be stupidly clear. Instead the AI is cluttered and figuring out anything is a headache.This is a serious issue and one that could potentially break any enjoyment you can get from the game.• AIBasically, war is completely broken. The game expects you to hand over control to the AI, because manually managing fleets sucks, as is having any sort of handle on what is happening.However, the AI also can't handle it either. It makes stupid decisions, leaves fleet stranded without fuel, leaves your empire-wide open and your empire gets destroyed against enemies the advisors suggested war against.Its a disaster, and currently war just isn't functional. That just completely breaks the game's back.• PacingSimilarly to Paradox 4X games, a lot of time is spent waiting. However, in those games like Hearts of Iron 4 you do feel like you make big macro decisions, you can make smaller impacts like micro-managing fronts or individual units.Here the game expects you to essentially play as a spectator, and your only real point of interaction is selecting research.This is also a back-breaking issue.What needs to happen to make the game playable.UI needs to be reworked, especially in terms of visibility and Empire-borders so you understand what the hell is happening and whom you're at war with.War needs to be fixed, with some sort of frontline system and the AI needing massive improvements.The lore is also dull as hell, but that is a minor issue.I wish I had discovered these issues before playing for 10 hours, as I cannot get a refund anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Would compare to Stellaris, this game is very similar but also very different.Ships and military could be better, it is hard sometimes to manage fleets. Fleets require to be fully fueled before any long jump or operation. This is a very realistic mechanic, but also somewhat annoying. I understand that it simulates Space better, it should take a lot of time for a fleet to travel in space, not jumping around immediately like in Stellaris late game. But also if you have one-half of your fleet fueled, and another half not fueled, your fleet might be stuck for ages waiting for not fueled ships to arrive and get the fuel - this is a very important part to get used to. Another annoying thing is - endless notifications from Pirates, I even wanted to clean up a map from them just to stop notifications.Except for these parts, the game is a great space strategy simulator, not as casual as Stellaris.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, after having played for ten hours now I rather tend to think it's not really for me. It's far too confusing and I don't mean the user interface. Of course it needs getting used to, but you can learn it, and it is actually not as bad as the UI in DW I. No, what I mean is: In DW I it was much easier to see what is going on where - regardless if in the system or on stellar level. It's a graphic problem. Too dark. Ships too small unless you really scroll in very far - and then you don't see much more but your ship. And it's not at all optimized graphically when playing on faster time levels. Jerking like crazy. You can play on slow time control, of course, and I'd even recommend that because else you will get problems to cope with everything (unless you play with automation activated for most aspects). But then I'm wondering how many games are you going to complete during your lifetime? Well, right now I think I will just go back to Stellaris ...

_childDocuments_.review: I have bought the game on its release and up to date I have spent 300+ hrs with Distant Worlds 2. Unfortunately I can't recommend this game to anybody as it is false advertised:1. It isn't finished product. It is still in development and the game's playerbase is encouraged in its betatesting. There are lots of updates (every 1-2 weeks), which vast of isn't compatible with earlier game's versions. You will have to start a new game post-patch. It is worth placing a note, that people using AMD components are still experiencing problems with the game crashing all the time when they perform any actions like zooming-in and zooming-out on game's map etc.2. Lots of in-game content is in poor state. Espionage system experiences heavy "ironing out" at the time I write down this review (developers aren't certain what is it supposed to do in their game). Diplomacy system isn't working either, the higher level diplomatic agreements like defense pacts don't do anything. Trading system is opaque to the player, the game only gives you a hint that you have to sign as many trading agreeements as possible to experience any decent trade income and at last you will find out that it doesn't guarantee any cashflow. Some of the playable races have their distinctive victory conditions via trading, but they don't work at the moment. There are quite a few of races in-game, however just 6 are playable. Non-playable races are missing their ship models and sprites (when you perform any diplomatic action, there is a window in which a sprite of this race is played, these are only in case of playable races. In case of non-playable ones you are welcomed by a stationary background representing a planet's environment).3. The game is lacking tools for a player to track various aspects of their space empire. You have tables which shows you income sources and spending sources, but you aren't able to play any graph to present you how are these values changing over time. You get plenty of lists for ships management, planets managements etc. which don't possess useful filters. For example let's assume you are waging a war and you want to find your ships in enemy's viccinity to make up a fleet. In this case you aren't able to sort your units by their system location, in return you can sort them by the ship's name which is pointless. It is only one example, but the game is full of these type poor game's design choices.4. The most important game's aspect is a war as for other 4X games. Ship designing, amount of design choices is great thing in DW2, but fleet's behaviour is a great disaster and it will drive you mad at some point. There already was a general overhauld of fleet behaviour made by the Devs, unfortunately they didn't suceed in keeping fleet's coherence. Ships in automated fleets are constantly making bad decisions which drive to excess loses. There are often situations that the fleet AI suggest you to assign a task to the fleet like getting rid off minor danger somewhere in your space. Let's assume that you agree for AI suggestion. Some time you check if they already performed the task and you are frightened at this point, because half of your fleet has been destroyed by minor threat. You begin to search what's the issue and you finally find out, that your ships don't arrive in-place at the same time, the first arrived ship is engaging the target and the rest of your fleet states that, they have to fuel up right now, therefore leaving the lonely ship to be decimated. The cycle repeats till the fleet doesn't have enough fleet's strenght to assign them an another task by AI, and it finally stops. In the late game it is impossible to oversee every single action the fleets are executing and steer them manually. It makes the most important part of the game (fighting) a huge failure.5. Game's UI is causing large fps drops due to the game's engine issues (the Devs has stated that they have to "upgrade" this to work correctly). On the other hand the interface is illegible due to inappropriate windows scaling and behaves unintuitively. A one mouse slide over the one of UI icons (without clicking on) cause an oppening of a table or other fancy stuff all over the screen, then you have to close by clicking X icon. In the late game these random pop-ups cause the game to stugger.These aren't the only issues, I would say that they are the most apparent. I don't recommend DW2 at its current state (it will be in poor state for next 2 years or so).In case you are interested in this franchise it is safer to buy its predecessor. Distant Worlds Universe may have worse graphic but its development cycle has come to an end. Thanks to that you will get a fully working game with much more features and community modding support, all this for a lower price.

_childDocuments_.review: Slow, steady development.  Impressive simulation.  Good game to play while multi-tasking . . . make sure you are using the "prepare and ..." options sparingly since they take FOREVER to "prepare."  With invasion fleets, bring them in last after defenders are gone . . . troop transports are squishy.  Be the first to research stuff that private needs (larger passenger/cargo/mining ships, etc.) and then you make tons of money selling ships to private.  You almost have to micro colony ships when taking independent colonies . . . they will no longer want to join you by the time your ship finally gets there.  It has gotten better since launch.  The notifications are more easily customizable in the last patch.  I play with the Star Wars them playing from addons . . . CTD before I get to the end game, usually.  I keep following/supporting to see what the next update/patch will bring!

_childDocuments_.review: Juggling Resource: The Game.I gave this game a full weekend of some hard gaming action and... I'm not impressed.It is very slow moving.  You may play for a couple hours or more before you colonize your first planet and then you have to deal with the huge hit it takes on your economy.  It's nearly impossible to tell if your empire is making money or in the red because the entire game the "income" amount is swinging wildly all over the place.  You can have -1500 income and still be making money for some reason. You can be +1000 income and your credit stache is barely climbing at all.  That stache amount is jumping all over the place also.  There is so much going on it's nearly impossible to tell why your economy tanks all of a sudden... a lot of times I think it's the AI changing tax rates on your colonies.The weirdest thing about this game is that there is nothing to do about your dropping income... or your slow research rates.  You can research just a couple techs for each in the early game but they only improves ships.  How would you handle these problems in other games?  Build some trade centers on your planets or some new research centers.  Here there is little-to-nothing to do with planets except change the tax rates.  Kind of boring.The AI does lots and lots of dumb things.  I got a pop up to colonize one of the nicest planets I've seen.  Clicked yes to "auto" build the colonyship and send it to the new planet.  After years of not getting a message for the completed mission I tracked it down.  The AI built the colony ship in the one star base that was furthest from the new planet.  While warping across the expanse... it ran out of gas.  I checked my tankers and NONE of them were going to refuel.  I jiggered with things for hours trying to get one damn ship to refuel my colonizer.  In the meanwhile, an used colony ship is a serious drain on the economy.. so that was fun.I found a super fun exploit where I had 3 spies get most of my techs from me.  You see the pirates in this game will always be more advanced than you for some reason.  If you become friendly with them then you can send you agents to steal techs.  Set them to steal techs in 3 months and the good ones will have a 50% chance of being caught.  Just save your game and reload to get the desired out come.  I had every tier 1-2 tech in the game and many tier 3s pretty quicklly.  That's when I realized around the tier 3-4 tech range the game grinds to snail pace.  Techs take a minimum of 3 years. (1 game tick is a day mind you.) and there are no new ways to increase your research rate.  No buildings to build.  You can wait for a random scientist to show up but in 100s of years of game time I only had 2.War might be fun, but even with tier 3-4 warp techs your ships are very slow to move about your expanding empire.  You can't build too many ships without killing you economy.  So I have a feeling war is a lot of surprise attacks with you trying to get your ships in the right place as quickly as possible.  I only battled some pirataes and space critters, but after 20 hours into one game I was kind of too bored to care.

_childDocuments_.review: While it's painful to compare this to other games such as Stellaris there's no getting away from it, and despite initial appearances, to sit down and actually play, this is very different. It manages to be a more micromanaging rich game, yet at the same time you don't 'have' to indulge in it; the extra clicking is totally optional. Ever had a large empire mid-late game, and find yourself routinely clicking away... just wanting it over as much as anything, only interested in specific aspects. Well, here you go, and by default pretty much most things are automated rather than flicking switches on and off and constantly messing with automation settings. They way automation is done here just feels right.That might make you think 'then what's the point?' All I can write is try it an see. In the same way a long time ago the stop-clock mechanic put me off trying Paradox map painters but now I massively prefer that to turn based, this type of optional automation is now something I think every strategy game should have. If possible and you're a 'map painting' type of fan, you should try this game. Don't worry, there's more than enough menus and intimidating supply lines to play with 'IF you want to get involved. I haven't got anywhere near enough hours to go in depth, but if you're bored, like this type of game and want something a little different, give this a look. It won't cost you that much to find out anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, not that fun. One of the big advertised mechanics of this game was the automation, but they really rely on it like a crutch rather than using it as an interesting mechanic. When you do decide to actually take control and do things, they don't work intuitively: take trying to attack an enemy with a fleet of your own, you'd think it would be as simple as "click on fleet, then click on who you want them to attack", but nope, instead you have to place a target on what you want to attack, then your fleet will attack it, when the weather is good, the planets align, and they feel like it. Instead they will spend more often attacking random things you don't want them to attack regardless of your orders. But let's say you decide to just leave that and focus on your economy as what you manually control, well too bad there basically isn't much of one. Planets have little to no depth game play or mechanically. Everything is like this, they say its "deep, intricate, hard to understand", make it really annoying to gather information, give orders, and do things so that you automate it, then hope you don't actually spend the time to look into the systems because then you'd find that, if it wasn't layered behind the god awful UI it is simpler than 99% of 4X and grandstrategy games out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I first played this game around release and found it be incredibly unstable with frequent crashes and drastic slowdowns. A year later and with the release of v1.2 Aurora update I gave it another go. Most of those issues do seem to be behind the game now, it ran pretty much fine and I only experienced 1 CTD this time.However, still, for all the claims of vast depth and wide array of options and choices there are still gaping holes in your strategic, tactical and diplomatic options that would shame a 4X game even 20 years ago. Habitability and colonisation remain extremely shallow and planetary development is barebones at best. There is very little to this game outside of designing your war ships, and yet for all the hundreds of components and thousands of possibilties... there's very little point.The only positive I have to say about Distant Worlds is the simulation of a civilian economy. Its also quite shallow a system, just moving a myriad resources from one point to another (there are a lot but very few are really important to have) but I don't think any other games bother actually moving goods and just abstract it all out, if they bother at all. Also seeing the freighters and passenger liners zipping around (when they're not just sitting idle in a huge orbital cloud at least) makes the map feel a lot less sterile.

_childDocuments_.review: I am changing my review after 7h of playtime to not-recommended.Another game that developers did not bother to play themselves at least one time from start to end, otherwise it is impossible to explain some issues with basic gameplay:1. No option to disband ships - stuck on different age of the galaxy in nebula field? Your problem. Your ship will be hanging there forever and cluttering UI.2. Fleets are nice. Do you want to upgrade them? No, you don't - game does not allow you to do this unless you have all the resources ready in one station for the whole fleet, which will never happen. So you have to upgrade every ship one by one - which makes fleets feature useless.3. Want to "select all" in any list? (ship/station). Nana, you can't do that. For ships you can at least multiselect with Ctrl. For stations - tough luck, please click through 100 of stations to upgrade them.4. Have 50 asteroids in your home sector? Tough luck - all your explorer ships will be scanning every single of them for hour, while your enemy already will be colonizing second planet.And a lot of other details like that which, unfortunately, do not allow to enjoy game at all. And I did not even reach mid-game... Bugs and crashes are expected on day one, but these are basic gameplay fails. Should be playable after few months of patches and QOL additions. Don't buy now - waste of time and disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay wise the game is similar to DS1. With the difference being, that now the game pace advances much slower than before. When in DS1 you could achieve incomes of 100k in 10 years, you now will be stuck at maybe 10k or when you trying to adjust to the game, maybe even end up broke. Compared to DS1 it feels like you have much less freedom. This encompasses things like station design. While in DS1 you could freely design everything, and this means everything. Now you are locked to specific design limits, for example research stations limited to only one lab or spaceports limited to a certain size. I feel like the developers tried to simplify things for a broader audience but failed to do so.This is also in my opinion made clear by the font of the game, which is pretty much a copy paste of DS1 mechanically. It needed simplification, but the only thing it got was a different look, while remaining a complicated mess. Stellaris would have been a good reference when it comes to a good and simple UI design (ignoring its terrible dlc policy). Sound design is a big downgrade compared to DS1. DS1 had a long, diverse and dynamic orchestral soundtrack. This changed with DS2. Now you are left with one soundtrack, which is dynamic yes and changes depending on the situation. But compared to DS1, its vastly inferior. Ships are very inconclusive to what they are currently doing and why they are doing. You cannot que orders like in DS1. And when you select a ship inside a system to go to a point, you don't have a system side indicator that says where your ship is going. Diplomacy is a letdown. It feels bland. Basic things like resource trading is lacking. Pirates seem to come out of nowhereAnd bugs, various bugs. Independent colony can have zero troops, yet the invasion button still says that you do not have enough troops to invade it. Sending a fleet to repair and refuel? Have fun having your fleet teleport randomly to another galaxy. It will only take 30 years for them to come back.Now to the good. The game like DS1 has great mechanics. The economy is very complex and interesting to manage. Graphics wise it’s a beautiful game. You can do better, but compared to DS1, it’s an obvious step up.The designing of your ship and stations feels downgraded, but still is fun. Generally, all which was good in DS1, is back in DS2.The game in all feels like one thing. A graphics update. It lacks a lot of quality of life improvements which were already needed in DS1 like the UI for example. I doubt that the developers will be able to improve much since they released the game as it is. But prove me wrong.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I've been a closed beta tester for Codeforce on this project, so take this with a grain of salt. However, I've been quite critical of DW2's flaws up until this point, and I was disappointed with the state of the game's release along with my colleagues at eXplorminate.Things have changed. With the Aurora update, I feel Distant Worlds 2 has finally become the game it was supposed to be. Most of the stuff from DW:U (minus the DLC pirates content) is in there, but it's a better experience in nearly every other way. Combat is drastically improved (it's so much better than Universe that it's completely unrecognisable to that old game) and is a joy to play, particularly with the way the different fleet roles engage: there's a lot of nuance in fleet composition and positioning that even playing full auto is engaging and fun. The new fleet management options remove my main gripe about DW2, which was painful fleet upgrade management, and now there are a wealth of options (and better documented/labelled than before) to show you what you need to do to keep everything upgrading correctly, without manual interference.Aurora has brought a whole lot of small updates that seem small on paper but the effect they have on the overall gameplay experience is greater than the sum of their parts I think, and DW2 is shaping up to be the best space 4X hands down. There is one big annoyance for me: finding a fleet of derelict ships can often mean clicking on a dozen or more continuous popups, and these aren't a type of message you want to surpress as these fleets are important. Codeforce are aware of how painful people are finding this problem but they've yet to fix it. It's the one really annoying damn issue in an otherwise excellent game.Bring on the DLC!

_childDocuments_.review: Finally the game is where it needs to be, still a bit pissed over the excellent DW1 being abandoned and no longer working on Win 11, whilst this was released initially buggy and without much base game content, but now this is at a stage where I can happy recommend to others as a true sequel. _childDocuments_.review: It looks like it has a lot of potential but it really felt like an Early Access game for the 3.5 hours I played. Military ship behavior is erratic if you put them on auto. _childDocuments_.review: Picked this up during the winter sale and was really pleasantly surprised at how fun it is. I now recognize the whole DW series is filling an amazing niche in 4x sci-fi for which it's very underrated. As a veteran Stellaris player, I was interested in seeing how this game was going to compare. I went in with an open mind and heeded reviews saying it is more of a simulator than anything else, and was really happy with the experience I got. It took roughly 20 hours of gameplay to finish my first game, learning the ropes in the process and gaining the experience necessary to consider myself capable of taking down normal AI. During that time I had a lot of fun with planetary management, manually controlling fleet and invasion orders, and learning what each tech did. I was happy to find that you can really spec into any given area and focus heavily on it, effectively specializing your empire in certain weaponry, military tactics, hulls, or fighters etc. This along with the pre-defined species (which I was originally not a fan of, again, Stellaris vet) allows for a level of in-depth and extensive uniqueness for each faction and navy.Overall, I'd buy it if you like the premise, that being a very expansive and intricate 4x strategy and simulator hybrid (heavy emphasis on simulator, as in simulating a living breathing galaxy with civilian traffic, mining stations, planets, militaries, etc). I liked that premise and was shocked at how much more fun it was than I thought it'd be, and how much more true to that description it is than I had presumed it'd be. Definitely following development from here on out and really hyped to see what other amazing things comes out of this franchise!!!

_childDocuments_.review: DW2 is a frustrating 4X game because it has great ideas and features buried under a UI so bad you wonder if any of the devs have a UX background. And I know that sounds harsh, but you can't get around the fact that many fundamental aspects of the interface are made useless by avoidable design decisions:-First and foremost, is the depiction of space itself. Space is an incredibly large thing, almost entirely devoid of anything at all. Most leading 4x space games will get around that by exaggerating the size of galaxies and having a finite number of zoom levels (galaxy zoom, system zoom and planet zoom). DW2 tries to model every last little bit of emptiness, and the most convenient way to zoom from galaxy to planet is to mouse scroll... and scroll, and scroll, and scroll. I maxed out the zoom scroll speed, which helps a little bit, but my pointer finger still gets numb during longer sessions, and pretty sure my mouse scroll wheel is quickly reaching its usage limits.  - The main screen is filled with tons of tiny little icons which are unrecognizable from each other. Rather than display text details with the icon, you need to scroll over each individual one for a small tooltip to appear. That is assuming they bothered to program a tooltip -  some icons have literally no explanation at all. The worst offenders are the resource icons, which are dozens and dozens of blobs of slightly different shapes and colors. If iconography is not transparent or at least easily learnable to the average user, then there is no point in having it.-I know that "no one cares about the techno-lore", but I do damn it! Even if world-building content isnt at the top of your feature backlog, would it hurt to add a few sentences to the tech tree for context? The only way to understand the fundamental differences between the many different types of offensive and defensive weapons, modules, and other improvements is through an obtuse wall of numbers. - And good God, the AI automation. Some things work very well, such as mining, transportation and refueling. But others are infuriatingly broken or downright combative towards the player. Take military ship automation for example. At multiple times my military ships were literally committing suicide by attacking vastly superior pirate bases and space monsters in a galaxy, even though I had military automation set to "manual".- Or my favorite, the ship design automation. If you have ship design set to automatic, the AI will tend to deck out designs with missile attack systems and little else. If you update or create a new design with the weapons and configurations you want instead, the AI will ACTUALLY IMMEDIATELY OBSOLETE the design you just worked hard on, for no clear reason other than perhaps to give the player a big middle finger for attempting to subvert its clearly superior intelligence. You can set design to manual, which solves that problem, but then the AI will not even auto-update the designs you create with like-for-like upgraded components. Yeah, hope you like manually updating a dozen ship designs every time a new technology is researched! There is much more I could call out, from the unhelpful menu design, to the lack of a centralized ship inventory, to the confusing way that budgeting is handled. All these issues add up to a game that I cant recommend, despite the fact that I still did enjoy some aspects of it.

_childDocuments_.review: The recent hyperspeed update has made the game vastly smoother to run when one is further into the game. There is a lot going in the background of this game, things that are automated but most of things can be taken in hand and done manually. I enjoyed the original game for its choice of splitting the state and civilian economy, and actually having the latter and interaction with it be an important part of the simulation. Distant Worlds 2 has taken that side and taken it further. Meanwhile it is enjoyable how each race has its own story playing out, with their own objectives. It makes the galaxy more than just faceless races which are all trying to do the same thing. Take your time to learn how things work, and you will be rewarded with a great space strategy game!

The AI is actually quite good.They need to be better about repetitive commands.  There needs to be a way to reject a command and stop it from coming back again 5 seconds later.They need to be better about multiple star systems spawning with the same name.Diplomacy is the same for every nation, and extremely easy if you have a bit of money.Spycraft seems pointless, unless perhaps one of the races gets huge bonuses.  As it is, I have played to late game twice with two separate races and never been able to use them for more than stealing maps.  Counterespionage doesn't seem to do anything.I do really enjoy watching the free market work though.  It is kind of like a sim running while I am playing a space 4x game.

_childDocuments_.review: Not ready for full release - should have been listed as early access.  Good concept though - hope it receives further development to get to a good place in the future.- Stability - regular crashes with significant loss of progress.- Functionality - game systems aren't complete.  e.g. The fleet / ship role behavior is limited - a single "role" for each hull type directly contradicts the researches available for multiple hull roles.- Gameplay - the automation means the game will practically play itself by default - you have to actively look to turn off the automation for things you want to manage.  However, at least for fleet management, the majority of the challenge is trying to trick the automation into doing what you want it to do.  It doesn't feel feasible to disable automation for many tasks - it would simply be way too much tedious micromanagement.- Performance - heavy FPS drop in some situations - e.g. zoomed out on galaxy map and then opening the tech tree.- UI - Feels good to start, but very clunky when used further.  Lots of zooming in and out, misclicking on icons, some notifications don't bring you to the point-of-interest.

_childDocuments_.review: The most obvious point of comparison here will be Stellaris, so to put it very simply: think Stellaris but with fewer layers of abstraction (and with worse music). Distant Worlds 2 has a lot more 'grit' to it, and feels much closer to how an actual interstellar empire would operate logistically. For example, rather than mined materials instantly being placed into an omnipresent inventory, materials actually have to be mined and transported by a freighter to some storage point (usually a space port). If you needed those particular resources to build a ship at a different spaceport, they would again need to be transported. You may be thinking that this sounds like micro-management hell, but for the most part this is all handled by the private sector, which you have no direct control over. The private sector comprises civilian ships like freighters, passenger transports (for tourists and migrants), and mining ships. These ships will go about their business without needing your direction, bringing people and resources where they're needed. This sort of thing isn't just useless fluff, either. Of course, resources needing to be physically transported means that supply chains can be blockaded and disrupted. Denying access to an important strategic resource or using hit and run tactics to disrupt the supply chain of a superior opponent are valid tactics. Speaking of micro-management, the nice thing about DW2 is that you have an extremely fine degree of control over how much of it there is. Literally every aspect of your empire management can be automated, and unlike many other games that offer a similar feature, the intelligence of the automation is actually respectable. If you don't feel like poring over tax rates for each colony, let the computer handle it. Don't feel like making your own ship designs? Automate it. Tired of ruling an empire entirely? Automate everything and assume manual control of an exploration ship and see what's out there. Or a battleship and go hunt space bugs. Graphics are nice. Planets look great, ship designs are pretty cool. UI is passable, or if you're comparing it with the first Distant Worlds, miraculous. Seriously, it's a lot better. Feels like an actual videogame UI rather than a Windows 98 shell. Still has some issues on widescreen displays and some resolutions higher than 1920x1080 I understand, hopefully this will be sorted soon. Audio needs some work. The music is... odd, to put it graciously. Some audio glitches sometimes result in very loud bursts of noise sometimes. I recommend turning the sound effects slider down very low, and listening to the music for a bit before turning it off and replacing it with your own just to understand what I'm talking about. There's one track in particular that can only be described as the sound of large sheets of metal being scraped together.Anyway, great game, very excited to continue playing and to see how it's enhanced further through expansions (the first Distant Worlds received a transformative amount of love post-release, I expect this to be no different). Any fan of 4x/grand strategy sci-fi owes it to themselves to give DW2 a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: (Disclaimer: I play on Pre-Warp, slowest tech speed, few colony-potential worlds, single-colony start with high difficulty settings, usually with more advanced enemy empires, mainly one of each major species, so experiences may differ wildly between players / playstyles.April 30 2022 Edit: If you play on Linux, get the Modloader & patch. It completely eliminates crashes and opens you up to a bunch of custom mods. (You'll also be supporting mods by some good peeps, so thanks for that <3)Apr 13 2022 Edit: Nearly 200 hours and a dozen games in, I can say with certainty: racial research bonuses, espionage, & Caslon supply will make or break your early game stride. In a current test game, the cat-people-whose-name-I-forget technocracy had 7 colonies and over 600 tech points within the time it took to get my first extra-solar Human colony going. It took my human republic a century to get to stealth, sector commands, and officer schools, while fighting off intense, constant pirate and monster raids in the Caslon-poor galactic core. Meanwhile my ice-world catfolk are chilling on the galactic edge and making advancements at lightning speed while swimming in starfuel. After retiring the first few spies and admirals to reroll for better starting perks, I got an administrator scientist (25% discount to crash theory) and some spies with energetic, skilled orator, etc. If you can get a General with the RARE perk that all local leaders slowly gain skills, DO IT. Kill anyone with the opposite perk. Also, watch out for leaders randomly becoming double agents, I had to scrap my best scientist for that. RIP. Stealing tech from pirates starts off as a risky training tactic, but once they get around 20% concealment and espionage, it winds up giving you effectively the first 3 or 4 tiers of tech for free over a number of years. If you focus on getting better tech labs and economics after your first proper warp drive, followed by civilian ships (colony especially), the free tech will trickle in. You can even cherry pick which techs you want to steal via manual control, which is great for when you really need that next tier of reactor but already set a 5 year crash research for faster mining in order to buff the economy. Anyway, this game is amazing and I love it. Cheers and enjoy!)Honestly, its been frustrating watching all the major Let's Play's treating this like a slightly more detailed Stellaris (which the AI auto-controls effectively does - until players encounter the old 'too many mining bases, too spread apart, private economy crashing, oh god I'm bankrupt, now I'm being invaded, HALP!' newbie A4X mistake lol), as opposed to a game  like Aurora 4X, Space Empire IV/V, Children of a Dead Earth, etc, where you can do all sorts of incredible, crazy things in ways most games aren't built to allow. From logistical hacks, to custom spy ships, to sabotage, to tactical maneuvers, to ambush-bait shadow colonies, to PD-only turtle ships with max armor and counter utilities in order to draw enemy fire while your heavy hitters pounce from the rear flank, and your dedicated boarding assault marine ships mass-attack the enemy flagship, or even their minimally-armed transport ships in order to cripple their invasion... Its ALL possible here. You can even automate the entire game and just manually control a single colony, or fleet, or ship, and ignore everything else as it organically generates and evolves around you. Honestly, this is more than a single game. More than a Stellaris-like. More than an Aurora successor. This is a dream come true for Scifi 4X players, and I hope, a return to the open-world,  if-you-can-think-it, you-can-do-it complexity of old-school Scifi 4X over the modern bore of streamlined Stellaris-likes.DW2 is pretty much vanilla A4X with modern graphics - something I've been waiting, hoping, dreaming of, my entire life. You'll understand the mechanics and complexities intuitively without the need for much, if any, tutorial / reading; and I know for a fact that bunch of us from the A4X community are already enjoying DW2.Scenario idea: Try emulating a certain glorious Scifi series by building shadow colonies with which to bait vastly superior xeno forces into ambush while you desperately try to hide your tiny, technologically backward space federation - its a ton of fun.Personally, I enjoy hiding fuel harvester-tankers in orbit of a gas giant near the enemy empire, in deep space far beyond reach of my active logistical network, in order to refuel for a major strike / invasion, without the sensor profile of an actual base, thus mitigating discovery and retaliation chances. The AI thinks I can't strike the enemy empire, but with manual control and a bit of clever dormant tanker placement, its easy peasy to go far beyond effective range. Want to spy on enemy movement? Build a custom intel-gathering ship loaded with long-range sensors, extra fuel tanks, and fighter bays / construction bays / etc., then park it in the middle of nowhere to watch the enemy pass by and reveal their activity, tech levels, ship types, etc? You can do that here too.While Linux users require some Proton finagling to run; it runs - even on this unstable tropical volcano of a refurbished laptop. Recent patches mitigated a number of slowdowns and crash-inducing issues, and so they've become far less frequent. I've gotten (what seem to be memory leak related) crashes down to clockwork at roughly 1 1/2 to 2 hours of gameplay at max speed, outside going absolutely nuts wheel scrolling across the galaxy while selecting a giant armada at max speed at the same time as your spy finally steals the entire map of a giant empire. (This happened lol. Though a considerable amount of jank is the fault of my sub-par system, and subpar Proton patching, not the game itself.)All in all, I'm absolutely in love with this game and look forward to what else will come, in terms of future features and customization. As it stands, the game is already a masterpiece. I've put in thousands of hours into what was effectively a text version of this game, so I envision playing DW2 for years to come.Seriously, devs, thank you for this dream come true. <3
