_childDocuments_.review: I do not recommend looking in to this game until another full year after launch. I do not believe this should be taken as an opinion, either because the game is objectively NOT finished, and has significant issues to be resolved. Such as significant balancing, mechanic completion, AI work, crash fixes, as well as a slew of quality of life improvements.While I respected the devs and what they have accomplished with Distant Worlds 1 which is a great game, this one should have been advertised as an early access game (and probably a remake of the original more than a sequel) yet it's a advertised as a full priced $50 complete experience. Which it is not. As such, I've lost a lot of respect for them because it appears deceitful. It was evident to me that this was an early access game less than an hour into my first game. If the missing races end up as paid DLC instead of part of free updates (e.g. finishing the game) then I do not suggest buying this game unless you find it on sale, which for this developer, is rare. We already got bamboozled, we don't need to pay again to get what we should have already got. If they aren't planned to be introduced at a later time, then I think that's a bad thing because there are not enough races to fill the galaxy sizes this game is capable of without a large number if duplicates.With the exception of the above, and to provide a more beneficial review for others interested in the game, I'm going to cut them some slack and not place a lot of emphasis on issues that will be patched out, in time.Distant Worlds 2 plays almost identically to it's predecessor, and while it does have some much appreciated improvements, it lacks a fair amount of content that the original has and they are so similar overall, there really isn't much reason to play DW2 over the original in it's current state, especially considering the currently unrealistic price tag for an early access game.-Ship/Base Design-As a personal opinion I also believe that the ship and base customization has taken a step backwards, because you do not have the freedom to experiment and ability to specialize that you have in the first game. It opens up somewhat as you get more tech, but it never gets the feeling of freedom and creativity of the original. The limited number of slots is frustrating. You are constantly battling with two forms of ship "currency" in the form of number of item equipment specific slots and total capacity. I enjoy going for a strong economy and employing a quality over quantity design for my ships and bases. But due to the slot limitations, ships are largely going to perform similarly. Having a bigger economy will let you have more ships, but not really any better ships. If multiple empires have about the same tech available, their ships are going to be largely the same. I believe Distant Worlds 1 is far superior for ship and station design. the two governing factors for your ships is capacity (tech) and how expensive they were to build and maintain, both in raw materials to build the ships and how many credits it took to maintain them. You could build 1 powerful 5000 credit upkeep ship, or 5 weaker 1000 credit upkeep ships. But if your economy was strong and you had access to a lot of resources, you could field just as large a number of your fancy ships. It was a reward for doing well. But a loss of each ship hurt more, as it takes more time and logistical support to replace it.As you get a lot of tech unlocked, the component list during ship/base creation turns into an absolute mess. Even using the filters, I waste so much time looking through the list to find what I need, slots are filled with obsolete tech. Why are there engine slots I can't use? Why do engines and directional thrusters use the same slots? Directional thrusters only on the rear of the ship wouldn't work anyway. There are so many weapons, and it isn't remotely clear on exactly what they do or why you'd want them over something else. The game really needs a testing arena where you can spawn ships with various loadout and testing them out so you can figure out what they do and how effective they are. The weapons are also in dire need of some kind of description.-General Gameplay-Some game starts do not function properly. You can select an expanding empire age that say you'll have 7-8 colonies but you'll actually only have 4. And you'll have no resources stockpiled and only a single construction ship, so you can't even build any ships and get started. As a result, that game is effectively dead on arrival since you have no economy nor the means to get one started. I could use the in game editor to recover, but I don't know if the AI can recover and proceed, so I just gave up rather than risk wasting the time.Pirates are way more annoying, numerous, stronger, and with higher tech. It doesn't feel like they have to scout your empire out either, and they just know where to raid. I also keep running into super powerful Hive ships that you have no hope of stopping at early tech levels, so they'll just ravage any nearby colonies you have with impunity and your ships will blindly fly to their doom on their own as they try to attack a ship they have absolutely no hope of even scratching, even if they massed together. Let alone one at a time, over and over.-Sound and Music-The music is okay in same ways, but very bland and forgettable. You can place your own tracks in the game folder and it will play them, which is nice, but there are so many events (and apparently zoom level??) that the playing track will frequently and abruptly change. It's like listening to music with someone who changes the song every 30 seconds. Very weird and jarring.The sound effects do their job but they aren't notable.There are more things that I have issues with, but much of it I believe is going to eventually get fixed, so I'll stop here.Give the game some time to get finished, at least a year, then check back in.EDIT: And just like I said, they're selling the races that they cut out of the game for too much money.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to preface this by saying I REALLY want to like this game.  I actually really enjoy playing,  I enjoy trying new builds for my ships and all the in depth customisation.  However, the constant crashing and FPS drops is very very disappointing,  I have crashed out of the game so much I have essentially never actually quit the game properly.  In addition, it seems that there are parts of the game that are missing, for example, vassalisation.  I would have also liked to see more in depth economy, as it seems like you can open basically one steel mine and never have any issues with steel for the rest of the game.  I would have liked to see as you make your ships or colonies better, they require more and more complex items and more of them so theres a constant ramp up of demand as the game progresses.If this was early access, I would have held off, but buyer beware.  Look online to see if the crashing is resolved.  In the meantime, im just going to ahve to stop playing for a few months, which is really disappointing.  Had I known the game would crash this much, I wouldnt have purchased the game.  As it is, i have spent more than a few hours trying to get it to a stable state, and am well and truly past the refund window.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Some interesting concepts, unfortunately stuck behind an unfinished game.- Economy is split between civilian and state economy, you only have direct access to state economy but can direct civilian money to the state via taxes and building and resorts.- Strong automated systems, most ships are fully automated so that you can let them do their own thing until you are comfortable with how to direct them.Unfortunately the automated systems seem to have a hard time letting go when you DO want to direct your designs or ships. You might find your ships in a fleet across your empire when you need them.The help systems through the game are somehow both too long and drawn out, while simultaneously not offering the information you actually need. Many places have terms or statistics with no way to find out WHAT those terms mean specifically,CRASHES. I have yet to make it through an entire game without it crashing, I would recommend anyone playing to lower the auto-save intervals below 5 mins, as with many strategy games you can go a while without much happening, and then have a lot happen at the same time. Meaning that 5 minutes feels like a lot more lost time.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some of the most innovative mechanics for a strategy game ever.You can go full manual, but you can also go full automation or anything in between.The automation is not always perfect, but then the player wouldn't have anything to do if it were always perfect.Whenever the AI fails to do what you expect, you just take over that specific part and you can really focus on optimizing that specific part while the AI takes care of the rest.It is like you work hand in hand with an AI in this game and to be honest I think this is the future of humanity, not just in gaming. We will be augmented via AI.As said before, not everything is perfect, not every detail at least, but it is the right direction with many innovative and just brilliant Ideas. Just wished that this game would get a better score overall, so that the developers would know they made good decisions and now only have to polish the details of the game.Also, thanks for proper 4K support! I saw many development studios failing on properly supporting 4K in their strategy games, but this one does it very well. Nicely scaled UI and everything sharp.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: To start with this is a simulation.  Everything in this sim can be controlled or you can give up control.  You first have to decide what you want to control and go from there.  Because of the sim mechanics and the variety of species each time you play it is different.  This game allows for endless replayability.  The sim is constantly being updated in beta, which is the version I play since I don't want to wait for official update.  I find this very satisfying to play due to replayability and the unique sim mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I played the first Distant Worlds and really enjoyed it.  The game play and the style of game grabbed my attention in a way few games do.  I had high hopes for Distant Worlds 2 - that it'd be the Distant Worlds Universe and then some.  Unfortunately, it isn't as it stands now.  The way the game is now is that it is Distant Worlds Universe and less some.I'll touch on the crashes briefly since that will, hopefully, be fixed at some point.  This is the only game in recent (past six months to a year) that crashed on me.  I've played a lot of brand new releases and even betas - this is the one that kept crashing.  As noted, this should be fixed, so... whatever.Back to the game itself - there are an awful lot of restrictions and limitations that were put into the game.  Part of the appeal of Distant Worlds Universe to me was the open endedness of everything.  You could design your own ships, your own bases, and basically your own empire.  The game would play and you had all these fun options with which to tinker.  In Distant Worlds 2 - that openness is gone.  As I got further into the game and began learning about the underlying systems from the ship designs, technologies, to the economic system I discovered frustration after frustration.  The game doesn't explain what's going on even though, at first blush, it seems like it does.  There's this huge "galactopedia" thing that sounds great and then I realized that it's as out of date as most wikis become after a single patch.  The information in it is often out of date or completely lacking.  The "flavour" text is fine but the actual details, the stuff you need to make decisions on how to design something or how to solve a problem, are lacking.  To me that sums up the game in its present state:  lacking.At the moment this game is not worth picking up.  It might be worthwhile after some major patches and / or content releases.  Maybe when there are more mods.  Something more than what it currently is.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Update for Christmas 2024:One day I will get round to writing a proper review for this game.... It is just immense. Just editing this scrappy collection of text to add that although my below comparisons to DWU still stand, they keep updating it and it keeps getting better. Truly great game.Normally I will write quite long reviews, but I am enjoying playing too much to do that now.I will update this review later but I will say that as a long-time DWU player I am loving this game. The changes take some getting used to, but I am only 25 hours in and I am being pleasantly surprised in many ways.I highly recommend it and now I am going to go back to playing it.BTW I am playing in linux and it works fine.Edit after 200 hours.I can't help comparing it to DWU, and playing DW2 just makes me wish DWU ran on modern systems. There is really one reason for this and it is freedom. A stand-out feature for Distant Worlds was freedom. It gave the player so much in terms of a rich simulation and access to enough information to be so creative in gameplay that the freedom to design ships and bases, and place them in accordance to your schemes and plans was a perfect mix.In DW2 there appears to be the rich environment you would expect in this sequel, but the freedom for the player to design assets, and more importantly the freedom in how to deploy your assets is limited in some really frustrating and apparently nonsensical ways. It is like the player is being protected from making certain types of choice. This makes responding to emergent events creatively a very frustrating experience. And actually limits the richness of the game massively.That said, it is a good game and it keeps getting better with updates, and I keep playing it.Still, i wish DWU ran on modern systems....

_childDocuments_.review: As fan of DW1 I can't recommend this. The big issue is performance. Right now mid game is basically impossible. As everything slows down to a crawl or just starts teleporting around. Then the game will crash. I basically can't complete a game because of it.Besides the performance issue there is a lot of polish is missing. Weird menus, some settings are broken or don't work. Like you can't turn of pirates and they can attack you from across the galaxy. Getting asked to colonize stuff that you can't colonize. Diplomacy being super bare bones, and basically revolves around throwing money at them. Colonies not making money unless the population hits a billion. You start at 35 million and pop growth is 2-6 percent. The map becomes unreadable later on. Typos and other weird stuff that shouldn't have been missed.It really sort of hurts, cause underneath it all I see a really solid game. The scale and look is amazing. While exploration and growing early on is good fun.If this was early access I'd say it's actually in a good state, but it's not. Honestly just like the original it won't really shine until has an expansion or two. So just wait for now.Edit: Developer kindly ask to update after the recent big patch. A ton of good work has been done. The performance has been improved. The AI is smarter, and lots of other smaller tweaks that improved things. Unfortunately for me the performance is still rough enough that I haven't finished a game. As by the middle of the game the lag still slows down the game dramatically, and occasionally triggers a crash. I'm very positive about the changes that have been done and trust the devs to keep working on it but I'd still recommend waiting.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is Distant Worlds Universe, but more streamlined. Many people seem to be making the mistake of comparing DWU2 on release to the original after over 10 years of development and user mods.What you get here is the same mechanics you had in the original, but better presented in my opinion. Everything is streamlined, with much of the "fat" of DWU cut out. For instance, I recall in DWU that I would bee-line to Hydrogen asap because anything else meant restructuring my entire empire to shift from one fuel source to another. A huge PITA the longer you wait. Here, there is only one fuel source. Or things like - every ship design in DWU no matter your race was basically the same except bigger when your size cap increases. DW2 goes a different route with hardpoints being locked to your race. It's just locking you in in a different way, but in my opinion the flavor is a nice addition.For new players, I would STRONGLY recommend when you start a game to leave absolutely everything on fully automated, then pick 1 or 2 areas that you want to learn the intricacies of and set only those to manual. Figure out how that works, and move on to the next thing. If you are new to the game and think you are going to micro every aspect of your empire, you will fail.It can absolutely feel like "the game just plays itself". This is because the AI is better than you. This is a good thing. Celebrate that a game has an AI more capable than a new player. Then learn how to run your empire better than the AI. Once you do that, that "the game just plays itself" feeling goes away while still being available for the things you really just don't feel like doing yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not going to recommend a game when I stayed away for over a year and the game still struggles with the most basic of things. I still lost an entire fleet, in my first game, because I told two fleets to attack a system and they took two different ways to get there and one was slower. The flight path had them going in the same direction and next I look, one of them diverted up to an unexplored area on the other side of their destination before coming back around. No explanation. No warning. Just stupid.Fleets and ships still happily go further than they have fuel even though it's within the first circle which (I guess?) is the halfway mark. Somehow they always seem to find some way to be completely ridiculous no matter how sure you are of where you told them to go. My home starbase never has fuel because all the ships were coming out of there and the private market isn't stepping up supply regardless of having five other places I'm getting the fuel. I'm watching the other places. They have fuel. They don't have a bunch of private freighters lined up to ship the fuel to where it needs to go. There's not a big back up of private ships to be built. I don't care how complicated you make the game, this is not how a private economy works, and the private economy is basically the only redeeming factor of the entire game when compared to its contemporaries. I played DW:U (the first one), and it never struck me as broken as this. I tried for many hours right when this game released but it doesn't look like it's been meaningfully changed at all. Most of the problems I found still exist and the developers still say they're "rare" even though everyone is experiencing them. But there's DLC!I think it's time to admit that the UI/UX was never going to be able to handle what the developers wanted this time around and either work on streamlining it or simplifying it. Thing is, they clearly don't want to do that to the point I wonder if they are even able to see what the rest of us are seeing!It's not a game that just has a few bugs. It's a game in which you will never be able to tell if it's a bug, a feature, or you're just doing it wrong, or some setting randomly reverted. Most of the discussions you'll find while searching are back from 2022 when the game was even more broken. Even then, the developers waffled on everything and mostly told us we were just doing it wrong. You can, and will, put a Herculean amount of effort into this game to try to get it to a state where you can just play, or even just get a basic understanding of its systems. Not to mention you will find things constantly throughout playing which aren't doing what you thought, or what was logical. It's irritating and tiresome and should not take that much energy to enjoy a game in a genre in which I am extremely familiar. They need to put this game in front of your average 13 year old (or adult) and see how long it takes them to actually have fun. It won't be quick. Maybe I'll revisit this later and give the game a chance to change my mind.

_childDocuments_.review: Starts with everything, ship design; economy; diplomacy; research; battles automated and it runs itself. You can choose to then manually control anything or everything. You can even automate parts of what you manually control (which unfortunately can lead to misunderstanding). The more you understand the better it becomes and you can tailor the game to play the way you want. Hate micro managing, DW2 is the game for you; love micro managing, DW2 is the game for you.Unique (nothing like Stellaris, Galciv or X4) and is an independently fantastic game.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: A truly unique game. Be warned - this is not a 4X like you've played before. Instead, events play out in real time across hundreds or more systems. The economy is a huge motivating factor in the game, as it should be - you seek to expand to grab new resources, set up new mining stations, and enrich your planets. An entire private economy works beside your military fleets. You're generally intended to play with a degree of automation - fleets can be set with certain orders for example, like to "Defend with X range of system Y, only engage if you have the advantage", etc. Trade, construction, espionage, diplomacy, it's all modeled. It's a lot of game and there's a steep learning curve but there's a lot of reward to be had.The main downside in my eyes is the lack of attention paid to UI and graphics. The game is not a looker. It's a shame because I think a UI consultant/contractor could do a lot of good work here even on simple things like making more attractive menus and buttons. The ship graphics for sure could use a boost - as a space conquest game, part of the fun should be seeing your beautiful fleets drop out of warp and open fire, but the dated ship graphics really undermine it.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Have only played a few hours, but really liking it so far! As a total newbie to Distant Worlds, I'd recommend setting all automation to manual in the beginning in order to get a sense of how everything works under the hood, and then, one-by-one, automating parts that don't interest you and that would be better handled by the AI. My first game I started with the default settings and it felt too much like the game was playing itself with no idea of what was even going on.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is the long awaited remake of the original. The new Distant Worlds faithfully upholds the content, scale, tech tree and feel of the original to a level of fidelity generally unseen in version 2.0 games. Quite frankly the game is a dream to play and if you played Distant Worlds 1, you will slip right in. Such replay-ability and depth. Focus on commanding a squadron/fleet of ships and let the automation look after the rest. SimCity the Galaxy focusing on colonisation, resource distribution and logistics and leave the fighting to the AI. Or, in my case, find a middle ground where I dip in and control some elements. Fleet engagements where I see the need or want to see things go boom. Prioritise mining installation construction to focus on a key resource. Manually control an explorer to investigate an interesting location. Set taxation rates on fringe worlds to encourage growth. Focus my spies on technology or strategic details on a hostile empire. The list goes on.In Distant Worlds 2, you get to be the true Leader of a empire that spans 100s of stars, with in game AI support to support you as you scale up.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game but far from done it feels like. Buy with cautionEdit : Gave the game another go after the Fleet update. It's better... but there's something that's just not clicking for me. The music is meh at best. So many sound effects are missing. You click on a ship or a fleet and nothing happens, nothing is being said, you can't even know if your click registered, and that's true for almost  everything the UI. The mid to late game is severely lacking in challenges. It doesn't seem like the AI has any catch up mechanics, once you get the ball rolling, it's over. And it's not super hard to get the ball rolling either, click yes pretty much everytime a prompt pops up and everything works just fine. I'd give this game a "maybe" if such a rating existed, but I'll leave my Yes on just because I did play it for 70+ hours. I just have the feeling the game could be so much... more! I hope the Devs keep working on it.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: After playing many hours in the beta, and bouncing off the "final" product, I've returned after the "Aurora" update and I'm pretty frickin' wowed by how much better this game feels. Had this been the game that released, I'm certain it would have been received much better. The user interface is light-years beyond Distant Words 1. The performance has finally leveled out and I don't have any problems in the mid to late-game. The combat is much better than DW1. Hell, everything aside from the amount of races and the border gore is better here in Distant Worlds 2 than it was in DW1. BOTH OF WHICH CAN BE FIXED. This is finally a game I can easily and happily recommend. Here's to another 400+ hours in the Distant Worlds' Universe (pun intended).
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Oh I have waited. Distant Worlds Universe came to me as a great surprise. The level of depth, complexity and grandness, combined with the excellent level of automation was simply mindblowing. The only thing bothering me with DWU was the old fashioned graphics and the GUI. So I waited for DW2.Now it is here, and it is improving lots of the "old" aspects I was missing with DWU.Sorry to say though, it also introduces some new things.I am not going to list everything, but short to say it is a little "to grand" now, and it is missing some essential mechanics like queing orders (assigning a list of systems and planets to explore by ctrl clicking the suns might be a solution), it is a little to much waiting game... based on the pure size of everything... and some stuff has been remove that reduce the immersion I experiences in DWU.But all in all, it is a great 4X experience. It is not as complete as Stellaris, but it might get there. And I hope they will keep on improving it. For 4X fans, I suggest trying it, but go into it with a easy-going mind that thing IS different from other games. For not-so-much-fans-of-4x, this might just be to grand...

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a relaunch of the first game with some reinterpretations:While the first game did motivate you to use automation until you learn to do it yourself, the second game motivates you to automate anything, as there is nothing to decide anyway.I want to love this game. _childDocuments_.review: Currently the game is still unfinished, and will crash to the desktop without warning, even on the smallest galaxy setting and with pre-warp start.Other then that, from what i have seen from the gameplay, it seems when this will be done, this will be just Distant Worlds 1 with prettier graphics and a bigger tech tree. Of course i imagine for a lot of people, that is exactly what they are looking for, and fair enough. If the crashes were fixed, this would be a decent game.Sadly, that is what it will ever be as it looks like. No extension of the gameplay (In fact, until playable pirate factions will be implemented, this offers less as DS1. ), no new exciting mechanics or perspective. I understand why the makers did not want to take any risks, and a better looking Distant Worlds is something i wished for myself as well. I just hoped they would also try an extension of the 4x formula, or game mechanics that go into a more interesting direction. The game is still fun to play (Until it crashes again after you were lulled into a false sense of security and forgot to keep saving every 10 minutes, because it seemed to run ok for a few hours.), especially playing an early pre-warp civ and its first steps into space when you do not have to rely on the automation yet.But as it is, even if the crashes were fixed, it would still not be worth the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I thought this game had potential. After several days I realized that this game isn't fun because it has serious design problems. The game's unique automation seems cool at first, but I realized that it's a band-aid to fix the ridiculous micro requirements.By that I mean, most of your time will be spent doing pointless "busy work". For example, if you want to invade a planet, you build the troops, build the transport, load the troops on the transport waiting for a bunch of small shuttles to load them slowly, move the transport from one fuel station to the next until you reach the target planet (running out of fuel means your ships are effectively gone for several months as they crawl to a fuel station at snail's pace). Compare that process to a game like Stellaris where you just build the troop and click on the target planet and everything just works. Even mining is a pain. You build a mining station and wait for freighters, which the AI controls, to move it from the mine to your spaceport. So you end up with situations like: have 20 mines for resource X but have a shortage of X because the freighters haven't brought it back to your station. Tons of it are stuck in your mine b/c there's not enough freighters or something else you can't control. Since there's 20-ish strategic resources, you're almost guaranteed to have a shortage of something. Then you just wait around a few months and hope it's fixed over time. By then I've completely forgotten what I was trying to do.Yes, these mechanics are more realistic but they're not fun. Why do I need to manually worry about refueling every ship along a route instead of just having it worked into a range limit and speed? Why do I need to load colony ships, transports, etc instead of having them preloaded? I end up using their automation, not because it's cool or good, but because there's no way I can manage this much micro without it. The game forces you to play every role from general down to the ship driver. It's just not fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: DW2 has a nearly limitless number of automation systems to help run your empire. None of those automation systems work as intended and you slowly find this out as you play more. This results in you slowly changing one system after another to "manual" meaning you have to do more and more manual clicks on tedious things rather than enjoying the strategy. The automated systems appear to be both the linchpin and Achilles heel of the game. DW2 appears to have released way too early, too incomplete, and too buggy.

_childDocuments_.review: I can now send fleets to manully attack things. The automation is still doing poor job at multiple things. Almost every game is the same. There are some distinctions between races, which along with higher difficulity is the only thing that actually can make you play more then 1-2 playthroughts. I cannot still recommend it with current price, lack of decent UX and amount of crashes it does.- original review -This game is both great and terrible at the same time.Being fan of Sci-Fi games, this one brings lots of promises. The promise of automation and 'living universe' is grand, and it almost allows you to spectate things when setting everything on auto. Almost. Because, when you want to just do that one single thing manually, you need to dig through unofficial guides, discord channels and steam discussions to find the CORRECT automation settings that will allow you to do just that. Like attack pirate base with your fleet.On top of that, there is a great deal of stuff which makes you just irritated playing the game.Wars are disorganized mess of different class of units warping in with different speeds, and getting slaughtered. I don't really see the point in smaller combat vessels as well, because they barely allow you to do any damage. The game is full of bugs, at the time of writing this just happend to see that 'defensive pack' just doesn't work. And there is no way to invite ally to join you in war or wage war against someone. There are milion of strategic resources, which just gives some bonuses. We could just get rid of 2/3 of them, buff existing by 2/3 and the gameplay will be exactly the same.There is a lack of automated settings, like automatically migrating races that are unsuitable for specific planet.Finally, there are random crashes here and there, but from what I read its not like everyone will get them, im just unlucky one here - Zoom in, crash. Click some icon, crash. Not too often, but can happend once or twice during a 2-3 hours session.The good parts?The automation settings are grand, so you can automate most of the boring, mundane things. Want to have a meaningful spies - just set the correct targets, select missions you'd like to run, and feel cozy sitting in your starbase and getting all that enemy techs stolen. Absolutely the best out of any X4/GSG I encountered. Same with building these mining stations, or recouping fleet losses and troop loses. The colonies you get really allow 'tall' play. Most of new colonies won't bring anything except influence range for the next 20-50 years. And only then if your homeworld is a tad crowded and passanger ships brings up migrants. You can design every ship and base type, which means you can make these mining stations into heavy fortified outpost that will make any pirate run for his life.Overall: It still need a lot of polish and a lot of bugfixing to justify the current price. The graphics are kinda outdated, so if you're looking for fluff its not for you. The automation settings for fleets gets in the way of manually controlling the fleets more often then not.

_childDocuments_.review: It's still a mixed experience, but stil its unmatched. The "private economy" is one of these special features - all goods are really transported around - by a private economy. They build ships and trade those goods to or from other empires and within your empire.The other feature that makes DW:2 great: The possibilities to configure how much you want to control yourself. Leave everything to assistant? Possible - just control a single ship, while assistant managed the empire? Sure! Technically still not 100% stable - i experienced a crash a day (but those days involved many hours of having the game running).If you look for a complexity monstrum with a large scale - and the ability too zoom in from galaxy to a single ship (no seperate system maps like in Stellaris), then it might be for you. Quite CPU demanding.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is an enjoyable slog. It seems overwhelming but it is not. It seems complex but it can be boiled down to simple commands. It is a more hands off game. The number one thing I learned is "Don't Worry". Are pirates bugging you? Don't worry, you'll crush them in time. Is diplomacy a joke? Don't worry, they're spy fodder. Did a hive creature just eat a mining station? Don't worry, eventually your space stations will make sushi out of them. Just sit back and watch the pretty numbers jerk around, and your searches to complete. Click on everything you can mine or anywhere you can put a research station (tourist stations are rarely worth it), don't forget monitor stations can be put where you are not, and finally select every creature to investigate; even if it takes several years for your military to finally bugger off.

You'll probably do a couple restarts after you figure out a few new things and get the hang of it, but you'll have a blast as you do.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played the first game quite a bit. But I just really don´t see much of a reason to play this. There is apart from graphics almost no real difference to the first game. None of the major downsides were improved. Factions feel as bland as previously for instance with essentially no difference between species and government types. The UI is somewhat improved but still terrible and the game is still quite bad at telling you what is going on. If you have the first game there is no reason to get this. Sure graphics have been massively imporved but 0 times 10 is still 0. You probably don´t care about graphics much if you play games like this and the graphics are hardly good enough to justify buying it.People also like calling this game deep. It´s not really all that deep. There is a lot in this game but these features generally have the depth of a puddle. Very few things in this game are more interesting than some stat changes. It´s a very straightforward 4x. As someone who plays Auroroa 4x this is far closer to Stellaris than that. And of course Stellaris has great visuals and immersion not to mention the great and simple to understand UI going for it. This does not. For the price I can´t recommend it and frankly if you have thew first game there is almost no reason to play this instead even if it were free.

_childDocuments_.review: Will echo some of the other negative reviews and say I'm struggling to find the 'game' part of DW2. My only meaningful interactions with the game seem to be setting up tech research and upgrading ships to use said tech. Perhaps if I were to reduce the amount of automation I'd have more to do, but I feel that just creates more chores rather than engaging gameplay.Its a shame since the whole private sector part of this game is oddly fascinating to me and creates a real space empire management feeling that other games in the genre lack. There is potential here and I will keep an eye on the ongoing development, but ultimately its hard to recommend a game where I spend most of my time waiting for something to happen.

_childDocuments_.review: My review as of beta version 1.1.0 (long read)I initially bought this game back at launch to support developer, but I knew that it would take a while for it to get "up to speed" with the first game. I played Distant Worlds Universe a little, so I knew that I would like the new game. I also have experience with Stellaris, Endless Space 1 & 2, Shadow Empire and Civilization and a bunch of other 4x. I waited for a year until the game seemed to be good enough, and I jumped right at the latest 1.1.0 beta update. There were IMMEASURABLE amount of bug-fixes and updates to it - I kept track of it. I thought that maybe this is the time to try it out, and boy I was right. If you like sologame simulation heavy 4x strategies this game can definitely get you interested. It is broad, detailed, and does a lot of things so much better than similar titles. Its main focus is warfare and "trade routes" management, so if you like deep population economy system like in stellaris it might be lacking in that department. Luxury resources just add bonuses to population growth / hapiness, and there is not much flair to that yet. Still, this game does something that no other 4x dared to - simulation of every civilian ship moving the cargo and passengers within your space empire. This unprecedented level of detail for economy is something I really like, because in the endgame your empire feels alive with all these little shuttles zipping around. These ships can be attacked by pirates or cosmic fauna, they do things on their own without your intervention and you need to protect them from all nasty things that galaxy might throw at them. What I find most important in this game is that because of how deep the simulation is your choices matter. Gameplay example - You enhanced your ships with new hyperdrives? Well now they can react faster to pirate raids, and you can finally stop paying them tribute. Unfortunately there is no "refueling" point down the road to your latest outpost, so fleets literally can't get there in one jump. Which means that you now either need to create a separate fleet to protect this new outpost or sign a protection agreement with pirates so that they stop bothering you. This interactivity of choices is really welcome.Another gameplay example - I started the game trying to peacefully coexist with pirates. Some pirate faction proposed me to buy a datacube with interesting info for large sum of money - I thought that it might be useful in the long run. To cut it shortly the cube was a fluke, and my demands for money return were met with laughter. Obviously I started doing everything possible to exterminate these scumbags, but their base location was uknown, and to add to the insult they used money that I gave them to buy 2 top of the line destroyers and started raiding my possesions. My ships were to slow to catch them, and even with manual maneuwering of fleets thier shields were too tough for my weapons, I was unable to make a dent in pirates hulls. I realised that I need more punch to my weapons, so I needed to tech rush, which in turn mean that I need to scout for suitable locations for research bases. After researching good scouting equipment I created 20+ explorers and they started to move from one system to another, slowly reveling research locations. I was raided without mercy, but it became principal to deal with these dorks, also judging by which bases were raided I was able to gauge approximate location of their base and moved my fleets so that I would intercept their raid attemtps. After 20 years of tech rushing and retrofitting my fleet I was ready to deal with them, but unfortunately their base was really far from my homeworld, which meant that by the time my fleet got to the pirate lair system ships fuel was mostly gone. Third of my fleet stranded without fuel on the edge of the system, while most of the ships initiated fight with destroyers. I still was unable to quickly crack them open, but at least we got into a stalemate this time, which meant that as long as I keep my fleets engaged these destroyers fuel would just run out. When it became clear that pirate cannot win this engagement it tried to jump out of the fight, and just by pure luck it jumped straight into my ships stranded at the system edge. They were able to anchor it just for the time needed for my main force to finish the ship. This is what I meant by "choices matter". ------------------------------------------Gameplay pillars of 4x games - Explore, expand, exploit, exterminateExplore This game certainly is less intricate than stellaris in its events and discoveries, but it still has some lore and events here and there. Expand The "tall" vs "wide" gameplay is very pronounced due to your border system being at risk of raids at all times. Newfound colonies require vast funding until they would became productive, so pacing yourself while expanding is of critical importance. The planets differ by their quality and habitability to different races, the system overall is good enough.ExploitOne of the strongest gameplay systems in this game - every planet / asteroid can be a source of precious resources required for your empire growth. Population on planets can be enslaved to work for you, and protecting your investments is of highest importance.ExterminateSpace combat aspect is the strongest thing in this game, with planet invasion combat being less intricate but still good enough - comparable to ES2 you have rock/ paper/ scissors situation with army. Overall this game is very well suited for warfare.---------------------------------------Comparison with StellarisI have 550+ hours in Stellaris. I really like this game, spent a lot of great time with it.The game is beautiful, and as of 3.7 update is a joy to play. It is very visual, and have better interface than this game. That said, DW2 have much better fights simulation (In stellaris there is almost no tactics to fleets engagement, and no ship captures are possible) - for example the placement of your ships matters due to weapons having limited arc of shooting. This makes maneuvering drives important. The weapons are not just "DPS shootas", they matter enough to be impactful if you counter your opponent build. The ships components can break down in the battle, and make them useless. The ship warp drive might consume more energy than reactor produces, making the ships slower than what they should be. I would say that Stellaris is for the times you want to build space utopias, while DW2 is for the times you want a slugfest. ----------------------------------Cons- Simplistic graphics- No interaction with planets population besides taxing them, no deep "jobs" management like in stellaris- No way to queue actions with Shift, not a big deal considering amount of automation- Somewhat hard to understand logic behind fleet stances and automations- This game probably require you to read the guide first. - Besides 3 super luxury resources no resource feels "impactful" to your empirePros - Relatively dependable AI (just dont let it build research stations and mines outside of your "defense perimeter")- Detailed private economy with ships moving cargo everywhere- REALLY detailed space warfare, where different ship components matter- It can be a glorified screensaver (set your empire to total automation and no input is needed from you at all)Its a shame that this game has "Mixed" review due to the state it was launched in, and I want it to change. Gamedev supported the first game with frequent updates for a long time, and I have no doubts he will continue doing that with 2nd part.

_childDocuments_.review: I held off on trying DW2 for a long time. DW1 is one of my favourite games of all time, and I wasn't sure whether the depth of that game would fully translate to the sequel. DW2 is a thoughtful iteration on the mechanics of the first game, and while I think the first game does some things better (pirates are more fleshed out, for example), at this point of the development I think DW2 is the superior title. Give it a try if you want to try a space 4x with a compelling and dynamic model of galactic economy, lots of room for experimentation in combat, and the ability to fine tune what parts of the enormous empire simulation you are controlling at a given time. DW2 still has its rough edges, the most obvious being in the presentation of flavour text. You can tell it's developed by a tiny team, but that makes it even more of a triumph in my eyes.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is my Game Of The Year 2022 for sure.After a rough release with a lot of problems the devs invested a lot of work and time into fixing the crashes and performance issues.It has by far the best automation options in any game I have seen so far which allow you to learn all the mechanics at your own pace and volition. No micro-manage overload needed! In this game you really can feel like the leader of a sprawling empire full of different branches. You have an economy that you can influence but not control. You have Admirals and Ship Captains that actually use their fleets/ships on their own. You give them the mission, they try to finish it.The research tree is massive without being overwhelming. There are species-specific techs as well as techs for every corner of your empire.All in all I enjoy this game so much that I produced videos since its release until the end of the year and beyond. Enjoying every new patch and looking forward to what the devs and modders will bring to it in the future!Definite recommendation if you enjoy grand strategy.
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. I cannot stop playing it. Its very difficult in my opinion and it requires a great deal of time to figure out how things work. At first glance I did not immediately like the UI, but its grown on me a lot. It actually has a ton of functionality and its pretty well thought out. I felt that ship design is satisfactory. Its not like DW:U, but honestly that's a good thing. It was just plain broken in DW:U. Ship design in DW2 is more restricted, but better balanced. Late game you can still do some crazy things.Progression in DW2 feels really complex. Like there can be many ways to develop your empire. Should you focus on technology, or growth? Should you spy, or trade tech? You can also customize the galaxy in many ways to completely change the feel of a game. Pleasing all empires seems impossible, making friends with some upsets others. Are pirates using you? Or are you using them? My favorite feature of this game is the surprises. There are things hidden all over, like in nebulas, or after taking an empires capital, or a pirates base. You can end up acquiring artifacts, and other things, that provide big bonuses. My biggest complaint is performance. It can be improved by turning off various settings like lens flair, hiding ships, and making sure to close certain menus as to not keep tons of objects highlighted. I also get the odd crash here or there, but they are quite rare, only one crash in my current 20+ hour game, they only happen when i zoom in to a planet so its not totally random.Nebulas seem to cause a huge performance drop, reducing them at game start may help. Also nebulas seem to be a bit broken at the moment as I cannot colonize anything in them no matter the distance from another colony.Also, colonization max range should be dependent on tech, not game settings! I really hope they improve fleet automation, and just automation in general. We need more settings.

While the AI is capable of running your empire for you, I would recommend handling certain areas such as warship design manually, as the AI is better at some things than others. Overall, a great game and a good return on my money.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply amazing. The otherwise ginormous learning curve has been granularized by the out of the box automation of everything in the game. You can learn by observing what is going on and gradually take control of areas as you get more confident and minimize the otherwise equally gigantic micromanagement soup. The graphics are an adorable splendor that I have never seen the likes of in space themed strategy games before. I mean, you can see the lights from cities on continents on the dark side of colonized planets, and you can see the atmosphere, you can even see clouds forming, dissapating and morphing around. Looking at a star, I realized, for the first time, that these behemots are gasfilled balls of fire. The game itself breaks a boundary for me between my understanding of what turn based versus real time means. The game is both actually. The time runs, and then you can pause it (or it gets paused) at events that you can then spend some time on, either in real time or in a paused state (turn based-like). This makes for a whole new experience, one that takes the best from both genres and kind of intermingles them. It's as if you could pause time and use an appropriate amount of careful deliberation on your next moves, before you resume it and watch the effects. I love it. As mentioned in some of the reviews of this game, there are still stuff that needs expanding on, but the possibilities and potential seem vast. The customization proces of the ingame universe in all its splendor is truly impressive, and the scale of things is out of this world. That there has been placed an equal amount of care in the grand scale aswell as the minutiae details of the close encounters in this world, gives this sense of actually being there. You need no more star wars or star trek, you can go to this game and get the real thing, the entire awesome and incredible cosmos. Now I hope what I have seen so far in the game continues and gets better as I play on, but even if it should not, the experience of what I have already seen in the game, is like taking a sky dive for the first time and feel weightlessness, - it's a game changer.

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps the most conflicted I've ever felt about a game. I really wish they have an "Eeeeeeeeeeh" rating. I haven't played DW:Universe (the previous game) so my perspective is relatively fresh.Pros:*Tons of fun designing ships and determining fleet doctrine. There's so many weapon paths you could conceivably play 20 games and never use exactly the same trees.*Excellent in game wiki that explains most concepts (although some are missing).*Highly customizable automation interface. You can rule in absentia in this game, and that is hilarious.*You really feel like you're managing a huge empire with dozens of science and construction ships, which the civilian economy and their ships really reinforce. I like to stress this point, because this is really where the game's advantages over, say, Stellaris lie. By the time I reached 1/10th of all galactic territory, I had more government ships than an entire galaxy in Stellaris, and my Civillians were legion.*I like the pirates. No real reason, I just think they're funny. Giving them military refueling and putting them in contact with all my enemies, then watching their reputations drop as their ships raid the heck outa them will never cease to amuse me.Cons:*The automation AI can sometimes be remarkably stupid. Please stop loading temperate species colonists onto the ships bound for ice worlds. This nearly bankrupted my empire before I could fix it.*The automation AI sometimes overrides you decisions and make bad decisions as a result. STOP BUILDING BARRACKS, I ONLY NEED 1 TYPE NOT EVERY SINGLE ONE.*The game is laggy and prone to crashes. Really laggy. The research screen is somehow the laggiest thing of them all, and it's not even rendering 500 civilian ships! I've only crashed a couple times, but good grief.*Diplomacy needs a real rework. I can be 400k score positive in a war with an empire and blockading all their planets, and they won't sign anything more valuable than "White peace and we give you some tech". Frankly, foolish reptile, if I weren't a democracy I'd be bombarding your planets into extinction. They really need an option of " Cede these systems and the stations therein to us". I'd have taken "You're my tributary now"! If you love 4x games and have a PC designed to fistfight God, buy now and work through the bugs. If you're still interested, give it 3 months and come back. If you despise jank in all it's forms, yeah maybe don't.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - I recommend Distant Worlds 2, but this game needs work. If you are looking for an in-depth Stellaris, or are a big fan of 4X Grand Strategy, this is the game for you.With that out of the way, here are my thoughts on my first ~10 hours of gameplay, where I have yet to complete a full playthrough.Pros:- A deep lore filled Universe- Colorful UI with deep menus that give you deep levels of control- A good community and active developers looking to make the game better (Active Discord server with support threads and bug reporting)- Decent automation AI that gives you control over multiple levels of systems, or AI control- Interesting democracy dynamics- Fully simulated civilian systems, with your own to compliment- Customizable galaxy size, shape, density- Win conditions are set by the player at the outset- AI is challenging and can be fun to play against- Time suck (yes this is a pro) as I find myself deeply involved in the decisions of my empireCons:- AI can be a bit hard to deal with at the outset, specifically when dealing with fleet automation- The later you go in the game, the higher the load on your CPU (as everything is simulated real time)- Combat can be frustrating sometimes when your ships decide to break formation even with tight formations set- I have not seen any crashes, but my game has frozen a couple of times- Once everything in your galaxy is explored, it does lead to the mid-end games, but that culminates in you completing your objectives to win AKA, no TRUE twists later on- The border system still confuses me, and what dictates "your owned systems" eludes me- Combat can be rather dull at times- Lack of empire creation/customization outside of modding one into the game- Repetitive musicOverall, this has been a fun game so far, and, similar to other 4X titles, I can see myself putting hours upon hours into the game. As mentioned, there needs to be some work done before I can say the $49.99 USD price tag is fully worth it, but I believe fully that the development team and the community will propel this game into even greater success than its predecessor.

_childDocuments_.review: Comparing this to Stellaris is a bit misleading; it's neither a multiplayer nor built around matched competitive play even in single player. Customisation is immense and though at the start the gamut of automation may appear to suck the fun out of things, it's very much a crutch for either new players or those looking to just chill and simulate. Even with most things automated player agency is still very much important, afterall if Paradox AIs are any standard to go by nothing can compare to a player's ability to long-term stratergise. Research tress are immense and complicated, very few of which are simple number boosts. Graphics are amazing for the depth of the game and surprisingly ships do change appearance based on loadouts.TL;DR this is very much a Space SIM not a Stratergy Game. _childDocuments_.review: I've only got a few hours into the game but I will say that despite its complexity it's very approachable due to the numerous automation options. Definitely more approachable than Stellaris (which is an excellent game). Is it innovative? The functioning of the economy is certainly unique. Other aspects are just borrowed - the specialists are taken from Endless Space 2 or Civ. The research tree certainly looks like Gal Civ or Civ. Diplomacy is reminiscent of Gal Civ or Endless Space. The exploration is similar to Stellaris as is the ship design. That being said, borrowing ideas isn't bad - it all works. It's really nice to be able to automate almost everything and then only initially play what you want. For me, I just controlled the research and my fleet. As I get more familiar, I plan to take a bit more control from the AI. I will say that only the most hardcore player could ever play with everything on manual - too much. BUT, the option is there if you want to. The AI does a good job at controlling things for you which is nice. Still a definite thumbs up (8- 8.5/10).

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. I want to love the game. For those who have played the earlier incarnation of the game, I feel that you will not take a lot away from the newest incarnation of Distant Worlds. The game is certainly prettier to look at and after a few hotfixes in during the first week of release it finally runs well, even on a computer that has an older generation video card (1660 Ti). The game remains an incredibly dense 4x, which runs optimally the more you allow your burgeoning empire to run itself, much as its parent game. It is slow however and the ability to speed up the game is limited to a 4x speed, which means that plowing through the early game can be a bit of a slog as there is not a lot to do past sending out your scout and selecting which resources to exploit first. The pre-warp phase could be optimized to go a little quicker, as technological advancement moves at the pace of a one legged sloth.  As time goes on I may change my views on the game, but with less than a 24 hours of game play I think that it is worth playing for those who loved the original Distant Worlds, but it remains almost as obtuse for new players.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Get it if you have already been waiting for this game for years and just have to get a fill of DW - else wait.This game is a step in the right direction, the graphics and feel are improved and the UI is better. Game doesn't look like it's straight out of the 90s anymore and plays fine on all resolutions.Currently the biggest issue that I have with the game is performance - on a machine that should have zero issues - Ryzen 5950X, Nvidia 3090, 64G of RAM....like come on the UI should be responsive - and it's just not. I have no idea what the issue is - it sure feels like it's a bug - is this thing running in debug mode? CPU, GPU etc are all under 20% utilization and the game stutters...UI while an improvement is still not great - the automation is still sometimes less than helpful "Hey do I send the fleet X to Location Y?" - how about you SHOW me what was there so I can decide? Nope? I'm just going to roll the dice and send my fleet into a potential meatgrinder? Ok. Oh and after that an hour later you'll ask me to send another fleet into the same meat grinder and I'll do it again because of course I forgot that Location Y is a death trap. (They have the "Show Me" button for other options - but not this?)Economy is messy because as far as I can tell, I can't force automation to maintain a minimum balance.  Meaning I cannot set the AI to always leave say 300k in reserve so that I can spend it on things I want to do. Instead I either have to outright turn ALL automation off or watch my balance ping pong from -30k to 250k over and over all while I just want 300k to dump into research. The map is still a nightmare to read made worse by the poor performance of the game - some of the AI faction colors are so similar that it's hard to see who is who - seriously there are 4 AI in my game who are different shades of purple. 3 AI that are different shades of teal....I actually attacked the WRONG purple base once when in a war with a different purple faction..I'm still enjoying the game because - well I'm a huge fan of the concept - but the technical issues and lack of polish really spoil the experience. I suspect that 3 years and 2 DLCs later this will be totally worth it for everyone, but right now I can't recommend it to anyone who wasn't already looking forward to DW2.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the new Distant Worlds. I would give this a "Hold off until initial bugfixes" if I could, but I would definitely recommend the game over not recommending it currently.I played the old DS1 (DSU) and that game was good. I was quirky and corny at times, with almost cartoonish civs, but I loved the systems and how the game played in general. It was only the discovery of Stellaris that got me to stop playing DS1.This game really has much more depth to it and customization than just about any other 4X I've seen, except for the lack of custom civilizations at this point. Hopefully that gets rectified, as that is a big sticking point. The start screen allows enormous amount of customization around the size, how many stars, and shape of the galaxy. You can even differentiate between AI and the player if you want to make the game easier... or harder.Everything can be automated. By this I mean the systems, your empire itself, how research works, your colonies, your ships, exploration, expansion, entire wars, everything. You can set everything in the game to be automatic if you wish, and you would basically be a passenger watching how the civ develops at that point.You can learn how systems work and take control of specific sections of different mechanics. You can even have the AI make suggestions for you on what to build, where to build, where to colonize, what ships to make. Many of these are intuitive, for example when building a mining station for asteroids, a white circle shows which asteroids will be covered by the station.They have a very similar ship and station designing system as Stellaris, where you can have it set to automatic and all of your ships and stations will be automatically upgraded AND automatically retrofitted. You can also make your own designs, and then watch as the AI goes to dutifully retrofit to the new design you created.Now, for the downsides. Bugs. Performance issues. Crashes. I will be clear: I fully expected these issues, and they are definitely present. I fully expect that these will be addressed, and my recommendation hinges upon them being fixed. If visual bugs and crashes will deter you, then just wait until these reports go away.The UI could also use a nice overhaul, but UI was never this developer's strongsuit. The UI is passable and won't be causing me any problems personally.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best 4x game (and generally one of the best games) I have played since Alpha Centari.This game has a lot of depth and is extremely satisfying.  It's a simulation that is fun to play, which I much prefer to the over "gameification" so prevalent in strategy games these days.  I love the espionage and ship design systems.The UI could be a bit better but is adequate.  It is a complex game and all the information is easy to find once you know where to look.The game is still under development and seems to be moving in the right direction.Note, this is simulating all the space traffic (civilian and military) in the galaxy.  It is a very resource intesive game.  The more CPU cores you have, the better.  I'm running an Intel 8700k (6 cores @3.7GHZ) and can comfortably run a galaxy with 700 stars.  They are recommending 12+ cores (24gigs of RAM) to run a 2000 star galaxy.  In a couple more years, when it is time to upgrade my PC, I will be choosing my CPU with this game in mind.Edit: 4/13/2024I've changed my review to do not recommend because the UI still has some major flaws that are not immediately apparent.  They won't become apparent until someone is well past the 2 hour mark.One of the major features of this game is the ability to design your own ships.  Each race has their own unique ships with their own unique capabilities.  Designing your ships could be a lot of fun.  However, because of the UI it is extremely tedious.The biggest problem comes with the way upgrades are handled.  The game recognizes hulls and roles.  The automated ship design will use one of those 2 (depending on what you've selected) to upgrade your ships.  However, there IS NO WAY TO DESIGNATE your own roles.  So if you are using the escort hull as a platform for several different roles you will have to manually create their upgrade paths every time you get new technology.  If you leave it to the automated system then all of your designs will converge to a single one.For example, lets say you have one escort design equipped with point defense to defend against fighters and missiles, you have another one set up with beam weapons for general combat, and a third set up with ion weapons and boarding pods to capture enemy ships.  You want to run this in a combined fleet.  The automated system will upgrade all 3 designs to the last one you created.  The way to avoid that is to turn off all the ship design and upgrade automation.  Each time you get a new piece of tech, whether it's a reactor, a better shield or armor, more efficient crew compartments, or better weapons you will have to manually create the new design and then manually connect the upgrade path.  It becomes extremely tedious very quickly.The solution is to allow the player to define their own roles.  For example: PD escort.  Now every time I create a new, better design for this role the already existing automated systems will do all the tedious work for me.This is such an obvious feature that I have seen a number of players in various forums ask for, that the developers have ignored.  Instead of making much needed upgrades to the UI they are tweaking already fully functional factions.Unless the faction they are tweaking is one you play yourself, you will not notice the difference.  However, you will notice the poor UI regardless of what faction you are playing.

_childDocuments_.review: On release I put about 125 hours into the game and have recently returned to the game (as of late 2024)The game shines in that you can set up auto-matic realm management. You can either have the AI Do tasks without notifying you OR suggesting and then auto-executing OR Suggesting and then not doing anything unless you approve OR Disabling Automation for manual mode. All aspects of the game can be automated in this way. From taxes all they way down to the lowly constructor ship and on up to entire fleet creation.It is reminiscent of Sim City games where the city council would suggest you build power poles in the city to supply power. You would then manually have to go and place those poles to provide power to specific areas on the map.In Distant Worlds 2 you don't have to bother with that granularity of completing a suggestion manually (unless you want to) because in the game as soon as a suggested pop-up happens and you approve it the AI takes over and completes the task without your further intervention. You can sit back and tend to other tasks or just watch as your approved orders are carried out.  The gameplay happens when your orders encounter speed bumps such as hostiles, TECH walls, Fleet logistics, ETC...You can fiddle while Rome is burning or you can lead a valiant flight of handcrafted fleets into battle and smash the hordes of barbarians at the gate. It is all up to you in this well-crafted sandbox.

_childDocuments_.review: Revision 4/23/2022:After a few weeks and another 15 hours of playtime, I have decided it's my moral obligation to update this review and turn my thumbs down to an up.My primary reason for this is due to the diligence of the developer and their solid efforts and real progress in supporting this title and addressing some of its technical issues.Also I must acknowledge that some of my own game settings and play choices contributed to some of my performance issues, as well as my own machine's specifications.With that said, since this review was originally posted, I was able to play a save for over 3 hours until it crashes.  The situation has improved substantially, and it is obvious that this developer is dedicated to providing continuing support to this title.Which is really a good thing - I want to see this game succeed and age like fine wine.  It is truly incredible how detailed and dynamic this 4X real time simulation gets.  The granularity and options for different strategies and playstyle are amazing to behold.I want to commend the developers for their effort and progress on improving this title since launch and can say resolutely that I am a happy owner and that it is worth the money despite the issues.Happy conquests!Original review:I've played several games of Distant Worlds 2, and at this point feel able to submit a partially informed opinion:TL;DR:  This is an awesomely deep real time grand strategy 4x game, with compelling systems and a robust suite of AI management features that let you scale the level of complexity that you have to personally deal with to the point that the game will literally play itself.  However, technical issues often prevent the game from scaling to endgame without crashes or performance problems and eventually make your empire progressively slower and more frustrating to grow.  Needs fixes, optimization, and maybe mods.This title is doing something very interesting with insane depth and detail that is able to be managed passably well by an AI.  It makes it possible to approach and learn this complex grand strategy at your own pace without overly diminishing your enjoyment of the game.  Don't know what's going on?  It's ok, you can relax - the AI is managing the details, you can pick and choose what to learn.However, the title is marred by considerable technical issues that impact the late game experience.  I have three games and a victory in one of them on the lower difficulties.  Even the smallest galaxy size and only 3 opposing empires still results in a late game experience that chugs at best.  I suspect it has something to do with the fact that your private economy is constantly building little NPC freighters and cruise liners and the like to move people and resources around behind the scenes, and as the empires in the game all balloon in size and logistical complexity, the game seems to bog down.  In my smallest match, I would crash twice every hour around the time all the other empires are discovered and finished expanding.  Even with autosaves, this has resulted in lost time and progress every time.  Crashes are frequent.As wonderful as a game as this is to play, and as awesome as the AI-management and sense of vast scale and complexity gets, this title is facing technical issues related to optimization, performance, and stability.I'm hoping that these issues get fixed and it becomes a more fully playable title.  Scaling up your empire endlessly is incredibly addictive and compelling until something in the code or my CPU starts melting.I really want to recommend it as this is a great grand 4x RTS with amazing vision.  But my experiences trying to play it have been too fraught with technical issues to put my seal of approval on this title.  I wouldn't tell a friend to buy it because I don't know if it'll even work well enough for them to ever finish a full match without frustrating numbers of crashes.I'm keeping this title around with no regret and keeping an eye on it.  I'm hoping some combination of continued patching or mods eventually causes the performance and stability issues to settle into something a bit smoother.  When I pick it up again next to check it, if it works better, I'm going to change this review to a thumbs up.  But for now, it's a thumbs down.
