_childDocuments_.review: Full-disclosure, my first review was negative due to a game-breaking bug. I made a stink about it on the forums, submitted some reports, and the devs are now fixing it. So, this game is very buggy but the devs do seem to give a damn, it seems like it's been getting better over the few years it's been out. --This game is extremely interesting. I've definetely never played anything quite like it. To get the obvious part out of the way immediately, the economy is in fact pretty complex. It's not too complex - easy enough to understand if you pay attention to what all the little ships are actually doing. It took me about 30 hours and a few failed runs to grasp most of the systems, but this game does have a helluva learning curve. I'd say it hits the sweet spot of being just complex enough with no smoke and mirrors, but not so complex that it all becomes meaningless noise.I played a lot of Stellaris at release, before eventually realising it was an incredibly shallow and unfulfilling experience. The comparisons to Stellaris are apt, as I essentially see this game as a deeper, less polished version of that.I'll start with the good:- Depth. Depth makes a great 4x game, once you learn how it works. This game hits the sweet stop of being deep enough that I never felt the need to speed up time, and always had something to manage, something somewhere that could be optimised, some ship that could be micro'd, some diplo or spying that could be done. Sometimes, even watching civilian ships go about their business can engaging. The military side of things isn't just blobbing, ship design means something and fleet positioning/tactics makes a difference. - AI seems strong enough, They consistently do well on normal difficulty, which according to the devs gives them no bonuses. At war, they'd attack my fleets when they were weak or in a bad position, and run away when it was clear they were losing the fight. My first war against the rats was looking like it would be a cakewalk as I had 4 fleets of heavily armed cruisers against their pitiful frigates, but they jumped on me as I was repairing and refuelling at a planet I just captured, and utterly destroyed my fleets. I didn't respect the AI, and it punished me. It's no genius, afaik, but it's no pushover either. - The SCALE. I've never seen anything like it. Stellaris just makes each system an 'instance' and lets you warp between them, but this game is actually just one big single map with all the planets and stars a (semi) realistic distance apart from each other. You can eventually pan to the next system without having to zoom out from the starting magnification - it'll take a bit, but you can do it. Ships without hyper-drives can theoretically fly to the next star at sub light speeds - it'll take them a hundred years, but without constant refuelling, they could do it. Ships are tiny little specs next to overwhelmingly huge planets and stars, and the vastness of space between planets - and stars - feels so real. It's wonderful.It's easy to understate how much of an impact this has. When the space you are colonising and warring over feels real, it's so much easier to connect with your empire and the sci-fi world that is unfolding before you. And outside size, there are just so many little freighters and patrol ships and pirates running around that the world you are playing it feels so much more alive then your typical 4x game. This is sort of a 'gamefeel' thing, but this game really feels like a SPACE game, whereas most Space 4x games feel so small.  It's a big issue with a lot of 4x; why build an empire if it nobody is living in it? This game solved that beautifully. And now, the bad. It's gonna look like the bad outweighs the good here, and in some ways it does, but I think those two strengths are so important that my overall review will remain the same. - Presentation is... rough. The art style is all over the place. Half the alien races have non-animated ugly portraits I believe are from the first game, thankfully all the playable ones look decent. The music is confusingly bad, I turned it off almost immediately. Little to no splash art showing the surface of your planets, the appearance of your cities, etc. Even little things like the generated names for planets and stars are all very uninspired. This is some of the most dry Sci-Fi i've ever seen. It's easy to say 'you're supposed to create the flavour through roleplay!" which works in games like Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld, etc. but I'd prefer an inoffensive but consistent artstyle (ie. Rimworld) over a jumbled mess, which ends up becoming distracting and immersion breaking. - The tutorializing is awful. For a game as complex as this, it needs a good on boarding experience. This game doesn't really have one. You'll get massive text-dumps that seem to repeat themselves a lot at game start. Expect the first 40 or so hours of this to be frustrating and confusing. - The UI sucks, controls are bad. It never feels like you can quickly navigate to where in the menu you need to be or find a ship you're trying to look at. So many tiny buttons that are difficult to click on, so much headache. It's not the worst I've ever seen, it's usable once you get the hang of it, but it's certainly very rough. Even the camera control seems janky. Zooming feels syrupy, quickly slowing to a crawl when you feel you aren't quite close enough, and zooming back out takes way to long. The immense scale does kind of drag you back here, admittedly; I do spend more time then I'd like panning or scrolling or navigating a mess of a menu to find that one ship in that one star system 400 lightyears away so I can click on it to jump to its location. Playable, but often janky. And finally, the one thing that should convince you not to buy this game unless you REALLY like the unique concept of it.  The bugs.This is one of those games you can't really trust. It has always been on the back of my mind with everything I do so far; every mission for every ship, every colonisation, every time I research some new gameplay-changing tech or launch an invasion... "What if it's bugged?" "Is this working properly?"To go back to the tutorializing problems, half the time I thought the game was bugging out was actually just poorly signposted intended behaviour, and half the things I assumed to be intended behaviour turned out to just be bugged. The bugs in this game are pervasive, and nearly game-ruining at time, and I've spent a lot of time troubleshooting and had to make a lot of forum posts asking "bug or am I stupid?" and the answer was usually "bug". I mentioned that the devs seem to care and actively fix things, so that's a big plus; I hate to imagine what this must have been like on release. The AI on the private economy that runs in the background is the most egregious example. Much as it is deep and fun to watch, sometimes civilian ships just do baffling things. Freighters seem to love picking up the one resource you don't need while your economy crashes and burns, for instance, and I don't think I've ever seen refuelling ships actually work as intended, they seem to have lobotomites as pilots. ---Overall verdict: it's good, but deeply flawed. Do not buy this game lightly, if you are not starved for the deep and meaningful space 4x as I have been since Stellaris crushed my dreams, give this a pass. If you aren't the kind of person who appreciates finer details and can forgive a shaky foundation and a lot of frustration, you will not enjoy this game.If the game does seem like a great concept and you think you can handle the jank, pick it up, though I recommend getting it on sale. I would NEVER pay 60 bucks for this beautiful hot mess of a game, but for the 40$ I spent including dlc? Yea, I don't regret my decision.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a very complex simulation running here, down to being able to check individual systems being used or damaged during combat. This is a slow burner. It will take time to figure out how to play. Give yourself that time. My first game i automated most of everything except research, and then took suggestions on that anyway. It helped figure out how things work, and the AI generally does a stellar job taking care of everything, but it's not a lot of fun just watching the game play itself. Instead, take this opportunity to understand what kinds of things you'd like to automate, and when. The automation itself is extremely modular, and you can set guidelines for entire categories of gameplay, or dive down to only set it for certain colonies, fleets, or characters when you tire of micro-ing them. You get to craft your own gameplay experience in this 4X, and you should. Don't complain about nothing to do if you're automating everything. Notifications can be set (or removed) as needed, if you feel like you still want some suggestions from the AI (or feel overwhelmed). It helps to play the game at 1x speed, and i've personally never gone above that. Just relax and watch your ant farm mill about while you call the shots, where you want to call them. There is plenty to do. I've personally not experienced a single technical hiccup with this game either so far. (Ryzen 7, 32gb, 1070)

_childDocuments_.review: A terrible sequel, marred by the leap to 3d.Distant Worlds Universe is a fantastic game, that allows you to control an Empire, as much as you like. It's entirely possible to automate everything or nothing at all. It's greatest weakness was the absence of a few Quality of Life features and late game performance issues.Sadly, this isn't Distant Worlds Universe. It's Distant Worlds 2. The devs, for reasons that make little sense to me, have opted to develop this game with a 3D engine. As a result performance is predictably worse than the previous title. The UI is somehow less intuitive and all of the old problems and foibles of the previous game have been realised anew. Now alongside new issues. A year after release and the game is still a hot mess, with terrible performance and bugs aplenty, features that don't work or work poorly. To their credit, they continue to chip away at it, but honestly, the damage was done in the early development stages and there is little they can do about it now.I very strongly recommend people avoid this title. It's not going anywhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is not terrible, not great.  I rate it a 7/10 if you are a new player (you don't miss what you never had) and 5/10 if you are coming from DW. I recommend buying it, if you love 4x but otherwise wait for either a better presentation of the game or lower prices. The modding community definitely is needed to correct some UI/AI/game play flaws of DW2 in its current state.Frankly I am disappointed with the release state but did not return the game. There are bugs but I am ok with that. I get its a small team and willing to let them iron the bugs out on a larger release due to system configs and such. My problem stems from the UI choices, weak AI, and 'dumbing down' of game play with generalizing of resources and their management, ship design, and focus on automation over manual control.   The positives are: the engine is 3d, the load time is seconds not minutes and some of the menu organization is excellent.UI choices:  There is no 360 all axis camera control.  Why make a 3d game world and then restrict the camera movement to the a locked Z axis and only rotation along the X and Y.  While in Ship Design mode you have full camera control. Obviously its possible in the game engine.  Further it is difficult to center the camera currently on a particular ship.  There is no button on a specific ships info screen to follow it.  This seems very odd that such a simple feature it left out (maybe I missed it, and if so please let me know where it is). Currently you have to fiddle with clicking on the ship model to have the camera follow it.  It does this occasionally and may be a current bug.  Also when a ship is selected sometimes you can bring up a menu for build choices when you right click on a destination planet (when there are multiple options) Example: Sometimes on home world at game start the explorer ship may access a menu allowing to either refuel or survey the planet.  Other times (before it has been surveyed) it just refuels with no options offered.  So again you have to fiddle with the selection process.  It is annoying but not game breaking.   ****EDIT I have learned that you can click or click & hold for menu options to appear or to center on an object and while there is no clickable option that I can figure out to set camera to follow object, you can, use the keystroke ( l ) to lock on the selected item.  It is still a little fiddly but it is workable******No search option in the Galactic Encyclopedia, in 2022 its just not acceptable to lack a word search.No comprehensive list of all ships that is sort-able, as the Research tree is sort-able. This is not terrible as you can find the various ships in their associated menus but you have to dig through them if you want to go from warship to constructor to explorer.The UI elements are locked in place and the game/windows can not really be spread across two monitors. This is a complex 4x game we should not only be able to adjust font to our screen settings but also move windows around to support individual game play and management.  This is not a huge issue but makes the UI feel more 2015 than 2022.Weak AI: It just is... the choices it makes are very limited and combat is predictable. This is disappointing given AI should have been significantly improved from DW.'Dumbing down' of management/game play:  Resources no longer divided between luxury and normal, and the miners harvest everything with a single mining component (maybe I am wrong here but it sure seems like that so far). Resource management really feels gamey in DW2. Ship Design is restrictive due to 3d models. Now this may change with expansions so I hold out hope and final judgement on this. In DW2 current state you are only able to add certain components to certain predetermined locations. I will say I do not like paying for DLC that improves basic and expected game play.I think the above 'dumbing down' is in order to gift the AI so automation is more reliable. So in essence the current game design looks to be leaning more toward automation while you occasionally turn it on and off to interact with the 'ant farm'.  Overall I am disappointed with the design choices given its 2022 and there are many 4x space games out there to consider and improve on. These choices do not seem to have been taken here or implemented well.  Its crazy that in some ways Aurora C# is still a superior game in management and design but that game is really Excel spreadsheets in space. I have hope DW2 will be patched up and brought into the future. Where it belongs. 4X SPACE PORN FOREVER!!!!!!!I recommend DW2 but with reservationsAll EDITS SO FAR ARE SPELLING AND GRAMAR MISTAKES

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is a great, great game. I have not played the first installment, but I've played a lot of other space 4X games.Distant Worlds 2 is complex in a good way. It is not visually as polished as Stellaris or Endless Space 2, but it has DEPTH. You have tons of tech to research, meaningful decisions to make at every turn and the combat is just fabulous. Last time I played this micromanagtement heavy, yet entertaining game was Space Empires IV and V. You can automate it. Even fully. You can go Master of Orion 3 and just let it play itself. One of the biggest strengths is that you can automate ANYTHING. For example I find spying tedius and I am not overy into heroes here. I let the game manage that and it's doing fine. I let it design and upgrade ship types I don't care so much about. I manually design my main combat ships. I may leave smaller fleets on auto to either defend a certain area or attack minor threats. But the biggest draw is combat. Oh my... The ship building and combat in this game is beyond fabulous. Why? Because it matters, makes sense and you can actually see very well and clearly if the choices you made make sense. For example the ship need so be properly rotated as the guns have firing arcs per hardpoint. Including PD. So if the enemy shoots at you, you need to be properly rotated in order to do something about it. Of course you need to be rotated to shooth yourself too. Nice, but not that impressive, right? Except you can also PD direct fire weapons. So where do yoo put your PD? And which type? Putting it on the front of a kiter could be wasted as they'll mostly try to run away from the enemy. What kind of weapons do you use? Short range? Okay. Do they have to bypass armor? Or shields? Or perhaps both? Are they AoE? Every shot you see and it counts. If you use AoE weapons, they explode in an area, as they are supposed to. You have EMP, counter EMP, boarding parties, fighters... You have it all... Standard three layers of defense, each interacts differently with wepaons and vice versa. And components have several version. Usually 2+. For example do you have economic reactors that are weak(er) or do you want supercharged fuel-hungry beasts? Well, if you go with the beasts, your fleet might end up standing on the spot waiting for refuels a lot more than you would like! Ever was stuck mid-invasion, because your ships can't more or fire? Yeah, that happens here a lot. Decisions, decisions. Did you chceck if you have resources the weapon you have reseached? Logistics and resources are super-vital. They are NOT just number in the upper bar. They are units somewhere in your cargo and you need to bring them to a station to buid a ship. Economy matters, logistics matters, techs matter, diplomacy matters.Downsides:- HORRIBLE music. Your ears will bleed.- At first unattractive graphics. Until you understand that what you see are actual models with the things you have designed. So not a placeholder.- UI is a fight at first. After you lean it, it's good. You just need to suffer through the muscle memory / memory part until you know where things are and how to get to them and control them.- May be had to get into. There is a juicy reward after that learning wall ("curve" doesn't do justice) though.- Fighters have same ultimate weapons for both interceptor and bomber. Personally, this is biggest letdown for me.- There is an issue with tankers. They supposedly work as they are supposed to, but the result is... ...well, you have to learn what is happening to understand it and hopefully manage it. Until then it's just pure rage when your fleet parks in front of enemy homeworld without fuel and your tankers go fishing instead of refuelling the fleet...This game is not really a rival to Stellaris or Endless Space 2. Each scratches a different itch. Distant Worlds 2 is very much about logistics, ship design, ship combat.It's awesome. If you are willing to work for it, go through the initial phase of confusion, leaarning and frustration, it's very much worth it! I hear some people enjoy it on almost full auto, so anything goes.EDIT: I have 100-200 hours more because I played the non-Steam version quite a lot as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Played Distant Worlds Universe and loved it for the asymmetrical play and freedom to do practically anything you liked? Well, don't look here for that. Basically everything that made DWU so unique and fun is dumbed down or just plain gone.In DW2 you CANNOT:- build wherever you like.  Want to stake a claim in a border system by building defensive bases around the resources? NOPE..have to have a settled colony to build around.- want to throw a lab module or two onto each mining station since they will be out there doing their thing anyway? NOPE, the lab module will only fit into the mining slot and then guess what, you have an invalid design. (yes this can be modded, but why does it have to be?)-Want to build research labs a-plenty to get a scientific edge and nearly go bankrupt pushing the limit of your economy in the name of science? NOPE.  You have to find a special ruin or obelisk or whatever to build around.- Want to go resource shopping on a list of explored planets and asteroids for that one item your economy needs? NOPE, there is no list like that in DW2 (that I can find). Shortages of materials didn't even seem to matter anyway.- want to try and slip in a mining station in a nearby system that your neighbors think is theirs? Nope, if it is in their sphere of influence, you just cant build there. Never mind that your hubris of trying to stake a claim would likely end up bloody anyway, you are just forbidden from doing so, you silly git!All that aside I figured lets try some good old warfare and invasion.  Should be simple enough take my entire fleet(s) and just click on an enemy planet and invade it, right?Declared war on a neighboring race of bugs who TOLD ME they were jealous of my "overwhelming power" so I declared war just to see. Selected fleets and told them to attack. Apparently that overwhelming power comes with totally incompetent leadership who cant even parallel park their air-car because none of the fleets arrived at the same time nor did they take the same route. Sure enough we beat their fleet, eventually, but not until after our fleet scattered, split up and divided themselves in ways that defy logic causing unnecessary losses. Ok, mistakes were made,  Lets INVADE!. My troop ships were loaded to the gills with eager young warriors looking for blood.  NOPE NOPE NOPE.  Forget it son! We gonna blip outta here and refuel first.  Where are the tankers?  Well, they were the first to die because they DID go straight to the enemy system, while the warships went site seeing at nearby systems first.Automation on all the way is mildly interesting to watch, nothing else.  Automation partially on to allow you to do some things is a click fest.  Automation off so I can do all the things just becomes a slog of shaking my head in wonder at how they could have dropped this so far from the DWU tree.This is just a smattering to the disappointments that await you in DW2 if you knew how great the predecessor was. When the planning for this was done they took all the good stuff in DWU and flushed it down the loo and slapped a "DW" sticker on the box for us suckers. By the way, it is cleverly designed to make you burn through the 2 hour play return limit in eager anticipation and belief that surely you are missing something, or some automation needs to be changed or some setting needs to be flipped that will make it play the way you are hoping it will.  NOPE.  You bought it.  Now have fun desperately trying to enjoy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Distant Worlds 2

_childDocuments_.review: The automation is spectacular and your empire feels alive. It is capable of completely running itself in your absence if you choose.  Fleet battles are exciting, graphically pleasing, and interesting.   The game is fully customisable and modifiable.  The diplomacy has been very well crafted and you feel as though you are dealing with genuinely alive universe and alien empires that are all seeking to fulfill their own unique agendas, often at your expense.  It is important to colonize planets early to stay competitive (if your particular customization selections allow for this).  Overall- superb and only getting better.  The game is vastly superior to Stellaris in my opinion, and much more engaging.  There are less story arcs than Stellaris, but everything else about this game is better than Stellaris, from the economic and military realism, to the ability to customize micromanagement.  This game is a classic in its field.  It gives you a real game in its latest iteration, without any hidden political or other agenda.Work remains to be done to extend and enhance the game through DLC and continued content and maintenance updates, but it is already fully playable.  Do expect crashes to desktop about once every three hours at this time if you use the latest experimental beta (February 2023), and about once every 12 hours if you use the latest regular version.  Usually you can simply restart the latest autosave and continue with the same game.  It is recommended you file a report with the developers when this happens, as they are constantly updating the game and it is improving weekly.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game if you're into simulations and some degree of hands-off play. It is an experience. I do recall it took many attempts to get into the first one and several long reads through the manual. My favorite way to play this game is to select one or two parts of my empire to control and leave the rest to the AI. In my only full game thus far, I controlled only research and ship design. My empire was crushed pretty quickly because I overly focused on colonization and civilian techs. For my next game, I'll just handle military ships and fleets leaving the AI to design and build them. I also plan to play one where I only handle the spying and diplomacy.I really hope CodeForce continues to grow and improve this title. Not just more species but also a deeper sim. I'd like to see planetary government, building, development and related tech get more interesting. Make losing them harder to stomach.

_childDocuments_.review: Distant Worlds 2 is a very different look at the genre of grand scale space empire building games. While this is a positive review there are quality of life things that put this game back to 2010 era of games.UI is very unfriendly. - It's oftentimes hard to find things you need. Modules, technologies and other items have no descriptions to them outside of stats. Compared to Galactic Civilizations or Stellaris it feels odd and saps a lot of life out of the universe.- When selecting multiple ships or managing a fleet player can only see individual names of ships and their class while their type or "current model" aren't show.- While trying to micromanage fleet engagements ordering ships to engage particular target makes them completely ignore all other enemy vessels between them and the target.Automation is a large feature of DW2. Something that makes managing a stellar government much easier and takes a lot of pressure off the player. However it too has a large number of quirks.- Ship hulls autofit isn't optimized. And even if you make any changes the moment new module comes out the game will completely replace all the things you did following its own logic.- Macro stuff like colonizing independent planets is poorly optimized. You can reach the required relationship level with a populated world on which you need to set a colony in order for the planet to join your empire. However by the time it takes your colony ship on automation to fill up with colonists and get to the independent world many months will pass and your relationship with the world would likely deteriorate to the point where they will consider attempted colonization to be grave offense, making all the credits spent as gifts go to waste.- Ship orders are extremely limited. Barebone special actions. Sometimes a manually controlled fleet traveling far will have stranded ships that ran out of fuel and will take years to get to nearby systems.- Your leaders will not age.- No culture of any sort. Only straightforward economy and supply chain simulation.These are only few of most glaring quirks of DW2.Still, however, this is an engaging game that's roughly on the level of first versions of Stellaris. It's a great start, should DW2 have mod support and planned DLCs.But at the current state it leaves you wishing for more.

_childDocuments_.review: DW1 is my favorite 4X game of all time.  I only stopped playing it because the game stopped working on my newer rig and OS, and it didn't seem like the developers was going to do any updates on the old platform because they were busy working on Distant Worlds 2.  Sadly, I cannot recommend the game in its current state, as it crashes frequently and is missing a great deal of content and functionality that existed in the first game.  If this was released as an early access title, which it most certainly is, then I would not review the title and wait a while.  However, this is a bugged out and watered down 3d version of distant worlds.  Below are my major gripes.Planets don't orbit the star, and moons don't orbit the planets like they did in Distant Worlds 1.  Frequent CTD's for no reason.  Lots of content that was in DW1 is absent from this title, like hiring mercenaries or ordering pirate raids.  Lots of factions are also missing from the game.  Likely because there wasn't enough money to model all of the ships.  Eras are missing from the game.  In summary, this game feels like it is a beta, but is being sold as a full release.

_childDocuments_.review: DW2 has been sitting in my Steam library for quite some time before I decided to dive in recently. I kicked it off with a weekend of trial and error alongside watching DasTactic YouTube tutorials. I proceeded to sink 30 hours into the first week of playing. Keep in mind I also work 50+ full time hours a week. Game is amazing! Takes me back to the early 90's and a board game called "Silent Death".  A space skirmish game with metal miniatures. I had written house rules that allowed players to build an entire solar system around this base game. My friends and I would sit around rolling dice, generating our planets, moving our ships. When we encountered one another, we'd turn it over to the Silent Death board game for resolving the space combat.DW2 brings that whole tabletop, pen and paper experience back for me and It's spectacular.One "role play" flourish I would love to see in future updates. --  "Ship stories" A ships log (journal of discoveries and battles) for each vessel as well as the ability to custom paint your ships with war paint or nation colors.Thanks for this wonderful game. I can see my starter 30 hours turning into 300 very quickly.  Also shout out to DasTactic for all his help.

_childDocuments_.review: I am updating my review, after the game has received several updates to the game. I wish there was a "middle option", because I would recommend this game with a few caveats. - The game is a lot of fun. There are some nice quality of life changes in the game from the original Distant Worlds Universe. The UI is better, and if you liked DWU, I would recommend this game.- The updates have addressed the performance issues. I haven't had a crash yet. And my game has held a steady 60 fps while playing into the mid to late game. The game will occasionally lock up sometimes for half a minute, usually it seems to happen when major story events trigger. - The game still lacks content for most of the races from the original DWU. That game had about 20 playable races. While they are still in the game with assets imported from DWU, only about 6 are actually "playable". I understand why, each of the playable races have their own ship set, which is full dynamic 3d models, as opposed to in DWU which just had a sprite get smaller or bigger based on what was on the ship. Each playable race also have a fairly expansive story line. However, the lack of playable races leads to a lack of diversity in the galaxy empires, which would be particularly evident if you turned off independent worlds. - I still am not a fan of the dynamic music system, which will rapidly change the soundtrack that is playing based on what you are doing. In theory that sounds great, but it is really annoying when you want to hop into the research screen, ship editor, or just dart around the galaxy map, and the music track that is being played will change constantly.=== Original Review ===As someone who really enjoyed DW1, I want to enjoy this game very hard. This game is NOT finished, it should be labeled an early access game. Most of the races from DW1 while still in this game, but are unfinished, they lack updated artwork (It seems like they just imported static images from DW1), and the game is very poorly optimized and buggy. The game will crash, completely lock up, or just have FPS tumble to the single digits every so often, especially the farther you get into the game. I had to turn of rendering civilian ships by the early mid game, because every time I zoomed out to full galaxy view game would grind my game to a halt, with serious input lag, which is a shame because I always enjoyed watching the swarms of civilian ships zip around my empire in DW1. I also liked to have long range sensors displayed, but that also causes the game to slow way down. I noticed in the early mid game that I don't like the randomized tech trees, which caused messy tech options to show up the farther I got, and I'm not sure if it was a bug, but I wanted to further advance my reactor tech, and I could obviously tell that more advanced reactors existed, but I had no visible options on the tree to unlock any reactors past the first quantum reactor tech. Another aspect that I find rather jarring is the music in this game, which is bland and repetitive, which is a damn shame considering I actually liked the music from DW1. Not to mention the soundtrack system will rapidly shift from track to track based on what you are zoomed in on, which while cool in theory does not sound great when you are jumping from system to system rapidly, while managing your empire and fleets. I would agree with other reviews that this game is not a squeal, but an incomplete remake of DW1. I really want to love this game, but I think it might be better to wait for the game to be fixed and finished.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, this should probably be marked as early access. The pieces are there for a great game, but it's not there yet. Firstly, it crashes. I'm a few hours in to a game and there's a lot happening, but my game crashes roughly every 20 minutes. Sometimes it freezes and comes back, other times it doesn't. Secondly, some of the mechanics are too tedious. Organising troops to individually get into a carrier and then attack a specific location takes a long time and is not at all intuitive. It was bad in Stellaris, it's impossible here. Even after playing so many hours, it still takes me about 30 minutes. Imagine my frustration at finally doing this only to have the game crash immediately after the invasion. Over and over. When you click into a new system, the camera starts zoomed into the centre of the system's sun. You have to click and drag to move the camera, but any clicking also deselects the last unit you selected. Because of this, you need to scroll through your huge list of units and hope you can remember the fleet's name. If you can't, the game doesn't tell you which unit is near your camera and which is on the other side of the galaxy. You can try to find your fleet by clicking into neighbouring systems and... unzooming from the centre of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sun again.Finally, there are weird design decisions. The game defaults to 12 opponents, but the colour palette doesn't give 12 real options. It's almost impossible to distinguish between two shades of pale blue or two shades of washed out green. There's no 'border' between the colours, so it just melts from one shade to the next. If you're colour is blue and your two neighbours are also blue, good luck working out whose territory your ships are in. I seriously played 6 hours of a game not realising that I had a colony on the other side of the galaxy because I assumed it was a different blue to mine. I am not colour blind, but this game made me understand their condition just a little bit more. The tech tree is huge but completely unintelligible. There's not even a vague hint as to the difference between 'ion thrust' or 'vector engines'. The 'ship design' screen may as well be written in Mandarin because it made no sense at all to me. The game told me my battlecruiser had a slow turn rate which could be fixed by using a different thruster. Of course, the starship construction screen doesnt provide any stats for the 15 different thrusters and doesn't recommend any in particular, so if you want to fix the thrust issue you have to close the ship builder, open the research tab, read the engine description, open a notepad, write the values for all the different thrusters, reopen the ship building screen - oh, it's crashed again. A final representative example of the shape of the game is this: without watching youtube videos, there is simply no way to know that researching 'colony ship construction' does not actually allow you to construct colony ships. The good news is that all of these issues can be easily fixed with a bit of time and love. I hope they do, because underneath all the rubbish is a solid concept for a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have around 250 hours in Distant Worlds Universe, participated in the Distant Worlds 2 beta and have a few dozen hours in the release version, and would strongly recommend DW2.This is basically the best mega-scale real time space 4X available. The scale is awe inspiring, and the civilian economy is unique within the genre and does provide different strategic challenges. It looks great. It is mostly intuitive to play. It's my favorite 4X, period.There are a few rough edges or odd design decisions that mostly arise from the grognard and very small development team, but these are quite minor in the scope of the overall game, and that approach also led to the greatness of the series.One major caution is if you are looking for rich pre-scripted stories, similar to the events in Stellaris, you'll probably be disappointed. There are stories and events in DW2, but not at the same volume or richness of Stellaris with all DLC and mods (yet). For me, that's fine - the mechanics make the story. Think of RimWorld compared to a traditional RPG - that's like Distant Worlds 2 compared to Stellaris.Similarly, if you're looking for lots of colony management, you'll also be disappointed. There are some meaningful upgrades and knobs to tweak at colonies, but you won't be micro managing build orders on planets like in Stellaris or other 4X with lots of city/colony management. In DW2 far less time is spent on planet buildings and populations, and more on decisions around where to expand new mines and colonies; research paths; base, ship and fleet design; diplomacy and espionage; and, war and conquest.Regarding direct comparisons with DWU: For those on the fence:

_childDocuments_.review: As one of my favourite gaming series (and with 178 hours with the game at time of launch) I thought I would write a review. Before I start, I am an unashamed fan-boi of Distant Worlds and have loved the game since version 1 so many years ago. Distant Worlds was one of the games I launched my YouTube channel with - so I do have a bias in favour of the game.DW2 will inevitably be compared to Stellaris and I don't think this is fair for either game. Stellaris is designed to work with multiplayer and so must maintain a level of balance. Distant Worlds has so many procedural aspects to the galaxy creation that the events and strategic problems that crop up (not scripted btw) lead to a real sense of story that Stellaris could never really achieve. Distant Worlds is as much a story/simulation with a living galaxy as it is a strategy game. Having said that, if you like Stellaris I think you will also enjoy Distant Worlds.Distant Worlds 2 may be too slow in places for some gamers who enjoy a fast pace. And if you ramp up the speed you will most likely miss out on many of the small events that may crop up. The game builds - slowly - but when a crisis occurs you will have to really think things through how you can change a situation to work in your favour. And these crises can be diplomatic, military, expansion blocking, espionage, or resource control. What are you willing to do if you find that a friendly neighbour controls a valuable Spice World close to your common border? What will you do if an aggressive neighbour had found a derelict grave-yard and suddenly appears with a ship 10-times more powerful that anything you have? How will you cope with the early pirate menace that is constantly raiding your mining stations and home world? Pretty much anything and everything can happen in this game – and all because of the living breathing galaxy that is completely randomly generated. You may find yourself surrounded by factions with the same beliefs and values as your own and have a very peaceful game – or you may find yourself surrounded by factions that want to eat you for dinner.The game has a definite early, mid and end game. In the early game you are just trying to survive against pirates and get the tech to start exploring and expanding. In the mid game you will largely have dealt with the pirates but will then be contending with your neighbours. This can be a time of war, subterfuge and intrigue. In the end-game there will be some dominant empires with incredible ships.One of the great innovations with Distant Worlds is that the numerous resources in the game have to be used at the specific location they are needed. The only global resource is the Credits. Everything else is either at colonies, on ships, or on mining stations. If you need 64 units of polymer to build a Destroyer but only have 62 units at the star-base, then you’d better hope that a freighter is on its way because you aren’t building that Destroyer there without it. Every component you design ships with a specific resource cost. Another innovation is that you only control the state economy but there is also a private sector that runs all the mining operations and freight transport in your empire. Your job is to protect them and to build their ships for them – but you don’t control what they do. Another innovation is the degree of automation you can setup within the game. You can play where you really are just watching from afar, or you can be controlling every little aspect of the empire (which, believe me, is waaaay too much!). You also have your colonies and ships fully automated and then just choose one or two to manually control. There is no other game even close to what Distant Worlds does in this regard.Take your time with the game and enjoy the ride. Don’t try to push the pace if you can help it. I can see that many of the reviews have been written with only a handful of hours down – that really isn’t enough time to get out of the early game. And the early game can feel frustrating because the pirates will be much more powerful than you are for a time. Stick to your bases and don’t go hunting until you can swarm them with sizable fleets. Hunt down their bases when you have Frigates with strong weaponry and Point Defence protection. If you try to be aggressive in the early game you will be smacked hard. It may be better to allow the pirates to raid your mining stations freely while you try to protect your home-world. And don’t buy too much protection from the pirates – it may bankrupt you (I no longer pay them anything).The game is going to be actively developed into the future so rest assured there will be constant improvements over the coming months and years. I haven’t had the same crashing issues that I’ve read other have had. When I have had the occasional crash it tends to be when the game is trying to load in new 3D assets because I’ve suddenly zoomed in on something new. What I do now is it I’m zooming and notice a slight stutter is to let it load then continue zooming. It isn’t a fix – but it may stop some of the issues.I’m really looking forward to seeing what people will do to mod the game into the future. In terms of negatives, it would be great if there were more factions but the more I play the game I haven’t really missed the others. They will come slowly over time but the 7 factions in DW2 play with much more nuance than they did in DW:U. For example, the hard-points on the ships are different for each faction. Some will be smaller but with broad fields of fire, while some, like the Boskaran (aggressive insectoids) are large and only face forward ‘There will be no retreat!’. If you are playing as other factions and have to deal with Boskarans you may need to find a way to focus on manoeuvrability to get in behind their ships.Another negative that many viewers miss in the orbiting planets. I missed them as well at the start but am used to it now.Queuing orders is gone from this version and I do miss that.There are small QoL things that have been improved a lot prior to launch but there is still a little more to do to bring them along. I can never play Distant Worlds Universe again after playing Distant Worlds 2. A great addition to a great and innovative franchise – but as I said, I am a fan-boi!

_childDocuments_.review: Not gonna lie the game has a lot of performance issues and crashes pretty frequently. There's also a few QOL features missing (why can't I queue ship orders?)That being said, it's also the most in-depth and intricate space grand strategy game out there. Space actually feels like space. It's massive and requires conquering numerous logistical challenges to expand into. You can't just fly from one end of the galaxy to the other. Your fleets need fuel hubs to operate from and numerous types of resources to build in the first place. It isn't necessarily a Stellaris killer. Both games are so different from each other that practically the only similarity they have is they take place in space. Stellaris is all about building a unique culture and exploration. It's very space opera. Distant Worlds focuses far more on the logistic side of things and is more 'realistic' in that sense. Both are fun time killers depending on what you're in the mood for.Anyway, back to the bugs and such. Reason I'm recommending instead of not is that this team seems to be moving very quickly to fix them. This includes, apparently, working this weekend, which is more than what I would do, personally. I hope this was a collective decision and not that on the part of some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ CEO forcing them to work overtime, but given it's small team, I think the former is more probable. All that means the issues present are gonna be resolved pretty quickly. And after that, they'll probably be cranking out new, most likely free, content. For that, despite all the bugs, they deserve another recommendation.Keep on keeping on, lads.

_childDocuments_.review: Just my 2 cents, people aren't wrong when they state that DW2 is more of DW: Universe. Personally, I don't take that as a negative, since DW2 immediately feels much smoother in terms of gameplay than Universe, arguably the players largest hangup with that game. As a player who prefers mostly manual control with basic automatic defenses (mostly so I don't need to micro every planets system of escorts, or can have dedicated defense fleets without having to be super aware of every planet) DW2 is much smoother as far as general gameplay. The automation works like I expected from Universe, which is a definite improvement, & didn't require me having to take 30+ minutes of fiddling & look up an old forum to get an understanding of how to kind-of make it functionRegarding the change to ship-building, I do & don't like the new system. As far as DW: Universe is concerned, the designs are now somewhat rudimentary in comparison with basic ship chassis' not having much, if any, additional slots for components that would immediately go into my basic designs in universe when unlocked. However, while they are somewhat basic in comparison, they are also much better balanced compared to Universe & have more QoL. Personally, I always hated how Universe's design would let the player, but not the AI, build an Escort as if it were, say, a Battleship & the only thing preventing that were (A) techs that limited construction size, (B) your budget & (C) the players conscience. That said, now ship roles make much more sense with the limited component slots & slots in general reduce the irritation of having to repeatedly replace components, as upgrading a manual design now automatically introduces the new components in place of the outdated counterparts, & facilitate easier construction of ship designs for new playersTLDR: The new design system may not be ideal, as far as customization goes, but makes sense to me as far as retaining a semblance of strategy (vs making one/two design super-ships) while also expanding the QoLLastly, as far as stability goes, I did have the game crash once in a Pre-Warp start, near the beginning with only my home planet colonized, which is not ideal to say the least (comparatively speaking few ships in the actual galaxy vs late-game) BUT I believe the game was attempting to auto-save while calculating some event in the galaxy which I'm also fairly certain had Universe at least lag on me before, too, if not outright crash once so I'd say, if you're concerned, hold off for a couple patches since late-game will probably be rough by comparison & make finishing a game difficultOverall, I'd say 2 is a nice improvement where I wanted it in comparison to Universe, if imperfect as a sequel, & if you enjoyed Universe it's probably worth picking up if you can reconcile the ship designer changes & some potential instability. For anyone new to the series & on the fence, this & Universe are both solid games so I'd suggest doing some additional research & picking whichever you think you'd prefer more. Universe, at this time, has more options for player empire choice & a diverse galaxy whereas 2 has more QoL in comparison & I'd say is generally a more polished concept

_childDocuments_.review: Played previous versions of DW hundreds of hours, so of course I'm going to give this one a thumbs up. All I really ever wanted was Distant Worlds Universe but with better visuals and UI/UX. With only 24 hours in DW2, I do not pretend to have a comprehensive appreciation for where it is successful and still lacking. I am aware of widespread discussions of non-trivial flaws with the game as it stands. However, I was there when DW first launched. Despite the promise the game had from the beginning, it was VERY BADLY BROKEN at original launch. CodeForce listened to their community (who were overall very constructive) and fixed it progressively. The transformation of the final version of "DW 1" from how it started to where it finished is quite possibly one of the greatest successes in fixing a broken game in history. Right up there with No Man's Sky.Is DW2 'perfect' right now? Probably not. But I can already see it is good, and it has primarily delivered what I wanted: DWU but with better graphics and UI/UX. The game is highly moddable/customizable, and the community has grown enormously compared to the beginnings. Codeforce seem to be the same hard-working, sensible folks as they ever were.So in sum, this game is good enough to warrant a positive recommendation already and is almost certainly going to get better and better.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a player coming from the original Distant Worlds 1. My expectations of this game is a improvement over the first in the terms of UI and some gameplay elements. Here is my thought process so far as I play the game as a complete beginner. I might update my review as time goes on, but I wanted to imprint my initial feelings and impressions here. Initial Impressions of the UI. Its certainly bigger and clearer than the first, since its compatible with modern systems, but it does not feel intuitive. The only thing that really was like a "ah hah!" moment was when you zoomed out from your home world and they had all the planets at the bottom of the list for easy viewing. Other than that, it still feels cluttered, janky, and I'm often going through a list of menu's to find what i'm looking for. Let me give you an example. Take the Research menu. This list is super long (not left to right) but rather top to bottom. They have tabs on the right side to allow you to switch between each section, but that doesn't mean it makes it any better looking at this giant excel spreadsheet. In the old DS1, they cut this up with tab categories. Why they decided not to do this here is confusing because it just makes it a pain to scroll through the whole thing. When you click on a ship, you can now see the cargo they have and you can see it transferring from and to stations or whatever that ship might be doing. This is a Godsend personally and this is what DW1 was lacking. You would always have to manually go and find out. Now its just there, which I love. Ship Models:I just need to get this one off my chest. The models look absolutely stupid and made by a 6th grader.  If you have ever played Supreme Commander, a game that came out 15+ years ago, have better models. I am not kidding. In DW1 the ships were 2D, but atleast you had one hell of a image to look at, and you can scale it upwards to represent a "bigger threat" when it had more components added on it. This just feels like lego starwars or something. I mean they are just so dam static.  I'm playing Zenox and I was expecting there to be some kind of flash or blinking with the ship designs to represent life or a presence, but its just not there. Take Eve Online, when you go to a space station, you see flashing lights, so you know someone is home. Perhaps the bigger orbital stations have some flashing lights, but I can say for now, the smaller ones do not. Limited Ship Design:In DW1, you could load a ship up with 100's of generators if you wanted to. Why? Just because. Of course, you had to be able to afford it in terms of ship yard that could allow you to build a huge ship, but the flexibility of putting anything and everything unto a ship, even multiple of the same type, was there. I can't say for sure as I haven't played much but after designing and putting on my new ship drives for FTL on a exploration ship, I realized that, that feature seems to have gone away. Now you have preset bays and components. To me this is not in the spirit of DW1. This was what I loved most about that game and its charm and that seems to have been taken away for very limited building templates. If that's the case, I will likely not continue to play in the future. Why? Because it means I can't spam 30 resource mining extractors on a mining station if I wanted to. The game will just tell me nope, build what WE say you can build. The Home World:I might have gotten a bad first world, because its like Saturn. The concept of having a Saturn like planet is cool! But the rings are on top of all my ships, so they are hard to find under the rings and actually block me seeing my own ships! Its like putting a filter around your base and asking you to enjoy it. I mean its my HOME planet, so I'll always have to deal with that. Maybe a reset with a new planet will fix it, but that is annoying. Crashes:The game had crashed on me once so far before I even got a year into it. I have a 5900x so I do not lack in the CPU department. Thats a bad sign for early game, because it makes me wonder about later late game stages. Will I have more common crashes? Either way, when something didn't move, I had to think about was the game gonna crash on me again. No gamer should have that feeling. Auto Saves:So far i'm 8 autosaves in and they just seem to be stacking up rather than overwriting one another, at 25 MB each. That's a lot of storage in the long run. I'll have to check the settings later to see if I can do anything on my end, but talk about eating up space just to eat up space. So far, I can only say why is this the default setting, rather than an overwriting save every 2-3 saves or 5? I don't need 8 autosaves!Music:Kill me. On the design screen, the music lasts for like 2 minutes, then repeats, over and over and over and over again. It was driving me insane, and I was just designing ONE ship! I think i'm going to have to mute the music in this game. It is no Stellaris by a long shot. That has been my experience so far. Overall some changes are good and I like those changes, but i'm not feeling good or optimistic in the direction so far. If this was all the changes they have made, they could of just improved the UI to the first one and left it at that. I will continue to play more because I really do like DW, so hopefully further gameplay will change my mind and its a bad first experience.I will update my review as I continue to play if things become more favorable.--------------------------Further UpdatesAfter playing the game longer, 1 fear has come true, in that the ship design is preset. When I unlocked Frigates, for example..  They have "types". Heavy, Fast, Fleet, ect. Each one has a different component configuration. This means the FREEDOM to build the ship how you want rather than a TEMPLATE is gone.  How does this make the game BETTER? Its a STEP BACK. Fire FightsOkay I am sorry but seriously. Go play command and conquer 3. Look at those beautiful laser fires from 15+ YEARS AGO.  Then look at this garbage of a "laser fire" or a "bomb blast aoe wave" is here. It looks like it was scribbled and made by a 2 year old. This just isn't fun or enjoyable anymore. Its not the first game because it has down grades. Things are templated out, so there is no freedom. PiratesThey just get better stuff and better gear. And no i'm not talking a little bit of here and there, i'm talking superior in every way. As Zenox, my race has superior shielding recharge, but when I took damage on my ship and looked at the damage their ship was taking, they had superior shield recharge. Meaning they are running with the latest and greatest. You can still kill them but your going to have to out-gun them 3-1 to stand a decent chance.Also, perhaps its likely a special weapon they get, but they are doing damage not only through my shields but also through my armor and hitting directly on my hull! What weapon by-passes both defenses and just says F it, I will go straight for the kill. Oooookay. Overall my impressions is I enjoyed the new UI changes and what not, but this is NOT the same game. You don't have the freedom to express yourself like you did in the first one. You do NOT have great fire-fights or visuals. Infact, it looks like a 2 year old throwing paint on the wall. ITS THAT BAD. Don't believe me, go watch a YT video. It will bore you to tears. I don't know why they decided to go this "3d route" when no one requested it. We just wanted better 2D. Oh well. That is my review. If you want a slightly better UI experience but turned down visuals and turned down gameplay, this is "part 2". I will however, being go back to part 1.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick review - I've got a lot more playing to do before I write a more complete one.I play 4X games weird.  I like to use big galaxies (or worlds or whatever) with just 3 or 4 other empires in them.  I also like things to be generally peaceful.  Monsters/barbarians with some bigger (but temporary) military challenges are fine, but I enjoy trying to win more on the explore/expand/exploit fronts than extermination. _childDocuments_.review: I have to say this is the most regretted $50 I have ever spent on a game.  I have played and loved 4x games for many years,  and have put ~90 hours into this one ( not all on Steam ).   I was hoping against hope that the disappointing 20h impression was wrong, but not so much.  This game is not even ready for EA, it should still be closed beta IMO.A lot of the noise, and ALL of the dev attention, has been dedicated to crashes, instability, and performance issues. I have had NONE of that, my complaints are all in execution and playability.  I have played ONLY the smallest maps, with many problematic features culled out, just to see if I could get a grip on the core game, with both scratch and advanced starts.The UI is abysmal, elements on top allow mouse actions on underlying levels, presentation is too detailed and unexplained to be useful, actions in context are almost always missing, forcing you so use cumbersome non intuitive workarounds for the simplest interaction between entities. Popup overlays are distracting and poorly done. The AI in general struggles with too little context and needs so many blacklists and oversight controls that it is best described as hapless in many cases.  I have to say I am impressed with the comms and the patience displayed by the devs, but I do not see this game EVER reaching the potential that was implied by many of the surface level play throughs out there, and it is going to take a long time for it to be pleasantly playable as far as I am concerned.My advice is to enjoy your summer and check back in the fall, and even that is optimistic IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: AI broken, several recent "fixes" introduce "WTF is it doing now?" level problems. It's painfully bad for a game who's hype involves it's simulation and levels of provided automation. Avoid.Aurora Update (March 28th 2023): This is worse? Some things were made better in the previous update, but this update seems to have reverted or broken the same things in new different ways perhaps? Example: New game with Aurora  and the new DLC installed (don't ask me why I gave them more money...). Pirates in my home system. My fleets (who are half the strength of the Pirate base, have no point defense, and appear to intentionally ignore small craft attacking them in favor of rushing the pirate base keep getting killed under AI control. Put the fleets on manual control, tell them to refit. AI tells them to run off and die to Pirates. Change their AI settings to use the fleet settings, set fleet to engage when attacked, manual control. Fleet runs off to die to AI. Set fleet to do not engage, manual control. Fleet runs off to die to Pirates. This is worse.Update v1.0.4.8: This patch focused on fleet and ship AI, but we're still annoyingly broken. Some things are better, but "Prepare to..." still appears to be the default action. There's a big section of the patch notes talking about how you must configure these settings in different parts of the AI to ATTEMPT to make the Feet AI not be stupid. However, these cause the AI to continually prompt me to send fleets to investigate hostiles which happen to be pirate bases that I have a treaty with. And in cases where there are legitimate hostiles, the investigating fleet heads over there, attacks a single target, and completely ignores the others in the area unless they get into combat while the fleet is engaging the first hostile. And on the nature of continual AI prompts, colony ships under AI control still cause continual pop up prompts to go colonize planets that are horrible choices. And if you do send a ship to colonize an independent colony, and another empire beats you to it, that colony ship gets stuck unable to do anything without setting it to Manual and giving it additional commands. Back to being uninstalled, and I'll try again, maybe after the 1.1 branch.Original Review: As others have mentioned, the control scheme and AI, especially the ship/fleet AI as it stands (even with the new beta as of the time of this review) is staggeringly frustrating. The current default command is "Prepare to..." when giving orders to a fleet. So if you have a fleet selected, and just click on a target to attack (That's on screen mind you, in the same area the fleet is in) It won't engage the target. Your fleet will jump out to "prepare". And even in this instance, it won't do it anything close to intelligently. My favorite example is doing this in an asteroid belt, my ships jumped out to "refuel at...". But they didn't pick the closest fuel station, which was in system. They didn't pick the closest shipyard, which was 1 system away. They didn't pick their home base, which was near by. They picked my homeworld, on the other side of my empire. Oh, and did I mention that at the time they decided to jump out to fly across my empire to refuel, they already had tanks that were 95%+ full because they already had "prepare to...." attack? And that they were flying to a station that was out of their existing fuel range, and would have to refuel on the way there? This isn't a unique example by any means. One time 3 pirate ships were attacking a mining station. I assigned a fleet to "investigate". The fleet jumped in, attacked, one of the 3 pirates, flew right past the other 2, and jumped out to return to their base. And it doesn't seem to matter how you have the automation configured. Yes, there are detailed videos and guides out there talking about how the automation settings for ships and fleets interact, how they override each other, how this setting causes that to be ignored, etc etc. I honestly don't care. as a player, I expect ships set on manual in fleets set to manual control, to follow basic instructions (refit, move to, attack) and they don't. I expect ships in close range of enemy ships that are actively on an "investigate hostile" mission to actually engage said hostiles. Distant Worlds is known for the expansive AI and detailed simulation. Distant Worlds Universe is an amazing game. This iteration is not, and I'm almost questioning if the same people are behind it. AI problems that were solved YEARS ago in Distant Worlds, that shouldn't be happening in a 1.0 release, are all over the place in Distant Worlds 2, and it's a shame. I want to like this game, but I just can't in it's current state. The developers say they're working on these AI issues, but IMHO some of their decisions to address things have actually made playing the game worse, and more frustrating (like making the default click action "Prepare to..."). I'll come back in a few months and check things out again, because I do hope they succeed, but for now, stay away.

_childDocuments_.review: V2. Well 2 years have passed my original review (27 hrs). The games stability and performance has improved greatly. Along with most of the GUI and control issues. Honestly, it isn't enough.-The amount of automation by default gives a very false idea of all the games systems. The global automation menu being tucked away doesn't help either. We should be able to have this preset before the game as well.-Stability issue with engine. The UI still has a severe performance impact in galaxy view. The game suffers from momentary random pauses(i don't know what's causing this).- After all this time I still don't have enough control over my fleets. It is much better than it was, but missing functions such as regrouping and home bases makes organising manual fleets a pain. Retreat functions leave ships idling even after they go back above the damage limits. Requiring you to find them and manually order them or order the entire fleet and disrupt what the rest of the ships are doing. Navigating around planets is really annoying because you can't control where they arrive.-Ship design is too restrictive. Before we could put whatever we wanted in ships as long as it met the role restrictions and we stayed below the maximum size. The ships would get bigger based on the final size. Now we have ship slots heavily restricting what we can do. Yes this came with reactive models, but that could have been done based on ratios of equipped modules. Granting us that flexibility with the bonuses.-Camera Rotation is locked to certain angles. We need a mode that allows full orbiting. The game is in space. Why put a limit on this.- Movement of the units is not smooth atm. This made sense with the nature of distance, speed and "tick rate" with Distant Worlds 1. Now it is extremely noticeable and hard to ignore. Especially with slow moving units. Units can't fly over planets and must go around them now giving a huge tactical advantage to attacking forces.- UI Scaling issue. It is resolved for most by changing the DPI Scaling options for the exe.+ Almost Every feature has been carried over from Distant Worlds 1. Except the world editor, but I suspect it something has to do with things being 3D now.+ 3D models and themes are simple and that's perfect for this game. The aesthetic choices are really interesting and shockingly unique.+ Smaller ships representing the workings of the main ships is a nice touch.+ Automation for anything you don't want to deal with is available.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this game as there's a lot I like about it, but ultimately I can't...The problem with Distant Worlds 2 is that whilst there is a ton of depth, there's almost no accessibility to that depth. Even simply managing a fleet is an exercise in frustration as there isn't a good balance between automation and manual control there.Want your fleets to simply conform to a specific template and repair/replace/refuel automatically? Well, tough. The game makes it seem like this is possible, but in reality it isn't. It won't rebalance fleets to the correct number of ships and even removing ships manually just re-adds them even if the template says something completely different.The home bases make no sense, the AI will assign fleets to the other side of the universe when you don't even have the technology to get there. End result: a useless fleet for a few dozen years as it flies across the void. Sigh.This would be a fantastic game if it worked as intended but right now it's just not enjoyable to actually play. The messages which are meant to be helpful quickly become a source of irritation and frustration. You get overwhelmed by useless ones you just want to dismiss with no obvious way to disable specific types.The ones you do want, you end up missing unless you watch the messages like a hawk. I spend more time dismissing messages to get to the ones that are important than actually doing anything fun. If there's a way to customise what messages are delivered, I didn't find it. Developers could take some learning from the Paradox games here, where you can categorize that type of messages are delivered in what way.I had a vastly overwhelming military to anyone else in the universe, yet I couldn't effectively deploy it anywhere. Even in my home system I struggled keeping tiny fleets of pirates at bay, despite having 5 fleets that were 10x their strength per fleet.I "fought" 5 wars against the AI in which not a single shot was fired and not a single ship even went near one another. What was the point of that? What was the war even over? Where is the war progress? What do they want out of it? None of this is indicated anywhere.I've spend a good amount of time watching tutorials and reading the manual. It's not overly difficult to grasp, but the UI and the way things are automated just doesn't work very well in a couple of places. That unfortunately makes the whole thing unravel.

_childDocuments_.review: This has been at the top of my wishlist for a while, I was a huge fan of Distant Worlds Universe and still consider it to be one of the best 4x experiences out there. It physically hurts to downvote this, but I can't in good conscious recommend the game in the current state for the current price point. If you want to slap a AAA sticker price on a game you really need to earn the right to do so, Distant Worlds 2 is a buggy mess that feels like it needs another year or two in early access to fix critical issues and fill in the areas it falls short of the previous entry.The critical issues and main reason I have to say avoid this one for now, are frequent crashes and horrible performance. One of the main selling points for this game is that the engine has been rebuilt from scratch to run in a 3d environment with multithreading and 64bit support, it's supposed to run much better than DWU even though it's switched from a 2d game to a 3d one. Right out of the gate if you zoom out to the galaxy view the game is a slide show, this becomes progressively worse and by mid game you see ships update positions in galaxy view like once every 5 seconds, dragging the view around feels extremely laggy, but the UI and mouse seem to be running in a different thread and continue to move around the screen somewhat smoothly. The game might physically run with a lot more going on in the galaxy, but it doesn't look good doing it and wont do it at any appreciable speed. Zooming in on any systems to see what your ships are doing will frequently result in a hard stutter for a few seconds and occasionally a crash. There's been one hotfix so far to address some of the crashing issues, but the game is still crashing for many people.The UI is another serious issue, trying to do anything with it is often a battle. The game uses some weird mechanic where the UI will fade in and out and lock into position or disappear depending on if you've clicked in the window or not. It's not at all intuitive, often locks open when you don't want it to, often disappears when you are trying to do something, and information is spread out through an absolutely staggering number of sub-tabs making it difficult to find what you are looking for if it even exists (an example of UI bloat is there are like 6 different tabs for viewing the various types of ships and stations you own, when a single searchable/filterable list would have worked better, and trying to locate your colonies requires diving into another sub-tab instead of being pinned somewhere more easily visible). On default settings the game will inundate you with message spam and suggestions on the right of the screen, you can leave them flashing on your screen for like 30 seconds at which point they fade on their own, or try to dismiss them by right clicking on them. I say try because you will often fail, you have to click on a certain area of the message to succeed and the messages change size after a few seconds, if you try to dismiss them early before they shrink they tend to shrink just as you click to dismiss it causing you to instead lock open a larger message on your screen which you now need to find a new button to close (this has happened to me many dozens of times). There are also bugs related to this system, occasionally you will get new messages popping up seconds after pausing the game, and occasionally you will get 5-6 messages and suggestions popping up in a very short period of time that all decide to instantly disappear for some reason before you can read them (there is no message log for automation suggestions). Another amusing UI issue is opening the steam overlay while playing the game will likely blind you as for some reason it jacks the gamma of the overlay up to like 1000 for whatever reason.There are also issues with the AI. Automated non-combat ships don't seem to attempt to flee until they've been hit by an enemy attack, but you get a message the instant any enemy in the area decides they want to attack this ship even if they are on the other side of the system. If you do nothing about it you will generally lose the ship as it flies directly in the maw of some large angry creature, if it's an exploration ship or something you can control you can give it a flee order and then set it back to automate. This happens a lot, between pirates and alien creatures and the hundreds of automated ships you have flying around you get several of these messages every minute, you can either go insane trying to order them to flee every time or you can just ignore the messages and let them die and have automation build a new one. Fleet AI is also often suicidal on default automation settings, throwing fleets of your early game ships at threats they have no hope of defeating, or worse picking a fight you should be able to win but only showing up with 1-2 ships at a time while the rest straggle behind refueling or whatever. This is partially because the power rating system the game uses to determine how strong something is, is very bad, and something that is rated at 300 will often easily stomp an entire fleet of ships at 100 rating.Comparing the gameplay of Distant Worlds 2 with Distant Worlds Universe, DW2 falls short in many areas. Multiple gameplay concessions have been made for the sake of switching the game to 3d and trying to make things "pretty." Planets and asteroids and such no longer orbit stars, there are no asteroid belts any more that I have seen just clusters of comically low quality asteroid models in fixed points of some systems, ship design is limited to a slot system so turrets can line up on the 3d model (gutting the previous game's freeform ship design mechanic which was a true highlight of it). Star ports are built in fixed locations next to the larger 3d planets which makes them more or less useless in defending said planets (enemies can just raid from the other side of the planet avoiding your defenses). Most of the major factions from the previous game are unplayable and have no ships models, but still exist as minor factions with art assets lifted directly from DWU. Expansion features like playable pirates and advanced interactions with them are missing. Other than that almost everything else is copied more or less exactly from DWU with only some minor changes to things like luxury resources and colonization. The gameplay is functionally identical, just less.The end result unfortunately is that DW2 currently feels like an inferior and buggy "budget 3d" version of DWU. It is not worth $50, I'm not sure it will be worth $50 when the bugs and UI issues are fixed. Undoubtedly as a Slitherine published game the devs will release a series of equally overpriced expansions, which I'm sure eventually at some point will make DW2 into an amazing experience full of content, and then they will release some bundle with all the expansions included like with Distant Worlds Universe, and probably at that point in time it will be very much worth buying. Until then, I would suggest firing up DWU instead, or grabbing it during a sale if you haven't done so already. If you can't stand 2d games and DW2 looks really good to you, probably wait until a significant discount, by that point most of the major issues should probably be fixed and the game should be in a more polished state.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually review games as there are plenty of people who can sum up everything there is to say better than me.That being said, Distant World 2 is by far the greatest surprise I had in a couple of years. Everything that other games are doing wrong, this game nailed perfectly.The most common gripe I have in other games, specifically Paradox-made games, is that they tend to become more and more totalitarian-like in their approach to modeling the society they want to represent. Take Stellaris for example -> you as a driving force behind the galactic society have to control every aspect of society, and you have to micromanage everything from trade, civilian buildings, planet management etc. There is no private sector. There are no private traders or miners.  The universe, without your agency, is a cold, dead place.Not so with DW2. The universe is a vibrant and rich tapestry even without you, and your task is to nudge the events around you in your favor. Just because of that approach, this game is a breath of very fresh air in the 4X market and I hope this game will have a die-hard community and be alive and kicking in the next 5-10 years.Also, I can't wait for the Star Trek mod for this games.
