_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed this game when I played it, but I say this lovingly:I would never recommend this game to my friends. This game has persistent crashes, bugs and totally unreliable instances of game play. The game crashed near hourly and had tons of various lag issues. (Example: Large piles of gold can cause serious lag/sound issues/crashes) Considering this game is not a high graphic output game, there is no excuse for the poor optimization and performance at all. The very obvious lack of any developer communications to the player base is alarming and the lack of updates to this game to resolve the never-ending list of bugs and crashes is unacceptable.For all the faults and frustrations I had while playing the game, I did enjoy the action and character building in game. I love that the mod community also enjoys working to expand the game and the features within. I purchased the game because I'm a sucker for the graphic style and RPG elements that it really DOES do well. It was kind of my alternative dungeon crawler game for a while. The game's music kept me floating along as well, it's catchy and pretty enjoyable overall.Some games are brilliant. Some games will fall flat on their face for not resonating well with the target audience. There are some games that are cult classics because they have a very loyal base, but at the end of the day if you can't be bothered to follow up and improve the game to be able to continuously run -AT A MINIMUM-, your game should be nothing but "refunded".I would give this game a score of 27/100. (I don't have a real metric, I just felt the game was only able to run for a 4th of my playtime) The game could be both brilliant and resilient if it could manage to stay launched for more than 30 minutes to an hour at a time. It has many great concepts and a ton of wonderful community members that want to add content and enjoyment to the game for others to experience, and I find that when a community is willing to do that it can become a masterpiece.This game will never become anything like that without the support of the creator to finish what they started so it can be enjoyed without the constant pressure of frustration and disappointment.
_childDocuments_.name: Hammerwatch II

_childDocuments_.review: I've finished this game today, killing every boss in the game and (as far as I'm aware) discovering every secret. After all this, despite having good fun here and there, I cannot give this game a positive review.First off, there is really little content. Completing everything this game has to offer so far took me 24 hours. However, around a quarter of this time was spent on doing tedious things. First extremely boring thing this game makes you do is backtracking. More often than not, when going through some large dungeon and finishing a task at the end of it, you need to go back to the entrance, while there should be a shortcut of some sort. Another thing that added dead playtime for me were rampant bugs. I play the game in 2-player co-op, which is so riddled with bugs, that it's not even funny. I played the game across three days, and on the second day the game has crashed for me around 15-20 times. For some reason, sometimes when you load into a level, the player who isn't hosting the game can just crash and have to reset. Another annoying bug is that the game sometimes desyncs and you're kicked out of the game. At some point I was just used to being kicked out or crashing, as this occured at least once every 30 minutes. I cannot even imagine how mindnumbingly annoying these bugs must be when you're playing in a 4-player group. Also, a few hours of my playtime was just retrying the bosses, as some of them were quite hard. If I were to erase all of the time spent on the aforementioned things, there would be just very little stuff to do. Much of my actual playtime was also spent on walking through pointless caves, just filled with mobs to grind experience, and occasionally find some secret chest. It would be great if some of those contained some interesting event, or a sidequest, or honestly just anything to differentiate these caves from one another. I feel like the devs didn't even try too much, as 90% of the caves have literally the same name pop up when you enter them - "Mysterious Cave".However, as I feel wrong only pointing out the flaws, I can say that there are things this game got right. The pixel art is definitely top-notch, also combat is really fun. Some people say that all enemies are just damage sponges, but I don't feel like that's a problem. This game aims for a diablo-ish combat, where enemy design revolves more around quantity than quality, which I wouldn't necessarily consider bad design. It feels satisfying to destroy hordes of enemies, and some of them do actually have mechanics that distinguish them from others. Controlling your character is fluid, abilities are fun and I haven't encountered any clunky mechanics. The diablo-like loot with occasional legendary items is also really fun and feels rewarding.This game has some great qualities, but I feel like they're largely overwhelmed by lots of tedium, most of which is in the game clearly by design, and not by mistake. I'm looking forward to seeing it get fixed with bugfixes and quality-of-life changes, as well as receiving more content (probably in form of a DLC). However, at this point in time I cannot give this game a positive review.
_childDocuments_.name: Hammerwatch II

_childDocuments_.review: A good spin-off game with a very poor name.Hammerwatch as a series has been consistently fun for me although naming this one as a direct sequel is misleading.Hammerwatch: The first one being a static dungeon crawler with permadeath to beat with friends (and a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good end clear condition).Heroes of Hammerwatch: The dungeon is now randomly generated but there's appreciable amount of permanent progression to make each run easier and character progression exciting.Hammerwatch 2: More than mostly character progression, you now get character customization options. Fun minigame, rewarding crafting system and creative build options.The problem is just : Heroes looks more like a direct sequel to HW1 than HW2:Hammerwatch 2 is essentially the Diablo of Hammerwatch.The overpowered builds are fun to crack, the variety within each class is impressive, rare equipments are meaningful options and exciting to find.The one awful thing is the writing, but this is not a series where you should bother reading any story tbh.The story keeps talking detours not only in objectives (good, makes you explore) but in narration :"This guy told that man to tell me to tell you that this relic forged by that lad inspected by this friend commissioned by this creature is now guarded by a Golem in this castle..."Get to the point already istg...Despite the writing it's a fun good game, just know: every Hammerwatch game is a spin-off. Counterintuitively, if you liked HW1 and want more of the same you'll find something closer to that in Heroes.To highlight that this one is still not a direct sequel it should've been named something like "Chronicles of Hammerwatch" imho Mustn't be great solo but always a blast with friends, just don't bother reading any dialog knowing where to go and what to kill is more than enough.

_childDocuments_.review: To preface, I was extremely excited about this game. I was even part of the Playtest and I had extremely high hopes. It's unfortunate that I have to give it a negative review.This game is absolutely loaded with tedium. It is an absolute pain to explore the areas in this game. You run into so many dead ends you're constantly forced to slowly walk back towards areas with even MORE dead ends --both dungeons and overall world included. These dead ends don't even have a crumb of incentive (unless you consider wooden scraps and 10 gold coins to be)... I feel constantly punished for exploring in this game which is disappointing considering this open world switch-up of the series.The time system... dude. I'm sure there's a gameplay reason for NPC scheduling, but it adds even ANOTHER layer of tedium. All the loading screens are bad enough... Here's a fine example of this system not working in your favor.-Go to dock to take boat-its 0400. find out its only open from 0600-2200-walk all the way back to inn that is on the other side of the village-LOADING SCREEN-walk all the way back to dock-LOADING SCREENFrom first read this may not seem like that big of a deal, but when you have already been constantly waddling into dead ends with nothing, this could be the final straw in making you alt+f4.This game is simply not rewarding enough for all the tedium it throws at you.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me first start off by saying I have played Hammerwatch 1 and Heroes of Hammerwatch and I loved both of them. It's a rare game my friend group and I have always agreed on and played together. The other two while slightly different still felt like a Hammerwatch game and were great in their own ways. Hammerwatch 2 though? In its current state, I can't recommend this game. Dev's, if you're reading this, I'll try to outline all the issues I can find because I truly want to pour my time into this game as the base of this game is great. First off, controls. As others have mentioned, items you newly acquire will have its own button that needs to be mapped but can only be attached to a button if you have the item with you. Namely the bow quest one, having to waste gold on both the mini game AND the bow. Speaking of mapping, I had to abandon playing with a controller because the remaps don't work, and the 2 trigger buttons (R2 and L2) don't even register or work when you try to map them (and yes they work with other games). The day and night cycle. Like, I get it, but its such a pain in the butt. Make passing time free and a menu option that's instant when you're solo, and a vote to sleep/wait until a certain time with a multiplayer game. Allows you to still have the time sensitive things with out the wasted time (and gold) to go to an inn. Classes. My friend also reviewed this and couldn't recommend it as he played a paladin and hated it. A paladin should be tanky, can heal or mitigate damage in some way from the get go. The block is just pathetic, needs to be buffed, and isn't even a 360 block. He was dying so much I could real time sense the fun draining in his voice. And after playing all of the classes, the sorcerer is the only class that feels complete. All melee classes are pathetic, the ranger is lacklustre and kind of weak, and the warlock or w/e has to keep sucking in souls for weak and unreliable spells. A sorcerer should have a bubble of some sort but its better off being a skill for the paladin to take some more hits (on top of a massive buff to defence). Saved worlds instead of saved characters, and multiplayer. Having the saved characters in both previous games, and now locking characters to a single game is awful. You have to completely start a new file, do all the tedious stuff again, rebuild and re-grind your way up, JUST to get a chance to see if you like that character and if you don't, you have to restart. Not saving characters individually like the old games that are able to go into a world, is for me one of the worst aspects of this game. I love the RPG elements but not for the sake of ruining everything Hammerwatch was. Not being able to join a game as whatever character you want so you can switch on the fly with friends, is a huge detriment, as others have stated.And if were on the subject of saving, SAVING. You have to remember to manually save at the end of each session, with no prompt or warning of "Would you like to save?", or you know, autosaves..... What the actual hell? This is such a basic thing in basically every game, and it makes me incredibly disappointed in your team as a long time fan that this was either a choice or overlooked. Look. Like I said, I want to love this game. I'm rationing money right now but when I heard this game was out I didn't even bat an eye or look at the price tag, nor read any reviews. I just bought it out of love and excitement from previous games. But the things I mentioned NEED to be addressed asap to keep the glory of this franchise going. Please please please, listen to your fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Hammerwatch II

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Hammerwatch, I absolutely adore Heroes of Hammerwatch. But this game, it ain't it chief. For reference, I have been playing solo, as a wizard, on insane difficulty.A major step up from the previous games, gorgeous high end pixel artThere are 3 categories of enemies I've encountered.    1. Fodder, you blast through them without a second thought.    2. Health Sponges, kite them for 30+ seconds per basic enemy.    3. Gotta go Grind, perfect dodge for 10 minute straight or go grind exp for a few hours.As you level, most enemies slowly move from 2 to 1. Category 3, though, have very high movement speed and typically 1 shot you.No complaints, but not earth shattering either.Pretty minimalist, again, nothing special but not bad.The leveling curve could use some work. Early game felt too slow. The skill variety is a lot better than previous games. Each tier of skills feels like a significant change from the previous tier. I really like how each skill also has a variety of ways you can choose to improve it (range, AOE, provide additional buffs, new status effects, etc.). If not for the combat systems problems, this system would shine more and be a lot more rewarding.I've only slightly been paying attention to the main story, but it seems passable. You killed the dragon in the previous games, there's a new threat, gotta go save the world. The amount of direction you get from some quests makes them a bad scavenger hunt. The guidance in quests ranges from "go east and enter the cave" to "go find 4 bottles of wine somewhere in the game". If you're going to have quest descriptions this vague, please give me a quest arrow.This section is very specific to this game. Death in this game, at first glance, is not too punishing. You die, you lose 50-60% of your gold, and you choose to revive in town or the nearest entrance to where you are. This part works reasonably well. Dying also makes 5-6 hours in game time pass. Here is where the problems start. There is a day/night cycle, so if I choose to respawn in town and enough hours pass that it turns to night, all of the NPCs have gone to bed, so you can't sell anything you've collected. Fine, just go sleep...but that costs 100 gold, and you only have 80 because you died. You now have 2 options, leave the game running until the NPCs wake up or go kill yourself to make time pass. Then there are quests that automatically fail if enough time passes, such as if you die a bunch while fighting a boss. In my save there are now quest NPCs who call me scum every time I talk to them because I took to long getting them scraps of cloth or whatever.If you have a group of friends who you can play through the whole game with, this is probably a fun game (just don't play on insane). If you will end up playing this game solo, probably pass on it. Even at lower difficulties, I don't see the harder enemies becoming fun. The level requirements to fight these enemies will be lower, but they won't suddenly feel "fair" in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: There is just too many things not thought through in this game.For example, you have poisonous enemies in the very beginning. This means you most likely are going to die already at the beginning if you are any type of close combat character.However this pales in comparison of the sin that is the end game. In one of them there are walls that are supposed to move when you destroy a nearby orb. This does not happen for most players. We LITERALLY had to cheat to get to the boss of this place! Specifically go through walls since it doesn't work. This means that most players will have the "cheat" sign up to the right because the developers did not play-test the game to this point. The disconnect seems less though, which is good and all, but an entire endgame dungeon being like this? Devs... PLAY-TEST YOUR GAME.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of the original Hammerwatch, I was so excited to play this game with friends. Unfortunately I didn't find much of what I loved about Hammerwatch - chiefly challenging, engaging, densely designed levels great for coop.My friends and I couldn't bring ourselves to keep playing the game after spending the majority of our time progressing quests. The classes remain very well designed and they are fun to play, but the issue is the combat is so scarce, repetitive, and easy, you don't really get a chance to really use what the classes have to offer.In the original Hammerwatch, you have to work with your friends to take down swarms of advancing enemies who are defending their spawn points, on a uniquely designed and dense map. In Hammerwatch II, we just fought the same small packs of enemies over and over in large, empty caves or fields.Overall, I'm disappointed this game is more about generic open world RPG exploring and quests rather than challenging, engaging, coop gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: They killed the magic of the original HammerwatchYes, I know, it sounds horrible. But that is the sad truth. It is still a decent game, but it is very far away from the original game in playability. Is a different game, so for those who like these kind of games, where you have to do countless stupid quests like deliver a letter while slaying pirates, it is your game. But the original Hammerwatch was so much better. Just load your game and you are in the action, no bs, no stupid meaningless tasks. Now, in Hammerwatch 2, you WASTE SO MUCH TIME IS UNPLAYABLE. - You have day/night, so if you want a shop at night, sorry, wait. Or you want to fast travel? sorry wait- You want to sell something? go to the SPECIFIC shop that deals in that merchandise. - you want to explore this cave? fine, do you have a rope? nope, then you cant explore it, go buy one. Wait is night so you have to wait. Ah, and thats not the shop that sells ropes. - You got the hook, so now you can explore areas that were not reachable before, so go aaaaaaaaaaall the way back and try to remember where you could use the damn hook to explore those new areas- You got new gear while exploring. You want to organize your inventory? nope, all is scattered around, and no way to organize it neatly. Just guess what was the last things you picked!It really makes it very hard to open the game, knowing whats waiting for me there: meaningless tasks, stupid quests, unnecessary waiting, and so on. The original hammerwatch was game on from the 1st second. The game mechanics, combat, leveling up and so on are ok, more or less like the original or better (like skills), but the rest of stupid in game mechanics have killed the spirit of the original game, in my opinion. I have no idea why Crackshell would want to do a game like this. They had it right the first time, dont change it!!!!! You could have done hammerwatch 2 by just adding some more classes, and some additional levels, and I would have bought it right away! Like Temple of the Sun, what a suberb dlc (and free!).I hope the fix some of the nuisances via DLCs/patches (like day and night, please remove that asap)

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: After watching other gameplay and reading some other reviews, I now realize that my understanding of the game is very incorrect. The value of purchasing this isn't the existing pre-loaded campaign, it's the freedom to create your own and play scenarios created by others. I think the purpose of this is closer to a Dungeons and Dragons campaign simulator than it is a developer-content created experience. What I did NOT review involves using community created or expanded campaigns. I do think there's a lot of potential here, but at the same time, that doesn't change the expectation of buying a game, and jumping into a smooth experience.____Begin reviewThis game isn't what I'd hoped it would be. As someone who played Heroes of Hammerwatch, this is my perspective. Game saves - Your character only exists in a single save file. Be that either locally or with someone else. You cannot move a single player character to online or vice versa. Nor can you use a character from one save in another save. What this means is that if you join a random online game, you get to create a character at the same level as the party, but you can't take that character into another save. It's nice that the game gives you the character levels, but because the game is more gear-focused for progression, you are still a bit behind even if you "jump in".Time -The game has a time mechanic like many other games where day shifts into night, then eventually back to day. This modifies some of the lighting and shading effects, and is genuinely beautiful. It seems like 2 real life seconds are a minute in game. I might be wrong/off, but that's close enough. The issue with this is that this seems to be an arbitrary hurdle to progression rather than something that adds interesting events or changes to the game. Specifically, many NPCs are only active at certain parts of the day. Notably on the starting island, no NPC is available during the night. If every in-game minute is 2 seconds of time, it can take quite some time to get to the time you want to be at. Ah! But there IS a way to change the time - sleep at the inn! Because sleeping at the inn costs in-game money, this feature isn't available if you have very little gold. Worse, because it is night, you can't sell loot to an NPC to earn enough to skip time. This was a huge problem early on, that after I had a lot of gold, went away. But it's still very annoying to even see.I will note that some of the quests don't actually need to be started from an NPC to gain progress, but others explicitly do need you to speak to an NPC to receive an item to hand to the next NPC in the quest chain. The other glaring issue is that you cannot turn in quests when the NPCs are asleep at night.The time mechanic is bewildering in its implementation, and I have to wonder what would happen if the devs changed the NPCs to always be available. What would be the meaning of "night" in the game? What purpose does the time mechanic serve? I didn't play much past the first island before this review, but other than a night/day cycle and the NPC lockout issue, "time of day" seemingly has no "positive" effect on the game. No new effects or enemies. No exciting events. No secrets hidden in the moonlight.  There's nothing interesting about night that would encourage me to spend time there. I very much admit I could have missed it, but there is no redeeming feature here. Starting the game and gameplay - The game feels very open and appears to give you the choice of how to tackle its various quests through slaying monsters and collecting quest items for NPCs. The combat is quite engaging and can be fun, but it's definitely important to level your health so that some enemies don't immediately flatten you. There definitely feels like risk/reward gameplay here, and I really like that about Hammerwatch II.I really disliked the user interface for the first 30 minutes or so. It's quite confusing, and the game does not do a good job of introducing all of the features to you. That feeds into my issues listed above with game saves or the time mechanic. If there really are interesting positives here, the "tutorial island" should ideally highlight those, and provide a brief and direct explanation. After a while and through pure blind experimentation, the UI is actually quite robust and provides a lot of customization. The combat is fun an interesting. I played a couple of different classes to get the feel, and eventually settled on Wizard. The wizard has a powerful ranged attack, and compared to some of the other classes that are more melee focused, seemed to give me more time to breathe and move around to avoid enemies. But when I was playing melee, I was getting killed over and over. Yeah, it's definitely a skill issue, but it's very much easier to play at range in this game. As a paladin, even if you block, many enemies can and will give you damage over time effects. So, it's simply easier to dodge and attack from range.There are several interesting side-features like fishing, potion making, and enchanting. I hate to hammer (ha) on this again, but although there is a very vague tutorial, how to actually participate in these activities isn't obvious in the beginning. Nor does the game provide good hints for how to progress. For example, the potion maker is the first quest I think most players might find. Great, you can go and do it, come back, and you're given a potion flask. But... no charges for the potion. So, do you need to talk to the NPC to make more? How do you get charges. After playing, there are several ways, but it's odd that you don't seem to get charges on receiving your first potion. Further, the drops for bottles necessary for potion crafting seem VERY rare. I only came across one "large" potion bottle in the tutorial area. Interestingly, "large" is the smallest potion bottle size. Where are the smalls and mediums? Why does it start at large? Just another odd quirk of this game. And to highlight another strange feature, there are "hookshots" in the game, and points to use them throughout the first island. However, you don't get the hookshot for quite some time. It seems odd to place items just out of reach in early areas. Maybe the intention is for people to come back and re-explore, but given the random drops I've received, there's no guarantee the item you spent 10 minutes backtracking to find will have real value.I finished the main island in my time, and there are definitely a few rough difficulty jumps that the game doesn't alert you to. I set out to explore early on and learned that lesson. If you stray in the wrong direction, expect to face very tough enemies if you move too far outside of where the game expects you to go. One other odd quirk is that there is no "fast exit" feature for dungeons. Once you've killed the boss, you have to backtrack all the way out of the dungeon. Many modern games have a small teleport square or secret passageway that opens up. This is basic modern game design that doesn't exist.As a mild spoiler, you finally gain the ability to travel off of the island. I was very excited to do this, and when I was ready, headed to the ship... only to be told it's "too late in the day" to sail.I closed the game after that.
_childDocuments_.name: Hammerwatch II

_childDocuments_.review: I must admit, I was initially hesitant about purchasing Hammerwatch II due to so many negative reviews. However, I took the plunge, and am I glad I did! Hammerwatch II has proven to be an incredibly enjoyable and refreshing addition to the series.Unlike its predecessors, Hammerwatch II takes a different approach, deviating from the static dungeon crawler formula. The game introduces a handcrafted world with a fun storyline, providing players with an immersive and engaging experience. The emphasis on worldbuilding, quests, and exploration adds depth to the gameplay, making it my favorite installment in the series.One of the standout features of Hammerwatch II is the character progression and customization. The diverse classes offer creative build options, each with its own unique playstyle. The game rewards players with a satisfying sense of accomplishment as they navigate through the challenges, with a tiered gear system that adds meaningful variety to the loot. Discovering new and exciting gear is great fun.The addition of a rewarding crafting system adds another layer of depth to the game, allowing players to tailor their equipment to suit their preferred playstyles. The fun minigame also adds a playful element to the process, making it even more enjoyable. I always want to see more unique enemies, more unique gear, more unique items, more places to explore in a bigger world, with more puzzles and minigames, but I do appreciate the attention to detail in the world-building of Hammerwatch II. The quests and exploration contribute to the game's overall appeal. For someone like me who values quests with a large world to explore, Hammerwatch II delivers even more than the others in the series.In conclusion, Hammerwatch II has exceeded my expectations, proving that sometimes negative reviews don't tell the whole story for everyone's unique tastes. With its character customization, crafting system, expansive world, tiered gear system, minigame option, and so many quests, it has become my favorite in the series. If you're a fan of the Hammerwatch franchise please be aware this is not more of the same game. It is different, so if you are looking for more of the same, then Hammerwatch II may not fit your needs, but if you want something different from the others, then I highly recommend giving Hammerwatch II a chance. You might just find yourself pleasantly surprised, as I did.Note: I've only played multiplayer, and there are a few bugs so far. For example, player 2 was unable to buy or sell anything for some reason, so we played our own little roleplaying game of "the vendor does not like you so you have to drop the gold for me to pick up and then I'll go buy that item for you because the shop keeper likes me." :P

_childDocuments_.review: The biggest mistake many people are making is going into the game thinking that it is a rogue-like, as Heroes of Hammerwatch was, but it is an open world RPG.  It is very dynamic with it's mechanics and equipment.  Building a character is not as simple as "if Paladin then dump all into strength".  It is all beautifully designed.

_childDocuments_.review: edit: just found out some quests have hidden timers you can fail if you don't do them fast enough? When has that eeeever been an enjoyable mechanic?? Whyyyyy.A solid basis for a great game is here, but it needs some changes to ease tedium and friction. That and a few puzzling design decisions are enough for me to not recommend the game at the moment.Good:- The pixel art looks great. In fact, both the sound design and visuals do a great job making the game world feel alive.- I've only played the wizard, but the abilities are fun to use. I especially love the concept of a grimoire that lets you discover new spells as loot. I also like that you can change how abilities work depending on how you invest your skill points.- I haven't had a chance to try mods or mod tools yet, but I've heard the support is expansive, which I always love to see. It usually means good things for a game's longevity.- The castle/cannon minigame is a fun addition.- Lots of little bits of humor scattered throughout the game that keep things fun and light.Bad:My thoughts echo what many reviewers have already said. The multiplayer save system is awful. Sadly I don't see myself using it at all, as I don't always play at the same time as my friends, and I have no interest in maintaining a separate character for each of theirs.Additionally, there is a lot of friction and tedium in the game's current state. The day/night cycle is visually beautiful and immersive, but it's a pain in the ass. Time frequently skips around when you die, so you only have access to NPCs for everything from quest turn-ins to merchants half the time at unpredictable intervals unless you're at a tavern and want to pay to sleep. Much of the looting is tedious with minimal reward for the time invested. You spend a lot of time smashing containers for very very minimal returns - mostly junk items like planks of wood and tiny bits of gold. Oh and walking over tons of items on the ground like mushrooms in caves and crops on farms. Maybe I should be mad at myself for recognizing I will never use the items and still compulsively collecting them.  Dungeons are big, which is great, but they're not designed with exiting in mind, and you will spend a ton of time backtracking. You also cannot scroll the map in dungeons to view areas you've already been through, which is a feature I'd like to see added. As-is I find myself getting easily disoriented in the large and procedural-generated dungeons.  The readability of the game also needs a lot of work. The menus and inventory are not intuitively organized - I frequently find myself wondering why they chose the icons they did for things like the inventory categories and what the icons are supposed to convey. Inventory is also missing things like autosort and filtering tools. Bugs have been present but manageable. I've experienced a few crashes during transitions, which is mostly frustrating due to a lack of autosave and lost play time. I also was unable to complete an early quest because activating a keybinding for the shovel did nothing (I had to search steam threads to even figure out I had to set a binding first). I gave up and moved to the next area, where the shovel worked normally. One thing unrelated to gameplay that really peeves me is the day one DLC. The game is already a high price relative to similar games (a little less than $25 with the 10% launch discount), and the devs removed ~1/3rd of the character customization options from the game and locked them behind a $6 micro transaction. Not cool.I get they're a small team, and a supporter DLC with things like a soundtrack and artwork are a good way for dedicated fans to support the game, but locking out in-game content with it is super lame. I don't think it's unreasonable to say players should have access to a game's full content when they purchase at release for full asking price. Effectively they are pricing the game at $31 but asking you to split the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Didn't think I'd be doing this, considering I really liked the first game, but for the moment, I have to insist on a negative review. I've stopped playing until it's fixed and will happily edit my review if that happens. The big thing that plagues this game (in SP) right now is the astounding lack of QoL. It is fun to play, but sooooo tedious. The worst things:-The amount of backtracking is insane. People have known how to design levels with minimal backtracking for 30 years now, how is this still a thing? -The game uses a time system which passes extremely slowly, yet NPC's are only active for a part of the day, and it's different for each one. You can rest in some spots to pass the time, but this costs tons of money. It's making you pay to pass the tedium, for NO REASON. -You get the grappling hook WAY too late in the game, you have to revisit all the dungeons and places again. This should've been present right in the first dungeon where it can be used. -Quests don't tell you where the quest giver is. They hide in caves and whatnot and you can't find them back once you solved them.-You can't scroll on the map, it only moves when you do. So you can't scan around to see where you need to go.-Some quest givers just decide that they're not interested anymore and permanently give up on the quest. Very disheartening. Honestly, the gameplay loop is fun, but it just feels like this game takes unnecessarily long to play without adding ANYTHING to it. Whomever playtested this should feel ashamed, all this should've been picked up on during the very first tests. It's fun to play, it should just take less than a third the amount of time it does right now.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first review I've ever written, but I feel this game deserves it, especially with all the negative feedback that it's received.This game does what it sets out to do very well.  This isn't a Diablo clone, or a sequel to Heroes of Hammerwatch.  If you come to this game with that expectation in mind, you will be disappointed.This game aims to create a story driven ARPG experience, with skill based combat that is difficult to master, and provide a variety of heroes that play in genuinely unique ways, and require sensible planning for skill and stat distribution when leveling up your heroes.If you want to mindlessly wade through monsters like in Diablo, then this won't do it for you.  If you want a hectic Heroes of Hammerwatch rogue like experience that you play on repeat in an effort to master the game, this won't do it for you.If you want to take the time to master a challenging combat system with the hero class you choose, and thoughtfully build that hero as you take them through a story driven campaign, then you will like this game.  It does this very well.Regarding the negative reviews and common complaints upon release of this game: yes there were issues.  However it is clear from the last 2 patches, that the devs are dedicated to making this game shine, and removing the minor issues which plagued this game on release.  I've already beaten the game on hard, and will return and play it again soon.  This is a gem, and the devs are continuing to polish it.

I'm not sure what changed in Hammerwatch 2 from Heroes of Hammerwatch, but my friends and I were in a constant loop of crashing and losing progress every time we zoned out. This was, according to another Steam forum, fixed with the "Persistent Mode" version of the main campaign but it does not do as was claimed and we were still constantly crashing and losing progress.For now, I intend to refund the game and revisit it later, if this issue is fixed. I hope Crackshell manages to sort out whatever is causing this instability because I really want to play this game with my friends, I loved the previous entries.

_childDocuments_.review: Do not look at the Mixed reviews, this is a solid coop action RPG well worth a buy. If you are looking for original Hammerwatch, look somewhere else, because this is the evolution of the franchise with an open world to explore and meaningful progression much richer than the other games in the series. Hell! Much richer than many many other RPGs!Just a few classes but really deep in what they can do and well characterized, with a plethora of meaningful abilities that change as you put more points into their specialty. Enemies are a mix of new and old but they deliver what they need to do: keeping you always on the edge, looking for that corner to kite them to to abuse them with your spells, like in the other titles. The quests are simply great and meaningful. The devs are clearly respecting your time here, bar a few fetch quests that could have been avoided. The real gem is the amount of lore they put into them, with detailed descriptions and interesting bits on the world and its characters, often on the funny side for a good laugh. And I absolutely do not understand the people criticizing the quests themselves. They are varied and clever and you need to use your brains to overcome them. Perhaps this is the real reason they do not like them...One of the minor negatives is the mild repetitiveness of the locations which are outside the main quest, with mainly caves in various forms, although they are sprawling mazes full of secrets and items, like when you ticked the "Expanded Floors" in the HoH fountain but even more complicated since there are multiple entrances and connections to adjacent caves and dungeons. I absolutely love this kind of puzzly level design but I understand people who get lost. Another one is that the interface is quite confusing at some points, with the worst UI choice being the "Rumor journal" which is sometime needed to progress to check what to do in a quest (on top of the extensive quest text) but it is basically hidden at the bottom of  one of the character menu screens.Finally at this point after all the patches, the only real stinker is that your coop mates will lose connectivity at random during loading screens and they need to be invited in manually if you set your game as private. However the case with the disconnections, all in all, Hammerwatch 2 is truly a blast, especially if you play in a 2-3 player coop without cheesing the quests looking on the internet for the next steps. Do not do that, just read carefully and be mindful of any visual cue at screen. They are plenty It merges classic Hammerwatch gameplay with old-school RPG: think Gauntlet meet Ultima 7.After a year of patches, this is the best coop indie RPG of the last few years and I have a glimmer of hope that they will release more content and DLC for it, like another massive quest in its glorious tiny epic world which we all love since the first chapter.EDIT: added a few lines after more hours.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR This game has a higher base difficulty tuning than your average game. Hardcore gamers will adore this game. Casual gamers will need to choose an easier difficulty than they're used to. I talk a bit about why the negative reviews are laughable and inept.--- Intro ---So this is the best game I've played in 2023 and the negative reviews are from people with the leanings of the average game journalist. The following is a summary aimed at addressing criticisms I've read in negative reviews and why I think most are laughably inadequate. I play on the hardest 2 difficulties depending on friend group, and have played all the classes except wizard.--- Valid Criticisms ---* Character saves cannot be ported from 1 file to another (devs have immediately responded to feedback and are adding this)* Very occasionally, as in once in 20 hours, you may have a quest time out. I empathize with this one a bit.* (?) There might be issues with controller bindings. I use mouse and keyboard so I dunno about this one.--- Misinformation and Invalid Criticisms ---* (Lie) no fast travel* (Lie) abilities can't be rebound* (Lie) no ability to wait* (Skill Issue) It costs gold to do things* (Skill Issue) "Melee classes are hard"* (Skill Issue) "I dont know where to go" It's included in the quest description smh* (Skill Issue) "I lose gold for dying" Yes, you're punished for dying* "Why is it not a carbon-copy of the previous game?" --- Conclusions ---I can only assume most of the people complaining were expecting more hand-holding, or they just wanted a Heroes of Hammerwatch 2. This game has tunable difficulty switches out-the-box, and the campaign has already received QoL mods for people not interested in engaging with certain mechanics (i.e., routing NPC schedules, losing or spending gold, discovering new places and quests, traveling for longer than 20s). Seriously, the modding tools are insane and will probably enable these people tune for that more casual experience they're looking for. As for my own opinions: The gameplay, difficulty, and art are what primarily attract me. The graphics are downright gorgeous. I can rarely find combat in this genre that actually demands you pay attention and can furthermore be practiced and mastered. You can create character builds with deep synergies that can also interact with your equipment builds and other player builds. Classes are a secondary way of modulating difficulty and can help your friend group by giving extra crutch or challenge for each person (I.e., rogue is difficult, ranger is easier). On hard difficulties, you can survive most mistakes, but you need to react quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game, but it's full of bugs, at least in multiplayer. My friend had tons of issues while trying to play while I hosted a lobby. Throughout one playthrough, my friend crashed multiple times - nearly every time we loaded a new area. We encountered a bug after a crash that corrupted my friend's save and forced them to revert to an older version of their character. We nearly avoided a bug that would have softlocked us near the end of the game (a quest required a rare item that we already had in our inventory, but it wouldn't recognize the one we had, so we had to find a new one. This item is also used in crafting and is a finite resource, so if we had used all of them, we would have been stuck after 30 hours of gameplay). The debug menu can be used to get out of some of these bugs, but it makes gameplay far less enjoyable.If these were fixed, there are huge caves and a nice overworld to explore, a fun storyline, and a rewarding crafting/enchanting system. I actually really enjoyed these additions after playing Heros of Hammerwatch, which is a great game, but can feel a bit repetitive at times. Loot, boss fights, and character progression are also well thought out. Perhaps the bugs aren't as apparent in singleplayer, and in that case, this game would be great, but I can't really recommend this as a co-op experience in its current state, and I'm not sure if the developers intend to update the game anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: I have tried so hard to enjoy this game, and at its best moments, it really reminds me of how much I loved the first entry. The expanded level mechanics for classes, a day/night cycle, open world, more advanced questing, I thought, how could this be anything but awesome?!Unfortunately, it manages to not be. The open world and day/night cycle ultimately become more of a source of irritation, as you often end up backtracking and/or wandering around in confusion due to poorly communicated direction. In one case, my friend and I spent hours fighting through a dungeon, only to discover we weren't supposed to be there yet and we'd gone to the wrong place. In another, we trekked across the map to complete a quest but the individual we were supposed to turn it into was not in their house and we had to go find somewhere to sleep in order to pass the time for them to return (which is not free). I get what the devs were going for, but in practice it becomes less about fun and exploration and more about annoyance. Even little map markers would help obviate this. In the end, it seems like the devs added open world for the sake of doing so, rather than thinking about how to fill it with content that makes it not irritating. In spite of that, we tried to power through, but somehow recent updates have made multiplayer bugs worse, not better. I have a reasonably decent internet connection, yet the last two times we've tried to play I lag and/or get kicked out every 15 - 20 minutes and have to reconnect, only for the same problem to crop up. To try to end on a positive note, the Walls of Gadir minigame is pretty darn fun, it's sad that we often spend time playing that instead of doing actual questing due to mechanical and technical annoyances.Please listen to your fans and fix stuff. There is still so much potential in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a pretty high barrier to entry.  Thats the first thing that has to be said, it still has some of the hallmarks of the previous entries, but definitely feels closer to other ARPG games in the genre than the previous ones do.  Some of the original games charm is gone, but the arpg combat feels more polished, the build variety is pretty interesting and I've really enjoyed my time with the game.I've tried pretty every class and feel all of the classes are pretty good, though some are extremely punishing to play on higher difficulties, especially in the early game, but every class does still have just enough to get through.  After you tier up you should consider doing a realignment of your skill points each time, sometimes you will commit to suboptimal builds to clear a section and would be much better served with a different skill build when you tier up.I have not played any of the multiplayer so i can't speak to the performance on that.All in all, its a pretty good ARPG, if you're a fan of the previous games, theres a decent amount to enjoy with this one as well and if you're willing to put in the time, its definitely worth the price of admission.Some notes:  You need to pay attention to the quests you accept.  I spent a couple of hours initially kind of lost not being able to find npcs that i had taken quests from because it doesn't even list who the npc who gave you the quest was in the quest, nevermind where they are located so you can get lost very easily.The day night system is a bit inconvenient at times, frankly the game underutilizes the mechanic enough that theres really not much value in it outside of inconveniencing the player, making you have to sleep to be able to find the npcs you're looking for.  It feels like something where the mechanic had a much bigger ambition than what actually was delivered in the final product.Don't be shy about selling consumables like mushrooms to generate funds, this is not a game that rewards you for hoarding hundreds of items.The crafting system needs a smoother introduction frankly, stuff like cooking, and crafting of items is vitally important to the game, particularly with some builds that need additional regen but are easy to overlook despite how vital the benefits are. (In early game, you can make mushroom soup to get +2 regen to all stats, which will likely give you more than 2x your regen in all stats, but you need to craft or buy a skillet to be able to make food, you'll also need to buy onions from the veggie seller to be able to cook it)There are going to be some things that are up for dispute because of the old school vibe, I don't mind how little the game holds your hand.  With that said I feel there's probably a balance that needs to be struck where you can introduce and teach the player some of the tricks a bit more directly, it would probably lead for a much wider audience to enjoy the game without feeling lost and adrift, while not really being off-putting to the existing audience.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Heroes of Hammerwatch from launch and was even a part of some the DLC beta testing and this kind of feels par for the course.  They often release with a lot of weird decisions, but they do take in player feedback and make even big adjustments if it's really what the community wants and is actually viable.I will also say have not beaten the entire game yet so obviously some things might get better, but the parts I've played of the game shouldn't have had these issues anyways.The game feels like it came out of a vacuum where there wasn't enough of the actual audience giving feedback.   There are a lot of things you might not notice if you've played the game too much already, programmed it yourself, or had "rose tinted glasses" about since it was your idea/work.There's also a LOT of development time put into neutral/negative features:*   Visually cool except when one of them stands in a chokepoint or you get sandwiched by a couple of them.  Then it becomes annoying.*   Again, visually looks cool...but in gameplay it's a huge hinderence, especially when connecting to the previous issue where you are sometimes just watching a dude walk to the store at 1 mile an hour.  It also costs a decent amount of gold early game to control the cycle so your first experience of the game has a high chance of being arbitrarily screwed over.  I couldn't complete the potion quest once because I didn't realize they'd be asleep and I spent my money already.*  Being Concise is vital if there's no voice acting.  I can promise 90% of the people confused about where to go and what to do are because they just got tired of reading so much fairly dry text.  If the game get's to a state where I could recommend it I might just make a language file that trims down the text to a reasonable state.A couple other problems worth mentioning:*   This was in Hero's of Hammerwatch so I'm kind of lost as to why it wasn't included.  Rather than some of these other features, having the ability to scroll around the map seems way more important.*  My friends and I literally have a new group meme of going "Good Cave" anytime we go somewhere and get nothing out of it just because of this game.  Of course we look for secret walls and sometimes find one or two, but it's crazy how often we go into a cave and come out with nothing but a small chunk of XP.* I don't think I need to mention that playing multiplayer, randomly being consumed by the void and then spawned *dead* at a cave entrance we've never even been to is a problem.  I'm sure the developers are working to address those kinds of bugs, but it seems like the game wasn't stress tested with the host/client having spotty wifi/internet.Some suggestions for the game:*   Please...maybe your engine doesn't have a layer system to let certain collision boxes not exist to others, but if you're going to have NPCs get in the way like that it needs one.  Maybe the host is able to just push past them, but non-hosts still seem to suffer from NPCs (including enemies) being immovable objects like in "Heroe's of Hammerwatch".*   I would make the sleeping fee incredibly small if you REALLY want to keep it, but I think it would be a case of sunk cost fallacy to even have it.  For most of the playerbase, having to sleep to get the shops back open is a negative especially if the shop you go to check is really far from the Inn.  .* : Fixing this is obviously easier said than done to keep it balanced, but there really does need to be more loot rooms.  If you don't want as many item rooms you could also add gold rooms, flower rooms, crop rooms, per-player single-use potion refill rooms, etc.  Just there should be more than "break boxes/tables for some wood", "find maybe one garbage common boot per cave", and "fight 100 wolves/bats for a single attribute point and a chunk of xp".  Hell, a literal room that just has a per-player single-use XP fountain would be more exciting to find.  You really gotta tap into those kinds of moments that make players eyes go wide more.*   This is definitely the hardest to address because it's roots are caused by a story that assumes players will care a lot more than they do.  "Hammerwatch" and "Heroes of Hammerwatch" have not cultivated a story oriented fanbase.  They have a roguelike fanbase who play those kinds of games because they just care about the action.  I'd be willing to bet not even 5% of the playerbase who have beaten the games who know anything besides "We go smacked dragon and won."    Rather than having the Hookshot quest be like go here, then go to this guy, then go to that guy to get a password to get into the back entrance, it would've been more aligned with expectations for the quest to go "Go fight this group of bandits!" and we just go there and fight them and get the hookshot from the boss.  I just want NPCs to throw me at challenges and dungeons in a very straight forward way.  The game either needs substantial script/quest work or adding constantly visible waypoints.  The latter feels kinda lame, but is certainly the fastest to dealing with player's getting lost on the "what do".*   My friend spams down a couple traps down and it insta kills a group of +2 bonus player THICC skeletons we aren't even supposed to fight yet, but my Paladin judgement hammer that sorches the ground with holy flames barely even registers on their healthbar then goes on cooldown.  The early game just feels really unsatisfying for some classes.  I swear the Paladin's hammer is actually a pool noodle and I wouldn't even be mad if it actually looked like one.  It might be worth just sitting down and making a spreadsheet that does some calculations on abilities like "Damage per Mana" and "Expected number of target's hit" as compared to a character's expected "Mana Per Second" so you can identify what values feel good and then make sure that's pretty consistent.  You  factor in a character's relative safety, but that doesn't matter as much as you'd think since none of the characters really try to get hit.  Paladin just runs out of stamina from blocking if he tries and takes damage most of the time anyways so it ironically discourages me from even using the shield.  I might've used it if it had an ability like "Your next shield block triggers a significant AOE effect" rather than "I hope you invested in stamina to do little thorn damages even though mana is way more fun and used for more things".

_childDocuments_.review: Before purchasing, know that the publisher has abandoned this game. The developer is no longer authorized to patch or add content. A friend and I played the campaign via co-op on the second hardest difficulty with relatively no issues until a point where he'd crash during every stage transition (there are MANY of these). After searching the official Discord, we discovered this particular crash bug has been around for awhile and is caused by a unique item dropped by the giant spider boss. As long as that item exists in your game instance, certain players will perpetually crash. Discarding them on the floor is not enough. To fix: ALL players must sell ALL copies of that item to a vendor and wait a full 48 in-game hours for the shops to cycle inventory.Hammerwatch 2 is like a modern incarnation of Gauntlet with quest progression, sandwiched inside a bland medieval fantasy shell. The colorful sprite aesthetic with visual damage numbers is a bit reminiscent of older 2D PSX titles and boasts high visual clarity, even at points when 20+ mobs of enemies are constantly chucking mini bullet hells. Five unique classes have 16 unique skills each which allow for varied build customization. I can't speak to the balancing of everything but I was able to work out a couple of serviceable and distinctive playstyles using the ranger. Convenient respecing makes it mostly painless to change builds to something better suited for late game if your initial choices don't pan out, that's always appreciated.The story picks up immediately after the first game, which I didn't play, but I wonder now as I write this if there's an explanation to why the party starts out at level 1 when they just ran an entire prior adventure. Meet up with a resistance movement, kill a dragon, dethrone an illegitimate puppet ruler, defeat the necromancer mastermind. The game tells you exactly what's gonna happen and it unfolds with no surprises. Keep narrative expectations low as this isn't the kind of RPG that offers dynamic story consequences. Instead of cinematic set pieces, tension, or character development to encourage player investment, long winded exposition is vomited from forgettable NPCs I suspect were named with a random word generator.There's a vast and dynamic open world advertised but it's really just one moderately sized hub area, a smaller second hub area, and a tiny starting island-- all peppered with generic caves which use the same exact tile set and inhabited by a single regional enemy type. Some caves contain a hidden random drop chest, some a side plot progression mechanic, but an alarming amount have seemingly no purpose but to maybe serve as an area to farm a bit of experience and materials for a crafting system you'll likely not utilize outside of side quests. I stopped actively picking up useless mushrooms and still had close to 1000 by end game. The vast majority of these caves feel like they were procedurally generated a single time, then given a playtest pass for functionality. Really, like a fire demon wolf cave could at least tint the screen red and have some wavy heat visual effects to differentiate itself from the other 20-30 caves. I initially thought the cordoned off regions of the world map's edge would open up, but at about 75% through the game it is clear those areas were meant for future DLCs that will never be. This makes the world feel too small for the scope the narrative pushes. For example: there's emphasis placed on travelling to a far desert for an important quest but it's just an empty screen of sand with a lone NPC chilling in his studio apartment pyramid with your fetch item. This is not an isolated incident and it really makes everything feel disappointingly small in a setting hyped up to be a sprawling adventure. The design in general inadvertently discourages exploring until a crucial hookshot traversal item unceremoniously drops from the main questline just before the halfway point of the game, as without it you're just missing too much.There are a handful of main dungeons that were clearly handcrafted compared to the caves and those hold up a bit better, though some are very long winded time fillers like the sprawling cultist temple built by an architect with a hallway fetish and a 3+ floor troll cave complex with multiple entrances and exits. Of course it uses the generic cave tile set but at least there's some bone furniture feng shui. There's no equivalent of 'town portals' or convenient fast travel in the wilderness, so after completing a dungeon, it's necessary to manually backtrack all the way out which is an interesting design choice seeing as games from as far back as the ancient late 1900s solved this issue by adding an alternate exit at a dungeon's end or a one way shortcut back to the entrance. Enemy design is uninspired: three types of wolves, multiple palette swaps of three types of bugs, boars, three classes of troll, different flavors of undead (fresh or frozen), assorted human fodder in Halloween costumes, and for some reason, shamblers from Quake 1 (why?). The bosses all feel distinctive and are definitely the highlight of the game's combat, with the exception of the dragon which constantly cycles into an invincible flying state, making it the most tedious fight.The day/night cycle curiously just serves to lock out any NPC the player needs to interact with from roughly 10:00PM to 10:00AM. Maybe for immersion? The music and lighting changes. Certain sidequests are on a timer or only unfold over time. Some randomly placed graveyards in the overworld will spawn undead enemies at night. That's all the differences I noticed. The feature feels very under cooked. Perhaps the devs could have given players a reason to fear travelling at night. Maybe introduce items or events that only appear during certain times of day. There's a main story NPC that jokes about you needing to return to him in specifically 10 hours after completing a task, as if the game is self aware that the mechanic is forced to justify its own existence.I appreciate RPGs with co-op multiplayer because we all know there aren't enough out there, but I can't recommend this game in good faith as the setting has no soul, the exploration leaves much to be desired, and multiple game features are inconsequential (day/night cycle, most itemization outside of balancing resistances, crafting, cooking). The entire game feels like a proof of concept that wasn't properly fleshed out. Great sprite work and boss fights alone can't compensate for all that. I'm not trying to throw mad shade at a small dev team, you can tell there was love and sweat put into the title, but for a $25 asking price in a highly competitive market-- this did not stick the landing. Best of luck to the devs on their future Heroes of Hammerwatch 2 title.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a "Ehhh" button to select for this game. It's a good game but to me it seems like it needed another couple or 5 months of polish and bug fixes and quality of life changes.It feels a little bit rushed.  A lot of the dialogue (English) doesn't make sense or is incorrect. Quests are sometimes cryptic and some of them are timed (why?!!?!?! that's a TERRIBLE idea for an ARPGish open world game!!!).You get so many items clogging up your bags, and you have NO IDEA what to do with 90% of them since there is no toolip or anything explaining why this item exists.  is it vendor trash? is it a tool for later? Is it a quest item??? Who knows!!! You'll have to guess. If you drop it or sell it and it ends up being important later, too bad!  Fun, right?  ....Right?Leveling is pretty slow and tedious, with you needing to reload and kill things over again to get a little boost. I don't like how skills are set up.  Unlocking higher ability tiers is expensive and a bit annoying.  The game wants us to apply our skill points but punishes you if you do.  I absolutely HATE 'holding onto' skill points to use later, but you just about have to if you want the build you prefer.   1500 gold to respec, too? Good LORD!!!  Assigning hotkeys is a clunky mess, and the game doesn't automatically do it.  For instance, the little bow shooting range quest to get a bow, you have to pay 500 gold to play the game, then extra 250 (I think?) to buy the bow to play it.  But after you say "yes" and get the bow, the game instantly starts, without any button assigned to shoot the bow....so after you rush to assign a hotkey to shoot, the game is over, and you wasted 750 gold you can't get back.   To play again, another 500 gold.That happened last night to me and it made me so angry I alt F4'd and haven't logged back in since. Which brings me to my next major issue: EVERYTHING costs gold, even the passage of time costs gold, way too much gold...you have to pay to pass time so that you can turn in quests since for some reason there is an annoying pointless day and night cycle where NPCs are unavailable. And if the timer runs out on that quest? Too bad! Now you get to hunt that NPC down to talk to them to get that quest out of your inventory. Just...Ugh...  It wouldn't be so bad if we could just choose to use a 'wait' command to pass time quicker and for free like literally every other game out there has with a day/night cycle. You can sell all the flowers and stuff you pick up for a pitiful bit of gold, but not every vendor will buy everything in your bags, and vendors have a finite amount of gold to trade with.  This is a game, not a banking simulator. It's not necessary to have all this going on.  These devs just LOVE making things cost gold and making gold hard to come by.  It's not fun to force us into this economy.Also, I'd really like more classes.  I don't really jive much with any of these.   Wish there was a Druid.

Even though it says ARPG, the best features of that (solid multiplayer, boss farming for epic loot) are not going to be in this game. No repeating content - like most story-driven RPGs (but not HnS ARPGs) the content is cleared once campaign-style. (in other words it's not Diablo2, Titan Quest, Torchlight, Last Epoch, PoE, Grim Dawn).1. I know it sounds ridiculous, but this is not a troll post. _childDocuments_.review: 90% of the negative reviews are people expecting Heroes of Hammerwatch 2, which is neither the title nor the description of this game.The other 10% are people complaining about multiplayer save files only being available to the host.  This goes hand in hand with the first invalid complaint.  I doubt the people posting negative reviews about it here are complaining about the exact same functionality in Baldur's Gate 3, which is more similar in genre to Hammerwatch 2 than HoH.  The quest system notably would not work if you could play your character solo, then bring it into a friend's campaign, having finished quests that the host world had not completed.  This is extremely typical for the genre, and imo a good decision.tldr; Game is good, game is fun, me play gamePlaying around with your build and min-maxxing gear is pretty accessible. I'm interested to see how things play out in the long term, as well as the scope of the game.  To me it has the charm of a classic RPG, where not everything is explained to you outright, which brings a feeling of true discovery.I really love crafting and enchanting my own gear, especially with the large amount of crafting materials that can be gathered.  Making your own potions adds more to your build, allowing you to select what potions to have equipped that best fits your play style or role in the party.  The food buffs are actually good and pretty important, making it valuable to find ingredients, which I also enjoy.As is with all Hammerwatch games, the combat feels very fun and rewarding.  There is a lot of ability variety within classes that make builds feel very unique.Overall fun game so far, hoping the scope and variety expands through the game.tldr; some systems are annoying or fail to impress, but it doesn't ruin the gameI do have complaints about the game, and some are mentioned in the negative reviews.These are ordered biggest complaint to smallest.Quest writing has been sub-par so far.  Especially in the starting area.  The quests for 2 of the dungeons on the starting island are "There are (wolves/pirates) over there, please go kill them and I'll give you money".  I talked to some NPCs and they did mention pirate raids causing issues, but it just felt like it had no weight at all.  Not everything has to have a massive story line, but when the motivation for completing a dungeon is essentially a fetch quest, it takes away from the experience.The UI is rough, especially for combat.  Massive bars spanning the entire vertical length of your screen that are pushed to either side is not readable at all. It's also very weird that EXP is there, it was relevant for HoH but not really in this game.  It also makes the UI even worse, since 2 of your resources are on the left, and one is on the right, but the far right is not relevant to combat at all.  The UI is also almost impossible to navigate with a controller, especially inventory and shops.  I find myself reaching for my mouse every time I want to trade or level up.The dungeon areas are... large?  That's the best way I can describe them.  Large, full of dead ends, and they usually contain the same 5 enemies throughout an individual dungeon.  I find myself asking when the end of the dungeon is, or when I'll see a new area or enemy.  More variety would be nice.The shop system is not intuitive.  They seem to be scattered around the town with no real label.  When you talk to the shopkeeper, they usually say what they sell, but there is a 0% chance I will ever remember where I want to go when it is relevant.The time system is just... weird.  It probably shouldn't be a part of the game unless it plays a major role later.  It really just seems like a gold sink.  It's difficult, but you can get "stuck" in a situation where you don't have enough gold to rest at an inn, but it's night time and all of the shops are closed, so you just have to wait it out if you want to progress.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me begin by saying this IS NOT Heroes Of Hammerwatch 2, nor is it trying to be! Hammerwatch 2 is a superb sequel to Hammerwatch I, combining the best of Hammerwatch's original combat with the deeper customisation and itemisation of Heroes of Hammerwatch. This is not a traditional rogue-like. If you are looking for a rogue-like - Hammerwatch Anniversary edition is a incredibly good remaster of the Original game plus contains three campaigns instead of the original one campaign (including Shaftlocke Tower, which was the campaign for Heroes Of Hammerwatch, redone in the original games style)This is a labour of love and while there are some bugs it is a fun new game and a lovely continuation of the series taking it to an open world format. Like the original game and its spin-off it will NOT hold your hand nor guide you every step of the way you are expected to explore and discover for yourself.It is getting an unfortunate amount of negative reviews that quite frankly are not deserved by people who clearly did not bother to check the trailers, multiple developer diaries, Q&A's and other such things explaining the game and what it is and isn't. There are plenty of valid reviews of course - the game has its issues. Multiplayer is janky and buggy, save files are a mess and other problems are around but the development team are working on it and patching. This is a small studio, not some AAA studio and if we can accept the utter-trash that is releasing these days from big developers like EA in buggy messes we can afford to be patient and wait for fixes here.TLDR: Game is fun and good with friends, if somewhat buggy. Worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of Hammerwatch and Heroes of Hammerwatch, I can understand the mixed reviews. However I can say the game is still fun for fans of the franchise, but you have to keep in mind it's meant to be more like Dungeon Explorer / Diablo than its rogue-like predecessors. If you're looking for a spiritual successor / evolution of the Gauntlet / Dungeon Explorer series, this fits the bill nicely.The other big thing weighing it down at the moment is the controller support that feels spotty. it shouldn't be necessary to use the right stick / mouse to navigate the menu, and the binding of items / skills is needlessly complex. It really feels tailored to keyboard and mouse play at the moment and I hope these get ironed out eventually so it becomes a better portable / Steam Deck experience.Very enjoyable with friends, as with other Hammerwatch games.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the mixed reviews: This is a GOOD game. It has the hammerwatch style we know and love despite the different format. The format is done correctly and is a fun world full of challenges and secrets to discover and things to interact with and engage with. There are a variety of difficulty options, though this game does get very crazy at the harder ones so I suggest starting with a dose of caution, and it runs well enough.Most of the major concerns that a lot of old negative reviews have are now fixed. Though there will still be negative reviews from three groups of people:- Those who dislike the new format (despite hammerwatch having a history of constantly changing its format as the years progress)- Those who dislike the difficulty (choose an easier one)- And those who dislike the fact there is no fast travel.Quite frankly, this last point is bad enough that if a mod did not exist I would have given this a negative review. There are plenty of times when you must backtrack significant distance or climb back up to a boss area. Sometimes there are faster paths and shortcut esque cave entrances, sometimes there is not. Without modding this game it would become extremely tedious and annoying whenever you make a mistake and get to spend the next 5 minutes on a walk of shame back to where you died.So modded, the game is good. Not modded, all the good is overshadowed by a MAJOR point of frustration.Oh and the issue with cloud saves making things weird sometimes seems to be around. One of my friends who was playing with it turned on experienced a crash almost every time we loaded a new area. Turning them off fixed it, but a  bug that causes you to be unable to play the game should be fixed ASAP even if there is a workaround.TL:DR: GOOD GAME, USE FAST TRAVEL MOD, TURN OFF CLOUD SAVES.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, but such appalling design decisions that I can't recommend this right now.- Map only shows a small area around where you are, you can't look at everywhere you have been.- No icons above vendors so you have to memorise what services they offer.- No waypoints mean you can spend ages looking for something with very little info to go on.- No teleport out of dungeon mechanic. You have to seriously trek back all the way through the dungeon.- EXP, mana, stamina bars are vertical on the screen. Why?- Gamepad controls for UI are terrible, you will end up using the mouse for inventory management.- No easy fast travel when out in the field.- Area map is useless as it doesn't show your location.- Game can randomly crash if you die and respawn.There is just too many baffling design decisions that really hold the game back, I just hope they fix it up with quality of life improvements as I know it can be a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: A few weeks after release and the multiplayer still has some game-breaking issues,  and a few design choices that turn adventuring into a bit more of a slog than I'd usually like....- Certain areas will cause all remote players to disconnect, and fail to reconnect until the host leaves the area or restarts their game.  One such area is a hedge labyrinth to the northwest of the main town; probably because of some of the scripted events running when you enter the room. - There are far too many "mysterious cave"s pockmarking the map... every once in a while you might get lucky and find a hidden treasure, but most of the time you spend 5-10 minutes fighting groups of mobs for not much to show for it- Relentless backtracking. Some quests have you travelling from one corner of the map and back multiple times. An option for quick travel would be great, but instead you have to traipse through the same landscape over and over again and fight the same handful of mobs that have respawned again. I think I'll still keep playing it because there's certainly some good to it, but if I knew all of these issues beforehand? I think I would save myself the trouble. Maybe with time some of these issues will be addressed.
