_childDocuments_.review: So I am just around 19 hours play time.And the TL;DR is I am enjoying myself.I've started 3 characters, with my main character being a level 27 Paladin. But the others being a 5 Ranger and 7 Wizard.The only way I can describe this game is Maximum Entertainment trying to evolve their system, but in doing so losing the heart of the originals. The game isn't a Rogue-Lite anymore, it's an ARPG. Which to me is fine, but if you loved the Rogue-Lite/Like of Heroes of Hammerwatch (HoH), or Hammerwatch itself, this game will be a shock at first.But. The game FEELS just like the originals still, just open world now. A different level up mechanic which I do enjoy, though it's not as robust as PoE/D4/LE. Your limited in which abilities you can upgrade, which means you'll likely fall into everything being unlocked if there is no level cap (similar to HoH). Idk if there is anything past maximizing your skills.I'm really enjoying my Paladin, and the gear I find and end up using is focused around the abilities I use a lot.Pros/Cons:Single vs Multi: There is a difference as Single player characters can't join a multi now, so progress is separated a bit. --- Mixed FeelsThe Story: So far the story ties in really well with the other games, and I'm a fan. Though what I am not a fan of is how my character responds to dialogue. I would've just preferred "Next" button instead of "Yeah yeah, get on with it" rotation of responses when it's incredibly important info. Sure, not everyone is going to read the quests, a lot of people just want action, but that so far is my only negative on the story. It's pretty a generic hack n slash plot, but, because of the other games, it does feel like the world building is there and prevalent, which is why my nonchalant responses to this lore bothers me.--- ProRunning... Running everywhere: There are networks, abilities, and items that increase your movement speed, but my god do you do a lot of running if you are going in blind. A Mount in the over world/outside of dungeons would be nice, as since I am blind, I've ran back/forth from quests just to deliver or acquire stuff constantly, or I am just outright lost.A Mount and Compass (another potential item) that point to a check-boxed quest would be a massive help, but it does feel "Old school" without that feature. So maybe make the compass point be an optional thing when you start your game (which does exist already)--- ConChallenging Combat: My Paladin is on Normal, my Wizard/Ranger are on Hard, the combat is tough until suddenly it isn't. Through personal experience with the foes, to the gear, and ability unlock, there is just sudden invisible thresholds that make you feel like fodder, to suddenly feeling incredible. And I think they did a good job finding that. The game can be a bit grindy at time, but that's par for the course with ARPGs--- ProDay/Night: In the other games, Day/Night really didn't do anything. In this game, Mobs respawn on the timer, citizens sleep, shops close, travel stops, and quests turn in/acquiring is gone (All but the main storyline). You can sleep at an Inn or the Church for a cost, but never so much you'll go broke, but there is no buff to sleeping as far as I notice. So you can just keep on clearing mobs that respawn depending on how much time has passed.--- MixedHow this game handles dying: Death isn't like the Rogue-Lites obviously, so how does it work? It costs a % of your money, and you can respawn at the nearest town, or at the beginning/end of the dungeon for a higher % of coin until you pass a threshold and can't pick that option any further. When you die, you lose several hours to resting/recovery.So far, I have only failed a single quest, so I'm unsure if there are others that can if you just keep dying over and over.--- MixedHow to offset death: In other Hammerwatch-world games, you have potions. It's the same here, but you get 3 Potion Slots that you can fit with upgraded sizes, multiple options Mana/Healing/Mixed etc, and more. It leads to better customization of your character, and so I'm a fan.--- ProCrafting!: This is new to the game, but Food/Buffs and Gear/Quest items you just gather and can sell enmasse are a thing. Crafting so far hasn't produced anything incredible in terms of gear, but the food buffs and quests have been nice as I just had the things on hand for ez experience from repeatable quests.--- ProItems/Loot: In the Rogue-Lite/Likes, your loot resets at the start every time, win or lose. In this, it's a ARPG, you keep finding more and more loot and equipping it till something replaces it. But the loot you are using HEAVILY impacts certain classes more than others, and is a nice change of pace.Paladin is Shield and Mace: it never changes, but some maces upgrade some abilities in different ways (pro)Wizard is Wand and Book: I hated the Wizard starting spells and was looking for means of changing them, and then I realized your items impact your damage type/spell (right click). Being at only level 7, I wonder how many spell options there are, but so far I like the small variety I have seen (Orb, AoE Blast, Laser, in different magic styles. Fire/Frost/etc.)--- ProMultiplayer: I have yet to play this way. But I am looking forward to this mode. There is an option to make the Loot Shared or Instanced, which I love. I want to play with Shared Loot and then try to help everyone get stronger together. Instanced Loot seems like the easier option, but it's less interesting if the goal is to go on a RPG experience together. I'd say the recommended party layout would be 3 players with 1 focusing in each of the 3 stats.--- ProWith that, I will be trying to finish the game soon. Aside from the constant feeling of being lost (especially in the Sewers which are a horrific nightmare of stairwells and levels), I have greatly enjoyed my time in the game.I hope this review helps you make your decision

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, it is a bit too... cumbersome for that. It picks up where its predecessor from 2013 left off. We have just defeated the dragon Worldfire in his castle on a small island and are now trying to leave the island on a ship organised by the resistance. Of course, this does not turn out to be as easy as planned. We move our tiny but wonderfully drawn and animated character around with the gamepad in twin-stick fashion. LS to walk, RS to move the head or our weapon in one direction. With RT we strike, with RB we shoot with our ranged weapon, with LT we block. The exact abilities, however, depend on our chosen character. It is not so much a simple action game as a full-blown role-playing game. We can interact with countless things in the game environment - buttons, levers, doors, NPCs. Useful things are picked up as soon as we walk over them. So we run around in typical RPG fashion, stealing the locals' apples and carrots, smashing every crate and barrel while decimating the wolf population and completing little side quests (bring me this, bring me that...) for the local population. For example, cleaning the cellar of vermin for the landlord, which has been part of every classic role-playing game since The Bard's Tale. Whereas the vermin here were not rats, but green beetles. The pirates' cave, however, is somewhat larger than expected, and the pirates have not only kidnapped the captain of the ship that was supposed to take us off the island, but have also stolen all the important parts of the ship. The leader of the pirates is then also the first boss opponent. Here it pays off if you don't play alone but with three friends in the cooperative online mode.The game menu is quite extensive - on the first page we see our equipment and other items, on the second page are the attributes of our hero (strength, skill,...), on the third page is the quest log, on the fourth page the skill tree, the fifth page offers information about the world and on the last page we have a very useful overview map. Conversations are in text-only form. The game made my fans howl loudly, but limiting the framerate solved the problem. It can be controlled with the gamepad, but mouse and keyboard also work well. If you fancy an indie Baldur's Gate 3 in pixel art graphics, you won't go quite so wrong with Hammerwatch II and get a detailed action role-playing game with countless items, quests and character values.Action-rpg, quite detailled but of course not as polished as the big productions like Baldur's Gate 3.

So you are looking around location for 2 hours and after that you are making huge facepalm that simple F button in the corner, not the button, but the place where you can simply jump - blocked you from playing further.In addition, a lot of locations in which it is not foreseen that the player can enter there without having a story item. _childDocuments_.review: The genre of the game has shifted substantially towards being a more modern ARPG, but save mechanics and QoL systems are extremely lacking.Characters are locked to whatever save they start in. These 'guest' characters also aren't shareable, so you better always play with the same people and never leave them out. The developers really need to separate character saves from world saves to allow for smooth drop in/out.It seems like money is shared on pickup, but all other items/loot aren't -- including items for quests. Combine this with the save system, and if a friend logs out of you game with important drops for a quest you're juts screwed.If you start a singleplayer game, it seems like you can't host it multi or visa-versa.Really needs some work.

_childDocuments_.review: The game definitely is fun, however there are some quality of life changes that I am amazed are not apart of this game. There's not a lot of explanation on what you're picking up. Be prepared to hit "c" and tab a lot, until you've memorized what everything is which is another one of my main gripes. There's not enough keybinds in this game. I shouldn't have to hit c and tab through to get to the quest journal (or click), or to look spend attribute points. A simple "I" for inventory, "J" for journal would do wonders for this game. Be wary on some quests as well as they are time sensitive, but there is no clear indicator of this. I've failed several quests due to exploring and not realizing that some of these quests had timers on them... why?Another gripe I have is that you are punished for exploring. So many needless dead ends which require you to back track a good distance.I am not sure why there are sleeping NPCs in a game like this. It almost feels like this game just wants to waste your time with the running into dead ends, having to wait or spend currency to rest at an inn just to speak to a shopkeep. In addition to waiting at a dock for the exact appropriate time to travel. (waiting, waiting, waiting)It took me awhile to figure out that the game clock is on the map -- which leads into... why is there no minimap built into the game?(For those that want the "not officially completed version, hit tilde and paste ui_hud_visible_minimap 1). The overlay does not have nearly enough opacity for me to feel happy leaving it up all the time. The game itself is beautiful, but no one will experience it because they're hitting tab every two seconds into a jarring map overlay. Town portals? That'd be pretty cool too considering some of these dungeons are *huge*, and I've spent more time running backwards than actually playing the game. Even a quick exit option, or a option once you've beaten a dungeon boss/completed the dungeon having an additional exit would be beneficial.I haven't delved into the "completed" multiplayer experience, but it's similar to Baldur's Gate 3 in which a person cannot keep that particular NPC/character that was created. I'm a bit saddened by this, but this isn't an end all for me. It's functional, enough, however be prepared to feel a little salty over the chests not dropping items for both party members as it's similar game Heroes of Hammerwatch.Overall I see so much potential, and I'll still play the game -- however it's hard to give this a solid positive review when it ultimately feels rushed and like my personal time playing the game isn't valued and appreciated. Maybe I'll change it down the road, but for now -- make it player friendly and not "creator of the game, I know what this all means/does" friendly. I'd wait to purchase, but you'll likely still have some fun playing it if you choose to buy.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really excited for this game and wanted to enjoy it, but I encountered so many little annoyances in my first half hour or so of playing that I had to refund. A lot of the design decisions here are legitimately baffling. Why are stamina, health, mana, and experience represented by vertical bars on both sides of the screen, taking up unnecessary screen space and preventing you from seeing all of them at once? Why is there one overlay map that only shows features in a particular radius and one "area" map that has no details at all, making it basically impossible to get a sense of any location that isn't immediately next to you? Why do quests not identify the quest giver or have any sort of in-game marker, forcing you to roam around with your slow walking speed until you happen to speak to the one particular person who gave it to you? Why is there no wait button, which means you'll be spending essential gold just to pass the time until shops are open? Why are item and ability descriptions so vague? Why are hidden walls basically impossible to find but often hide important switches or items? Why is the camera so tightly zoomed and walking speed so slow? Why do some quests have markings on them that are never explained? These are just a few of the things that immediately jumped out to me after less than an hour of playing - I can only imagine what else I'd have to deal with if I kept going. Maybe these things will get fixed with some aggressive patching, but for now, it was a real headache and I don't recommend it. Beautiful pixel art though!

_childDocuments_.review: edit 3: the game has been abandoned in a still broken state and the devs have moved on to heroes of hammerwatch 2. don't trust them with your money ever, they've taken and ran with it once.edit 2: there have been no updates to the game since september, and the game is still left in a broken state. buyers beware, there are countless bugs.edit: It's been a few weeks and there have been no updates to the game, multiple major issues remain entirely unpatched that further ruin the already subpar experience this game has to offer.Gameplay on it's own is fun, but there are too many issues surrounding it to safely recommend;Respeccing costs a significant amounts of gold. Genuinely, why? This isn't an mmo, why does this need to exist as a gold sink? It punishes experimentation, and in tandem with the respawning fee it disproportionately punishes 'bad' builds. Someone who stumbles into the good skills will never need to respec and die less, someone who doesn't has to slog through dying and losing gold and then respeccing to fix it and losing even more gold. I have not played a single game where prohibitive respeccing was ever fun.This gets further compounded by the bad UI; there are no skill previews, the descriptions of skills suck, effects aren't explained (how much is +30 range? what is vulnerable? what is stun and how is it different from minor stun?). You're basically gambling when you buy a new skill on if it'll actually be useful, and if not, enjoy eating the massive respec cost.The respawning fee is also a needlessly punitive mechanic, and is circumvented entirely by just saving and loading. All this does is make my online group have to quit and rejoin and slog through another loading screen. We'd eat the cost, but respeccing costs literally all of our current gold already.The UI is also severely lacking. The game does not feel like it's meant to be played with a controller when opening menus sometimes uses the dpad to highlight menu items and sometimes pulls up a cursor to browse like I'm playing a console shooter released in the past 10 years. The radial menu system confusingly lets you navigate it normally with a stick but still has a cursor show up anyways?Balance also seems iffy, I'm playing paladin in a 4 man group on serious difficulty (but afaik scaling is only enemy health?), and basically any attempt to melee anything results in quickly dying from enemies hitting like trucks and dots stacking for the entirety of my maximum health. I've specced fully into the armor skill, wearing as much armor as I possibly can, and using the best shield I've found for pure defense, and I can block a group for all of a fraction of a second before my stamina is instantly drained and I'm stacked out on dots.I really want to circle back to the respeccing fee being the biggest issue though, the unclear skill descriptions wouldn't matter if it was free to experiment. Being trapped in a melee build wouldn't be an issue if respeccing was free. Why does this mechanic exist? What gameplay purpose does it serve?edit: oh my god the bugs. constant crashing on screen transitions that require everyone to close the game and rejoin. characters getting outright despawned for literally no reason forcing everyone to rezone to respawn them. summon skills instantly despawning and going on cooldown more than half the time (really annoying for paladin's banner). shops for non-hosts randomly copying the hosts stores.more than half the entrances on the map go to mysterious caves with literally nothing in them, not even secret walls, why is there so much filler content? why is there so much walking back and forth? after killing doomhammer we had to trek all the way back to the castle to be told to wait a few hours to talk to the king to end the game? why waste our time like that?

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Great game. Nothing like HoH. Don't expect that when coming into it.Biggest complaint you'll see on the reviews/forums revolves around multiplayer. It's a fun game and I love the ARPG gameplay over the turn-based gameplay of BG3 and DoS2.

_childDocuments_.review: Very different from Hammerwatch 1 and Heroes of Hammerwatch, in a good way. They're all fun for different reasons. Hammerwatch 1 is like the Gauntlet series of games (Gauntlet Legends, Gauntlet Dark Legacy, etc.), Heroes of Hammerwatch is a roguelite that's heavy on meta progression (upgrading your town after each run for permanent boosts), and this game, Hammerwatch 2, is like a Larian Studios game but without turn-based gameplay. The classes are varied and have interesting talent trees.The two big reasons for the low review score are: people expecting this game to be like the previous two Hammerwatch games, and people who don't like the fact that if you play multiplayer, your character is tied to the host's savefile. Your character doesn't exist outside of the host's savefile, which isn't a dealbreaker if you don't mind only playing with your friends.

_childDocuments_.review: Its all the things of hammer watch but deeper and with more to explore.However and a big however. And as i view hammer watch as a primarily multiplayer experience I would give this a thumbs down for anyone looking to random match make.The reason is that your character save is local to the host. When you spawn into a open world it gives you 90% the gold of the host and matches you to their level, but once your done that world and your character are gone. Saved only in the strangers game.So wavering thumbs up from me. Solid smooth game play. Good single player, good gamer buddy game, terrible rando match made game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm absolutely loving this game, but I think I understand why a lot of people are having trouble with it. Big picture, this is not really a continuation of the normal Hammerwatch or Heroes game style. It's really an evolution into a new genre almost. It feels like an MMORPG mixed with twin stick action and worlds from old school SNES RPG turn based games.In my case, I was really wanting something that scratched the WoW itch. Can't get into the modern way Blizzard has done the game, and Hammerwatch II has been perfect for me. Love the character skill choices, gear options and reading through quest dialogue.I can see where some quality of life changes could help. Rather than a complicated crafting system or day/night cycle, might have been better to go with mounts for easier movement. Gold loss can be a bit too punishing especially since it's needed for things like resetting the day cycle to talk to people. Also quests that can expire probably wasn't the greatest move, but it seems like you can mostly ignore these things and just play through.If you're an old school RPG gamer looking for something with better gameplay though, absolutely recommend this game. Combat and class customization feel very satisfying and the world is fun to explore. Definitely recommend the game based on the right expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: it's more hammerwatch 1, but with extra sprinkles. given that crackshell made 2 similarly styled games before this one, i expect more progress to be made from hw1 and hoh instead of stumbling over themselves irt ux. not to suggest they haven't tried - they definitely have with things like the circle wheel for function navigations, bindings and more comprehensive settings, but it's still lacking. my coop group is carrying the game - i would never play this solo.examples of bad ux off of the top of my head: - debuffs aren't explained unless you do external research or have played the other games (partially incorrect: see addendum).- respeccing has a relatively high cost, at least in the early to mid-game, which discourages experimentation (compounded further when the abilities don't explain what they do in sufficient detail)- death cost schema heavily incentivizes reloading the game instead of accepting the death cost- the ui still leaves something to be desired - four bars on the side of the screen that are as far away as possible from where eyes will be at mid-action. partially corrected by having points be visible at the crosshair as an option, but still.- enemies can STILL attack with no animation.some other reviews have mentioned time being a factor and i personally have been fortunate enough to just be in the right place at the right time whenever i needed it.addendum 8/18/2023:thank you for the dev response - hopefully this also gets read, but steam reviews are a horrible way to have correspondence with the game developers or whoever is responsible for managing consumer relations. i have additions to make to my  review while i'm on my soapbox.i tried to omit bugs in my original review, but infinite loading screens in coop for specific maps in the default campaign (wishless resting place, some caves) is tedious when it's a diceroll whether you get through or not, forcing non-hosts to have to restart their clients. paladin losing their banner seemingly randomly is extremely agitating, paricularly on 4p serious difficulty. for this alone, i can't recommend the game in its current state for coop unless your tolerance for these kinds of issues are high. i also notice some strange inability to use skills as wizard occasionally when they are off-cooldown while mashing. my keyboard supports n-key rollover so i doubt it's a hardware issue.while digging through the codex, i found the debuff page buried in combat mechanics - so i stand corrected on that count. i believe left values are for lesser debuffs, middle values are for normal debuffs and right values are for greater debuffs. personally, i would like to see these debuff results in the tooltips somewhere. some things like lightning's resistance reduction are also not explicit.i don't mind the sleep system to forward time. most npcs with a schedule are near an inn. there is an edge case where you can't afford being in an inn though and i haven't encountered it yet. however, what i do mind is stamina being consumed outside of combat because traversal around the world is fairly slow, especially in coop. there is dexterity privilege that manifests as QoL. revives should also be instant when no one is in combat as dying through console to work around party stacking for map changes is a common occurrence in my playthrough. i would also settle with heavily increased movement speed out of combat, but solutions addressing this would probably feel bad in practice. both h1 and hoh are significantly more linear so these problems don't end up occurring nearly as much in them since time spent roaming around is significantly reduced.i think i've spent 50-60% of my time in the same cave-styled layout in the game which feels symptomatic of playing on serious difficulty due to the constant hallway fights. currently at  and am backtracking to clear the sidequests, so i don't know if it feels better eventually.all of this to say that hammerwatch 2 is probably an upgrade over the first game in a vacuum. it suffers from bloat. a lot of the systems in the game feel shallow or poorly thought out, such as warlock's scaling in the mid and lategame, the aforementioned "optional" death cost, enemies blending in with the background during boss fights, and wizard needing to mash 3-7 keys constantly in the lategame. it definitely has more character than h1, but it feels super unfocused and i'm not having that much fun with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerwatch II definitely does not deserve the bad reviews. There might have been some issues at launch, and some (a lot of) people were expecting a different game. I very much enjoyed the Demo and got exactly what I wanted: a great, somewhat old schoolish action RPG with lots to explore and try out. I am very glad this is not yet another "rogue-like".The pixel art is beautiful, lighting and sound effects are awesome, the music is great and gameplay with the classes I tried so far (wizard and paladin) is a lot of fun. I was hesitant to buy the game, due to poor reviews. But once I did, I experienced no bugs or issues whatsoever. I installed the fast travel mod, and while not necessary, it removes some backtracking and potential annoyances and increases the fun of dungeon delving by 300%.UI and controls are a bit weird, but I grew up playing games with worse controls. Once you get used to it, its no issue any more. There is a death penalty and respecs cost money, but if you play a while, money becomes a non-issue.TL;DR: Great game, worth buying, especially on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has been out for 2 days and I already managed to sink nearly 15 hours into it. So far I’ve had a love hate relationship with it due to the general difficulty of the game but I cannot say the experience hasn’t been overall enjoyable. If you got this game expecting it to be alike Heroes of Hammerwatch or Hammerwatch 1, you will either be disappointed or pleasantly surprised. This time the game went into a different direction by opening up the world; it no longer follows a strictly linear progression alike in previous games. Now, despite liking open world games, Hammerwatch to me was a break of sorts where I could just follow what the game tells me to do, without doing the tedious exploring, resource collecting, having to figure out my next step, or getting distracted by side quests. This cannot be said about Hammerwatch 2, which is a semi open world game with many activities that open world game often entails - crafting, enchanting, exploring, cooking, fishing, tedious side quests and so on. Whilst it does retain the atmosphere and look of the previous games - it isn’t the simple roguelike you play to take a break from, eventually tiresome, open world games - it is now kinda one of them. Whilst I do recommend it because it is a great game, I must mention I was minorly disappointed to discover that the game has become a lot more expansive and it no longer has that feel of being a quick and simple game I can just ‘play for a bit’ without overly committing to it (I still sank many hours into Heroes regardless but I didn’t feel like I had to). This could be a big upgrade to some who wanted the game to become more expansive, or it could be a slight disappointment to the boring gamers like me who kind of want to replay the new versions of essentially the same game. Regarding the multiplayer issues some have mentioned - I personally do not care about it. It seems to be the same as Hammerwatch 1 where someone else’s character was also locked to the save. It wouldn’t hurt to have a similar system to Heroes of Hammerwatch where any character could just join at any point but this isn’t really a multiplayer focused game so if you’re a multiplayer enjoyer - don’t bother because this isn’t really a game for you. Just because it has the option it doesn’t mean that it needs to be played with others to be enjoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute gem of an indie RPG. It might take a little while to understand the game's systems -- Hammerwatch II is much more complex than either Hammerwatch I or Heroes of Hammerwatch, which threw me at first -- but once you do the game becomes completely satisfying. The world is beautiful, the maps are intricate, the RPG elements are nicely developed but never unwieldy, and the game doesn't hold your hand but it also isn't ever obtuse. I am having an excellent time with Hammerwatch II; I haven't enjoyed a game this much for ages.I'm surprised this game hasn't gotten a better reception. It's probably because Hammerwatch I was a very different (and very undemanding) game, so players expecting more of the same might be disappointed. But the devs know what they are doing. if you're willing to meet Hammerwatch II on its own terms, then there's a really great time to be had here.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really disappointing that people have reviewed this game so poorly.As someone who enjoyed the first Hammerwatch (and didn't end up playing Heroes), Hammerwatch 2 has been amazing. Seeing the game go from a simple little pixel art dungeon crawler with fairly static characters and a super simple "story" (there wasn't much of a story at all), and has now evolved into a beautiful highly detailed open world, with multiple biomes and areas to explore, character progression, lots of loot, solid enemy variety, and tons of bosses, it's just admirable to see how much work went into this beauty. Yes there are some issues, bugs, crashes, and people aren't a huge fan of the day and night cycle. But for the most part I made it through the game with friends with nothing particularly game breaking getting in the way, a couple situations where a save and exit was required. And sure, wanting to run to a shop in the middle of the night, and instead having to stop by the inn isn't ideal, but I don't hate it for the fact that a day/night cycle makes the world feel a little more alive to me.It's a proper RPG now. And people review bombed it for not letting you take characters across saves on release?? I didn't see Baldurs Gate 3 get the same treatment. And this isn't WoW where getting carried to the end game unlocks a bunch of stuff to do. Experiencing the story and the challenges along the way is the whole point. But then the devs went ahead and changed that anyways!People didn't read the description of the game and got upset that they were wrong about what this game has to offer.Anyways, the short version is, if you're looking for a beautiful little pixel art RPG to run around with friends or alone for a few dozen hours, then I can't recommend this game enough. The classes are fun to play, the world is a joy to explore, and the story isn't half bad if you actually read the full quest texts in the journal. It's a proper little RPG, expanding on the world of Hammerwatch.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun but also very flawed experience. It's clear a lot of polish went into the final product, but that polish is spread so unevenly it creates a sometimes baffling experience. Sometimes, you can play hours on end without any problems; other times, an entire dungeon is bugged no matter what you do, and you have to teach your friends how to use noclip console commands just to avoid a complete softlock 25 hours into the game. Sometimes you'll explore a big, interesting, and entirely optional dungeon and get great rewards for your time; more often, you'll clear out a dozen random caves scattered about the map, none of which contain a *single* reward besides enemies to farm (which infinitely respawn naturally anyway).Is it fun? Yes, at least doing a playthrough with some friends. If you ignore some of the clunkiness, the combat is fairly engaging, and the progression system offers a ton of customization (almost too much, since by the endgame half of your keyboard will be bound to some skill or another). Bosses are generally pretty decent, but fall across a wide spectrum; some are needlessly confusing (to the point that, even after beating them, my friends and I aren't sure how they actually worked), while others are extremely exciting and well-designed challenges, requiring not just character levels and stats but also genuine player skill and teamwork to get through.Is it infuriating? Also yes. Minor annoyances are everywhere, and you're bound to run into a few major ones over the course of a playthrough. Often, they aren't even bugs, but intended features (the dark fog is the worst mechanic anyone has ever dreamed of, I swear).Do I recommend it? Yes*, just expected plenty of scuffedness and preferably bring some friends along for the ride. When it comes to suffering, the more the merrier.

Every class is a mere shadow of the powerful bone smasher it was in the last game. The game play loop was not enjoyable, exploring was barely rewarding. The only thing that mattered was secret walls. The equipment system and adventure system was just more filler compared to Heroes. Don't even get me started on the walking simulator part of the adventure. Did you beat the dungeon? No portal back. Did you go through an entire mountain range but now you gotta go back to the main town? Have fun walking. I see why the fast travel mod is topping the charts, what a nightmare. The day/night cycle did nothing but annoy the player and could make the player fail TIMED QUESTS (what a useless feature) because the quest giver was asleep. This game was a long journey filled with eating a lot of sand, very boring and dry. I wont recommend this to anyone, but i will hope they make a Heroes Of Hammerwatch 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Besides the minor annoyance that is dealing with the day night system being locked behind costs; I haven't much to complain about besides the game's undeserved review score at the time of writing.As a friendly reminder, steam reviews tend to aggregate based on how well a game meets expectations rather than the actual quality of the experience. The same seems to be true for this game. I'm not sure if its an issue with the steam description or what; but it seems like a lot of the negative reviews seemed to have a very specific understanding of what this game is supposed to be. Which I guess is "Diablo but pixel graphics".This game is more of an adventure platform. Modding tools that are of insane quality and complexity to enable the creation of what are effectively entirely separate games (such as tower defense or racing sims). The default experience is a wonderful adventure action RPG with classes, bosses and procedural loot galore.This game is not Diablo. If you expect that, don't buy it. However, if you, like me, are tired of playing games that label themselves as "action rpg" and then turn out to be more akin to theory-crafting simulators with the vague notion of a game stapled on top; this game will absolutely feel like a breath of fresh air; and I hope to see more games like it.---------------------------------------------------------------------Anyways the main complaint from the reviews so far seems to be that there is something wrong with the notion of character saves being tied to the host's save for multiplayer. And how this is somehow in defiance of the tag of "co-op". Simply, I don't understand this take at all, it sounds completely silly. Let me explain:"This game is not a co-op experience" "how so?" "I can't play the game in another server with my character and progress alone without my companions, I only have the option to play with them." "Isn't that like, literally how co-op is supposed to work?" This seems like anti-logic to me. Being locked into the world you joined with a character for that world is pretty standard fare for a lot of rpgs and adventure games. Wanting to play your character you were playing with friends in an outside environment sounds like a way of playing the game without them, and seems antithetical to a co-op experience. Infact in my experience doing this is a great way to ruin the experience for everyone else unless there's some "level" or "difficulty" scaling mechanic built in to accommodate it, and even then its like "dang man yaknow I kinda wanted to experience that with you but whatever I guess".---------------------------------------------------------------------In addition, today I had the displeasure of reading one of the worst takes of all time: where somebody simultaneously made the deliciously outrageous claim that this game is more like an idler than an ARPG and yet had the absolute audacity to claim that "Torchlight/Diablo" are better models of an action RPG that definitely are not idlers.For anyone who has never played videogames before, Diablo and Torchlight are both games where you hold down the left mouse button for several hours until the game auto completes itself. There is no user interaction besides theoretical build crafting, that only becomes relevant after you have already invested 60+ hours into the game. This is obviously an extremely hyperbolic way to describe these games, but you get the point. Hammerwatch is most definitely significantly further away from being an idler than the likes of these games and I think anyone who has played all 3 would unanimously agree on that front.This take has to be a troll, and if so, good work sir you managed to get me steamed up enough to write this review. If not, just, dang man, RIP. Bad takes all around.

It's not Heroes of Hammerwatch 2, so don't go into it expecting the same kind of gameplay loop. This game is a lot more like if classic Legend of Zelda games, Diablo II, and Hammerwatch I had a lovechild. Fantastic gameplay all around, and the ability to spec out different skills in your tree really adds depth that this series hasn't had before. This game takes all of the mechanics and quality from the original Hammerwatch and cranks it up to 10. Music is fantastic, graphics are literally jaw-dropping for a pixel-based video game, animations are super crisp, etc. etc.Some people will complain about more RPG elements that were introduced, such as a day/night cycle and a supposed time-limit on certain quests. In my several playthroughs of the first few areas so far, (I've done a few multiplayer runs and a couple solo runs up to about expert level) I have only encountered a single quest that timed out, and it's because I genuinely forgot to turn it in. Additionally, quests that are about to time out do warn you in your quest tab, unlike what some reviews I've seen have said.Other issues I've seen people mention include not being able to port over characters to multiplayer runs and the fact that loot was not instanced on game launch - but in less than a week, the latter problem was patched in an update - and they're already working on solving the former as well.This is a fantastic game if you're into more classic ARPG's. I will repeat what I have said earlier, in that it is definitively NOT Heroes of Hammerwatch II, but it never claimed to be. This is a solid game to pick up at any point in time - it is absolutely worth full price and I would have gladly paid more than what the listed price was.I fully anticipate that this game will receive a lot of love from the devs in terms of QoL updates and patches, and I'm really excited to see if they also launch DLC like they have in the previous entries to the series. On top of all of this, the modding tools that have been provided for content creators are absolutely insane and I'm also ridiculously excited to see what kinds of content the community will be able to come up with, given enough time.TL;DR - This game is absolutely worth every penny. Don't expect HoH 2. If you like classic ARPG's like Diablo II or games with open world elements like classic Legend of Zelda titles, buy this game immediately.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who tested this game, I can say the devs did a good job of communicating with the community and involving us in the development process.  And personally I've been enjoying it, but a few things need to be explained I think, because people seem to be coming into this with expectations on what this game is, when it's not those things.This game is NOT a "looter RPG." You aren't meant to farm bosses over and over for loot. By the same token, you aren't meant to just bring your character across multiple games, because your characters are individual saves for individual runs of the campaign.The game is also not a roguelike, as Heroes of Hammerwatch was a spinoff. Hammerwatch 2 basically added more RPG mechanics on top of Hammerwatch 1's core gameplay, but it focuses on a more open world design. You go around, you kill things, you get some loot, and continue on with the story after you finish the current part. As someone who enjoyed the relatively simple hack and slash nature of Hammerwatch, I can appreciate them adding some more depth and exploration to it, while keeping the core gameplay of 'Cut through hordes of monsters.'Do you like to go through a dungeon and just kill everything? Yeah, this game does that.On top of that, the mod tools are pretty darn robust and capable of a lot, as we've been shown via the preview showing off entirely new games made in Hammerwatch 2, like a Jump King clone. Though I'm hoping we see some good new campaigns.As long as you understand you're getting a more traditional RPG with action gameplay, instead of a full on Diablo/Path of Exile/Etc, I think this is well worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: I've changed my thumbs up to a thumbs down.There's too many bad design choices.Don't get me wrong, if you liked the first game then you'll probably like this...... maybe.My biggest annoyance so far is the inability to mark my map and no quest locations.You'll pick up a quest, go do said quest and then you'd better hope you remember or drew a map of the location or marked down on your hand drawn map where the quest giver is or you'll be wandering around where ever you are till you accidentally come across it.Not to mention if you want zoom out on the map meaning you have literally no idea where you are.You have a basic map in your inventory but again, there's no real information on the map other than the location of cities or towns etc.Exploring in this game is so dam boring, normally in most RPG's I'd be exited to find a cave to explore, NOT IN HW2!It feels like I'm being punished, by that i mea you find said cave, explore said cave, clear said cave and what do I get?NOTHING, well not nothing i did "Find" some mushrooms and a few gold, other than that NOTHING.Multiplayer.Normally not a bad thing. NORMALLY. See the thing with HW2 is that you can't take your main char with you into someone else's world meaning that you have to start a new char that tied directly to who ever you joined.They'll have all the gear and levels, you on the other hand have some xp lvls to spend and that's it.Can't just join other people's games with your main, you have to start all over again.Why?Sweet baby jebus, the design choices are weird?On another note, it might be a bit of a controversial opinion, but when you're in a dungeon hows about NOT filling the screen with fog every couple of seconds.Not only does it eventually effect my eyes having to constantly focus and re focus, but when you're dodging traps and the enemies are firing at you as well as enemies chasing you down to get into melee, you also have these legless skeletons just appearing.All of this is going on while the fog rolls in and rolls out every few seconds, making the game a chore and incredibly annoying.I'm not sure what the dev's were going for here but it's a stupid design decision that needs to be addressed ASAP.Also (I don't know if this is just me?) but the dodge mechanic doesn't seem to cancel out moves, you have to not be attacking in order to dodge, normally not a problem, but when you're in a fight and it starts to get hairy, I'd expect to be able to dodge out of the way, but nope, you need to not be attacking in order to dodge.Please Dev's if you see this, think about adding markers or quest markers.If you enjoyed HW1, give it a go, but IMHO I'd wait a few months till they address some of the problems.

_childDocuments_.review: edit: with some babyrage angst, I'm changing this to not recommended. More than 2 months later this is still an endless pile of bugs and problems. To be fair some are because they tried to cater to the vocal community asking for persistent pc-specific save files for multplayer. However this whole thing is such a mess I'm really disappointed. Sorry to all who tried their best, but this game has surely damaged this dev's reputation and is a disappointment. (/end edit)Begrudgingly recommending. I was expecting so much more from this game, loving hammerwatch 1, but in reality the release feels like early access and like no attention was paid to details. Check steam discussions and you'll see all the drama. I actually feel pretty bad leaving so much negativity for this game because I was extremely hyped for it.To give credit where it's due, the art is better than what I expected. Most everything looks great, as far as set pieces/enemies. The combat too remains good. The skill trees are meaningful enough and significantly change your character. Character skill progression feels good. Classes are pretty different. These areas of the game are obviously where it excels Kind of everything else is broken or designed terribly. These devs have no idea how to handle a genre like this (this game isn't like Hammerwatch 1 at all except similar combat). This would get EXTREMELY long with all the stuff I've run into, so I'm just going to quickly list some of the endless negatives in the following wall of text. I assure this is only scratching the surface.NEGATIVES: Can't reach stores over their counters. Day/night cycle serves no purpose except to waste your time, removing vendors and quest turn ins. Cannot re-enter store window after exiting unless you walk out of range. No local co-op (wow, what?). Awful map covers ENTIRE screen, no options except opacity, cannot zoom out, cannot view the fully detailed map all at once anywhere making you run in circles. Painful epilepsy-causing near-death warning. Most of the world has well-made set pieces yet in reality the bulk of the world is just barren plains and trees. No way to know your base stats without manually removing all your gear. No way to exit a huge dungeon after beating it; need to trek back out for no reason - sometimes there is a shortcut a ways back. Skill descriptions regularly completely fail to describe the math or keywords of what they do (edit to be fair: most keywords are explained, but annoyingly on a completely different screen instead of on the skill or a popup). Lets you bind items to 1-3, even though these are secretly specifically for potions; the bindings won't work but the visuals indicate nothing is wrong. If you don't have enough money to buy an item, it's like 50% covered by an icon and you can barely tell what is it; you could have enough in commodities but this makes it hard to browse and check what you'd want. Disappearing NPC/quest turn in. Apparently this is because the quest can fail with no warning after x time, but it's stuck in the quest log with no mention. There are 9million different types of stores but they have the same icons and no mouseover info; have fun running to every single store checking what it is. On release, items would straight up disappear when dropped to trade to friends (this was fixed though). If you drop an item for a friend, you can't move at all until someone takes it or you'll pick it back up. Menus are 2005 clunky crap.  Especially with a controller (which is often perfect for fighting in games like this), because it just turns random menus into a handicapped mouse cursor you control with the joystick. There is no key bind to go straight to your inventory (wtf?). This game requires constant inventory viewing, item dropping, comparing items, so this is unacceptable. No shortage of bugs/softlocks (again I'm sure they will get fixed but ugh).Frankly I want to keep writing. The amount of bad decisions made with this game is upsetting. I think they took on more than they could handle in basically moving the series to an almost entirely different genre of game. I have some confidence they'll fix the bulk of these things but I don't find it very acceptable for a released game. Some of the above problems are also just obvious stupid design choices that don't need to be fixed per se, because they may not care or think they're fine for some reason. In the end I'll say I can still recommend the game because the combat and progression are pretty good, and online co-op is decent (except your character is only accessible on the host's machine so they own your character and you can't play it alone). Just know that when you're doing anything else, it's probably clunky or works like crap. The combat, art and character growth absolutely carried this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Cons:The game needs a few more weeks/months in the oven maybe. I've not seen many bugs, but crashes are frequent enough to be annoying... as fast as the game is to launch and get back at it.The game needs a difficulty option between Normal and Hard. Normal makes the game INCREDIBLY easy, and hard makes the game somewhat overpowering ( though do-able in a party ). I feel like there's a happy medium between these two difficulties that needs to be explored.Pros:The combat is different to HoH which my friends and I played a ton of, but it grew on me pretty quickly. Starting off on Hard mode, it posed a crazy challenge that basically required us to be a team which felt really unique.All of the classes feel like they play a role in the party, though I think the need for a Paladin is a bit absurd on harder difficulties being the only decent group healer.The crafting/itemization of everything feels really cool. Seeing that modding is available to this, I'm very curious to see what other people may add to this down the line if that's an option.The map design is good on the premade stuff. It's a far cry from HoH which was mostly completely randomized dungeons which the "Mysterious Caves" seem to take the place of in this.The bosses ( so far ) are each unique and fun.Things I'd love to see:MODDING! I'm very hyped to see if people can make their own maps and worlds, heck if there was some kind of map editor to do custom scenarios for the public I can see this game really taking off. Player made content will always come at a faster rate than any team can produce, and as a DM of D&D, I'd love to put my own adventure into a scenario for people to play - I think that'd be really special. All of that, of course, hinges on there being a great map editor/scenario editor. . . I'm thinking something like the dev tools from Neverwinter Nights or the Neverwinter MMORPG. Then modders+map makers can combine to make truly unique additions to the game.NG+ and NG++ etc modes! The added challenge and endless reward cycle of playing your favorite class to new game + modes and adding variety to those NG+ modes would be cool. I may have foot in mouth syndrome here, have yet to beat the game but given that the level cap is 50 - I don't imagine it's AS endless as HoH was.

_childDocuments_.review: Foolishly expected a rogue lite similar to Heroes of Hammerwatch, which I put about 100hrs into and LOVED. So my expectations weren't great coming into the game, that aside, I LOVE RPGS. The game play feels solid enough. But the open world take, and especially the dynamic time system really ruins it. Wanna turn that quest in so you can unlock your first health potion? Sorry, that NPC is sleeping. Go to the inn and pay to pass time, or run into a dungeon and die and lose 15% of your gold and hope that whatever time it spits you out at the NPC is awake. Tracking quests is a hassle and not intuitive, theres no good way to keep an eye on progress or see where youre supposed to be going without literally stopping the game and opening the menu. Theres also an INSANE amount of materials that you gather with seemingly no purpose that its overwhelming. I dont have much further to say on that note, because to actually use them I'm pretty sure you have to find a toolbox- which the aforementioned inability to track quests prevented me from doing so. A big part of why it didn't click for me is that everything is overwhelmingly slow and tedious, whereas Heroes of Hammerwatch was a very fast paced always in the action game, with clear objectives, items, upgrades, etc. Hammerwatch 2 is a much more traditional RPG, but it kind of feels like it pulls you in many different directions, and the dynamic time cycle makes it even more confusing. Ultimately if you like slower paced RPGs with lots of things to do, this might be the game for you, like I said the core gameplay feels good. But if you wanna jump headfirst into dungeons, and consistently upgrade your character and equipment in a powerfantasy, go back to Heroes of Hammerwatch. I've yet to find any games that quite match that experience, and I was hoping this title would further carry that torch, but for me it missed the mark.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a bad game, but it could have been MUCH better without the poor save and loot systems.  It's clear that there are a lot of good updates/additions to the game compared to Hammerwatch 1, but unfortunately they came at the cost of multiplayer.  Despite what the marketing tells you, this is a single player game with some second-class citizen functionality for co-op.  You can't use your own character in multiplayer as a guest, your character will be tied to the host's save.  So unless you plan to play through the game exclusively with the same people for the entirety of the playthrough, don't go into this thinking it's like most other multiplayer games where you get to bring your own character in, make progress with a friend, and then leave back to your game with ANYTHING from that play session.  No experience, no loot, no quest progress, nothing.I would genuinely recommend just playing the first Hammerwatch and especially Heroes of Hammerwatch instead.  Heroes is a stellar game with an progression system and well designed multiplayer functionality.  It's a genuine shame they did a 180 with this game in terms of these systems.  Hopefully they hit the mark with Heroes of Hammerwatch 2, if and when they ever decide to make that.

_childDocuments_.review: To those unaware, yes, the game as I write this review is actually having mixed reviews as of lately ; and mmmNo, I kind of get some of their point, but find them being a non-issue.The state of multiplayer as of now is inconsistent, some latency/bug issues, but the experience remains playable and enjoyable (especially since the class synergy is more prevalent when you factor that most buff abilities are very effective with some specific classes). The modding aspect of the game, albeit requiring some adaptations compared to HW1 modding tool, is really complete and allows for a plethora of ideas to take form (modus did release a presentation video showcasing that).Now for the elephant in the room, the save system. As a solo player, the save system is completely normal ; you start a new world, create a character linked to said world and play the story.It's when it comes to multiplayer that opinions diverges ; notably, having your character tied to the save, and the save tied to the host.For the unaware players providing feedback regarding that, Classic Hammerwatch did have the exact same system and that posed no issues whatsoever.Of course,HW1 and HW2 are absolutely not comparable, the former being an Hack'n Slash while the latter is an RPG with various gameplay elements inspired from a plethora of games.Back to HW2 and its save system tho, as I said, since your character is tied to a save, you cannot, similar to HoH, bring an overleveled, or overstuffed character with epic/unique gears to said save, and wander from world save to world save.The save system is literally similar to BG3 this way, your friend create a save, you create a character specifically for that save and only one for that save. So I'm heavily concerned when a positive from a game this caliber is considered a drawback for a co-op couch RPG like Hammerwatch 2.But enough regarding the save system, another point I entirely agree with and expect the devs to soon fix or work heavily regarding it is the loot system, as it is now, the loot is shared, meaning chests and whatnot will contain a singular item for your 1/2/3/4 member team (so yeah, it's obviously gonna end up in bickering situations due to that). Instanced loot for these kind of game is nonetheless, important especially with latejoining.All those discussions aside, the game feels and play smoothly ; great pixel art/aesthetic, fluid gameplay with a lot of tinkering, and the replayability will mostly be about doing higher difficulty runs or finding all the secrets/achievements (or playing mods, like Tranquility Shores) ; and a really engaging soundtrack from start to finish (the night version of some themes are ASMR tier in all honesty)So yeah, consider this game a "BG3"-like (I say like but it's its own genre all things considered) ; and with that, forge your own opinion on that.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerwatch 2 is extremely fun. If you love difficult game play then you will enjoy this on "serious" mode. There is so much to love. The pixel art is insane, fun fights, well rounded characters, quests, boss fights, loot and other great ARPG elements. The multiplayer on hardest difficulty is no joke. Played with three friends and got to the first boss and got wrecked multiple times. People are talking about the host saved data for the online multiplayer. Where basically the host is the one who has all the saved data of all the characters who have joined. Pretty much if you want to progress then that host(your friend) has to be on for the group to play where you left off. That is something that I honestly don't care about. I'm playing with core friends/family and we will most definitely beat the game together. If anything comes up then just play it single player until your multiplayer crew is on. It's definitely not a deal breaker; if you really enjoyed the previous Hammerwatch games then you will surely enjoy this one.Although I will say the UI for the health, stamina, xp and magic bar have some weird placement lol. Nothing major though, you can easily adapt to it. The UI for everything else including the menus and player stats/inventory are all standard and look normal.Also the quests are cool, they add flair to the game and aren't tedious. They went the old school route where you have to read and find where to go. The quests are easy enough to complete and find. The quest areas are not huge and are easily found by just walking around and killing stuff if you are too lazy to read. The people complaining about the quests and not having indicators or way points are just whiny and lazy. When you complete or find new quests they are marked on the map for turn ins or pick ups.As far as bugs, I have seen none, but that could be based off of anything. Type of computer or OS system you are running. Runs perfectly on my 2018 gaming laptop. Overall a solid game so far. I can see myself putting in many hours in solo play and in multiplayer with my crew. Don't let these whiny people steer you the wrong way and not enjoying this fine game. Watch some Youtube videos and make a decision for yourself. Watching game play is way better than a written review.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the game, it is definitely a time sink and the quests can be somewhat difficult to complete since the NPC's aren't always where it says they are because of the Time mechanic, if they could have key NPC's not move during the day/night cycles it would be much nicer.Combat is good, ranged is definitely good to start with (Wizard is a nice one for learning the game)A lot of the mechanics aren't explained but seem pretty easy to figure out with a little exploring.VERY IMPORTANT: This is a game where you are expected to check every single corner of EVERYTHING, it is very different from Heroes of Hammerwatch, you can't just sprint past enemies unless you are much stronger than them since they will chase you until one of you die. There is a hookshot you get later, don't worry about trying to find hidden ways to get to those odd posts sticking out of the ground, they are there for when you feel like returning so you don't have to do the whole dungeon again.The equipment drops are quite generous and there are some fun unique items you get from killing bosses and finding hidden rooms.You can spot hidden rooms on the map so you don't need to visually check every wall.Buttons have been very obvious about what they trigger so I'm not constantly backtracking to figure out what the lever I flipped just did.The puzzles I've found so far have been fun and challenging, you can logic your way through most of them by trying a few times, but there are also some that require you to find hints first.Playing with friends makes the game way more enjoyable, whether you are a crew casting fireballs to obliterate everything or a balanced adventuring group with a counter to every situation.

_childDocuments_.review: This is boring af. Completely missing the charm from the other Hammerwatch games. Way too much micromanagement here.UPDATE: No quest progress tracking, or indication of where you're supposed to return quests. Some pretty weak UI decisions all around. No indication of what is required to advance through the 'tiers' of experience. Turns out it's gold. You buy it. And around the time you finally discover that, (and consequently need more gold)  there is no merchant around to buy anything from you. _childDocuments_.review: What keeps me from playing this game more than an hour at a time is the unnecessary tedium of a few in-game features.Within the games day/night cycle, npcs stick to a narrow schedule which includes quest givers. If you don't remember a NPC's location, the quest text more often that not offers no information of where to find it. If you do remember, it might not be around due to its schedule. You can skip time for gold at an inn, wander aimlessly or simply afk until enough time passes. On top of this, there is at least one overlap I've come across so far of a multitude of quests demanding the same item, a few bottles of wine, which you can primarily get via a repeatable quest, each completion offers some bottles of wine - not enough tho, which makes these quests time gated and annoying.Aforementioned annoyances could be solved by simple text or number edits, reduce the number of wine bottles per quest or increase the amount sold by the vendor after each turn-in, expand npcs schedules - for example the ship to travel between regions only sails from 05-16 hours. Why not from 05-20 hours? Or, you know, travel whenever for additional coin? And please include a sentence at the end of each quest with the npcs location.There's also the frustrating reality of dying, or dying in a dungeon. Dungeons tend to either be irrelevant little pockets or endless labyrinths. If you die, you lose a substantial percentage of your gold and time passes. If you choose to respawn in town, enemies will respawn.The solution is obvious, either don't die or save often and quit/restart. This way of doing things destroys any immersion but is simply too good to pass up.You are punished for amassing gold/waiting for an opportunity to invest said gold, instead of mindlessly deducting 30% of my total gold, why not let respawn cost scale with level? If you cannot pay, you cannot respawn somewhere else beside the town. Make respawn in the town free, there's enough drawbacks already to do so. So what if that becomes a way to fast travel? That would not hurt anyone - at least it would practically remove some of the painful backtracking you have to do every damn time.Unless some QoL patches drop soon, I cannot recomment this game, even if you enjoyed previous installments.And as devs have pointed out in review comments, I'll be on the look-out.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a terrible launch, which is why a lot of the reviews are mixed. The only other legit complaint I see is people who want this to have local coop, but other than that, every major issue has been resolved.An incredible indie RPG that held my attention longer than Diablo 4 did. It has mod support and custom maps (although the community is too small at the moment so we don't have anything crazy yet).Great class design with enough depth to find your own build, but there's definitely certain skills that are outright better than others. It can take around 5 hours before you start to see a classes full potential, because as you level up, you'll have to find a certain NPC to increase your classes mastery, unlocking the next level of skills in your classes tree.Now that the developers have added separate character save slots, you can easily hop world to world and grind all you want.Shared loot was a mod until the developers added it to the core game. Fast traveling is a mandatory mod in my opinion as the base game campaign has a LOT of backtracking.Mods and even custom maps are entirely possible within this game, but unfortunately it's just not very popular and so it'll probably take a long time before we see any custom maps that compete with the main campaign.The pixel art is some of the best I've ever seen.. but some areas have way too much visual noise. It's hard to tell what's going on when my entire screen is covered with fog. I wish there was an in-game option to disable the clouds and smoke layers (or a mod) because while it's very pretty, it's more annoying than practical.I'm not even kidding. It's crazy to me that this small indie team, despite all the initial issues, made a game better than a triple-A studio.The classes have way more depth to their builds, the world is massive and actually makes sense being open-world and while difficulty has some huge spikes, unlike it doesn't rely on getting stun-locked to death like Diablo 4 does. It should've been here day 1, but it is there now.. so why complain about it? Because not having it day 1 cost me a 5 hour save file.Lots of quests require tons of backtracking over multiple maps.Scripting errors within the main questline can soft-lock your world save. I've had to replay through this game 5 times and was only able to beat it on my last try because THANKFULLY nothing bugged out.The developers listened to our cries and made it so world save and class save are different. This was not the case until an update in September 2023. This is a positive and not a bad thing, but it's responsible for a LOT of the current negative reviews...honestly they're not too long, but considering this is a pixel game it should be faster. I assume because the main campaign is basically just a giant modded adventure created by the developers, the game engine is generating each map rather than caching them like in other games. All higher difficulties do is make enemies one-shot you more than they already did. On easy you can usually rush through a lot of useless areas and you'll still have a decent challenge.Without question: USE. THIS. MOD. I don't care how "hardcore" you are, going 5 minutes into a cave to a dead-end without ANY fast way of getting out is just wasting time. Later in the game you'll run out of potions pretty quickly too, so often I'll farm an area, fast travel to town to restore my potions, and fast travel back to the dungeon floor I was on. The difference of doing this without the mod? 20 minutes of your time.EVERYTHING in this game drains your gold, and losing a % of gold on death is just stupid and stressful, especially when a select few areas are wildly overpowered and will have enemies one-shot you even on easy difficulty.If you're unsure which class to main, start a file and cheat some levels to experiment, then restart when you find a class you like. Or if you don't want to waste a ton of gold to reset your stats, you can just cheat to respec. You can find a list of console commands here on the steam discussion for Hammerwatch 2.Honestly, it's crazy to think how much content was crammed into this little indie game. There's still bugs, but the team is very small and working very hard to fix them, even changing fundamental design choices to satisfy us (like persistent save files).I honestly think this game deserves a lot more attention and am kinda shocked it's still getting so much mixed reviews. Hopefully it just pops off some day, because mods and custom maps could add insane value to this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've read the other reviews then you already know that this is probably not a game for the ADHD raised-by-smartphone generation but if you're a bit older and want a more classic feeling adventure game then this is a wonderful choice.Is there back-tracking? Yes. But back-tracking is an important part of breaking up the game's pacing and if you're playing it with a bit more chill then it's not "tedious" - the characters actually move very fast and if you open the map, even distance places are accessible very quickly. Occasionally the idea of traversing the map feels more daunting than it actually is and it seems that the foreboding has stuck with some players more than the relief has.Are the environments repetitive? Well there's repetition but that's not the same - they're not boring. The different areas feel meaningfully different and different strategies are needed for different enemy types etc. Having enough time to work out and deploy these strategies is an important part of what makes the game enjoyable and you need to attempt these combat engagements multiple times in a single area for this effect to manifest. It adds to the experience, in my opinion.If you're the kind of gamer who looks up youtube videos for the most efficient way to farm specific crafting materials in your favourite game rather than just playing it in a more leisurely way then yeah, maybe this isn't the game for you. You need to be able to embrace the value of modulating game-pacing and a path to mastery. That said, it's not that I don't mind tedium or repetition - I am quite sensitive to these things since my time for gaming is quite limited. I just think Hammerwatch || strikes the right balance, which, evidently, isn't the right balance for some others.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of this game is great, such as the artstyle. There are obvious graphical improvements, and it makes strides in animation from the previous two. Getting good loot is exciting, and so is progressing my character. All the skillsets seem to be well thought-out, and mesh with each class's strengths/weaknesses, which makes combat really satisfying.There are some problems with this game. I want to see them better, really badly, too. I agree with a fair portion of the comments about game mechanics like having characters across multiplayer campaigns, but my main issue is a different issue.In the beginning of the campaign, when you leave Castle Hammerwatch, you get to hear that familiar catchy music from that same level of the original Hammerwatch. You then find the exit to Castle Hammerwatch by walking down long corridors, fighting minimal enemies along the way, while picking up mushrooms and wood for unknown reasons. In this sequence, you are blasted with wordy tutorial pop-ups you have to exit out of (default setting on tutorials is set on ALL, rather than 'important', so you get a lot). As you're leaving Castle Hammerwatch, the music fades from a familiar jam to utterly forgettable ambient fantasy music. You depart through a forest containing no enemies, headed towards a town with an NPC. You must do her fetch quest in order to create your first health potion.This initial sequence ironically highlights what is missing from the game, and it's the player's first experience.The campaign is frontloaded with MULTIPLE pages of story, yet it feels like you have no place in that story. Why? Because you're out farming wolves in a huge dungeon and gathering leather for some reason!In the original Hammerwatch, you didn't need much story- the music drove you forward, and as a result, you killed literally everything in sight (all of them). Now I have fewer enemies to kill, and demotivating music.In your game release post, you said "..And with the addition of Full Modding Support, you can create new adventures of your own."I guess we'll have to, because the only campaign that ships with the game isn't interesting?This game broke the streak of me loving every Hammerwatch game. Please listen to the community's suggestions, as I cannot recommend this game in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Big love for Crackshell and I've put many moons into the first Hammerwatch and Heroes of Hammerwatch. That being said, the game is good, but need some tweaks. I will state that generally, I recommend the game thus far. However, here are a few notable concerns currently, though I will change if they are indeed addressed by Crackshell:1) Currently, the game has issues with needing save files instead of individualized character progression like Heroes of Hammerwatch, and unlike the original Hammerwatch, it is not a session-based roguelike. If Crackshell can remedy the limitations on save file-character exclusivity and the symptoms seen by that in multiplayer, most of the issues would be fixed. This is not a complicated issue, just a necessary quality of life change, as well as literally limiting the function of the game to notable degree. Perhaps the modding community could solve it given enough time, but they should not have to.2) Secondarily, the aiming and movement is a bit wonky. The fluidity that Heroes of Hammerwatch saw in movement and combat is impeded to some degree by the added visual flair (which is impressively good for the art style and I appreciate), as the collision and skill system makes the actual "feel" of the game significantly slower and labored. The art and visuals should not come at the expense of the actual game fluidity, especially for this game genre. If the aiming and can brought up to the same consistency as the game's predecessors and the directional movement can be tightened a bit more so that collision-based abilities and movement stop feeling like walking on ice, the other major concern I have would be addressed.I hope this is received with the support I intend it to be communicating. Overall, things are grand, but you don't need me to tell you all the things that are good, especially if you played either of the other two related Hammerwatch games. Currently, 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a complete letdown for sure. This doesnt feel like the good aspects of hammerwatch to begin with, All the previous games including the first one felt snappy and you felt like even if you challenge was based around the game it doesnt really feel like your character is being weighed down with artificial problems. The attacks of all the classes feel sluggish and dont feel satisfying like in the first game, Ive only upgrade them because i have a hard time dishing out damage  to the threats in my vicinity in the first place because of stupid cooldown mechanics, Not because of stamina or mana limitations. Every aspect of quest finding with the frustrating feeling of where to go, In the previous games every objective was communicated to the player to finish the level was easy to grasp. This game really tries to be what its not and flips the bird to all logic and simple qualities of life/necessities associated with rpg style questing. Never had i ever had a quest fail just because i took too long, Well sorry if it supposed to be realistic but i dont care for it. There is no purpose for such a ludicrous decision to have a quest run out and even not give any waypoints to begin with. Realism doesnt always equal fun, its a game for crying out loud. Quality of life tools in your log would have alleviate frustrations that outright ruins the game.I find it really easy to run into an area or group of enemies that are waaay over leveled more than i expected, call me foolish for trying to engage but the areas being easily accessible and also being not given a clear idea to the player you arent supposed to go there with the forced exploration from said problems really can feel like artificial difficulty. Ranging from a boring time to all of a sudden screen bomb because the enemies they you attacked were too strong to deal with and they one or two hit you. The game didnt feel smooth in the first few moments and felt as if there were ideas pieced together with duct tape all over it then shipped. I would have loved the simple formula that teaches the player very clearly and well progressively with a fun combat system that isnt just higher stats equals i win. First game was fun in the right circumstances, HoH was infuriatingly punishing and grindy unless you have friends to cheese the game, now this is like just levels of 1 step forward for graphic style and many steps backwards in so many ways that cant even permit the excuse of "Skill issue". Crackshell does it again making a game worse than the last.
