_childDocuments_.review: I looked at some videos of Monark (MO) to get a better sense for what the game would be like. There seemed to be mostly good points, as long as you didn't play on a console where the framerate tanks. I'd be playing on Steam, which wasn't one of the problem platforms, so I figured why not try it out? MO doesn't play like a bog-standard JRPG, but it should feel familiar. Exploring the school is rewarded with items and lore dumps. Making progress requires responding to NPCs conversations correctly, finding clues in the surrounding environment, and inputting combinations to open safes for important items like door keys. Some of this takes place without any fights or fog, but to make progress, you have to risk your own sanity, which feels creepy. Oftentimes, I didn't really want to explore, but had to dive into the madness. Battles take place in arenas, but instead of a grid system, you'll move units freely in a circular range. Placing them behind enemies often deals more damage, but that isn't the only factor you have to keep in mind. Enemies can use all the same terrain advantages, so it's not always just about seeking the highest damage potential. Based on their level and what moves you've unlocked for each character, you can alter stats, inflict status ailments, target several foes, or heal allies.One area where MO misses the mark is with the game's balancing. I only had any issues beating a boss when I got to the final ideal for lust, whereas the previous ones got steamrolled so fast they were lucky if they could do anything. Even when I had to take a few attempts, ultimately I beat that boss without much hassle after adjusting my approach. If you removed the peons from boss fights, each of them would only take a few turns to beat, which I think is disastrous in an RPG. These should be impactful, engaging fights that take time, effort, and a solid strategy to work through. However, in MO they're just huge disappointments.Around level 30, enemies get a significant gain to their HP, having far more than you do. It's true that your damage output makes up for that, but each fight's losing condition includes the protagonist (PG) dying. Therefore, you can easily face a game over if enemies gang up on the PG and wipe him out suddenly, when you otherwise had no fear of losing that fight. At the time I quit MO, I was around level 40 with 6 units going into each battle, and was getting so sick of the grind. It's monotonous having to babysit and level up that many units in a game this slow. Although not game-breaking, I encountered minor issues with the controls. When walking past NPCs and other interactive items, sometimes my character wouldn't line up properly, so I'd have to keep moving around until I could engage with them. Similarly, while in battle, aiming an attack to hit multiple foes can be fidgety, instead of allowing for precise adjustments.  JRPGs have a reputation for over-the-top, convoluted stories, and MO was no different. Making matters worse, it has a terrible intro, as the first few hours is packed full of dialogue and tutorials, with infrequent bursts of gameplay you can control. What's sad is how I can summarize the main plot of this section in a sentence, when it takes hours to go through it in game. A cursed school is granting students wizard powers based on the seven deadly sins, they've made the campus a warzone, a proud loser has a hate-boner for your ally, and you're going to mind screw him thrice in order to strip his powers away because you're a wizard too Harry. Regardless of what reality-bending powers any of the pactbearers have, nobody has the power of succinctness or good writing.   I'm no expert in game visuals, but even I can see how bad the 3D models are. Character's faces look lifeless, items clip through their bodies, etc. Even if they weren't going to look great, the lack of creativity in the enemy design is also annoying. The one area with interesting visuals comes from the monarks, but they get pitifully little screen time. They should be a primary focus for MO, the titular foes granting these destructive powers, yet they never even utter a single word. Be prominent in your own game! Some character development of them could have explained why each student was singled out, the reason each sin related to the power it gave, and overall show more about the daemons behind everything that's going on. Vanitas is the one exception, but this doesn't make up for the others having zero presence. Besides, he's tied to the PG, so of course he gets special treatmen Despite not liking MO, I can't say there's anything wrong with the music. I find the songs well composed and capable of setting the right atmosphere. Although the boss fights themselves are unremarkable, their accompanying songs are rather intense and make them seem more interesting than they really are.  🌟 Writing so much dialogue and information for 100+ students must have taken a lot of effort. 🌟 Some of the writing is funny, and a few characters are enjoyable.  ❌ Since MO emphasizes beating enemies quickly for better rewards, it undermines much of the potential strategy you'd use, such as boosting the stats of units. It's another factor that doesn't fit with the game's overall design.❌ I despise how using any move aside from your basic attack gives a negative side-effect to that unit. Using a more powerful attack costs HP, and spells not only increase madness, some will put a unit to sleep, or worse. 🔍 You'll want to pay attention to how much spirit you earn from beating a stage, as once you find a profitable option, it's useful to keep restarting that fight. Restarting the battle maintains all that you've earned from beating fights, but resets your madness to what it was at the start of the fight. 🔍 Going mad in battle is incredibly bad, so avoid it as much as possible. If that happens in the overworld, it only kicks you back to the infirmary. You might as well heal while there to restore everyone's sanity.🔍 Since you'll automatically lose any battle if the PG dies, keep his levels high. What really brought this game down for me was all the plot contrivances. In real life, some people have horrible personalities without the benefit of some sob story to explain it away. However, the plot of MO relies on people who are killing students to have sympathetic backgrounds, “I killed teenagers because somebody was mean to me.” Personal tragedy isn't a get out of jail free card. The writing really tanked when happenstance leads to all of the avoidable deaths being retconned. Even the writers didn't want to bear the consequences for their actions. I find the overall portrayal of human nature facile, and they squander their own world building by treating the monarks as window dressing instead of plot-centric characters. Perhaps if I wasn't needing to grind so much to get through tedious filler fights I'd have finished, but the story certainly wasn't engaging enough to convince me to continue. I wouldn't recommend this title.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily has one of the best, well-balanced, and actually challenging combat systems I've seen in a Furyu-produced title. _childDocuments_.review: Gehe.The reason I picked up this game was because I saw it had combined elements of Chess and the Seven Deadly Sins. Although with regards to Chess, it's moreso only on the side of theme and character + map design, while the story itself is where the Sins become emphasized.The soundtrack for this game is pretty good, and all the BGMs fit well with the ambiance/story sections they are associated with. What I really liked was how there was a song for each major battle as the song is reflective of its respective antagonist. Voice acting wise it was pretty well casted, I played with JP voices so I don't have an opinion for the English VO. None of the voices seemed out of place so kudos to them there. For gameplay there's nothing really special regarding the open world, although there are some collectibles and NPCs to talk to in between story events and I'd say it's worth your time to look for collectibles as they do offer bits of lore and hints towards the story itself, as well as progress towards achievements (relatively easy ones considering you only need to find half of the respective collectible type).A con for me about the overworld movement is that the base running speed felt too slow and fast travel only works for entrances to buildings (no going to specific rooms/areas), but that's just because I wanted to look for collectibles and read all the NPCs reactions to game events (lots of  dialogue reflecting story progression a la Falcom's Trails series). I would have liked to see fast travel for different floors/sections of buildings because every time you move rooms the game has to autosave. There are some puzzles to solve, but none of them are too difficult as long as you are paying attention to what's going on, and collectibles will even provide hints/answers to the puzzles.Battles take place in arenas, with varying layouts (to a degree). Once you reach mid-game there will be hazards to avoid and walls to destroy as well, these are not too great of a difficulty increase and just incentivize you to pay attention to positioning and making use of the game's defer system. Map movement is free and you are not locked to a grid. The battle system itself is the regular RPG menu system. (For comparison, Trails of Cold Steel comes to mind.) While the menus aren't perfect due to how cluttered they can be, once you unlock more skills for your characters, you are able to favorite skills and those favorited skills will appear at the top of the skill list. The only time you will see proper organization of skills: Attack/Offensive Spell/Buff/Debuff/Other is when you do a (party) resonance. The difficulty of the game isn't too high and the different systems that are used in combat don't take too long to learn. Just remember to (de)buff and maintain the madness meter, which is essentially a berserk mode (easily done by doing a Party Resonance with an Awakened and Maddened character in range) and you'll be fine.Plotwise, it's the pretty stereotypical JP high-schoolers vs. some antagonistic force, but with the basis of the 7 Deadly Sins in mind, the story leans more towards darker/realistic themes. Where the story shines in this game is with each character you meet and interact with, both protagonists and antagonists. Hell, you might even come to love and hate some of the NPCs granted you interact with them enough. The story is split into multiple chapters where you are partnered with 1 of 4 potential party members, giving enough time for you to understand your partners (once you reach the final chapter you will be able to put anyone in your party). For each antagonist you encounter and fight, you will find yourself learning more about them and their motivations. I'd say the story itself is about 20~ hours long and the rest of your playtime will be inflated by the amount of grinding you choose to do. It's pretty well done and the only times I felt uninterested were after a long session of grinding levels, but that feeling would quickly go away as soon as I hopped back into progressing the story. That being said grinding isn't too bad in this game as there's a double speed option in battles and once you unlock 2 Legions (Lust and Pride) and get some levels in them, grinding becomes exponentially faster. You are also able to redo fights after beating them while also keeping any drops/currency you earned so that also is helpful for saving time. Levels in this game are tied to the skill tree, so every skill you take/upgrade = + 1 level, 99 total. You realistically don't need to max level each character outside of the Protagonist(his death=soft game over, starting over from battle prep screen). The other human characters can be on par with enemy levels and the Legions can be even lower since their stats can be supplemented by equipment. Equipment varies by rarity; Normal, SR, SSR, and EX, and can be easily farmed.All in all I'd say that it's a pretty good game, but I would recommend on waiting for a sale if you're not looking for this specific genre of game. I'd say you should watch a gameplay video of the combat and go on from there. One thing I must note is that every time I closed the game there would be a computer wide lag in a majority of any other window/applications I had open: internet browser, Steam client, etc. to the point where it would say not responding on any of the affected windows. Nothing heavy enough to cause a crash, but enough to be extremely annoying and time consuming. I don't know if that is because I have my OS on an SSD and the game on a Hard Drive and the games files get saved to %userprofile%, or if its because I played in multiple hour sessions and all the saves need to sync to Steam or what (I still got the lag after turning off Cloud Save so I don't know what causes this).(line for 2022 steam nominations)

_childDocuments_.review: Monark is my new favorite game. I love its story. I love its characters, Kokoro especially. I love the world-building, the themes, and the way it changes up the JRPG turn-based combat formula with all of its systems like deferrals, assists, and madness and resolve.Most people ought to buy this on sale for about 30 USD or less, whatever is their equivalent.This is a very niche title, much like Lancarse's other work, the Caligula Effect 1 & 2. Like their predecessors, Monark is a very fascinating game that is very niche, has great music, and won't appeal to everyone. It has a lot of flaws inherent in it like the grindiness of the game, the difficulty and convoluted nature of the puzzles, and the fact that the game expects you to be able to sink in countless of hours in it if you want to get the "full" experience, that is, True Ending and most of the challenges it has to offer you.In that sense, it feels similar to NieR Automata, where repeated playthroughs, persistence, and investment are key. I won't say that Monark is anywhere near as tightly engineered and polished than that, though, oh goodness no.In short, I love Monark. I want it to be successful. I can't wait to see if this gets the Caligula 2 treatment of a surprise sequel with everything that we hated in the first being fixed and vastly improved in the second.But most people will not like it, most people will not say it's worth this much at launch, and I can't wholeheartedly recommend anything but a "Wait for sale." or "Buy if you're a niche JRPG fan with money to burn."If you'll excuse me, I'll have to go back to incinerating my enemies with the sheer, blazing heat of my Fiend of Lust's horniness.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't lose to the unfairness and absurdity of this world.The keyword of this game is "理不尽". Irrational, absurd, unfair. It's a major theme, a lot of the characters say it frequently. The game itself has this really compelling theme of fighting against the unfairness and absurdity of the world. The cast has a lot of depth and a lot of things, be they character traits or what you might think is going on, aren't what they appear to be at all.The combat system is quite brilliant as well. It has a large learning curve to the point where even as I finished the game I feel like I'm learning new things about how it works, but it really encourages strategic thinking. A lot of other reviews say you need to grind up levels a lot but I beat the last boss quite handily while being 30 levels below by abusing Resonance.

_childDocuments_.review: Mostly going to say no because of a bug. The bug won't affect everyone, but essentially the bug is that the game does not behave well on some CPUs (multi-core issue). There is a workaround of setting your affinity to only use every other core starting at core 0.The story does let you pick your order to some degree, but mostly ignores your order during cutscenes, such as some characters having revealed their transformations already and then acting like it is their first time transforming, certain cutscenes not acknowledging people already there, etc. Cutscenes also sometimes show scenes different from the actual field.Do note that the map markers can sometimes be a little off in terms of positioning, so if you are at a the marker and nothing is there, it might actually be in a different area and the marker just isn't being clear about that.The game has personality tests and such that really make you want to use a guide because of the stat gains for them, which can reduce the amount of farming you have to do, which is a bit of a shame because it would have been nice if they had made every path give similar rewards so that it didn't feel like you were losing out by not picking optimal options.The story so far is okay, but can be fairly predictable due to the tropes/archetypes used.The music is nice, especially the boss fights.Note that there are some limits for the resolution. Depending on your settings, some resolutions do not work well, especially if changed while the game is running.For anyone wondering, I am running off an Intel i9 with a RTX 4080 and 64 GB ram.

_childDocuments_.review: I think it is a  good game - not £65 good but maybe £35, it kind of has an xcom like combat system which i really like, it is adaptable combat which prevents you from just face tanking the enemy - the various systems make thinking about an adequate strategy actually useful since each character has their own specific role - trying to force them into another role is possible via skills but difficult since face tanking is a good way to end up KO'd and the early game combat changes significantly depending on your responses to the introduction but of course it isn't perfect; the mid game pacing is kind of atrocious, I understand wanting the player to grind but this was a little ridiculous since it effectively forces you to player a single side level like 40 times to get to a level that won't result in an instant KO. Another issue is the lack of customisability - this story pretty much gives you the perfect opportunity for character creation that is actually integrated into the plot - You're the pact bearer of vanity but you don't get given any room to express that vanity barring some really weird pre-made outfits which are incompatible and overwrite your combat armour, there is also another reason as to why it shouldn't have been an issue but that is revealed later in the story. Finally barring the skill system there is no way to improve the main character, no weapons or armour, not even a lucky charm - To summarise the story is well thought out, as is the combat, the human character development is good (about as developed as you'd expect a bunch of rebellious teens to be), the skill system is awesome but the equipment system and customisation system are incredibly limited so no real ability to insert yourself as the main character appearance and equipment wise which is unfortunate.

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this are a prime example of why Steam needs more than just a "good or bad" option for its reviews, because, yes, I do recommend this game... if it's heavily discounted. 75% discounted at least. It is incredibly simple, with repetitive gameplay that does little of note and a dull, poorly written story. But, despite all that, I did have fun with it: just not £50 worth of fun.It's worth noting for all the Shin Megami Tensei fans who might have heard of this game as being worked on by "former employees of Atlus" that those employees consist of a single co-writer and a composer, so take from that what you will. You're not getting SMT levels of depth with this story at all, even though it certainly tries, at times, to evoke a deep and emotional feel, dealing with things like depression, self-doubt, abuse etc, but the poor writing hold it back. The characters are uninteresting and unmemorable and all of the villains are one-dimensional tropes you've seen countless times before. What's more, by the end of the game things just sort of... happen..."This guy's actually evil, this person's evil too, here's a new character, now this other character's the villain, now they're doing evil things, why are they doing evil things? Because emotions and they're sad and depressed now go fight them."It feels as if they knew how the story should unfold but didn't have the writing skill to actually write that story out in a way that feels meaningful; it just doesn't flow well at all.As for the gameplay: It's turn based, but with a tactics sort of feel. You move your characters around, position them and then choose an ability to use. You can also defer a character's turn to another character for some added tactics. Positioning matters to an extent since there are things like back attacks, counters and assist attacks depending on where characters are positioned. There's also the MAD and Awake mechanics. You have two meters: Awake, which you raise through just fighting and using the "Resolve" skill, and when it fills up you enter a super state that increases your stats. MAD is almost the same: you increase it by getting turns deferred to you or by using certain abilities. When this fills up, you enter a similar super state but lose control of the character who attacks the nearest unit, whether its you or the enemy.The protagonist can also use the Resonance skill to share stat buffs and abilities between one or several party members. Resonating with a mad character while awakened will give you the Enlightened state, which is a sort of super-super mode, increasing your stats even more while letting you keep control. It's an interesting mechanic and adds more tactics... Tactics that you will very rarely use because the regular battles are often too easy to warrant going through the trouble of awakening or enlightening your characters. The only time I actually felt like I needed to use those mechanics were during boss fights, and even then you could probably win very comfortably without them.Speaking of difficulty: the difficulty curve in this game is complete and utter trash. After a few hours you'll notice you're getting absolutely destroyed by every encounter. The only solution to this is to grind. A lot. The way encounters work is like this: you're transported into battles by calling numbers or answering phone calls. You can find phone numbers lying around which you can call for optional battles, and you're basically given a free optional battle at the start of each hostile area. Aside from that, every area has a single battle that you have to search for. There are no random encounters, you simply find the optional phone numbers or the plot phone calls and fight those as you want. I'm pretty neutral on this, I don't think it impacts the gameplay in a negative or positive way much, it's just a thing that's worth pointing out. As for the grinding, there's a lot of it. After every act you're more or less expected to grind a decent amount before moving on to the next story fight, and this grinding sure as hell doesn't help when you start noticing how repetitive the battles are.There's one more thing I want to point out before the end of this review: the endgame. I'll avoid any huge spoilers here. By the end of the game I was incredibly burnt out, but the game just kept going and going, and the endgame felt so painfully drawn out. Every time I thought I was about to fight the last boss, something else popped up to keep the game going for several more hours.And then, after all that, after pushing myself through the crappily written plot and boring characters, the game has the sheer audacity to pull a sad twist out of its ass and then has a character come to me and say, more or less, "Damn, that ending sucked, huh? Hey, I'm gonna teleport you back to before you picked your ending so you can go grab the other three endings and then we can talk about getting you a nice one, okay?"...Yeah, I'm not doing that. Bear in mind that because I never went and grabbed the other endings, because each route has several hours of gameplay to go with it, so I'm just assuming that doing so nets you a better ending. Also bear in mind that I'm telling you this as someone who played through SMT Nocturne half a dozen times to get every ending. No loading earlier saves, I played the entire game several times to get every ending, and yet I couldn't get myself to play the endgame of Monark several more times to get half as many endingsTL;DR: Monark isn't a bad game. The plot and writing is bad, and the gameplay is repetitive, but it isn't overall bad at all. With that in mind, like I said at the beginning, I'd recommend getting this on a *heavy* sale. Do not buy this for full price like I did...

_childDocuments_.review: MONARK is a game that makes no secret its megaten inspirations (Shin Mikado Academy, anyone?) while also trying to find its own identity. The positives I can say for this game lie in its combat system. It's almost like a cRPG where you can move your characters a certain amount and launch an attack. You can either use "Arts" which are physical skills that cost HP, or you can use an "Authority" which is akin to a special attack. Keep in mind that there is no Magic Points or Spirit Points in this game. Authorities raise your MAD gauge, and when it reaches 100 percent your character loses control and attacks everyone near it with absurdly high attack but reduced defense, and if they're not killed or cured after 3 turns, they explode. There's also the Awakening mechanic which allows you that but with no downsides, and an Awakened + Mad character becomes "Enlightened" which furthers the attack boost and allows the characters to execute broken moves, and both allies and enemies are affected by this. However, while the systems are in place, the combat encounters themselves feel lackluster. Enemies can gang up on you and perform assist attacks with seemingly no end, allowing them to deal 4x the normal amount of damage in a turn, and there's always more enemies than allies. Their solution to this seems to be to make enemies aggro only in a specific range, meaning I had to "huddle" my characters to focus on one enemy at a time without going too close to other adversaries, who kind of just wait their turn. This is immersion-breaking, since the environments are small isolated floating islands where everyone there should be aware of your presence. Speaking of the environments, let's compare this game to one of it's more fitting inspirational parallels, Shin Megami Tensei If... Both games feature you as a nameless high schools student who gets caught in a seemingly sudden event that separates their high school from the outside world and fills it with demons. Despite being a SNES game, I unironically think SMT If... does a better job setting up its world. Students are panicking, they're scrambling to find makeshift weapons and survival tools, the council and instructors are acting absurdly weird as though they're possessed by some malicious entity, it makes sense given the emergency and depravity of the situation. This game though starts off with you getting caught in the insanity mist with one of my least favorite plot devices in fiction: Amnesia. The game throws a few characters at you that try to establish their relationship with you, but it did not personally make me feel invested in the story. The game's very unclear as to exactly how long has passed since the incident happened. Where the Mist isn't, students are free to chat around with each other and gossip around with other students, as though the school drama was hardly interrupted by being imprisoned in the most irritating place imaginable for a teenager. They're free to talk about love and rumors and teenager stuff which is not the reaction I'd expected.The story is a mixed bag. It's formulaic as heck, each section you have a party member that has powers that helps you defeat a PactBearer that you both have mutual animosity towards. The pact bearer embodies one of the Seven deadly sins, and to be honest they're actually quite interesting conceptually. They've let the poor circumstances they've had corrupt them in their attempts to make the world a more "fair" place, and their intents are very humanizable and relatable, and would make the player reflect on their actions in real life. This is good, because that's what sins are, bad things that EVERYBODY, without exception, has done. However, it becomes so formulaic that when the formula attempts to branch out in interesting ways, it has to snap back because the formula is prioritized over artistic experimentation. Overall, I would recommend getting this game on sale, but I'd say it's worth $20 or so. It's not optimized well and has stutters even on high-end hardware, and is generally an unfinished game. However, it's very hard to actually FIND on sale considering the last time it was on sale it was for $38. So I would just not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very messy game. Gameplay has 10 different mechanics and characters have 20+ options, but very few of them actually matter (namely deferals, PSY buffs, and Resonance). The story starts in media res, but takes a painfully long time to explain how and why things got there. Outside of the brief exposition from pactbearer ideals, we never get a glimpse of what the characters were like before the anomalies started, which can make their characterization murky. Date's motivations come off as weak compared to the other protagonists, while Nozomi straight up disappears for most of Act 2. Finally, Yoru and the Monark of Woe do not have satisfying conclusions to their stories in Act 3.However, I still genuinely enjoyed my time with the game. The boss battle music is absolutely incredible, and the character portraits are excellent. The voice acting is generally solid. The gameplay, while repetitive, is satisfying. The characters are generally interesting, with the character chatter in the TSC room doing wonders to make the characters likable. Most importantly, it manages to nail the major emotional beats in its story in a satisfying manner. Overall, I would recommend getting the game on sale. I would also firmly recommend getting your hands on the album of Monark boss themes. PS: The achievement to fully level up every character to 99 is completely psychotic compared to every other achievement in the game. It exists to add 10+ hours of rather mindless grinding to the playtime of anyone hoping to get 100% completion in the game. It really should be changed to something else.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still clearly in the earlier stages of this game but here are my thoughts after just over 6 hours of game time.This game reminds me of the persona series of games, more so persona 4 with the fog and what not. The art style is what you'd expect from an anime looking game, and the music is soothing, invigorating and compelling all at different moments which is what you want from a game like this imo.The collectables seems to be many and most seem inconsequential other than to give you back story into previous events tying into the whole greater lore of this story or just provide useless background information on the rest of your school piers who are just extras to you playing the main protagonist.The main characters of the story however, feel full of life and have reasons, emotions and baggage. _childDocuments_.review: I don't have many hours in, but if you like JRPGs with (at least at the beginning confusing but) intriguing story, potentially deep characters with great japanese voice actors, besides the voiceless protagonist, this is the one.Besides, the music is amazing and by no later than the first boss encounter you have to bop your head. You just cannot not do it. Ash and Nihil are superb.Edit: 1 and 3/4 years later and over 60 hours in, I am not sure I can recommend this game anymore. It's still not bad. It is basically the same as the first hours. However, it is more of the same. There are differences, sure, but the gameplay loop stays, sadly, the same. The most infuriating element for me is one part of the fights... the main protagonist is never allowed to fall. Never. This punishes risky moves and forces you to use your team members to be focused on, so you can deal damage in a safe distance. And this makes fights slow. But the risk to getting crit damage and fall and having to repeat this level again and again is just so frustrating. Also, enemies of course get stronger, so the risk of putting yourself in the mid is way bigger, forcing you to play really slow (and losing on spirits, the currency to level up your characters, urging you to grind some levels).Over all, the music and voice acting keeps getting better and better, but sadly, I cannot ignore the issues in the gameplay. It's sadly turning into a drag. Get this on sale or if you are a huge fan of tactical turned based fights and a love of repeated fighting on different small map layouts.

_childDocuments_.review: I will put the TLDR at the beginning of my review, so you don't need to scroll all the way to the bottom to find it. Basically, a fun Persona/SMT-like game that could use a little work and a few tweaks. If you like those games, you can find something to enjoy about this one.Please note that I have not yet finished the game, and may update my review then, though my review has little to do with the story and mostly the mechanics, and seven hours in, I feel like I have a good grasp on the mechanics. I will attempt to  be as spoiler free as I can, but spoiler warning to cover my bases anyway.The premise of Monark is nothing new, particularly since some of the people who worked on Shin Megami Tensei made this game. High School Students find themselves trapped in their school with a mysterious mist that causes madness and must use the power of their personalities to overcome the obstacles. Nothing new about that premise in 2022. However, it brings a few innovations to the table, such as it's free movement combat system and it's customization options.The core gameplay loop is as follows. Wander around the mist, head to the Otherworld and stop the mist then proceed to the next level of the building you are in. While walking around in the mist looking for the way to the Otherworld, you will find yourself attempting to solve puzzles to remove obstacles in your way, all while monitoring your sanity to make sure your party doesn't go nuts before you are able to progress. First, madness generates extremely quickly, even on the easiest difficulty and there are two ways to remove it, items or visiting the medbay. The items are relatively easy to come by, the doctor gives you a handful if you're below a certain amount when you visit him, but once you're out of those, you have to go back and visit him. It's supposed to create a feeling of tension and a sense of urgency, but in actuality creates a sense of tedium more than anything. Being able to fast travel back to the medbay at will removes the urgency about madness and makes the threat of insanity non-existent.To attempt to spice things up, there is a mechanic called "Death Calls" that cause those who are already insane to attach you, and if they catch you, you are sent right back to the medbay. You also have the option to answer the Death Call and be thrust into a difficult fight. However, you can eliminate Death Calls altogether by using a special code given to you by an NPC at the beginning of each floor that has one. This thrusts you into a fight that you are supposed to destroy the object responsible for these Death Calls. Once you have destroyed that object, you have no more Death Calls for the remainder of the level you are on. However, the object that can destroyed in one hit and is usually reachable in one turn, allowing you to bypass the combat, and the only real threat of the mist.Before moving too far from the "exploration" portion of the game, I want to talk about the puzzles used as obstacles in the mists. These fall into two categories. 1) Finding enough clues around the area to then use dialogue to remove the obstacle or 2) Extrapolating some information from your surroundings to solve the puzzle. The second of these two puzzles is the most frustrating, because sometimes it isn't obvious what you are looking for or at. **Spoiler Alert** The most frustrating puzzle to this point was one that required me to have in depth knowledge about Tchaikovsky and what he wrote, as well as piece together that some desks were arranged in a certain way when the camera wouldn't let me rotate it in such a way to put two and two together because of the angle I was stuck looking at. That one I had to look up the answer for because I could not figure it out.Next up, is the currency system. The currency of the game, "Spirit" is used for two main things, leveling up your characters and creating support items. However, spirit is shared among all your characters and every time a new character is recruited, they start at level 1. Up to this point, unlike most JRPGs, I have not found a very useful way of grinding large amounts of spirit. There is the ability to repeat certain fights over and over again, but Spirit rewards are minimal if you aren't acing every encounter, which in the early game is extremely difficult, making grinding a even more tedious process then grinding usually is.The battles themselves are interesting. The free movement and turn-based combat makes the game feel more like a Strategy RPG rather than just a regular JRPG. However, resource management really needs some work. Your stronger abilities either cost health or increase your madness. Most of the time, I felt as if using my basic attacks was the best way to go, as I couldn't afford to lose my own health, but restoring my other characters required the sacrifice of another character's health or risking going mad. Now going mad is not a bad thing in combat, so long as you can end the combat in 3 turns as a mad character will be knocked out at that point. Human characters, as opposed to the Daemons you could command, also have a charge-up referred to as "Awakening." I have only ever awakened one character, and that is because it is a long process. You awaken a character by taking damage, dealing damage, or using an ability to charge it up. Charging it up is the best means, as it give you 25% of the necessary charge as the other methods give you 3-6%, however, it costs a turn in combat which could be used to to deal damage instead, and with how important it ends up being to just remove enemies from the field, the trade off is just not worth it.The animation and cinematics are decent, not the greatest thing, but not the worst I have ever seen. The ability to customize your Daemon's is fun. Choosing their equipment, appearance, voice, and even names is enjoyable.The last thing I wish to comment on is the story, which I will come and update when I have finished it. From my first impression, the story is interesting and has promise, but it so far is not groundbreaking. Which is fine, not every story is going to be the greatest story ever told. In general, the dialouge sounds stiltled or forced at times. However, I did have a legitimate reason to care for most of the characters.Overall, I would give it 3 out of 5 stars. It is a fun game with some flaws, and I hope we do see more Monark with improvements in the future, but I expected more out of a veteran crew who had more than dipped their toes in the water before.
_childDocuments_.name: MONARK

_childDocuments_.review: The music in this game is a huge bop, the character art styles are amazing and the story is pretty good. I feel like if they had put more resources into this game it would have been insanely good, but unfortunately it lacks some aspects that would have made the whole experience better.The maps that you fight on are pretty much all dull and the same with minor changes. There is no variety in enemies that you fight at all (other than the main ones) and it becomes boring going against the same ones over and over.Overall it's a very grindy game that requires patience and a love for this type of genre. It's not a horrible game and I would still recommend getting it and giving it a try because there are some parts in the story that hit really hard!P.S. Ryotaro  is the goat!!
_childDocuments_.name: MONARK

_childDocuments_.review: How far will you go to save the ones you love? Could you face the threats that surround you? Could you face yourself? Your world is plunged into madness when the mysterious and deadly Mist surrounds Shin Mikado Academy. In order to save your friends, you enter the Otherworld, a Daemon-filled dimension beyond the real world. Within this enigmatic realm, you must learn to harness your Authority of Vanity and conjure a battalion of Fiends, whose power comes from the Ego of their master. Develop your Ego through various psychological tests to enhance the power of your Fiends, and lead your forces into battle to fight with and against the seven "Pactbearers" that are corrupting the academy. Embrace the power of your madness to gain strength, but take care not to delve too far, lest you risk losing yourself. Fellow students and instructors will lend you their aid in your quest to resolve the anomalies throughout the campus.
_childDocuments_.name: MONARK

name: The Fabulous Fear Machine
detailed_description: The Fabulous Fear Machine is a narrative-driven strategy game with a pulp horror style, from the creators of Do Not Feed the Monkeys . You’ve just become the newest Master of the Machine, and now you must generate fear and expand your influence by playing Legend cards: those scary stories, urban myths, and conspiracy theories that lurk in the dark corners of the mind. To clear a path for your Legends to grow, you’ll dispatch your Agents to new locations on the map, harvest and manage resources, decide how to deal with events in the simulation, and spy on the operations of your foes. What are your deepest desires? Power, wealth, glory? Everything you’ve ever dreamed of is within your reach, with The Fabulous Fear Machine . Pick your poison. From cryptids like the Black Dog, to urban legends like Bloody Mary, to conspiracies like Reptilians—with over 80 Legends to choose from, you’ll craft a custom blend of terror for each city you visit. Horror evolved. Plant the seeds of fear in fertile ground. Watch and listen to how the media reacts to your Legends. Feed them, then see them grow more powerful and effective. The job done right. Your strength is in strategizing; leave the dirty work to your Agents. Send them to explore new locations and infiltrate your enemies, making interesting choices along the way. An equal and opposite reaction. Rivals and the forces of good alike seek to undo the Machine’s influence for their own ends. Plan accordingly, or you may find your own Legends twisted into inspirational stories, mascots, or other sugary-sweet clichés. A tale as old as time. You’ll direct the stories of several Masters operating in different regions of the world. Along the way, explore the history of the Machine, its enemies, and the Agents who aid you. Presented by AMC Games and SHUDDER. Early development of the game was supported by Red.es and FEDER (European Regional Development Fund).

_childDocuments_.review: The presentation being a huge throw back to Tales from the Crypt and EC comics was enough to make me get this game. There's a very fun gameplay loop of managing your agents and playing your cards right. It's not the most challenging game, but it has its difficulty spikes from time to time. After a quick tutorial, you get a cheesy presenter, horror puns, a steady drip of gameplay mechanics with each level. The game is broken down into mini chapters, each with their own protagonist(? lol) with dubious morals and see how they go about their stories.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: I have played just a short time but will say that I am very much enjoying it so far. The art style is extremely engaging and the mechanics are fun to figure out. The humour is brilliantly well written and I haven't yet found the learning curve to be too steep. The developers should be very proud of a polished game like this for a launch. All that being said and again kudos to you Fictiorama, I have one very significant big Irish bone to pick. I, nor any of my countrymen, ever take very kindly to our country being referred to as part of the BRITISH ISLES. A simple mistake I know you obviously did not mean but if in a future patch you could at all see your way to replacing this rather indelicate blunder everyone here, and the diaspora around the world no doubt, would be eternally grateful . . . to be sure. P.S. Ireland and Great Britain is the generally preferred term for the region. Though by all means refer to it as Ireland and its outer regions if you like! TL;DR Game is really great, Ireland is a distinct place from Britain.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: An honest to goodness hidden gem. I only know about this game because I follow a thread of new steam releases. I wish it had made a bigger splash because I think it's really fun.This game combines four things I love - map painting, urban legends, four-color comic style art, and penny dreadful morality plays. The narrator is an evil wish-granting machine that ties together the story of three protagonists who trade ethics for power through spreading fear and panic, then of course get their just rewards. Great stuff.If I had to nitpick I'd say the second story felt a bit short, and the legend cloning mechanic in the third story felt unnecessary. I also wish the nature of the legends you used played into events and such more. But those are minor concerns, the only real letdown to this game is that it's a shorter, smaller scale game that will leave you wishing there was a part two to play more of. I think it's priced fairly as is, but it goes on sale for 40% off during major sales if you prefer to wishlist and wait.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a lot of fun, and I had a fantastic time 100%ing it. The art gave me a strong hit of nostalgia for my wayward youth sneaking off to read horror comics, and I loved the "evil Zoltan" stand-in for our beloved Crypt Keeper.  Overall, it's a pretty simple game, with mechanics that look complex at first but are not too hard to master. Some elements (namely the audio 'scream' when a legend gets evolved) got really, REALLY old by the time I had chased down my last legend. However, the game itself is short enough not to overstay its welcome, and the fun of the lurid pulp tales kept me engaged.I hope the devs consider making an expansion. There are so many more spine-tingling tales of vice and villainy, death and depravity, magic, monsters, and mayhem to play with!
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game, it's been hard to walk away from. If you enjoyed Cultist Simulator or similar games, you'll find a great deal of enjoyment in this game. The stories are interesting, the strategy enthralling, and the game just has a great sense of style over-all. Hope to see some DLC expansions for this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: A game different from most strategic titles, and interesting to play. At first it may seem bizarre and complex, but managing your agents ends up being engaging and fun. The comic style is amazing and manages to evoke the pulp atmosphere of the magazines of the time, it reminds me of Creepshow and other B-horror movies.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Not really for the faint of heart who can't handle sexual or gorey imagery on the cards or in the story. A brutal recreation of the EC Horror Comics that actually has interesting commentary about how easily people can be made to panic with the cards representing things that people still fear to this day, like Viral Challenges encouraging kids to hurt themselves for internet fame or people being afraid that an entire nuclear arsenal is left unmaintained underground, just waiting to explode and destroy humanity. The story is okay, albeit likely the weakest aspect. Not the machine itself but the twists. They feel rather tame and honestly a bit too repetitive with the twist being everyone going to kill the person who makes the wish. Not a single person, a huge crowd/swarm. It made the future deaths after Jen feel repetitive and rather boring.The rivals are okay as well, but not really remember-able. The best were the Zepplin/Children of M but even then its more for their mystery rather than their writing. The challenge behind them is good though. I also like that they aren't pure, they are just as vile as you. Cards are the best part. While I wish you could build a deck rather than being pre-assigned one, the artwork is great and a lot of the topics listed on them are relevant to today. The Local legends was also very well done. It just had me wishing for more to be included. The game is pretty challenging even on Normal difficulty but not stupidly broken. It feels like losing is because of a mistake you made rather than the game being unbalanced. Ways Devs could improve game- Mod support if there's no plans for dlc (Think Plague Inc)- The ability to read the stories of the other people who work for the machine when you complete their story in game- Reduce the lightning effect at the end of Santos' campaign as its way too bright right now. - The ability to replay old campaigns with your new card decks to unlock secret legends that required cards from future campaigns. Overall - 8/10. A solid albeit niche strategy game. For people who love card games and resource management, a great game for you if you can handle the dark and blood filled themes.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe a 3 out of 5 carrots. The three smallest carrots.It's definitely unique so they get an extra carrot for that. Love the pulp horror style. I like the overall theme. The narrative makes me want to continue to see what happens. A game of sowing fear and expanding influence was right up my alley but the gameplay is not as engaging as I had hoped.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: The dialogue in the initial campaign is pulp all the way through, and some dialogue choices play on that awareness of the genre while also having in-game consequences. The premise that everything takes place in a pulp comic book casts a long shadow over the narrative, in the sense that it refuses to take itself seriously. Stories within stories, that’s cool, but I found myself caring little for the characters.Fictiorama Studios became better known in 2018 with , a voyeur simulator that allows players to unleash their inner stalkers.  allows you to act as an agent of Fear and Legend in a world drenched in the pulp surrealism of conspiracies, dark fictions, and lies. It’s intended as a dark mirror of our world, but it gives the player control over it.Satire is a fine instrument rather than a blunt one.  avoids bludgeoning the player over the head with a simplistic moral. It is meant to be more than the sum of its gameplay and narrative. Choices matter, though not as much as they might seem to. For some players, the strategy component of spreading Fear and harvesting Oleum might be enough to carry the game’s unique flair and style, at least until the novelty factor wears off in the initial campaign.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Growing up on Creepshow, Tales from the Crypt, Goosebumps, Twilight Zone & other anthology horror media- The Fabulous Fear Machine has all the makings of being in the conversation with said titles.Divided into three stories of people wanting unimaginable power, this Fabulous Fear Machine can provide your deepest desires, all you need to do is feed it FEAR. Spread fear to the world by recounting urban legends, conspiracy theories, & just downright savage human behavior. Use agents of chaos at your disclosure to infiltrate cities, establishments & even good Samaritans trying to bring you down. But is corrupting the world all to achieve these three malevolent beings goals worth a buy? Let's find out//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//You'll spend majority of your time in maps, all are easy to navigate- the HUD is nice, the sounds are okay- there are times where I wish there was voice acting, (you will get some at the end of each chapter but that only made me wish it was all fully voice acted) but the star of the show? The artstyle, seeing the tarot like power up cards, the Legends- are the cards you lay down on the map to spread fear- and they look magnificent, it made me want to unlock all the artwork just to look at it afterwards, and while I would rather not spoil what some of the legends can convert to, pretty much everything from Nessie to Sewer Crocs to La Llorona are in this... and some are much more gory than others//Gameplay//I cannot emphasize this enough but it is very much a NARRATIVE driven strategy almost board game like game at its core. You start by putting "messages" in each region you want to take over for example, you might want to push the narrative in Ireland that "Natural Remedies" are bad in Ireland or only certain brand of pharmaceuticals work in Scotland.. Then with an agent of chaos that you can direct to explore towns as long as you have the necessary Oleum or fuel that can be gained from having fear in a city. You then establish posts that can get you resources such as blood, political favors, visions, pop culture, science, destiny among others that you will need to evolve your legends or to take down a certain foe that will try to stop your evil plans. Legends are placed on available towns, for example installing "Sharpy the Clown" in Dublin will see the residents of the town be terrorized by a clown that looks a lot like Doink. Well he's gonna need blood so after exploring the Dublin Castle- I'll install a "blood" drive there so my agents can harvest blood all while the fear of Doink I mean Sharpy is spread when Sharpy is ready to level up a ton of words will come out & picking one that fits the picture will give you a bonus. Upon meeting all the goals on the map, you will win and go onto the next page of the comic as it will fill out with your character doing evil deeds.//Price//17.99 USD//How many hours estimated//I beat the game in under 10 hours and I messed up twice during my playthoughs so I think I may have even beaten it faster, however I am still going back to collect all the artwork I missed. So I'd say I'm spending about 15 hours total on this//Is it Playable on SteamDeck?//While it is, and I played it for about 2 hours this way with no impact on my battery life, playing it on mouse & keyboard was the way it was meant to be. When dragging an agent with the SteamDeck, sometimes I'd lose him or drop a Legend in the wrong place. But it is still very enjoyable despite my small qualms.//Final Thoughts//What you really get is an anthology horror series within a lite strategy game and being a fan of Political Machine, Risk & Creepshow- I'm the personification of the Fabulous Fear Machine's target demographic. Every time I saw a card for some cryptid, conspiracy theory or talking point on cable news networks- I grinned. The tongue in cheek commentary of our very fears in society mixed with some more occult believers made for an awesome time.I only wished that we could just play on a map against a CPU opponent(s). Because while I did very much enjoy the experience of the Pharmasis Girlboss, Political Patsy & Megalomaniac Zealot- I just kinda wanna pick a map and infest it with fear. In the third chapter of the game everything gets real complicated and makes you strategize in ways that change the fundamentals & the harder it got, the more fun it was. And the more enemies attack your base, with your fuel depleting and only having limited movement, it was in those moments that I wished for a FREE MODE even more. I made a few silly mistakes like picking a town that had their borders CLOSED but it wasn't till after i reseted the mission that I realized I could've just moved the message from one portion of the map to the next. Events were something I didn't take advantage of enough at the beginning but they were crucial in later missions- so pay attention to all the small details...I was sort of expecting me to pick a character and going into the world, but alas I had not read the description that i mentioned earlier NARRATIVE-DRIVEN. So with replay-ability sort of shot, is The Fabulous Fear Machine still worth your money? Absolutely. For under 20$ USD, you get a fun game with a niche horror story. A campy horror I love especially around this time of year.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the first campaign out of 3 on normal difficulty. The story plays out like a comic book and is genuinely captivating. The mechanics are unique and challenges seem balanced and there are plenty. I have fun getting legends to max level and collecting them in the album. The tutorial does a good job covering all you need to know, now it is up to you how you spread fear with the machine to accomplish your true goal. And be wary of your rivals trying to take you all the way down!
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely unsettling game, play it if you can stomach a lot of dystopia and fairly extreme cruelty and negativity. Powerful narrative even if the lead-up to the ending makes you think there is more to it that is not quite delivered.Gameplay is very clever and takes some strategizing. Make sure to study the tutorial well, the mechanics are not complicated at all but the game is highly strategic on normal difficulty and requires fairly deliberate action even if there is room for 2-3 big mistakes on each map.Completed on normal difficulty in around 10 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: It's not an overly complicated game.  Very leisure, but can get tense at the end of objectives. Once you get down the basic mechanics (tutorial is bare-bones at best, but the scenarios all have special objectives -- but that's a good thing) Where the game shines is the voice acting and story lines.  It's basically Tales from the Crypt/Creepshow meets card-based game.  Amusing.  Stories are basic, but fun.  At the cost, it's worth it.  Also ... politics of stories in game, very even-handed.  Shows the hypocrisy on all sides.  Well done walking that line.I do hope devs continue the concept, but give me some truly creepy stories for DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: This game is both strange and boring.  I will grant that it has a unique vibe, and cool art, but it's just not really that fun.  It's got a pretty steep learning curve and the tutorial is lacking so it makes it relatively inaccessible.  That may just be me, but there are a lot of better games out there that I'd rather be confused by.   I gave it a for real go and just couldn't get into it and there's nothing special about it to keep me around to continue trying.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Starting a new game will take you to the screen selection page. Here you will find the Tutorial and three stories, Double Blind, Shaking Hands and Saints or Sinners. Also, on this screen you have a book which will record your progress as you unlock Legends, Guide Fears, Utopias, Arcana, The Power, The Form, The Passion and The Occult stories and cards. To begin with though you can only do the tutorial if this mis your first time playing the game. Going over the tutorial will take you over the basics of the game and give you an understanding of how the game mechanic works.  The object of the game is to take control of the Fear Machine and to spread fear so that you can have your wildest dreams come true. The Fear Machine is a fortune telling machine and the character looking into the crystal ball who is going to grant you your dream wish is Kirlian who along with his Agents will help you. In exchange for your wish, he just requires knowing your story which will play out as you progress, although be careful what you wish for... Currently there are only three Campaigns, and each campaign is divided into missions. The first and third campaigns each have four missions while the second campaign only has two missions to complete. Each of the campaigns will unlock after you have completed the previous campaign, with the first campaign unlocked after completion of the tutorial. Once you have selected a campaign a small cartoon style intro will begin with you finding the Fear Machine and Kirlian waiting for you. After chatting a bit and agreeing to the conditions you place a coin in the slot of the Fear Machine and your dream will now commence. It will then detail the current Mission objectives, the number of missions in this campaign and your starting Agents who will help you spread fear across the lands. The Agents will do you work across the lands, visiting locations extracting the necessary essences, infiltration and explorations, they are your hands on the ground. The first campaign you play as Jen Hammond, and you have just been hired by the Phadro Pharm as their youngest researcher. Although you have far more loftier ideas in mind and want to seize control of the company and spread its influence in the pharmaceutical world across the globe. To do this (and in the other campaigns) you must get your message out to the people. At the start of each new campaign, you will have to place the messages needing to be transmitted into the regions. This will be the message you will transmit once you have earned enough fear, once all messages have been transmitted you will have completed the mission. Before you can spread your message, you have to take control of regions through the spread of fear. Once a region hits a certain fear limit you can then send out your message to the people. You will have to do this multiple times across several regions to complete the current mission objectives. You will also have to keep your rivals at bay as they will try to reach the same audience and get their message out instead of yours. Once you have placed your messages into the various regions, next you must get the fear started by placing the Fear Seed into one of the regions on the map which is indicated by a red striped area within the regions. It is from here that your fear will spread and progress your growth across other regions on the map.  In the first campaign, you have three regions, England and Wales, Scotland and Ireland, within Scotland and Ireland there are one location in each, whereas in England there are two locations. Fear will spread from the Fear Seed, but it will need feeding if it is to spread across the regions. In the Psychic Centre there are four categories of fear, these are The Power, The Form, The Passions and The Occult. Each of the categories contains two types of Terror. Selecting a category will display the cards you can use to spread terror and fear. The categories also detail how much terror they will spread but you can increase the terror through the upgrading of the cards when placed on locations.  You will use the cards of terror from the Psychic Centre and place them down in the locations. However, first you must visit and explore each location with an Agent before you can add cards and increase the terror in the region. There could be two or three places to visit in each location. Once a place has been explored you can then add a card of terror, providing you have the resources.  To place a card will require Oleum, this is the fuel which you will gain through the spread of fear and terror. It is also used constantly as you progress, without it the game will end. So, you must try and keep in stock as much as possible so creating fear from multiple locations can help keep a steady supply of Oleum. You can earn Oleum from events although at the same time events can cost you Oleum. At a location you can Implant various resources, one of those is a refinery for the Oleum without which you won’t collect any. As there are more than one place at a location you can also implant other Resources which can be extracted from that location. You must use an Agent to perform an extraction of a resource and there is a total of eight resources which you can collect. These resources can be used to upgrade the cards four times, increasing their fear. You can also use any extra resources and convert them into Oleum if you find yourself in a pinch. Every time a card is levelled up you will add to its story by choosing from a single word from a bunch of eleven. Not all the words offered will follow on with the story of the card so you must choose wisely.  You won’t get punished or anything if you don’t get the correct answers, but you will miss out on some much-needed bonuses that can increase the terror quicker throughout the region. Pay attention to the cards as you level them up and you may just spot a clue here and there. There will be some events happening, sometimes you won’t have to do anything, other times though you’ll need to send an Agent. You can also send your Agents to infiltrate your enemy, they’ll uncover secrets which can then be used against them. It will take some resources to use against the enemy and it may take you some time to deal with them but the quicker you do the better. You can also upgrade your Agents; this will allow them to extract resources and perform faster. Once you have spread enough fear and terror throughout each of the regions a little popup will appear that will allow you to transmit your message. When all messages have been transmitted then the mission objectives have been completed you will then move on to the next mission until all missions of a story have been completed and your story will have played out. Positives  + Fantastic artwork + Decent stories + Can be challenging but easy to learn + Enjoyable to play + Has achievements Negatives  - No cards currently Use the Fear Machine to spread fear and terror throughout the land, frighten the people into believing your message and not that of your opponents as you strive towards the goal of attaching your dream. What will you do to make your dreams come true and will the price of your dreams be worth it? 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: A puzzle game about fear-mongering to spread your goals, with a little Tales from the Crypt. The primary challenge comes from attempting to not just spread fear across the map, but the right types of fear in the right regions while having to juggle resources produced to feed these fears and playing defense against rival organizations. Extra challenge in trying to do all this while achieving 100% fear in the mission.A short 3 episode campaign is provided, which is enough to give you a challenge and teach you mastery of the mechanics but still leaves you longing for a little more to put that mastery to use. While the story of the game's campaign is concise and ends precisely where it should, I'd welcome an episodes expansion or a free-play randomized sandbox mode if they chose to.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Moderately fun, if somewhat undemanding game. Touches quite directly on some of the modern social landscapes and how fear is wielded to the advantage of grifters and powermongers, including commentary on pandemics (albeit a poor one that initially leans into the reactionary ideology rather than against it, but the ending at least turns that around) and certain recent elections, but also not anything particularly insightful. Some of the writing for the direct characters is hamfisted at best, but the rest is good. It's not very difficult and there's a lot of waiting without necessarily a lot of forethought and planning. You will probably be playing this game like a turn-based one, holding down RMB to speed up the clock and then stopping when you need to pause to make a move. I'm not sure why it wasn't made turn based to begin with, honestly. The first story is not really challenging at all. By the second, though, you are racing against the clock a fair bit more, and the rival you're given by the second stage is a legitimate threat that may require some give-and-take. However, the game is still fundamentally the same. Spread the right kind of fear in the right places, manufacture different colors of skittles to spend on leveling up fears and progressing events, and hold down RMB during all the time inbetween.At the $9 sale I got it for, it's a 7/10. At the base asking price of $18 though, I'd bump it down to a 6/10. Buy on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Reading about this, I was immediately intrigued about the concept of spreading fear to push your particular agenda, although even after seeing the screenshots I was unsure how it would work gameplay-wise. I definitely like staring at maps though, so I picked it up pretty soon, at full price even.So a bit of a gamble, but it definitely paid off because I thoroughly enjoyed it. The gameplay turned out to be rather straightforward, with new mechanics added or basic ones slightly changed every so often to keep it interesting. In terms of complexity or originality I guess it's nothing to write home about (assign certain messages you want to spread to regions, pick the right conspiracy or horror stories for each region/message, acquire resources and fight enemies with the machine's minions, level up the stories and minions) BUT since the whole ordeal is executed very well it kinda  something to write at least a positive Steam review about.Not to mention the whole visual style and presentation. The illustrations are so well done I didn't want to miss a single card in the album, so after finishing (which took me 12-13 hrs) I played through half of the levels again to get 100%.If I had to criticize something it'd be QoL-related, like the fact the game always automatically starts on normal speed even though I like to play with faster speed, pausing whenever there's something to do... I forgot it would do that pretty much every time, which led me to reload a lot since I can't stand it when a minion is idle for a week, especially this early in the level. Then again, it probably wouldn't make much of a difference, since my second criticism is that the game is a bit too easy overall (and I usually like it relatively easy). There was one level I had to restart twice, other than that it was a walk in the park. So for future DLCs or sequels: I wouldn't mind failing more often, within reason.As for the themes and stories, the philosophical implications if you will, it's kinda silly to assume that spreading any kind of urban legend and conspiracy theory would further whatever goal you're after, but since the game doesn't take itself too seriously (despite the serious nature of its topics) it's easy to suspend your disbelief. In the three scenarios you're playing (which I'm not gonna spoil), the idea even makes sense in a way and there often  connections between the stories and the goals, but abstract "fear" is just not enough to explain the phenomena we're dealing with here. Good thing that's not the point of the game. It's to tell dark stories in an entertaining manner, and I think it's doing that absolutely fabulously.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: This felt like an amazing combination of Plague Inc. meets Creepshow! The pulpy comic book style was beautiful and worked so well for telling the story. For such dark topics, it did help make things much more vibrant without taking away from the creepiness of things. The art style and themes are incredibly consistent throughout the game. The stories are very interesting and revealed with great twists as well as timing. Difficulty builds with different mechanical layers that keep gameplay interesting as well as challenging. It felt like this game was so thoroughly thought out! Try out the demo for yourself as that is what got me into the game! Overall Score: 8/10 Gameplay & Thoughts:
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly unique strategy game in which you inspire fear through paranormal events, cryptids, general violence, and conspiracy theories to fuel a machine which can grant you anything you desire. The gameplay is fun and the game introduces things at a pace that allows you to easily learn how to play. On top of the theme and the gameplay, the art style is awesome and evokes classic horror comics. If you're into strategy/simulation games and enjoy the horror genre/want to play as a supervillain, don't hesitate to check this one out. I would love to see a few more campaigns or a sandbox/endless mode added to the game though, as it is fairly short. The length/amount of content on offer is my primary complaint, but this can easily be resolved by free update or paid DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: The Fabulous Fear Machine is a strategy game with a strong main storyline where you must spread fear around the world to further your evil agenda.The game is quite elaborate so to go into all it's mechanics here is a bit much, but essentially you must take over towns then use your controllable "agents" to spread fear and harvest resources in each town which you then use to handle random events and defeat your rivals. It is far more complex than that but thats the key essence here.The game also has some wonderful story with it working on a "pulp comic" style, comic book panels play before and after each mission detailing each characters plot and evil deeds (which are horrifically and awesomely graphic) and you also unlock cutscenes by completing objectives within missions with more comic panel's to reveal story. The main gripe I had with the game was I found it very hard HOWEVER I do not play this kind of game at all for the most part so I'd imagine if you are a strategy gamer you'd probably have a considerably easier time than me managing everything.Overall TFFM has a great plot, great visuals and fun if quite complex gameplay. Recommended
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Played it for 4 hours, thought "this is a slow start but I can see it getting good soon," played for another 2 hours, "wait it's not getting better, maybe there's some twist towards the end?" played for another 2 hours "oh it's over. That was mid." 2/5Fun art style but gets old fast. Game basically plays itself on normal, and I didn't see an option to play a 'hard mode' - if it gets unlocked after beating the game, I'll pass; there's basically no replayability as there are only 10 missions total (12 or 13 if you count the tutorial, which you shouldn't), and nothing like a 'skirmish' mode that I could see. Maybe replaying a mission lets you skip the cutscenes/dialogue but I didn't care enough to see. I only lost a mission twice, once because I misunderstood the win condition (my fault, but not exactly an intentional challenge) and once because I deliberately picked the worst starting location I could find to see what would happen (the answer: nothing really, and then you lose)I could be ok with mediocre gameplay if there was a strong narrative, but the game doesn't seem to have much to say besides "haha aren't people stupid and/or evil?" I get that the 'pulp' style typically has pretty flat characters and kind of nonsense plots, but it got boring quickly since it didn't have really meaty gameplay to fall back on - see Tropico for a game with a similar narrative style but (more) complex gameplay. There are hints of some more interesting stuff with the Zeppelin and Mae Ludd, but most of the narrative is just terrible people making quips at each other and then a page or two of a classic-style comic book. The aesthetic is fun, and there are hints of interesting mechanics in the game - you just don't need to bother exploring them because there's so little difficulty. It feels like an overlong demo for a full game (I expected the "real story" to come after the three provided campaigns finished) but there is no full game. Also, while the game is very unsubtle in its critiques of reactionary social movements (it lampoons evangelists and anti-immigrant nationalists), the first campaign being "An Evil Pharmaceutical Scientist Fakes A Worldwide Pandemic to Get Famous" is either just comically tone-deaf or deliberately playing into the same kind of reactionary politics the other campaigns make fun of. I think the former is actually more likely, because the campaign ALSO rips into anti-vax movements, but it's just an eyebrow-raising framing. Also none of the critique (for any cause or ideology) is particularly funny or interesting; as I said at the top, the only thing the game seems interested in saying is "haha aren't people stupid and/or evil?"Honestly I think that if this game took a pivot into being a roguelike or at least rogue-lite, it'd be a lot more interesting. Some of the design feels like that was part of the original intention (agent stats, 'Somber Place' location modifiers, cut+paste legends, 'rival' dialogue that's incredibly generic), but for whatever reason that's not what we ended up with.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Short but enjoyable resource management/worker placement game. The artwork and fun comic theme help to carry the relatively narrow gameplay. Once you've made it past the learning curve, the scenarios become very easy to 100% complete even at the highest (normal) difficulty. Additional campaign DLC would be welcome, in the meantime would recommend waiting for a sale drop below $10 unless an ardent fan of management games or the pulp horror genre.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little gem of a game.  The aesthetic is imitating classic horror comics like Tales from the Crypt and pulls that off remarkably well.  From the art style to the campy, over-wrought dialogue to the rather shockingly gruesome violence in the inevitable twist ending, it all feels so damn authentic and true to that genre.  The actual gameplay is deeper that I expected, though still pretty simple.  Essentially it's an infection game, except that instead of spreading disease you spread fear.  To do that, you send your minions to different cities on the map to harvest resources like Fear, Blood, Politics, etc which you then use to place Legends.  These are essentially stories that can be used to terrify the populace and can take the form of everything from legends about monsters in the woods to  conspiracy theories regarding chemtrails and Big Brother.  Once you get a certain amount of fear in a province you win.This is the type of game where context and aesthetic can paper over a lot of cracks.  The flavor text is a joy to read, the art design is great, and the stories are fantastic pulpy fun.  Probably won't change your life, but I definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Fabulous Fear Machine
