_childDocuments_.review: Shadow Gambit is a new take on stealth-strategy from Mimimi, the new masters of the genre.As with other games in the genre, you control a small number of stealthy specialists, and progress by carefully taking down enemies one at a time, as you have little chance in outright combat against multiple enemies.In Shadow Gambit, the focus is on freedom and variety.Each of the game's maps are large and open islands, with multiple missions taking place on each, and you have the freedom to select which three of your eight playable characters should go on each mission (with a few exceptions where one character is required for story reasons.)Each of the eight playable characters has a unique skill set and most feel quite different to play, so your choices of who to take can significantly change your strategy on each island.The downside of this freedom is the missions can feel a bit generic, because they have to be solvable by any set of characters, and so can't have complex setups that require specific skills.  This can make the game a little easy at times (though it feels a little strange to say that about a game where you will be saving and reloading constantly.)The story here is lighter than Mimimi's previous games.  You control a group of cursed, undead pirates who are fighting against a group of religious fanatics - and specifically their leader, who plays the role of the primary antagonist.Both groups are hunting for a specific treasure hidden by another (now dead) pirate.Each of the characters also have their own side stories, but they mostly deal with their past rather than there being any real drama between the characters themselves.  The characters are quirky and amusing, and some have interesting histories, but don't except anything as complex as the characters in Shadow Tactics.The backstory of the setting isn't very well explained.  We never learn why the pirates (and others in the region) are cursed with undeath, and we don't even learn if they are cursed because they are pirates, or became pirates because they are cursed.  There are some hints at it, but it's never fully explained.This is a solid game for fans of the genre, with more polished gameplay and more variety of characters, though sadly the focus on variety and freedom leads to a less compelling story overall.Pros: - Refined stealth-tactics gameplay - Eight unique characters which all feel different to play - Interesting maps, with each island feeling different - Freedom to approach missions how you chooseCons: - Most maps are re-used multiple times for different missions (though the missions usually take place in different areas.) - Can be a bit easy because every map must be winnable by any combination of characters - Less focus on story

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent sequel, the greater range of flexibility per-mission was a great change and most other changes were also good. Not a fan of the island/crew/mission badges staying invisible until after Act 4 instead of after the first time you complete the mission, and the silliness sometimes intruded in places it wasn't welcome, but those are fairly minor complaints. _childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: This is yet another great game by Mimimi. However it is a huge step down from Shadow tactics and Desperados 3. The game is much less linear, which unfortunately is very detrimental to a game like this. The characters are unlocked in almost whichever order you want them to, which sounds cool, but leads to the characters being pretty bland and their relations are almost irrelevant.You decide which 3 characters you want to bring on each mission, again a cool idea, but it means the levels are designed for every single combination of characters, which leads to the levels not being nearly as sharp and well designed as the other Mimimi games i mentioned earlier.The final thing I want to mention is the difficulty. The hardest difficulty in Shadow tactics and Desperados 3 is explained as not being recommended for a first playthrough no matter skill level, which I agree with, since it will take away from the story that the game is so difficult. The same warning is in this game, but here the game is so easy that I wouldn't recommend playing on anything but the highest difficulty, unless you want to breeze through the game. It is still a solid game that I would definitely reccomend, but their similar titles are significantly better, both in story and gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Best game in recent years! Totally worth the wait and price!Game play is awesome as always. Voice acting is nice, story is interesting, but not by any means the focus of the game.The team system has been changed into 3 people per stage, and you get to choose who to bring on each mission.I wasn't fully on board with this idea before the release, but I have fully confidence in Mimimi after their last few releases.The new system plus the way they implement it. It doesn't feel like you are getting handicapped for not being able to use your fav char in each mission, but adds a variety to the mission which make the game so much more interesting and replayable.Sidenote:As a gamer, it's rare having a developer and now a publisher that really care about gamer and the games they are making. I really want to support Mimimi's ethics and enthusiasm for the gaming industry. When did releasing a game without major bugs become the golden standard?Mimimi not only release a game without major bugs, but gave gamer more than what we are asking for! Which I believe should be recognised by the gaming community. Shouts out to Supergiant Games for Hades, can't wait for Hades 2, and Larian Studios for their recent success in Baldur's Gate 3. Please keep the good games coming!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: This one is a gem. I played Shadow Tactics of Mimimi before. Loved it too. But this... As a Monkey Island fanboy and all into the pirate stuff... this is for me. Every new character you unlock has a tutorial, which is great! You could critique the fact that you have to unlock all the characters in a long process, but this has up- and downsides. I don't think it's a valid point. I'm someone who likes to get used to a character before trying another, so the unlocking pace is perfect for me.For those who think the maps are repetetive. No! You have a lot of different areas, all completetly different and about 3-4 missions in each terrain. The maps are huge and every mission in a terrain is in a different part then the other missions.

_childDocuments_.review: MiMiMi has been bringing to us state of the art RTT's games from Shadow Tactics through Aiko's Choice and Desperados III. I was counting the days until the release of Shadow Gambit and, again, their work is really impressive. Besides the beautiful artwork and the attention to every single detail, what stands out the most is how satisfying is the gameplay. Each task can be solved in infinite ways, which gives the players freedom to try and find their own path. After 63.6 hours of playing I finally reached 100% of the achievements, with 91.2% of badges completion, on hard level. Although my recommendation doesn't change at all (it's a great game), I have to say it can get boring if you are running for the achievements due to the limitations of crew tales steps one can get done between missions.And that's so because the main story finishes too fast. After killing the big boss, what's left is play again the same missions, which is odd - for example, you can have all your crew (including the hidden 9th member) and even so play the missions to rescue them or the ship just to enable more steps to finish the remaining crew tales.Besides that, Shadow Gambit is all about the characters skills. They made a really good job creating such cool abilities. I did have a good time anytime I pick John, a massive hard killer. Toya and his Shadow Tactics aura became to be my favorite. Gäelle proved to be very useful to help the others to reach locations no one could achieved without her. Pinkus and his body theft also helped a lot to solve hard problems, such as Suleidy and her bushes or wander dusts. Quentin, Teresa and Afia are more simple, but also helpful to specific situatins (Quentin to hide bodies, Teresa to snipe, Afia to kill from medium distance).I don't care for storytelling, so I have to confess I did skip every single dialogue, so I don't get the criticism from some thumbs-down reviews about an eventual lack of character's depth...we're playing games, not reading books, people! I'm all about the fun, and besides this things I pointed before, Shadow Gambit offers many hours of fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: While the game play is technically much improved over previous games, "Shadow Tactics" and "Desperados III", I find Shadow Gambit to be a little tedious at times, replaying the same maps and grinding through cheezy stories for each crew member.Just for me personally, the thematic mish-mash of undead pirates who are the 'good guys' doesn't quite work. In the PotC movies, such characters held up because the undead pirates were a supporting element, a surprise to be revealed and feared. However here in Shadow Gambit, the undead pirates are the only characters that exist, in a poorly fleshed out world, where the villains are some faceless robed cult.  It's a world of style but no substance.All that said, I've had a good time playing, even though I'm not invested in the story and find the dialogue long-winded and poorly written.So if you can overlook these shortfalls, or want a cartoony, light-hearted undead pirate game - tactical rpg - then I highly recommend.

I really miss some tough nuts that require a lot of observation and strategy and sometimes even luck.70% of the game feel like I could manage them with a single character and melee attacks only - which is quite sad for a stealth game.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: 2 hours in and this might be my all time favorite stealth strategy game. And I played the genre since Commandos series (1 through 3) a long long time ago. Team hit it out of the park with this one, only shame is maybe it's a little overshadowed between the release of two titans this year. I wish Mimimi Games the best possible result with this launch, Supporters Edition totally worth it in my eyes.While it's not the same sort of game by a long shot, those who enjoyed the sandbox aspect of doing things your own way in Baldur's Gate 3 may also find some enjoyment in the sandbox aspects of this game too!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say - Mimimi Games did it again. When it comes to RTS/Stealth (Commandos like) games they not only revived the genre few year ago with Shadow Tactics but they keep raising the standard with each game they are making. There was amazing Desperados 3 and now they gave us Shadow Gambit which pushed things even further. I'm not gonna lie I was a bit worried at first with the setting of the game that includes magic, that it might be a bit too much. But oh boy I was so wrong. It opened the arsenal of abilities and possibilities to new extends. One of those is ability to freely select team members you'd like to take on a mission. This gives a lot more replayability to the game. However, there is a bit of a downside related to it - enemy setups had to be solvable with any team members combos so the game is a bit easier than previous Mimimi games and you will feel it especially if you are a veteran of a genre. Overall I do recommend the game to everyone. If you have played the games in the genre you will love it. If you haven't yet - well it's a perfect time to start because you are missing on an amazing time with a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: BEYOND MY EXPECTATIONS.The game is like the combination of its siblings: "Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun" and the franchise "Desperado", but so much better. It has the spirit of freedom, the "not-giving-a-f*ck" mindset in "Desperado"s, the bromance, sophisticated yet mesmerising story in "Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun".What's new is that it offers a near non-linear gaming experience. Unlike its older sibling where you unlock new characters along a fixed storyline, Shadow Gambit allows players to, apart from one "starter" character", pick any follow-up character in offer to unlock. Also, a stage consists of multiple spontaneous missions which players can choose up to their preference. Similarly, a mission has multiple starting points, and there are amusing side missions to learn more about each character's background and personalities.*SPOILER ALERT*Having Toya as my second character has kept me nostalgia. Many of his voicelines are similar to Hayato in Blades of the Shogun (as well as his ninja background). Is the developer getting lazy here?. I have just unlocked Pinkus as my third character recently, I have yet found him a familiar character. Perhaps I will add some to this review when I find some similarities in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: The story is great, the skills of the crew are interesting and the characters are fun and differ a lot. The setting is very appealing with pirates and magic. I like that they went in a new direction which isn't tied to history, that way they could invent new and exciting abilities for the characters. I also like to go back to maps and finishing them in new ways, it's an efficient use of the assets of the game and with such great maps there is no reason not to.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: +1Stealth mechanics are fun and challenging without being annoying. Characters seem to have more in-depth personality than most other games. I also like that the crew members do similar tasks slightly differently, so there's more to them than just their skills. For example, Suleidy kills/KOs the enemy faster than Afia (better for Stealth mechanics during takedown) but Afia stays crouched after grabbing the body, while Sueidy stands up with the body (worse for Stealth mechanics after takedown).If I could change one thing, I would have waypoints added to the Shadow Time. Thus I can queue a takedown coupled with a follow-on body dump so that each crewman would takeout the guards and then body-dump and hide after their takedown. Since each takedown is conducted at different speeds for different characters, I have to jump in and out of, and execute, Shadow Mode multiple times each encounter for individual crewmen (unless I just haven't figured out, or found via Google, how to chain actions correctly).
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: I am historically not a huge fan of this style of strategy game, it is often too finicky and frustrating for me to really sink my teeth into. Shadow Gambit is the latest in a long line of similar games by this developer, and it shows. This is an amazingly well polished game with intuitive and deep mechanics, and a cast of characters who are just as engaging for their unique personalities as they are for the diverse abilities they have in game, and the unique approach they each allow for. Shadow gambit is the greatest realization of this genre of game that I have seen, and I cannot give it enough praise. Go for it. You'll have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Pros    • Fun sandbox gameplay building on the standard stealth-strategy formula    • Smooth controls (including gamepad support)     • Varied well-voiced cast of characters    • Fantasy setting allowing for some unique, interesting character abilities    • Loads of content and replayability    • Nice graphics and pretty environments    • Decent story which even ties in the quicksave and quickload mechanics    • Great soundtrack    • Well-optimized and bug-freeCons    • Some characters can be slightly annoying    • The sandbox nature causes non-story missions to have “random” goals    • Basically only two environments or a combination of both: a tropical island or an inquisition fortressAfter reviving the stealth-strategy games with Shadow Tactics and following up with Desperados III, MiMiMi decided to take the genre in what I consider was an obvious direction: they detached the setting from reality and made the game as sandbox as possible. The result is Shadow Gambit: A Cursed Crew, MiMiMi’s best game which is unlikely to be topped as the studio announced closure just a few days after release.After ninjas and cowboys, the new setting is Lost Caribbean, a stretch of sea with several islands. There, among humans live the Cursed, undead who managed to escape death by drawing power from “black pearls”. The story follows a Cursed pirate Afia, who strikes a deal with the sentient ghost ship Red Marley to find the treasure of Marley’s former captain, Mordechai. Afia becomes Marley’s navigator and has to resurrect and work with Marley’s seven crewmates to achieve her goal and beat the inquisition led by Ignatia, the main antagonist. The inquisition’s main aim is the extermination of the Cursed, but they have also their eyes set on recovering Mordechai’s treasure. Fortunately, Marley has powers to manipulate time, which are basically an explanation for the game’s key mechanics: quicksave, quickload, time fast-forwarding and the Shadow mode (more on that later). I would say that while skilled at writing dialogues and fleshed-out characters, MiMiMi aren’t as apt in writing the overarching stories. In that regard, Shadow Gambit does not shock, but the story still has a few twists so I would say it is their best one. The characters are brilliant though, each with a unique personality, quirks, and secrets. The dialogues are witty, though the open-ended nature of the game results in Afia and Marley appearing in most of the dialogues.If you played MiMiMi’s previous games, the core gameplay will mostly carry no surprises for you. You control several characters who each have different skills to use and have to overcome or avoid enemy garrisons and patrols using stealth to achieve your objectives. However, instead of the usual skills like tossing a stone to distract an enemy, your crew in Shadow Gambit has access to a variety of magic powers which mix up the formula quite a bit. Several characters have some form of teleport, which allows you great freedom of movement. Some are built around a certain gimmick, for example, the canonness lugs around a cannon that shoots people instead of balls, with which you can hide bodies, get your crewmates to high ground, and more. The overarching structure also got improved, as you don’t follow a set string of missions, but you can choose an island to land on, which mission to undertake there, a place where to land and which crewmates (usually up to three) to take on the mission. Once your objectives are complete, you also have to make your way to one of the island’s extraction points and return to the ship. This results in a great deal of freedom in how you approach each mission. The enemy variety is also greater than in previous games, you still have the standard enemies, enemies who do not respond to distractions and strong enemies who require two characters to beat (this time, no character can beat them alone), but now there are also connected characters who revive the other if he or she is incapacitated and snipers with great view distance. Key tools in your arsenal are also the time-manipulating powers: the quicksave and quickload are kind of a staple of the genre, allowing you to retry a failure immediately, the Shadow mode enables you to perform several actions at once or control their execution, and a bit overshadowed but for me a must have-feature, the time fast-forwarding, thanks to which you can make a patrolling enemy move to where you want them much faster. As it is usual with MiMiMi games, the player has perfect information about everything, from the enemy viewcones (though only one can be visible at a time) to skill sound radiuses and durations. Thanks to this, the player can form a plan anytime and execute it to satisfaction.The Red Marley serves as your hub and headquarters. You start the game only with Afia and have to resurrect the rest of the crew using black pearls you obtain as a reward from certain missions. This is another degree of freedom as you can choose when to unlock which crewmate. Once unlocked, you can take them on missions or do “crew tales”, short missions on Marley’s deck that reveal more about the crew. There is also a training area on the Marley, where you can play tutorials for each crewmate to learn their skills. Each crewmate also has an upgrade which makes them even stronger and further broadens your options. The missions on the islands either move the story or you can receive materials to unlock the crew. There are more of them and the game offers you replayability in the form of challenges. These can forbid you from using certain skills or require you to perform a certain task during the mission. The challenges are split into three categories: crew, island and mission ones. The crew challenges require you to perform a certain feat with a given character, the island ones can be unlocked in any mission on that island and the mission ones are tied to a certain mission. Sometimes you have to replay the mission several times to beat all the challenges. All in all, there is a boatload of challenges that offer a great deal of replayability and if you want to reach 100%, it will take a lot of hours put into the game. If it sounds like repetitiveness sinks in later on, it does not, as you can modify the missions as described above. The game also offers a lot of difficulty options with four presets so both new players and veterans can enjoy it. Thanks to the strong character skills, I would say the game is not that hard even on the highest setting, but it can take time to overcome each enemy setup.The art aspect is as great as everything else, the graphics are nice, the voice actors did an excellent job in bringing all characters to life, and the soundtrack by Filippo Beck Peccoz is pleasant to listen to as always, be it sea shanties you hear on the ship or tense tunes heard on inquisition-controlled islands. I would have one small nitpick with the levels: there are basically only two environments, an inquisition fortress or a tropical island, so the variety is not that high. But the developers at least made each island unique in some way. The game is well-optimized and I did not run into any bugs – sometimes the viewcones are a little finicky, requiring perfect positioning to eliminate an enemy without being seen by another, but that is likely a fault of my strategies and I can’t say the viewcones are inconsistent with their indicators.

_childDocuments_.review: I was thinking writing a positive comment and recommend the game, but after I read that Mimimi studio is shutting down, I changed my mind and do not recommend it. Why? Long story short - the only reason I wanted this game to be bought is to give financial support for their next project, the same reason why I bought it. I played demo, did not liked it but decided to support them and give them second chance. Now about the game:  THE STORY: Oh boy, where do I start? I wanted to write "Spoilers alert" but then I thought there is nothing to spoil. BTW, Is this the same studio that made Shadow Tactics and Desperados? I had to double check. WHY you make a stealth game with a fantasy children's bed story? Do they not know what audience played their games? With this project, it is clearly evident that they wanted to attract new younger people and hit it big, they flopped and went bankrupt. I bet the most of the recommendation is positive because of their previous games, but we have to be real now. Kids nowadays do not have the patience for stealth games. Give them COD, Apex Legends, Magic, something to burn, shoot, explooode etc. WE WANT AS MUCH AS REALISM AND PATIENCE in stealth game because that is why they are stealth. THE CHARACTERS: I saw the characters the same as a generals sees their soldiers on military map. I did not care about their stories or where they did come from I just wanted to perform my task and shut up. I did not care to hear..oh and there is a lot of talking gibberish, on every mission they were conversing uninteresting cheesy stuff with amateurish acting voice, after they were finished I had to click in Tasks to see what is it to be done, really. Some are so annoying and give that you-have-to-admire-me vibe and made me more sympathetic to the enemies so I knocked them out mostly. Maybe children would like to hear their stories, but again there is metaphysics involved that children wont find it immersive (Like characters saying that death is not the end, black magic, etc.) The story is like someone giving you ice cream but with ketchup topping only. I can not talk about the story much, leave it to you maybe you will like it, and because honestly I lost interest. It is about a dead captain that made cursed ship and you have to get this crew together again. If you like the stories in the previous games from the studio, expect disappointment.GAMEPLAY: Firstly: EAAAASY, ez,ez,ez,ez!!!,..I played on cursed with 3 saves only. Many times I did not saved once, and I do not consider myself stealth veteran. Times I saved was because of misclicking or getting my character mixed (which happens often) or similar. The game is so easy that you have to make your own challenges if you want to enjoy it and I do not like making my gameplay difficult when I have a lot of easier options, I want to start on hardest mode and have no other choice to pass except the hard way. Example: HIDING BODIES is so easy,(grow a bush on it, done, put it in your chest, or drop an anchor above it to sink underground); HIDING from enemies piece of cake(grow a bush again, go underground again, teleport etc.) ALARMED enemies go back to their hut where they spawn form, so you have dead bodies lying all around and enemies say only "They are gone!" and return to normal, ENEMIES can not climb vines, so you just run there duck and wait for the alarmed ones to go inside, so MANY DIFFERENT WAYS to play, because the many repeatable skills the characters have kills the reward factor, there is no part in the game where you have to sweat. And the kills you have to trigger that make cannon shoot or box to fall add to the fact that they aimed at younger and new audience that likes to win without challenges, they forgot about the people that played commandos, and how rewarding was to kill 1 or 2 enemy.  Here, no punish to your mistake, nor reward to your "walk-through" Also those different relics you gather on the island where you choose on the map are different because of the story only, they all give you same thing - soul, (what you need to revive another boring character that is not necessary) In comparisons to Yuko from Shadow Tactis, I saw her like my daughter and send Mugen mostly to do difficult tasks because he was older and experienced soldier, and would accept death as samurai. In this game I did not care when character died, I was happy even when that annoying sailor with his dead fish (that says "Im felling Blblbl-balloons" the most annoying) died and continued without him which you can do here because the devs even knew how easy they made the game and that you can go on with less character to complete the mission.MECHANICS: The only thing I liked. It is smooth and I met minor bugs.WHAT THEY COULD DO instead of this children's story for grow-ups: Make medieval robin hood, that has more stealth and realism. Pirates and magic? Pirates are not Stealthy, why the heck they chose Pirates? Pirates are noisy and aggressive, they have Cannons and are most of the time drunk to sneak around. On top of that cursed, they supposed to cut some throats to be cursed, why should I sympathize with them? Magic in stealth game, tricky and risky. Magic goes with Baldur's Gate yes, with combat, but in stealth games you have to put boundaries to magic. Stealth with fantasy? Make for example Early Colony on Mars, you play as natives that hide underground, and sneak around to make their colonist Terran enemies job difficult with shapeshift (spy), attracting attention with their bug-like pets, etc. Or another fantasy genre with animals, the lions have a catnip network and like to push it on rat societies, few rats want to stop it, the time should be in Chicago-mafia 1930's time, Zootopia-like characters....Anything, but not forget that in this stealth isometric games the aim should be an audience that have patience, which are grownups mostly, what they like? So Easy, what we liked about the previous games? As it shows FEW liked pirates. People think that they flopped because the release time (Baldur's Gate) yes and no, no because they are completely different games. So why so many recommendations, you will ask yourself when you try this game, well People saw pirates, gave it a chance, played the demo, some have done it because they liked the previous games and had hopes for the next to be as them also and some bought it for support, as I did. But I spilled the beans since I know that no other game will come from the studio. End it with Desperados, or buy it on sale if you have no stealth game to play.To the Developers: It was hard for me to not recommend a game made from the stealth game legends and I find it hard to write that you messed up with this one, BUT the ones you made before this we will never forget, those are cult games. Wish all the best for all.

_childDocuments_.review: After sinking about 23 hours into Shadow Gambit - Cursed Crew (and it didn’t even counted the hours I played offline with the steamdeck) I’ve got some mixed feelings about it. On one hand, it’s not a bad game by any means, but on the other, it didn’t quite hit the mark for me.Let me break it down: I usually give a game a fair shake before passing judgment, and despite my efforts, this one just couldn’t hold my interest. It felt like I was going through the motions without anything really grabbing me. The gameplay loop got repetitive, and there wasn’t anything new or exciting to keep me hooked.But hey, it’s not all bad. The game has its moments, and I can see the effort the developers put into it. However, it feels like they missed the mark compared to their previous titles. The whole vibe of the game shifted to something more goofy and less serious, which didn’t sit well with me. Plus, the difficulty took a nosedive, making things feel too easy compared to what I expected from the studio.Overall, Shadow Gambit - Cursed Crew is a decent time-waster, but it’s not something I’d rush back to play again. If you can snag it on sale, it might be worth a shot, but don’t expect it to blow you away. I’d give it a solid 6 or 7 out of 10, acknowledging its potential but feeling a bit let down by the execution.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: This is a yes if you're just looking to have fun. Perhaps a lean yes if you're looking to be a completionist.It's the now closed Mimimi so it's in that same vein as Shadow Tactics. Bigger crew so you get some more interesting mixes of playstyles with the team's different powers which actually enhances gameplay a bit. Same lovely artstyle with a fun mix of places to explore. The plot is enjoyable enough. Unfortunately the highs are pretty short as game comes with a number of downsides.There's a lot of talking in this game. Far too much talking. I got about halfway through before finding out right click advances a lot of it without skipping. And every crewmate you add has a five part tale which is full of you guessed it... talking with minimal human input needed to activate thing for portion.While all the islands are fun and unique, the downside is that all the missions on them barely change the map other than the mission component. So if you're the type of person that wants to fully explore and murder everyone, you kinda end up getting bored after a while. And since most of the missions are all set to three people, there's no diversity there. Really could have used some more mix of things.This also hurts the storytelling because you somewhat wonder why you couldn't have done some of these things while you were there the first time. In Shadow Tactics, each level had a clear purpose for advancing the story while these just feel like dragging out a lot of the gameplay.Getting the final achievement is a slog - unlocks at 85% completion. If you're doing all the crew stuff, you'll get around 50% pretty easily when you beat the game. But after that, you're constantly redoing things or wrapping the final crew stuff which gets you around 70%. And with all the badges you can earn, it is a little frustrating because so much of it feels like padding.Focused a lot on negatives but this is probably a 75-80 on 100 point scale. With Mimimi closed, you might as well see if it goes on a Steam sale. I'll probably go back and get through the DLC at some point but I've burned myself out on this for a while. A shame Mimimi closed because I like their work but I think they overscoped this and with all the voice acting had a budget much larger than this niche genre could support.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love Desperados 3 and Shadow Tactics but the more I think about Shadow Gambit, the more I dislike it.First of all, the whole theme with undead, ghosts, skulls, souls, soul energy thing, strange inquisitors and their rituals is really boring to me. If the game presented real pirates and more realistic environment, I would be much more pleased.The bland characters and story are not helping either. They are not a real team, they are just few individuals traveling on the same ship and their side stories are simply silly, although this concept itself has potential - but no, instead we get some (woke - Gaelle) diverse ethnic characters without deeper connections. Sure, they come from different regions and they might have minor roles on the ship, but what makes them unique? Nothing, really. The humorous tone of writing is not bad but sometimes feels like it was too much (uh, skeletons drinking?, fish student, skeletons doing... er, poetry; skeletons repeating simple phrase, etc). Btw, "Sakana" means fish in japanese.Well, I still liked some of those characters, to be honest. Toya and John with sir Reginald, for example. Mostly because I like their accents and the design a bit.Oh, but what was with those quotes from Commandos?"Coming right up.""Consider it done." etc etc.Is that suppose to be a tribute, or a reference? Maybe, but it feels like the devs cannot come up with more original lines. And hearing it from those bland characters sounds kinda insulting, to be honest. The game is forcing me to play all locations too many times. Why go there separately for black pearl, and right after that for soul energy again? And then potentially few more times for some more side story trial? Yeah, I know, more hours in the game. But it would be better to have some more islands available instead of repeating the same ones over again. In combination with the simple storyline and characters it felt a bit tedious, although the gameplay itself is not really that bad and there were some moments I enjoyed. Ok, I take it that this game is more like experiment, however, in comparison with previous titles, Shadow Gambit is overall a disappointment to me. I hope the devs will come back sometimes in the future and the next game will be more linear again with higher difficulty and likable, deeper characters and their conflicts.

_childDocuments_.review: Desperados 3 was perfect. _childDocuments_.review: Another great entry from Mimimi for the Stealth RTS genre. It is the first game I bought on release date and I was not disappointed.Switching to an Open World approach adds more Hitman like freedom and removes a bit of that puzzle feeling from Shadow Tactics and Desperados 3. Still, there have been enough moments where at first I was not sure how to proceed, but figured out a way. I see the advantage of having a higher replay value of the Open World with self set challenges and different ways to your target.The difficulty is modest. I played it on Legendary and it had a good casual difficulty. I guess Cursed is not that much harder as the only effective change is the faster detection. In good RTS tradition I did not kill anyone intentionally (how should I know the inquisition can't swim), did not raise any alarms and did not use firearms. The only really challenging map was  It needed some try and error and I learned a lot of the characters I brought. But in the end even that worked out. That is the amazing thing of the level design: Regardless who you bring, there always seems to be a way. So the difficulty of the game is not (just) what you select when starting the game, but the challenges you set yourself during the game. I count this as a plus, because this game has something for experienced players as well as newbies.I love the new characters. They are iconic, over the top individuals with great voice acting and interesting skills, that would not be possible without the fantasy setting. During the plot, you have to progress the individual background story of the characters you find most interesting. The writing of their plots and the dialogues are really good.When I first heard of the new setting I was not sure if I was going to like it. But the humor and the overall idea of having a game plot about save scumming convinced me. The lovable characters also helped a lot. And it adds something fresh to the genre.The overall story arc is solid, but nothing exceptional. They consist of "get three of these and do five of those" too often. There are some highlights at the end of the acts though and the characters background stories that you unlock in Act 2 (I think) are much more interesting.If you liked Desperados 3 or Shadow Tactics I don't see how Shadow Gambit was NOT for you.For everyone else: You can pet a bearded monkey skeleton!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on this game.  On one hand, I absolutely love the theme, the colors, the mechanics.... they were very fun.  I put nearly 30 hours into it.  On the other hand, I didn't finish the game because after 30 hours it was just too repetitive.When I first bought it, I was worried that it was going to revolve around reaction time and that I wouldn't be able to keep up, because I am not a fast gamer.  I was very happy to find out that, no, this game really caters to nearly anyone.  It has quite a good pause mechanic which you can use at any time to line up a simultaneous strike, and it works really well.  It was a ton of fun to pull of a coordinated attack on 3 or 4 guards at the same time!But like I said above, I never finished because even though there is a little bit of a story, the main thrust of the game are the  missions and they just got very, very repetitive.  Eventually it just felt like I was grinding through them just to see the story move forward, and then realized the story was pretty light anyway so I stopped playing.I don't want to rate the game poorly, I did love my time with it for sure but it isn't something I see myself coming back to finish.  I enjoyed what time I played, and I'm done now.  That's the best way I can summarize it.

_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: A truly fantastic game to close the curtain on Mimimi studios, and likely, the whole RTT/Stealth genre. I'm sad to see them go, but at least they can go with a bang and not a whimper. Shadow Gambit is an excellent follow up to their previous games (Desperados 3, Shadow Tactics) and gives the player a much more sandboxy game to play with. Unlike before, you can freely choose any party of 3 characters for most missions, save for some character specific missions, which makes for a much more replayable game than the ones that came before. The game does as a result perhaps suffer from a slightly reduced difficulty, as missions have been designed to be able to be completed with almost any crew combination, but I personally haven't felt that at all. Some combinations work better than others in certain missions, but nobody feels weak, and everyone is fun to use. The game has massive potential for DLC and expansions, but sadly it seems like we won't be getting much of that due to the studio closing down.

_childDocuments_.review: Some years from now, when we’ll look back and examine the lifetime output of Mimimi Games, a developer who arguably single-handedly revived the entire ‘-like’ real time tactics genre, it’ll be another feather in their cap that Shadow Gambit, despite being , still stands head and shoulders above so many other games in so many other ways. .When I say Shadow Gambit is unfocused, what I mean is that . I appreciate Mimimi’s willingness to innovate on the formula, but I don’t think diverging from the core structure of the genre did them any favours in this case. The entire point of these real time tactics games is that they confront the player with unique missions set on unique maps and then challenge us to finish those missions using a specific set of characters. Thus, the designers can build missions to take advantage of these characters’ specific abilities or even force the player to use a combination of characters they might not have considered viable until then. In that way, real time tactics games were always more 'combat puzzle' games than anything else: Here’s your objectives, here’s the abilities you get to use – now figure it out!Shadow Gambit, conversely, is structured to be very open. . While this may sound like a good thing, as it . You see, since there are always multiple missions set on each island, the developers couldn’t design these maps in such a way as to perfectly fit any single mission. The maps are  (a lighthouse forever caught in stasis as it explodes, an island built around the carcass of an enormous anglerfish…), but as you’re playing missions on these islands over and over (with mostly the same enemy placements, to boot), you’ll soon realise that their layouts are designed to be too open so they can accommodate any given mission, instead of being laser-focused on being the perfect map for one specific mission.Since you can choose which characters to take on each mission, the . Which is a shame, because . One character can create bushes as cover wherever she wants, another can possess enemies and walk around disguised in their skin and so on and so forth. But all missions are designed to allow any combination of characters to succeed, which . Thus, Shadow Gambit sometimes reminds me less of the tightly designed combat puzzle games ,  and , which Mimimi have made until now, and more of free-form sandbox games like  or mission-based games that frequently re-use maps and enemy placements, such as . As far as I’m concerned, Shadow Gambit never becomes as tedious as  was in its worst moments, but that’s in large part down to how good everything else is in Shadow Gambit.You see, . The maps and missions may not be specifically designed for them, but that doesn’t take away from the sheer joy of pulling off impossible supernatural group assassinations like clockwork. But what really made me want to write a positive review about this game is everything built on top of the gameplay: , and each of your crew mates gets to shine thanks to lots of interactions in-between missions on your ship, the Red Marley. And .In particular, : Mimimi evidently realised that these two functions are essential to how people play their games, so they decided to turn them into diegetic magic time powers which the Red Marley can use to aid you in your missions. Sort of like how  explained the roguelite cycle of dying and re-trying as part of its premise. And just when you think Mimimi will leave it at that and simply use that concept as an in-world explanation for why you can save and load, Shadow Gambit also tackles the in-world implications of this system. If you’ve played  back in the day, you’ll be familiar with how .Honestly, when I had played Shadow Gambit's first couple of hours, I wasn’t entirely sure how I felt about it, as all the downsides of the new, more free-form and thus less focused approach to gameplay and missions will hit you right away. But . I still think if you’re looking for a REALLY tightly designed combat puzzle game, you’ll enjoy Mimimi’s other games more, but if you’re able to put up with Shadow Gambit’s structure and the slightly generic missions that result from it, you’ll be able to enjoy all of the game’s other qualities to the fullest.

_childDocuments_.review: For fans of Shadow Tactics and Desperados 3, there's plenty to like about Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew, but I personally found the experience to be a bit of a mixed bag. Unlike their previous efforts, this one's a lot bigger in every sense of the word. More playable characters, more missions, more abilities. But that expanded scope comes with a cost, I'd say. Characters are escpecially shallow. In both Desperados and Shadow Tactics, each character is allowed somewhat of an arc. But in this game, what you see is what you get. A chef? He only uses cooking metaphors. A canon-lady? She likes cannons. Treasure Hunter? You guessed it, he likes treasure. And on and on it goes. None ever rise above their station or particular stereotype. And while that can be fine, it would have helped if the characters themselves had more than one or two lines that they repeat for minor actions. If I had a nickel for every time the chef called someone a heavy customer before carrying them, I would have been a rich, rich man.Another casualty of the game's increased scope is the level design. Both Desperados and Shadow Tactics featured five characters. And most of those characters were present for most of both those games' missions. That allowed each level to be designed around both the strengths and weaknesses of each character. Sometimes you came across a heavily-guarded area wherein you could much more easily slip inside with a disguise, or a group of guards wherein you could lure one of them away with a bottle of Sake. And while each mission featured multiple ways of completing the various objectives, most of the time each mission gave a certain character a chance to shine. But in Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew you've got eight playable characters. And for almost every single mission you can choose which character to bring with you. And therein lies a problem, I think. Since you're free to resurrect whomever you wish first, no mission can be designed to heavily favor a certain character, or make another obsolete. And that results in a much easier and open-ended mission design that I felt robbed the game of any and all challenge. Rarely was I ever stumped what to do. It isn't bad, per se. But I did find the game growing stale the further I went on as I was never challenged in the slightest.Now, it ain't all bad. Levels are for the most part well-designed visually, and despite the somewhat lackluster writing, some of the characters have a moment or two where they are either interesting and/or fun, and abilities in general are quite awesome, both visually and technically. Though, I'd go so far as to call some of them flat-out over-powered. But if there's something I'd call genuinely bad, it's the atrocious pacing. See, in order to progress the story, you need to unlock characters. To do so, you need a piece of Soul Energy and a Black Pearl. Each island (mission) has both a piece of Soul Energy and a Black Pearl. But you cannot grab them both during a run. No, you need to play one mission wherein your objective is a piece of Soul Energy. And then, once you've completed that mission, you have to play the same level again only with a Black Pearl as your objective. Each island (mission) needs to be played twice. Nothing carries over between runs, either. So if you don't wanna raise a single alarm and really be patient, you'll have to do so twice. Then, further into the story, you're required to play a couple of missions that'll have you go back to islands you've been to before. Only difference now is the character you're forced to bring along. Meaning you'll have to play certain levels up to three or four times. Having done that, I eventually said ♥♥♥♥ it to stealth and just ran to the objectives as I couldn't be bothered clearing out the same section for the fourth or fifth time. It is a baffling decision that I can only assume was made to pad the run-time. But bigger don't always mean better, I'm afraid.So, what's the verdict? If you're a fan of stealth games in general and Mimimi Games' previous efforts, you'll find much to like here, and much of the same. Moreso, you'll find a game that'll try your patience with tediousness more often than with a genuine challenge. Thus, I'd wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow what an awesome game! Just watched the credits roll, and in a year stacked with amazing games, this one still stands out. The characters, music, level design, difficulty, and attention to details in this is are so well done all around. I'd heartily recommend this game to anyone who likes stealth, pirates, RPGs, and/or good writing with great voice acting. It might be easy to pick the same 3 characters for each mission and roll with it, (I'm partial to Suleidy, Pinkus and John myself), but the game encourages you to try out different combinations of characters and rewards you for taking characters you don't often use after awhile. Plus it's not mindless. It doesn't let you just brute force your way to a solution, it often requires thinking and careful planning to step away from a mission unscathed. Just a really well polished stealth gameplay experience. I'm sad to learn that the studio closed down recently because after playing this I was looking forward to anything else they may have put out. I definitely want to go back and check out their older titles now based off of this game, and I got a little choked up seeing the wall of "Thank you" messages from clearly passionate, hard working developers who just wanted to make fun games.Well Mimimi, mission accomplished, you made an AMAZINGLY fun game. Hope everyone at the studio goes on to do great things and hope anyone reading this gives this game a shot, because it deserves it!

The previous games were excellent but Shadow Gambit has some tracks that start to wear a bit thin after a while.It's still a good game and well worth playing but  its predecessors were more to my taste.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely brilliant. It's a stealth strategy game where you usually control 3 undead pirates and go to town on an island killin' and plunderin' the Inquisition. Mainly killin'.The quicksave and quickload - always so integral to Mimimi's games - has been beautifully integrated as part of the story along with the pause to plan your coordinated attacks, and I really like that you can select whichever characters you want on the mission.Speaking of the characters, they all have their own - usually pretty amusing - personality quirks, backstories, crew stories, and quests. And they're absolutely top notch. The Cook's crew tale being a particular favourite!The crew all have different skills and they're all good at what they do. You'll quickly find your favourite crew members and they probably won't be the ones you expected when you read the bio's. I skipped the doctor, Suleidy, because I thought she wouldn't fit my play style. In actuality she now my favourite character and can pretty much solo an entire island (barring the special enemies).Overall it's a truly brilliant game. It's taken everything that was excellent about the previous titles and added so much more. A crowning achievement and a new high bar for the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This will probably be my indie game of the year.The devs have really outdone themselves with this one. Their first game was a masterpiece in so many ways, their second was still very good but sometimes felt a little like just more of the same. This one though breathes so much uniqueness and creativity and that already in the first few hours.So far it really got everything: The amazing tactical gameplay the studio is known for, great voice acting and actual great fun writing, good music and all the other design the other games were known for. But on top of that you now have so much more freedom, a Hades-like hubworld with story elements and fun interactions, and out of every single character I've unlocked so far everyone of them feels unique and great and I just wanna keep playing with all of them.I'm writing this review early because I couldn't put the game down and that is a sign that I want other people to play it to. This game is worth your time, I don't regret waiting for it for so long!The game is still great and all my previous points continue to be true throughout it.However there are three mayor things that I am a little disappointed about:The first one is that the even though I like the story of the game, especially the enemy faction, it can't at all compete with their first game Shadow Tactics. It's good but at no point was I ever really emotional invested or felt the urge to push the story forward. At fault is probably the openness and freedom in which you can chose you missions.And the second one is that it just wasn't ever really challenging for me even on Cursed difficulty. Since you have so much freedom with abilities, landing/exit spots and who you even bring with you; the game seems to struggle with presenting you actual though puzzles. The older games were very linear and didn't give you much freedom but in that there was challenge. Seemingly unbreakable fortresses would slowly crack because the devs knew what you had, what you didn't, where you could approach from and could design it all suitably.And finally the last one is that you revisit all the island too often. It's not that it's too repetitive since you usually don't visit two thirds of an island in the first mission and come back for it in future ones. You never approach the same location from the same direction which is good.But still, I saw the ten island spots on the map and through badge progress and I still hoped for an extra giant flagship or fortress to pop up on the map to catch me off guard.Nevertheless it was still fun and I will continue to look forward to the next Mimimi game and hope that they make it even better.

_childDocuments_.review: A good example of a game in a quite rare real-time tactics genre (a.k.a. Commandos-like). Gameplay mechanics are almost identical to the previous games from this studio (Shadow Tactics, Desperados 3) and are very entertaining just as before.Game setting is by itself fairly novel - a cartoonish and magic-filled pirate world - but unfortunately the storyline is very bland and in most cases just distracting from the actual gameplay. Map and mission design also seems like a downgrade compared to previous games because authors were clearly aiming for quantity (replayability) at expense of quality. In any case, if you are a fan of this type of games then this is a go-to choice, especially for the lack of any competition. If you are new to the genre then try Blades of Shogun and Desperados 3 first.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Shadow Tactics and Desperados 3, and knew this would play similar.  I followed previews before release, and it looked like a solid but maybe formulaic follow-on...but I  like this game, and it certainly stands on its own.  It's odd; I'm not a massive pirate fan, but the pirate theme mixed with authoritarian religious goons really works.  Maybe it tickled my love of the Hammerites/Mechanists from the Thief series...It feels a little easier than previous games as you can chose who you take into a mission and it needs to be a bit looser to accommodate that, but it also makes it feel more like an immersive sim which is awesome.  I'm also a bit further into the game than when I first reviewed it, and the story is pretty darn cool; nicely done, devs.

_childDocuments_.review: The burnout is real with this one.  I have been a huge fan of this studio and still sad to hear that this is their final project.  Unfortunately this is not as good as it should be.  While playable there are too many issues that will not get fixed and too many design fails for me to recommend this.  Purchase at a steep discount to lessen the disappointment that will follow after playing and finding a finishing point.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: A perfect ending to the unofficial trilogy, and probably the best game of them. The real shining take away from this is that the characters are really fun and offer unique gameplay for each one. Though at first I didn't find the use for each, with different combos of characters on a team, it became more obvious how they could be used in tandem to achieve some really cool results. The levels offer enough variety to encourage you to find this as well, which is a nice incentive to try things you wouldn't otherwise have. I will say on top of that, they really nailed the story and the character arcs as well. The story keeps it moving at a nice pace without becoming dull, along with creating a nice world with which to explore.  The crew tales are key to this as they provide context for the characters while also giving a nice distraction from the otherwise lengthy missions that can be quite taxing. I found the conclusion to the story was a beautiful end to not only the game, but also to the studio if need be. Overall, go pick the game up! It's great fun and unlike anything else out there/

_childDocuments_.review: A few hours in I was thinking I'd begin this review with "I don't normally recommend games this days, but this one is an exception". However, as I played more I realized that no, it's not.I want to like this game. It's modern and smooth to play. It's pleasant to look at. The magic abilities power fantasy can be enticing. The savescumming is legitimized by the story in a clever way. Even the odd setting and the whole "cursed pirates versus mad-cult-meets-spanish-inquisition" thing somehow works without being irritating. I really hoped I'd enjoy Shadow Gambit more than I actually did, because at first glance, it does just what I thought I'd like to see in a game like this: replayability, open world elements, the abiity to choose between characters, more player freedom. "Beware what you wish for"...With no prior experience of making RPGs or immersive sims, Mimimi tried to make their own Dishonored. The results are rather predictable - a cast of empty, forgettable characters-stereotypes. The lead Afia Manicato is no Emily Kaldwin, and Red Marley is no Dreadful Wale. I just can't bring myself to care about any of them, as the game doesn't do a good job of portraying backgrounds or motivations beyond constant dialogues that serve as exposition dumps. "Crew stories" are literally just that - go here, listen to a cutscene-dialogue, go there, more dialogue, repeat. Dragon Age of 2009 puts Shadow Gambit's attempt at this to shame. It all feels like Mimimi made a mishmash of things, with limited budget and little understanding what made them fun in their respective games. There is now about a dozen characters that fall into different archetypes and feel like some heroes from Overwatch. There is little diversity in their skillset, and the whole progression is just unlocking their "skill upgrade" through grinding the same maps multiple times - and even that is only available for some of them.This failed experiment could be forgiven, as thankfully crew stories are just an optional feature you don't have to engage with, if it wasn't for all the implications it had on the traditional real-time tactics part. And that was heavily dumbed down for casual audiences. And while I'm not a huge fan of hardcore myself, I feel they really overdone it there. Alarms are now meaningless and barely have any consequences, moreover they are even beneficial as they allow you to draw enemies away and slaughter them one-by-one. Dying is also trivial, as any character is able to revive his or her teammates. Even though there are plenty of abilities geared towards stealth play, there's no real need to do that - it's entirely feasible to brute force your way to the objective. And given how maps are huge and how you'll have to replay them multiple times - stealthing them through quickly becomes a tedious chore. Tediousness is in fact a recurrent feeling I get after playing - which is why I can't bring myself to stomach more than one mission every time. As of this review, I have reached the end of Act 2 as well as dabbled a bit into DLC - and I honestly feel no desire to continue and don't really care how the story ends and what happens to the characters I'm not invested into.Perhaps it's a harsh thing to say, but I'm actually not disappointed at all Mimimi is closing doors after this one. It feels like they've exhausted their creativity and did everything they possibly could for the genre. Even this game rides quite heavily on Shadow Tactics' nostalgia. As it is, Shadow Gambit is trying hard to come across as more than a reskin of previous games - and while it certainly succeeds at doing so, too many changes here are not welcome ones.TL;DR If you want a stealth game with great characters, progression, replayability, immersion and non-linear design - play Dishonored 2. If you want a great real time tactics game - play Shadow Tactics or Desperados 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadow Gambit is a very nice and kind-hearted game. The characters are well-designed and have excellent voice acting. I haven't played Desperados 3 yet, but compared to Shadow Tactics, the characters are significantly more overpowered, and the abilities are quite crazy and funny. As a result, the game is sometimes a bit easier. However, there are moments when you encounter challenging puzzles, where everyone can see everyone and you have to coordinate a perfect attack with 3-4 characters simultaneously. It's incredibly satisfying when you succeed. If you need more challenging gameplay, try getting most of the coins in missions. Some players may not like the "open-world" aspect, where missions can be completed in a random order, and you have to revisit most of the islands 3-4 times through the game. But I think the islands are quite diverse, nicely designed and interesting enough. It's nice that once you become familiar with the environment, you can invent new and more effective strategies with other characters. Thanks to that, the story is perhaps a little less epic. It's basically an adventure of funny undead pirates on a ghost ship looking for the dead captain's lost treasure and finding friendship along the way. The soundtrack is awesome on its own and I recommend checking it on Spotify, YouTube or buying it on Steam. I was delighted with the game. Good job Mimimi devs!

_childDocuments_.review: Just like it's predecessors a solid game. Graphics fit the purpose, sound is good, controls are great .... if you like this kind of games then there is little reason to not get this one as well.There is drawbacks though. It's the last game from this developer since they closed doors...sad, so much for my "Blades of the Shogun 2" hope.Seriously: Despite it being a great game and the 3rd from the developer, it is also the weakest.In previous games you got characters fixed to the story and missions would have fixed character line up, often bringing all playable chars at once. In gambit you start mission 1 with a fixed char. For mission 2 you can choose 1 out of 2, for Mission 4 who can unlock 1 more out of 6 chars. The remaining chars can be unlocked in w/e order whenever you have the resources. Also you can freely choose what character to bring to a mission, but you can bring a max of 3. This means characters are vastly less unique, most of the chars have a distract/bait skill as example. The difference between the use/playstyle of characters being hvly limited. With most characters having similar skill effects and the 3character limitation, it also opens up BIS teams. It also means levels are vastly less impressive. E.g. in Blades there would be an area incredibly hard to enter without the spy, in order to use the spy you need to first get the disguise from another hvly guarded area which hvly favors using the samurai, but the samurai cannot easily get there due to his limited mobility. Gambit has none of it. The disguise mechanic is completely gone and mobility penalty has lost most of its value. Every map is made generic enough to ensure that w/e character you bring can get past it.This brings gameplay down to either bringing your most favorite  or the most OP char collection and then finish every lvl by repeating your favorite skill combination over and over again. Where the previous games forced you to adapt and change your approach by making certain characters unavailable or making bringing them into play a challenge, this game doesn't even attempt to give you reason for either.If you haven't, play Blades of the Shogun and/or Desperados 3, both are better. If you still feel the itch for these kind of games after that, then you can go for Shadow Gambit.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew is another installment in the genre of tactical stealth games from Mimimi, developers who brought us Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun and Desperados 3.In many ways, this game stays true to the style of the other two games, and if you've played them, you'll be very familiar. For those unfamiliar, you control 1+ characters per mission, each with their own unique abilities, and must work together and utilize each character's skills to accomplish your objectives. You need to maneuver around and/or distract enemies to take them out, while avoiding being seen. There's many ways to tackle each mission and this game actually offers more than the other two games in that regard, which I'll cover later.The following gameplay aspects which more or less stayed the same:* You can save/load during each mission* Hotkeys assigned to each character's skill* Enemy viewcones have essentially two ranges; up close and far away, where you will always be seen up close and can be crouched in the enemy's far-away vision* Badges/achievements for completing missions in a specific way or completing optional objectives* Adjustable difficulty modesThis game also introduced some new aspects to the game, and I'll share some thoughts on each based on my experience:* No minimap. You are forced to use the large map to get your bearings, which can be difficult to keep on the larger maps.* Certain missions require stealing/obtaining keys, and keys are usable only once, forcing you to save them or find more. This is nice because it keeps you from just getting the "easy" one and blazing through the mission* Manual saves and quick-saves have been merged into a single feature (called memories), and you only keep saves for the current mission you're on (but you can have 20 saves per mission). This means, saving and loading specific missions to go back and farm badges is not possible.* Missions and characters are mix/match in a sandbox style fashion. That is, you can choose which missions to do first (in most cases) and with whom you want to complete them with, like a choose-your-crew approach.* Characters can be upgraded to improve/unlock skills to make them more deadly, completing missions is how you earn these.* New enemy types (not just the normal "grunt", "captain", "brute"): kindred ("connected" grunts, which need to be simultaneously eliminated), custodes (units upon elimination yield an exit point), Iudex (enemy snipers)* Multiple entry/exit points per mission, pick where you start and exit each mission, slightly changing your approach each timeIn some aspects, I think this game got easier compared to the others (though, I have not completed it yet, so my tune may change) on the normal difficulty (so I'm hoping the higher difficulties amp up the challenge)* On normal difficulty, it can be possible to kill enemies inside an enemy viewcone, but if far enough away, they will die before you're spotted, making it easier to cheese your way through some missions* Many enemies are seldom watched by others, making it really easy to pick enemies off one at a time, relying less on subversion and distraction.* Patrols are often in the path of a hazard, which can be used to eliminate all of them at once. This concept isn't new to the game genre, but so far, I feel like it's too abundant.tl;drIf you are a fan of the genre (you liked Commandos, or the previous Mimimi games), you will enjoy this one too. It's got enough new polish that it's worth a try and I'm having a blast playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game after playing the demo, and it has exceeded them. And I'm not even close to halfway in yet!Pros:1. The art is gorgeous2. The gameplay loop is so satisfying and even when something is difficult it never gets to the point of being annoying like most games do because you are ENCOURAGED to save scum--it's actually an integral and intended part of the game and a core part of the plot and is made hyper convenient (near instant hotkeys, almost like playing something on an emulator...I LOVE IT SO MUCH!)5. A stealth game that is ACTUALLY ABOUT BEING STEALTHY AND MAKES IT REWARDING??6. Badass POC female protagonist, and a good diverse cast (clearly not just thrown together for oooo diversity points. They're all actually cool as hell and I love them and the positive representation.)7. I like all of the characters so far, even the villains8. Great voice acting (and I am picky about voice acting. This is high quality. Intentionally goofy sometimes, but that's a good thing.)9. Great sense of humor (Toya's questline is so dumb, I love it)10. Interesting storyline11. Because you can save anytime, you can play for 10 minutes and leave and not get stuck having to abandon progress in the middle of a mission12. Badges/achievements13. I love pirates so much, dudeCons which are mostly user ineptitude in all likelihood:1. It frustrated me that I couldn't use WASD to move the camera around until I figured out I could move it around with middle mouse. I don't know if there's an option to use WASD for the camera, but it would be nice if not.2. Likewise, sometimes it's annoying when you want someone to run somewhere but they just slowly crouch-walk because you didn't double-click. It'd be nice if I could see multiple enemy vision cones at the same time, not just the eyeball that you can place with right click. Badges/achievementsSuggestions:Due to my first three cons, perhaps a slightly more in-depth explanation of controls and varying control options would be nice? _childDocuments_.review: Why do people recommend Shadow Gambit, when it is "inferior" to the previous stealth strategy games from the same producer?Easy: It is a new approach to the genre! Although this entails some flaws, it is worth recommending.The biggest change in Shadow Gambit (in comparison to Shadow Tactics/Desperados 3) is the "open world" approach. You can choose which crewmate to get first, you can choose which missions to take on and then you can choose which of your already available mates you take into that mission. This has two consequences: More freedom for the player and the maps/mission have to be designed in a way that it is possible to achieve the goals with every possible combination of characters.In comparison to other games, Shadow Gambit gives you more choices. The downside is, that the missions are more generic (and therefore easier in difficulty), because there is no specific set of available options to solve a situation. But this is the problem with every game that has an open world: More freedom for the player comes at the cost of mission design.In general, I am not very fond of open worlds, but I like this idea here. In other stealth strategy games there is always a character which I did not like. Being forced to use this character in certain missions annoyed me. In Shadow Gambit I can choose to ignore him/her.Overall I would argue that Shadow Gambit is not superior or inferior to other games of this genre. It just does things in a different way, which I really appreciate.But I get why some negative reviews dont like this game as much as e.g. Shadow Tactics.Sadly Mimimi-Studios are closing down. After supporting the game with patches and two upcoming content updates in late 2023, the company stops producing their awesome games. Thanks Mimimi for all you've done! Best of luck in the future to everyone!

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of Mimimi and the games they have made in this genre, I had elevated expectations for Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew. While the tone was a little more lighthearted than their previous games in the genre (which is a slight detractor for me) and the setting was not as interesting to me personally (I'm not really into pirates), the tried-and-true RTT/Stealth Strategy gameplay shines through here. At its core, this is a game about going on missions where you issue orders to various combinations of your crew in teams of (usually) three pirates. It's about stealthily executing individual and group actions to meet objectives across several missions on different islands. It is methodical. It requires a lot of trial and error (quick saves and loads are not only a necessary mechanic but also a narrative conceit!). It is satisfying in its strategy. I enjoyed the varied characters and abilities, especially when I found a good combination of characters/abilities to approach the mission in a creative way. I have purchased both DLCs for this game but have yet to play them. I am excited to have two additional characters to play with.I am happy that there is much to do here once you complete the game. And I'm glad that the developers provided a thorough in-game challenge log to keep track of the post-game challenges. My only complaint here is that when this unlocks, it's all a bit overwhelming because you suddenly see all the challenges for every mission and character all at once. In previous games, I was able to see and complete challenges for each mission after they were each initially completed. I preferred this as an option. I also wish there was a way to pin individual challenges because having to navigate back through multiple tabs of the challenge log can be tedious.In the end, I am sad to see Mimimi leave us, but I think they did so with a great game. If you played and enjoyed their previous games, you should enjoy this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game in about 30 hours. It’s pretty great! Buy it if you like desperados 3 or shadow tactics.The characters are great and all feel “overpowered” in their own right. Some things bug me however:- Only 6 or so big islands that you visit over and over again. They are quite big, but enemy placement doesn't change from mission to mission. So it gets stale after the 4th or so visit- No special premises for missions. I wish there would be a mission were you weren't allowed to kill anyone, or one where you have only one character in each corner and you need to unite them in the middle- Punishment for being detected is not harsh enough. The guards are running around for 30 seconds (on cursed difficulty) and summon some more troops that go away after 30 seconds. Why do the extra troops not stay permanently? Sometimes the easiest methods is just shoot an enemy that annoys you and just wait 30 seconds till all is normal again. - Only 5 enemy types is a bit bland. In desperados 1, there were only susceptible to some forms of distraction, or went to a higher up when they were disturbed. - No sound traps? All NPCs are just set dressing. No dogs that bark, no chickens? - The coin system. I don’t want to repeat the same missions over and over again to fulfill a special requirement and gain coins. I would like to have that revealed BEFORE I start a mission, so I can play and plan accordingly. The “start and end at specific point” coin assignments are not exciting. I’d rather have a couple good coin assignments per mission that add spice.  Some of the coin assignments feel just like busywork.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty good. Pretty similar overall to previous stealth tactics games by the same company (Shadow Tactics, Desperados) but mostly improved, with some sidegrades.The main gameplay change is that you can use any comp for majority of the missions. This gives the game more of a sandbox flavor, something which I felt really helps in a game like this; it feels a bit less like playing a straight puzzle game and instead feels like there's more room for creativity with the various abilities.The biggest issue with the sandbox approach though is that most of the game is fairly easy, since it has to be forgiving to arbitrary comps. The couple of missions where the group is fixed tend to be somewhat more difficult, which was ultimately more enjoyable. Many of the maps are nearly soloable even on harder difficulties, at least with the right character.The vigor (upgrade) system was well-implemented. Essentially an experience bar that gives you perk points to buy upgrades for each character, the amount you get is increased for bringing a character that has been benched (basically +1 for each mission they've sat out, compared to +3 you get as the base mission reward). The upgrades are nice but for most characters not that critical (though some are), so it's a great system for providing an incentive to experiment with different characters without forcing the player to rotate through all of them if they don't want to.The story and the premise is pretty fun. The characters are memorable, and with 8 crew members (plus a postgame character) it's a pretty full party, especially since most missions are limited to 3 characters. The integration of the save-reload with the plot was fairly well done, and the individual character missions were all quite enjoyable (the 'crew tales' were more hit-or-miss; the problem is that the 'any time' nature of those essentially disallow character development). The biggest issue with these sorts of games though haven't really been addressed - there isn't much in terms of development throughout the game in terms of gameplay, and the enemy variety remains the same (the latter is particularly bad here, as you run into all of the very limited enemy types quite early). This does make the gameplay get somewhat repetitive fairly quickly, as you can only solve the same type of situation so many times before it gets to be routine. The story was good enough to carry the game despite that, but it would have been nice to have seen a more nuanced development system, especially given the very elegant levelling system.
