_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Veteran of this genre here.I have played almost every game from this genre starting with desperados back in the days.First lets get one thing out of the way: I have not seen any impact from sweet baby inc that would twist the game in a certain way to ones agenda.This one has the same promise as Robin Hood: Legend of Sherwood. You have a base (ship) and plan your missions. There are also fewer maps but some are gigantic and you will complete multiple missions on them.Missions: DO NOT try to clear a whole map for every mission. The maps are designed so you plan your mission and your way on your own. You get to the objective and then leave. Many people complain about replaying a map for the 5th time but this isn't bad since you don't really play the same part of the map in every mission except if you are bad at planning. The different locations are astonishing.Characters: You will collect pearls and soul energy as a reward from missions to revive characters on the ship. This is how you get new characters and you will play a tutorial right on the ship. You can only pick 3 characters per mission on your own. To make you play different ones each one that wasn't picked will accumulate one skill energy point per mission that you get once you pick them for a mission. You can also abandon a mission and then pick again if you feel like you made a mistake.Skills: The skill energy points will fill a progress bar and once full you will get a skill point. You can then invest   1 of 8 of these into a single skill that will boost one skill of a crewmate. For some characters they are a necessity for others they are near useless.Story & Dialogue: I have not finished the story yet but lets say it is way more interesting that desperados. You are literally an undead crew on a talking ship against the inquisition. There are a lot more dialogues than in previous games but they are actually entertaining and humorous. If you don't like it simply press and hold space to skip.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: This will not be a proper review as I usually do, because I am unable to finish the game. I'm already clocking in at over 20hours and almost half of it was going through the same maps over and over. Why? Well, this is why I cannot finish the game and the reason why I'm going to downvote it. Before you read any further, I am a HUGE suporter of Mimimi. I loved Shadow Tactics and Desperados 3 is one of my favorite games of all time, check my review here if you dont take my word for it  Sadly, Shadow Gambit while it has the ingredients of what Mimimi does best, they cheaped out on what made their previous games great: level design. Instead of difficult, linear, masterfully crafted level design, now most missions are more open-ended and can be approached through multiple paths. This in turn makes the game far easier. To make matters worse, they've decided that instead of crafting multiple and unique islands/levels, you'll have to revisit the few of them the game offers. And you will not just go back once or twice! Nope. You will literally have to do some levels 4-5 times! Small spoilers but at the end, once you have your entire crew, in order to find the treasure, 4 of your companions have to do missions related to their story which involves playing the same maps you've played already 2-3 times., and each of those 4 have 2-3 missions related to their story, that means you're going to play the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game again for another 10 to 15 hours at least, when you're quite literally at the end. Whoever thought this was a good idea, sorry, you failed, and I hate you and I hope you're reading this. This is not an open world game or an rpg, it's a freaking stealth-focused puzzle game, where you have to masterfully reach your objective. 20'ish hours is ideal for such a game, maybe a little more if you do not force your players to replay the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ same maps over and over for MORE THAN HALF YOUR GAME. Look, despite my thumbs down, I'd still recommend you buy the game with the a huge caveat that it wont be as entertaining as their previous work. This is clearly a manager or some higherup's major scre.w up, for deciding the path the game went and releasing the game between Baldurs Gate 3 and Starfield. Like...it was literal financial suicide even for big games, let alone a small indie game. It hurt me when I heard Mimimi was closing, because I'm a huge stealth fan, and it hurts me even more to give this a thumbs down. C'est la vie I guess.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Yet again a Commandos-style stealth strategy game, this time with pirates. But this time Mimimi Games' approach seems to be on the less serious side - which definitely makes for a lot of fun playing around with all the available skills and devising powerful combinations. The story itself is very straightforward, but I enjoyed its focus on gameplay mechanics that usually stay "external" and essentially unexplained. Furthermore the difficulty is customizable, allowing to change individual aspects like enemies' reaction speed or impose a limit on quicksaves.On the other hand I'm missing the tension of the previous games a bit: every character is strong enough on their own to pretty much waltz through an entire mission without assistance (even on higher difficulties), significantly reducing the need to meticulously plan an approach - even once discovered you can (most of the time) just wing it and overpower enemies in a head-on confrontation.All in all, I'll still recommend the game for anyone looking for more content of this genre, as long as you don't expect it to be a huge challenge (or if you're fine with self-imposing additional limits to make missions more difficult).
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: ***Full disclosure, I made all the gameplay trailers for Shadow Gambit!***I LOVE this game! Before I got this job I hadn't played Shadow Tactics or Desperadoes III, but I've always loved stealth games and this really god its hooks into me. How deep? Well, after 400+ hours logged on this game from making the trailers, I dove back into the game to play it "for real" from the beginning. It's been great to see the game all finished and polished up. For me, playing games after working on them is RARE, especially for one I worked on for over a year total.I'm so hooked on the mechanics of queuing up the actions of each crew member and intricately timing my moves to take out the guards one at a time. They're very satisfying to use (also good for getting cool trailer shots, btw) and it's the best when I surprise myself by coming up with new solutions to each situation. I'm by no means an expert, but I feel like making the trailers was like training for my experience of playing the shipped version of the game, haha.I love trying out different combinations of crew members, and some which I initially thought I'd use less I end up loving when I'm forced to use them. I have so little time to play games because of my job, but I can't stop playing this in my downtime. There's still so much more game for me to play, nevermind the badges for each character. I feel like I'm going to do my best to explore every nook and cranny of the game before I'm done.Another joy of playing it in its final version is hearing all the music in context (I always have music off when capturing footage). The music is excellent across the board, and I had great fun collaborating with Filippo on the Release Date trailer's sea shanty (I wrote lyrics and he did everything else)Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Damn is this a hugely fun game! Loved their previous work but this is next level. Now played 20+ hours and must post a big thumbs up. High level of polish on every aspect of this game: addictive intuitive gameplay, vibrant graphics, wonderful music and sound design, dialogue and writing are both clever and superbly wrought, and the voice over talent is ridiculously good. Voice work can make or break games and this talent is outstanding, I literally look forward to each line of dialogue. Lots of thought into every aspect of gameplay. Finally, as in previous games, watching mission end map replays is so enjoyable. Highest marks from this fan, Give it a try you'll have a blast. Cant wait for Shadow Gambit 2!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Yarr! This game caught me by surprise, like a cannonball out of the blue! A tactical stealth-game with a PIRATE-THEME? That sounds as silly as, I dunno, a Viking Assassin or something. But, it makes more sense when you realize, you're not just playing as a salty crew of pirates, but a CURSED crew of GHOST-PIRATES! Or undead pirates, anyway - most of your crew still have some amount of flesh and bone to them. So of course, you operate in the shadows, sneaking around the sentinels of the Inquisition, which has some odd vendetta against unnaturally immortal outlaws...In short, the game's excellent. You control anywhere from one to eight pirates, coordinating their actions as they systematically winnow the ranks of the Inquisition and carve a path to their objective, whatever that may be. An innovative sort of 'real time with pause' approach gives you both the tension of dealing with enemies that move whether you're ready for them or not, AND the ability to carefully consider your next move without getting stressed. Better yet, there's a quicksave-system that's fully integrated into the plot - your sentient ghost-ship has time-control abilities, as it turns out! So, far from being one of those games that tries to make you feel like you're 'doing it wrong' if you want to go back and fix your mistakes because 'actions are supposed to have consequences!' or whatever, the whole game is DESIGNED around trial-and-error. You try something, get gunned down by an Inquisition hit-squad, then jump back to the moment before to try something different while your crew sarcastically go "What, back here AGAIN? I didn't like it much the first time!" or similar rejoinders.Actually, the characters you use just have a ton of personality in general! Each of them is highly distinct, weird and charming in their own way - and through various conversations, side-quests and onboard mini-adventures, you get to know them quite well, from the sophisticated and over-the-top arrogant Quartermaster, past the towering, poetry-loving Cannoness, to the bluntly Scottish carpenter and his pet undead fish, Sir Reginald. They're all DRIPPING with personality, and as a noted philosopher once said, personality goes a long way...So, I invite you to give it a try! Once you get into the swing of it, you'll find yourself wondering where the hours went - why, time will seem to just slip right away from you the moment you look the other way...
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely top-notch!  I loved Shadow Tactics and Desperados 3 (those are how I first discovered this "stealth tactical real time strategy with pause" genre or whatever your call it), and this builds on top of those games with tons of creative new abilities for your characters.  Being able to create cover wherever needed, or launch up onto higher terrain, or just pop up from underground to ambush the enemy never gets old.  These games have have always used quicksave/quickload as a core part of their gameplay design, and Shadow Gambit has now found a super clever way to work that into the story itself.  They have also added a few nice nuances like a ability upgrades for your characters, and some 'downtime' story telling between missions that fills in some backstory.In terms of critiques, some of those awesome abilities they introduced are perhaps a bit  awesome - it's easy to always use the same couple characters who have your favorite abilities, especially once upgraded.  The fact that you can visit the same islands multiple times is cool but I feel like this may have restricted level design in order to allow for any combination of characters to always have a way to pass through (thereby making things too easy if you find a certain group of OP characters to use).  Instead, I think it would've been more interesting to have additional missions that were specifically tailored towards the strengths/weaknesses of different combinations of characters.  Other minor nitpicks include the fact that I felt that some of the crew stories dragged on a bit too long, and I wish the ability upgrades were a bit more fleshed out.All in all, this is a fantastic game.  Even if you've never tried stealth or strategy games before, if you set aside just one hour on some random weeknight to try this out, you will become hooked.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Masterpiece!You shouldn't miss this game, truly... 10/10I feel like they only to aimed to entertain and it's such a flattering experience for me to be part of it.Hats off to the developers and producers!-If you really like stealth games, this could be one of the best experience for you.-Creating your own strategy will give you one of a kind satisfaction.-You don't have to like pirate-like themes to enjoy this game because their only aim to give you that stealth experience and free will to conduct your own rules: kill only or knock out etc.P.S: Try harder difficulties if you really want to feel those sweaty moments even if it's your first time.

_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Mimimi have been a consistently good developer of stealth tactics games, and Shadow Gambit is another great entry into the genre. You play as a crew of cursed undead pirates battling against the leader of a dogmatic religious organisation, slowly reviving the playable characters as you go in any order you like and getting to know them through personal missions and small playable sections called Crew Tales on your ship between missions.It's a game bursting with great mechanics, tactical considerations and a compelling story.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: The story, gameplay, characters, puzzles, and even Von Presswald were nice. I especially liked the voice acting. Sure, some parts of the story could've been better if we compare it to Mimimi's older titles, but I feel like I got my money's worth.My only real complaint is that Cursed difficulty wasn't cursed enough for me.. I guess this is what OSRS does to you.Strongly recommended, 11/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: This is at least the third game from this developer in similar real-time stealth RPG genre...if that's it's own genre. They've all been good, and fairly unique. It's well worth the price, though there is a demo if you aren't sure that you'll enjoy it.The stealth aspect isn't too difficult, though you can ramp it up, and presents unique puzzles. Overall, it's not something I'll play all that often, but I have bought all their past games because they're all good, polished, and are great to play through. There is little replayability (for me), but that doesn't really matter given it's inexpensive. It's like $1-2/hr for entertainment at full price, which is great value.If you're not sure, just try the demo. If you're still on the fence, buy it as you'll probably end up enjoying it. Great dev. Doesn't cut corners of rehash sequels.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the games Desperados 3 and/or Shadow Tactics or generally these types of games, then you will like this one too. _childDocuments_.review: A good tactical game, which, due to the wide variety of characters and the combination of abilities, does not have time to get bored during the passage.I advise you not to try to complete the game 100% for now because of the large number of bugs that make it impossible. _childDocuments_.review: An impressive continuation of Mimimi's oeuvre. One word : replayability. Instead of a linear set of levels, you return to one of several maps that each have multiple exit and entry spots. You can affect the difficulty of missions simply by choosing the right entry. Additionally, a huge cast of characters (including one secret character) increases the different combinations of skills and abilities further.I'm looking forward to any DLC for this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best entry point into the genre for the Mimimi stealth titles. While Desperados 3 and Shogun have their advantages, the flexibility of Gambit's level design encourages you to try different character combinations and strategies, as opposed to being dealt a setup and finding the pre-planned solutions.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: It will be a while until we get another stealth game that is as creative and polished as Mimimi's swansong. Put off by the games' prior settings/tones and difficulties? Returning player to the genre/dev's catalog? There's never been a better time to pick the game up. This can't be stated enough but the island centric gameplay with a chance at "pre planning" your entrance, exit and picking your 3 member party remains UNMATCHED in terms of gameplay and self imposed challenges(we can debate on how the story is delivered, the story and banter is cool however). A squad full of agile swimmers that are amazing up close with micro intensive utility or a less mobile squad with a longer range that needs more planning to get from A to B? The choice is yours. This also works mostly because of how whimsical everyone's kit is, and it's quite impressive that 8 crew "main" crew members and 2 new additions are all fresh. Sure there are classic abilities we've come to expect like audio lure/distractions and visual blinds, but fully playing into unrealistic magic is just great, both at full map clears or ghost runs. It's the ultimate isometric stealth strategy sandbox.If you liked the Guns of Savo Island/River Kwai levels from Commandos 2 and the town structures from Castle Colditz/Robin Hood/Shadow Tactics but with a high gothic taste, a mix of cutesy eldritch nonsense and an alt history colonial era undead pirate Carribean setting then yes, do go and play it. Expect classic objectives like infiltration, sabotage and espionage, but also wacky things like treasure hunts and "collectathons"/pseudo escorts/rescue/escape scenarios.This whole gameplay design was "teased" in 2 levels in Aiko's Choice and it simply works so well. We're still waiting on The Stone of Madness, Commandos Origins, Stargate and many more indie efforts, but the bad after taste of War Mongrels has gone away with this pallete cleanser. Still waiting on a game that does more dedicated indoors and inventory management a la C2 because Partisans 1941 and Gone Rogue lack the polish.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Certainly the most fun of their games yet. the variety with the characters is excellent, but may trivialize the early missions. You cannot pick the wrong crew mates in the beginning, its that easy. However, the maximum difficulty will fix that right up for you, punishing mistakes instantly. However, if you sharpen your reaction speed and have an accurate set of fingers, you may still find the game challenging without being unfair, at said hardest difficulty.Regardless, this game is quite fun and a must have for RTT fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: With care and passion a thank you letter to Mimimi studio for everything they gave us. Youre the treasure I found not long ago. You always be the shining beacon for all of us that loves and appreciates tactical strategy stealth games. There will be no other like you because youre the one. The one that showed us what quality of your games are and that magic will stay forever with us. Never say never. I don’t say goodbye to you because I know we will meet again. Like lightning in the bottle you imagine this is only possible one time. Well with Mimimi its possible every time they release a new game. Shadow Gambit is no exception. Brilliant, charming, classical and every best way you can imagine. A pirates life is no easy way aroung but with this crew everything is possible even unpossible things. Meet Afia Manicato in a thrilling journey to hunt for a treasure. But what you find will be much more valuable things than treasures itself.Stealth strategy game at its finest. From every island you go into to the deck of your Red Marley. The world is crafted in beauty. Every mission and every scenario is filled with brilliancy. Big moments and small moments filled with the smallest details. Controlling every crew member is different and unique. Every one of them brings life to the game. There are many options for newcomers and even for hardcore fans like yourself. Personally for me the game is same quality as Shadow Tactics and Desperados 3. One of the best experiences you will have in every aspect of this game genre. I would recommend this for everyone who loves pirate theme games. <3

_childDocuments_.review: We're the folk of the sea, we put rum in our teaWe got grog in our hands, and our feet in the sandsThat's what we do, that's why we liveThey were a mighty crew, until they ran aground... the ship!!I enjoyed being a stealthy cursed pirate, unlocking Jester made me quite irateI look forward to the DLC, I wish the devs luck wherever they be
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game, especially if you liked Shadow Tactics and Desperados 3. It is clear what Mimimi were aiming for and I think they achieved it. Sad to see them go.Pros:+ Great gameplay and art style.+ Excellent design of characters and abilities - with some exceptional voice acting.+ Good main story and setting.+ Games runs well.Cons:- Characters' personal story-lines are not as emotionally engaging as the previous Mimimi games. However, this is understandable given the large number of characters here.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome stealth strategy from Mimimi as always. Unlike any previous game in this genre, this one doesn't go with tight setting, i.e. preset team composition and guard placement that basically requires a very narrow solution method. This one is more sandbox. You can take pretty much any one of your crewmates into a mission. Some say that it makes the game too easy. I don't share this sentiment. Although there are plenty of solutions to any situation, it's not too easy to be boring. It also offers a great replayability, as changing your crewmates changes the way you approach the mission. Also, if you are a hardcore gamer, there's a plenty of badges that are "tight" and will put your skills to a test.It's sad that for Mimimi, it is their last game. They basically revived the stealth strategy genre and brought new and refreshing ideas into it (they even created this new and imho very fitting name for it). Luckily, I have recently noticed other similar high quality games (such as War Mongrels), so hopefully, the genre will live on.Some great things that deserve appreciation:- great "sniper" character - just one "bullet" which can be picked up and used again,- treasure hunter character - not so great by himself, but totally awesome in combination with others,- generally awesome abilities to rapidly change positions of your crewmates, haven't seen it anywhere else before, great,- save/load mechanics are part of a game's story, kind of emphasizing, that they have always been the stealth strategist's greatest power,- awesome idea with post-game unlockable character, which can transform to any other one, total beast.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to love this game, like I love commandos, Desperados: wanted dead or alive, Desperados 3 and Shadow Tactics.But... it's just not as good, It's taken me months to progress as I get bored with revisiting the same locations & the easy gameplay. I'm just occasional grazing the game.I've found progress too easy, the enemies are easy to pick of one by one usually with just one character, you can even run around rather than creep through the level - try doing that in desperados or shadow tactics!  It's nothing like picking your way through the intricate view cones of Desperados 3 or Shadow Tactics..... Use range weapon, shoot, run and hide in cover, sit out the alert response, rinse and repeat....On a personal note the graphical style does not suit my tastes, not gritty and real enough, it's too cartoony and for me spoils the immersion.It's not a classic, perhaps what it is is a  good gamey introduction into the more demanding games of this genre.I've played in on the steam deck and it runs very well on the deck
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Learned of Mimimi studio right after they shut down their team, sad to see that Shadow Gambit's their final swan song, got excited thinking that they would release more similar games in the future, oh well. Will finish the 2 other stealth game they have as well! Shadow Gambit's really fun though, trying to go for 100% achievement and it doesn't feel like a chore because of how fun their gameplay mechanic is! Def a buy if you love stealth or strategy games! Here's hoping Mimimi studios will come back in the near future.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Just as great as Shadow Tactics and Desperados if not better because of the clever story integration of the quicksave-load mechanic. Mimimi games have outdone themselves with the story. Without spoiling it, the  quicksave-load is not just a feature here, but its actually woven into the story which was quite interesting and a lot of fun. You are more versatile than ever, since its up to you which characters are available to you and who you take on missions. If you liked any other Mimimi title you'll love this. Even if Pirates is not your thing, this will draw you in!Recommended without reservations!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: Shadow Gambit is what happens when a studio takes every lesson from their previous games and perfects its genre. If you've never played a real-time stealth tactics game, the allure here is that the stealth is a highly rewarding set of tension-filled puzzles that can be approached in open and creative ways. You get to mastermind kills, distractions, and infiltrations with a mix of planning and improvisation that is unique to Mimimi Games. In short, this game and genre makes you feel clever about every 3 minutes. Shadow Gambit removes the frustrating friction of stealth games without eliminating all the stakes and consequences that provide challenge and tension. This game has an impeccably clear ruleset. Outcomes to your actions are predictable, meaning you can plan and risk strategically. The rules for hiding, the ranges of sight cones, the timing of patrols all become incredibly easy to internalize over time. This leads to breaking up the methodical planning with quick intuitive play. Abilities and mechanics offer many self-expressive approaches and solutions to the game's varied encounters. And the large cast of characters offer seemingly endless combinitorial synergies. This is such a wonderfully fluid and snappy stealth action game.But what elevates Shadow Gambit is its inspired cohesion of design and theme. Every design and aesthetic decision comes off as deeply considered, resulting in a game that is immediately a joy to play. Quick saves are encouraged and called "memories." Character abilities and limitations perfectly suit personalities and the world. The story even has twists that put twists on the mechanics. And all of this woven together in package full of high levels of production value, great art direction, colorful dialogue, and fantastic voice acting. So, aye, this is a game worth your doubloons.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow Gambit: The Cursed Crew

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this up when it was on sale, and it's one of the best blind game purchases I've made in years.  It's insanely engaging, and the adjustable challenge levels are nicely done.  This is a game that makes you step back and think about what your next move will be, and you'll enjoy the hell out it for making you think.  It's really rare that a game pleasantly surprises me this quickly out of the gate.  Will (try to remember to) post an update upon completion.  If you're on the fence, and aren't entirely sure about "stealthy" type games like me, just buy it.  It's a blast!

name: A Musical Story
detailed_description: Join Us On Discord About the Game GAME LENGTH: A Musical Story is a tightly designed experience. A single play-through will take most players around 2-3 hours. Achieving a perfect star rating on all chapters will increase the play time to around 4-6 hours. A Musical Story is a rhythm game set against a 70s backdrop. Explore the memories of Gabriel, a young man trying to come to terms with his situation through the connections to his musical memory. Each correctly played melody opens a new chapter into Gabriel’s past, bringing him closer to the truth. Key Features Rekindle Gabriel's memories with rhythmic button presses in time with the music Storytelling without words – discover Gabriel’s journey through music and visuals alone Gabriel's story comes to life through a beautifully crafted art style A unique original soundtrack featuring 26 songs Play every song perfectly to unlock a hidden chapter A Musical Story is the debut game from independent French developer, Glee-Cheese Studio. They are: Charles Bardin (Game Design + Music), Maxime Constantinian (Programmer), Valentin Ducloux (Music + Integration), Alexandre Rey (Artistic Direction).

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: "Rythm game" is a partial misnomer for most "rhythm games", but A Musical Story is truly deserving of the title.It's an interactive 70s psych concept album with beautiful art, and that's enough for me.I think rhythm games are an underexplored genre -- I blame this largely on Guitar Hero's introduction and then popularization of many genre conventions that newer titles can't seem to shake.Guitar hero (and many others) gamify music by asking you to hit the correct inputs as they pass under a line (or using some other visual indicator). However, this often emphasizes input complexity rather than any sense of actual rhythm. You could have no grasp of the beat at all, and the visual indicators would still carry you through the experience.Put another way: guitar hero and rock band are far more interested in your fret hand than your pick hand.This is interesting, and maybe a little sad, because we call these "rhythm games", yet rhythm is the aspect of music they emphasize least.There are rhythm games that buck this trend - "Rhythm Heaven" and "Osu!" come to mind immediately. Yet these are really exceptions to the rule.Rhytmn games also tend to be random assemblages of music rather than cohesive albums. This is a little disappointing for multiple reasons. For one, something like a leitmotif in a rhythm game is far more impactful than in a non-interactive medium, because you get a direct mechanical reward for identifying the repeated phrase. For two, albums are cool, and tying the arc of an album to a mechanical arc is doubly cool.There are, again, exceptions here: the 2019 game "Sayonara Wild Hearts" advertises itself firstly as a Pop Album and secondly as a video game; Guitar Hero 6's story mode includes a full playthrough of 2112; Ape Out's integration of gameplay and soundtrack along with the album motif is very cool.All of this is to say: if you, like me, have ever thought "I wish there was a stripped-back rhythmn game that challenged me to play interesting and unconvential rhythmns a la Rhythmn Heaven, while playing through a bespoke album with gorgeous visuals a la Sayonara Wild Hearts", then you should play a Musical Story. The story is also pretty alright, I suppose.You could argue that not loving the story is a pretty sever condemnation for a game whose title is literally "A Musical Story", but I don't think it's a huge deal. I can't think of a concept album that's revered for it's narrative twists and turns, but folks love them anyway.I'm not trying to say that A Musical Story is the best rhythm game ever, or even that it's a "Great" game.But it's at least very good, and it's not quite like anything else I've played. That's all I really want from a game anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, blame the Steam Rhythm Fest for this :P And as an upfront disclaimer, this review again is meant to be settled in a rather neutral region. It’s not like the game is bad, no no, so please don’t get me wrong. Actually I absolutely love the original music (great 70s tracks), the congenial rhythms and all the work that definitely flowed into the creative cutscenes. But a lot of things still were off in my opinion, so please let me elaborate my personal problems in this special case.Urgh, yet where do I start. First of all, A Musical Story definitely has the potential to bring people closer to “music”, like I already said, the rhythms and all the different vibes really show what music can achieve, provoke and do to your mind, no kidding. But the problem here is, the way they handle the rhythm aspect gameplay-wise, oh boy, it’s rather counter-productive to that initial goal. Honestly, the game definitely gets too hard too fast. Like, half of the achievements revolve around completing levels at the first try (this obviously is even needed for another alternate ending), but this actually is super tedious and frustrating. We’re talking about (in later levels) 7-10 rounds with extremely variable rhythms and unintuitive controls, in which you also have to memorize the (initially) hard to grasp music and rhythms. And even then, one button pressed “too early” would kill this try. But to make things even harder, at every new retry you have to ALWAYS watch all of the cutscenes and intros, and add to this that at every restart your starting point is always cryptic. There is no “1,2,3 ....”, instead you’re thrown into a “flowing start” and always have to anticipate when you’re supposed to continue after the introductory round. Sorry, it’s a bit hard to explain, but maybe you get the drift.Long story short, just for a subsumption, I’m actually used to progressive metal with loads of breaks/changes or minimalistic electro music, but it still was very hard for me to achieve or anticipate those hard goals in the first try with those extremely narrow reaction corridors (for my wife it was even more frustrating in later circles). And just think about it, why should I learn super complicated tracks from a random/unknown game when instead I could rather spend my time in a better way, like making music yourself, or playing something else that empowers you better. Anyway, still a thumbs up, if only for the great music and the consistent cutscenes. Maybe check out the demo, and if you like it, give it a try on sale, and play it mainly for the experience (and by the way, you could also cheat those super hard achievements with some workaround to see the alternate end, but that’s another story not meant to be told here).

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the narrative story to this game, plus the musical soundtrack. It definitely has a 70's psychedelic-rock, Woodstock, instrumental vibe to the whole experience. I assume that Jimi Hendrix was a huge influence on this game. Keep in mind, the narrative story is told through the music and handcrafted art-style & animations. There is no narrative text (only chapter labels) and there are no voice overs (except briefly at the end). Because of this, the story is rather simplistic, in fact, there is a whole chapter devoted to refueling the van and and another to having a flat tire. Despite this, I enjoyed the narrative experience, mostly because of the trippy visuals & the chill music that really carried the vibe of the story.Unfortunately, the gameplay loop was a rather discordant experience. It starts out chill enough & the controls are simple. You basically hit either left or right or both, and then just hit the note and hold when needed. I did notice that there was indeed a visual lag, especially when doing rather fast notes between input and when the game would register the note. I had to memorize the tune and play the tune by ear to get the timing right during these sections. I just found this core gameplay loop to get more frustrating as the game went along. They just added more notes and upped the tempo, forcing  you to focus on timing each note correctly, rather than enjoying the audio / visual delight as it happened.I grew to dislike the gameplay loop. However, I enjoyed the other parts of the game enough to trudge along until the end. There's no way I'm replaying the game though to get perfect on each chapter to unlock the secret chapter. That's a shame, because I would really enjoy seeing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting little rhythm game that tells a story.  The story isn't overly spectacular, but music is pretty cool, even though it feels like it never gets to the good parts of each song and instead always feels like you're building up to something that never comes.I have some major complaints with the game however.  There's no indication of where you are in the current part of the song, would like to have something you follow or even bars to indicate where the notes are relative to the beginning of the bar.  It's also sometimes pretty difficult to tell when the line restarts, I had to tap my foot sometimes with the beat and go along with that.   Sometimes the first note I feel should actually be before the bar starts too, like at the end of the last line instead, it doesn't feel very consistent.  Funny enough the last couple levels are the easiest in the game because they change the mechanic for one, and the others are just less complicated beats that follow proper musical flow.------------------------------Control Scheme I Used:Used Game mostly, but also tried with keyboard.the game is only 2 buttons, either L/R or D-Pad/Buttons for Gamepad, or Left/Right on Keyboard.------------------------------Worth the current price (CDN$ 17.49)?  That's fairly cheap, but I'd still wait for a sale on this one.What I actually paid:  $4.18------------------------------Completionist Review:DLC Achievements:  No DLC.Rating:  Nothing special, you have to perfect every level.Can be completed in one run:  Yeah you could.Chapter Select: There is chapter selection, and it tells you which levels need to be perfected.Did I need/use a guide?  No, don't think one exists and it wouldn't help anyways.This took a bit of time but wasn't too bad.  Some levels I had to replay many times though because the timing felt wrong on them, or it was super hard to tell where the beginning was, etc.  Sometimes if I had to hold down a note it randomly let go, but that might have just been me or my controller acting up. _childDocuments_.review: You know how in Dark Souls, if you die at the boss, you have to go back several minutes and fight the same enemies over and over to get to the boss for another attempt? This game's idea of "perfect play" (which gives you in-game stars and achievements for playing the level perfectly) is worse than that. You can spend minutes getting every single sub-section on a level right on the first try, but if you accidentally press the last note of the last sub-section a tad too early (which is all too easy with the lack of rhythmic cues in some of them), you have to redo the ENTIRE several minute's worth again (and perfectly again, no less!) just to get another chance at getting that last bit perfect. If you fail again... you get the picture. You can't even skip the story cutscenes in-between those subsections to speed up the process; you're forced to watch the (highly boring) stuff again.Pair to that an extremely long-winded story that spends an entire chapter, through endless little cutscenes, telling a tiny bit of the story that could be told in a single comic-book page... and I was disappointed. I refunded the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A Musical Story is a rhythm game about a jam band who decides to travel to play at a musical festival...but it's also about addiction, love, friendship, and the true value of music. The story itself is a rollercoaster that manages to find a sweet spot between emotional and intimate. The music to score the adventure is usually excellent, with inspiration from 60s/70s prog rock and jam bands and other icons such as Jimi Hendrix. The soundtrack is really why you take this journey, but the game sometimes doesn't know how to handle its own music. The gameplay comes in the form of a ring, where you must mimic an instrument's notes/beats by repeating the line back. Typically, it's about a measure or two of music at a time, which can range from slow, meditative pieces to faster rock anthems. The game's primary issue comes from its ability to time out to the player when to press the notes. There is no visual guide as to where on the ring you are, and the spacing can not only change between songs, but even within a level. This combined with several of the 24 chapters being very ambient, slow pieces with no backbeat to anchor to leads to a frustrating few sequences that result in many failed attempts to find the obtuse beat. There are no accessibility options that truly help with this either, like a metronome which would play out a steady beat to assist. I am a musician and have been playing instruments for over a decade and I struggled to understand some levels due to the sheer chaos. On top of all of that, you must do a perfect run of every individual level if you would like to see the true ending, which requires a lot of patience and practice. All of this said, I really liked A Musical Story. Its art is astoundingly gorgeous and with no dialogue, the characters still tell an engaging tale of music and romance and heartbreak. I don't know if I'd recommend this to anyone who doesn't play music. There are other titles (Rhythm Heaven) that appeal more to non-musicians that still have a great set of songs. But, if you feel like casually playing through this game, you'll probably have a good time. If you're going for completion, expect a difficult handful of chapters to bump up your playtime by double.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: Life has a sort of rhythm to it.  You feel the ebb and flow throughout days, weeks, and months.  Small tasks that get you bounce your feet all the way to monumental occasions that demand an orchestral finale in your mind.  I’m sure right now you’re either listening to something or you’ve had a tune in your head for a little bit while perusing the internet.  It’s cool.  Me too.  Music can envelope emotions wrapped tightly to be ripped open with the right chord or note.  It can bring like-minded people together with similar tastes, or divide in favor of what they enjoy.  For some it’s a side-dish to a well balanced meal of lunch, for others: it’s every last crumb on the dinner table.For Gabriel, the guitar was his solstice in a life of controlled monotony, applying stickers to bean cans in a factory for longer than your granddad’s entire vinyl collection.  But constructed practices with the ever present jam session brought Gabriel and his friends to small gigs around town, laying down progressions and rhythms that spoke louder than words ever could.  When a multi-day festival sets its stakes in the heart of Pinewood, the band pull together a beat-up van held up by their hopes and dreams and set foot on a journey of friendship and heartbreak.The title screen places Gabriel tattered in bandages lay dormant on a hospital bed with no explanation.  With music traveling everywhere with Gabriel, the musical backdrop for our story is built up by the player.  Using the left and right arrow keys (or triggers on your favorite controller), you’ll construct Gabriel’s time with his band starting with a silky bassline, eloquent drum tempo, or a soulful acoustic lick.  These pieces mesh together to create one of the best soundtracks so far this year.  Overflowing with emotion, scenes unite guitars, synths, keytars, even just the rhythmic tapping of two drumsticks to strike a chord through every minute of A Musical Story’s 3 hour runtime.  I got chills on multiple occasions just feeling the passion provided through each strum or key played and I was instantly hooked.Gameplay is laid out in a form similar to musical Simon.  Notes are displayed on a curved track and once shown must be played perfectly to continue forward.  Once each layer of the song is completed the scene blooms to show a moment in time for Gabriel during his trip to Pinewood: traveling the road, stopping at cheap motels for a smoke and drink, or bringing the instruments out for an impromptu jam in the forest.  These memories are pieced with beautifully paletted visuals, each scene looks like a oft-remembered dream: muted in intricate details but popping with color and personality, that when combined with the gorgeously crafted soundtrack wastes no time pulling you into this world and not letting go until the credits roll.Gabriel’s story also pieces together the struggles of a man filling the holes in his life with addictive tendencies.  Anytime not at work building his craft as a musician, there is booze at hand and drugs close by him: a nasty byproduct of the 1970s musical revolution.  These scenes throughout the game are terrifyingly brilliant seeing the shadows of Gabriel’s past refusing to let go of the dreams of a better future, with a wild crescendo near the back of the game.But while these scenes combined with the soundtrack are as gripping as they are fantastically orchestrated, the freedom given to some of the 16 beat lines also makes the back half of A Musical Story a little too messy to flow comfortably through.  The latter half sludges the tempo to a crawl, letting menacing synths bury the need of a metronomic guideline and letting the futile plinking of guitar strings lead the player through a quicksand-like turn of events for Gabriel.  But this also makes the jazz-like structure of the instrumental tracks very hard to play correctly, causing me to miss notes constantly on the back half and eventually turning on the auto-assist and abandoning A Musical Story’s achievements given for playing a chapter perfectly through.  That one XKCD comic came into mind a lot and I realized if the added bonus of being perfect wasn’t embedded into my mind from the start, this story would’ve progressed so much smoother with less restarts and expletives muttered under my breath.But once you remove that tracker from your radar and just let yourself become immersed within the sultry tones of a band facing the tough challenges of a dream forged by miles of asphalt, you’ll see what a hidden gem A Musical Story really is.  Easily providing a Soundtrack of the Year bid behind enough interactivity to keep you engaged, this is absolutely worth an afternoon to sit down, tune your instrument just right, and follow the notes of a path well worn to a dream into the great wide open.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: The art, the music, and the story are excellent. The gameplay mechanic is a mix of a "memory game" and a rhythm game, and can get very hard especially midway in the story when the rhythms get very complex and sometimes practically just random effects without any underlying rhythm. That by itself wouldn't be a huge issue, except the devs also decided to do this very cruel design choice: "Play every song perfectly to unlock a hidden chapter". This means perfecting everything on first try, with assist off. Perhaps 1% of all players can do this. I certainly can't even with a lot of previous rhythm game experience, so I will most likely see this "hidden chapter" on Youtube later. Also, once you realize you will never be able to do that unlock without spending more hours and patience than most people can afford to, you'll be tempted to just refund the game after the main story, since it can be finished easily under two hours. Which makes the design choice even more odd. But that said, IMHO it's worth the asking price for the art, music and story alone.

_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: In some cultures playing rhythms and polyrhythms represents the hardships of life as well as the fact life will always go on. This game plays with this concept in a way no other does. The story is somewhat predictable but is charming, effective and still has its surprises. The real star is the way the events in the story play out in musical form. It's much more than an emotional piano riff when things get sad. The rhythms that are asked of you in the moment really force you to stop, listen and think about the music and rhythm which in turn helps you connect to the characters in a way no other game does in my experience. It truly connects when you start being able to predict the next scene based on the rhytm you just played, or when you notice surprising chords and and progressions followed up by some story revelation or plot-twist when you finally master its rhythm. Its really a game like no other.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've played lately, and a big surprise.In short, this is a very different take on a rhythm game, with great emphasis (and success!) on narrative. It's like a playable concept album, with very tasteful layering of tracks, and the music perfectly fits and changes with the mood of the scenes.It also presents a uniquely challenging use of rhythm - not as a deviously fast sequence of inputs, but as an interplay of different rhythms and long silences that requires you to figure out the underlying rhythms and keep them all going in your head.I give it a whole-hearted recommendation for doing something different and . It is also a fertile template for more rhythms games and can be taken in slightly different directions.That said, the game has some problems. They are not serious for a casual player who only wants to get through the game once, with mistakes. These problems become a lot more serious if you want to unlock the "real ending", which requires you to play every song perfectly - here, the game's flaws start to show, and the high difficulty can make for a frustrating experience. That said, I also found it rewarding, and is where the meaningful gameplay is to be found.The game works as a "call and response" loop: you hear the short section being played, along with the on-screen cues, and then it repeats as you play it yourself. This is simple but effective. In early levels, you get an extra repetition (sound only, no visual cues), to get you into the groove.The patterns aren't very fast. This is not a japanese style rhythm game, or Through the Fire and the Flames in Guitar Hero!If you miss one of the inputs, the same track keeps looping, until you get them all.There is initially no visual indicator of where the track is (aside from the success/failure of the notes), but one will appear, intermittently, the more times you fail the sequence (and you can permanently enable/disable it in the options).This is one of the game's biggest faults, honestly, which I'll address later.Each level is a series of these loops, usually relying on the same underlying pulse, but playing different patterns and iterations. In the harder later levels, these are very different from each other (sometimes too different), which can make it quite difficult to get through the level in a single go (because it becomes a lot harder to memorize and prepare in advance for what is to come).The game is also not very precise with its input - in fact, some of the faster levels have a huge tolerance, so that your sense of rhythm can be very off and still "succeed". This, in a way, alleviates the need for input delay control and so on, but it also means the game is not as snappy as most other rhythm games (for example, there is no distinction between normal, good and perfect hits, which is something that typically makes rhythm games a lot more satisfying!).For a normal playthrough, in which you aren't trying to perfect a level, all of this is fine. If you miss a note, the track will just play again, but each one lasts for 2 bars, a few seconds, no big loss.The problem is very different when you're trying to perfect levels, because, in the second half, they can take longer than 5 minutes - and a single mistake requires you to restart the whole level.This is compounded by the nature of the difficulty - (1) poly-rhythms, (2) unclear pulses and (3) long notes. By which I mean, (1) you are hearing one rhythm in the background and playing another (sometimes playing both for different instruments), or (2) perhaps it isn't even clear what the underlying rhythm should be, because the track is silent, or sparse, or (3) there are long periods of silence between notes, and they start in some weird off beat that is difficult to keep track of.I have two things to add about this: So yeah. Perfecting every level was sometimes a very frustrating experience. When every rhythm is slightly weird, paired with long levels (5+ min) and very different sections from one another, it becomes very easy to make a small mistake, requiring a full restart. Several levels took me close to 1 hour to perfect.Maybe I suck, but the game could have done a better job at this. Even allowing some margin of error by letting you "recover" from a miss by a streak of good notes, for example (of course, better input would be required).The other big problem I have with the game, and one that could have helped with difficulty, is the lack of feedback.I like the idea of not showing you where in the measure you are. That makes things very easy, and stops being about the music - it becomes about following a little dot on the screen and pressing the button when it reaches a note. The current implementation forces you to listen, feel and remember the music. It's a very good attempt!But there are problems: Given that merely tracking a dot on the screen is a terrible solution, what could be done?Well, one idea, for me, would be to add some pulsing visuals in the background, playing the underlying rhythms. Players aren't supposed to be fully fledged musicians keep track of the multiple rhythms!Another would be to divide the circle on the screen into measures, to act as a better guide to the player, a visual pulse.These could be customized in the options, of course.And, of course, I'd strive for better input detection (dealing with all the annoyances of input delay, etc. that other rhythm games already deal with). This would allow you to give better feedback on perfect vs. good notes, for example (particles, sound, whatever), and also to slightly modified the background music to play the notes when you hit the buttons, rather than as mere playback. Mostly because then the player can actually hear when they are offbeat and self-correct.This idea of self-correction (or lack there of) is one of my biggest disappointments with the game. It's not a killer, but it's a weird miss for a game that takes musicality so seriously.It's been a while since I bothered to write a long and more or less organized review like this. I hope this is taken as a token of love!A Musical Story is a very unique approach to rhythm games, and it deserves a lot more attention than it got.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful rhythm game with a story.  You probably should be using a headphone with a jack if you want to play with headphones, as the game suggests.You play through segments of each track to unlock the story. As others have noted, the themes form a continuity throughout the sequences.  However, know that you will be missing a lot since the tracks reflect the events, characters and emotions of the story. Game-play is not hard, and if you continuously fail a segment of the song, an additional visual cue appears to help you out. You can finish the game in a few hours with this mode. However, for perfect completion challenge you have to turn the assist mode off.The only downside I can think of is that a bonus chapter is locked behind perfect completion of 24 chapters, each composed of several segments. It is not impossible to achieve, and the game is enjoyable and the soundtrack captivating, but it is sort of a grind and requires patience. You can find a video of the bonus chapter (and in fact the whole game) on youtube, but if you like the visuals and the music do not spoil the fun for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: graphics, ideas, music are all well designed, a great enjoyment indeed.however the game gets annoying halfways towards the ending. It was not until you pass all chapters that the game told players to perfectly finish every chapter to get to the music festival ending. The process to perfectly pass a chapter is sometimes difficult and boringly long as you have to follow the rhythm perfectly right after listening it for only 2 times. You also have to continuously follow about 4 different rhythms, without missing one single note. At the same time, you cannot skip any CGs and openings, once you failed a note you have to restart the whole chapter again, and that was a big waste of time.I really did adore the game at first but got frustrated when trying to perfectly clear all chapters and get to the PINEWOOD ending.

Art, story, and music fit together perfectly.Be sure to take the advertised game length into consideration when deciding to buy this at full price or wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are expecting this to be a rhythm game then you might be disappointed. It is 90% about the story and artstyle. It seems 10% of developing time was spent on the actual gameplay. There's no visual cues for the beats even when there's no other instruments to play off from. At several sections you're solo with your guitar, no beat and trying to guess the bpm. It's a pretty game but that's it.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: I suck at rhythm based games. Signal sent from my brain has a 60% delayed response chance to reach my finger and I always felt jealous towards people who are good at them. Just last friday on my commute I saw some soyjack looking guy playing Hatsune Miku Project Manhattan or whatever on his fancy foldable smartphone. I literally couldn't see his fingers moving. I was in awe. He eventually managed to perfect a track while balancing himself on a rough subway ride with nothing to support him but his thin legs. That day, I witnessed what we humans are capable of as a species if we tried. I shed two tears, one to recognize his effort, because I knew such a feat is only achievable via enduring hardships of the kind that's unthinkable for us common people; And another out of shame, because deep down, I knew I would never reach his greatness no matter what I achieve in the future.But even for a hopeless loser like me, this game felt fairly easy with its adaptive difficulty system, very generous timeframe for playing notes and sequences divided for every instrument that is played in the track. In the last few levels, they try to artificially ramp up the difficulty with the longer length and unnatural notes shoved inbetween but even with them I felt that this game was way easier than the rest of rhythm focused games I've played in the past.The story can be summarized with the sentence 'Camping trip gone wrong gone sexual' and with its charming handdrawn visuals and music setting stage properly it's hard to not be engaged in a story it's trying to tell, and it also helps to reinforce the part of the game that would've been otherwise boring. Game's worthy of its name. Definitely give a playthrough if you have it sitting in your library. Recommended price <4$.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a real, real shame. The art is beautiful, the music absolutely stellar, and the storytelling is wonderful and creative. Unfortunately, the gameplay itself fails it atrociously. The simple mobile rhythm game set up works fine for early, simple tunes and charts, but it becomes a nightmare once it starts introducing more complex, syncopated rhythms on top of rubato tempos and at times completely inaudible beat. With no markings to track beat and/or measure, some songs become an exercise in frustration and simply memorizing the rhythms over repeated plays. And you WILL repeat them, as you MUST perfect a chapter in order to unlock the final ending, and any mistakes whatsoever will force you to start the entire sometimes 5+ minute chapter over from the *very beginning*, making trying to fight through the previous frustrations that much more infuriating.I find myself feeling not like I'm failing at the challenges the game is offering but that the game is failing to provide me the tools required to succeed. Tell me "git gud" if you must, but for an indie game seemingly focused on providing an artful, narrative experience, I shouldn't be having to tap into my inner FromSoft player to keep from throwing my keyboard across the room trying to play it.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a gem of its kind. Telling a story without words, and succeeding at it.The music is great, the visuals appealing, the story touching. Emotions are felt.The gameplay is not fantastic though, but get the job done. Sometimes it feels repetitive, or challenging when going for the stars (full perfect), sometimes it is just plain brilliant.The ending is perfect.Bonus point for a chapter with asymmetric meter.Duration is around 2h if you don't go for the stars; you may need to double or triple that for all achievements.Overall, I would recommend, but understand that this game may not be for everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game with a great soundtrack that carries the experience. The artwork fits perfectly with the 70s vibe and really gets you into the story.The gameplay is pretty simple - just two buttons required - and the difficulty ramps up as the game progresses - at times to the point of frustration but as you fail it starts to help you more. Sometimes it feels like the chapters aren’t going to end when there are 6,7 or 8 melodies to crack. I’ve only played through once and unsure if I’ll go back to get the fully perfect game and open the bonus levels. I played on Steam deck and my advice is to play it out loud. I found my headphones had just a small sound lag and it can affect timing if you’re really getting into the rhythm. It makes it that but easier to get those perfect chapter achievements Overall an enjoyable and mostly relaxing couple of hours listening to some great music. Recommended for rock music fans most of all
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: A rhythm game, but not for everyone who loves this type of game.   Using blue, psychedelic, and soul music for a rhythm game is a bold choice. Usually, most gamers are accustomed to rock or techno music, which is easy to catch on the beat. However, this game focuses on the melodic part of the guitar and keyboard alternate with percussion which is very hard because it heavily relies on irregular melodic, not rhythm. Most gamers' reviews comment that it is not rhythm accurate. As a matter of fact, it is accurate but not "on the beat" as we used to play in many games.The songs remind me of Uriah Heap or The doors, which is (again) not enticing to play as a rhythm game. I love the artwork and the story, though. The downside is you can not get a good ending with easy difficulty. Getting "all perfect" to progress half of the story is pretty frustrating.   Because I was not engaged in getting a good ending, and the game didn't have upbeat music, which is the selling point of the rhythm game. I don't recommend it for gamers in general, except for those who are into 60's era music.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice game but it didn't really click with me.Unlike other rhythm games, the only cue here is the music. The song of each chapter is divided into sequences. Each sequence is played initially and it will seamlessly loop until you hit the notes perfectly. It sounds simple enough but as someone who doesn't play music, it just made me anxious most of the time because I couldn't tell when to play the notes sometimes (and I like casual rhythm games). The visual indicator is still available through the Assist Mode but you'll have to ditch it if you want to unlock the bonus level.I found the story to be pretty lackluster. Here's a summary:  The songs were great as set pieces but nothing really stuck out to me. But this is more of a personal taste and if you're a fan of the genre, you might appreciate the music more than I did.Unfortunately, all of this stuff was enough to discourage me from attempting another playthrough which is disappointing since it seems like the game was designed to be played at least twice. Not to mention how tedious it is to replay chapters because of all the animations and sequence intros you have to sit through.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: First, I wish this had some sort of accessible lag compensation, there's an assist mode but I had to switch to a lower latency setup to finish the game because the lag kept throwing me offFairly short call and response rhythm game with a visual narrative. It's kind of like an interactive music video set in the 70s. Very well done visuals and music, and I ended up 100% it because I enjoyed both
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: There's a kernel of a delightful game buried in here, but the storytelling is so incoherent and dull that it feels like an absolute slog to get through. The joy of the game should come from seeing the story of compelling characters unfold when you nail a difficult track, but instead it's more of a loosely connected and highly repetitive slideshow.The rhythm mechanics are so simple that I can't see hardcore fans of that genre playing it for the gameplay alone, and I got nothing out of it as someone mostly there for the story. It takes two hours to tell a story that would fit in a shallow, 3 minute music video. Really disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not entirely sure what's going on with the story.  Jimi Hendrix smokes weed and it drives him insane and he decks his bandmate and runs off in the woods naked, then later he's high again and crashes his hippie van and nearly kills himself?  Better luck next time Jimi.  Anyway, it's not appealing, nor is the art. There appeared to be alternate paths on the map, which might mean different story branches, but I didn't know how to access them.  Maybe you have to get a perfect or high(er) score on the stage it branches from, but I didn't feel like playing more and trying to unlock.  The gameplay is actual rhythm / music based, and it's alright, that's why this has an upvote from me.  If you don't have the helper indicators turned on, it gets pretty hard.  There are only 3 controls: Left, Right, or Both, and sometimes you need to hold them down. The gameplay is to listen to a pattern, then repeat it with exact timing.  It's difficult because the duration of the "clip" you have to reproduce is pretty long.  And most of the stages have intentionally off-beat notes that are harder to keep in-mind.  You can get a Star on stages (and extra achievement I think) by doing 100% perfect without even a single miss.  I achieved that naturally on some of the early stages, but getting it PERFECT became very hard once you're a few stages in.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: A very different rythm game than usual. You are not asked to play notes in rythm with reflexes but you have to memorise a ~10s music that will stay on loop until you hit every note on time.While the game can get very tough it adapts the difficulty if you struggle too much and helps you. It makes you discover a lot of classic rythm used in late 60's-70's rock and also unusual rythms that are very interesting to understand and replicate.The music is super interesting to listen to and we have the feeling that we are actually a part of a band playing it. This is helped by the wonderful graphisms of the game that immerges in a trip to woodstock in the late 60's.I totally recommend for non-musician but also to musician, the rythm used are very fun to analyse while playing !
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: A perfect linear story-driven game with stellar music!The story is great, the art is stunning, the level design is perfect, sometime a bit hard but never impossible to get though!Approximatively 2h30 without doing any perfects, a lot more if you want to unlock that special chapter!I absolutely recommand it!
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lovely game. Music and animation are clearly great — you get that just by watching the trailers and that remains the case throughout the whole thing. What I'd like to single out are the rhythm mechanics. It's all too common for a rhythm game to punish mistakes with a series of error sounds that take you away from the music and eventually lead you to a fail state. The way this game perfectly loops each scene until you get all the notes right makes sure you're never out of the groove. You keep trying until you get a perfect bar, but you can make mistakes over and over again and everything will still sound pleasing and you can't ever fail the chapter. It's super refreshing to play a rhythm game like this, I really loved it.I will say though that the requirements for the bonus stage are somewhat frustrating. Later chapters are harder, of course, but also way longer, which makes perfecting every scene a bit too much. If the bonus stage opened up at like 80% stars this would already be a lot better, allowing the player to see the whole content while still posing a challenge. The 100% completion would be fine as just achievement fodder. I'm glad I finished it all, but I *do not* want to play chapter 19 again.
_childDocuments_.name: A Musical Story

Hunt werewolves, fallen angels, and other damned creatures in a vivid slow motion love letter to action classics. Fight your way through a reality-shifting motel, floor by bloody floor. Save the victims of Draculae, lord of the vampires. Destroy the villain you loved--even if it means dying yourself. Somewhere in El Paso, Texas, a three-story motel gained another 46 stories... all below ground. So, yeah. This is going to get loud. FEATURING Original hip-hop soundtrack. _childDocuments_.review: This game has Remedy as a special thanks in the credits.Yeah, no shiт.It has Remedy everything: Max Payne's slo-mo, monologues, shootdodging and painkillers, Alan Wake's floating furniture and cheesy but awesome song stages, Control aesthetics right down to the big bald-letter poof at the start of every level. Oh, wait, Control had rockin' song stage too.The thing is - El Paso nailed almost all of that. Like, dead on. Knocked it right out the gоddamn park. It's like Strange Scaffold is the only other studio in the world that could grasp what made Remedy games in general and Max Payne specifically so effortlessly cool.The story part especially. Like all the best Remedy games it has that mix of fun videogame nonsense with something genuine and tragic, and it all works. And the voice acting is just superb, way better than trailers will lead you to believe. Almost every cutsene just glued me to the screen, especially that "one good day" one, Jesus Christ. I won't be surprised if some of this stuff will hit someone waaay too close to home.It has some problems tho, The devs loved Remedy so much that they even took Remedy's platforming, Remedy's bossfights, and Remedy's Part II - Chapter 1: The Baseball Bat. None of that was good in Remedy's games and none of it is good here, that one boss in the middle especially. On top of that - shootdodging is kinda useless, the game in general is way too easy on intended difficulty and there are about 7-10 filler levels that really should be cut for pacing.None of that stops me from loving the hеll out of this game tho.

_childDocuments_.review: This game appeared on my steam store page like a back alley watch salesman. Unassuming and promising a Rolex for $17.99. I of course bought it, worth it for the story if nothing else. 10 hours later and I'm left questioning my life choices. How many times had I brushed off what looked like a terrible game, a cliche knockoff, but it was actually a diamond that just needed a bit of polish? Had I been missing out my entire life? I returned to the steam store page to search for the next masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It's a love letter to Remedy, and a really good one at that. Imagine Max Payne but instead of mobsters and drug addicts you are fighting mummies and werewolves. The familiar bullet time is there, and so are your painkillers. Molotovs, Uzis, dual pistols, shotguns, you want them, you got them.But you also get the crazy nightmare levels, and you also get some Control-esque weirdness to go along with it. And if that wasn't enough, the Strange Scaffold team got a pretty well developed narrative going on, and a surprisingly effective original soundtrack that works even if you aren't a fan of the musical genre that's mostly represented in it.It's not 100% bug free and there are rough spots and some repetition, but overall, this is the kind of game that I would 100% recommend to any Remedy games lovers. Trust me, you won't be disappointed!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Once in a while a game comes along that reminds you these things can be art. . . If you've ever been in an abusive relationship, this game will resonate with you heavily, bring back painful memories, and remind you of what it feels to cling to those good memories through all of the cruel acts of trying to emotionally destroy each other.The game-play alone was enough to sell me on this, a love-letter to Max Payne with vampires and werewolves; The gun-play, slow-mo, movement, level design, and soundtrack are all phenomenal. But on top of that the story is a work of art.I cannot recommend this game enough to someone!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I have yet to finish it but I will say I recommend this game due to the amount of heart it has. Is it repetitive at times? Oh yeah. Is there a lack of depth in combat and level design? Sure. Is it blatantly a Max Payne homage? You betcha. But it’s the story, the voice acting, the character, the strangeness of it all, and the overall sheer amount of passion and love that went into this that KEEPS. ME. GOING.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: So, how you're going to feel about this game is going to break down to which of the following two things you feel more strongly about.Solid vibes. A moody, introspective story. Excellent sound design. We-have-Max-Payne-gunplay-at-home.ORA witch. It has an attack that deals 75% of your bar. The attack is an aoe. The attack moves very fast. The attack has tracking. You can't jink the attack, you have to dodge roll it. The witch teleports when you move. The witch only sound-cues the attack at the last possible second. The witch often moves behind you. The witch is very tanky. Guns are inconsistent against the witch. Witches spawn alongside melee enemies that punish you for standing still. Witches are common and spawn in numbers.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: While technically about the end of the world, the design, writing, voice acting, and even the soundtrack make the story of El Paso, Elsewhere so deeply personal that it feels intimate. And I'm saying this about a game with werewolves in it.This game is something special. If you like artsy indies then pick this one up. It's a can't miss.Also if you get stuck on a level while streaming, the lead developer will jump in your discord call and read the lyrics to Alice In Chains songs until you beat it.
