_childDocuments_.review: This is not the game I needed it to be.Getting the pros out of the way: basic atmosphere is on point. The voice acting and the music are great and did a lot of the heavy lifting for getting me invested in the game. The gameplay itself is...not so great.- The Max Payne influence is very apparent, but the mechanics implemented simply don't make sense. Bullet time dives work in Max Payne when you need to clear out a room of gun-wielding criminals before they have time to shoot back. But in EPE the majority of enemies use melee attacks, so diving just means you're lying on the floor ready to be dogpiled by the enemies you didn't manage to kill. There's no reason not to just use the dedicated slow-down-time button instead.- Plenty of reviews have mentioned the repetitive level design, but I don't think any have mentioned the extremely messed up spawning system. The game will spawn new enemies when you hit certain triggers, but the spawn locations are illogical and sometimes extremely cruel. One level in particular will spawn angels directly above you, where you won't know they exist until they've already started firing.- On a related note, enemy design is really not great. The brides and their teleporting force you to yank the camera all over the place to keep up, which of course means you can't see the conga line of zombies about to crash down on you.- The game runs out of ideas by the halfway point. They don't have any more enemy types to offer so instead you get 'elite' enemies which are a different colour and do more damage. Level design isn't about new and interesting challenges so much as throwing more and more enemies at you at once. And using 'the void' as a narrative excuse to throw assets together doesn't really work.- Gunplay feels bad and inconsistent. Sometimes enemies die to one shot, sometimes they don't. There's a dead zone right next to you where guns just can't connect so your only option is to spend a stake or die.I'd still have been somewhat satisfied with the game if it ended on a high note with the sort of payoff I'd been hoping for, but it doesn't.  Perhaps this is more of a personal issue than a narrative one, but after pushing through the less-than-stellar gameplay to get there it didn't feel like the outcome I wanted.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This one was a really hard review for me to write, because I like the artistic approach that the devs took here. They also made the voice acting work and everything, and I do applaud them for that. The thing is, after around four hours, I did find myself not having fun anymore. It got very repetitive, and the actual gameplay isn't great - the shooting is sometimes quite off with the hitboxes, the Max Payne Style slo-mo fades off really quickly. I'm a huge fan of Max Payne, but I do think that at some point they took too many ideas from the series, and in the end didn't execute them as well as Remedy did.So the final question of recommendation, I would have to say from my side, no. As much as I would've loved to give it a thumbs up, I couldn't - just like I couldn't really finish the game.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could love this game but I cant. Music is great, aesthetic and visuals are wonderful, story is fine, but it feels like the MP mechanics are well done but tacked on in the wrong game. Levels are claustrophobic and twisting with enemies that either hide from you or run straight at you. Max Paynes gun combat was great because you used cover and angles to fight enemies that shot at you. There a moments where the combat works, typically with a mix of enemies in open areas with columns, but when you get surrounded by a bunch of melee enemies that damage feels like it comes out of no where and your dive becomes a hindrance. You can lay on the ground after but everything runs straight at you so you cant stay there for long. Long range enemies float high up at the ceiling and the tight hallways mean diving to the ground often cuts of your line of sight. The enemies and levels do not allow these mechanics to shine. On top of that the there are a few guns that feel super effective, but the shotgun is a lead pillow that only seems effective within literal swinging distance and the uzi has a spray pattern that makes csgo AK seem like a laser. The molotov is basically there to stop rushing enemies but imagine if you had actual guys behind cover and you could throw it to clear them out or shoot it in air. Theres something here and the music is really fun but the levels are so monotonous and the game feels way too long for what it is. Youll be seeing the same environments over and over and over with a weird hostage/ key mechanic and a floaty awful feeling stake if enemies get too close and it just feels like the wrong game for max. Lot of great talent here but feels like a first game, confused and super buggy.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I took this game’s opportunity to literally play as my friend. It’s weird. You likely won’t have this experience. But it made this my most memorably powerful experience in games this year. Xalavier Nelson Jr. helped get me my first paid video game trailer gig in 2015 (in which we used his voice to explain Super Flippin Phones). This was the first time of many that we would work together, working directly with his voice and it was well before he released his first video game as a creator. Our career paths intertwined over many games, and I'm very familiar with his and his team's creative work. So I feel like I can at least be objective when I say that this was Xalavier's first game that I personally adored in nearly every way, shape, and form. Sure the difficulty isn't consistent, some levels could be trimmed, and the enemy variety is limited by the game's scope. But I sincerely feel like it's the best Remedy-adjacent video game that I played this year. Like I replayed Control and Alan Wake 2, but I liked this more. A lot more. I didn't expect that, and other players willl almost definitely not have that experience. But I have to be candid about why I loved this game so much. In sum, El Paso Elsewhere is an indie game that worked extremely well for me.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

Some stellar voice acting made this a really memorable experience for me. The combat can get a little stale but everything else more than makes up for it. Definitely worth your time!Check out  for more recommendations!

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: - Max Payne with vampires, that's always going to be cool- Narration/Voice acting, James especially is very well written and voice acted.- Presentation, the style is just cool, I just wish it went further and got weirder -StoryCons: - Very drawn out. overstays its welcome- Gets repetitive very quickly - Gunplay is off, weapon reloads are slow for this type of game as well - Enemy and level variety. 20 levels in you've basically seen everything, and you still have about 20+ more to go. - Lack of indicators, either low health or projectiles. Can't count the number of times I died to a lock-on fireball nailing me from off screen.   - Balancing. Beat the game on the intended difficulty and still died quite a bit. Some enemies are a joke and other are just annoyingly god-tier. - Damage. Sometimes a weapon is a one-shot kill, other times it takes 4 shots to the head. The game can't decide if the weapons want to work or not.   I really wanted to like this game more, but there just isn't a ton here worth spending the duration of the story to see. The gunplay is just okay, and the lack of enemy and weapon variety make the game very redundant.A sequel where the tighten things up could be promising, but unless you're really desperate for a slightly different Max Payne, then I'd suggest picking this up on sale or skipping it outright.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A totally accurate depiction of what happens if you really think "I can fix her" and follow it to its logical conclusion: you’ll chase your abusive vampire waifu down into a hellish plane of warping unreality, distorted memories, and supernatural violence until finally one or both of you ends up splattered up the walls. If you do manage to survive the experience, you might well emerge changed for the worse.This is one of those mood piece games in which the ambience is good enough to elevate some quite basic gameplay. The vibes created by the outstanding script, voice acting, soundtrack, and setting are immaculate, but the gameplay is basically just a reskinned Max Payne (the way it actually is, not the way you remember it). I love Max Payne as much as anyone else who grew up playing it but the gunplay always felt a bit light - it was always a game of aesthetics. The levels and enemies are quite repetitive, and the game is maybe 30-40% too long, but I found myself pushing through to hear the one-liners, musings, radio recordings, elevator chats, and music. There are some very unpredictable difficulty spikes - you'll be happily nodding to the music, headshotting vampires and blasting werewolves, when suddenly several heavy-hitting enemies will appear surrounded by mobs and you'll struggle not to be 1 shot by a projectile while you scramble to get clear of the swarm. I also think that there are perhaps too many narrow spaces for the bullet time/shootdodge to really shine as much as it could - you end up with odd camera angles and banging into walls. It's not really fair to accuse the game of being fully style over substance, but it's definitely further over to the style side of the spectrum. I don’t want to sound overly critical - none of this means that the game isn’t a good experience, or that the incredible neo-noir atmosphere won't drag you in and encourage you to persist. It’s undeniable that a lot of love has gone into this game and it's got a lot of character as a result. Overall a very fine 7/10 game that has more soul than many games with superior mechanics - I'd not be surprised if it earns a cult following.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A game that dresses itself up as a crazy, violent, psychodelic romp that tells a heartfelt and very human story. I went in expecting parallels to Max Payne, and it was a lot closer than I'd expected. Monologues, bullet time, and insane visuals all came together to make something entirely unique while reminding me of one of my favorite childhood games.The music is a treat, as well as the voice acting. Strange Scaffold does something very interesting with using breathing as a part of the dialogue that makes everything feel more exhausting, I can't get enough of it. The story that the game tells feels very personal, and the final boss/ending feels incredibly bittersweet.Unfortunately, I do think the game is a bit on the long side for the amount of weapons/enemies you run into. I was determined to see the story through to the end because I was so enthralled, but I'd have liked if the experience was cut down by a few hours. Don't let it stop you, though...the cutscenes are more than worth it.Highly recommended. Also breakshitkillpeoplebreakshitkillpeoplebreakshit
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Decent gameplay, but not good enough to carry the length of the campaign, it gets tedious about halfway in.Love the art style, blending of environments and music.The way the environments are constructed feel dreamlike, you start in apartments, get to a cemetary and the parts are combined in nonsensical ways. This gets more interesting as more environments are mixed together.The voice acting is great, and it's interesting to see toxic relationships explored in a videogame, not something I often encounter. Recommended if you don't mind repetition, otherwise stay away.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is never more than competent when it comes to gameplay, as its limited enemy roster takes little advantage of its mechanics while the repetitive levels make the campaign padded out despite its short length. What turns Elsewhere from a mediocre Max Payne throwback to a certified cult classic is its story, aesthetics and soundtrack. This is an introspective and personal journey so tightly woven with its music that neither can be truly appreciated without the other. While the game parts of Elsewhere never quite fit together, the love its small team poured into every other aspect makes the experience worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Neat third person shooter with a good soundtrack and a SURPRISINGLY HEAVY STORY Like haha fun Max Payne dive shooty man but suddenly you're watching someone slowly destroy themselves for just the faintest chance of reaching through to their abusive ex, massive power imbalances in relationships, and all the myriad ways someone can use love to manipulate and control.I had fun, story was fantastic, shooting will drag on after awhile though.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Max Payne-alike that misses the mark on what makes those games so compelling. Bland and repetitive combat that lacks satisfying damage feedback, and a diving/slomo action that seems to work against you. Some wonky aiming issues and enemy pathfinding problems don't help matters. Altogether it's very easy with the hardest enemy being the videogame itself.I'm not bias against low-poly aesthetics but rule number one is not to use high-detail lighting that emphasises just how simple character models are (think "This Fan Made Zelda In Unreal Engine!" articles) rather than complimenting them. The limited set of assets gets a lot of creative use but after a while you're going to close your eyes and just see copy-pasted motel rooms. Flash neon floodlights taking inspiration from that trend of 10s cinema but is mostly style over substance.Level design is tedious, with a confused pattern of rescuing (or killing) hostages and getting keys but are just different ways to unlock your path from A to B. Being able to see outside the room boundaries I think is meant to be a stylistic choice but it makes everything feel a bit cheap and unfinished.I can enjoy self-indulgent writing but El Paso Elsewhere takes a lot of time to not say a lot. Audio logs aren't particularly insightful and have to be stood next to to listen (a good chance to reload all of your weapons at least). The plot is just fine, presumably quite relatable to people who have experienced the game's themes but otherwise quite concise in its message.Highlights by far are the soundtrack, very clipping. esque hooks without the abrasive sound, and the voice acting of the game's duo.There's just not quite enough going on for El Paso Elsewhere for me to recommend, but there's a lot of promise undearneath it. Halving the length of it so the gameplay and writing can say more with less, and much more visceral combat, would be my first step. It's a drug-fueled paranormal nightmare that I wanted to finish early for the wrong reasons.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Plays like Max Payne, looks like Hotline Miami if it were 3D, and features a premise that has more in common in Constantine.A game that legitimately stands on its own, and while the simplistic gameplay does start wearing thin towards the end, the strong visuals, the banger soundtrack, witty wordplay, the amazing performance by the lead dev (!) voicing the main character, all of it honestly props the gameplay up. Better yet? It's all wrapped up in a gut wrenching, emotional story about toxic relationships and idolising "perfect" past days instead of looking ahead.This game managed to surprise me even if I was already looking forward to it.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It’s been a long time since I’ve seen a Max Payne clone, and El Paso, Elsewhere is certainly the best of them. However, that is a very low bar to clear, and I think there are plenty of faults with El Paso, Elsewhere that hold it back from being a true successor to Remedy’s iconic game.While most other clones of Max Payne tried to add onto the bullet time mechanics, El Paso, Elsewhere basically just lifts them as they were. You can enter bullet time, shoot-dodge, or do a combat roll. Being a game that wasn’t made in 2001 though, it’s done much better, obviously. Jumping doesn’t feel like it arbitrarily cuts off like it does in Max Payne, you can perform any action you want without actually needing to go into bullet time, and guns are actually accurate. It’s not just the mechanics though, it’s also the goofy side shows that are now on the radio, the brooding protagonist, the level of interactivity you have with the environment, and even the quit screen reading like a hardboiled novel.What really separates this game is the full on supernatural element. You’ll be spending your time fighting vampires, werewolves, biblically accurate angels, and spooky ghosts in surreal mishmashes of motel, graveyard, and medieval castle settings; all in the same level. You’ll barely notice the low-fidelity look of this game when looking at the environment design and lighting. This game can look gorgeous when it wants to, especially towards the end. With all of the dark pathways lit by unnatural greens, purples, and yellows, it’s a great game to play during the halloween season. Unfortunately, I don’t think the sound design is as good as the visuals. The soundtrack is great, even the corny rap tracks feel at place in the game, but the guns lack any kind of punch to them and enemies don’t really have much going on beyond generic gurgling and growling. And since enemies are either melee attackers who beeline for you, or AoE ranged fighters who hang back, they actually undermine the usefulness of bullet time. There is literally no reason to shoot-dodge in this game, and it will actually get you killed more often than not. You are better off just rolling away from any attacks because you are invincible when doing so, and then shooting them when you get back up. I found myself forgetting I even had bullet time for most of the game, even on the Challenging preset difficulty.Speaking of difficulty, I highly recommend NOT playing on the Challenging preset. All it really does is max out the damage dealt by enemies, making nearly every hit an instant kill. Thankfully, this game lets you customize quite a few aspects of the game individually, including difficulty. Don’t like the camera placement? You can change that. Feel that the game is too fast or too slow, you can change that. Want to adjust enemy health, health regen, and ammo capacity separate from one another? Damn right you can change that, and I would recommend doing so, because the game would be too easy otherwise. Personally, I think buffing enemy health and speed to overcome the frankly quite stupid AI, reducing ammo capacity, and increasing bullet time drain are much better ways of giving yourself a more enjoyable challenge than any of the presets. Also, at least double the speed at which you take pills to regain health. The animation for it feels way too slow by default, to the point where you don’t even have time to use them in an intense fight.The hardest part of this game is the first half of it. Not because the game itself is challenging, but because it feels directionless. This game’s plot doesn’t really get going until around chapter 25 or so, which is halfway through the game. Each level may be short, but doing so many back to back, many without even cutscenes in between, really drags the pacing of this game down to a crawl. Even when the game picks up in the second half, there is still a lot of filler to get through. This is by far the biggest thing holding the game back, because beneath the moody monologues is a really good story about addiction and abuse, and overcoming them, with characters I came to love by the end.I think there’s a lot to appreciate in El Paso, Elsewhere, despite its glaring flaws. There are tons of small details that made the game a lot of fun. Enemies getting ragdolled into oblivion from a close range shotgun blast never got old, the game over screen being “you keep going”, which fits in with the themes of the game , or just the smoke trailing from your gun after unloading a mag into a crowd of vampires as you move around. There’s also a handful of frequent bugs like enemies getting stuck on objects, or hitting you while facing away from you that also stick in my head. It’s a mixed bag in the end, and I do think the good outweighs the bad. At the very least, it has me excited for future Strange Scaffold projects.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This feels more like a meme than a game. It's just a bunch of random elements stitched together to create a vibe, with very little substance and a lot of repetition. It's a short game at 8-10 hours, which I like. But there's 50 chapters, and they all feel the same. I'm quitting the game on chapter 15 because it literally has me running in a circle the whole time. The "bullet time" dive mechanic that they're taking from Max Payne also makes no sense in this game. Every single level is a series of narrow tunnels, with very few exceptions, so there's usually nowhere to dive.It's crazy to me that the current top review is praising the soundtrack, because the music is awful. It's either early 00s-style techno that sounds like it was created by AI, or even worse, Liam Lynch-level ironic cornball rap. At least I think it's supposed to be ironic. Either way, it usually kicks in during the most intense fight scenes in a given level, and it's so distractingly bad that it got me killed a couple times. It also sometimes plays over the main character mumbling his noir dialogue to himself, which renders both unintelligible.It kills me that Lakeith Stanfield is even considering making a movie based on this game. We truly are circling the drain in terms of culture.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It plays like Max Payne but with mummies and werewolves and ghouls. The storytelling is poetic. The music is badass. It's all very cool. And too long, frankly. At 8 hours and 50 levels, both the gameplay and narrative outstays its welcome a bit. This is one of those games that could do with a Director's Cut or whatever to cut out the filler levels, get it down to ~35 levels and it'd be a better experience. Still an enjoyable journey tho.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: There are parts about this game I really liked. The voice acting is very good, and the music feels fresh and sometimes perfect. (Imagine if Max Payne started rapping along to the soundtrack in his emotionally-dead voice.) Some of the story cutscenes were well-composed.But there was more I didn't like about the game. It's far too long for such simple, easy gameplay. The gameplay doesn't make enough use of slow-mo or diving to justify it.  The graphics never make use of slow-mo (a few times stained glass shatters and falls, but these moments are far and few between.) A few set-pieces were evocative, like the endless bathrooms, but a lot of the game is set in flat and generic settings. The weapons all feel like the same gun with different fire modes.There are also small annoyances, like how much time it takes to consume several pills at once (why make this change from Max Payne?); the fact that the audio logs wouldn't play if you left their location (!!); the lack of pre-set difficulty options (that I could find).I think it would have been great as a three-hour story mode, with plenty of arena or time challenges afterward. As it is, the uninspired gameplay in repetitive levels is unfortunately leaned on, padding a better story that also feels pointlessly dragged out.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It's a well made indie homage to Max Payne. The art direction is pretty darn good, I am not a big fan of rap music but I can tell whoever made the music put a lot of effort into it and I definitely respect it. There is a decent variety of guns and they do feel different enough that I find myself switching between most of them throughout each level. The voice acting it really good - the voice actor for the protagonist did a particularly good job. My only real criticism is that it is fairly easy for the vast majority of the time and extremely repetitive while it does go on for a bit too long. It is good they made the chapters short so you can drop in and out and not play too much due to the repetitiveness of the game but I am finding it is overstaying its welcome and I am having a hard time finding the desire to finish it. If they cut out maybe a quarter of the game I think it would have landed much better. Still, it's a good game and worth a go if you like the Max Payne games.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 game ruined by excessive fluffstory is amazing and the voice acting superb, but the dev clogged it up with 30+ levels of nothing, which makes it very hard for me to recommend. I personally beat the game, but only through sheer determination of seeing how the story ends and after beating it i don't want to play another second of it.id say out of the 50 levels only 20 or so were really worth playing. it takes way too long for the game to ramp up in complexity and the copious amount of health and ammo made it very hard to die, compounded by the fact the only thing you adjust difficulty wise is how much damage you take and how much health you can heal, (Neither of which matter when every level has several healing items in them.) you either make it so health items don't matter at all due to how abundant they are or that you die in one or two hits. there's no in between.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: should you buy it? idk, but here's a list of my thoughts on it:- the music is fun and weird and one of the main reasons I bought this game- the gameplay gets repetitive and boring way too fast. the only thing that saves it are the difficulty spikes, but I wouldn't say that it's a good thing- there is only 1 hour of fun and enjoyable gameplay in this 6 hour game- shooting and movement are clunky, there's way too many moments when I stumbled into an enemy behind a door which oneshot me before I could even do anything. I am also convinced that melee was added to let players do at least something if an enemy gets in their face, because guns literally won't work. oh, and if you get stuck anywhere without a melee weapon, then you will just die. there is no way to get out of that situation.- but hey, respawning is faster than it could've been (still way too long imo)- the artstyle of cutscenes is very atmospheric and at times even beautiful- the artstyle of levels is all over the place, with most of them looking extremely messy. artistic choice my ass, you could've made these look better (proven by some of the latter levels inside - the story is solid. it isn't crazy good, but it still fits the game very well. it's human. it's raw. it's real. I liked it-  chapters is way too long. indie games aren't where you pad for longer playtime, you could've cut like half of them and gotten a way better game that doesn't make the player say "god, when will this end already" every 20 minutes- cuts to cutscenes are jarring and would've benefited so much if they were properly integrated into gameplay. i believe that removing loading screens would've made for better pacing.- bosses are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. the devs looked at souls-likes and somehow decided that rolling around is the most fun part of them, so their bossfights are just roll, shoot, roll, shoot, roll, reload, roll, shoot... imagine what I felt when I realized that the final boss of the game was anyways, even though I pushed the "do not recommend" button and said a lot of mean things about this game, I still really appreciated the passion that went into it. I appreciated it enough to finish it, which is a rare thing for me. really hoping that the next game by these guys is going to crash the negatives I've pointed out and ace the positives.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This is a worthier successor to Max Payne than 3 ever was.Intense, moody, silly, hard. Doing a LOT with less. Voice acting that mixes with rapping while the bullets fly in truly sublime ways. The ending hurts. The story hurts too, in a good way. It made me feel things. And it was absolutely worth the price of admission. I'll probably play through it again at some point.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is a third-person dungeon-crawling shooter featuring a vampire hunter chasing his ex-vampire-girlfriend into the void. The game's style, story, and characters are the absolute highlights and were able to carry me to the end. A gripping story of love, trauma, and the scars left behind. James as a character was especially great. The snippets of him reflecting in the elevator between levels were a great reward pairing nicely with the rather short in-and-out level design. Watching him slowly grow more restless the longer he spends in the void and seeing him forced to face the trauma of his past was fantastic stuff. The surreal aesthetic that the void conjures works well with the experience. Additionally, the gunplay is fun, with the slow-mo ability and head-shot damage doing a lot of heavy lifting in creating a satisfying loop. My personal biggest issue with this game is the enemy variety and environments. The enemies that were there were solid, but there just wasn't enough variety for the length of the game. Shooting the same werewolves and shambling vampires gets pretty dull by the end. While I generally enjoyed the level design itself, the environments leaned heavily on reusing assets. While the reuse is explained and justified story-wise, it results in a rather large number of levels being visually indistinguishable from one another. That coupled with a lack of verticality in level design made many levels play out very similarly. Either rescue civilians or find the colored keys to progress. I think both of these issues would have had less impact if the game itself was tightened up in length. As much as I loved the story, the levels just didn't always do it for me and I was forcing myself to finish by the end. Overall, this was a good time and the game's story and style charmed me. Just need some more variety and a tightened experience.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is incredible. All I was expecting was a Halloween flavored Max Payne send up and while I definitely got that I think it's unfair for this game to live in that shadow. It takes so much from that series but rearranges and tweaks those things to achieve it's own identity.I love urban fantasy. Dresden Files, Vampire The Masquerade, Blackwell. A supernatural underworld just below the surface of humanity. Often treating humans like cattle or at least disposable for their own purposes. I find it so interesting and El Paso is no exception. The little bits of worldbuilding we get paint a similar picture but this one is much more abstract.You play James Savage who is currently in a three-story motel that just got a 46 story expansion all heading down, courtesy of his ex, Draculae. She's taking part in some sort of ritual that will end the world and has plenty of hostages. Whatever this ritual is doing is causing The Void to warp reality with trauma into a nightmarish thrill ride all the way to the bottom where they'll confront everything that made their relationship come to this.All supernatural chaos aside their abusive relationship manages to feel very real in the little ways they interact and the voice acting helps this exponentially. It's clear to me the writer knows what this kind of relationship feels like. It's not afraid to poke fun at the melodrama of two ex lovers confronting each other either. These two characters the story revolves around are flawed and fleshed out and I really enjoyed them.James' descent into this hellish motel feels incredible. Diving past ghouls, rolling through their slashes and slow mo blasting them in the head. Saving hostages in between brief bursts of violence and popping enough pain pills to kill himself 50 times over just to tank through The Void's horde of supernatural horrors. If you hold down the dive button you can stay on the floor until you're out of ammo and need to get up to reload. Like I said it's Max Payne. The one main tweak in the gameplay besides enemy variety is an instant kill stake that you get 5 of and break various pieces of furniture to get more. Break ♥♥♥♥, kill people. That's the gameplay loop and god is it addicting.Which brings me to the music. It's pulse pounding and intense in a way that feeds perfectly into the gameplay. Other times moody or relaxing but always experimental and playful. Any time a track with lyrics comes up feels like a treat. It's one of those total package things where the visuals, sound design, gameplay and music are all working together perfectly. The entire OST has me seriously considering getting the vinyl.El Paso, Elsewhere is a must play. There's so much I didn't mention because I want you to unravel the rest of this one for yourself. I'll definitely be trying to 100% this in the future and it's safe to say I'll be replaying this for many years to come.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, it's just not for me; I got really bored about a quarter of the way and forced myself to get to about half way through the game until it was becoming a chore I wasn't looking forward to. The writing is decent, the voice acting great, but the repeating low poly generic monsters over and over with really simple mechanics just got to be a slog.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A bit repetitive. You could argue this game has 3-4 hours of ideas stuffed into a 7 hour package, but the gameplay was good enough to keep me playing. YMMV though if you don't like repetition. It's 50 levels but most are very similar. What kept me going was the great core gameplay and the fantastic story. I look forward to seeing what this team makes next and seeing if they can keep pushing this formula forward into even better games. Highly recommend for people who like 3rd person shooters
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A game that overstays its welcome. The graphics, story, music and voice acting are all fantastic. But the shooting is incredibly just...okay. There is really no reason to use it. Just okay, maybe pick it up and try it out on a sale. Cannot rec now.

_childDocuments_.review: i hope to change this review when i finish the game, but right now i'm rather disappointed.the style, music, story, voice acting, cutscenes between levels, and the Pill Cop radio play are great so far. but you put all this effort into remaking/refining max payne's shooting/dodging/pills mechanics, but then the One Enemy for the first five levels is just a melee enemy that walks at you? there is almost literally no reason to ever shoot dodge. when they introduce the second enemy it's a little better, since they can at least jump at you kinda fast, but still completely kite-able. max payne was built around diving into rooms containing other people with guns. the shoot dodge was to make it less likely for enemies to hit you with bullets, it has barely any utility against melee enemies.another max payne staple was that, although most of the enemies were just Some Guy, they had some great personality to them - you could often eavesdrop on petty and funny little conversations before diving in and clearing out the room. enemies also had a very distinct bark for when they took enough damage to die, which was a fun way to let you know when to stop shooting. again, the enemies in this game are identical, monstrous, non-speaking, melee-only generic guys, who only run directly at you (with less-than-great pathfinding around corners), and their death noise sounds just like the noises they make while they're chasing you (and are clearly just a guy whisper-grunting into a mic).at least there's hit markers, which is something that doesn't bug me in games. there are red weakspot hit markers for heads, etc, but it doesnt actually affect how much ammo you use to take them out all that much. the base zombies take 2 or 3 bullets depending on the gun, and werewolves can usually be taken out with one shot from any gun. weakspots are, then, pretty useless - if weakspots were an insta-kill they'd be really fun to aim for, and it would make the more hectic encounters a fun practice in target-picking.the levels are okay, if a bit samey. i was excited when the hotel gave way to a cemetary, but then the next level was *also* a cemetary, so i took a break.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Max Payne with a goth vampire mommy, including the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up parts of Max Payne. I do quite like how it's written. It's depressing as hell and funny and bittersweet. It's an aesthetically pleasing game, and it feels good to shoot and stake enemies. Each level is never just 'another level' there's always some sort of gameplay or aesthetic gimmick going on. The humor is that trademark Xalavier goofiness combined with a truly depressing narrative about addiction and abuse. We love the meat oblong.Now for the negatives (and apologies for how long this is, because I did really like the game). I think enemy behavior is simple, and has a tendency to be a little cheap. Enemies can swarm you or attack before you notice them. Having to go down a corridor to fight a puppetmaster is tedious. They're an enemy that runs away and summons smaller minions that track you down and head to your direction, but in a small space you wind up shooting them without progressing towards the main body, because more have shown up. Bosses can be trivialized with the slow motion mechanic and the Uzi, disintegrating a health bar before staking them. This does make the final encounter anticlimactic. Also the aim assist is a *little* heavy and can get in the way of precision aiming. I think that it's a little weird that the game is like 'wow you did it you saved the hostages' after you get the good ending, because the good ending is achieved basically just by playing the game. You sorta have to go out of your way to kill hostages to get the bad one. It's kinda like the Bioshock kill the little sister binary choice in that it's not really a hard decision. It's not really a negative but it's sorta got me perplexed. I can't imagine anyone seeing that ending on their first playthrough on their own. Edit: Xalavier did a whole TikTok explaining it, and it's sorta what I thought they were going for. It's that saving or killing hostages both mean one less sacrifice for Draculae, and  that it's a choice that the game has to contend with narratively. But my issue here is that it sort of isn't pragmatic to do that. It'll save a second or two per hostage maybe, but if James decides to kill all the hostages, he's just a freak, but he's never treated as such. Killing the hostages doesn't actually make his life easier. In a perfect world, Strange Scaffold gets like five times their budget. Most quibbles I have with the game are scope or polish related. They made a satisfying, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up shooter. It looks great with its low poly aesthetic and modern lighting. It sounds *great.* I love the horrorcore soundtrack. I love the different genres it goes into. You're always hearing something new. This game is unique and special and I've been looking forward to it for a long time. It's absolutely worth checking out at full price, but the experience could be smoother.Edit: I originally brought up a bug that caused weapons in a level to despawn upon death, forcing me to do a deathless run of a level that had you retrieve your weapons after losing them. The bug has since been patched. They did also adjust puppetmaster behavior, looking at the patch notes, so it's possible that you won't have the same issues that I did.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Charming love letter to Remedy and incredibly intimate. If you are the type of person who enjoys a piece that feels so evocative of the main person behind it, you'll definitely appreciate El Paso's narrative. Gameplay wise it's a fun and chaotic, albeit somewhat easy, third person shooter with a rather limited enemy roster and weapon amount, compensated by just how much the game somehow squeezes out of the level design and variety using the same assets. It dangerously gets close to wearing out it's welcome, but as a game to play in bursts with a simple loop, there is a lot to like about this one.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I wanna recommend it because I like almost the whole game, the story is really good and well written, the gameplay loop is pretty fun....but....There's two big problems. 1. It's way too long. It feels like a complete slog after enough time and gets insanely repetitive. This game is honestly maybe 2/3 or maybe even twice the length it needs to be. 2. There are two boss fights in this game that are both just atrocious, the game doesn't prepare you for them in any way at all and whatever the trick is, I never figured it out, I felt like I just lucked into beating them eventually. The boss fights are actually such a big problem I think the game would be better if it just did not have them at all to be quite honest.As small as those flaws may sound, honestly, they kind of ruined it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It's....not very good.The levels are incredibly repetitive, both design wise and just the general structure, there's a few good ones but for every one of those there's 5 filler missions. I guess there was a need to pad out the playtime to justify the price tag but i would've greatly preferred it to just be 2 hours shorter.Combat is alright but the glaring issue is that there was a reason enemies in Max Payne had guns, when they don't they're really not much of a threat to you, for large chunks of the game you likely wont take any damage. And the 2 regular enemy types that have projectiles can be sniped from across the map on most levels. And while Max Payne was an obvious inspiration to this game, bullet time and all, it really doesn't play much like it at all. Most of your time is just spent running around picking up ammo boxes/stakes/pills etc while circling around small combat arenas and enemies spawning around you, felt more like your bog standard boomer shooter then the carefully planned combat encounters in MP.There's also some really clunky stuff with the combat that kills the pace, why is there a long animation when popping pills instead of just having the healing be delayed to prevent spamming? Why cant you cancel weapon reloads by shooting(especially with the shotgun)? Why does every weapon besides the shotgun have a giant deadzone when an enemy comes close to you so you wont hit them even if the crosshair is right on them? Well i guess the last one is to make stakes feel more useful but it really doesn't work well and just feels jank.Great voice acting and a decent story can't really save the overall package, maybe get it on sale if you're interested in the story.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly solid game, start to finish. It's hard to describe, because the joy of this game is experiential. Thematically it's like Hotline Miami crossed with Control crossed with Max Payne, all spun through the raw and vulnerable heart of the neo-noire genre. It's a constant switch between scenes of fever intense music with twisted reality, and the ache of lonely addictions and loss.If that sounds high-concept, it's not. It's plain and straightforward, and that's what makes it a joy. The writing, directing, VO of this game are sharper than most films you'll see. Absolutely give it a go.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most economic use of game assets I've ever seen, it fully explores every interaction with the first weapon and enemy before moving on to keep things fresh, and recontextualize them with things later game. _childDocuments_.review: I really loved the original Max Payne, it's arcade elegance mixed with just enough depth to allow you to pull off some really satisfying and cool manoeuvres and on higher difficulties it demands those manoeuvres of you. But the really compelling thing about Max Payne is it's writing, Sam Lake is fantastic at somewhat campy but entirely sincere writing. Writing which can, on its face, feel trite and undeserving of its reputation, but nonetheless is spectacular when actually experienced; he's sort of the Stephen King of video game writing if Stephen King was as good as people say he is.Enough talking around this game, I bring this all up because El Paso Elsewhere does not just replicate the gameplay of Max Payne but embodies the virtues of Sam Lake's writing style without owing itself entirely to Remedy's games. It is a very singular experience, it is deeply moving, personal, sincere and of course very campy. You feel it from the very start, the protagonist James Savage's monologues are very overindulgent in the best of ways. Flowery in the direction of pulp, all of Max Payne's talk about angels and demons and the night sky are paid homage to in every line, fitting for a game featuring 'biblically accurate' angels, vampires and eternal night. It's fun and lovely to listen to and spices up the game as you go through the arcade style levels all made up of the same assets. At first, the story does just seem like a piece of pulp fiction, like a noir serial that needs to tell its story and end within a restrictive word count. A man's ex - who IS a vampire - is trying to end the world and he has to stop her, classic! But then the tone shifts, I couldn't tell you where exactly but at some nebulous point it does, you feel it happen but in hindsight the exact moment is foggy, like a reverse wave function collapse.I don't want to go into detail on what this story is about, but it is clearly a very personal expression of Director Xalavier Nelson, and he has an extreme clarity of vision, it is truly resonant. I can see him in James, and I can see myself, and many other people in him. I really didn't go into this came, expecting to review the story as 'deeply moving' - though that is a phrase I use a LOT - yet here we are.It's carried too by the incredible vocal performances of Nelson and Emme Montgomery. I want to draw attention to Nelson in particular because not only does he pull off a fantastic performance as James - nailing the gravelly, defeated tone of a noir protagonist, coupled with a few snappy quips and humanising moments of shock - but the man has pipes. Every few levels, the soundtrack has lyrics, these songs are very indulgent synthy hip-hop which for some reason reminded me of CSH's , they're very cheesy but really fun and all serve to make their respective levels feel narratively significant; they really get the blood pumping too. Which is not to diminish the excellent OST of the rest of the levels, one of my favourite soundtracks, ever, probably.The gameplay is satisfying but drags a bit in the middle, once you get to the back end of the game and the difficulty picks up, as the game becomes meaner and more strategic with it's enemy placement, it picks up; however once the novelty wears off and before this spike in difficulty (though this is never a difficult game) it does become a bit samey. I don't understand the inclusion of the slow-mo dive other than that it was in Max Payne. Enemies don't shoot bullets so you don't really have any reason to dive aside from a few encounters with projectile firing angels and brides. However again it is only in the later levels these enemies demand you  to use this ability and, even then, very sparingly, it was cool when I needed it but it was really just a sparsely used get-out-of-jail-free card. There is a great variety in the weapons, they all feel good and have their uses, all throughout the game, and while ammo isn't scarce you cannot just use one weapon because ammo is plentiful in its variety, you don't get a tonne of ammo for one gun, but a lot across all guns, this is great. This rings true for the enemy variety as well, there are many enemies that are all interesting (though I found the armoured knights to be a bit silly since you don't need to hit their weak points if you have a shotgun). But the game doesn't utilise them properly - which is to say, in thoughtful combinations - until the latter half. Also I hate those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ werewolves, like straight up.Overall, this is a fantastic game and I loved my time with it, it will be VERY hard to forget.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels like a depressed Gen Z tried to condense therapy in a Max-Payne-meets-Path-of-Neo-sized pill.The gameplay is straightforward but does not get old due to the map diversity and weapon choice. The level design is different from other games as you're not given a minimap, but instead are offered a very intuitive no-roof layout with markers for where you need to go, shining like beacons in the sky. The weapons feel like unique tools fit for different situations (e.g. Close Quarters vs mid and long range fights) and the player feels like that choice matters. The little tidbits of lore and random debauchery strewn across the game levels are every bit as mesmerizing as the story that unfolds across the different scenes between missions. One finds oneself compelled to seek out every detail, learn every part of the characters' tale. And it is a story that manages to touch and awe without seeming heavy-handed, even though it is one of tragedy, grief, and the protagonist's efforts to not sink under their weight.I think the most striking aspect of the game which really pulls everything together is the sound. The tracks always perfectly play the line between hyped-up combat motivation and spiraling descent into madness! The way the conversations, recordings, music, and menu interact with one another, especially in the later part of the game really flesh out the atmosphere that this game creates - a very intimate personal journey through a scarred relationship and the possibility for healing.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A game full of character! The cutscenes ooze noir, the music is pumping and the levels can have a mind of their own at points, showing the power they have over their domain. However, those levels are often flat and combat boils down to "walk backwards while firing" with little reason to use the slowmo or dive. Overall, I think the game is worth it for the experience, even if it could've been a better shooter!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely apologize for this review, but I just can't go on with this game. I don't even like to review games I don't finish, but this game feels like such a repetitive chore that I just can't psyche myself up to open it again. and that SUCKS, because there is so much to friggin love. The story, characters, atmosphere, music and general direction are all GREAT. It's literally just the game that isn't very good, but "the game" is the table stakes here (these vampire puns are intentional) and I simply can't get past that. After close to 3 hours and 20 levels, I grew so tired I looked up the chapters and time-to-beat to get an ETA on this on to find i'm not ever close to a halfway point. Just the endless cascade of the same enemies, all in very similar levels, all with the clunkiest mechanics simply isn't fun. Unlike the OG Max Payne, diving doesn't feel fun or cool -- It's actually a hinderance most of the time. At a certain point I just adopted running backwards while shooting the things chasing me 90% of the time, foregoing "bullet time" completely. I'm sorry Devs. I love your vision. I love your style. I just don't love your game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to find something not to like about this game. I disappeared into it for almost 3 hours and had a great time. I want to go back already. Idk I can't explain it I just had a really good time and I think you will too. Get it.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I flip-flopped on whether or not to recommend this game or not. On one hand: The writing and acting is superb, the cutscenes stylishly directed despite the lo-fi aesthetics, and a varied (and long!) score which bounces between witch house bangers and the developer's best CLIPPING impersonation. On the other: Dull, monotonous gameplay that largely misses the point of what made Max Payne and bullet-time fun. Compounded by a somewhat bizarrely bloated runtime. (Seriously, you could have cut out 15 levels here for a dramatic improvement to the pacing.)What ultimately tipped the scale for me was a bit of news that came out while playing. There's a film adaptation in the works, starring LaKeith Stanfield. Assuming it comes out, and retains Xalavier's writing chops, it will be a much better way to experience this story. Admittedly, I'll miss the likely absence of the protagonist's murmured, intimate and very-closely-mic'd narration, though not so much that I'll miss how tedious this game was to play at times.To get into some more detail about the failings of the gameplay, the key mistake here is the game's insistence on nearly every enemy being a melee attacker. This decision laid bare for me one of the fundamental appeals of Max Payne. Bullet Time, and the Dive, exists to counter *ranged* enemies. Even more specifically, hit-scan enemies. You dive into a new room to throw your attackers aim off, because if you get shot more than like three or four times, you're smoked. The dream, then, is to dance across the battlefield as bullet trails soar past you with inches to spare, and land a decisive shot before it's too late. Diving in El Paso makes you an idiot. No reason to do it, no bullets to dodge. There are enemies that shoot slow-moving projectiles, which you can largely dodge in normal speed if you're awake. The closest the dive comes to being essentialized is the Knight enemies, which have a large weak-spot on their backs -- easy to target if you dodge past them -- but why do that when they easily go down to a stake or a well-placed frontal shotgun shot?So instead you quickly discover that the best method is to use the slow-mo, stand still and play point-and-click on enemy heads before they can get close to you. And if you're out of slow-mo, just kite backwards!! They can't do anything!! Because they don't have guns!!!!This results in gameplay that outwears its welcome by around 90 minutes, which seems bad for what should be a brisk 6-8 hours. My friends, my 6.8 hour playtime felt every bit its length. As I suggested earlier, cutting 15 levels would be something of a remedy, as every third level or so presents some fun gimmick, either in visuals or audio, in a way very reminiscent of, uh, Remedy. Keep those, cut the Doom WAD filler.  While we're at it, change the combat. Shoot, maybe remove it altogether. The cutscenes are all great, so maybe make it just that? And then also have actors emote the story, using their faces. Then give me a big bowl of popcorn. Wait a minute...This story spoke to me a great deal, which is why my tone is a little snippy. I earnestly, truly, hope that the film adaptation is able to retain the stylish edge and intimate feel that El Paso, Elsewhere has, while doing justice to its love of violence in a way the game could not. Then I could recommend it with my whole chest.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A loving homage to Max Payne (and, to a lesser extent, Control), El Paso Elsewhere doesn't just copy Remedy's formula. Instead, it puts its own unique framing on it with impressive results. Solid writing and soundtrack prop up the somewhat basic gameplay, but - at least a third of the game in - that's quite enough to keep my attention. EDIT: having now completed the game, I stand by my initial impressions. In fact, further into the game, I finally started grooving more with the gameplay and walked away quite happy with it. The dynamic difficulty settings that can be further customized - up to and including effectively immortality and infinite ammo if you'd like - was a godsend, as a boss fight in the middle of the game is kind of ridiculous. Wouldn't be that way if not for the lack of saves between boss stages. Normally that's a huge mark against a game for me, but here, because I could tweak the difficulty to get through it, it wasn't that big of a deal.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A Max Payne alike with a 1:1 copy of the original's gameplay. I like it, the sound design is great and the story is nice. I didn't mind the rap, I always like it when games try something different.Even though a lot of the levels play very samey I enjoyed most of them, especially when they shifted walls around. I would have liked some more vampire tropes; somehow it felt like story and setting would have worked without the word "vampire" too. Probably because you only run around in some strange realm where everything is twisted and different anyway.Had some frame stutter, and some bugs so I had to replay 1 or 2 levels, but nothing serious. And sometimes the elevator doesn't open via E - it only works when you approach it from the side? That was strange.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly what a odd decently refreshing game.We have had games that do the slow time shooting, and obviously this is inspired by the Max Pain games.However, the game just such a interesting story concept and does a lot with a little.The voice acting is incredible, and the music is great, although maybe not everyone's bag.I was still just so engrossed and wanted to keep going to see how the story resolves.The only issue I have is that there is too many levels, Weird to be complaining about more content, but it does feel like it's drags a little near the end between plot points. But that's not a big negative.Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes action and something different!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: In a year of a lot of writing, a lot of quite good writing for games,  slides in at the last hours of year with some of the best neo-noir you'll hear. Touching, affecting, and shockingly intelligent, Xalavier Nelson Jr. (writer, director, star, composer, etc) manages the impossible of marrying an a pitch perfect neo-noir with a narrative involving vampires and an elevator that screams your sins at you. As it's infamous trailer puts it, it really doesn't seem like it should work, but it really, really does, in my estimation because Xalavier knows how to take the emotional core of it all seriously while still dragging a thread against a much larger world. It's the sort of thing I used to love anthologies for; little window glimpses into another reality without falling into the trap of over-explaining. It's a hard balancing act, and  flies. As a game, it's as much a homage to the original  as anything can be, and despite having some indie quirkiness about it (I swear the crosshair is misalign depending on where the gun is on your character, a dangerous fault in 3rd Person Shooters), it plays smooth, fast, and furious. It's pounding, vibrant sound-track is a perfect. But like it's Remedy inspiration, I think people will remember it's performances and it's narrative more clearly than it's gameplay.I almost missed  and like a lot of others I feel it shot directly to the top of my best of lists. I implore you not to miss this, you will not play anything else like it this year or any other this decade.I await Strange Scaffold's next project eagerly.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso elsewhere at its core is a very well done homage to the original Max Payne games and it nails the shooting as well as the neo-noir style from them games. With a total of 50 chapters i did think the game could have used a few more area types as the levels can start to feel a bit stale, the gameplay itself can also get a tad repetitive. For me, the story and atmosphere was the real highlight and definitely carried me through to the end of the game. I was also impressed with the quality of the cutscenes and the unique soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: The worst thing I have to say about El Paso, Elsewhere is that there may be too much of it. Cut out or combine some of the many motel/meat factory levels, get to the parts where the game gets weird and subverts your expectations faster, and it would be an unqualified recommendation.But it never stopped being fun to play, and the story did a beautiful job of drawing me onward when I began to wonder if I'd blasted enough hallway-dwelling mummies for one video game. Content warning for substance abuse and domestic abuse, by the way. James Savage has really been through it.In short: The boomer shooter impulse has caught up to Max Payne, bold and experimental attitude toward storytelling included, and I'm very happy about it.

_childDocuments_.review: A very direct homage to Max Payne 1 and 2 (not 3). With EXCELENT music, voice acting and storytelling. Gameplay wise don't expect anything super deep, but if you are into neo-noir and a great narrator / inner monologue, this game is for you.It's also kinda longer than I expected, I thought it would be done in 4 hours but I think it's gonna be closer to 6. edit: just beat it, great game. A bit too long, it ended up going for almmost 8 hours.Kinda wish it was about 10 levels shorter, there's a few in there that didn't feel all that great. But it still left a great impression on me.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the coolest game I’ve played all year. El Paso, Elsewhere is a really fun third-person shooter with phenomenal voice acting, writing and music. It’s the full package. The cutscenes are gorgeous. I loved the set designs for the levels that you delve into as you descend through the void. Seeing “YOU KEEP GOING” on the screen every time I died was cool as hell and I bought a copy of the soundtrack as soon as I finished playing which I’ve never done before. Playing this game felt like being at a buffet that coincidentally had all of my favourite food at it without me even knowing. I feel greedy playing this game and want more. On a gameplay level, while I did really enjoy it, some of the boss fights weren’t as balanced as I would have liked them to be. I found most of the boss fights to be quite easy, (including the ), in comparison to crowd fights with one notable exception, (being ). However there is the option to modify the game to suit your level of difficulty if you’d prefer. The game hit me on a raw emotional level with its story and characters as it deals with heavy themes of addiction and the fallout of an abusive relationship. By the end of it I really felt for James and wanted to see him live on to see another day despite knowing it was always meant to be a one way trip which made the ending all the more impactful to me. It’s also really funny when it wants to be. Overall I loved this game and I’ll definitely come back to play it again some day. It has my full recommendation. ()

_childDocuments_.review: The gunplay feels nice but the cramped, limited cover combat areas combined with how all enemies are either melee or fire gigantic explosives makes shootdodging worthless. The game also takes way too long to introduce new enemies and weapons, for example you spend at least the first 5 levels with just the pistols against one enemy type.The saving grace is that the story and its delivery is shockingly good and the some of the levels look pretty.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Score w/o Context: 3.75 Star HotelThe Context: Hotels aren't usually known for their interior architecture. It exists to ferry you from the lobby to your room, with very little in between. Of course, sometimes it also guides you to the continental breakfast, with all its delectable bounty (or terrible but that doesnt fit my beleaguered metaphor). El Paso is similarly elevated by its excellent voice direction, soundtrack and story, making each sojourn through similar halls and hells worthwhile despite the repetition. Within the first few chapters, both the tone and gameplay loop you can expect for the vast majority of your playthrough are firmly established. A man is hunting his ex, Lord of the Vampires, down through an increasingly weird hotel, trying to stop a world ending ritual and gunning down any who get in his way. Hallways shift and werewolves prowl, but you always end up at the beginning, descending further each chapter. Despite the supernatural skin, this is a noir setup at heart, complete with tortured protagonist and inner monologues aplenty. The conflict between the two leads is believable and palpable whenever they interact. The soundtrack touches on any number of genres, but always manages to stay consistent, driving you forward at every opportunity. If the levels were halved, or more varied I think I would've had a near perfect game.Despite the initial fun of slow-motion and diving headfirst through crowds of enemies, I found myself growing tired with the 5 or 6 enemies that populate the entire game. While there are reprieves where the level design shifts to platforming or a boss fight, not enough of them varied to keep things feeling fresh for my entire playthrough. I also ran into a number of bugs in 15% of the levels that slowed the game down significantly.Still, I found myself drawn to the end. The breakfast outweighed the hallways, and each level conclusion reminded me why I kept playing. The heart beats ever onward.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A weird mash between Max Payne, Hotline Miami and Control, this game feels like a dream.I mean that in the literal sense - the sub-floors are alive with a sense of humour. They'll throw a hoard of vampires and werewolves at you whilst surrounded by toilets. They'll have recordings of a couple asking each other how the transformers have sex. They'll make you zig-zag in a cemetery that was a common date place for said lovers (one of them is a vampire), and it'll also have toilets.When you think you know what joke it'll throw at you next, they'll transform into neon voids and get you doing platforming.Overall, it has a rich story and the music somehow just works??? I suppose with the absurdity of the game it just has to.

_childDocuments_.review: Played 2.1 hours, wish I had refunded a few minutes before. The first Max Payne remains is my favorite PS2-era action game, I have had a passionate love affair with PC-first low budget indie games since Minecraft's original launch, due to the ability that format gives the developers to pursue unconventional ideas, and take the time necessary to adequately execute on a concept. The best of that format (Outer Wilds, Disco Elysium, The Case of the Golden Idol) offer novel, polished experiences that, outside of occasional Nintendo releases, we almost never see in the AAA or even AA space.This game is not low-budget, it's cheap. The 2.1 hours I have spent with it feel more like 10, due to the grating, repetitive nature of the level design. There are a total of 2 repeat enemies so far, with single encounters with 2 others. Each of these has exactly one mode of attack, and is used in the same 2-3 ways throughout the levels. The levels themselves have so few assets, recycled so gratuitously, that they often feel like pre-alpha leaks. They do not build one another, offer twists or new obstacles, or even any particular strategic challenge in the combat. The 4, generic weapons so far are just as effective against each of the enemy types. The reason Max Payne's combat worked so well was that the slow-mo diving changes the approach to combat against ranged enemies a great deal. With these melee enemies, the slow-mo ability hardly makes a difference. It is a surface-level aesthetic imitation without a basic understanding of the foundations.Even if the game has just one more level to go, I don't want to see it. Writing this review was more stimulating.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Don't sleep on this one. This is something special. Yes it's channelling Max Payne- and doing an excellent job of it. But you'll stay for the soundtrack and the narrative and the unforgettable, funny, disarming lead voice performance.Genuinely, this is one of the best games all year. Made by extremely good cool people. <3
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso Elsewhere is a Max Payne style third person shooter with quirky cutscenes and dialogue detailing the toxic relationship between our lead and his vampiric ex-gf (who is trying to end the world).The game is fast paced third person shooting action with a good variety of weapons and dialogue, excellent music and fun gameplay. It does drag a bit through the games 50+ stages with some of them feeling very much the same particularly near the end but the cutscenes and story break it up just enough to smooth the pacing out.The game has multiple endings and secrets to be found so there is lastability here too for those of you looking for multiple playthroughs and overall it's worth a play for a fun , stylish third person experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Well...it is great for the price. I love the music and the combat style reminds me of Max Payne for sure. Though, large part of the game is easy, it takes time before it gets difficult. The story, well it takes times to get into it. A lot of monologue. _childDocuments_.review: Tough call on this one. I really enjoyed learning the game, systems, etc. Once mastered though, I started craving some sort of challenge. Upping the difficulty just increases the damage scale from 2.0 to 5.0, so more than double, rather than changing enemy spawns or behavior. I read a lot of reviews of people getting burnt out at level 10, feeling like 40 more levels would be a grind. It does seem to get harder and harder as the levels progress, and when I started, I wondered how people could be getting burnt out. Well for me, I started to feel that way at level 15.Edit 1:I have been playing now on the hardest difficulty to try to make things challenging. I am noticing that the regular mobs and dogs are nearly one-shotting me, and everything above that, like witches and werewolves completely one-shot me. Makes me wonder what the point of healing is. The levels are getting harder, but in ways I am not a huge fan of. They like to spawn things right next to you or in ambush locations like dark souls. One area has a lot of grass/plants, which hides the dogs very well. Combine this with the witches tossing huge one-shot (my difficulty choice of course) projectiles at you, it starts to feel cheap rather than challenging.

_childDocuments_.review: Worthwhile homage to its influences. The control on this is so tight the muscle memory of playing max payne 2 just reawakened up within minutes. The fantasy noir blend works really well for a surprisingly enthralling narrative between slow mo dodging pistol clips into mummy skulls. Its soundtrack is a...choice that grew at on me by the end but hearing the lyrics kick in might knock the wind out of you the first time it happens. Definitely pickup if you're a fan of its Remedy predecessors.
