_childDocuments_.review: "Moooom, can you buy me Max Payne pleaaaase?""No, we already have Max Payne at home!"This is what this is. Kind of. But also not really. But for real though, this is a barely thumbs up from me.I reaaaally didn't like "EL PASO - NIGHTMARE" (see my review for that) and I hoped I would love "El Paso - Elsewhere". But in my opinion this is highly overrated.So let's go over the motion and get this Review over with.Graphics:I am soooo tired of Low Poly Graphics. Still I have to admit it fits here and after a while it even kinda grows on you. And even though the Game has some beautiful moments in some levels, it all looks dull and boring for the most part. Especially the first half looks super boring and samey. Sound:Pretty good overall, not much to complain here. Weapons sound good for the most part. But I have to say the "moaning sounds" of the enemies got on my nerves after a few levels.Music:Even though I don't really like "Rap/Hip Hop" I still found the Soundtrack to be really good. There were also some Rock Crossover Tracks and I think that every level had a different track and they were all really good.Strange choice but still also very fitting.Voice Acting:I mention Voice Acting here because the Main Character Voice Actor (I think it's also the Game Director) did a really good job here. The other Voice Actors did a decent job also, but the Main Character steals the Show.Story:I don't want to spoil anything here but this is basically some kind of supernatural Vampire Story with abusive Girlfriend elements. The story was what kept me playing in the end. because I wanted to see it through to the conclusion.Still it felt also kind of strange. Not even sure if I liked it or not, but I could identify with the main character at least.Btw. I hated the main antagonists name so much, I don't know why. But everytime the Word "Draculae" came up I had to cringe a little.Gameplay:So, the bread and butter for every Game. How is it? In short: I found it to be pretty boring.I mentioned Max Payne before. This is a third person shooter, you have a time slowing ability that fills up with more kills, you can roll and you can dive.Over the course of the whole Game you fight the same 5 basic enemies, 1 "Mini Boss" that appears a few times and 2 bosses. There is not much variety here. If you've played "EL PASO - NIGHTMARE" you already know all the enemies.But this Game is much easier and less frustrating/annoying than "EL PASO - NIGHTMARE".The Diving Mechanic did only see use in one room, where I dove 150 times in a row for an achievement. Otherwise there was NEVER a need to use it. It was basically completely useless.You just tap the time slow button, one tap every enemy in the head and that's it. Rinse and repeat.For some enemies roll came in handy at least.Overall I just wanted the Game to end but it overstayed it's welcome. 50 kind of short Chapters but it still was way too much. If it weren't for the story, I'm not sure if I could've finished it.First I played in small chunks because I got bored early on. Then I really pushed myself through the last 20 Chapters just because I wanted it to be over with.The Game is also very repetitive. Not only with the levels but also with the shooting. Enemies just run/jump at you and you shoot them. Some will shoot projectiles (some can also one shot you) but it is not enough.Shooting or rather the aiming felt off sometimes and overall it felt like a more janky/clunkier Max Payne even though most of it played well enough.Also you really have to push through the first chapters where EVERYTHING looks the same and everything repeats a 1000 times.By the end of the Game you know every single asset that was used by heart.And again, same with "EL PASO - NIGHTMARE" there was actually also one Achievement that didn't count even though I KNOW I got the requirements. And since this one Achievement didn't work and I'm missing only 2 for a 100%, I am not even going to attempt to get the second ending (even though I know that I am not even required to play through the full Game again).So, there are many things that I mentioned that sound super negative. And some of it really is in my opinion. But I still respect the Game and the work put into it and that's why I'm barely giving it a thumbs up.Also there obviously will be people that really enjoy this Game.I think they even have a movie planned for that. Wonder how this is going to turn out...

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere wasn't a game that I wholly enjoyed, but I can see why other people would. My personal issue is primarily that it's got a third person camera in a game with a ton of narrow corridors and small spaces, which makes actually seeing what's happening around you often a fiddly and annoying experience, and that the weapons seemed somewhat random in whether they put down enemies instantly or not, particularly the shotgun.The shotgun in general feels kind of ill served by the game's mechanics because if you're in slowdown, the fire rate between shots is so slow that you can barely fire twice before you run out, forcing you to slowdown, shoot, unslow, reload, slowdown, shoot, etc. which is effective but feels unintended.The movement and combat felt like it would be a better flow in larger, more open arenas, rather than the cramped spaces the game delivers, but what rescues it from being a game I actively disliked was the soundtrack. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the soundtrack slaps. You could ask me to shovel out a stable while that soundtrack was playing and I'd get hyped for moving ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in industrial quantities.

_childDocuments_.review: Short: Imagine Max Payne (like, someone took it  but trying to kill his vampire-queen ex and shooting through her horde of her monsters in her maze-like pocket dimension. It works somewhat and is fun, but it is flawed by putting Max Payne run-and-gun design into a survival-horror scenario, repetitive level design and enemies as well. The game does have good writing, it tries to make every dialog meaningful and impactful, but it over-relies on cutscenes. It is still a descent-to-good game overall, my down-thumb is because I feel that the focus went to the cutscenes rather than the gameplay itself. Long version: Let me try to boil down my opinion into a critique of a gameplay element: your right-click is a slow-mo dive that anyone who played Max Payne is familiar with. In Max Payne, you did this because you had to enter doors and go around corners where goons with guns that would shoot at you as soon as they saw you. The dive made their aim more worse and the slow-mo allowed you to the time to gun then down, giving you a critical advantage.None of the enemies in this game carry guns that justifies this mechanic. Instead, most of them are either melee enemies with zombie-like tactics or magic casters that fire near-undogable projectiles at you with large splash effect. Using the dive is bad because you have a short time window to shoot everything down. Instead, you are better off carefully moving forward and using slowmo to headshot enemies before they can reach you or fire at you. The player would be much benefited with a lean mechanic rather than a slowmo-dive. This is reflective in the lever design as well. The conceit of the level design is that you are entering an unreal alternative/pocket dimension constructed of elements of the real world and memories of the main characters. This is to justify a maze-like design that is very simple from a gameplay perspective and hefty reuse of assets. It becomes repetitive and boring. Some levels try to mix it up, but these are few and attempts at enviromental storytelling feel few. This issue of neglected focus on the actual game is also revealing with the game's two (maybe three?) boss battles that REALLY do not work well with Max Payne-esque movement design. I actually discovered that the roll mechanic is BETTER with those bossfights than the standard dodge, because you are able to duck below attacks. The enemies are visually interesting at first but are one-trick ponies with very little intelligence or tactics. They are stupid, have difficulty with the terrain and can be just gunned down. The game even does the thing where it just reskins old enemies and makes them tougher, but otherwise not much changed. The terrain also leaves soemthing to be desired. The game's conceit is that you are in a pocket dimension that constructs maze-like levels. Yet most of these levels feel nonsensical (unlike Max Payne's level that at least tried to imitate real-life locations), despite the significance the game gives them in the story. The story is finally what gave me a dilemma whether to reccomend the game or not. The story is good, there is one, it is connected to what you are doing, there are characters with motivation present, there is a plot, archs, drama.There is another aspect to critize and that is the graphics. The graphics are low-poly and do not try to impress with fancy features or massive textures. It instead tries to go for stlye and occasional effects. I applaud this notion. However, I feel that main characters should be given a slightly higher-poly models. The darkness-instead-of-eyes effect looks cool on static art for the game but during cutscenes it looks stupid. The gunplay is simple and the weapons have some room to be critized. You cannot switch between shoulders and I think the bullets start from your character and go towards your crosshair, sometimes resulting in situations where you miss because of the character's positioning. The camera is also awkward in tight spaces and there are more than there should be. The weapons are mostly standard fair and have some room to critize. You have only dual pistols and cannot select between dual or single. The shotgun is a near-melee weapon. What I dislike is the unstaged nature of the reload animations, you have to wait for the entire animation to happen rather than the reload happen in stages like in Helldivers 2 (where once you dropped the mag and inserted the new one, you don't have to do it all over again just because you had to dodge before you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ the gun). So why did I pick a thumbsdown? Because most of this story is told through cutscenes and those feel like the focus of the game. What environmental storytelling there is, is mostly the equivalent of audiologs (the game does not go as far as have random tapes but they are functionally that) scattered sometimes around the level randomly. What story there is, it is told outright rather than seen. Sometimes the level design TRIES to tell you the story but it doesn't tell you the story that the cutscenes are and you could be forgiven thinking that half of the levels are randomly-generated. Why are cutscenes a problem? Because I am a believer that video games should be interactive story mediums and if you want "cinematic" experiences, just make it all a damn movie. If your greatest creative focus for a video game is the cutscenes, then make your project a video of some sort so I can have popcorn in my hands rather than a controller that I am itching to use already. I understand this is a debetable position, but in the end, a review is an opinion and this is my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, and this is something we see a lot in video games.  Someone does something really cool and others want to do their spin upon the formula.  When it comes to the full dichotomy of third person shooters, there are a select few that when they arrived completely flipped the genre on its lid: and one title that spawned hundreds of shooters with its additions to the gaming world was 2001’s Max Payne.  With its popularization on the Bullet Time mechanics and achievements in low-pitched and grungy noir storytelling, it was a title that put one studio, Remedy Entertainment, on the map and another studio, Rockstar Games, higher in the clouds.So while the gaming world is now 12 years removed from the Max Payne franchise, love-letter imitators have circled the empty wagon in search of inspiration.  The newest title to greet the flock is Strange Scaffold’s El Paso, Elsewhere.  Instead of in the gritty streets of New York we start our story in the flat, desolate desert side of rural El Paso, Texas.  You play as James Savage, a vampire hunter with a love of painkillers right in line with your resident undercover cop as we join him on the crescendo of his journey to locate a vampire named Draculae and stop her before she ends the world.  Draculae is also James’ ex-girlfriend.  So you can see how this could be complicated for James.El Paso provides a small tutorial to get the feel for the descending floors of violence ahead of you but if you’ve played Max Payne you’re already ahead of the curve.  Fluid movements allow run n’ gun gameplay but you’ll have a bar dedicated to how much time you can slow which allows for precise aiming in hectic situations.  You’re equipped with a dodge roll that has a pretty generous amount of invincibility and a dive which is farther than a dodge roll but not necessarily as efficient.  There is a jump button to help with scaling furniture and some light platforming but it’s mostly used for specific points in the game and not something you’ll use often.James carries a litany of weaponry that’ll be used to stop the hordes in front of you.  Pistols, Uzis, Tommy Guns, Shotguns, Explosives: the arsenal is brought out for James and it’s well stocked.  Stakes are used as James’ melee option but they are limited, you can refill your stakes by breaking wooden structures which is just an odd design choice having to ram your face into every wooden structure to be properly equipped for battle.  Guns lack a particular punch in visuals and sound with the exception of the Shotgun which absolutely deletes enemies and was my main weapon throughout the game.  There’s something barbarically enjoyable about a close range shotgun blast morphing an enemy into a wall with a loud shrill of buckshot and a Dragonball Z-like instant teleportation into another area.  Hilarity ensues far longer than it probably was intended.The vampiric army James has to mow down consists of your usual suspects: mummies, werewolves, priestesses, puppet makers, biblically accurate angels (no, really).  Enemies hit hard and quickly so maintaining distance is vital to survival.  Distance though, is very easy to obtain as most of the enemies are not smart and are very easily exploitable.  Mummies will walk in a straight line to you so it’s easy to cater them into a hallway and casually dispose of them.  Werewolves will always provide an audio cue before jumping which is an easy tell to remove them with a shotgun blast (very satisfying to hit in the air regardless), and the angels fly high enough in the air you can pick them off from several rooms away since most of the levels do not have ceilings.Enemies consistently sway from overtly easy to sigh-inducing hard due to two scenarios: size of crew and choice of position.  For tracking, I played on the defaulted Intended difficulty, but you can use sliders to choose the correct difficulty on damage done, damage taken, infinite ammo, etc.  It’s a very nice touch that caters to fine-tuning the correct amount of sweat to feel during battles.  When dealing with a normal pack of enemies, the writing is on the wall on how to handle each one, but slamming a large amount in a small room is less on making competently hard battles but more on a trial-and-error on what to do when they all spawn.  No room in El Paso is hard per se, but instead is startling because when 8 enemies pop on screen in areas you’re not ready for with a jump on how to kill you, that’s not prepping a smartly positioned battle, that’s prepping for the inevitable second try with extra information.This happens when the design does not meet the demands.  In Max Payne, the Bullet Time and acrobatic dives work because you knew enemies would do and would punish you for not making use of all the tools provided.  You had to use those moves because if you walked into a room and just started shooting, you’d get plugged with bullets and die immediately.  El Paso suffers from the opposite of this.  Constantly throughout my 9 hours I succumbed to checking corners and shooting warning shots into rooms to proc enemies because I was tired of losing health by playing the game like it feels like you should.  Enemies hide directly behind closed doors and breakable areas, forcing damage taken and in some later levels an instant death.  Random rooms will spawn cannon-fodder alongside y-axis-abusing priestesses (who kill in 2 hits) and angels (who kill in 1 hit) that will send you to a title screen from way off-screen.  You want to go guns blazing, and the game wants you to go guns blazing,  but you’re instead penalized by dying repeatedly because a majority of the enemies hit like trains and doing the cool stuff gets you killed.  El Paso forces a sense of passivity that makes the game drag its feet across a staggering fifty levels, which feels about as passive as the gameplay as most areas are bland room-to-room setups that offer very simple puzzle-elements that are required to move on to the next area.  Hostages are strewn about each level for you to save or kill, which never really gets explained why they’re there other than a moral objective for the game’s two endings, and sometimes colored hearts are needed to open doors?  The whole concept of floor-to-floor progression felt very disjointed and played more like plot filler to give James a reason to descend these many floors.And I’m sorry, but I cannot let this soundtrack go.  Some levels are backed with rap songs tuned to spoken-word by James himself in an attempt to infuse the music provided with the internal mental struggle and violent tendencies instilled throughout his journey and it just does not hit.  It’s jarring trying to play the game and hearing these songs come on as it’s hard to aim when you’re laughing as hard at the game instead of the songs providing the fuel to continue forward.That said, what shines brightly throughout El Paso was the writing and the cinematography splashed throughout the game’s cutscenes.  You can really feel the writer’s room working extra hard to provide a desolate man hopped on pills and going weeks without sleep drudge through each floor with a molasses-slopped interlude piecing together a puzzle he does not want to finish, but must.  I would love to kick back and watch a show built around this style of writing and camera work, but it’s a shame the narrative is surrounded by what the game eventually became.  It’s been documented the troubles that came with El Paso’s development and how the unhealthy structures of creating video games nowadays played a hand in creating a potential rift between expected dream and confirmed reality.  But when the end product is like what El Paso, Elsewhere eventually became, sometimes it’s a hard pill you have to swallow.

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere certainly remixes some elements found in the old Max Payne games, but the gameplay is quite different from Max Payne, and in my view, it is a bit broken. I''ll give a few examples:* The enemies you encounter here have either meelee attacks, or shoot slow-ish missiles with splash damage. Because of that, bullet time is only a gimmick. I did not come across a situation where it actually helped, let alone where bullet time was required to win a fight.* The enemy AI is bad - you are often able to shoot monsters before they even register your presence. If you turn up the difficulty the game is still not easy because everything kills you with either 1 or 2 hits. A zombie or werewolf that spawns on top of you in a narrow corridor will still get you sometimes.* My impression is also that there is a rather sudden increase in difficulty around 2/3 of the game and some of the boss fights are much harder than the rest of the game.* The character's meelee attack (stakes, obviously) is also a questionable design choice: given that enemies are either meelee and able to kill you in 1 or 2 hits, or are airborne, there is no point in using it at all, except for when the game forces you to.Apart from the gameplay, I found the story decent, the visual presentation nice and the sound quite good. The voice acting and great music is probably what made me finish the game, regardless of its shortcomings.While I do not recommend this game because it has too many design flaws, it is still a passable sort-of-retro arcade shooter with a good presentation. You might want to play it for that, but do not expect something like Max Payne.One final nit-pick: running the game locked at 60 FPS on UHD resolution makes my RTX 4080 draw 200+ watts and turn its fans on. Given how the game looks, this took me by surprise. With some playing around I found out that the post-processing effects and the colorful-noise-shader you see in the background of the ceiling-less rooms are what takes all this processing power. Turning down the rendering resolution a lot mitigated this for me, and because the textures and geometry are so low-res, the game practically looks the same. I know that achieving a better level of optimization than present here might not be worth it for an indie game.

_childDocuments_.review: A visually pleasing, bland, low-action shooter, dripping with adolescent relationship cringe.This game's one strength is the aesthetics of the levels. Visually, they are interesting to look at. A neon red sun at the horizon under a patchy, shifting green sky. Dim lighting of every color scattered throughout. Fog-covered graveyards, mausoleums, sketchy motels, rooms that are upside down, objects suspended midair by a mysterious force -- there is always something cool to look at.The rest of the game is either plainly not compelling or actively unpalatable.The map layouts are bland and don't feel very fun to explore. The idea is you are supposed to find all the hostages in the level, rescue them, and then backtrack through the level to the beginning, but in "hard mode", TimeSplitters style. However, there is often not a very clear direction forward, and you are meant to walk around kind of aimlessly to find some hostages, which unlocks a door somewhere else but it's not clear where. So you have to walk around the level again to see which gate was unceremoniously opened. There are some gaps near the floors that you can roll under, or some waist-level barricades that you can dive over, but there's hardly any advantage to doing it, since the enemies are so easily dispatched just by kiting them around.The "save the hostages" goal of most of the levels feels really unrewarding, almost like an afterthought. You find a random NPC crouching in a room by themselves, saying "I don't wanna die!". Then you save them by standing next to the holding E, and they pump their fist and say something corny like "Wow! You're my hero!", then disappear. Completely unsubstantial.The enemy AI is way too simple. In some levels you can jump onto some height, like a hedge or gravestone, and the enemies will walk in a circle around you, and you can take your time picking them off. The enemy variety is low, the enemies that you do see have simple melee attacks, or jump at you in a way that is dodged by just strafing, which you're doing anyway.The Bullet Time, diving, and rolling techniques are completely unnecessary because the combat is so simple and easy. Most big encounters with lots of enemies are taken care of by retreating into a hallway and picking them off as they funnel in -- yawn.The voice acting is awful. The protagonist's actor has this "too cool to actually try" kind of tone with the delivery of every single line. It comes across as flat and uninspired, and makes the main character feel really lame. There are little lines that needlessly play "Nice, ammo", when picking up ammo or "Always need more pills" when picking up pills. You advance to a central hub in a level, and a bunch of enemies appear as the door closes behind you, and the thrill is watered down when the protagonist pipes up to flatly say "♥♥♥♥.... that's a lot of monsters.". The main character's past is revealed by finding and activating film cameras (which only play audio for some reason?), rewarding the player with a clip of two people talking to each other like they're 16 years old and have a crush on each other "would you like me if i was....... a vampire?" "then i would really,really,really like you!".Too many things are pointlessly explained by the main character instead of being left to the player to discover. For example "I guess that beacon lighting up means I killed enough monsters to proceed." Ok? Did that really need explaining?The plot is mostly the main character talking to himself in an elevator, with thrilling topics such as "it's so hard to be good, because you have to keep doing good things, and also not do bad things" and "i have this problem, where i think too much about stuff..". Feels like someone is trying to sound deep and smart.Lastly, the soundtrack ranges from weak EDM to unbearably cringe rap. The EDM is tolerable and even a little enjoyable on some levels, but the rap is vocalized again by the main character's actor (I'm sick of hearing his voice), and the lyrics are so cringe "I'm a ♥♥♥♥♥♥' demon" that i ended up muting it.Overall, the gameplay offers no challenge or excitement, the music is bad, storytelling is cringe, and visual design can't carry the dead weight. I would not recommend this game to anyone unless it goes on sale for maybe $3 or less.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most theraputic games I've ever played. Amazing how well it lets you vent your frustrations. What frustrations, you ask? Imagine you're a millenial, your parents are still alive, and they own a ton of junk. Like, a lot a lot of junk. Perhaps even one room in their house is filled with so much useless crap and furniture that it has been downsides into a corridor you can't walk through without tripping over something, and getting rid of even one bit of it is a no-no because possession is 9/10ths of the law. Thanks mom and dad. This game is a hotel full of those kinds of rooms, and maybe even some rooms that are completely normal but the furniture in that real life room-turned-corridor really BURNS YOU UP and GOD does it feel good to smash a wardrobe to pieces in a single attack. And tables! And stacks of chairs! Why can't I dodge straight into a bunch of set pieces and watch them crumble to bits in seconds?!Oh, and you get to shoot supernatural monsters in abstract rooms with way too much sector lighting. Good fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of Remedy games so the Max Payne style gunplay and tone, and to a lesser extent the Alan Wake/Control inspired supernatural stuff in the level design was really clear and executed really well. In the gameplay department, the game is simple, a bit repetitive, but enjoyable enough for me to say I had fun the whole time. And that's what matters.The story didn't really grab me, and the game went on just a bit too long (50 levels), which was compounded by the fact that a lot of the levels look very similar. I am normally a fan of the edgy noir style dialogue (as was executed well in Max Payne) but something here didn't do it for me. It could be the writing itself and the humour that I didn't really vibe with, but also probably the voice acting...I don't really know how to say this nicely, but the main voice actor (who's also the game director) loves his own voice maybe a little too much. Don't get me wrong, he has a pretty good voice, but it's maybe a bit too overacted with his whispery vocal fry tone, and the mic picking up his mouth noises. You also hear the voice A LOT, including in some of the music, so that did get a little tiresome over the almost 10 hours I played this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Max Payne style combat flows really well with a nice variety of guns to shoot and enemies to kill. _childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I'm usually the type of guy who plays games for escapism. It's hard to get me to stick with a narrative or long cutscenes. Despite that ,this game has made me change how I consume media and I absolutely cannot recommend it enough.Gameplay: The game plays like Max Payne through and through. While I hadn't played Max Payne before, just watching gameplay footage side by side tells you what you're in for. The bullet time mechanic is really fun but you never really need to dive. There are only 3 enemies that shoot projectiles and all of them are slow moving with large weakspots. The level design is wonderful and trippy. It feels like the devs ran out of level ideas halfway through but the last few final levels are an awesome sendoff. What you're really here for is the story. While the levels started getting stale, I powered through them just so I can get to the next cutscene. The dialogue and voice acting is absolutely top notch.Sound/Music: There are not many sound effects for NPC's or monsters. The vampire groan gets particularly grating. The music is going to be a highlight. The slightly cringe rap singlehandedly rules the soundtrack. I listen to a few of the songs on Spotify often. The vibe matches the aesthetic of the game perfectly. Overall, the game does drag in the later half. About half of the levels could be removed with nothing of value being lost. The diving and dodging feel half backed. The enemies don't have much variety. Despite ALL of that, the pure VIBES this game gives off makes it an easy reccomend to anyone, especially fans of Remedy games. The soundtrack and gameplay mesh to create a breakup album of a game that does not pull any punches.I don't think any game has made me so excited for a cutscene. El Paso Elsewhere is a gem.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the kind of acting that reminds me that most games have serviceable acting at best. That drip-feed of narration is half of what kept me going through the rest of this. The combat was clean, though there's a general lack of consistent feedback for when you're taking damage.What nearly stopped me from finishing the game were the few bosses, mainly on level 30 and 50. It went from a fairly forgiving shooter to something that required Dark Souls timing, and the controls are not set up for that level of precision. It required constant rolling and I got killed while healing or reloading so many times that I actually deleted the game for a few days. I know I could have just fiddled with the difficulty settings, but that that point I was so frustrated I found it easier to just walk away for a while.But that is the joy of the large list of settings you get when you start a level. You can customize just about every aspect of the difficulty. So that's what I did, I played around with the settings and got past it.And I'd say it was worth it, because there's a genuinely satisfying ending beyond that. The writing in this game has an appreciation for grief that you don't often see in the medium. Well worth the time, and forgiving enough that most people can see the ending if they want to.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Right off the bat: If you are a fan of Max Payne, just get this.This game is clearly tributing and inspired by that, but has a neat occult story involving vampires and a protagonist who stuck it in the craziest of crazies. Rather than have a smaller number of large levels, this has 50 levels, but which are much smaller in scope. Fights are often in tight quarters, which did happen more than I liked, but you're always equipped for it. Personally, aside from a couple of levels, I never found this particularly hard on the normal difficulty, though I suspect it would be much trickier with a controller.Where they really nailed it and did well by their Max Payne inspirations is the combat. Every weapon is punchy and while there is a lot of ammo around, you'll often have to switch around and pay attention in combat, especially since the guns won't automatically reload when you run out of ammo. And of course, there's bullet time and it's executed perfectly here. Using this regularly, but sparingly is key to having smooth combat encouters and I had it down pat well before the halfway mark. Accompanying this is one of the most banging soundtracks I've heard in a game in some time. A combination of a great score and electronic/rap combo tracks with vocals by the game's Creative Director, they add an incredible amount to the combat flow. The game would have been good without this soundtrack, but it's great with it.I personally really enjoyed the story as well, particularly how it comes together at the end. There are multiple endings and I only saw one, but I was satisfied by it. There aren't cutscenes after every level, but there are enough of them to keep the story moving without feeling like you're constantly being interrupted.If you like Max Payne or just third-person action games in general, I think you owe it to yourself to try this. Not everyone will jive with the low-fi graphics, but with the way it plays, I think you'll quickly not care about that.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere, is a moody, Max Payne inspired shooter where you go on a one-way trip to stop your ex from destroying the world. This game itself was a fun experience. Although there were tense moments and challenging fights, I overcame them by dedicating extra focus and effort. For me, I found the gameplay to be a solid experience, but what I think the game is most enjoyable for is its story between the MC (James) and Draculae (his ex). To put it simply, this game is quite the reflection of a hurt man trying to wrestle with his feelings, against his goal to stop his former lover.I strongly recommend you play this game! With strong writing, fun game play, and even better music, you won’t be missing out!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game not expecting much, and got one of the best written stories I've seen in a long, long time. The core game play itself isn't super special, but its very fun and you end up getting a decent amount of weapons that all play different and have their own uses. The movement isn't perfect, but it forces you to have good positioning and once you're good with it you can enjoy feeling stylish while you kill a whole room of enemies in bullet time. It took me about 10 hours to beat game on Challenging difficulty, and with a soundtrack that dares to be different and a story that grips you so deeply you don't want to stop playing, this game is worth its full price.Game play rating: 7,5/10Story rating 9.5/10Overall 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Certainly influenced by Max Payne, El Paso Elsewhere is a run and gun arcady bullet time shooter with massive amounts of atmosphere. Had a lot of fun playing through this one, plus the game gives you the ability to add modifiers to your playthrough which can change up the gameplay drastically from run to run. _childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute Kino! And I use that word very lightly!Growing up, I developed quite the fixation on Max Payne. It being the very first game I could categorically call my first Narrative Experience as everything beforehand on the N64 and OG Xbox was something I was kind of just engaging with on a “Pretty Spectacle, Pretty Colors” sort of vibe until Maxy swept me off my feet with his eloquently spoken sarcastic musings on Norse Mythology and Pulpy Talkalongs to cope with his own personal trauma.It also helped it was the best action game I had ever played at that point.And nothing else really hit that itch of level detail, interactivity and immersive Neo-Noir Atmosphere except perhaps it’s Sequel, with nary a game really out there that could match dual-wielding-shoot-dodging style with only a few coming close like Enter The Matrix, Wet, John Woo’s Stranglehold, Total Overdose and El Matador (It’s a fun game, shut up!) but absolutely none of them matched the Writing Chops of Sam Lake so my lust for Neo-Noire Pulp always left me blue-balled--Oh Hai El Paso Elsewhere!El Paso Elsewhere is a Supernatural Third-Person Neo-Noir Romp right out of the early 00’s, feeling like an amalgamation of Max Payne and practically half a dozen other games like they all flew out of the blender yet it absolutely lands firmly on its feet by staying true to itself, as despite it’s Meta moments and perspective shifting it absolutely tells it’s story with a straight face and while it makes room for a joke or two, it takes it’s subject matter very seriously despite the sheer bluntness of the Paranormal Situation the main lead finds himself in.That is absolutely Sam Lake. James Savage feels as genuine as Max Payne Himself.But the narrative truly is more than just waxing poetically on Esoteric Mythology and Snarky Observations. The Bulk of the story is an astonishingly deep and methodically spoken narrative of a Broken Romance, Emotional Abuse and Pyschological Torture that I truly wasn’t prepared for nor was I expecting it to be better written then many movies I’ve seen explore these subjects, especially as despite how real these people sound and feel you could honestly count the number of polygons on their character models with both hands!Speaking of which, the actual Graphics, while despite resembling something from 2000 or earlier are still drenched in atmosphere despite their low-fidelity and are paired with great sound, whether it be punchy gunfire or rabid snarls of nearby enemies punctuated by a highly varied soundtrack I wasn’t expecting to jam out to!Gameplay is nothing but sweeps and dives, obviously. But the care in the level design to funnel both the enemy and player into tight-quartered battles is very well done for the most part with heavy destructibility to keep the firefights tight! Coupled with one of the most overtly detailed Custom Difficulty settings I’ve ever seen, I was openly replaying some levels with different mutators just for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles!So, what DOES El Paso Elsewhere not do very well? Honestly it’s just mild annoyances. Some enemies can get too close but that’s what stakes through the heart are for, some levels start to feel a bit samey with the reused assets and perhaps the game could have been trimmed by 10 levels or so and I would have loved if the game did not despawn ragdolls and debris so quickly but really, it’s an all around solid game that would feel too dismissive to call just another low-poly throwback shooter.It’s just a fantastic blend of some many different inspirations and slapped together with such care and precision that it becomes its own animal.I Couldn’t Recommend El Paso Elsewhere more! On a side note, I could honestly fall asleep to the Voice Actor who did James Savage, he should seriously consider doing audio books!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is a very fun stylistic adventure where you play as James Savage, a combination tribute character to Blade and Max Payne, as he battles his way through legions of vampires, werewolves, and angels in an effort to save the world. Your girlfriend is actually the queen of the vampires and is attempting to complete one last ritual to fully ascend to her throne and rule over the world, and you have to descend floor by floor in the motel she is hiding out in to root out that evil and destroy it once and for all. El Paso, Elsewhere as a whole takes inspiration from Max Payne, Blade, Control, Hotline Miami, and more to present a very cool story with a pretty simple gameplay loop. You'll pick up an arsenal of weapons throughout the levels and traverse some neat environments to take out the vampire/werewolf/angel horde, doing sick jumps and flips and slow-motion rolls and such to keep looking badass, all while popping dozens of pills to keep your health high (this man has died of several dozen overdoses how the hell is he still alive). El Paso, Elsewhere's narration/story/voice-acting is surprisingly well-written and dramatic for a smaller indie project, and even remembers to not take itself too seriously every now and then. The soundtrack is pretty fun, featuring some rap vocals by the main character himself which is cool to see. If I had one gripe with El Paso, Elsewhere, it's that it definitely over-stays its welcome. There's 50 levels to play through to complete the whole story, and while there are new environments and plot moments to experience, the gameplay and enemies get pretty redundant after a while, and I think the length would have been just perfect at 30-35 levels. Overall though, I think El Paso, Elsewhere is a super enjoyable experience and I highly recommend to anybody with a vague interest in some simple Blade-Max-Payne-style vampire-slaying.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This was a very enjoyable experience. The levels are short and sweet and the gunplay feels solid, though there was some jankiness with the aiming at enemies in very close proximity. All of that combined with stylish and moody visuals set to an equally moody soundtrack (with more rap than I was expecting!), make for a great game. Highly recommended if you enjoy your games with supernatural elements, bullet-time and brooding, self-reflecting protagonists on a mission.

_childDocuments_.review: "...El Paso, Elsewhere is Strange Scaffold’s homage to Max Payne games of yore; a fatalistic trip towards self-destruction. James Savage knows he only has one option: kill his ex, Draculae, to prevent her from ending the world via primordial sacrifice; and likely, himself, in the process.Level by level, encounter by encounter, James’ snippets of memories come through, drip fed like a parasocial hit of dopamine, a window into his ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up life and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up relationship he had with Draculae. In the incessant shooting; in the swarming groans of enemies; in the ceaselessly irreverent soundtrack; these moments of quiet honesty punctuate and juxtapose the loudness of everything else that’s going on; James’ words are a solace in the middle of a storm....we’re reliving James’ nightmares; the horrors of dread and pain intertwined with love, knowing these things will never be disentangled from each other, or from him..."A diary entry about IMMORTALITY - Signalis — The King in Yellow — El Paso, Elsewhere — Isle of the Dead — Stories of Your Life and Others / ArrivalOn dreading the future, facing fear, and how to move forward for the sake of love - for the sake of yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a truly unique experience!The Music & Dialogue is great and every gunshot feels impactful.Literally lighting up the room with every enemy I shoot and diving last second out of the way of projectiles creates combined with the slow motion effect a cinematic gameplay.There are moments where I just thought: DAMN that was cool. The brutal energizing songs raise my pulse and want to make me break ♥♥♥♥, kill people (ingame/ it's a song reference).These wolves, jumping out of the corner and me just sending them flying mid jump with the shotgun is just hilarious. Very enjoyable.This is one of those games that just makes you feel like no other game.

_childDocuments_.review: PillsPillsPillsThe voice acting was so engaging that I could listen to James and Janet talk all day.Once the music hits it's hard not to find yourself bobbing your head back and forth to these hypnotic beats.The monster variety is cool and the levels are quick yet challenging. _childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This game helped me get out of an abusive relationship. It captured that feeling of being trapped and chasing that one good day with a person and never knowing if anyone could ever love you in a way where you made them think life was good. It captures the prison that puts you in. And it captures where I'm at now, which is recovering from all that. Trying to figure out how to be a person again, and figure out what's real and what's not. Trying to figure out what love is again. Trying to figure out a lot of stuff really. I actually wrote down the full Ferris Wheel monologue to show it to my therapist. I've never done this but I even messaged the developer on twitter just to say thank you(he responded, which was also really cool). I give this game as high a review as I can.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Max Payne, so of course I had to give it a shot.  The voice acting and music are solid.  The game functions well but the gameplay loop fails due to the enemy design.  Max Payne style dodging and bullet time worked for Max Payne since the enemies had big damage and range, really needed that more here.  It probably deserves a "meh" button, but I honestly don't think I'd recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Positive but with caveats. Story, voice acting and music make this game better than it is.Gameplay is so damned repetitive, needed something to enhance it as by level 37/50 I am really bored. _childDocuments_.review: First off, the voice acting and writing are phenomenal, really good performances. I love the story, the whole idea behind it, this would easily make a good mini series. The gameplay however is whole other story, basically, you think you're gonna get Max Payne with vampires, but that gameplay really doesn't work for the enemies in this game. They are mostly melee enemies, and the bullet time dodge is practically useless as you're not dodging any projectiles. You're better off just triggering the bullet time while standing still and getting easy headshots. It just really doesn't work and it also stays its welcome way too long. There are 50 levels and they get incredibly tedious and repetitive. Would have been better with maybe half of them, maybe even less.All and all, I liked it for the story, the gameplay is quite mediocre.6/10
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: To me this game is refreshing. Many people compare it to Max Payne which is fair but it finds it's own unique place and for me surpasses Max Payne in a lot of ways. It has a great quality of making you empathize with the main character and the supporting cast in a way that most games could only hope to stumble into. This however, is no stumble as every level the mood and the dialogue along with the level design itself seem to be in harmony even when the game world continues to unravel.Alongside the feelings and vibes of El Paso Elsewhere the gameplay is so fluid and punchy that while much of the missions follow a similar formula, you never get tired of blasting a werewolf into the great beyond with a last ditch point blank shotgun blast. It also rewards and fosters your skills as a player as you keep playing. As the game gets more complex with more enemies all of which have really unique designs and mechanics, and weapons that all seem to have a purpose. You will find yourself managing some really impressive performances that leave you with an exhilaration that few games reach.All in all I wish I picked this up sooner because it shows that the Indie scene still blows all of the big releases out of the water.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a fun (if repetitive) 3rd person story shooter that could have used some tightening up writing wise. The OST goes from being pretty good to being not great (I wasn't a fan of the raps) and the boss difficulty spikes were a bit annoying.  I really appreciate the swings they are taking and can't wait to see what else they are working on!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I stumbled across this game by accident with no expectations going into it. This was probably for the best as I was so happy to have stumbled across this unexpected Max Payne inspired game that I was giddy with nostalgia when playing it. The soundtrack is incredible and incredibly silly but that is it's charm.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A tasty third person shooter with slo-mo bullet time ala classic Max Payne,  El Paso Elsewhere is a very smokeable action game with amazing art direction, killer voice acting, and 60 excessively fun, albeit periodically repetitive levels for you to blast, duck, and dodge your way through. This is an art house action game in the vein of something made by Remedy, albeit on a much a smaller scale. Wishing the developer(s) the best for their future endeavors.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This game features Max Payne-esque gameplay with a dark and deeply personal story with excellent voice-acting, and if you pay attention, you WILL feel things. I'm very much looking forward to what Xalavier does next.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: If Max Payne and John Costitine had adopted a child, and he grow up to be just like them, except he dated Dracula who was actually a very depress woman who now wants to destroy the world because of her mess up life. thats the game in a nutshell..... buy it, 48 levels to beat the game with a protagonist you'll actually love and empathize with.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Great narration, excellent voice work, nice general idea. Music can be hit and miss, but the effort is definitely there.Gameplay is mid, though. Bland melee enemies for the first dozen (!) of levels, I almost fell alsleep. Eventually ranged enemies arrive, they spice up things a bit... though there's still little reason to use dodges (of which there are two kinds for some arcane reason). Enemy AI is very weak, they constantly struggle with pathfinding, get stuck in the walls and doors, "brides" tend to ignore player and nearby combat, etc. Monster variety is really low, "Mega"-variants of monsters are just reskins with a bit of extra damage or survivability - in practice, not making any difference whatsoever.99% of combat is sleep-inducing trivial and boring, 1% are ambushes spawned right on top of you and enemies hidden by camera and claustrophobic level design (still trivial though).But yep, still a thumbs up. Narrative and voiceacting makes the shambling gameplay tolerable.

_childDocuments_.review: A bizarre, funny, well acted story in an interesting setting, with some of the best writing in the medium, mechanically and visually feels like playing a mixture of Max Payne and Control except with frequently boring repetitive gameplay and a length that has it stay long past its welcome.El Paso, Elsewhere is visually similar to a Playstation era title with the movement and controls of the first two Max Payne titles with some of the colors and environment styles that can feel like you are playing Control. The story involves your character entering a motel to stop his ex, the lord of vampires, from destroying the world. He believes his addictions as well as the battles themselves will lead to his death. As you enter an elevator you are transported to the void and are slowly lowered down where floor after floor you must fight through an area while attempting to rescue people who have been captured to be used as sacrifices. As you your journey goes on the environments shift from the motel to areas that were important to your ex's life and some by extension important to your life. Memories of both your lives are discussed with entities you meet, each other, and can be further expanded on by finding projectors in stages themselves. Radios are also scattered around with often humorous stories or references to noir style monologue filled with increasingly ridiculous metaphors. The visual style and writing are the highlights of the game and can make it worth playing on their own merits. Though another issue is that it takes about 1/3 of the game for that writing to go beyond just being entertaining to reaching that next level.The problems with the game come from the dull enemies that don't fit with the Max Payne bullet time style gameplay. That there are 50 stages and you only start to see more interesting things around 20 stages in. You are only given enough enemy variety for combat to be interesting and a bit varied, if the enemies were even fun to fight (which they typically aren't), around stage 26. Nothing interesting is ever done with the hostages you want to save, they are just sitting around waiting to be saved, there is no threat to them, no timed deaths, no real issue even if they do die from you killing them other than a slightly different ending. Even when the enemy variety is better and the stages become more interesting you are still doing the same thing over and over and with how long it took to get to the second half of the game I was just wanting it to end, keeping the slightly higher quality of the gameplay from making much of a difference at that point. As there can often be points where something narrative wise might only happen over other level it would have felt like a much better experience if about 1/3 of the stages had been cut.There is a dull weightlessness to the combat where bullets hit enemies until they die and rarely feel like they did anything until that moment, you can take a massive hit that takes off 60+% of your health and not even know you got hit unless you look at your healthbar, the stake melee attacks are powerful damage wise but there is no visceral satisfaction for hitting an enemy with one. The entire Max Payne style gameplay of using a slow-motion toggle, diving, rolling, etc is almost entirely pointless due to the boring melee focused enemies and how you move with where the reticle is in relation to your body always makes aiming a bit awkward. Rolling becomes more useful about 27 stages in when there are some enemies with AoE attacks you can try to roll out of the way off but you never really want to dive into a room in slow motion shooting things because it isn't practical with these kinds of enemies and isn't even fun due to lack of any real response to your shots and lack of things like the killcam Max Payne games had. The only positive thing I can say for the gameplay is that there are great difficulty settings where you can alter anytime you start a new game or continue your current one, you can give yourself infinite ammo and stakes, change the speed, change how much slow motion time you have, change enemy and weapon damage, enemy health, etc and from playing on the base settings for 35 stages when I realized it was never going to become remotely enjoyable and I gave myself infinite stakes and ammo so I at least wouldn't be bothered with picking up supplies or needing to melee objects to try to find more stakes.It's a game that I am glad that I played and will continue to think of in the future, especially now that the gameplay is over.Has the annoying frequently found problem in PC titles where it doesn't disable your controller when using a keyboard and has no ability to turn off controller rumble, so if you keep a controller plugged in you will likely want to unplug it.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: hard to put into words,One hand i would like to say there are definitely moments of this game that were enjoyable, The cheesy EMO rap was fun at times but other times it was kinda annoying. I was enjoying the game  and i get to around level 35 and i realized i was no longer having a great time with the story telling any further. It's just like a repeat of the same topics repeatedly and it grows boring, then you toss in the fact this game has 50 levels, FIFTY!. i literally had to quit the game to keep checking to ensure i was making progress to finish the damn game because i wanted to quit at the end. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bosses, man i was playing on challenging and getting instant KO'd within seconds, their attack patterns have zero wind up either. I found them so frusterating that i decided to cheese the game by adjusting the speed they move at down to 00.01 just to move on past them after attempting for 2+ hours to make progress.Let's talk about the story, it doesn't really seem to go anywhere after having seen both the good and bad endings, ultimately boring.Gameplay wise its a real nod to old school gameplay found in the mid 1990's, Its fun on its own and it can be a bit challenging on the higher difficulty settings. ultimately i can either recommend or not and i think this ain't it chief.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a banger soundtrack, a nice story (if you like it edgy, and I do), and solid dub.  It wears the Max Payne's inspirations on its sleeve. Grey main character, bullet time, even pieces of a fictional in universe story played through radios (and I am part of the Address Unknown fandom), But it doesn't deserve a thumbs up. Why doesn't it though?It's mechanically disjointed. In Max Payne, the whole point of the bullet time (beside balancing unfair fights) was to make the gunfights cinematic, see the bullets fly around. Here it doesn't serve any other purpose than to kil the enemies faster.Speaking of enemies, most of them attack in melee, which make the bullet dodge useless about 99% of the time, and the few enemies that use ranged, either produce explosions, which negate it too, or don't attack often enough for it to be practical.The dodge-rolls are barely untroduced and nearly useless until the first boss, halfway through the game. You better learn fast then.The level design is inexistent. It's flat, boring and labyrinthic. At this point, I'm crawling through because I want to know how it ends.So why the thumbs up ?Potential. El Paso Nightmare sucked big time compared to this. This game is leagues better and I believe the developer will end up doing an actually great game in the future. And for that, they'll need money, and I want them to have it.So, sorry if this thumbs up is the one need to the rating on the positive side, and you've bought this game thinking it would be good. It's not. But the next one will be.

_childDocuments_.review: Not really my thing. I'm recommending it because even though I don't necessarily like it, it is written well and some people definitely will enjoy it. As far as the gameplay goes, it is well executed and feels great. It gets a little repetitive toward the end, but overall, pretty good. I'm not the biggest fans of the original "hip-hop" tracks but some of the instrumentals are really, really good. Again, this wasn't really for me, but if you are into the melodramatic style of Max Payne then you will get something out of this.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly loved playing this game and its attempt to recreate the feeling of Max Payne with its own twist. Like Max Payne, its story is quite interesting and its bittersweet ending wasn't what I expected but had me thinking about it well after the credits had rolled. The music is 100% something i didn't expect to be so good. Its so good that im occasionally listening to it on my off time. I think the only issue I had with the game was some glitches and some of the levels. There's a level that almost made me put down this amazing game. _childDocuments_.review: Claustrophobic Max Payne, shoot werewolves and mummy vampires as you turn around dark corners, there's little reason to jump dodge though, so it's mostly about using your limited slow-mo time to hit perfect headshots as fast as possible, your crosshair is a tiny, tiny little dot in the middle of the screen and even the shotgun doesn't spread much further than that, every shot has to be done with maximum precision, so you go in a room, turn on slow motion, hit every shot as soon as possible, headshot after headshot, clear, into the next room, repeat. Very hypnotic, so long as you don't meet the puppeteer enemy, that guy is a bastard.Only problem I had is that, at around 7-8 hours long, the game is TOO long, there are stronger variations of the base enemies but that isn't enough and it gets very repetitive, at around 50 chapters long, I feel like this game could be 10-15 chapters shorter. Thankfully the story is amazingly written and the soundtrack is a bop and they both cap off wonderfully so it's worth seeing it to the end, just, take your time with it so you don't end up bored like me.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty decent! very stylistically really cool at face value and the soundtrack is fun albeit a little goofy. but the gameplay never quite reaches a satisfying level. and I've heard it's insanely long for what it is. which is a shame because overall it's SO CLOSE to getting the "max payne but mixed with modern remedy weirdness" thing right, but lack of polish and cohesion in the gameplay really bring it down. things I'd fix: -reticle doesn't quite line up with where you think it should. -diving doesn't give you free slow-mo like in max payne so its easier to just use regular slow-mo and never dive, -especially when the tight spaces and bumrushing enemies mean diving puts you at far more risk of camera ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.-enemies break down doors but you can't see them through the debris until after the auto-slow stops.-strafing left and right feels odd because of how the character controller moves in relation to the camera-over reliance on the door and key thing-painkillers don't heal a lot on intended difficulty, they feel super weak-the protagonist's actions are also in slo-mo, the point of slo-mo is that you can execute crazy moves very quickly, this leads to a lot of waiting out reloads that are 4x as long during a slowmo event and such-lots of deaths feel cheap because of these issues. also this is just a nitpick but it could be so much weirder! granted I haven't played much yet but the environment  is already feeling samey, except for the bathroom level, that was funI really wanna love this game, and i think its worth a look if you like indies, a few users have said it could use a directors cut and I wholeheartedly agree, some extra polish and cutting out the chaff and i think this would be an A tier indie title well worth the purchase
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is a fantastic game, with beautiful visuals, story, and set pieces, not to mention the killer soundtrack. These are the best aspects of the game, and why its definitely a game you should take the time to experience yourself. These are what is specifically going to keep your interest, as while the rest of the game is serviceable it doesnt hold up to the runtime as well. I wont go too much into this to keep it fresh, just know that this is the best part of the game.The gameplay was solid, though it felt a bit shallow at times. Some weapons felt redundant and that they filled similar rolls. Despite this, I do not advise neglecting any part of your arsenal or movement options. I personally neglected to use the dodge roll for most of my playthrough, which while it doesnt really affect gameplay most of the time it was basically required in a select amount of fights. My opinion about level design is more positive than gameplay, but I dont think it reaches the same heights as other features. Simply put, it feels like theres alot of filler in the levels, which is good if you like gameplay but I think it takes away from the best parts about it.While not exactly problematic, the enemy AI was lacking complexity, with one major exception. Throughout my playthrough I had to iterate my strategy against the puppeteers several times over, analyzing the AI, its weaknesses, and my kit before I finally felt like I conquered the enemy type, and I really wished there were more enemies like this. To clarify, I dont feel like the AI is badly designed, its actually well designed for the intended roles of each enemy type. The problem is that when the enemies are so simple and the roster is so limited the gameplay has a tendency to become stale quickly when separated from the story and new setpieces, which is something that happens alot.Overall, despite its shortcomings I still recommend this game. The usual gameplay is only serviceable, but is significantly enhanced by the story and setpieces of the game. If features mentioned in the first paragraph isnt the main reason why you would want this game, then I would recommend waiting for a sale, but its definitely a game to try out.(I made this review almost immediately after completing the game)

_childDocuments_.review: El paso elsewhere is stupid good It wears its inspiration on its sleeves, the graphics are crunchy fun. Stylistically a wonderful fit for this homage to Max Payne of old.The soundtrack Fits it so well, With some bangers  imo That rivals Tony hawk soundtrack to a degree. I don't usually listen to a game's soundtrack often. This one has been an exception adrenaline pumping as you do what James does best. Broken up by wonderfully campy moments as the melancholic story unfolds, the story unravels itself in greater detail as you progress. Egging you both on, figuratively and literally fall deeper into this madness. There is no 4th wall, we descend together from the start. That is El Paso, Well written and believable characters. With gut punches being the only thing promised and a chance at closure for the protagonist james. This game seeks to challenge you emotionally, mentally and your reflexes. Giving you the tools, time and  encouragement to do so.  The intended difficulty is a bit high, Specifically the enemy's damage. Which I get, it’s to add urgency and panic. Teaching the player to be calm and methodical despite the pumping jams. Helps flesh out James a bit imo. Sometimes the bullets don't track properly with what the reticle is showing, easy to compensate. Sometimes I had to completely restart the level as the game progressed. There are some cracks that start showing through more and more. Non progression bugs. not a lot, but there. The longer ya play, the more the cracks start to show up. It kind of rips you out of it and you lose all your progress for that level. Restarting from the checkpoint hasn't fixed it in my experience either.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a huge surprise and clearly an unsung landmark game from one of the best years in gaming. Where do I start???Incredible action, perfect enemy balance, amazing voice acting and narration, stylish visuals, a soundtrack that completely slaps, and it controls like a dream on the Steam Deck! My only gripe is the game starts to spin its wheels in the last quarter of the game. Almost feels like the dev felt pressured to have exactly 50 levels. Definitely could have wrapped up a little sooner than that.Still, the ending is incredible and I loved the story this game took me on. If you’re a fan of gun-fu and Max Payne, you need to play this ASAP!

_childDocuments_.review: Is an OK game. the main problem I see with its design an wanting to become a sort of "Max Payne spiritual succesor" is that it doesn't work most of the time. Most enemies are melee-based and come in groups, and you don't become unkillable during slow mow like in Max Payne 1. So the result is that diving has no purpose, it doesn't help you avoid projectiles (Enemy projectiles are ALWAYS explosive) and against regular enemies only serves to get yourself cornered or stuck against a wall and get yourself killed. The other problem it has is that is repetitive, and it takes its time to show you a new idea, concept, weapon or enemy to the point of being a little bit annoying. Yeah, this thing wants to be a mix up between Max Payne and Noctune, but it doesn't get quite right neither of those.Having said all that, is a good game, worth your money, and has some redeeming things  Narrative and cutscenes are ok, (it doesn't explore a lot of stuff, flashbacks would have been nice, or tying up properly the Elevator voice plotline that the story suddenly drops for no reason, but whatevs, there are no perfect games) action is good, and the OST is certainly interesting. I think it was worth the price, but don't go in thinking (like I did) that this is going to be something like Max Payne, because its not. Its...similar, but that's it, the combination is good, but some pieces doesn't fit as nice as they could.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I came for the Max Payne style gunplay. Stayed for the raw emotional story about abuse and the trauma that comes with it.I'm incredibly impressed with what is for offer here. The writing, voice acting and visual design all adds a sort of texture to the story. A human tale of one miserable breakup between two people coated in an end of the world style flair. The real shine comes from the impressive camera direction in cutscenes. Most of them take place in the same location but the level of creativity on display make that location feel rich, constantly shifting the tone from safety to suffering.The gunplay is strong but does have some content pacing problems. New enemies and weapons show up at odd intervals leading to long stretches without anything new to offer. However, due to the short length of the game it's less of a deal breaker and more of a noticeable blemish. The enemies all showcase specific weapon weaknesses, which is good to keep the players switching from old reliable. It's likely not going to be the thing you remember this game for but it is still incredibly entertaining to bullet time dive through a window. Just this time it will involve werewolves in a bathroom.I really recommend you check this one out. It's another great example that we don't need photo-realistic AAA graphics to tell an impactful and moving story.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It's the kind of game that only comes out once or twice in a year, the story keeps a tight focus that's punctuated by the game design. It didn't have quite the design chops to make me cry (high-impact moments didn't feel distinct enough from the regular gameplay loop), but it's raw and visceral and made me feel like the characters were real people. I loved the decision to make James a folklore researcher who's always trying to stop and puzzle everything out, it really fits the game's cerebral vibes.Now, gameplay: 3rd person isn't too bad, it works to get you invested in James as a character and it isn't too much of a problem. The weird off-center makes it easy to miss in close quarters or firing through doorways but stakes and certain weapons like the shotgun help offset the difference. The slow-mo isn't as helpful as it'd seem, flinging yourself through the air at high speed isn't great for your aim but it is hilarious to body-check tables with. Also rebind dodge to spacebar as soon as you can, it's way more valuable than jump and it's not accessible where it is on the C key. Overall, the shooting hits a nice balance between frenetic and methodical, different enemy types will force you to check your corners for werewloves or make aggressive pushes to find that one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ puppet man, and the audio cues will tell you exactly what's about to smack you in the face even if the camera won't let you see it. Your gunshots also tend to blend with the music and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'s some good music.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso is a different kind of boomer shooter. Instead of taking Doom, Quake or Half-Life as inspiration it is a Max Payne clone with a twist. Instead of shooting gangsters and drug addicts in New York the player is put into the role of a guy that fell in love with a vampire queen. Too bad for him that his ex-girlfriend now wants to end the world with a dark ritual. So he has to descend into 50 dream-like levels and fight vampires and werewolves to save humanity. The graphics are simple, even worse than Max Payne 1, but the artstyle is on point. The bizarre color palette and surroundings make for a great atmosphere. Regular ingame-cutscenes with fantastic voice acting and heavy-hearted writing add to the strong vibes of the game just as much as the original hip-hop soundtrack. The gameplay is simple. There are 50 levels to go through, each of them built as a small labyrinth where the player has to find keys, rescue hostages and escape to an elevator to the next level. Most of the levels are easy enough to navigate. Don’t expect to get lost often or lose track of where to go. Visual clues and light pillars in the distance are easy to follow.The game is played in a third-person-perspective and heavily relies on using bullet-time mechanics to quickly shoot enemies before they hit the player. Lost health can be replenished by painkillers. Enemy variety is quite solid with good encounter design. There are also plenty of weapons to choose from and the game features a unique melee mechanic. Melee is limited by wooden stakes which can be replenished by destroying furniture.I agree with everyone saying that the game can be repetitive. But I think the playtime of around eight hours is still completely fine. Just don’t expect to do that in two or three sittings. I preferred playing the game over several weeks in short bursts but enjoyed every minute of it.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I played on the highest difficulty option, but there are sliders that let you customize damage your taken and dealt at any time, which is good! The game felt sufficiently challenging in a "Everything kills you in 2 hits max, usually just takes one though" kind of way, but the player is lethal enough for it to never feel like a trudge through spongy enemies. My only real complaint about the otherwise good combat system is that you seem to deal significantly more bullet damage while in slow motion, making slo mo more of a required way to play rather than a helpful assist for when there's too much heat on you. Aside from that, the dive move tended to get me killed way more than if I just rolled and spammed slow motion headshots, but that could just be a fault of my own, still glad its in there.Other than that? I didn't believe a Max Payne homage about killing your vampire ex-girlfriend would have such a powerful narrative, but everything about the cutscenes is incredible. The voice direction, shot composition, and razor sharp writing elevate a solid, if flawed shooter into a classic that could easily stand beside its inspirations. Strange Scaffold crafted something special here, and I cannot wait to see what they do next. 9/10Edit: The game took me like 8 hours to beat with a handful of deaths. My playthrough was during a time I had no internet for a few days, so the 0.2 hours Steam has me listed as at time of review is incorrect. Hope the film adaptation they've been in talks for goes well.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Top-tier sound design, it's creepy, startling, trippy, and energizing, with some excellent music. I don't normally play shooters, but was drawn in by the excellent reviews and the slow-motion mechanic, and very glad I was. I enjoyed the gameplay and level design, but especially the story (it's worth trying to find the radios and projectors for more story tidbits), and of course the sound. The visuals are a bit weird, simplified and old-school in the main, but higher-resolution, eyeless and warped in the cut-scenes; I ended up liking them, although the sound and story is where the game shines more.I played the first 10 levels on "Intended" but ended up switching to "Story" sometime after that (when Intended got too hard for me) and appreciated the fine-tune settings, including a speed setting, which let me get past the main bosses without too much frustration (after first attempts seemed impossible).The game is a bit long (50 levels, some quite short, but latter half levels are significantly longer than early levels), and is repetitive at times, but usually is remixed enough or changed entirely occasionally to keep things fun. Several bosses were too fast/difficult for me to beat on story mode (without setting tweaks, as mentioned above), but probably are doable in normal mode by those who are better at shooter games.One setting that was missing was the ability to tweak the slow-motion yellow bar. If I could've made that refill faster or be bigger, that would've been preferable to me than changing other settings like enemy damage or pill health refill.There is a good variety of weapons, which are almost all "necessary" for certain types of enemies or situations; you'll want to keep switching weapons.  I found the strikebreaker the most versatile, although I also used the shotgun and rifle frequently. The molotovs were a mixed bag - occasionally very useful, but also can do a lot of damage to protagonist and sometimes allow flaming enemies to attack you.The story is hard to describe, but is a mix of abusive relationship recollections, fatalism, drug abuse, regret, longing, and monster-hunting and pending apocalypse. Voice acting was great.Overall, fun to play, looks good, sounds great, fantastic story, highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: steam really needs a "meh" option. everything about this game is good, except its length. sadly, 50 levels feels way too long and drawn out. but the story and characters are excellently written and voiced, the music is fantastic, and the gameplay is alright for what it is but halfway through you've seen everything.buy it on sale, and do so knowing that you've seen everything when you hit the halfway point.

_childDocuments_.review: buy this, you won't regret it. Its amazing, truly a masterpiece with the soundtrack, gameplay, and story THIS GAME DOES NOT MISSNow after beating the game. This is in my top 3 games of all time. The soundtrack rivals halo in its uniqueness and way it blends themes for the player in the different levels. The Story deals with the cycle of abuse and I rarely see this portrayed in such a true and organic/believable way. Just like a Vampire a abuser can suck the life out of their victim. If you need a reference look at 343 Industries and how it treats Halo fans. In all seriousness this is a beautiful, amazing, fun game worth every cent and I wish there was more but I am excited to play the rest of strange scaffolds catalog.
