_childDocuments_.review: Glad I played it. Brooding love story, with original Max Payne controls. Feel like 50 levels was a bit too much to tell the story. There's a lack of enemy variety and mechanics change halfway through the game, so there's a lot of the same until the end. However, I enjoyed the story and atmosphere, and hope there's a sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy indie games and when everybody talked about a love song to Max Payne with vampires I was sold. The voice acting, soundtrack, level design are all top quality. But as good as the level design is, it's not made for the bullet time use. It feels clunky to use because there is not enough space to actually dodge and often you hit something fom environment. It's a 7/10 for me. Dissappointed on the gameplay side and enemy variety.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Great vibe and fun writing.  Excellent soundtrack, and it ALMOST scratches that Max Payne itch.  I has the exact same controls/mechanics, but I think the levels/enemies aren't really designed to take full advantage of those mechanics.  After a while it begins to feel a bit shallow, but it's still a fun time that clearly a lot of love was put into, which tilts it into the positive for me.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: As others have said, a great homage to Remedy games. I played while also playing through Alan Wake II, and it was fun to see so much of Remedy's identity in this game. There are a total of  levels. And as others have said, they can get repetitive. There is no leveling up. You get all of your equipment pretty early on. So don't come to this game looking for some satisfying upgrades or anything like that. However, the story and atmosphere of this game is amazing. I enabled unlimited ammo, unlimited pain pills, and made myself invincible (the game has these sliders whenever starting and there's no "penalty" to using them). I happily breezed through the combat in order to experience the story. And it was 100% worth it!  Also, there's so many songs that the developer made for the game. Rap songs with lyrics about what you're doing in the game. So cool!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This game is actually really fun and I am enjoying it. Sadly, until the developers patch it slightly I cannot in good faith recommend this game to ANYONE. If you die, you have to quit the game. You WILL start getting micro stutters, and every death makes these worse and worse until the game becomes completely unplayable. Alt-F4 works fine, but the fact this happens at all is awful. Very enjoyable and fun, but this issue is too big for me to ignore.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It's got an undeniable sense of style, especially in the music and narration but also how it plays with the light from objects (like, a key that emmits light to be easy to find also being used to make shadow puppets).It's like a mix of Max Payne (duh) and Painkiller and plays really well, though I'm not 100% convinced the Max Payne DNA needed to include the slo-mo dodge. Never found an instance where it helped more than got in the way. Swapping between weapons to tackle different enemies in big encounters felt great though.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Love the game! heavily inspired by the Max Payne series. So if you enjoyed those games very likely you'll enjoy this as well. The soundtrack, the gameplay, the environments, voice acting, a story you want to see to the end. With challenging but fair levels. I have almost no negative comment. If you into 3rd person shooters. This is a solid buy!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Story is really good. Apparently there's multiple endings? Maybe only 2? Directed very well. Enemies are interesting enough. They make the whole scenario feel real even tho it is ridiculous. Music is phenomenal and even themed around the level and current plot elements.When they give you the back story of James and Janet/Draculae. It is a totally messed up scenario to be in that the main character realizes and has to come to terms with.The game play did start to feel kind of repetitive towards the end. The only thing that changes is the levels and the story progresses. The art style is gorgeous. The level design is really good tho. There was a lot of effort and thought put into them and you can tell. The pathing for them is so good actually.Yeah uh 9/10And shout out to my friend for gifting this hidden gem to me.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Never thought I'd end up describing a game as Max Payne-esque, or that Max Payne-alike could be a genre, but here we are.  Wears it's Remedy influence on it's sleeve, but has a distinctive art-style that sets it apart.  It's fun.  The dive mechanic doesn't really work here, but everything else is great.  The music didn't grab me at first, but gets better in later levels, or it grew on me.  Either way, it's worth picking up the soundtrack with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing you might notice is the low poly art which may turn off a lot of players from purchasing a game but this is not a game, it's a beautiful work of art attached to a game.  What really stood out to me besides the story was the level designs were exceptionally well planned out, artistic style is simple but Strange Scaffold really used that to their advantage to control every detail for the users experience in cinematics and world design, the music not only enhanced the game but I actually enjoyed it which is a rare thing in the span I've been gaming, and did I mention the story?  The shooting mechanics are fun however they do lose their luster as you play, but that's not why YOU KEEP GOING.Bottom line, if you have the money to spare and want to support a game developer that should be supported buy now.  If you don't have the money to spare then add this to your wish list and wait for a sale because it would be criminal not to.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This an enjoyable rendition of Max Payne, with some monsters added in. Its story is well made and carries the experience, and kept me engaged throughout. Riveting voice acting, writing and monologues, in and out of cutscenes. The level design is very fun to explore and feels varied and fresh each new level, with mash-ups between settings feeling surreal. One level goes more heavily into horror and it is fantastic *chefs kiss*. The artsyle is perfectly incorporated, and the animations / texture work is very good. Can not express enough that this game is worth a look and I liked the overall experience, even with some of the points I bring up next.The gunplay is alright, enemies have a handful of varieties, but the game soon runs out of new things to show you aside from the different level settings. Enemies are spawned in very 'monster closet' esque styles sometimes, leading to some corners instantly killing you without due caution. Cant imagine it on 5x damage mode (this games version of 'Difficult'). The music is solid.... except with the lyrics. They are genuinely not fun or themed appropriately (in my opinion) to listen to in the levels they accompany, I had the game music turned to 0 for about half of the maps. The game has nearly 0 verticality which felt like a missed opportunity, I found myself never using slo-motion to dive due to the enemy design usually punishing its use.Got it for a discount, but I feel its worth full price and overall was a blast, keeping my attention and making me want to continue finishing the story even with my nitpicks with the gameplay. Hoping it gets a sequel and this studio keeps making such enticing games!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Music, vibe, and presentation are all excellent.Gameplay is awful and extremely repetitive, there are probably 25 levels too many (there are 50 in total)halfway through I decided to just put on infinite ammo and reduce the damage taken down to half, and I very much appreciate that those are there and readily accessible because I otherwise would have just uninstalled and instead I beat the game to the end.Only play if you are either a particularly huge fan of original Max Payne gameplay, or if you are exceptionally sold on the game's vibe. listen to the song "BREAK ♥♥♥♥" online and you can probably decide based off that alone.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: A (tribute? homage? just a great game in the same vein of?), for lack of a better description Max Paine-like. The cutscenes and narration hit a great noir-doomsday vibe. The level design makes good use of the surreal framing mechanism and environment aesthetics. The action feels like classic, but smoother and without the aged engine jank. Edit: The OST slaps, buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is a love letter to Max Payne that also comes into its own with its story and characters. While nailing the original feel of Max Payne 1 and 2 in many ways, it also takes the formula in its own direction to make for, in some ways, a better gaming experience.The game sees you playing as James Savage, a pillhead with a truckload of trauma and guilt who's only remaining goal is to kill his ex-girlfriend, Draculae, before she completes a ritual that will end the world. The format of the game is very much like Max Payne 1 played entirely in the nightmare stages, but in the best way possible.El Paso's strength in writing lies not in the plot itself, but in the details. As far as video game stories go, El Paso does a magnificent job of capturing the contradicting feelings many of us have about our relationships past and present. The way in which details are revealed about the characters does a great job of manipulating the player into having different feelings about the main characters at different times. The way you feel about James and Draculae very much contorts as the game progresses, leaving you feeling like you've lead a similar path of disappointment and retribution as the characters have. El Paso mainly conveys its story through multiple bite-sized cutscenes that are miraculously paced, small audio log equivalents in the environment, and quips from James periodically about what's going on around him. Many game stories don't do much for me, but the relatable and raw nature of what El Paso has to say left me addicted to finding every projector and secret I could in the off chance I'd get another mp3 of James and Draculae interacting. The writing and the voice acting are really impressive for the scope of the project we're talking about. James and Draculae both have demeanors that are very believable throughout and you feel for them both to an extent. The way the script itself is constructed really works with the talents of the voice actors, too. There are incomplete sentences all over the place, not to mention conversations that dart back and forth between topics, as if you were talking to your buddies or an ex of your own. What makes the serious notes all the more effective is that El Paso does have a sense of humor it proudly displays from time to time, but never so much that it cheapens the game's atmosphere.I'll be controversial and say I find El Paso, Elsewhere more fun to play on a base level than Max Payne 1. Video games have a certain language they speak and El Paso speaks that language fluently with its enemy design, level design, and combat-puzzle-style gameplay. While Max Payne 1 saw you going through hotel after corridor after enclosed city street gunning down normie goons with pistols, El Paso sees you gunning down and staking a variety of otherwordly baddies who range from melee meatheads who just charge you and get in the way, to supernatural snipers who hurl giant energy balls at you from a distance. This type of gameplay, more in the DOOM tradition of varied ambushes, makes the mechanics more fun to play around with than the heavily thematic selection of limited enemies in the Max Payne games. The sound design of El Paso deserves to be mentioned, as it plays a big role in the atmosphere and gameplay of the whole experience. Haunting, otherworldly stuttering is not only part of the enemy soundscape, but also part of certain songs in the soundtrack. This leads to moments of paranoia where you're SURE you're alone in a room, then you hear an enemy right behind you. You turn around only to discover you are indeed alone and the soundtrack tricked you. On top of this it's hard to ignore El Paso's soundtrack. WhileI'm inexperienced with the genre and not all of the songs completely land for me, the majority of them do a good job of making the whole game feel like a modern high-budget music video. The metaphors and imagery present in the lyrics not only compliment El Paso as a full project, but can also stand on their own.El Paso's visual style works really well for what it's going for. Though low poly graphics have become increasingly common, this game earns that style by being a direct throwback to the Max Payne games. On top of that, the horror aspects only work better when left more abstract. The creature designs are unsettling, especially when paired with James' commentary on them. The game utilizes colored lighting very effectively, truly making you feel out of space to a similar degree as Remedy's own Control. The aesthetic styles the environment switches between all add to the game's overall atmosphere, but go on to be enjoyably disjointed with rooms and assets being smashed together in ways they seem they shouldn't.El Paso, Elsewhere does a great job of fully realizing all aspects of its creativity from writing to sound design to gameplay. While a spiritual successor to the Max Payne games, this project also creates a world of its own that's amazing to get lost in for 10+ hours and leaves you with a delightfully bittersweet feeling not all games can pull off.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: The pieces fit. El Paso, Elsewhere fills space in ways I found unique and interesting. Gameplay feels incredibly fluid, though it's environmental design can be awkward at times. Enemy AI is also lackluster. By the end of the game I found myself using bullet time less and less, You won't be dolphin diving into every room or around every corner.Biggest props to the direction, cutscenes were amazing as well as stellar performances.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I just heard about this game a few weeks ago and decided to buy it during the holiday sale.  It took me a couple of hours to really get into it but I am so glad I got it.  It is a very creative game that really feels like a brilliant homage to Max Payne and other Remedy games while making its own path.The voice acting is really good and the story is well though out.  The audio is nice and crisp and the soundtrack fits the game nicely.  Graphics are good and game looks great on an ultrawide screen with just a few issues with the subtitles sometimes during cut-scenes.The game is throwing something new at you all the time and keeping you on your toes.  Near the end of the game it did crash a few times but overall ran great.  Another amazing thing that does not get mentioned much is that the game loads very quickly and there are NO splash screens at boot.  The game loads straight into the main menu.  Thank you so much for that QOL feature that more games need to follow.  Really makes it great to start the game and you're playing in no time.I enjoyed it a lot and did not want it to end.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is what happens when you take Remedy's budget away and force a studio to rely on knowing that formula better than the big league studio does.Gripping, brief cinematics pepper an intense third person shooter haunted house. Outrageously sublime soundtrack, beautiful lighting making those PS1 era polygons glow, and voiceovers that send a chill up the spine. Huge content warnings for victims of abuse and those struggling with addiction, but this game sets out from the jump to deal with those topics head on. As someone who's dealt with one of those, I felt very seen. It's a little long and could have stood to drop about a fifth of its levels, the my god, the payoff. Nobody's perfect, but at least this is unique and hits WAY above its weight class. Strange Scaffold deserves all the money that ever went to its AAA  competitors.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible game. The soundtrack, the voice acting, the Max Payne style gameplay, the graphics. All of it is so good that I can't not recommend this game. If you're in the market for a great third person action shooter, just grab this one.My only complaint is that there's not more of it to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more than just a throw back to Max Payne.  Its surreal, trippy as ♥♥♥♥ gameplay loop is an experience you'll never forget.  This game is by no means perfect, nor is it a masterpiece.  Infact this game can be jank at times an repetitive.  But just like the games central theme once you start you just can't put this game down.  Its fun, weird and its worth experiencing the once, twice and... Yeah buy the game.  Its good!!!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: My view on the game is mixed.The vibes are the best part of the game, hands down. The voice acting and script is extremely good. The brooding tone delivers on its heavy themes. There are also some very funny jokes thrown into the mix. Some of the memory scenes made me upset in a good way, since it really captured the feeling of loving someone who hurts you. Under all the fantasy there is an understanding of real trauma.The gameplay ends up feeling stretched too thin. This means that when the story takes a backseat of takes a less interesting detour, the whole game ends up feeling dull at points. I ended up wishing for a shorter experience.The gameplay has so much potential, but fails to deliver on many points. The enemy variety is not super good, leaving the level design samey despite the game doing a lot to try to spice things up with level layouts. Only the projectile enemies pose real threat. The guns also lack distinctive features, and due to ammo being so plentiful managing your arsenal does not provide tactical depth. The game misses the mark on why Max Paynes leap and time slow mechanics work. In those games you fight against enemies with guns. Without that the leap is almost always a mistake and time-slow is not a core part of the experience. The clunky movement works when diving to dodge bullets is necessary. Against El Pasos mostly melee enemies the movement just stifles player expression. The 3rd person perspective is unoptimal. A lot of the fighting is done in tight spaces and in melee range. As such aiming and hitting enemies can be wonky. Since leaping is unnecessary and usually a trap option, seeing your characters full body is not needed. Small nitpicks:-Damage feedback is minimal. It's easy to lose track of how much life you have-Hitmarkers would sometimes be buggy and not show up-Enemies have powered up versions that are barely any different-The key rebind menu had issues with ctrl and shift keys. Resetting input to default fixed the issue.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game but overstaying it's welcome.Max Payne -style shooting with a kind of fever dream /drug fueled setting and story. Had it ended at lvl 30 instead of lvl 50, it would have ended strong and probably had me wishing for a sequel. However the game drags on. The gameplay isn't very deep and really doesn't support the long runtime. The last 15-20 lvls had me hoping every lvl would be the last, even though the lvl design started to be interesting around that point. Still, it´s worth playing. At least the first 20-30 lvls.

_childDocuments_.review: Knew little to nothing going into this game but easily one of the best games of 2023, El Paso, Elsewhere is going to be a game that sticks in my head for a while. _childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: There's nothing quite like it. I mean, Max Payne is a hell of a lot like it, but El Paso, Elsewhere brings a surreal, dreamlike story about processing an abusive relationship that hits different than anything you'll find anywhere else. The gunplay rules, and gives some very satisfying feedback; the shotgun in particular blows back enemies like a cannon, and the uzi is a fun little spray-and-pray gun once you find it. But there is a repetitiveness to the action, and the game tips its hand pretty fast. Once you've seen the first handful of enemies, the game doesn't have a lot more surprises in store, either in its level design or its enemy encounters.And that's what will make or break this game for you: if you're cool with some repetitive (but very satisfying) action gameplay in service to a unique story with stellar writing and performances, you'll have a great time. If you're looking for something mechanically deep and intricate, you won't. Do I wish there were more creative enemies and challenges? Yes. Do I wish the Max-Payne-style jump-dive was useful in any way, instead of being an active liability in combat? Sure. Did I run into some odd glitches and the occasional technical issue while playing? You bet. But I had a great time anyway. Try and appreciate this one for what it is, instead of harping on about what it's not.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I was drawn to El Paso, Elsewhere early in its press coverage, between the cool title and obvious Max Payne homage. I was sold on it when I read a review - I believe RPS - describing it as a love letter to the period of time where a tortured man in a trenchcoat diving in slow motion while firing dual pistols was the pinnacle of cinema. As a 32-year-old manchild I was probably the target audience here; suffice to say it wasn't surprising when the main character revealed he was the same age as me (though he's looking a bit healthier and coping better).What I wasn't expecting was for some of the best and most honest writing I've seen in games for a long time. It's goofy and pulpy, sure, but manages to be knowingly so without remotely stumbling into "well, THAT just happened!" Marvel territory, a feat I honestly wasn't sure *could* be pulled off any more. Vampires, exes, run-down motels, addictions and a stubborn refusal to let one's demons get the better of them - for all the excellent hip-hop soundtrack, it's a game that ticks all the boxes of being an all-timer Mountain Goats song.The gameplay is good enough to stand by itself, but only just. Significant drawbacks become apparent over the course of its probably-too-long 50 levels / 8-9 hour running time. The enemy variety isn't great and takes too long to get going, I think it's a good 5 levels before the second enemy type is introduced and overall there are only really four or five "regular" enemies total. The levels are similar - the designs are cool and atmospheric enough, but I did not really need 10-15 levels of the same graveyard tileset. It feels unusual to wish an 8-hour game were shorter, but El Paso wouldn't have lost anything for being 30 levels rather than 50. Maybe one spot where it did not, but should have, taken inspiration from its beloved Max Payne 2 and its 3-hour campaign. Games like this should be replayable - perhaps some kind of arcade mode or score attack - but this one just drags out too long for that to be appetizing. The shooting, bullet time, dodging and so on all feel great, thankfully, and it never gets old going in and out of slow-mo to headshot some snipers before mowing down charging vampires. As video game sentences go that's a very video game sentence. I have some other minor gameplay quibbles - hit feedback is poor, many times I died because I didn't realise I'd actually been struck and brought to low health, the bullet time shoot-dodge is kind of pointless when "normal" bullet time gives you much more control, time and direction, and the weapon variety/balance isn't very good - but nothing that spoils the game. Bottom line - it's more than fun enough to play, with some understandable rough edges that are a frequent minor annoyance.Also the boss fights were boring bullet sponges but that goes for every game of this style ever made so fair enough.People are divided on the music. I know nothing about music but I loved it. It's  a pity some of the more standout vocal tracks don't play more than once; not that the more "ambient" music on the non-landmark levels (sidenote: I don't know which levels are landmark levels and wouldn't have known that was a thing other than the achievement. I assume it's the more set-piece and unique ones with cool music and more dialogue, which presses the question - why are there 40 non-landmark levels?) isn't good, but I absolutely loved climactic battles set to the mad chant of BREAK ♥♥♥♥ KILL PEOPLE BREAK ♥♥♥♥ KILL PEOPLE. Ultimately it feels appropriate that a game bursting with love for the reliable old 7/10 budget shooter would turn out to be a 7/10 itself - and close to an 8. More games like this, please - made sustainably, priced reasonably, not 100 hours long and wearing their bursting, bruised but still beating hearts on their sleeves.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: This game is literal perfection. The gameplay, inspired by Max Payne, merges everything perfectly. Every weapon has a utility. Every enemy is different enough to change your strategies and try different thing. Every level is a masterpiece. Every song kicks in at the perfect moments to create the perfect combat encounters to create the perfect experience. The story is top-tier and covers topics I haven't seen before in another game. Every single aspect of this game just lands so, so well. The characters, especially Savage, is just... Amazing. The performances are amazing. The writing and humor is amazing. It is scary how amazingly good this game is. I'm going to follow this company closely, because this game left me wanting so, so much more. Everyone should play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: My opinion of this game fluctuated so many times I wasn't sure how I was going to feel by the end, the game is easy at most points but then some specific encounters are just obnoxious, the teleporting enemies that throw glowing orbs are especially awful and frustrating, almost made me quit the game, the levels are interesting visually if a bit too repetitive, the game is probably 2-3 hours too long considering how little it mixes things up, but the story is genuinely heartfelt and interesting, the two only characters in the game are engaging and I was legitimately interested in learning about their relationship, the fantastic voice acting is the icing on the cake.In the end, the game is a solid 4-5 hours experience stretched out into 7-8 hours, the gameplay is decent enough bordering at times into frustration, the story and the characters are what sell the game for me.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: It's a treat. A hidden gem worth discoveringThe game often leans on the verge of stalling, but never really gets there, always pulling something new at the last moment - an enemy, weapon, setting or gimmickEnemy variety  is too low and guns  feels quite unbalanced (i stopped using shotgun due to his low range) but overall it's nice game, oozing with style and atmosphere
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game. Fantastic soundtrack, decent action, gripping story. Only issues I had were minor technical bugs (stuttering after using molotovs or high explosives and some odd black fog that would try to take over the screen) but they were solved by restarting checkpoints. That aside, it was a fun ~8 hour adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is fun and claustrophobic, not exactly groundbreaking, but it works well enough and will click if you like third person action shooters. Where the game truly shines though is it's personality. It is absolutely oozing with charm and soul, a decent soundtrack dense enough to fill every new stage with something you haven't heard before, and a well crafted vibe it carries through until the end. The story is campy and oftentimes funny without being unserious, and it strikes a kind of strange harmony I could appreciate. VA's did a remarkably good job considering. True low budget indie gem.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Really neat idea, but the combat, enemy and level design gets old very fast. While the initial selling point of "Max Payne with vampires" was exciting, after a while I was disappointed at how little the game design actually plays into those mechanics. For example, the shoot dodging is practically useless because of the claustrophobic level design and almost all the enemies are melee only. Most of the time you end up smacking into a wall while the enemies beat you down. It wasn't long until I was only using the basic slow mo button as it's way more useful. The music, voice acting and story are what kept me going.Overall I still recommend checking the game out. It does some really neat things with the music and art direction that are worth experiencing.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: For  the first time ever, I bought a game because of the hype soundtrack in the preview video. Now that I've played it a bit, I can already tell this game is gonna be an awesome romp. Writing is on point, vibe on point, and music is PREEM.  You will know in your heart when watching the video if this game is for you. And i sure hope it is!
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: I have finished the game. Took 6h to do it on the hardest difficulty and get what Is considered the good ending. So not a very long game. But it was one hell of a ride. I was so invested. The poetic speeches. The deep meanings. The story. The gameplay. It all just works. This game is an excellet showcase of amasing ideas coming togheter and playing with the limitations instead of trying to hide them. Utilizing what they got to make something better. This game is a 9/10 for me.. If you love max payne and  the whole bulletime slowmo shooters. Then this will be a good one for you.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent gameplay, beautiful and detailed environments, an absolute  of a soundtrack, and a love story that goes for the maximum emotional gut-punchage possible. I purchased the game only yesterday and couldn't stop playing it until I beat it- and then had to go back and get all the achievements for it too, because I wasn't ready to be done with it.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: The story, acting, atmosphere, and music are all excellent. I am recommending it mostly off of those aspects. The noir tone mixed with the interesting worldbuilding, all following a protagonist who, despite his edge, is very compelling to listen to. The gunplay is solid, getting headshots and managing ammo is fun, but the game is really let down by its level and enemy design. The claustrophobic levels mixed with enemies that can very quickly drain your life had me feeling more stressed than badass mowing down enemies, knowing that I could quickly be ambushed and swarmed and dead in a couple seconds. Thankfully checkpoints are forgiving, but I still hated the feeling of balancing on a tripwire the whole game. I played on Intended difficulty, but I will give major props to the devs for incorporating plenty of options for adjusting the difficulty. The game goes on for more than I think it should, to the point where I stopped playing a bit around halfway through. Maybe I'll come back and finish it eventually, but I just wasn't having enough fun to keep going. I recognise that's probably more of a me thing, but if you're like me and don't handle the tight corridors and stressful encounters well within the first hour or so - you're probably not going to enjoy forcing yourself through 7 hours more of the same. Plenty of levels could be cut to better pace out the excellent cutscenes and story dialogue.My biggest grievance with the game is that diving is unfortunately more of a hindrance than help due to the tight environments and melee enemies who can quickly swarm you while you're slowly getting back to your feet. Your camera view will also shake up and down during the initial leap, so its really difficult to aim in the first couple seconds of a slo-mo dive, wasting valuable meter. You're better off rolling for avoiding enemies and using the slo-mo while standing so you can keep moving around and aiming fluidly.This game feels like a perfect 7/10 - Really good in some areas, lacking in others, and whether it makes or breaks it for you will come down to your own personal preferences.

_childDocuments_.review: 'It's good, but flawed. _childDocuments_.review: I haven't been so thoroughly blindsided by an indie title in a while. I tried this not expecting much, but walked away reeling. The voice acting is absolutely amazing, and the writing is some of the best I've seen from a small title in ages. This blows all the recent AAA titles dog water excuses for "plots" so far out of the water that I'm pretty sure they've become dust in the atmosphere. Add fun gameplay to the mix and an emphasis on letting the player have fun, and you have a game that I'm glad I bought without a sale. There are a good few things this game stumbles at, but the fact that a game about killing your vampire ex girlfriend has better VA and story telling than most games in general makes them all seem diminutive. Since there's a lot I want to praise, I'll start with what I do NOT like. It will be quick.-The shotgun is weak and inconsistent. Paired with the bullet time, it just blows. You get 2 shots max when leaping, which is just underwhelming.-No Dual uzis. That sucks big time. -Too many maps without music. Too many maps with lackluster music. Some maps have absurdly good bangers, but half are either silent or just bland. -Really slows down at the end. The maps become more maze-esque and it starts to drag. -Terribly optimized. 3 maps in particular chug frames for seemingly no reason. That's about it for what I don't like. Now, what do I love? H O L Y S H * T the voice acting. If you told me that the main character's voice actor had his family held at gunpoint for several line reads, I'd believe it. The sheer emotion that was put into almost every line was just heart wrenching. Some lines were delivered with such raw passion that it bordered on distressing. I never expected such genuine depth and talent in a game that seems so surface-level silly. It's Max Payne, but with vampires and demons. How deep can it be? It's deep. I won't over-hype it by saying it's Mariana Trench deep, but it's at least deep enough to crush a poorly constructed submarine with several billionaires in it. The prospect of having to confront your vampire ex, which was briefly shown in the trailer, drew me in immediately. I was really curious to see what they'd go for with it. I did not, at any point, expect things to actually be so...devastatingly real. I cannot, for the life of me, believe a 20 dollar indie game about killing monsters to stop your vampire ex girlfriend depicts  better than 99% of multi-million dollar media. I'm still nursing a horrid case of whiplash from how quickly my expectations were shattered. This game's author is an absolute master of "Less is more". Rather than throwing in constant filler or cringey jokes or constant expository cutscenes, you get almost everything drip fed to you bit by bit. In so many recent games, I find myself wishing for LESS exposition because the story is such a horrible drag. In this, I found myself craving more, yet equally pleased to be left wanting. Every bit of backstory or relevant information given about the main character or his ex all have exquisite purpose. The way this game balances its serious tones, both overlying and under, with humor is master class. There are so, SO many one-liners in this game that are equal parts memorable, meaningful, and damaging. It's hard to go much into how this game does any of that without spoiling things outright. So, I'll just talk about all that last and spoiler it. I'm normally one to skip the audio-logs or text logs in games that give extra bits of lore or plot, as those usually just seem like lazy afterthoughts, but they're really, really good in this. They not only add increasingly sought after breaks in the tension with uplifting comedy, but also add soul crushing depth to events that become clear later on. So, gameplay. It's fun. It's a lot of fun! Especially because the devs let you pick to have infinite ammo if you want it. I started the game without infinite ammo and got 11 or so levels in before deciding...yeah, I want that. Way, way too many games now have this disgusting and cancerous mentality that it MUST be some over the top thing where you prove yourself as a gamer by playing it. It can't just be fun. In a game where you slow-mo jump around blasting vampires, fun is exactly what I want, and precisely what I got. The combat does not have depth to it, and more often than not, you'll be taking damage from sheer BS. The dodge roll has a weird timing to its i-frames, and they love putting enemies around corners. The game is a LOT of fun in the first 15-18 levels, but it really does start to drag on towards the end. It feels less like kicking in doors and more like wandering hallways. I liked the gameplay, but it just started getting tired towards the end. You have far more guns than I expected from a game like this. It gives you options for basically every scenario, and I liked that. As previously mentioned, though, I think it's straight trash that you don't get to dual wield uzis. Huge missed opportunity. I can forgive that, though, thanks to infinite ammo. I just REALLY wanted to spit unfathomable amounts of lead. Probably for the best, though, because the game is very poorly optimized. I'm not too sure how you fail to make your game run smoothly when the graphics are...what they are, but that's sadly the case. Stuttering and frame drops are a huge issue on 3 maps in particular. Thankfully, I only ran into 2 bugs that made me reset the game. I fell through the map on the first major boss fight, and then had an enemy ragdoll through the map and just break the entire game. It dropped to 10 frames and the audio started freaking out biiiig time. Funny, but annoying to have to restart. All in all, the gameplay is not actually why I'm recommending this. I thought it would be the big draw, but it just wasn't. The story is absurdly good. Good, and horrifically, painfully, tragically down to Earth. Again, I know I keep saying it, but I was not expecting such master class writing from a game about something so seemingly cheesy. This game is such a pristine example of how it is possible to take any plot, no matter how seemingly inane or even generic, and make it shine like a radiant beacon in the dark. So long as you execute it well. And my god, man, this executes it so well. So, onto the spoilers about this game's unforeseen topics. Do skip this if you intend to play this game. I'm serious, here, if you are even considering playing this- Stop reading and get it. Or, stop reading and wait for a sale to get this. Do not spoil it for yourself if you intend to play it. This game is SO worth it. Okay, I had 2 whole pages of extra review here, but Steam hates detailed reviews, so I had to delete it. Just buy the game. It's beautiful. It tells a heart wrenching story with the most down to Earth suffering I've seen from a game, full stop, in a package that entirely warps your expectations. Masterful writing, exquisite cinematography, and a genuine and emotional story told in a unique way. Worth every penny without a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is a supernaturally charged love letter to old-school third-person action shooter games, primarily Max Payne. While it's darkness and brooding atmosphere may make it appear like another Max Payne game at first glance, it's the story that really stands out. Max Payne's unique grizzly, emotionally tortured sense of brooding is hard to replicate in other games, but El Paso, Elsewhere manages to be reminiscent of its highly regarded predecessor straddling between the surreal and strange. All of this is wrapped up in what feels like a typical gritty horror story starring tortured protagonist James Savage, barely able to cope with a terrible situation that involves the end of the world. Not to mention his crippling emotional baggage caused by the antagonist of the game, the one that will bring about the end of the world and his ex-girlfriend Janet, aka Draculae, Lord of the Vampires. The story is also one of twisted love that has left the pair with serious scars. The relationship between James and Draculae is one of the game's most interesting offerings it brings to the table. It's a story that never feels boring and oftentimes will leave you feeling a genuine sense of sadness and empathy for not just the tortured James but for Draculae as well. She doesn't show up until much later in the game but her personality is told to us by James who knows deep down a good person might be there, but the terrible things that she's done and plans to do keep her from fully realizing it. Turning her into the monster he fears (and loves) deep down. It's not the most simple relationship they share when you throw in ravenous, nightmarish creatures into the mix.James's struggle is not only to fight back against an onslaught of vampires, werewolves, undead abominations, witches, and even fallen angels to save the world but regain his sense of self. His struggle to deal with the fallout of his relationship with Draculae and the issues that caused the pair to split still haunt him and fuel his barely controllable drug addiction. He wants to help her and be the one person that might make a difference in her life. But, as with real life it's not always that easy, and the further he descends into the void where she is performing the ritual to end all life James will have to fight harder and just keep going in the face of overwhelming odds. Maybe even learn more about himself too. It's a self-reflective story of love, pain, loss, self-understanding, and improvement, and above all else learning to love others (and yourself) while trying to do better along the way.As mentioned, the game's mechanics and action are very solid with slow-mo action like it's 2001 and it's really fun for the most part. There are fifty levels of high-octane action and thrills that do tend to drag at times. The game's level design can be pretty creative and surreal sometimes leaving you guessing at what you'll see next. The downside is some of the levels lack those creative moments and tend to repeat themselves and while the enemy roster is decent and provides a fairly tough challenge they do become a bit repetitive as there are only a handful of them. These limits however do not hinder the game's fun factor but your mileage will vary. There's one aspect that doesn't get old and that's the music and audio design.The game has great overall sound design with the music being arguably one of the best aspects of the title. There's this surprising mix of rock music and rap songs sung by the main character with lyrics as you blast and dive your way through the various levels. Seriously, this soundtrack is very creative and surprisingly impressive in its own right let alone being featured in a third-person action game. The soundtrack is on YouTube if you wanna hear it in its entirety and I highly recommend it as it not only reflects various narrative themes of the story but is just a banger to listen to as well. El Paso, Elsewhere is the kind of game that even the trailer's marketing says "This shouldn't work" but this game works very well and I only encountered a few bugs. Considering how much effort and overall style are present in this final product I have to say I'm impressed with what I experienced and I hope to see more from this world in the future. The mood, atmosphere, story, and game play all come together to create both a loving homage to its influences all the while carving out its own unique place in the pantheon of third-person action shooters. Give it a try, well worth the asking price.Have fun escaping this monster club.

_childDocuments_.review: I expected a great retro time with good aesthetics. I got that.I also broke down sobbing more than once as this game's thematics began to cohere around what it means to find yourself in the aftermath of gaslighting and emotional abuse. This is handled with incredible deftness, all without ever breaking the keyfabe of its hardboiled noir meets horror nerd storytelling conceit. Nor is the game isn't as dour as I make it sound, or as dour as a lesser game playing in these themes would be, and instead its incredibly playful and funny on top of its heavier thematics.This is one of the most emotionally meaningful games I've played in a while, and it feels good to be caught off guard like that with how good a game is. And how, on a more personal note, stories can meet you where you are and remind of your own work to heal from harm done.Oh, and the soundtrack ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slaps.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: For so long I've waited for the day where I see more games taking direct influence from Max Payne. It's one of my favorite games of all time but I feel it only scratched the surface for what can be done with that gameplay style.That day comes today. El Paso, Elsewhere is positively drenched in Max Payne influence; the gameplay, main character, and even general presentation are all highly reminiscent of the early 2000's shooter. Thankfully however, this game is not just trying to be Max Payne again. It has many similarities to it but this game really is trying to do it's own thing, and I think it's a great success in that regard.It may look and maybe even feel like Max Payne a lot of the time, but the way the game is designed reminds me a lot more of classic shooters like DOOM or Quake. The levels, while small, can sometimes feel maze-like as you look for colored keys to unlock colored doors, and the enemies that inhabit these levels, instead of shooting at you, rush you down with melee more often than not, Even the few ranged enemies that are in the game have big, flashy, relatively slow projectiles that can be dodged even outside of bullet time. Despite this change to enemy design, bullet time and the shootdodge feel just as good in this game as they ever have. I was surprised to be reminded of Max Payne 3 of all things while playing. Headshots are usually one hit kills in this game, and it is very satisfying to dive over a counter and pop three enemies in the head before you even hit the ground. It's a very good mix of the fast paced action from the first two Max Payne games and the preciseness of the third one.So the game is fun of course, but I was also surprised at how much the story resonated with me. It's a little bit out there at first, but once I realized where it was going I was absolutely hooked. James Savage might seem a lot like Max on the surface, but as the game goes on you start to see a lot of his own personal struggles and vulnerabilities. His VA is great and gets a lot of moments to perform his heart out while also maintaining an element of cool. I should also probably the mention the soundtrack for this game is very... unique. I don't know if the rap music here would work at all outside of the game, but in the game it's fun and amps up the energy so Idk it's fine.As for criticisms, the game really struggles with keeping it's low variety of enemies interesting throughout the whole game, even with two boss fights. Even though the game is only about 5-6 hours, I feel like you could remove at least one of those hours and not really miss out on all that much. With that in mind, the short levels this game offers are both a blessing and a curse. While it does make it easy to jump into the game and have fun for an hour, it also makes the game feel a lot longer than it actually is when there are so many of them. Overall I think this game is pretty cool: a new take on a familiar gameplay style that doesn't get enough credit. If they make a sequel I will gladly play it.

_childDocuments_.review: . It's a charming homage to old action classics like , because it pretty much is  but you're shooting/staking creatures of myth and you're trying to kill your vampire ex-girlfriend. I could go on about how the guns all feel fun to use and the levels somehow never feel like they're just repeating each other despite there's only like five settings and six enemies in the game but what really sells the game is the tone. Xalavier Nelson Jr voices the protagonist James Savage and provides most if not all of the music and that, on top of the brilliant cinematography and pacing, grounds the game rock solid in an unforgettably dreary, surreal, and haunting atmosphere. Thank goodness for that because I feel like the game goes for a bit longer than necessary. I clocked in nine hours and it's solid to play but its biggest issue (of which it has very few) is that the combat never really has the room to expand as far as it could. All of your seven weapons are too similar to each other to warrant changing them for most encounters, levels are mostly passageways that are far too cramped so your dodge and dive abilities aren't particularly useful and you spend most of your time downing enemies from doorways you can barely see past, and you have so much ammo that I ended up using guns simply to make room for all the ammo I was tripping over. I do recommend  but do keep in mind that the combat might wear you down.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere is a throwback to Remedy's neo-noir classic Max Payne 1/2. You know the routine: dive, shoot, go into bullet time and pull off a bunch of impossible consecutive headshots; but this time, there's mummies, vampires and werewolves in a surreal dreamscape 2-star motel with 46 stories descending into the void. Also, there's puppets. Too many puppets. The cutscene direction and writing are top notch, you really feel for James and Draculae by the time you're through (around 7 hours, based on my playtime) and some blocking shots and vistas in the cutscenes really wowed me. The OST is another highlight, and it fits in insanely well with the levels and gameplay, with some choice needle drop moments. The only complaints I could really bring up are practically nitpicks, I had a nasty visual bug that'd wind up blacking out my entire screen, and a few times a button prompt would be kind of finicky to trigger, but it's a small team and they're still actively patching the game as of writing. Overall, if you're a fan of older style TPS games and an interesting, weird story, I'd give this a look.
_childDocuments_.name: El Paso, Elsewhere

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game with a slow start, and not sure when it decides to end. The game feels like a labor of love but one of those ones where the game was designed *exactly* as the dev wanted while getting sidetracked with ideas that sounded cool but felt like tonal whiplash or don't work as intended. Biggest gripe is bullet time is only used for the first 10 levels, then the rest of the game wants you dark souls dodge rolling because your bullet time dive actually leaves you more vulnerable than useful. The boss fights just dont feel good, and feel like someone looked at a paragraph describing a souls fight and thought "yeah, that'd be cool to add to my game". Then this complaint might seem odd but holy hell the game is long and padded long not fun long. 35-40 levels would have been good but my brother in christ the game is still going. and what is tragic is there's a few decent and well laid out fights (monster club and ouroboros) being my favorites. but i pretty much universally hated anything that was  because they wer elong ass mazes with closer than close quarters and more monster closets than doom 3 in the bathroom themed stuff. Now, why would i complain this much? Because the game when it has a great pace going feels fun- the story is pretty interesting and Savage is a moderately interesting character though he should maybe tell less at times. I thought i could finish it in one sitting but all the padding burned me out for the day and i'll beat it tommorrow. Only closing comments is the Rap is jarring because some tracks are good, others are flat out not good and kind of interfere with the tone of some levels.

_childDocuments_.review: EDITED EDITED: So Neo-Noir is a thing. Well I just look like a knob now, don't I?EDITED REVIEW: I wanted to add some thoughts to the review I made for El Paso, Elsewhere as I felt like I should add onto my thoughts and opinions as the original was not much to look at, and wanted to express more but didn't at the time. Original review will still be below this edited review, even though its not a lot to look at.After my original review of the game, I jumped back in and am halfway through on an evil playthrough currently. I bought the soundtrack on Bandcamp and even bought into the Makeship plushie they had for Draculae (It failed its funding period, but oh well). The game left that much of an impression on me, but I was a bit clueless as to why. It was great, definitely inspired by Max Payne in terms of gameplay which is a great game to use, but couldn't put into words what was the 'thing' that got me.Then it hit me. I mentioned it in the original review where I said that the story was very film noir in terms of its characters, its writing and atmosphere, despite the setting. That was the part I was missing. The story isn't a  Film Noir inspired romp with a hell setting (Well, it kind of is). It's a template of what Film Noir can become in terms of story, character and emotional expression in the modern day.The story scenes themselves inbetween almost each level could make the story great, but the soundtracks where LS takes over the vocals, give me a much deeper understanding of James's inner turmoil, emotions, the havoc he causes and the wreck he was left as by Draculae. He feels so much more fleshed out as a character and the story as a whole due to this change.The changes made to the theme of what we could consider Film Noir in this game with the mix of gritty, character focused storytelling and its introspective, intoxicating rap soundtrack could absolutely be utilised elsewhere (No pun intended). Other video games, movies, TV shows, audio drama.All I'm saying is keep an eye out for other forms of media that will follow this type of writing and story beats going forward. El Paso, Elsewhere is not a revolution of Film Noir storytelling, but its an evolution of it to modern day that wouldn't surprise me if it catches on.ORIGINAL REVIEW: Absolutely amazing game. El Paso, Elsewhere grabbed me from the start and I didn't want to stop playing until the very end. _childDocuments_.review: The storytelling style in this game is simply excellent.  The low-res visual style may not be for everyone, it will definitely be a turn-off for some, but it runs buttery smooth and they definitely went in a very cinematic direction with the cutscenes as the camera work is very dynamic.  The game overall oozes this sort of neo-noir style that I can't say is necessarily tongue-in cheek but breaks the fourth wall in a way that feels just right.  It's fun without being silly, and that extends to the gameplay.   I had a hard time describing it when recommending it to friends but the best I summed it up was "Think about a supernatural themed Max Payne demake and you'll be most of the way there."  Run and gunning while trying to survive with the limited ammo (though as you go, if you are staking enemies enough to save ammo, you will build up enough to use weapons liberally) adds a layer of difficulty that takes getting used to at first, but once you get your groove it feels solid.  New weapons pop up soon enough that combat doesn't start to feel stale, and feel good to use.  (Note: I played on the "Intended" difficulty level) The bullet time leaps are more a survival necessity than a cool factor, buying you precious seconds to kill impending threats to your health, or to escape, as you start to have encounters with higher enemy density that will kill you before you have time to heal.Another thing I appreciate is that the game seems to handle checkpointing and respawning rather fairly compared to games of its ilk.  I died my share as I wouldn't consider myself a particularly skilled player of fast-paced high difficulty retro-style games, but never felt like I was being heavily punished for it.  You are sent back a ways but have all the items and ammo you had when you reached that checkpoint originally, no restarting the whole level or being stuck with the ammo count you had after dying.  Gets you back in the fight quick which contributes to the overall faster pace this game feels like it has compared to your average game.On the note of fast pace, this game has a spectacular soundtrack that definitely contributes to that feeling.  So far every level I've played has had something great with a very driving feel to it.  It's also quite an eclectic mix of genres that helps keep things fresh, definitely interesting.  As for negatives, I would say it can feel repetitive, so maybe long sessions of the game could get grating after a bit since there are only so many environment types, and the gameplay loop is somewhat simple, some of the voice lines in-level from fighting enemies, picking up items, or saving hostages can repeat a few times.  I feel like for me at least, the game uses its positives to offset these, most levels have something new to them, even if sometimes just storytelling-wise.  Give it a try, what have you got to lose?

It feels forced to keep the love story heterosexual, and ends up being a bit too derivative even considering the referencial way in which it is written. I can't think of a reason for this choice over a female protagonist or a gay romance. Either would have helped the story feel more unique and the character a bit less flat.

_childDocuments_.review: To be clear, I'm writing this after playing this game to what I think is the genuine end of the first act, so maybe halfway to a third of the way through the game, and I have been taking an easy pace through it. This game is a Greek tragedy with bullet time and vampires, and the character you play is simultaneously the protagonist and the chorus. The controls are genuinely good, the art style is fantastic -- as someone who never really touched the Max Payne series, this game makes me want to go back and give those a try once I'm done here. The various weapons are all fun to use, but ammo and recovery items are paced to your difficulty level, so you'll often find yourself running out of ammo often if you're trying to do an all-pistol run or something.Important note, no spoilers but fair warning: the story may hit you a little hard if you've had a really, really bad relationship before -- that said, I personally think the treatment of the various "sensitive" subject matters in this game has been solid so far, and all of that stuff makes reasonable sense in the narrative. It's clear that a lot of care went into making this game and making it well: there are a few things I would prefer this game do differently (melee having an ammo limit will always feel weird to me in these kinds of games) but those are matters of taste, not a design flaw, and I've yet to run into something in this game that I don't like because it doesn't work or doesn't fit the concept. It's a good game that stands well on its own and, as I've been told by the folks who watched me play it, a "damn fine" entry for the genre as a whole.

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso Elsewhere is one of my favorite games of 2023, the game play, story, and overall aesthetic are a wonder to behold. The game play is a love letter to third-person shooters paying homage to games like Max Payne while still retaining its own individuality. The variety of weapons allow you to take a different approach to the enemies you encounter. Overall I enjoyed each gun's distinct advantage in encounters. I found myself switching between guns rapidly to dispatch waves of enemies or when navigating the claustrophobic hallways with harrowing blind spots. The Story is a deep narrative regarding two broken people trapped in an abusive relationship where both sides can't help but hurt each other in the end. The overall concept of a realm outside of heaven and hell soul bent on the ruin of existence itself was masterfully done adding a layer of mystery. The game establishes that the journey your taking is one way and you feel the tangible weight of that knowledge as you progress. Many of the cut scenes within the game have so many great  cinematic shots that it really proves that art style outweighs photo realistic graphics.As the credits rolled at the end of my play through of El Paso Elsewhere, I felt like I had experienced something astounding in the world of gaming. A story of a broken man desperately clawing his way through the madness of the world around him and confronting the woman that he once loved. You Keep Going will always echo within my mind reminding me of the exceptional journey I embarked upon.

_childDocuments_.review: El Paso, Elsewhere overwhelms the senses with atmosphere and action.It's darkly humorous, playing liberally on Noir tropes. Somber, with a love-sucking story of loss composed by brilliant cut scene direction. And crackling with action that's had me coiling my hands around the controller with a steel grip. There's one instance where after you fling James through a window, he complains, knowingly, about how many more times this is going to happen until he reaches the inevitable end. Honoring your inspirations and transcending them to say something new, while making a game that feels damn good.I'm still not very far through it, so grain of salt, but El Paso, Elsewhere is the silky smooth, head-thrum-thrumming Noir love story more games, and media, wish they were.Don't look back. _childDocuments_.review: I've never had a game that quite made me mad like this before.I've had games that frustrated me, sure.  Games that pissed me off due to their very existence. _childDocuments_.review: I have played the game extensively on Xbox and double dipped on PC. _childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna throw myself on the mercy of the court and compare it to Max Payne, since the gameplay inevitably is going to draw those comparisons to it. When I think of Max Payne, I think of a man blasted out of his mind on painkillers talking in neo-noir platitudes while gunning down loads of bad guys with a gun in each hand. El Paso, Elsewhere hits those notes, but with less of the neo-noir and more of the internal introspection, and you're also shooting loads of mummies and werewolves. It's 75% of the way there, in terms of how it hits and how it performs, but the remaining 25% is in the way the game weaves its tale and the way the game can be picked up and put down between five minute short bursts. It doesn't quite hit its full potential, but it didn't make me want to stop playing, either. Also, the game's physics are weird enough that it allows you to send a werewolf flying out of the game if you shoot it just right with a shotgun, and that's something Max Payne can't offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily a love letter to Max Payne series its cool dive in to this love story grasping lots of interesting themes from classic one man army monologues  all the way to examples of dealing with depression and being in toxic relationship its a fun ride with an Amazing soundtrack worth your time i would recommend

_childDocuments_.review: It might make you cry. El Paso, Elsewhere has stylish, over the top action and will have you mowing down monster hordes with an array of satisfying weapons while jumping through tables in slow motion. The game's pulse pounding soundtrack will drive you through each level like a bat out of hell. And at the end of it all you might cry as you reflect on the journey of destruction and what it meant for the characters that have been so thoughtfully crafted by the dev team. It's a story of what we do with our pain, how we respond to it, and learning that every floor is a new floor. I strongly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Max Payne experience in absoltuely fantastic new coat.Immerse into a fantastic story, face hordes of (adorable) werewolves and other creatures of the night, all with accompany of really captivating soundtrack.I love how little details makes this game so fun to immerse into - the muffled sound urging you to escape, the halftoned textures looking so good on character models, PC commenting on the surrounding world (imagien that -one of biggest "sins" of modern gaming, yet tEl Paso execute it so well), sudden neon filled rooms, Chad Shakespeare...I am not a fan of rap music, and I loved the score, making certain levels feeling so much more dangerous and thrilling thanks to it.
