_childDocuments_.review: My true playtime is closer to two hours, I accidentally left the game running...I can't recommend it at full price. Would def recommend around 10 dollars or less though. The problem is that it seemed like you could do a lot more than you actually could. It appears at first like you can try and frame anyone but that is not actually the case, there are only a couple workable options. The story it hints at for different characters could be interesting but you never get the details (such as a gallery or something of news clippings). Regarding the news clippings some of them conflict with the game: you were photographed with x character before the trip but when you are on the trip it seems you've never met for example...It would've been a lot more fun if the options were in place for you to frame any character, find out more about your fellow passengers etc
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing. It turns out that getting away with murder is incredibly easy. The goal of the game is rather to explore the extra stuff. For example, can you pin it on someone? Can you murder everyone on the ship? The game however leaves little room for experimentation, so if you try something and it doesn't work you have to either reset the run and repeat many steps or continue the run and repeat many steps. It's like playing a puzzle game and only getting one chance to try out a solution every 15-30 minutes. And for what? None of the extra things I observed so far enticed me to explore further.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Is it a good game ? Yes. Is it a perfect game ? No. Is it frustrating ? YesThis game is great for a challenge. The art style, dialogue and gameplay is very engaging and enjoyable. But there are some little big things that let it down. Probably the biggest is the one that affects all of this type of game. You select a dialogue option, such as "I don't know where he is" only to have the game add incriminating information that you really didn't want it to like "I haven't seen him since last night". So you go from being innocent to going to jail for one random programming flaw. Some additional playtesting might have ironed these things out and make it less frustrating for the gamer.Hopefully if there is a sequel they'll fix some of these issues.Its good, don't get me wrong, just not great.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Once again I'm wishing for a "Meh" or "Just wasn't for me" button because I hate giving it a thumbs down when it isn't a bad game by any means. I just don't think this is the game for me.I love the art style, the concept, the characters, and the atmosphere. I just don't really like the gameplay. I felt so defeated after a few runs of getting arrested and felt even worse when I really had no clue how to successfully frame someone or get someone else to confess - this might just be a impatient thing of mine, but I ended up just looking up how to get away with the murder. I like that there's a bit of direction with the checklist, but I needed more of a push in the right direction because as many times as I planted all the things in Clarissa's room, it wasn't really clear to me what further I needed to do. I was missing just one little dialogue or move that led to that ending and then I'd have to do it all over again just to fail again. It was a bit frustrating to me. As much as I like the idea that not only is the ending dependent on your lying skills and choices but your time management and catching people at the right moment, this feature was also my worst enemy.So I truly appreciate the love and time and energy put into this game because it is a really well done game - I just don't think I'm patient enough to figure out everyone's timeline and combine that with what I need to do and when and do it all fast enough to finish before the meeting is called automatically while not being caught.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Overboard! is intended for multiple playthroughs. My first six attempts landed Veronica in prison. Each attempt I learned more, feeling my way forward by trial and error. Characters follow a predetermined path that only changes if Veronica interrupts them. On my seventh attempt I succeeded in avoiding arrest. This wasn't the “best” ending. I was told by my accomplice, that I should “do it again” because I had convinced the detective that my husband died by suicide. You don't get life insurance for suicide. I needed to frame someone.But after this seventh attempt I was tired of repeating this game. I took my freedom as a minor victory and set sail for new games.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little concept for a game, and the writing is pretty on point as per usual for inkle, but... I dunno, I felt a little underwhelmed by this one? I fee like the depth just isn't quite there, like, you can replay this dozens of times (and probably will trying to get all the side-achievements and endings) but the flow never changes significantly - characters usually have a hidden secret or two that range from "easy to find out" to "because the game discourages experimentation due to the time investment in a single loop i would not have found this out without a guide" which... ehh. The loops aren't -that- long when you know what you're doing, sure, but it can still feel like slightly too much, at least to me. I still did enjoy this, though I don't know if it has enough to warrant its $15 price tag either... cautious recommendation but recommended nonetheless.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: at first i was kinda annoyed thinking it was too short to pay what i did even tho i got it half off but i ended up getting obsessed with getting all the achievements and now im sad i have nothing left to do in the game.  it was a lot of fun and def worth what i paid for it.  i wouldnt pay full price tho tbh.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing little game with tons of replayability. You spend a 15-20 mins trying to cover up a murder and see if it worked and then do it again, with more information and a better plan. You start to get more ambitious. Why's one murder enough? Why not two? Three? It's an audiovisual treat and Veronica as the main character is one of the better playable villains in a long time. This is just distilled gaming goodness if you like things such as Poirot or dark humor.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Had a lot of fun with this one. It's an immensely entertaining and replayable text adventure straight out of Agatha Christie novel in which you're the perpetrator and your goal is to escape justice and frame someone else. It has incredibly good gameplay for a text-based game and allows you to scheme freely and encounter many unexpected situations. There are 6 characters to talk to aboard a rather small ship but there's tons of secrets to uncover and multiple endings to unlock. And experimenting is so fun I did 100% (although there still might be some dialogue options I haven't seen).I'm glad I found this brilliant little game.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Bought as game design reference.Its unique pov of "getting away from accusations" is fascinating, and is a first step towards a better detective game narration. As the phantom that haunts detective games for ages - the "who will validate player's solution" phantom, is finally given a blow in this game. Instead of validation, use cause and effects, which is simply a more dynamic, engaging way of telling a detective story. And really, the narration backend, ink, made also by the devs, is clearly powerful to allow them to do all sort of crazy narration experiments.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: I've got to say, I'm quite disappointed with this game. I don't often mind repetitive and slam-your-head-against-a-wall-till-something-gives games, because more often then not those games have characters and wit! Unfortunately, Overboard has opted instead for having cardboard stand-ins for an interesting cast and a sore lack of charm or humor or real intelligent choices the player could make,,, just LITERALLY ANYTHING to save it. If you don't like the core mechanic of "fumble blindly in the dark", there is nothing worthwhile elsewhere in it, and if you do like the core mechanic, there's very little meat to the game at all anyways. If you're really curious, wait until it's on sale for at least 30% off.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those fun little indie games to play over a weekend. You are on a boat in 1935, you push your husband overboard one night. Then you spend the next day trying to get away with it; frame/murder/other passengers, plant fake evidence, etc. A single run thru is just 15-30 minutes. Depending on your choices, you either end up in jail or free, or free with other perks. It's really well made, well presented, and has a lot of quality of life / player friendly touches to respect your time. There are checklists and hints to help you find other options.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: It was okay. Fun idea and storyline, but it was not necessarily a logic-based game like I expected. It is more so trial-and-error because you can never really know which dialogue option or specific action got you one ending over another. I wish there was a map of choices available like in Detroit Become Human.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Its been a long time since I've played a game that made me think about my next step as much as this one. Each run of the game takes about 20-25 minutes, and there are so many avenues to explore.I'm not the kind of person to replay a game just to see what happens if I pick a different dialogue option, but in this game i thoroughly enjoyed that aspect of it.Its a good game if you want some brain food to chew on.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting twist on the old school who-done-it mystery, cause you-done-it but can you manage to be found innocent? Quick game with multiple replays to make different choices. I've been enjoying it. The design and music are perfect for this period 1930's story. The characters and dialogue are reminiscent of black-and-white films. A well-rounded game, and my only complaint is that it's too short. Still, it's not as easy as you would think to get yourself off the Hook and into a nice hotel on land.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game because I was watching Youtube videos about mystery game design. I saw a talk from one of the devs discussing how most mystery games are about clues and suspects unveiling a single fixed story, and instead, they built a game where you, the player, use clues and create suspects to build up your own story of events. Then, the game uses the "parlor scene" to bring it all together.I was excited to play it, and it sure delivered. The game loop is addictive. It's dark and funny, and encourages you to uncover more secrets about your fellow passengers--so you can use those secrets to your advantage! I like that they show you which option you picked on your last play. It makes it easier to see your goals through. I love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: You know the saying "as wide as an ocean but as deep as a puddle"? I think this game might the opposite of that. I was NOT expecting much going into this, just a quick, 2010 flash-like game about trying to prove your innocence up against a few number checking AIs. What I got was something that was shockingly deep, and compelled me to 100% the game (and I'm still sure there's options I haven't explored). You'll most likely lose the first go around, even if you think you've covered all your bases. But the game is meant to be replayed again and again. You'll find out more each run through, and then use it the next go around (But it ISN'T a time loop. Information and items won't carry over, but the game does make it easy enough to skip through what you've already done)I highly encourage this game if you're motivated by achievements and flavour dialogue, but discourage this game if you desire a really meaty story or aren't that impressed by low budget affairs (the game stretches it's budget well, but if you have a particularly critical eye, it might not hold up. Def buy on sale. I got it for AUD$8, and it's not worth AUD$20.)
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: In Overboard, you play as Veronica Villensey, a wealthy socialite who has pushed her husband overboard on a cruise ship. Your goal is to get away with murder by manipulating the passengers and crew, planting evidence, and creating alibis.The game's non-linear structure allows players to explore different strategies and approaches to solving the mystery. The game's writing is also a highlight, with clever dialogue and a cast of quirky characters that add to the game's charm.Overall, Overboard is a refreshing and original take on the puzzle genre that offers a fun and challenging experience for players. If you enjoy puzzle games with a strong narrative and unique gameplay mechanics, Overboard is definitely worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: If only they had Load/Save files, then I could really enjoy this game.The story is pretty good and exciting, and I'm impressed with how thoughtful the gameplay is. You're on a ship with seven people, and you’re the murderer of your husband. Your goal? To figure out how to hide your crime or pin it on someone else before the ship reaches port in just a few hours! In the end, you either end up in jail or walk away free. There are so many conversations, decisions, and paths to explore, allowing you to truly master the art of getting away with murder.The only issue? You have to repeat the entire story because they don't have Load/Save files. You can only rewind the scene if you mess up a conversation, but if you want to try different paths, you’ll have to start a whole new game, which feels torturous to me. After about three hours of repeating the same scenes just to try a new option, I got bored. It takes the fun out of experimenting with different choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a gem: fun, sleek, surprising. Its gameplay and writing both are efficient & appealing; they "deserve each other" more than any game I've played in a while. For me, getting away with the game's central murder was challenging but not overwhelming; it took four (short) playthroughs, and now I am slowly mapping out more baroque & extensive killing sprees.And, as much as I want to recommend this game on its own merits, I also want to recommend it on its "meta-merits". This is a compact narrative game that uses text as its primary "rendering engine" but augments it with stylish art and snappy interactions… produced by an independent studio… that is responsible for developing and sharing an amazingly capable scripting language for interactive fiction that has benefited many other studios, developers, and writers alike. If a Steam purchase is always, in some sense, a vote for "more of this, please!" then… MORE OF THIS, PLEASE!
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Not in the same vein as 80 days where there was always some new combination that would take you strange and interesting places.In urgent need of a rewind function as what is actually quite little content is padded out by making you play the whole thing over and over again which even with the fast forward function is a pain.Guests follow set patterns so it is just a case of working out how to deal with it- vaguely amusing to try and work out ways of breaking it.  However many of the things that you think should work do not due to limited options (e.g. much of the material you can only plant in one specific place)
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept, but the game bit off more than it could chew. First of all, this feels less like a visual novel(ette) and more like a choose your own adventure. What's the difference? VNs usually have few choices with tons of text in between, here is a ton of choices with few text in between. So far so good? No, because the dialogue parts feel rushed and insignificant (even though they aren't).Let me just get straight to the point: it feels like it's just a matter of choosing a few correct options. I felt very railroaded, so to speak. I definitely didn't feel like I'm covering up a murder, more like I'm going through the motions. Especially since the game is "aware" that this is a repeating situation, ever characters sometimes say that "let's try again". I don't know, that feels somewhat jarring. Game sessions are short - which makes it seem like it lacks depth. The funny thing is, I saw that there's a lot of things that can happen, but for some reason it doesn't really feel that way.If you played Among Us and tried to get away with murder there, this is a completely different game. I would compare it to Elsinore if nothing else, or perhaps The Sexy Brutale, in the sense that they're all "explore the day" kind of games. I liked Elsinore, I loved The Sexy Brutale, but this... eh, pass on this one. Not refunding. I got one of the endings, refunding after seeing the ending would be dishonest.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: It just doesn't work as well as I thought it would. Clicking through dialogue trees isn't engaging enough to make re-treading the same ground interesting to me, and I got out of it on my second time through. Then the only thing to do is find the other ways to your freedom, but the game is so rigid that every time I had an idea I wanted to try, it turned out it was something I couldn't do, and I'd wasted a run on nothing. I like the art and the general vibe of the game, the writing is funny in an on-the-nose kinda way. But much like 80 Days, I think it's just a lot less replayable than it purports to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Overboard! Is such a fun twist on typical murder mystery games. It's complex without being confusing, and you're rewarded for misteps. It also has so much replay value, allowing for multiple endings and numerous plot lines to follow no matter what kind of ending you're aiming for. I highly reccommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: A remarkably fun game about getting away with murder - pretty much exactly what it says on the tin! Nothing's ever as simple as it looks, and there's just enough moving parts that it kept me thinking about it even when I wasn't playing it. It's not so complicated as to be *hard* per se - just the right level of difficulty. Just a straight up, wholesome good time! Ignoring the homicide and frameup job, of course.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: (Received for free due to helping with playtesting, but absolutely would have purchased anyway)Overboard! is a blast. It feels so satisfying every time you figure out some new way to hide something, misdirect, or even add to the body count. The game has a great system of noting and reminding you of things you've learned about but not yet addressed, so you always have an objective. Even when you manage to get away with it, there are several goals beyond that that really press you to perfect your run.Also comes with *really* fun music, plus the most hilarious discussions with God I've ever had.

_childDocuments_.review: 4/10: A sub-par choose-your-own adventure visual novel that fails to stand out in any way.It's pretty typical choose-your-own adventure fair, but it's not the best. I saw everything I wanted to see within 3 hours and am requesting a refund.Whatever you're imagining this game is like, you're being too generous. The key items have very limited usefulness and most of the characters can only be killed/threatened in one way-- incidentally, a way that 90% of the other passengers can also only be killed/threatened.Oh, and the game gets trivial pretty fast when you figure out who your accomplice is. And it's one thing in the Nonary Games where you can't figure something like that out until one of the very last endings, but in this game, I learned about it on my second run. (Of about 18 total)I think the entire game can best be summarized by this subplot:At some point you can learn of a rumor that the ship is sinking. You may think it's quite a side-story to go check out, and may spend a little bit of effort to do so, but I'm going to go ahead and spoil it because there is literally no subterfuge or twist here. If you talk to the captain, he will straight up tell you 'No, the ship isn't sinking, the person who told you that has precisely one character trait; Drunk.' AND THAT'S THE END OF THE SUBPLOT. Can you imagine if other murder mysteries did this?"I've caught word that there's a major conspiracy in our city." And then the mayor tells you there isn't one, and that's how the side mission ends.And I know this is petty, but this game legitimately has one of the worst, most unsatisfying secret endings in any game I've ever played. I'm not going to spoil it for you, but it is so far removed from everything else that's going on in the game, it ties up precisely zero loose ends and it's just... weak. It doesn't have any impact on you when you get it. It's just silly.4/10

_childDocuments_.review: i really enjoyed this!!! you push your cheating husband overboard and play through multiple stories/ endings. you can either get caught, pin it on someone else, blackmail someone into covering for you, pass it off as suicide or murder more people. learning about each character was interesting and seeing all the different dialogue options/ endings. one of the endings is a lil weird tho

_childDocuments_.review: It is a good game, but It certainly could have been better. Starting with the good stuff I really enjoyed both the idea of the reversed crime story and Agata Christie like atmosphere. Talking cross is also a great feauture. _childDocuments_.review: Overboard is a new game by Inkle Studios, the company who made Heaven’s Vault, Pendragon and 80 Days. Like 80 Days, Overboard is a piece of interactive fiction. It’s a murder mystery, with you as the murderer.  Set in 1935, aboard a ship destined for New York, you play as the recently married Veronica Villensey. At the start of the game, you push your husband, Malcolm, overboard, for reasons initially unclear.  And so, begins a Groundhog Day narrative cycle where you have 8 hrs (game time, not real time) before the ship docks and Malcolm’s whereabouts need to be explained.   Gameplay takes the form of a choose your own adventure story. Played from a series of beautifully animated static frames, you always have multiple actions or dialogue options to choose from, and each decision brings with it consequences. The other NPCs on board remember what you say, and how you act, and this all culminates in a final Hercule Poirot-esque scene, where the Major gets his little grey cells working overtime to solve the crime – which will most likely involve you behind bars on arrival in New York. But there must be a way to escape scott-free? And that’s the crux of the game. After each indictment, you wake up back at the start, with all of your recent knowledge intact. Previous choices are highlighted in green to help you decide which narrative path to take this time.  My first playthrough lasted about 5 minutes. I chose to take some sleeping pills, woke up hours later, and was immediately taken for interrogation. Expect to play through the game many times, as you learn what to say and do, who to speak to, and when, as you try to secure your freedom, Malcolm’s sizeable life insurance, and get away with murder. Overboard is clearly inspired by Agatha Christie novels and Alfred Hitchcock films. It most reminded me of ‘Double Indemnity’, a 1940s film noir starring a scheming femme fatale who murders her husband by getting her lover to push him off a train to claim his life insurance.  A super gem of a game!The game featured in my Indie Games of the Week for May 31 - June 6, here:
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: A short, yet hilarious choices-matter interactive storytelling experience. That's as many buzz words as I could get into one sentence. But in all honesty, this game was a lot of fun and the premise is extremely simple, with mechanics that allow you to skip dialogue you have already seen, re-make decisions you know work, and experience so many different paths. Totally worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever read one of Agatha Christie's murder mysteries? Have you watched Knives Out, or any of the movies based on Christie's novels? Do you like virtual novels and choices that matter? Do you ever wanna be the bad guy?If your answer is yes or if these are things that interest you, look no further than Overboard! You and a small cast of interesting characters are on a voyage to New York City circa 1935 and you must figure out what everyone knows about your husband's death. Here's the catch: the person that murdered him....... is YOU. The game begins with you pushing your husband overboard and you have until the ship reaches the harbor to alleviate suspicion and make it seem like you are innocent. The game's music is jazz recorded by the US Army (which is pretty cool) and the art is smooth and precise. The best thing about the game are the choices and sheer replayibility it has to offer. There are easily HUNDREDS of different scenarios that can happen because of you talking to certain passengers at different times and the ability to pick up items and use them in different ways. Another genius concept the game utilizes is a built in clock that records when you go to certain locations and talk to people. If you go to the upper deck at 9:30am, there will be a different scenario that happens at 2:12pm, etc. The passengers actively move around as time goes on so you can learn to track their movements and plan your moves to plant evidence, spy, or avoid them. The dialogue is very unique for a game as well. The conversations mesh realistically and situations can play out entirely different based on your attitude. The game also mixes in humor quite well. There were a handful of lines that actually made me laugh out loud most of which came from God himself..... yes, you can pray and hold a hilarious conversation with God and he will troll you for murdering your husband and also give you information. There is also a mini game tucked into the game as well. You can play one of the patrons in Pontoon (21) and you can change bet amounts and decisions. The game overall has a multitude of different endings based on your actions: you are found guilty, found innocent, get insurance money, and/or tie up loose ends. To get the best result, it will take numerous tries (without the help of walkthroughs, or course) and is very difficult to beat. Don't listen to the comment section saying it's easy to get every achievement, because it isn't. They 100% used walkthroughs and help to  get them all quickly whereas I'm 7 hours in and I'm not even halfway done with them because I'm doing trial and error and not using help.All in all, this game is a diamond in the rough for fans of whodunits and really makes you use your brain to try and get away with murder. Play it now!
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a ship murder mystery, but you're the murderer while the other crew members act like the detectives. The game begins after you (a married lady) have just thrown your husband overboard the night before. Luckily, no-one seems to know yet (or do they?). You quickly need to figure out what the guests know, hide any evidence and tie up any remaining loose ends. There are a wide variety of ways to do this; like pinning the murder on someone else or making it look like a suicide. You simply need to ensure your story adds up at the end, or the evidence will stack up against you. Time passes when you wander the ship, and of course you can't be in two places at one time: Being in one place at a certain time might mean missing out on an opportunity elsewhere.Most of the fun comes from the dialogue. The writing is excellent, and all the characters have interesting quirks and personalities. It is easy to completely mess your story up the first time around and end up arrested, but in each subsequent playthrough you'll use the information you gathered previously to perfect your strategy. The impact of a particular (dialogue) option is often implied, but never fully revealed beforehand. At times you just have to try one and see what the effects are. Often I've found the impact of certain simple responses to be far more dramatic than I thought, suddenly opening up entirely new strategies. Even an unfortunate dialogue option can reveal very important (or exploitable) information about a certain character for your next run. The game helpfully shows you the option you picked in your last run so it is easier to experiment. Eventually you will form a specific strategy and lie, manipulate, seduce or even murder your way to freedom.I found the main character to be very charming, despite her obvious tendency for murder. It is easy to relate to her, and the dialogue options that you are provided with will certainly express that sinking feeling in your own gut when you are caught in a lie. And if you subsequently get arrested, you can choose to go out with grace or by cursing everyone within reach. She also has her own quirks (dolphins come to mind) that you'll learn more about each playthrough, as well as her motivations for committing murder in the first place.The game is definitely meant to be replayed, since you won't get the full picture the first time around. There are multiple endings and even after you successfully get away with murder there are additional side objectives to unlock for your next run. But of course, eventually you'll have seen most of what is on offer. I guess my only 'complaint' about this game is that I wish that there was more content. I would have loved to help the main character 'unsolve' some additional murder scenes.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked 80 days then you may like this. I'd say it's tentative to how much you like the idea of a reverse murder mystery. Honestly, I think I'd have preferred an actual detective narrative for this kind of story rather than vice versa.End of the day it's enjoyable, but the scope is significantly less than 80 Days. Given the amount you can do in that game, the options and paths you took felt limitless, whereas this game is very much a rinse, repeat, trial and error sort of affair, which can honestly feel a little loose when it comes to common sense (The trigger points for what actually makes you succeed and fail during the denoument are rather inane)I'd like to see them do something far bigger in scope with this idea. This felt like a demo episode of what could've been a much more fulfilling experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Overboard! Is a game by Inkle wherein the classic whodunit formula is turned on its head; , Veronica Villensey, are the killer, having pushed your foolhardy husband overboard at the dead of night. Now, with just 8 hours to go before you sail into the port of New York, you must find a way to evade suspicion by the crew and other passengers, all the while using clues, objects, and choices to dictate every step of your way.Overboard is presented as a visual novel, with choices and impacts being marked down by red text on the upper edge of the screen. The game uses this to its fullest extent; tell the Captain you saw your husband earlier today, but during a later confrontation, admit to not having seen him since yesterday? He's going to find that awfully suspicious. The game has countless different choices, through both dialogue and physical actions, that you can choose to engage in before the boat sails into New York, either to clear Veronica's name, pin it on somebody else, or flounder and fail to avoid suspicion. Meanwhile, every action and dialogue takes a certain amount of time to complete, and the cast of characters have schedules around the boat that shift, so you're always kept on your toes to act.Overboard can be beaten within a few minutes if you just want to get to the end of a single scenario, but the sheer amount of choices, endings, and possibilities that you can find yourself in give it endless replayability; Do you run up on deck to hide evidence that you were on it last night, risking not attending breakfast? Do you murder the bellhop to get his key, at risk of having the corpse found? Do you investigate your late husband's habits and find an excuse for his disappearance? Overboard is a great little visual novel and reversal of the whodunit, with a lot of replayability, dark humor, and charm that makes it stand out as a title.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: I never expected getting away with murder would be this fun! I thought Overboard would be a straightforward piece of interactive fiction, a few different routes to a few different endings, a great story along the way. Instead what I found was a deceptively simple game with a ton of moving parts. Everyone you share the ship with has their own routines, agendas and information, all of which are stacked against you. When you start this game, you will almost certainly fail. It's through multiple (very quick!) playthroughs that you'll begin to piece together what's going on, what everyone's hiding and what gaps in their knowledge you can exploit. The result is a deeply replayable game where each session will leave you excited to try new things in the next. I stumbled into a sort of success early on, but it took me a couple of hours to truly grasp what was going on, and a couple more to use what I'd learned effectively. In that time I couldn't tear myself away. Each attempt is short and fast paced, but I found myself playing several of them, one after the other, without ever getting bored.This is served by the hilarious writing and the colourful characters. They all make distinct first impressions that give way to surprising depth given how little time we spend with each of them. This also creates an interesting shift from my first few sessions to my last: at the start this game was a puzzle to solve, but by the end it was a playground to explore. I'd already accomplished my main goals, and now I had the chance to learn more about the characters and see how far I could push them. Overboard is great. I'm sure people who aren't super into narrative games will still have a lot of fun with this because of its fast pace and its clear goals, but if you like interactive fiction you will love this. Specifically if you're a fan of 80 Days this should be right up your alley. It's not 80 Days and it's not trying to be, but I think it serves the same kinds of players. It sure did for me.In short, yes, play this game. You can play it in fifteen minute chunks but I can promise you it'll keep you coming back for hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Great mystery game with  short game play loop but lots of replay-ability. I enjoyed after each run, you were given new objectives to try and discover. It was also really interesting that there are multiple ways for success. There was a couple of sequencing issues with the writing, where it didn't fully make sense when you selected certain options but this only happened a couple of times. I wish there was a way to track what decisions I made, similar to the Nonary games but each run was short enough so it wasn't a big problem (only small nitpicks)Overall it was really enjoyable and I enjoyed learning about the characters, success wasn't as easy  to achieve as you may think.

_childDocuments_.review: : You play as Veronica Villensey, who killed her husband the previous night. You have to get away with it and also try to get the money from the insurance.: The game is presented as a visual novel with different choices you can make. You also have to move around the boat to look for evidence or talk to a certain characters.At the end of each run (15:00 pm) all the people are gathered to discuss what happened (is essentially the “emergency meeting” from Among us).: Initially you don’t really understand much, you have to play a couple of times (10 minutes per game) to catch on and plan a strategy. Overall the characters are predictable and if you get stuck you can ask (pray) for tips to God (There is a little church on the boat).: to get all the achievement you have to play a lot of times, but the more you progress the less time it get to complete a run (you’ll skip most of the dialogues you’ve already read).: It’s a cartoon style, it’s simple but I personally liked it. It fits the game. There aren’t many animation (at the end of the day It’s still a visual novel). Should you buy it? I don’t think the game is worth 12,49 €, I’d wait for sales.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally got this for iOS and played through a couple of times but it's a bit of a battery eater. Steam-on-laptop to the rescue!This is a fun little game in which you play a murderer and try to avoid getting caught by messing up the evidence. It's set on a transatlantic voyage on a steamship in the 1930's, so there are strongAgatha Christie vibes. There are lots of ways to fail (and end up in Sing Sing), and a few ways to succeed. The enjoyment in this game comes from putting together the clues that OTHER characters find, and determine how best to modify things to have them draw the wrong conclusions. Even a failed playthrough gives you new information that will allow you to make the next attempt better. And even a successful playthrough might not be the "best" possible outcome for getting away with murder.Piecing together all the moving parts is very rewarding. The writing is delightful and the old-timey music -- I'm given to understand that these are recordings of actual wax cylinders that are in the public domain -- makes it pleasantly atmospheric. Playthroughs are quick and it's easy to try, try again.Try this if you like clever plots, engaging stories, and murder mysteries with a twist.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a charming little logic puzzle of a game, in which you're essentially stuck in a time loop, not only trying to figure out how to deal with the evidence that incriminates you but also trying to figure out what makes your fellow passengers tick.  It's not hard to escape culpability for the murder -- I had the death ruled a suicide on my first playthrough -- but it took me several hours of exploring and restarting to not only work out the intricate timing of a run that cleaned everything up behind me, but also pinned the murder on another shipmate.  And then I discovered that there was some blackmail going on behind the scenes and had to work out a *third* layer of planning.  After I "won" the game, achievement hunting -- especially figuring out how to get the speed runs! -- forced me to throw away nearly everything I'd planned out and approach the game's central puzzle from another angle entirely, showing me just how much robustness went into the single central scenario.It was a satisfying experience throughout, with the game letting me chase a broad variety of solutions -- there are several pieces of evidence you can move around to frame others, and it's worth trying to use them all at once to see what happens -- and giving you a number of choices in which thoughtless conversation can come back to haunt you later.  (You can make everyone believe the time of death was the previous night, which places you at the murder scene; or the following day, which quickly raises other questions.)  It's a greatly entertaining onion of a puzzle with surprises at each layer, and while replay value caps out at around 4-10 hours of gameplay, it's well worth the price for that experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: It might seem a bit short on the first run, but there is a surprising amount of intrigue and depth hidden beneath the surface. It is fun to dig into the stories behind each character and find ways to twist the story even further. And as you would expect from an inkle game, the writing is very entertaining to read. A nice little treat of an adventure game.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Witty dialogue, gorgeous graphics and elegant design, endless narrative possibilities which you are encouraged to explore thanks to the short playthrough time... Getting away with murder has never been this fun.It's really Inkle's most compact game, focusing on what they are best at. Do buy it, it is an absolute gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly well designed and well written, with so many twists and turns you'll learn to exploit for the next playthrough! The "task list" and in-game hint system are also full of attitude and charm while making sure you don't miss out on anything big.You also get to read a bucketload of naval metaphors for being , 10/10 would kiss a certain someone again.

_childDocuments_.review: A game about getting away with murder. You have limited time to talk to a lot of people in the ship and come up with the perfect alibi for killing your husband. It's sort of a time loop thing, where each run is pretty fast, but you build on your knowledge of how everything works, sort of like Outer Wilds.The writing on this game is very good, the dialogue is very well written, on the first few runs when you're getting to know the characters, you can see each has their unique personality and a lot of depth, and the game let's you talk deeply with each of them, not just ticking boxes. On later runs, you're mostly button mashing to get to where you want, though.The game is very neatly and tightly packed. There's a lot of stuff happening at the same time, the world is moving on without you, and you can just interact with some of it, that's where the time-loop thing is a very good choice.The game is quite hard, I needed some online hints to get to the ultimate good ending with credits screen. Later on it does get a bit annoying to replay some encounters repeatedly, but I definitely enjoyed the whole experience a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: October 9th 2021 -  - 13h 18m - (100%) 8/10 - Got all of the achievements. Overboards art style and music work well despite that there isn't that much of it. The sound effects for each room give a very good indication of the room's atmosphere. The game's characters are enjoyable and well developed and most importantly, all of them have a secret you can exploit. Setting up the crime and timing your actions so everything goes perfectly make the runs satisfying to pull off. A lot of the time you have an idea of what went wrong during the meeting at the end. The checkboxes at the top left of the screen give you a general idea of what endings you still have to pull of, but figuring out how to pull them off is a completely different matter The problem is when you don't know how to change one aspect of the meeting. Even if you do it might not help you get a different ending. It is fun figuring out how to get different endings, but if you don't know how to get a specific ending, even after checking on god, there isn't much you can do. A few of the endings are pretty specific if you want to pull them off, which makes them hard to figure out.

_childDocuments_.review: What a charming game!  A reverse murder mystery where you try to get away with your husband's murder (and clearly, he deserved it, darling!)  The game play is short and sweet: A combination of visual novel choices and time management.  You'll probably fail a few times, but that is part of it's charm.  There are 5 major characters (besides yourself) and three minor characters (one of whom I am not sure you can meet?) to interact with and 7 locations on the ship.  Time is limited: You have from morning until later afternoon when a bothersome detective type will "summon everyone into the parlor" (restaurant in this case) to figure out whodunnit.  But the major players, while all possibly knowing things, may each have secrets or ways to manipulate them.  In execution, it is like a puzzle game, but the game plays fair -- unlike  early Infocom games like Deadline, it actually shows you the movement of other characters to different locations so you know if you'll be wasting time (or not) going to a specific location on the ship.  There are multiple paths to victory or defeat, and there is a bit of "Roguelike" in that each time you retry the game has a meta recognition of things you may wish to uncover or do differently.  Absolutely joyful, I hope this gets more buzz.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: In the past few years, Inkle has really won me over as a fan by putting out interesting and inventive narrative games like Heaven's Vault and Pendragon, giving interesting an informative talks on game design at narrative-focused game conventions, and maintaining their popular trademark design tool, Ink, which is available for anyone to use.  Overboard, their newest title, is a surprise release,  completely unannounced prior to dropping on the storefront yesterday.In Overboard, we meet an attractive young femme fatale who, in the opening scene, impulsively seizes an opportunity to get rid of her crappy husband by pushing him off of the deck of an ocean liner.  The next morning, we step into her shoes, and have one in-game day to help her cover up the crime before the resident Poirot-like detective connects the dots  and sends her to jail.  To succeed, you will have to lie convincingly and keep your lies consistent.  You must search the ship to locate and dispose of evidence without drawing suspicion onto yourself.  Meanwhile, find out what your fellow passengers know about the crime and bribe, blackmail, drug, or seduce them into silence.  If that doesn't work, find a more violent way of getting rid of any witnesses.  If you are really skilled, you might be able to pin the crime on someone else to collect that sweet, sweet life insurance money.Mechanically, Overboard is a text adventure but with pre-written buttons instead of a text parser, similar to 80 days, although the real-time clock of 80 days has been replaced with a more turn-based system.  The game's clock only advances as you perform action, talk to people, or move from location to location, and the game has a hard limit of about 8 in-game hours or so before the final confrontation plays out.  With each playthrough, there appear to be no randomized elements, so your own actions are the driving narrative force.Overboard is a very minimal, no-frills experience.   This is game that does a lot with a little; there's only one or two voiced lines, there's not many art assets, and the music appears to all be period-specific public domain recordings.  Overboard is a short experience designed for many playthroughs; one trek through the game takes about twenty minutes or so.  Helpfully, previously selected options highlight themselves if you want to continue down the same path you did before (or change things up), and a handy fast-forward feature allows you to breeze through scenes you have previously experienced if you choose.  So far, I have found a number of ways to successfully accomplish the main objective(s), and many more interesting ways to fail.  Each time you complete the game, regardless of the outcome, you are helpfully presented with a checklist of things to try to explore in your next playthrough.  Since each passenger on board appears to have something shady going on with them, there are tons of options when it comes to approaching them or playing them off each other.Honestly, the game's price point of $15 might be a little high when compared to similar games (or even other Inkle games!), but if you don't mind dropping $15 to support such an amazing studio (consider it a donation to help them make more games) or if you are lucky enough to catch it on sale, Overboard is quick, delightful, and extremely entertaining.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Whodunnits are always a gift, reverse whodunnits even more so, and this is the best of its kind I have played so far. The structure of the game is built around replays; every new attempt feels like peeling back layers of an onion as you reveal the many mysteries and secrets surrounding your fellow passengers, and figure out how to cover your trail. You don't need a perfect, flawless run to feel like you've won, which prevents the game from ever getting frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Going to be brutally honest with my take here and say Inkle is just a one hit wonder dev with 80 Days and I haven't really liked any other game they made since and I'm done giving them so many second chances.Overboard has a fantastic concept but as some other negative reviews have said all this game ends up being is trial and error. It's less roleplaying your way out of getting caught and more just bashing your head against the wall to figure out what the devs exactly want you to do. It really doesn't feel that rewarding and the writing isn't really that great to make up for that. Game looks nice at least.If you want a Groundhog Day loop murder mystery game I'd recommend Elsinore instead.

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful & clever narrative-puzzle game with way more depth than I initially expected. Overboard! essentially operates with a time-loop mechanic: each playthrough (which lasted about 5 - 20 minutes depending on my play style), you learn more about the secrets of your fellow passengers, their daily routines, and how to manipulate them to your own means. If the passengers turn against you, the story restarts at the beginning, with a few hints about what leads you might want to follow-up on next. If you successfully escape conviction, you're presented with additional levels of challenge to try again. In some ways, it has traces of a social deduction game (such as Mafia or Werewolf), where you have to figure out how to most effectively influence/taint the reasoning of the NPCs. The game does a great job of helping you keep track of what everyone believes, and the reactions of the NPCs always felt realistic and at the "top of their intelligence."For such a small game (in terms of number of characters and locations), the narrative is surprisingly rich (as I'd expect from an Inkle title). Even after getting the most straightforward "no jail" victory, I was compelled to keep playing to learn the full backstory behind every character. The "quick replay" functionality was a great quality-of-life improvement that really increases the replay value.You can play like a detective, you can play like a culprit, or you can play like a bloodthirsty bandit. No matter the runthrough, the world feels highly-reactive. For anyone with interest in story-rich games, playing detective, or social puzzle-solving, this one is definitely worth the price of admission to check out.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: This is like if the second act of Knives Out had a baby with Groundhog Day and was raised by Miss Marple. It has just enough permutations to feel interesting and fresh until you feel satisfied with the whole scenario, and the scenario itself is short enough that you don't feel like each playthrough is tedious.Nice writing, fun setting, good use of art and sound. Although the Blackjack minigame could be better implemented.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Overboard! is a fun twist on those delightful whodunit murder mysteries. You play as the murderer who kills her husband while on a boat to America and you have little time to arrange things in order to get away with it. There are many ways to go about this as the puzzle quickly becomes about understanding the ship, the people aboard, the time period's schedules, and in what order to react and respond to which events. You'll play through it several times, each time to gain more and more information and secrets to uncover. Can you get away with it, get the insurance money, and tie up all lose ends before the day ends?
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. You'll basically play through a murder mystery, but as the killer trying to foil the inevitable investigation. You'll go through a bunch of conversation trees and moving around the ship while trying to manage time. As you play, you'll learn the schedules of the other characters and can try to get information, items, and manipulate the other passengers.In the end, you need to escape justice, cast guilt on someone else, and tie up your loose ends. Along the way, the dialogue is very compelling and often quite funny. The art and music are a perfect complement to the narrative.After some number of attempts, you might want to look up a guide for the Septuple Homicide achievement ending. Or watch someone do it on YouTube. It's difficult to manage your time correctly, but the ending is well worth it.It depends on what you like. You can carefully explore and map out everyone's schedules, where/when you need to be for certain events, various outcomes from conversation trees evolving from the events you triggered.... There are a lot of hours of gameplay here, if that's your jam.I'm more inclined to look at notes from someone else's time to see people's schedules. If the game had internal schedule tracking, I'd be more likely to keep fumbling around to learn where people and obkects are through the game. If you could open a journal in the game where it displayed the information you've gathered over various playthroughs, I'd have liked that and spent a lot more hours playing this through.I also would have liked some way of slowing/pausing time while I was considering dialogue choices or where to go on the ship. I got caught a few times just because I wasn't clicking on options fast enough to get where I needed to be. There's certainly a thematic element to that ticking clock and rushed action, but it would have been a nice Accessibility option to give me a few extra seconds.This is one of the rare games where I'd even suggest it at full price. $14.99 USD is a bargain for the content. If this is on sale and you're looking at it, definitely worth purchasing.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: A fun murder mystery game where you are the killer and you have to try and get away with it. _childDocuments_.review: The setting, art, and clear amount of effort that went into the style of the game almost makes me want to recommend it. Unfortunately, while the first 2 hours are fun, digging in deeper into the game yields to repetitive walks through the same dialogue trees over and over. _childDocuments_.review: It's just not worth the asking price. I appreciate the concept - very much in fact, it is very fun to play as the murderer and basically try to get away with it, but it's just too little here. It's just a handful of characters, at a handful of places. You can play the game once in about 30 minutes and basically figure out what you can do with most, if not ALL other characters, since they fall in quite obvious categories.You can give this a couple of playthroughs, but after about 3-4 you are basically DONE with the game. On top of that, there is VERY little in the game or it's narrative that KEEPS you going. I got away with it the very first time, fumbling my way through. Now I could go for another run, to get some insurance money and be "better" with getting away with the murder, but that is literally it. Once you got it once, you got it and it's just curiosity, IF EVEN THAT, that keeps you going. In this state, although I like the presentation, it's not even worth a 40% discount at this time. Get it for like 2-4 bucks.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: A short, but highly replayable and entertaining reverse murder mystery story game where you attempt to get away with murder by any means necessaryAs someone who loves murder mysteries, the premise alone was enough to get me to instantly buy it, and i appreciate the idea that we play as the killer rather than as a investigator, because if you were to be an investigator and figure out the killer within the first few playthroughs, or see a spoiler somewhere, subsequent playthroughs of the game would only become gradually less interesting, as you would know whom you should catch at all timesYet, being the killer does not mean you do not have a mystery to solve: With each playthrough, there are many mysteries and clues which can be pieced together to uncover every character's role in the plot, their daily schedules, and how to take advantage of them. And on that note, something i highly appreciate about this game, is the ''objective box'' you can access during every playthrough: It helps to remind you what you should, or simply could look into during your playthrough, so you know where to start digging in case you feel a bit lost and wishing to try something differentAnother thing i do appreciate is this game's handling on the highly controversial and often overlooked topic of dolphins. Yes, they are evil. No, you can't convince me otherwise. Did you know they eat their own babies? Disgusting disease ridden creatures, all of them. I can't believe people actually like those evil psychopaths.-------SPOILERS below--------One thing i do not appreciate very much in this game, is that i felt much of my success was very reliant on the Commander's approval. Even if i hide every incriminating piece of evidence against me and frame someone else, i can be arrested afterwards simply because i did not interact with him enough, or didn't sleep with him without trying to steal his key, so he is convinced not to testify against me. Besides that, the romance scene is a bit long and unskippable, as i'm forced to wait for the music to stop before i can proceed.I highly appreciate that this game has a romance option that can be explored, and hey, i like the hat too, but i don't think having pursued it or not should affect so much on whether i get away with murder or not.--------------End of spoilers-----------------I have still not explored every possibility in this game, but i do very much recommend it to anyone who enjoys mysteries and choice-based games(and choices in this game do matter a lot, which is quite rare!) whether you want a serious mystery or something that doesn't take itself too seriously, you will likely be satisfied and feel rewarded either way.That being said, happy husband-murdering!''Dolphins, Malcolm! DOLPHINS!''
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: I see the other reviews and I'm surprised more are not complaining about the short length. I get the multiple playthroughs, but there is not a whole lot to get absorbed into, as far as the story, when it's this short. I played for about 25 minutes, got 2 out of 3 of the end game achievements, then sat in amazement for 10 minutes at how short it was. I, unfortunately, returned this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing. Managed to get off scot free on my second run and realized I didn't care to continue after the third one. I found the characters unlikable--maybe so we can kill them without remorse? But that made for uninteresting dialogues (and although she's a murderer, I need to kinda like the protagonist). Would have loved to see more of the rooms we're in too, beyond a vague color background. All in all it might be that finding out whodunnit is more entertaining than trying to get away with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is my favorite inkle game. Though each run is short, it's surprisingly challenging, and, realistically, you're not going to get the best ending on your first time through—maybe not even your tenth. Still, I never got completely stuck; there were always new ideas to try, and I got there eventually.One word of warning: this game does have some mild sexual content, which I found surprising (but not  distracting). It's not too explicit, but it's not exactly fade-to-black either.
_childDocuments_.name: Overboard!

_childDocuments_.review: Inkle's done it again! 80 Days was a masterpiece of a choose-your-own-adventure, with no two voyages ever being the same, and I can safely say that Veronica Villensley's voyages were always completely unique and completely enjoyable.Veronica's thrown her husband overboard. You have to make it 8 in-game hours before you reach America and can disappear. Were there any witnesses? Is there anyone you can trust? Anyone to blackmail? Can you frame someone? The answer to all those is a resounding yes.Each action has its consequences and depending on how you orchestrate a frame job, you might be caught out! It's a game of logic and wits as much as it is reading and understanding the different characters and their motivations. With such a colorful group of characters, it manages to stay fresh however many times you have to play to get the ultimate ending, the perfect getaway.Really a great game. The soundtrack is an amazing mix of early 20th-century big band music, which complement and elevate the scenes wonderfully in the game's 1935 setting. _childDocuments_.review: I mean I love murder mysteries…I mean literally love them, like read almost any review of any game I own and probably somewhere it’s going to say “wish this game was a murder mystery” or “wish this game was a BETTER murder mystery.”  Sure wish this game was a murder mystery, it should be.  I don’t know why the developers felt it would be better to make a game where you are the murderer and your goal is to get away with murder.  My best guess is they didn’t have the skill to tell an actual murder mystery.While the game not being a murder mystery is certainly disappointing, my real problem with this game is it simply does not have enough content.  This game feels like a demo, not a fully fleshed out game and CERTAINLY not one worth $15.  You just relive the same 8hr day over and over again.  It probably has maybe 4hrs of actual content and the rest is just you having to get the timings down right so you can figure out how to “win” the game.  This has more in common with a roguelike then it does an adventure game.  If you want basically a “murder mystery” adventure game that actually has content, a strong story, and similar time mechanics go play Elsinore.  That game is a masterpiece that is everything this game is not.  I will say I loved the art, characters, and sound design, the setting is also fantastic…sure wish the story was better.  Even though I feel putting a spoiler tag is almost meaningless in a game that cares so little for its story I’ll do it anyway as the rest of this review is going to have to talk about the actual plot. It’s easy to imagine a truly fantastic game from the elements here, but this developer sure didn’t have the skill for it.  The game needed far more characters and honestly it should have started with you boarding the ship in England and the entire game should have been the trip to America.  It should have taken place over like a 7 day voyage with each day being broken down into 24hrs and over the voyage you should have had the ability to explore multiple parts of the ship, talk to multiple people, gather evidence and options to deal with things and the ability to rewind time at will at any point.  Instead of the game requiring you to murder your husband that could have just been one solution to your marital issues.  More importantly the game should have focused on story beats with the individual characters.  Then after the 7 days are up the game should give you the option to rewind time and start over again if you want to try different things maybe with your character in game remembering what occurred.  At a minimum one play through should be like 10hrs long instead of the roughly 10min play through this story takes.It is shocking to me that this game is getting such high praise.  Go play Elsinore it’s far superior in every way, the developers should also play Elsinore as well and learn what a good narrative game actually is and then remake this game into an actual game instead of the demo it clearly is.

_childDocuments_.review: ✅Getting away with murder simulator✅Lots of paths and options➖Very time sensitive➖One-dimensional gameplay focusGame World: Overboard, as you might be able to guess, takes place entirely on a cruise ship in the 1930s. The game itself is a 2D, almost visual novel style, game. You traverse the ship via a side-view cut of the ship. There are only about 8 locations to go to over the course of 8 hours before your ship reaches its destination. Overall, the game world is fairly sparse, with only 8 locations and about 6 NPCs.Narrative: The narrative in Overboard occurs during those 8 hours of free time. See, you killed your husband last night in order to claim his life insurance money, and now you have to figure out how to get away with murder.Length: This is a short game, if you make all of the perfect decisions, which is unlikely, it will take you about 15 minutes to beat. It took me a bit over 2 hours, and 7 tries to finish it with the best ending. Mechanics: Despite the simplicity of the game world, I felt that the options and freedom of choice in Overboard is very well done. There are so many ways to go about doing things that all-in-all it mostly comes down to time and order that are your biggest threats. After waking up from murdering your husband, you start to explore the ship and realize that there are many things that are against you. Things like a lost earring need to be accounted for at a very specific time else you will have to figure out how to explain away its presence when the owner wasn’t supposed to be there. Still, there’s enough diabolical ways to influence people, or outright kill them, that you don’t need to deal with every single possible piece of incriminating evidence.Overall, I was impressed with mechanics, not so much the gameplay mechanics themselves, but more the possibility tree of choices that a player has to affect the story. Difficulty: I must admit, I was overwhelmed at first, definitely the first 4 or 5 playthroughs I was not feeling the game, but when I got to 6, I was finally able to formulate a plan of attack based on what I knew, and when it worked, it was a great feeling. So overall, my point is that Overboard can definitely feel difficult at first, but just stick with it. Quality: While graphically unimpressive, I did like the art style. It's got this kind of oldy cartoon vibe that fits in with the 1930s era. Everything though is fairly simple - UI, graphical options, there’s not much under the hood of this small title. Performance: No issues with performance and I encountered no bugs. i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSDSound Effects: Not much here, I didn’t notice a wide array of sound effects. There were a few lines of spoken dialog but not much else. Music: Music is sparse, but what I did notice fit in with the 1930s theme. This isn’t really a title to play for the audio. Overboard has a good amount of replay value purely with the number of choices and paths available to the player. Unfortunately, it's not uncommon to blow through 20 or 30% of the paths per playthrough, meaning it's very possible to run out of things to do within a few hours. Overboard feels almost like a super casual version of Deathloop. While I applaud its creativity, I can’t help but feel that it's as deep as an ocean, but wide as a puddle, meaning that once you get through the spider web of choices and paths, there’s not much else to do. Still, I think Overboard is worth a shot for at the very least a different perspective on your typical murder mystery game. Due to the price tag of $15 and the play time of ~2 hours, I would recommend you wait until this is on sale. You can find my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.  A reverse murder mystery where it starts with you murdering your husband by tossing him overboard from a boat, and from there on it's a race to get away with it.  It's meant to be played multiple times (I clocked nearly 20 playthroughs in my 5 hours until I got the perfect ending) as you learn more about others on the boat, and extract information from them, and get access to different areas to gather or plant evidence.  You can even go so far as to kill off other passengers to hide your trail.But the writing is excellent and the characters and puzzles are well put together, and I only encountered one jarring bug - I had just got the passkey from the captain and then as I'm leaving it describes him putting the passkey back on the keyholder. _childDocuments_.review: I've heard a lot how cool games from Inkle Ltd. are, but never really tried them. With Overboard! I was immediately hooked.The game is a reverse whodunit — you committed a crime on a ship (threw your husband overboard) and you need to spend 8 hours of game time (till the ship arrives to its destination) avoiding to get caught. And it is not easy, because there are a lot of characters on the ship, some support you, some suspect you, but almost everyone has their own secrets and weaknesses that in theory can be used in your advantage.The game is very short...but you will most likely fail the first time. Then you start again, knowing a little bit more. And again. There are tools that help you with fast forwarding parts that you already experienced, so it is never boring.Game happens in real time, so you need to plan your actions and think about your priorities, possible allies, etc. It took me 5 attempts to get a positive ending, but game is still very replayable after that, because there are many ways to achieve your goal, some easier, some harder.Overall, I highly recommend to try this game to everyone who loves good detective-ish games with a twist.

_childDocuments_.review: Overboard is the latest choice-based interactive fiction game from Inkle, whose catalog of award winning, modern-classic IF games includes the Jules Verne inspired 80 Days and digital ports of Steve Jackson's  gamebooks. Inkle's passion for brilliant storytelling shines through their games and Overboard is no exception.You are Veronica Villensey, fading theater starlet turned femme fatale in this refreshing twist on the mystery noir genre. The story opens with you hoisting your wealthy husband over the rails of a transatlantic ocean liner to his watery death, setting the stage for a frantic cover up as you lie, seduce and murder your way to freedom and a considerable life insurance payout.The characters and setting could have come straight from the pages of a Hercule Poirot novel. A closed circle of high society suspects traveling in luxurious art deco style are confined with a killer, nervously passing time until an eccentric detective with a funny mustache gathers everyone for a dramatic reveal of whodunnit. In this case, you're the killer and "whodunnit" depends entirely on your ability to weave a tapestry of deception.You're not the only person on this ship with secrets. Soon you'll discover your fellow passengers are politely keeping up appearances, each having their own character flaws to exploit and mysteries to unravel. You become the detective as you unearth those details which others would rather keep hidden, puzzling out ways to use their secrets to your advantage.You have 8 hours aboard the ship until you reach New York. Every conversation and movement advances the clock, requiring you to meticulously plan your strategy as you manipulate the evidence and craft your alibi. Each decision comes with consequences, so carefully choosing your dialog options and timing your actions is crucial. Something so simple as a rumpled bed sheet or careless slip of the tongue will mean the difference between a perfectly executed getaway and a life sentence in Sing Sing prison.Each play through is short. My first one took around 30 minutes as I carefully considered each conversation and dialog option. Subsequent play throughs average about 15 minutes and can be further streamlined with a fast forward option, allowing you to zoom through dialogs with choices from your last play through. It took me over 30 play throughs to unlock all the achievements and there are still variations of the story that I'm sure I haven't seen.Overboard's vibrant, stained glass art style suits the dark humor of the game perfectly. Although you're essentially a psychopath creeping around murdering, robbing and blackmailing your hapless victims, the atmosphere of the game is cheery and pleasant. Sound effects and music are sprinkled throughout, giving the core game loop of reading text and clicking through dialog options a lively, interactive feel.Overall, there really isn't anything I can criticize about this game. Inkle are masters of modern interactive fiction and anyone who enjoys the genre, or murder mysteries in general, will have a blast playing through this perfectly polished gem of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game!! I can't believe I've never seen a mystery game where you play as the murderer before. This game pulls it off well and seems to have a lot of depth to it. Characters move around throughout the day and you need to find who to talk to in what order to clear your name and hopefully frame someone else. Music, art, and voicing is also fantastic. only bug I have encountered is that the voiceover doesn't match the subtitles sometimes? _childDocuments_.review: What a wonderfully macabre game! Everything about Overboard is fun.Veronica is unapologetically the bad guy. Her husband isn't exactly a winner which excuses the game's inciting incident. This could rob her of some agency/delicious malice, but throughout the game we see Veronica has a heart. Two sizes too small in most cases, but a heart just the same. She's not a one dimensional villain. Overboard has 'best of the bad' endings - you're murdering at least one person even if you get away with it- (and one totally hilarious bat***t ending for an achievement) but there are no good endings. The genius of this is you're free to immerse yourself in the mischief of murdering, framing, and creating mayhem.The game offers a nice assortment of challenges. There's the overarching deadline which triggers the final event, so it pays to watch the ship's clock. Some actions can be accomplished more than one way, leaving the player free to choose and saving something different for a future play-through. Rifling through, or attempting  to rifle through your fellow passengers' cabins reveals a lot. Deciding what to use and how leads to some fun trial and error. A few of the secrets weren't revealed until my 5th or 6th run. The consequences of an action aren't always clear and the game doesn't hand-hold. Some locations or objects offer interactions that I've never found a use for and in true Overboard fashion are probably nothing more than red herrings. Some actions really leave you believing you've gotten away with it. Then the final passenger meeting comes around and Oh, if it isn't the consequences of your actions.Objectives are fun and varied, and while it takes several runs to complete them, there's not a moment of tedium. Each run is built around the objective you're currently tackling; framing someone, getting someone to confess, winning a pile of money bilking your shipmates at cards. This turns the objective into a satisfying run-long challenge rather than a box to check while playing through the same cycle of events over and over. Different objective, different series of events this time around.   One of the brilliant aspects of Overboard is that it's not a binary story line. You're not innocent/not innocent in the eyes of you fellow passengers. Some are on to your shenanigans, some have beef with you that predates your voyage. Some passengers have their own secrets to hide and will do and say a lot to make sure you don't discover the truth. This keeps the characters and storylines for each run from feeling one-dimensional. If you've played Inkle's '80 Days' (and you should!) Overboard offers the same quirky historical immersion. The Jazz Era/pre-World War feel adds immersion with music, dialog, and costume. There are also references to historical figures or events of the time that enrich if you enjoy history but don't distract if that's not your thing. The flavor of the era never overwhelms the experience. A small but fun conceit is that, if you fail a run or start a new one, Veronica 'wakes up' from the previous go treating it as a bad dream. She also frequently has a helpful tidbit for the coming run during this dialog.Lots and lots of twists and surprises, the king of which is just what Veronica is *really* after. Spoiler: killing her husband was the beginning, not the end. Each playthrough averages 12-15 minutes (YMMV while you get a feel for the ship's daily schedule and passenger routines. At about 13 hours I've done 60 runs easily and still have a couple of the more challenging objectives to tackle. Replayability is high and there's no reason *not* to play it all over again just for the voyeuristic dopamine rush of annihilating a shipload of people. Value for time, value for money, pure fun each loop.
