_childDocuments_.review: Overall Kingdom of the Dead has very strong art direction and music, but has a number of bugs and other small frustrating details that hold it back a bit. You can probably complete it in less than 3 hours.On the whole the game is relatively easy, even completing every level on the hardest setting. I probably only died maybe a dozen times, most of those on the last level and several from falling. Most bosses are somewhat underwhelming and die without much effort or thought as you hold sprint and circle strafe them until they die, but they have some cool arenas and designs. There's not much enemy variety, and you'll be facing mostly the same enemies you run into on the first level throughout the entire game. They follow along a mostly Doom-esque mechanical design, with enemies highly reminiscent of zombies, imps, cacos, pinkies, and lost souls for example. The zombies at least have some dismemberment which is fun, and even offers a bit of strategy to fighting them; you can blow off their weapon-wielding arm and then switch to the sword to finish them for easy alt-fire charging (more on that later).The weapons available are mostly fps staples with an old west coat of paint (melee, pistol, shotgun, rifle, machinegun, grenade, rocket launcher), nothing super inventive or interesting aside from the sword that has an alt-fire that just nukes everything in sight after killing enough zombies with it, sort of like the BFG from Doom. Weapons have alt-fires but, aside from the sword, aren't too interesting or useful. As an example, the revolver can be fanned to fire a burst of 3 shots very quickly, which is fun idea, except the revolver has pitiful damage and is mostly useless against anything that doesn't have a head for a one hit headshot, in which case, why use the fanning attack anyway? It'd take like 4, 5, 6 alt-fires to drop any of the tankier enemies without easy head hitboxes, when they'd die in probably 2 or 3 shots from the shotgun or rifle. This may all sound somewhat negative, but the weapons themselves are generally fun to use. The revolver and rifle both have custom spinning animations when you headshot enemies with them, which is super stylish and fun. The shotgun and gatling gun chew through limbs when you fire it into a pack of zombies. The sword nuke attack absolutely levels anything in front of you and lights things on fire, and it has a satisfying noise when it decapitates zombies. Whatever the arsenal lacks in inventiveness, it at least has a strong sense of style and personality that make it fun.Levels are generally very nice to look at because the game has an excellent art style, but the level design itself can be a bit rough or boring. The game is for sure at it's best when it gives you a bit of an open area to run around in, like the forest, but it feels that too often it limits you to running down narrow hallways, like in the catacombs and train level. I would say that the level variety is quite nice though, all of them are fairly memorable and distinct from each other. There's 9 levels in the game and you can complete each in probably around 20 minutes or less. There's some reason to explore in order to find more ammo crates or the extra lives hidden around the level, but they're only loosely what you'd call secrets. Each level also has an optional objective for the hard difficulties and a number of civilians needing to be rescued for the hardest, which I have mixed feelings about that I'll explain when I get to the parts of the game that personally frustrated me.Onto the bugs, I feel like people might've only loosely playtested the game in all honestly. There were at least 3 instances where enemies were stuck in walls and able to shoot me through them, and having replayed some levels a few times, seem to be a consistent problem, presumably from their spawn location being in the wall itself. There's some areas that don't seem like you should be able to walk through them but can, and would probably make you fall through the floor to your death, which is why I never experimented going out of bounds (more on death later). The snake boss in the train level seemingly got caught on geometry and just gave up within 10 seconds of the fight starting, leading to an effortless battle as I dumped 200 rounds of gatling gun into its face. Some sides of level geometry are untextured and let you see through the wall into the void. To the game's credit, I never ran into anything gamebreaking, but it feels like it could use a couple patches to get it up to a better quality. It's also debatable if it's a bug or working as intended, but the double barrel shotgun has some strange qualities with its reloading animation when using alt-fire. You can fire one barrel, then fire both barrels and get put into the reload animation, then fire the other barrel and get put back into another animation because the game only triggers the animation the 2nd time you've fired the alt-fire, which is strange on multiple levels.About my personal frustrations I've been alluding to, there's only 2 major ones. How checkpoint respawning works and civilians. After dying in the game, the game resets all your ammo counts back to a default (rather pitiful) set of values. It's pretty harsh exploring every level to stockpile 100 shotgun shells and 6 bundles of dynamite, just to die from something and get set back to like a dozen shells and no dynamite. The game respawns all ammo crates after death, which is nice, except that the game doesn't usually give you any near the checkpoint itself, meaning, depending on where you die, you could end up fighting relatively hard fights with only 10 rifle bullets to your name. I feel like this definitely could've been handled better. In the demo you kept all your ammo values after death, which had the potential for you to farm infinite amounts of ammo off of the aforementioned respawning crates if you had some near your checkpoint, but at least it wasn't frustrating, and frankly, if you're exploring (unless you die), you'll probably never run out of ammo for most guns anyway, no matter how bad of a shot you are.Onto civilians, keeping them all alive and saving them is a requirement to pass the hardest difficulty for each level. The issue is, it can be painfully easy to kill them accidentally. The enemies themselves seem to entirely ignore them, even after being freed by the player, which is nice I suppose, but it means that you have to be very cautious with your own weapons. The game likes spawning enemies around where civilians live, so AoE attacks can unintentionally decimate them before you even realize a civilian is in the area. I'll paint a picture of a scenario from the catacombs level. At a certain point, you come across a small stone semicircular wall with fire in it, and maybe a half dozen or so zombies rise up out of this area and approach you. If you're like me and save the sword alt-fire for moments like this when enemies are grouped up, this seems to be the perfect opportunity to nuke them all at once and move on. The problem with this is, and the game in no way indicates this, there is a civilian directly upstairs from this area, and the sword alt-fire will both penetrate the walls between the zombies and the civilian, and instantly kill him, failing your objective. It took me 3 retries to realize what was happening. From this point onward I was always very careful about not using AoE attacks in areas I can't see well, but it was both frustrating to realize what was going on in the above example, and to have to play the rest of the game carefully, knowing I could accidentally kill an unseen civilian through a wall at any given moment. As it stands I'd probably just say play the 2nd difficulty and just never let civilians even register in your brain.Steam is telling me this is getting too long, so I'll finish up in the comments.

name: Let's Build a Zoo
detailed_description: It's time to build a zoo! Let out your wild side, and create your own animal empire with this cute, expansive management sim. Import and breed rare creatures, hire the right staff, keep your visitors happy, and deal with plenty of weird and wonderful events. Then try your hand at DNA Splicing, and stitch together over 300,000 different types of animal, ranging from the majestic Giraffephant to the peaceful PandOwl! Build your own zoo with over 500 different animals at your disposal, then splice together over 300,000 different animal combinations Keep your animals and your visitors happy, with hundreds of buildings, foliage, path and enclosure decorations Hire the perfect employees to deal with a variety of life events Control everything that happens in your park, from what your animals eat to what eats your animals... Decide whether you want to run your Zoo above board... or break the law and pocket the extra cash Let's Build a Zoo lets you import a variety of animals from other Zoos around the world! Breed your animals and start families to expand your wildlife and fill your enclosures. But if that doesn't suit you... you could just create animals instead! With DNA splicing at your finger tips, you have the power to bind together over 300,000 different types of animal, creating monstrosities and oddities as you go! Ever wondered what a ChicKaka would look like? Now you can find out!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great zoo tycoon game. I enjoy the unique take on hybridization and selective breeding to offer some good variety of animals to choose from and manipulate. I have only ran a good zoo so far; trying to be environmentally friendly and sustainable. What I like about this game is that there is always the option to go the other direction exploit everyone for profit. Good humoured game and affordable.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: Great Zoo sim, reminds me a lot of Theme park back in the day in the way it doesn't take itself too seriously. Don't get me wrong there's plenty to do and if you want to you can drill down into whether you want to cut back on ingredients at food shops etc.Where the game shines is in the "morality" choices; do you buy/sell an animal to a black market dealer or report him to the police? Will you donate to the rescue shelter charity? Will you create a robotic lion to fool the punters? Will you buy that "meat processing factory" for your zoo etc.Also the crazy elements, do you build the genome facility to create hybrid animals (the Pig rabbit etc.)It's a great game and is enjoyable at the start it seems like you are forever borrowing from the bank but eventually visitors ramp up.;Pros:It ramps things up gradually so you can get a handle of things.It prompts you what needs doing in a non-naggy way.I like the basic graphics so it doesn't kill the pc and makes it seem fun (I also own Planet Zoo which does make the PC work a little harder lol).Cons:Some items are locked away until you complete tasks I get that this should happen but at times a donation to someone unlocks a new bus route etc (and it's sometimes not obvious).The morality system is good but some of the levels feel too highIt's unclear what you need to do to get a good rating from the inspector / youtuber visitingthe controls are fine but often I want to move somewhere else in the map whilst building (paths for example) click to drag like in most games ends up placing more tiles, only a pet peeve but it gets annoying after a while.I'd give this game a solid 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty fun for many hours.  And I dig the flavor, it's silly and cute and occasionally smacks you in the face with funny-cause-it's-true jokes about capitalism.It's also got a lot of micromanagement to do, and a lot of the micromanagement gets tougher instead of easier as you scale up. There are a couple tools you can unlock through research to make it a LITTLE better, but...I still can't figure out how to get to the bottom of the list of animal keepers without using my mouse wheel, and I NEED to do that to zone the new keepers so my animals don't starve, and the list keeps getting longer, and my mouse wheel scroll goes backwards sometimes because my mouse is stupid, and I suffer.  Of course that is partly a me issue, but I feel like it illustrates some of the rough edges in the late game experience. _childDocuments_.review: Okay. Okay, alright, okay. After 33 hours of this game (so far), I think I can say that I recommend this game pretty wholeheartedly.Allow me to explain: probably much like you, I saw this game and readied myself for some knocked-together zoo tycoon to take advantage of the popularity (and priceyness) of Planet Zoo and similar, given they have this whole gimmick of splicing animals together. Truly, I thought this game would be puddle-deep at best and maybe fun for <5 hours. HOW WRONG I WAS. Let's Build A Zoo is honestly so much more than it appears, and the game is deceptively well planned and considered! It's not just about gene-splicing, but rather it's about zoo management to a sometimes granular level. You can not only customise specific diets for different animals, or set up your bus routes with upgrades, or set up nurseries to maximise your animal variants, but also decide how much of the hotdogs being sold is made of hooves and eyeballs over prime cuts, or how much caffeine is in the sofa and coffee to encourage your visitors to zoom around faster. Every single square on the map is yours to do with as you please, and there's a marvellously satisifying sense of progression with both the tech tree and expansion in general. Honestly, I went into this with the lowest expectations and was more than impressed by how much this game has been made with tender, loving care. It's also very clearly been made for streamers and YouTubers who love making morally abhorrent zoos, so if you also love morally abhorrent zoos, this game delivers.However (and there's always a however) my biggest gripe with this game and the one thing that makes it a 4/5 (or, dare I may, even a 3.9/5) is the UI. I don't understand how on earth this UI wasn't changed before the final version came out, honestly. For a game with so much building and customising and finicky stuff, the menus are not particularly easy to navigate, things are divided into too many submenus (I WANT TO GIVE ALL MY SHOPKEEPERS A BONUS I DON'T WANT TO CLICK ON EVERY INDIVIDUAL BAR), and when it comes to remodelling, enjoy having to individually move/delete items, and individually paint every square, and looking for a single sprinkler in a giant enclosure and having to use a one-row menu where you scroll for 700 years to the right to find the One Thing you're after. Enjoy scrolling just in general, honestly. The menus are very small when I'd like them to be big and very big when I do not need all this information.It's the only thing in this game that I think brings it down in ways it really shouldn't; if the UI was better equipped for building (for instance, I'd rather be able to zone shopping areas or leisure areas I can move around later) or had mass-place or mass-delete (and maybe menus with filters for enrichment over decoration), I'd be over the moon, but right now I guess I'm going to manually upgrade every single water pump I have to collect methane because someone didn't add an 'Upgrade All' option. I have five million dollars; I can afford it. Trust me.Other than that, however (and hey, some people might disagree! However, my various Discord calls I've had whilst playing this game will attest otherwise to my patience), I really, really like this game. It's genuinely a really fun zoo tycoon that offers widespread possibilities. Heck, it's even a farming simulator, too! You can make a business selling unethical leather bags! Whatever you want to do, Let's Build A Zoo has a damn good chance you can actually do it... so long as you can find the correct menu and scroll for two miles in your attempt to find whatever it is you're looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love the art style and overall easy access of the game. That being said, the game is incredibly grindy to the point where new animals are got way too slowly. The animals you start out with are not exactly awe inspiring either. Rabbits, Geese, Badgers, Pigs are not particularly Zoo animals. I wish the all zoo animals were available from the start but that they vary in price. The research is super slow as it takes multiple days of waiting before anything gets accomplished. The structure mapping is also very difficult and unfair, item sizes are unfairly sized making it incredibly difficult to use the assets. Overall I enjoy this game, I just wish it was not as slow at times. The splicing ability raises this games score by a lot. Making fun hybrid animals is both funny and satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: I've got 115 hours in this game, so by no means am I an elite zookeeper, but I'd like to think I have a good understanding of the game. Much of what I will be writing may sound negative, but like I said...115 hours so clearly I enjoy the game. I'm still on my first zoo, having unlocked everything in the research tree and unlocked all the animals (no splices). Also, I've currently only completed a 'good' zoo. Spoilers below (especially in the CONS).PROSThis is a quirky little game that is quite fun. The research tree is extensive and allows you to use your preferred method (good or evil) to run your zoo. You can be sure to give the animals all the things they need to live happy little lives or if you're more sinister, use their body parts to make money. I love all the small decisions that unlock throughout the game. Having not taken any of the 'evil' ones, I'm sure they lead to other opportunities like the 'good' ones did. The game eventually sets you up for success, though this can certainly come sooner depending on your research choices. Heat maps! They're neato! They mostly work, and also help set you up for success, though the decoration and lighting ones are completely unintuitive.---CONSThis game is tedious as heck. There are so many quality of life improvements that this game needs to make it really good. First and foremost it needs fences as a decoration or utility. They are literally in the little screens it shows you when trading animals with other zoos, but there's no way to build them in your zoo. This makes visitor pathing an absolute nightmare. You either have to build every enclosure up to the edge of the path (leaving no ground or grass for decoration as you see in the videos or store screen grabs) or fill every single tile next to the path with a decoration item (also tedious and frustrating). The game also makes population management monotonous and tiring. It's basically opposite of the way it should be. At the very end of the research tree, you unlock the ability to enable exhibit control for specific enclosures. Personally, I went with trying to have one of each animal variant in larger enclosures built specifically for that animal. Unfortunately, instead of saying I want X number of male/female of X variant in this enclosure and having the Exhibit Control employees release them as you might expect with a game having population hubs that allow you to autorelease animals when they're overpopulating, you have to turn on contraception (how is this not an evil thing btw KEKW) and clone animals using the CRISPR, letting animals die off to keep your perfect exhibit. I'd much rather let the animals mate in the enclosure, allowing me to auto-release animals, thus further improving potential for removing animals from the extinct/endangered list. But for whatever reason, you have to do it opposite and let them die, instead of be released into the wild OR ignore exhibit control and manually release them whenever you're getting overpopulated. The menus in this game are horrendous. They're maybe set to a % of your screen size? They're huge, and unsightly. And scrolling through them is awful. ALSO, when using your mouse's scrollwheel in some menus, it will skip over entries, forcing you to manually click the down arrow to see all entries. This is especially horrible for janitor management while using heat maps. Heat maps! Ugh! They have so much potential to be helpful. And really, they mostly are. But it turns them on when placing certain objects and especially at night, they can make it difficult to see where you're placing your objects. Just let us have a 'perma day mode'. Also as said above, the lighting and decoration heat maps are next to useless. They give you a score that seems completely arbitrary because it for some reason seems to calculate these based off entire size of a land plot instead of basing it off of available spaces in a land plot. Enclosures can take up many spaces, not to mention shops, so your decorations and lights are already at a negative. I've literally had 10% lighting in a grid and it say it's good. That makes 0 sense. Visitors...This is a big one because there are many confusing elements. First off, emotes. In settings you have an option to turn off emotes. That's great, cause in a small very busy zoo, they can be annoying. BUT, they're also a little bit of what makes the game special. You'd think being part of that, they'd give you a guide on what they different emotes mean, but they don't. There's no guidance on them whatsoever. Had to look up what the caffeine emote was cause it didn't look like anything I could parse. Also, why can't we disable CERTAIN emotes. I'd love to see a research option, maybe for the security building, that lets you disable positive or negative emotes, so you can focus on only where your zoo needs work. Next with visitors, I'm not positive, but I think their decision to leave the zoo is based solely off of decoration. I understand why they went this route, but also I don't think it works properly. Having a boatload of blank space in your zoo that is entirely inaccessible to visitors seems to have a negative effect on their willingness to stay, even though it's hidden by staff entrances. This makes major expansions or alterations kinda frustrating and just having more land than you need a negative.Visitor pathing. Yes, I mentioned it above, but it's REALLY bad. I'd really like to be able to have ground types dictate whether visitors will path on them. No to sand/snow/grass/dirt, yes to everything else. They definitely don't take the most efficient route to their destination. Maybe that's to make it seem more real, but it makes managing optimization feel impossible. Attractions. Visitors LOVE attractions. But there are only 4 of them available. Sure you can place more than 1 of each type, but you can only customize the appearance of one of them, making the other 3 branded only to their default style. ----That's all I can think of right now, though I'm sure there's more that I love and hate. Like I said, I've got 115 hours in this game and will likely have another 100 before I'm nearing completion. I want to do an 'evil' zoo and also want to see if it's possible to make a profitable farm simulator using only crops. I'd recommend it for people who like cute little games with a bit of depth. I wouldn't recommend it for someone seeking perfect optimization of every block, because the effort you have to make simply wouldn't be worth it to me.

_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very cute little game, but don't let the pixel art fool you, there is a nice little simulator underneath the adorable appearance.  The music is nice and calming and is complementary to the gameplay.  Be sure to make use of your time modifiers so as to not spend inordinate amounts of time on each day when not needed.  You have to balance both the expansion of your zoo as well as the happiness of your animals and guests, all while making sure you don't go bankrupt.  It's not as easy as it sounds.  Take your time, focus on fixing one thing at a time, and eventually you will have a successful zoo.  Be it an Aquarium, Dino or traditional zoo.  It's definitely a good time waster  Well worth the asking price for me.  This is not going to be as complex as say Prehistoric Planet or Planet Zoo, but it's still a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game so much. While it looks like a simple & cute zoo tycoon style game it actually is a pretty robust management sim, letting you control almost all aspects of your zoo. Plus it has a morale system that is actually pretty fun/funny to play with, allowing you to make your zoo either environmentally friendly, or convert your zoo into a meat processing plant.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it, but I really can't recommend it. The graphics are lovely and cute and there are many different concepts here that have a ton of potential including a breeding and exchange programme etc. But everything gets muddied by how unwieldy the UI is on top of the extreme micromanagement involved. You're basically in charge of everything from ordering supplies (that I never remember to do and just resort to emergency ordering for an extra cost) to hiring (with a lengthy hiring process that requires you to put out a hiring campaign and wait for applications) to individually assigning zookeepers to individual pens. The last part quickly becomes unmanageable as you can only assign keepers by going to the individual staff profile one at a time and checking to see what they're managing instead of having a list of assigned employees per enclosure. There's a morality system which is kinda cool but there's little to no explicit guidance on how to manipulate your good/evil score except through random events and planting a lot of trees (or not) to improve your carbon score. This works in tandem with a really weird research system. Everything is hidden under tiles seemingly at random and you can only uncover them by researching the adjacent tile whether it's relevant or not. Some research topics are inaccessible unless you have a high enough good or evil score, forcing you to sit on your research points or spend them on random tiles. Everything is displayed with gauge bars, which don't really mean anything because you're penalised just for allowing your animals to suffer 1 pixel worth of boredom. This becomes a common event as you attempt to breed new variations of animals as you'll be stuck with a pen full of unwanted offspring that just keep increasing. The game also doesn't make your life any easier by automatically directing you to the problematic enclosure. Instead you have to click on one of the enclosures and then click to view all enclosures, and then go down the list of needs to find the tiny 1-2 pixel spec of deficiency which you then have to manually rectify by getting removing the excess animals by one way or another. It's also pretty inconvenient that you can't put your incoming animals in holding. You can get new residents by adopting from a shelter/exchange programmes/random events. The last option sometimes blindsides you by saying 'hey, do you want to save these animals from a forest fire? y/n' with no option to wait and suddenly you find yourself saddled with 5 incoming monkeys that you immediately have to assign an enclosure regardless of suitability, space, or any other issue. I want to recommend it, I really do because it's visually so adorable, but it's just so poorly executed in places that the flaws go beyond minor annoyances.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: I have been looking forward to this game for so long, and it's finally here and better than I could ever think! It has the classic Zoo Tycoon feel, with absolutely adorable graphics. However, the classic tycoons are quite cut and dry and this one is everything BUT that. There are so many ways to go about playing this game. Will you come over to the dark side? It's fun to play as someone without morals for a change. There's also a good selection of animals, customisation and in-game upgrades that keep you playing. Zoos may become large and many things happen at once, accompanied by the neccesary pop ups. But even though it's sometimes a lot, I haven't actually felt overwhelmed while playing. All-in-all I love this game and can't wait to play more of it. The price is really worth it!
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: I agree with a lot of the sentiments here that the game is so endearing and cute for a casual experience, but has some of the worst menus for a management sim I've ever seen. The menus are not fun to navigate and often require you to micromanage so much of your zoo that it steals from the charm of collecting critters and making fun little hybrids. Obviously I liked it enough to put a hundred hours in it, but my reviewer bias is that I enjoy micromanagement to some extent. YMMV.

_childDocuments_.review: HUGE EDIT: do i recommend this game now? yes, BUT;keep in mind that sometimes in this game you can have quite a rough start, as well as some mistakes can ruin your whole zoo. those are two things i dislike about this game, but now that i played more i discovered i liked it a lot more than before.once you get the hang of things, everything begins to run smoothly. it takes a little while but once you get over a few hurdles - mainly bus sizes and animal numbers as well as staff, then it becomes quite a chill and relaxing 'sit back and watch' sort of game, which i enjoy.the animals are adorable and the ability to splice them results in some wacky combinations, its funny to see just how crazy things can get. once you keep playing (maybe into your second zoo) you will get a hang of that skill point web, which will help you greatly. maybe look up a guide to know what/where to invest in, it can make or break some days for your zoo sometimes.there is a lot of managing stuff when it comes to this game, so if that is not your style, maybe this game is not for you. however, it does get easier overtime when you unlock more staff and skills, so dont judge this game (like i did) in your first few hours, it starts to get a lot more fun after that.a complaint i still have is it is a bit of a pain to decorate and move stuff sometimes, but i can manage now. definitely reccomend.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: Has something about it that reminds me of those wonderful Bullfrog games of old, you know, like Theme Hospital, Theme Park, Theme Park World etc. Doesn't feel phoned in, or like a cash grab / platform to sell you loads of content or like it's lacking a soul if that makes sense. Has the silly sort of humour you'd expect from a Bullfrog game. It also has a surprising amount of depth to it given it's graphical presentation, I was not expecting to have this many things to tinker with in order to reach optimal or desired output on my zoo, I went in expecting a cosy game to kick back with and lose a few hours on and whilst it can certainly be cosy, it's also very micro-management heavy.In the time I've played, I haven't really run into ways to automate things so if that bothers you, I'd consider that before purchasing. I'm personally all for it, but I can see how for others, as their zoo expands, it could become a logistics nightmare that could detract from the fun. The UI for me also isn't the best, it's not the worst thing I've seen, but it could be better.Art-style / direction is great, game still manages to look fantastic and vibrant. Most of the musical score is pretty good too.Plenty of animals so far to house in your zoo. I like the morality system too as it leans into choices that can have a long-term impact on how your zoo is run and the perception of it based on the little newspaper articles it throws out when something of note happens. There's always something to do, change, improve or manage and that loop hits my dopamine receptors pretty hard. Game somehow manages to nail both the concept of instant gratification & delayed gratification, strikes a fine balance for me.I wish the visitors would actually use the nicely designed pathways I've made for them and stop wandering off to touch grass though.I honestly quite love this game, the fact that this studio has managed to capture something for me that I haven't felt in decades, back when I played those Bullfrog games is something special. Kudos to Springloaded, Let's Build a Zoo is a pretty great little game. Will be picking up the available expansion soon and already wish-listed the upcoming one.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is interesting and is fun to play but the 500 different animals I think includes color variations of each one, then you splice them and it counts each splice as up to 2 additional zebra / pig is either a zebig or a pibra kind of thing. It can be hard to monetize and sometimes the AI and enclosures are pretty dumb. Breeding is hard to control and you either neuter the whole pen or let them get out of control. Some very frustrating mechanics to try to manage especially as your zoo grows.If there was some type of research available that allowed you to set population % for a habitat that automatically prevented them from getting out of control when you're at a larger scale it would be a much more enjoyable experience.Additionally the game doesn't really tell you that once you set down one path you are stuck going the good route or the bad route, I'm not sure if it's even possible to swap after you start heading one direction as this locks in a lot of the tech trees.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: Having a blast so far, I would definitely check this game out if the initial premise interests you. Mind you, I have only played a few hours so far, but this is what I have deduced in the meantime:Strengths:- Systems interact with each other and have depth to them without being overwhelming.- This game gives you breathing space for how you manage your zoo (as long as you don't blatantly mismanage it), but still rewards good planning and optimisation.- The graphics are pretty and sprites are easy to identify.- The Good/Evil system make your choices matter and unlock various perks and playing a certain way has its own challenges- The splicing system brings a cool new twist that help keep things fresh.Potential Improvements:- Some item descriptions could elaborate more (e.g. item stats/indications for decorations, how to source certain foods, etc)- Some menu interfaces are a bit obtuse (e.g. trying to hire more staff).- I didn't know I could turn structures before placing them with right-click until a few hours in. Not sure if I missed it somewhere. Overall solid game so far and it's clear that the devs put a lot of effort and love into this game. Let's build a zoo!

_childDocuments_.review: fun little game made only better by the DLC, with additional parks, new systems, and plenty of animals to raise (or abuse). my only criticism for this game is that in the transition to mid-late game the management systems get overwhelming -- there's nothing wrong with micro-management games and i enjoy plenty of those on a daily basis, but imo there are significant areas of improvement to be made in the game itself so the management is more seamless. i found animal keepers frustrating after a while, since digging through a long list of names to figure out who is assigned where and who needs to be reassigned where when my zoo was expanding wasn't exactly on my top priority when trying to figure out decorations, food and lighting, and animal wellness. the hybrid creation system in this game really shines and is one of the reasons i kept playing for as long as i did, and will probably go back for some casual fun times regardless :)

_childDocuments_.review: Let's build a zoo is the tycoon game I never knew I wanted, but now it's here it really hits a lot of spots that similar games never did. This game is pretty easy to pick up and has surprisingly in depth content, such as unlocking farms to grow crops to then use to bring down running costs of your zoo in feeding and in your food stalls etc. The research tree is nice and big, and there are enough animals and variants to keep you busy for a long time~ The devs are very active and attentive in the forums (and on discord), so any grievances that do come up are acknowledged swiftly and many have been addressed in the updates since the game's release. One of the things I love about this game is in its simplistic nature, exhibits are very easy to set up and a lot of the bother I find in other games (such as certain wall types only being compatible with certain animals etc) has been taken away, giving you more time to focus on the fun stuff. At first I wasn't keen on the super unnatural enrichment items like trampolines etc, but honestly after playing it for a while seeing an elephant on a trampoline or perched up on a tree branch is a fun quirk~ Would totally recommend this one. The vibe of the game allows you to play for as long or little as you like really, saving at the end of each day, unlike similar games that I always felt like I'd need a minimum of a few hours to sit down and really enjoy at each sitting, with this game I feel like I can load up and play for 20 minutes or 4 hours quite happily~I love the achievements and really hope they add more :)

_childDocuments_.review: The game has two sides: be super good, or be super bad. Or float in between. It's not shoving one side down your throat, don't be obtuse. My main issue would be the UI is kind of clunky and though it makes doing a few things more of a pain than it should be it doesn't kill the game.

_childDocuments_.review: In many aspects I really enjoy the game, with much of the core loop being fun. My issues come from a lack of information, issues with the UI, and weird design choices.The lack of information is an issue. Why are farms and farm processors different buildings and technologies, and why do you need both in order to make farms function at a basic level? You need 3 buildings (and fields) for farming to work and this is not explained in game. Farmers can only plant crops, crop pickers will only harvest, and the warehouse is needed to carry goods around. I spent months with just farmers, thinking they could also harvest, to find I had just been growing crops to tear out and regrow them. There is a lot of situations like that in game, so many things are just not explained and its hard to find any sort of guides to explain.The UI leaves much to be desired and pertinent information is commonly left out or missing in many screens. Likewise having more than a few zoo keepers or farmers to zone means you will be scrolling through a long and narrow list, rather than a page where you can see all employees of a type. This situation is weird, because the UI for the wildlife release building is likely the best, giving many options and information to make informed decisions, while the breeder's hut won't even let you change which animals will be bred. Also, farm fields cannot be edited to change their size, but you can with animal enclosures? You have to destroy the field and rebuild it, unless I was missing something.This leads to the last part, weird design choices. This game has an optimal build that effects zoo rating, but the optimal building is neither explained nor easily understood. Two food/drink buildings in a zone? Non-optimized. Too many trashcans/benches? Non-optimized. Instead of building a zoo that looks and feels like a real zoo, you commonly find people making there weird square grid zoos where everything is connected to subways and nothing else really. It looks neat, but I was trying to make a zoo that looked like a zoo and not fancy art with 10 lights per 25x25 square. You also cannot have multiple entrances nor adjust the road in front of the zoo to make traffic jams less of an issue. Why can't the subway connect to the outside world?I want to recommend this game but I can't with many of the issues. If there were guides on steam/on the internet or some in-game tutorials, then I would be more forgiving. I don't want to feel like I am stumbling in the dark when I just want to build a zoo, it shouldn't feel like a Paradox game

_childDocuments_.review: Let's Build a Zoo is a fantastic game that allows players to exercise their creativity and strategic thinking skills. One of the great things about this game is the number of different playstyles that are possible.Players can choose to focus on building the most impressive and profitable zoo possible, with a wide variety of exotic animals and attractions. Alternatively, players can choose to focus on creating a more environmentally-conscious zoo, with a focus on conservation and sustainability.There is also the option to take a more hands-on approach, by personally caring for and interacting with the animals in your zoo. This can be a great way to connect with the animals and learn more about them, while also building a strong relationship with your visitors.For players who prefer a more villainous playstyle, the game also offers the option to take a darker path. You can choose to sell animals to the black market or engage in other unethical practices in order to increase your profits. However, be warned that these actions may come with consequences and can negatively affect your reputation and overall success in the game.Overall, Let's Build a Zoo offers endless possibilities for players to explore and discover their own unique playstyle. Whether you're looking to build the ultimate money-making machine, create a more holistic and compassionate zoo, or even embrace a more nefarious approach, this game has something for everyone.- mDriveUnit

_childDocuments_.review: First off, if you liked Planet Zoo or the earlier installments of Zoo Tycoon, you'll like this game. If you kinda liked the previously mentioned games but thought it was a little too complicated, then you'd like this game as well. Let's Build A Zoo looks simple at a first glance but once you actually get into the game, you'll soon learn that there's a lot going on underneath the hood. There's a morality system - good vs bad. You can be a 'good' person by doing the obvious, releasing animals to the wild, donating animals, practicing reuse, recycle and reduce. Somehow this game has managed to add 'complex' elements while keeping them simple - you can decide how much prime meat or lower grade meat in hot dogs, for example and hide bad tasting low quality food by adding MSG, with it's own drawbacks. It's simply laid out and fun, honestly. As for the bad route, you can buy/sell from the black market, fatten up your animals to process and put right back into your food shops, it even goes as far as deciding when to take a baby away from it's mother as well. Let's not forget the gene splicing! I know I'm rambling, but I cannot say enough about this game. It also looks like they've got more updates in the works after they settle after their big launch, if you're on the fence, BUY this game you won't regret it! And don't let 'pixel graphics' turn you away because I know you're thinking it!

_childDocuments_.review: Update after 25 more hours of gameplay: Let's Build A Zoo is still a cute little zoo management game but the management is still such a pain in the ass. I built more nursery's to help breed population variants faster and that definitely worked but the gameplay loop here is just painful sometimes. You are constantly bombarded with notifications that your enclosures don't have enough water or enough enrichment which really just means your animals have bred themselves into being too crowded. This prompts you to go to the conservation center and comb through your livestock to see which ones you want to release into the wild. You CAN use a contraceptive on the entire enclosure or single animals but that tactic is far too tedious or flawed because completely removing species variants from your breeding pool just means you will have to back track and rebreed the whole chain again if you want that variant. And if you lose track of those steralized animals you could just end up losing a species altogether by having breeding partners die off. There are other chances to adopt later on but that still just seems like a boring way to fix a troublesome problem with animal management. There really is no system or tool in place to run your zoo while maintaining every variant of each species without just playing the game on a very slow setting and plodding along. And this is coming from someone who has only 20 of the 50 species. How the devs expect you to manage all these animals without just getting bored of this gameplay loop is a little ridiculous.However I still stand by the zoo design aspect of the game being very fun. I love expanding my zoo and decorating it. A grid based tool to measure where you are placing stuff would be handy but I've made due without. I am also still going to do another play through on the evil side of running things which honestly might just make animal management easier and less tedious because you won't actually have to care about your animals :/---------------------------This is still a fun game! But it has a lot of little issues that add up making it a bit of a pain to play honestly. Here are some of the good and bad of Let's Build A Zoo-Lots of animals! 50 some base species each with 10 different variants. Then DNA splicing lets you combine those into weird animals like Owl Ducks, Monkey Snakes, you name it. But there is a glaring issue I've run into and that's animal management. Your enclosures fill up very quickly since your animals can breed freely unless you apply a contraceptive to them or the entire enclosure. The problem here is your animals become unhappy, crowded, unclean because I just get busy working on other parts of my zoo. For example I put all my ducks in one enclosure until they started over breeding. Then I split them by variant and those ducks over bred. Now I am constantly having to go back and click one at a time to lower the count of these animals in every pen. If I was to apply a contraceptive to them, eventually if left alone, they would all die of old age. There needs to be a better way to manage the cap on each enclosure to enable to even attempt to collect and showcase all the animals available in the game otherwise it's a hopeless mess of you having to maintain hundreds of animals individually.-You can adopt animals on the world map almost daily which is a great feature to help you get some species variant you need to complete a DNA genome for splicing. Trading other zoos is also a feature but it feels like a very slow, grindy process. I initially thought it was going to be a fairly straight forward trading chain until you unlock all the baseline animals but instead you have to trade specific species variants so I have traded very rarely so far and don't have as much animal variety as I would like.-Plenty of Zoo design options and more to unlocked through the research features. I like how much you can do here but I also wish there was a refund feature to recoup some of the cost of items you just need to delete. If you unlock a new lamp you can't make sure all your lamps look the same without just blowing more money on a whole new set.-The shops you can open are fun and let you tweak the contents of your food to influence customers. If you make your food really salty it drives people to buy more drinks. And if you make your food really unhealthy it drives people to the washroom. There is a balance to how you structure your food stands-The research feature is a talent tree of sorts that lets you pick how you want to progress your zoo early on. I like the options it gives you but I would appreciate more transparency on where things are across the board. After your first play through there is very little guess work on where to go for each upgrade so the novelty wears off quickly-Morality is just a straight up cool feature. You can choose to play it good and go green with your farm, save the animals etc or you can play it very crooked by dressing up animals to look like something they are not or using a taxidermist to make robot animals. You can't do both at once and be morally ambiguous without hurting your zoo progression but I think that's fine since it encourages more replay-ability.-Later on you can unlock farming which lets you create plots of things to grow and help become self sufficient. This feature seems good but obtaining the seeds for what you want to grow is locked behind research which is a bit of a pain.-Feeding your animals is a problem. You are given a single warehouse to store you food and have to keep checking back and clicking a single button to restock. The issues arises when you speed up time and do anything for a few minutes only to find that you have run out of food and now your animals are hungry all because you missed a single click. It's not engaging in any way shape or form it's just a hassle.-Hiring new staff members is kind of a pointless feature sometimes. The fee to advertise for a job position is only $5 a day and over time people apply. Once you've hired someone the game asks if you want to take down the listing but unless it's a seldom hired position there is no point it taking it down other than time gating yourself behind waiting for new applicants when the current ones will just wait around forever.-Positioning staff around the park could use some work. It can be a pain to assign zookeepers to each pen or janitors to enough areas. It would be nice to see how much work a single enclosure needs as well and be able to assign the right staff to make sure your pens aren't a mess and your animals are fed. The fact that you only get one store room also makes the zookeepers jobs very dependant on your positioning and/or the subway system later on. I don't see why building more storerooms isn't an option.Overall I am still enjoying the game and will keep playing it but there are a lot of quality of life improvements I would like to see from the devs. It feels impossible to expand the zoo past a certain point due to all the animal micromanagement that is mandatory. I realise this is a zoo game and that comes with the territory but when I have to click 15 times to donate ducks every week it just isn't that fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. Played it for the past few days. Noticed some good things and things to be improved upon.I like how decorations are a factor, as most games like this, decorations are more of a sidepiece or updated later as dlc (prison architect). Currently, I'm between giving animals enough space (also in order to breed), two square pathways but I place things such as trashcans and water pumps. Not enough space for decorations, but I'm planning on expanding and moving things around more.Moving things around is a hassle. My water bowls are on the edge, so after the cage is moved, it errors the water bowl against the wall. It still works, but a bit annoying seeing all of those error x's against the wall. I got the other pathways opened, but because it's against a wall, it's an error. Another thing is the constant menu. Have to click on a cage, then click edit, then click the item then move. I kinda wish the delete button would work on clicking these items, instead of the different menus. Also, let's say you gotta resize the cage, well, there is an anchor at a random place on the cage, so now you gotta rearrange or move, in order to resize from the other side, since from what I can tell the anchor cannot be moved to a different corner.Menus are a hassle. Gotta click on buildings. Gotta click on employee name (out of let's say 24 employees) then zone, click zones or declick zones, then back to the next employee to choose a different zone. Zones. How do I know I need more animal keepers on one cage? I currently just have two employees on each cage, then i got a third starting on the ones I think are the worst. So each worker gets two zones, then so far each cage has two workers, maybe a third in the future if I keep getting alerts to hire more animal keepers. And Janitors? I got every square inch of my zoo with trash cans. Janitors don't see to have an issue keeping up, but if I chose a zone...the zone is one trashcan. At this point, I think my five janitors can keep up with the demand (but maybe I don't even need five, maybe two will do on my +7 area zoo).  Only one staff house, but it's the most needed one, and need to be near animals to help keep the workers going faster. I wish I could order food for more than 7 days, or have a shipment set for each week, instead of managing it. Btw, I ran into a bug where it constantly says I'm out of food for one cage, yet I keep refilling everyday for 7 days. Let's say, your rabbits died out. So you're trying to get the cage back running. I found one eventually. Then I would find the same gender in 4 weeks. Then maybe after 1.5 months, I find the opposite gender for the rabbit. Like, yes, maybe i'm not checking the world map everyday. But after checking three or four days straight, your mind goes on another project like redesigning, then you forget to check again. Maybe requesting for certain animals like common ones could be a thing?I rarely touched the nursery or splicer. Nursery can only house two pairs. Splicer can only do two. Have to have a line discovered before you can get really into the splicer, but even then I stayed away from it since it seemed to only show common animals skins mixed with other common animal skins. Maybe I just need to touch it more. With the nursery, it's on the sidelines until I check to see if one of them turned elderly. Lots of focus on green cage compared to other types. If you have to place a species in a cage they are neutral about, you may forget about them compared to the other +20 cages you are tending, then end up forgetting oh I should finally make that artic cage. This isn't that bad honestly, but best to just keep an empty cage of each type for new incoming ones.Copy and paste cages. I like my things uniformed. But since it's annoying to go thru so many menus to move items around, they are not really matching. So to end this... please let me stop starving my tortoises.

_childDocuments_.review: After 50hours with the game, I can seriously say that this game is not just better than any other 'zoo-tycoon' games, but literally ... that includes Pros: #1. 53 different animals, each with 10 sub-types, each of which can be spliced with any other animal... you want a Snake-lion, or a Duck-pig, or a Horse-monkey? You literally can.#2. The game doesn't have the completely arbitrary limits on the amounts of animals you can have in an enclosure like  has. If you want 500 horses in an enclosure, then you can.#3. The pixel graphics are preem#4. The buildable area is very, very big#5. It's just $20, which is significantly less than 90% of tycoon games on the market (I mean, f#cking Planet Zoo costs $100+)Cons: #1. Each time you quit/restart the game, all the zoo employees get spawned back at your zoo's gate, and they have to walk back to their posts. This is a time-waster of epic magnitude, especially when your zoo gets huge.#2. The DLC for the game is really bad imo, because it's a stand-alone expansion, so you're paying to NOT use the base content of the game and ontop of that you can't even use the expansion content in your existing zoo, so like for instance, I can't use any of the expansion content in my current 50hrs+ zoo at all. This literally made me comit to not purchasing any DLCs in the future, because I already got burned on the dino DLC, and the Aquarium DLC is stand-alone as well... so yeah, terrible DLC design.#3. Can't edit farms (only move, or delete the entire thing)#4. Buying food for the zoo isn't automatic (it should be imo)#5. The tutorial popups and general information provided to the player is lacking#6. I feel that the morale system is limiting, since you can ONLY go good, or ONLY go evil, .#7. You can't place empty buildings/shops... you HAVE to hire an employee to go with it (and the employee given to you is random, so it's often a sh!tty one). This makes it so that you have to then fire that employee, pay their severance and THEN you can hire an employee of your choosing to staff the building, which is just a very convoluted way of doing things.#8. It costs  to expand your building area (especially at the later stages)#9. Selling animals to the black market guy is a schlep. 'Bulk selling' needs to be implemented as a QoL improvement#10. The AI of the employees seemingly need some work, because I have 90 zoo keepers employed in my zoo, with only 12 exhibits (so that's 7 keepers PER exhibit) and yet I still sometimes get animals dying from not being fed. So something is screwy with the AI (sometimes).#11. No 'confine mouse cursor to window' option#12. The research tree is obtuse and it basically locks away the most useful & impactfull technologies behind other mostly useless crap, and ontop of that, the entire research tree is covered by fog-of-war so you can't see where the technologies are that you actually want (unless you cheat by looking it up online). I just really think they could have made this entire research tree much more user-friendly.#13. The game saves only at the end of each day. This sucks because you can't just save & quit when you want... you have to wait until the end of the day before it saves.#14. The entire game's UI and the enclosure management UI is actually quite terrible. Everything is more obtuse than what it needs to be and the UI needs a serious redesign.In summation, this game is fantastic. It's not just fantastic in the sense of it being a great Zoo-tycoon game, but it's a fantastic game, period. It's NOT a casual-friendly game though, so don't buy it thinking that you're gonna have a super relaxing experience, because managing a zoo in this game actually takes some brain power. Buy it... play it... splice a horse with a monkey...Here's my first hour or so of the game: My wishlisted games if you wanna be a bro: For more reviews, visit my curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I am not used to writing reviews but here goes.Overall I do recommend this game, I played it on the game pass last year but have bought it now on steam with the Aquarium DLC, so at the time of writing I have actually played much more that 25 hours. While I recommend it, because I think you get your money's worth of play time, it comes with some aspects that can affect how you enjoy the experience.Pros : I loved the base game so much that I was really excited playing the Aquarium DLC, hence my purchase. The base game has lots of things to love, starting of course with the beautiful graphics and a bounty of variants to discover, 10 variants for each of 56 species if I am correct (the collector in me lives for this). This keeps you occupied quite a long time and you can make your zoo and enclosures beautiful in the meantime. For some people the game mechanics of morality points etc is a drawback, but there is a sandbox mode available later for those who like mixing things up, so not really a drawback for me. Cons:  - more explanations would be nice to figure out how the different buildings and employees work. There is a lot of walking in the dark till you figure it out. Some poor wording choices and lack of update to descriptions make some dynamics complicated to figure out... it is just a matter of text that could easily be fixed with a tiny update in my opinion. For example, as you have more visitors, your employees will become tired quicker and have no energy and be less efficient, it says when you hover over the energy bar that you can schedule a break for them to recover. This is a non-existent feature, don't try looking for it. There is no scheduling hours, or shifts to alternate with a second shopkeeper. They will just be exhausted till the next day.Another thing, when you want to store something to use in your shops, it actually goes through the food store room of your animals where the animal keepers go. I thought it would go to the warehouse but no, there it will only be sold. It is misleading because on the farm processor, it says "select to amount to be stored for your animals, leftover will be sent to the warehouse" , I thought, I am not using this stuff for my animals so this is not the place to store it... turns out it is.So, some explanation about how this works would be welcome when you acquire the building, and some simple rewording.Finally, my biggest complain is about the Aquarium DLC. The real reason I am writing because I am so frustrated. Never, has it been so hard for me NOT to join the dark side. OMG. I am going out of my mind with grinding to collect the animals. To give you an idea, I have 140 days in game (20 weeks), I make 200k a day and have 4 million dollars overall. I have unlocked all the fishboat upgrades for weeks, and it is a miracle if I get 1 new species per week. It has been so from the beginning. When I got the first 2 upgrades I thought, the boat is finally gonna be a bit more productive. I unlocked all slots (6 fish) thinking it would increase the odds if it is all statistics. Nope. With all upgrades, I get maybe 1 new species during a week. _childDocuments_.review: I wish I could put this as a "maybe recommend" or a neutral review, because I see so much potential in this game even though it's held back by some weird, janky design choices. But if push comes to shove, I'd say "yes" on recommending it. This is gonna be a long review, but I can explain.This game is really charming with a solid pixel art style and a bunch of cartoony, unique ideas for stuff to put in your zoo. You can cross animal species in a lab, selectively breed animals to map their genome, track wild animal populations as you release new ones into the wild, and even directly deter protesters in multiple ways without even touching your enclosures. You can build a lot of extra facilities and run extra operations to the point where your zoo isn't even JUST a zoo. But the problem here is the progression system that gets you this elaborate zoo.First off, I really don't like the tech tree being a sprawling grid of largely hidden boxes. You can't really plan or prioritize much as a first-time player with your research, and you'll sometimes feel obligated to get upgrades you don't need TO EVEN SEE what upgrades you can get next. You effectively gamble your time researching to make progress, and then there's the morality system. Yeah, you need a certain amount of good or evil points, on top of the upgrades, to build some of the facilities.Now, this game has a good idea of either doing things as an eco-friendly conservationist or a reckless tycoon, but the problem is when these options become quantified and mandatory. You lose out on too much of this game if you go morally neutral, because trying to be a jack of all trades makes you a jack of none straight-up. Both of the two moral paths are as unfocused as the research grid too. I expected the eco-friendly path to focus on reducing park expenses and increasing positive press, while the corrupt business path focused on huge, new revenue streams with some new expenses to compensate. The truth is you can get facilities to reduce utility expenses, get farming industries, and obtain unnatural zoo animals on both paths. They only go in completely different directions superficially.For example, that "unnatural animal" part is due to this: The game will obligate you to make genetic Frankenstein animals when your lab is idle EVEN WHILE you're far along on the good path. Not only do those freak-show creatures have no place in my produce-farming, conservationist zoo, but I could have used my lab to clone animals from endangered species instead. How is this required and morally neutral? Like, robotic, captive animals are evil but potentially suffering, pig-rabbit chimeras are just "what it is"? If the game just improved its progression systems and taught me environmentalism with more subtlety, I wouldn't be thinking so much about this game's confused identity. It can't really decide to be goofy like Parkasaurus or kind of thoughtful like Planet Zoo.This sounds like a lot of complaining, but I'm doing it because there is a lot of potential and interesting ideas here. But with all the other confused or contradictory ideas in the game's progression, it feels a bit marred. If this game gets a sequel, a new update, or mods, it could be something truly great. Until then, I'll probably keep playing this game in small bursts until I feel like I truly got my money's worth out of this.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is innovative, the UI has regressed 20 years worth of development.Unlike Zoo Tycoon and Planet Zoo, this game strays away from min-maxing enclosures. Instead, your focus will be on min-maxing what variants you have in enclosures to have the best chance to breed new variants. Another new mechanic as far as zoo games go is morality. This is actually a really fun innovation. Turn your excess snakes into belts if you want. Turn dead animals into robot versions. Or: reduce pollution, go all-natural, get some windmills running, etc. The replay value here is really interesting because you have to become hilariously evil or good to access everything on both ends.As far as criticisms, the UI in this game is not thought out well. Almost no control works the way you think it should, but usually is the second or third choice for no discernable reason. The controls switch unintuitively between menus, certain menus like the enclosure allocation screen after adopting animals cannot be backed out of, and the pop-up screens do not close the menus that they just blocked letting unwanted actions go through. Most of the controls let you play with only a mouse, but the menu navigation is not quite tuned for it which sucks. If you want to do mouse & keyboard, the hotkeys are very limited and not in-depth. There are far too many intrusive pop-ups and unskippable ones, too. The path creation tool is too redundant since you can delete paths with it even though there's also a delete tool. It often leads to deleting paths you wanted to keep.Additionally, there is almost no lategame. The morality system swings both ways up to 200 but the highest tier unlock only requires 35. Kind of pointless. Nothing crazy to spend your money on either. Dinosaur island DLC takes far too long to let you unlock every dinosaur such that by the time you do, it's already been dragged out too long and there's almost no point in playing afterwards.

_childDocuments_.review: So, a LOT of my complaints were addressed in this latest update - it's now a lot easier to manage your animals as far as euthanize/donate - there's a new panel that shows you everything that's available for the action so you can do it in bulk. You can now paint floors in a large grid. You can now see new employee types when hiring. Basically, a lot of QOL stuff got added, pretty dang quickly. RCT fans will now be a lot happier - at least, I am. Definitely recommending this game with almost no reservations at this point. I like the game, but those familiar with similiar tycoon games may be let down by the data/reporting and UI of the game and may become frustrated by that. The game's art is good and there are a lot of systems to handle while managing your zoo to get it in working condition. It's fairly priced and I think it's worth trying. The remainder of this review will be me ranting for 3000 characters.Reviewing at around 12 hours of playtime, which is about 24 hours after launch. Keep in mind, the developers seem very nice and are responsive to bug/improvement reports, and my overall opinion of the game is positive. Just wanted to share some things that might stick out for some long-time simulation game players. I just want to get my biggest complaint out of the way first - the UI/interface. Do not expect anything like RCT2 levels of data whatsoever, though it honestly has enough content/systems that would justify it (and this is absolutely a compliment). There are so many different kinds of animals, and each animal seems like it has about 8 or so different varieties or so to discover. That said, when you want to do deep-digging into what is failing about your park, you don't have many mechanisms to evaluate the metrics. Let's take a game series that this game is being compared to - a Zoo Tycoon or RollerCoaster Tycoon. In that game, you have tons of panels that will display graphs, lists, sortable data on all the aspects of your park. In this game, you are reliant on an automated alert system that lives in the top left bubbles of your screen, along with the panels that list employees of buildings - but the latter is only accessible if you go to the park entrance or happen to be able to track down wherever that building is, specific to the employee, in the park. Sure, the bubble is great because it lets you fix things on the fly, but as far as having a prospective view? You're pretty out of luck. You can't view all your employees at a glance and what they're thinking and their happiness so you can quickly give them a raise across the board if needed (like a RCT), you can't list all the animals in a given pen so that you can quickly donate or euthanize them in cases where you allowed for overpopulation, and you can't see all your amentity buildings so you can quickly adjust them en-masse at a glance so that you can maximize profit. There are built in tick boxes for "apply to all [pens]/[shops]", but it's more about seeing the numbers so you have an overall view of your park.  Most importantly, remember the "Guest Thoughts" overall panel in RCT? Nothing like that is in this game. As far as your zoo animals being in danger- that sort of thing gets automated up into the top left alert bubble, so it basically does the work for you- but only at the exact time that you break the deficient limit of whatever is wrong.Instead of having graphs of available food for a given enclosure, you just simply keep spamming "fast supply" food every single chance you get - because why wouldn't you? Maybe I'm expecting a lot out of something that's meant to be a casual zoo simulator, but there are so many things to manage in this game I have a hard time believing that this game is meant to just be played by the average casual "I love zoos and want to run one" kind of player. There's systems like morality which allow you to branch your upgrades in different directions based on the way you run your park, which I've never seen in a simulation game before. Unfortunately, this basically means you are locked into doing one or the other as far as I can tell - and at the moment there's no way to experiment because you only have one save per game so if you "evil up" your park, you're breaking it for the foreseeable future. Either you go good and make impossible meat or you go bad and literally overproduce and butcher all the animals for their goods to sell them to companies to make into product. I'd like to see a way to have a hybrid, or for you to offset some bad with a ton of good so that you can justify seeing the entire game (and I admit, only 10 hours in - maybe this very thing is possible). This probably deserves its own header because I ranted way longer than I expected. * I really like the pixel art, everything is distinctive and you can watch hippos jump on a trampoline. This is good. * There's a ton of upgrades - if you love unlocking new thing, you can absolutely grind out to unlock new thing.* You will get sucked in, wanting to breed just one more new species - turns out, that never ends, and you end up playing 12 hours within the first 24 hours of release. * There's a ton of customization, but with the caveat that a lot of it is biome related- you'll probably only end up wanting to end up using the 'furniture' that matches the zones you make, but what do I know, I ain't you* You get to fuse animals together. Make a guinea pig + duck, its just a platypus. * You get to build tons and tons of buildings and paths. * Though you can fuse animals, it doesn't really seem like there's a point or benefit to it - they don't produce anything unique, they don't present any challenge other than having to unlock every species of a given animal before being able to use it for fusion- and the result is just that you get the head of one slapped onto the body of another. I mean, that's cute, but like, I expect some benefits from having fused animals. Maybe there are - I just have no way to tell I'm getting any increased gain from having them because of 'lol no in-game charts'. * 60FPS lock, this is not a huge deal, but a lot of us are on 144hz monitors now and notice when the frames drop to more than half of what they were. You get used to it, and it's probably some engine limitation, but I beg of you devs of all games, please just start using engines that are not frame rate dependent. We have ways to simulate 60fps calculations that translate to any framerate nowadays. * I just want to reiterate, please god, give me graphs and sortable data for the entire park, in one panel (with tabs) at a glance so I can actually understand my entire park and its inefficiencies, and let me do quick actions for each thing in that list in a fast way. Literally contact me and I will draw you a sketch of how it should be. The heat maps are great, but I have no idea how many people a day are leaving due to not having enough decoration, not having enough light, etc. * The game's initial keybinds ain't great. My advice: Set cancel to Q, set build mode to E, set pause time to spacebar, and then you can use 1-3 for the speed options. Try backing out of menus with right click first, then do a Q. Would like to see the ability to bind mouse buttons to things. The back button on the mouse is like, right there. Anyway, I like the game, it's not a ton of money, you'll have fun and get what it's worth. I hope to see it optimized so I can totally 100% all the species at some point. I will come back and update this review with an edit at the top if anything changes while I'm playing or if I discover something new. Again, I haven't 'beaten' the game, whatever that end state is, but I think I've played enough to get a good grasp of its general gameplay and most systems involved.

_childDocuments_.review: I debated on this game for a bit before buying it, and I'm really glad that I did. I love that you can decorate and design your zoo however you like (though with some restrictions) and you can choose between running a very moral or a very evil zoo. Pros:The game gives you a fair amount of creative freedom to design how you like, though a lot of items are locked behind research points. However, it's very easy to simply let the game run and collect money and points while doing other things. You only have to be present to close the save box and a couple pop-ups right after, but most of the day runs on it's own. There are a lot of hilarious references to pop culture and celebrities that give me a good laugh. There are also a lot of unexpected twists that take you by surprise and can give you a good laugh as well. (Like if you 'accidentally' put your welfare officer in the snake pen)You feel a sense of accomplishment getting a good score, though the punishments for scoring poorly aren't so harsh that it's discouraging. Though, if you WANT to get a bad score, you can as well. You have that freedom to be evil if you wish. I find I can sink hours into the game just decorating, rearranging, and working on my zoo. For me, the decorating aspect is my favorite, more so than the tycoon aspect. This game has given me a lot of laughs. Though I am half torn between laughing or being annoyed at the UFOs stealing my cows.I like how, despite it being a game with a lot of aspects that are not based on how things work in reality, there are a lot of things that are. I find the habitat and threat aspect very interesting. (I also had a lot of fun putting animals in time out for threatening other animals in their pen)Cons:The enrichment system can be infuriating. If you get a baby born in the zoo, if you don't add another toy within a short window, visitors complain and you are flashed reminders on the side to increase enrichment. Then, you will often get 'zookeepers blocked' messages because you have so many things in the pen they can't clean. 1 toy per animal is a bit over the top and makes the pens so cluttered and messy. I've gotten to a point where I just start getting rid of animals in a pen instead of adding a ton more ugly toys.Getting a variety of animals is very, very slow and even 70+ hours in I've still got barely any variety from when I've started. The amount of other zoos on the map is very small, and you cannot get new animals until you complete the current trade request. So if you do not have an animal a zoo wants, you are stuck until you do. This is frustrating when you want variety. Building can be infuriating at times, and you cannot move your map when you have the toolbar open to add buildings, paths, decor, etc. This can be very frustrating if you are trying to build a long path or make something symmetrical because you are forced to close the toolbar, slide your map open, and go through all the icons again to pull up what you need. It can get very tiring opening and closing the toolbar when trying to decorate because of this. The building box pop-up on the right hand side is also very large and can often block things you are trying to put down. You are given tons of shops to put down in your zoo...except the visitors seem allergic to most of them and they end up with little-to-no visitors. You often end up taking a loss because you are paying employees more than you earn from the shop. If there is some kind of trick to enticing customers, you are not told. Like many aspects of the game, you are left to figure it out on your own. This can be a frustration or fun depending on what type of person you are. If you like analyzing those sorts of things, messing with building placement and trying to figure out how to lure in customers, it can be fun. My wishes for the game:More variety of flooring, and/or edging for flooring. Fences! Unless these are still locked behind research points, I hate that there are no fences. It makes it hard to block off large areas from visitors. A better design system, or at least be able to move the screen over while putting items down to not have to open and close the toolbar. More uses for morality pointsMore zoos to trade with

But then after around 100 in game days it becomes a waiting game, there's no real challenge other than expanding, and that's probably what everyone here wants to do so that's a good thing, but the struggle from the beginning reminded me a bit of frostpunk (just a bit), so in the mid game I was left with a taste of wanting more of a  challenge, instead money just keeps on flowing and it feels like you're playing sandbox mode.I only listed the bad things but the game is great and you should give it a go, just try and ignore a bit the clunky UI that they're already fixing.
