_childDocuments_.review: I would love to love this game but in it's current state I can't. I love management games but there's a certain rhythm to making them fun and not frustrating. This is just frustrating. I had a pen of geese, the second animal you get, placed directly next to the store room and FIFTEEN zookeepers assigned to just that pen. I changed all their diets to nutritious and satiating and reordered their food often. Their food was always critical and I got an F rating on my welfare report which means I was penalized. I honestly think that pen was bugged because my other pens with only 2 keepers assigned did fine.There is no pause button in this game. **It's a building game that doesn't have a pause button.** Building any one area could easily take all day, which means you're neglecting your animals, and since you can't pause, the UI will interrupt what you are doing to give you a stat read out and cancel your progress when the day ends. I'm constantly getting stun locked by UI popups. It makes it frustrating to do ANYTHING because you can't even focus. Whenever I have to manage something, I take my cursor as far away from my park as possible to get some visual peace and quiet so I can focus. Not good design.And I hate *the way* you have to pick staff. What part of that is fun? Why would I want to micromanage a faceless NPC's pisspoor work ethic meanwhile I'm actively pissed off at them for killing my animals? When that happens in the sims or zoo tycoon you can literally kill that person. In this game the worst you can do is send him home without pay and then the game will punish you for that by turning off your power and progress locking you out. I feel like a little kid being shamed because my group members didn't do their fair share of the project and I'm powerless to do anything about it. Not fun.The animal management system is so micromanaged that it honestly discouraged me from expanding my park. I don't want more animals, that's just more responsibility and besides I don't have time to build an enclosure. It's the least fun part of the game- how did they manage that???I actually like the morality system, it reminds me of Stardew Valley, which I love. However, unlocking things in general in this game was just poorly thought out. Unlocking two cosmetic decor items costs the same and sometimes more than actual interactive items that allow you to progress the game in consequential ways. Which would you rather buy? This means that you're incentivised not to waste your research points on worthless cosmetics. But who waits until the end of a game to decorate it? By that point, the game is over. Your park has been built. You've just made decorating not just pointless but detrimental to your ability to progress in the game. Which again, weighs on you the entire time you're trying to build! Essentially, every time you decorate you are wasting time and resources and you will know this because you will get a UI pop-up distracting you ever 85 seconds.This game needs a balance rework. Badly. But I believe it has a lot of potential. I really hope I change my mind and am eager to change my review right along with it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game with such an incredible amount of content for the price. I'd go so far to say that it matches other sim/tycoons that offer a much heftier price tag for this experience. There's dozens of animals to unlock, all of which require their own little mini-quests of breeding certain other species to trade with other zoos, which you can then get all of the variations of as well.Plus you're offered quite a few of the bells and whistles of a zoo outside of just the pure animals; with hiring employees, designing park areas, figuring out where you want your hotspots of attendance to be, moral decisions on how to treat animals and either to exploit/treasure them, optional quests and requests, a farming system, and much more. For the most part all of these options are fully fleshed out offering additional layers to the complexity.My only criticism comes with the early-mid game transportation. In Let's Build a Zoo, not only are you responsible for creating a zoo worth attending, but you're also on the hook for getting everyone there via buses. In the early game, you're very cash strapped while trying to build for the future, and the first two buses are very expensive in relation to everything else. This is on top of a traffic system, where once you reach 8-10 vehicles, you actually won't have enough time in the day to get all the buses emptied and patrons into the park. This resulted in my playthrough having a 2-3 hour span where I was making the same amount of money every day because of the traffic, and I was forced to either keep spending the little I was making on bettering the park and making slightly more money, or just hard saving for the 2nd tier bus, which would take upwards for an ingame week at least. The vast amount that the bus cost also made it difficult to invest in more space for my park, as the price would climb higher with no financial benefit. Once you get over that hill however, the game is once again enthralling. No longer bound by a hard limit on revenue, finding additional ways to make cash is a great experience. While still bound by the amount of people you can fit on the relatively small buses, Once you get to a certain size it feels much less punishing, and you can focus on expanding your roster of creatures and other ventures. This game is absolutely worth picking up, doubly so if you can catch it on sale! I haven't had a chance to check out the DLC yet but I'm sure its great too.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit 12/19/2021 - I decided to give this game another shot.  Partially because I think the concept of the game is solid and partially because I didn't want to give up on the sound issue I was having.  I'm not sure exactly what was the fix, but during this time the dev team has been pushing out updates and communicating with their users very well via Discord.  I also happened to buy DTS Sound Unbound for an issue I was having with Halo Infinite.  I'm glad I repurchased the game and I haven't experienced my issue since I've reinstalled.LBAZ development team's delivery of a cute pixel art game crossed with a fun concept of zoo management crossed with, well, cross breeding - is a ton of fun.  I feel like this game is akin to a more fun, non-microtransaction mobile sim game brought to you on the full screen.  You can pick it up and put it down fairly easily (just need to get through a night to save), so folks who don't have a ton of time to invest nightly in gaming - this could be a fun one for you.The morality system is a huge plus.  You will have to get used to partitioning off parts of the zoo and learn zoning for your employees to be successful early on.Great concept, pretty good execution, fantastic pixel art, and really impressive community outreach for issues and resolutions.Original Post - I actually really like this game.  It has a fun concept, neat details to tweak, cute art concept.  I would have played this game all day yesterday if it didn't cause weird sound distortion on my computer.  I can only play this game for 1-2 in-game days max until my Discord, music, other videos, or the game itself become sound distorted.  The minute I close the game, the sound distortion disappears.  I've turned off hardware acceleration on Discord, attempted running other apps as admin for priority, changing from fullscreen to windowed in the game, but nothing seems to work.  I've never had this issue with other games.I'm on the fence of returning it and rebuying if this gets fixed.  It's unplayable to me until a bug fix.

_childDocuments_.review: Gave it a thumbs up because it is a cute game and the management is just deep enough to scratch that itch but not definitely not something I would call sim-level. It does, however, suffer from some serious progression and design problems that could use some attention. I will admit: I am only 3.5 hours into the game as of this review, so maybe (hopefully) there are solutions to some of these issues that are unlocked down the road.1. You unlock new items, buildings, and upgrades through research. However, you are only able to have one researcher at a time for at least the early to mid game, meaning the flow of research points is locked at a single rate for the majority of the game. I very quickly got to the point where my park was stagnating while I waited for enough points to accumulate each day. Also, the game will repeatedly remind you that you have unspent research points. Yes, game. I know. I can't help that it takes three or four in-game days to save up enough points to unlock the next bus upgrade.2. Additionally, the research tree is a random grid where the contents of each square are hidden until you unlock the square next to it. You can filter the grid to see what type of upgrade is in each square, but you can't tell exactly what it is. So you can very easily miss early-game upgrades that cause your park to stagnate until you inevitably hit a research wall then have to circle back to other parts of the grid.3. You unlock quests in the early game that don't or won't benefit your zoo until mid to late game. For example, one quest asks you to install a subway. The subway is how your guests get around a large zoo quickly. This quest also popped up when I literally only had two enclosures in my zoo so it was just wasted money. I feel like the specific quest triggers should be more closely related to the state of your park.4. You need specific colors/mutations of animals to unlock others. While the concept is nice, it turns your play-through into a random numbers game of luck trying to get the right mutation to trade for the next species of animal.1. So. Many. Button. Clicks. Certain tasks require you to click way too many buttons. For example: Want to hire some new staff? Well that involves you opening the staff menu. You then have to open the sub-menu for the specific staff type you want to hire. From there you have to switch to the hiring menu. On the hiring menu you have to click the button to allow applicants to submit applications. Then you select where you want to post the job listing. Then you have to click a button to submit the job posting. Then you wait for applicants to apply, before finally selecting the one you want and hiring them. Oh, and while you are actively hiring you can't click into other types of staff to see how they are doing. You have to wait until you either hire someone or close our the job posting.2. Some menus are hidden or hard to get to. Example: after some progression, you can start generating your own power, water, gas, etc instead of buying it from the city. Want to see how much resources you use vs create? Well the only way I've found to do that is to build a building that generates some kind of resource and open then menu from there. There is no top-level way to get to that menu from the main game screen.3. It's hard to tell what your guests do and don't like about your zoo. Your zoo gets a rating and you can view the high-level numbers that impact that rating by category. However, sometimes your guests get happy/unhappy symbols above their heads and it can be very difficult to figure out what is making them feel that way.4. Menus in the build screen are organized into single-row carousels. Meaning you can only see a handful of items in each category at a time without clicking the left/right arrows to see more. Again, it just hides more content behind more unneeded button clicks.5. Managing animal populations is a slog. Some of the early game animals breed like rabbits (one of which literally is the rabbits.) Since each pen can only handle so many animals, that means after a while the population needs to get thinned out. Doing this is annoyingly complicated. First you need to select one of the animals in the pen. Then you need to click the sell or donate button. This loads a screen with all of the animals in the pen, after which you go one-by-one to select what animals you want to get rid of. For the more reproduction-happy animals, this process could be required every couple in-game days. When you have two or three different types that you have to do this with, it gets monotonous fast. Yes, you can give your female animals contraceptives, but again this is done one-by-one and also means you can't work towards getting the different color mutations needed to unlock different breeds of animals.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Devs responded that they may add suggestions to the game so I'm changing my review to positive for the enthusiasm. _childDocuments_.review: -- Second Update --Third time's the charm. After the developer added the option for using the system cursor, all of the issues were resolved (Settings > Advanced > Use System Mouse). It's a great tycoon game, and the support is top notch; highly recommended!-- Update --The input delay was resolved by using the nvidia control panel to forcibly disable vertical sync for the game. However, with the delay gone, a new problem was exposed that was likely contributing to original experience: You can read my comment for details, but if you're like me and used to precise mouse interactions, I don't recommend investing in this game until there's a work-around.-- Previous Review --The input lag caused by the vertical sync kept me from even starting a game. I can't tolerate games where cursor input is not 1:1 with the OS. (And no, disabling the 60fps cap did not fix it).Maybe it's a great game. It looked like it. But, unfortunately, I will probably never find out as I refunded the game immediately.[RE: Developer Response]It would be quite bizarre that Let's Build A Zoo would be the only game that would require a system restart to prevent an input lag, when several different games (of various types and engines) had been open before and after without any issues. I'm happy to provide more details to help solve the bug, but the review is honest and helpful for anyone else who cannot tolerate input delay -- and is simply me sharing that I would not recommend the game for that reason (which many users won't have an issue with, as I'm likely more sensitive to input delay than the average user.)Here are my relevant system specs:OS: Windows 10 Pro NCPU: 3.2GHz Core i9-12900KRAM: 64GB DDR5-6000GPU: Nvidia RTX 3090 [Driver v497.09]Display: 4k144hz native (tried various windowed sizes as well, with no changes)It was clear that even with the frame limit option turned off, my cursor movement was being software-limited by a specific rate (behaving the same as VSync, which is why I presume VSync to be the culprit), so it ends up only capturing the input at that frequency, dropping anything outside that range, resulting in what feels like an amplified mouse acceleration. Again, for many users, this is probably not even noticeable, since most games have VSync enabled by default, but for someone used to 1000Hz input rendered at 144Hz, it is excruciating, and why I don't play any games where disabling vertical sync is not an option.Just to reiterate, since the review seemed to have been taken more personally than it ought, the game looks like a good game (which is why I purchased it), and my only complaint is that I wasn't able to play it due to the input lag.

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute management sim with lots to do and build. I've dumped a lot of hours into this game because it is excellent for endlessly tinkering with something low stakes that doesn't require a lot of brainpower.That said, the UI is horribly designed, and most features are very unintuitive. Selecting objects works sometimes, other times you need to go through a menu, other times you're just out of luck because there are too many visitors in the way. Want to move a floor light? Too bad, your only option is to wait until all the visitors have left the area.Want to select every male animal in an enclosure? Get clicking! While you can sort the order that animals are shown in(gender, genome, longevity, etc), there's no way to filter the view to narrow down what you see. This also makes the "select all" button virtually useless unless you want to apply an action to the entire enclosure. As an added annoyance, the checkbox is so small that misclicks are frequent. The research page is a nightmare of guesswork. If you're looking to unlock something specific(for example, the forest enclosure), you either need to look up a guide for where it is, or commit yourself to taking random stabs in the dark. There is a way to search for categories of research, but it won't show you exactly what you need. This would be fine if it were in a more typical research tree structure, as you'd at least have the assurance that you were on the right path, but the haphazard placement across the board makes exploration feel frustrating.There are many things that are doable, but hidden in obscure places(employee management via the heatmaps, for example). There are game features which are poorly explained and would do well with more management options(farm processing, population manager, nutrition hut). And most painful of all, if you want to rearrange your zoo, then you need to be prepared to move every single object individually.The notification system is inconsistent in design - some notifications will give a single popup, like employee level ups. Other notifications will appear in a side bar. This side bar includes both updates(such as new births) and statuses(such as the hunger of your enclosures). There is no way to filter out the ones that aren't currently relevant - most of the time you don't need a notification that my animals are properly fed. This means that sometimes you have to scroll down past a list of "everything is fine" statuses to get to the ones you need to address.If you pick up this game, also look up some user-written guides, because the game itself won't tell you many of its useful features. Yes, the game is cute and fun, but I will not be picking up any other games from No More Robots until the UI gets some serious improvements.Edit: I have edited this review - while I had tried to shine a positive light on a game that I am overall enjoying, the more I have continued playing, the more the bad UI is cropping up. In the early stages of the game, it can be easy to overlook these things. Midgame becomes overwhelming with things that look like they urgently need your attention because there is no way to prioritise notifications, so everything is an alert. Late game becomes an exercise in irritation as you try to expand your zoo without turning it into a bizarre patchwork.The more I play, the more I think I would be embarrassed to recommend it to people. I would be apologising for its shortcomings more than praising the things it does well.

_childDocuments_.review: This game can become such an addiction. The visuals are so pleasing. I leave the sound effects on because they are quite nice, but the music I switch off to avoid repetition while replacing it with an assortment of smooth jazz. The combination of animals with genetics and variations is mind boggling offering great replay value. After 200 hours I've developed a new hobby of taking screenshots while making small edits, and this has felt incredibly rewarding. Once mechanics of the game are understood the game becomes only limited by the player's imagination. I imagined something efficient with some good symmetry, and the game gave me more than I could have hoped. Additionally, in the brief time I have owned the game they have released a couple large updates which have added tons of extra features. Another interesting note is the developers listen to the community and make changes based on feedback. For example, the game released with 10 variants needed to use the splicer which was then reduced to 5 for ease of access. Second, sandbox mode released with a cost of 5000 investment dollars reduced to 2500 again to ease access for newer players. In conclusion, this game offers a great value for its price, and I believe anyone playing building and/or management games would enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like cozy management games with decorating, animals and pixel graphics, then this is a game you should try! The art and pixel style are well designed and the developers are active and responsive to players and release updates pretty frequently.There are lots of cute animals and buildings in the game. There are around 30-50 animals and each have 8 or so variants each. In addition, there is many different decorations and ways to expand your zoo. Whether it be through research; breeding your animals to make new species; capitalising and gaining profits, or just simply making a zoo - there's something for everyone, giving this game a lot of repeatability.Whether you play this game in a complicated or simple manner, I've never found myself personally hindered or stuck on what to do. If I desire to have a basic zoo simulation experience where I make a pretty zoo and decorate it beyond focusing on profits, I am able to do so. If I want to play more in depth, focusing on a morality system and the facilities, I am also able to do so.Despite all this, there are some issues I have with the game personally. These are rather small but worth mentioning:1) Animal breeding speed. I obviously see the benefit in having the animals breed fairly quickly so that you can unlock different variations and new animals, but it got to a point where I was spending a large majority of my time making  animals infertile and donating extras.2) Notifications.There are constant reminders within the game, which you are unable to dismiss. These include "new birth", "empty pen" and research points not being spent. Specifically the constant reminder of research points, when you are actively trying to earn more, gets a little annoying.There are some small bugs that still occur every now and then, but all around, I really like this game and I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty cute zoo building game with more of a focus on the managment side of things than realism, it has bit of a theme park flavor to it.I guess my main criticism is that there is a lot of Quality of life and a few UX issues in the game, some things feels a bit more bothersome than necessary to carry out! But the game is fairly good otherwise, and while a lot of updates are planned what is in there is very functional, it's far from a early access product.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: A complex business sim with a twist of fun.All the traditional economical levers are there for you to pull: gate prices, employee wages, decisions balancing morality and profits. But there are some new mechanics, such as being able to splice together different animals to create chimera-like creatures to draw patrons in.The visuals retro pixels but with the common modern twist of smooth unique movements. I'm old enough to have seen pixels go out of style and come back around in this new nostalgic wave over the past few years. I have to say I enjoy it. Its still pretty but allows a game like this to show you clearly all the details you need to see when looking from a zoomed out perspective.Two thumbs up, I look forward to building, maintaining, and tweaking my zoo over time.

A Guest review menu that you could access would help with better zoo planning, seeing which animals are the most popular, and seeing where the most foot traffic is would all be greatOkay, now for non menu related things-More shops. _childDocuments_.review: Love this game but why is there not a proper save feature?I spent hours working on redesigning my zoo. To maximize workable space, I made very tiny pens to move my animals into. I spent about 4 hours on this new zoo before I had to go to work and figured to just leave the game running and come back since you cannot save unless the day rolls over. If I let the day go over, my animals would have probably died from lack of space and water, plus many of the enclosures were not accessible to zoo keepers. Unfortunately when I returned from work, my game had crashed. It was very painful to loose all that progress.I still have a lot of the game to explore, but I really do love this game. The art style is very pleasant and the animal designs are very charming. There is a lot to manage and many ways to play, having a morality system for what kinds of zoo you can make is really unique! While Zoo Tycoon is the more popular zoo building game, I grew up with Zoo Empire and while that game had a much smaller cast of animals, the designing and managing of the zoo felt much more fulfilling than when I got my hands on Zoo Tycoon. This game really reminds me of Zoo Empire and all the positive qualities that game had.Besides being able to save whenever, there are a few other improvements I think would make this game more fun! The biggest change I would be happy to see would be animals having multiple favorite habitats. This would be snakes liking desert and rainforest, badgers liking forest and grassland, armadillos liking desert and grassland, and so on! I would love to have those animals in multiple areas of my zoo depending on their variant fitting one habitat over the other! Also being able to change the floor tiles in a habitat would open up so much more creative design!I have already recommended this game to a few people! I cannot wait to see what else they add in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a little time sink with adorable pixel art, have at it. Its genuinely really cute and relaxing to play if you don't mind how absolutely random the upgrade system feels or how there is no grey area when it comes to the karma system.My main critique is for the karma system. I hate that once you choose "good" you cant even do the slightest bit of "evil" or visa versa. So say you have like 30 rabbits dying because they are over-breeding and you have been using them to cut costs on feeding carnivores (a facility that you can only unlock if you have "evil" karma), as soon as your karma moves into in the "good" range, the facility shuts down immediately and will never be available to you again if you ever want to unlock and keep stuff on the good path. its more than a bit annoying, but its not game-breaking or anything. I still had a good time playing, and would still absolutely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: I only recently got this game and I've played other complex Zoo Simulators. I like the concept of the point n' click. Doesn't necessarily overwhelm your brain like other Zoo sims. This one takes the hat, it's pretty straightforward and once you get the hang of it.. it is really addicting. I like the option of good or evil (have yet to take the evil route). The story line is quite cute and I like the reactions of the visitors coming in n' out of the zoo. The options you get with animals without having to buy add on's is a plus and feels worth your money with how much they've put into the game. There are a number of routes you can take and what you can unlock. Unfortunately, debt is inevitable at first and over time as you start expanding.. it'll be less overwhelming (coming from the person who has 11k in debt already and only 6 hours in). If other zoo simulators are just sitting in your library, this option is your best bet to get that itch of building a zoo. Now... Let's Build A Zoo!

_childDocuments_.review: I've not been this addicted to a game in years. The original Zoo Tycoon it is not, but as good a comparison as any. You start out with two rabbits, and create a million (hopefully one day billion) dollar breeding empire, with fake animals, robots and a larger zoo than I thought was even possible. I couldn't recommend more. The animal combinations are amazing and pumping out the genetic abominations have been a blast to discover,Only a few problems I have encountered, - The game is a little overwhelming at first (and I'm still uncertain how the Zoo's value is determined from Publicity, Animals, and Facilities) but an engaging game loop- The notifications from the visitors buying things gets overwhelming when you have thousands of them, running around, the option to hide certain ones would be nice- Sometimes an exhibit just breaks because a keeper couldn't reach something, but other keepers are working fine and moving an object fixes this.

_childDocuments_.review: Lighthearted zoo management simulator that keeps you constantly engaged. Lots of variables to deal with in terms of animal welfare, human resources, visitor needs, environmental impact, and business management. You're not forced to do "the right thing" - you can be good, ambivalent, or evil. Room for creativity in building zoo and enclosure layouts. Also, the devs are very engaged with the community and responsive to bugs, issues, and feedback. Highly recommended for builder sim/zoo sim fans, especially those that find the Builder series expensive and heavy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so gloriously addicting.Pros: -Plenty of different animals, and the ability to make wacky crossbreeds-A morality system, and different buildings/upgrades based on good or evil-Super satisfying progression system-Cute pixel art and a lot of different decoration items-Can run on a laptopCons:-Gets grindy late-game-A little glitchy, especially regarding item collision-Building utilization percentage is strange and confusing-All animals act the same and mostly use the same enrichment items, even when it doesn't make senseI'd recommend it, though, especially if you loved Zoo Tycoon but can't often sit down to play Planet Zoo because of its graphics!

_childDocuments_.review: I think I'm going to echo what others have said.. It has a lot going for it, I kinda want to continue? But I have only played it for 7 hours and it's already overwhelming to try to micromanage. Trying to hire staff is difficult, managing zones for workers is difficult, hiring workers is difficult... Only having 1 store room? Animals need a lot more room than you have available? I figured they were trying to be "different" from other zoo building games- but why reinvent the wheel on QoL points? I love breeding things for variants, and the idea of splicing, etc.. But even breeding the things you want is a bit difficult. Managing your animals is difficult. Maybe it gets better the further in you get, with more research upgrades? But as much as I want to progress in the game, I'm a bit exhausted by it already. I bought the base game and the expansion on sale, and I don't think I'll return it in hopes that the developers fix QoL issues. But I don't know that I'll continue to play until some of this stuff is addressed.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great zoo building/tycoon game. The depth the mechanics of this game go are great. It's not just about building and managing a zoo financially and having animals. There is a morality system that allows for having a ethical or unethical zoo which grants access to different ethical specific buildings and things to do within the game. You can even build out farms to produce your own food to feed the animals or sell for money, there's a range of industry buildings to also manufacture goods from the animals for money. You can build your zoo to be eco-friendly to save on costs. There's so much to do in this game even without the DLC which does also look great! It's worth the price and a great alternative to the likes of planet zoo, even with its pixel graphics they compliment the game nicely. Also, although this game is marked as unsupported for the steam deck, I can confirm it runs very well on it with the only caveat being closing the game doesn't take you all the way back to your library but simply clicking 'B'/abort game in the bottom right does without any problems. Highly recommend this game!

_childDocuments_.review: This is the game you didn't know you needed. It manages to get the sim/tycoon genre exactly right. It invokes nostalgia for older tycoon games, but offers a fresh take. For example, there is a morality meter.The game-play feels meaningful and strategic, unlike many other tycoons where the focus is more on decoration.Overall a good re-imagining of the tycoon genre. _childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: Super addicting! The pixel graphics are gorgeous - the amount of sprite artwork packed into this game is impressive. There are so many variations of animals, so many items/buildings/decor. Breeding animals to get every color/variation and then being able to make hybrid species makes for fun gameplay. It puts Planet Zoo's breeding system to shame. I will say, LAND is the most $$ limiting thing in the 'story' mode - I often found myself with no room for exhibits or room to 'plan out' an area with paths and foliage. LUCKILY exhibits can be moved/resized VERY easily, unlike any other 'zoo' builder game. Hiring multiple staff at once is also weirdly restricted and difficult in the game? The whole 'job campaign' mechanic goes against the flow.I recommend this game if you are into the aesthetics of a bunch of baby monkeys bouncing on a trampoline while you serve pig burgers to unsuspecting VIPs (making evil meat is optional, theres a whole 'evil' route of choices)- it has so many animals, plants, shops, paths, toys, benches, etc to unlock through your campaign zoo. Or just go into creative and have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played much of the DLC yet, I only just started an aquarium and I have yet to play with Dinosaurs yet, so this is a review of the main game from the perspective of a person who grew up with Zoo Tycoon 2 as their favorite game.The game is a very simple zoo builder where you need to make a guest friendly zoo with lots of interesting exhibits, and lots of ways to make money, but what sets this game apart from other zoo builders I have played is the research system and the morality system. Research systems are a staple in the zoo builder genre as you constantly need to learn more about different items that can improve your zoo and your animal's quality of life, but this game takes it in a fun direction. All items, exhibits, facilities, and whatnot that you can learn about are in a grid, where you unlock each item one at a time to be able to unlock any items next to the previous one. This adds a fun element of gameplay where you have to work towards any specific upgrades you want by unlocking a pathway towards it! It's very fun and interesting to figure out different ways to get to a specific objective or seeing what new things you can unlock as you slowly expand the grid.The Morality system is where things get REALLY fun though. Throughout the game you have the ability to take either good or bad moral actions, things like using the black market, dressing up a lost dog as a lion and putting it on display, whether to use green energy or dirty energy, all these can have either a positive or negative impact on your morality bar, and depending on which way you go, allows you to unlock special objects.My first game, I was a goodie two shoes because that's just what I am. I gave my animals the best possible exhibits, the best diets, I got recycling bins and windmills for a cleaner more eco friendly park, and I reported any wrongdoing that came my way. I focused on making an eco friendly, customer friendly, animal friendly zoo that focused on conservation and releasing endangered animals back into the wild. I love playing like this! I like making a farm to grow my own crops so my food options are healthier and cheaper, I love donating to charities, and I love making a very kind zoo. Though as I kept unlocking more and more items and facilities for my zoo, I kept looking at all the evil options that sat on the grid untouched, and I thought to myself "How bad can it possibly be?"So for my second Zoo I have decided to become the worst person ever. I have decided that my main mission is illegal activies, polution, and scamming people. I painted geese to look like peafowl, I am stealing electricity to run my zoo, everything gets a concrete habitat, and all my food is the worst quality so I get a higher profit. This game really does let you either go the normal zoo route of creating a nice enviornment made for conservation and education, or the "how bad me be?" chaos route where you start to let the customers drink recycled sewage to save a buck. I think this gameplay element is VERY fun and something I rarely see Zoo builders encourage. Sure you can make bad exhibits or sell overpriced bad hot-dogs, but this game lets you take it to the next level. You don't have to fight against the game to be evil, it encourages you.If I had one criticism for the game, It would be that research points are very slow to gain making unlocking more items very tedious after a certain point. It's a very minor issue though.All in all, if you want to make a cute and pretty little pixel zoo, this is a good game for that. If you enjoy zoo builders and want something very simple with a lot of fun features, this is a good option. If you're a youtuber or streamer who wants to make the world's most unethical zoo for the ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles, this is absolutely a good game for that. I personally enjoy this game, and I want to give this game some love in the form of a review, that review being "I liked it and I'm gonna play more!"
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not quite what you'd expect. You can chose whether to be good or evil. If you choose good, you can have a wholesome zoo. If you choose bad, you can turn your animals into robots, donate them, have specific factories such as farm land (good) bacon and glue factories (bad). You can also make hybrid animals, such as a snake goose! You can change the prices and qualities on all stores and vending machines, You can also make your animals feeds more nutritious. There are a lot of things to do in this game. It is not quiet what I expected.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: Previously, I thought I had been burnt out on tycoon games, but Let's Build A Zoo is a breath of fresh air to the genre!  Behind these cute pixels hides a game with surprising moral ambiguity!  And morality plays a key point in how you progress in building your zoo!  Another more unusual feature is the genetic splicing system, which adds a level of difficulty, but attracts more visitors.Definitely addicting to play and highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful park builder! You'll find a lot of enjoyment here, don't take it too seriously and you'll have a wonderful time. There's a few gripes in terms of UX, but after the first big update they addressed quite a few of the issues I had, and this is a very very good sign of "on-top-of-it" developers. If the developers are reading this, three vital QOL additions would make this a beast of game: 1. Selecting multiple buildings/path ways (selector having options to select just buildings, just decorations, just pathways or all of the above) to move or delete. This would make a massive difference to a player like myself that likes to build and move things quickly.2. Duplication! Of buildings and of the above selection would be *chefs-kiss*, there's a lot of groups of buildings I create in duplicate and spend a lot of time tweaking their positions to match the other groups.3. Basic keybindings for delete and edit, although the main keys WASD is used for movement, at least some buttons I can rebind would make my "quick-playing" lifestyle a lot easier.Great game and well done!
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to play God before? Do you want to be an angry God or a loving God? Do you like cute animals? Would breeding new variants of pigs, lions, seals, etc be a rewarding experience? Do you like abominations? Does the idea of splicing a hippo with a monkey excite you? Than this might be the game for you! Let's Build A Zoo is a chill zoo building game with cute pixel art and a great sense of humor. The morality system adds a lot of fun to the game in my opinion. Make the world a better place or don't. Hate snakes? Turn em into wallets for a tidy profit. Do you have a deep emotional attachment to your pigs and would fly into a violent rage if anything happened to them? (Totally not talking from personal experience) Give them a trampoline and the best food money can buy. If you decide that your guests don't deserve nice things, change the quality of what they buy. Maybe they'll be more grateful once they learn you've been feeding them sewage and human flesh. Be the God you wanna be.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like management games and this one was pretty awesome at first. I really appreciated the art, how (at first glance) laid back this game was, and how (at first glance) no-stress the entire experience was.This game quickly evolves into a micro-management nightmare, and it was really sad to see unfold. There are so many different things that you need to pay attention to, and as the size of your facility increases, it just becomes more and more stressful to keep up with. I was looking for a casual experience where I could just chill and let the game automate at least some of what was happening, but it was very much the opposite of that. You need to manually check that everything's in order in virtually every single capacity. And it's not even that it's necessarily difficult, because it's not. As someone else put it: It's very overstimulating. The UI is honestly pretty awful and maneuvering it felt very unnatural. It made the entire process of dodging and dealing with 1000 different mechanics in rapid succession so much worse than it probably could have been. I was willing to keep playing until I popped in the reviews and realized this was not only a common sentiment but gets increasingly worse as the game goes on. The soundtrack was cool though

_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a lovely casual zoo sim! The animals are hilarious - each animal interacts with every enrichment item, so you end up with snakes jumping on trampolines and geese carrying around dog toys, and hippos jumping into cardboard boxes. There are lots of fun decorations and enhancements to uncover. I don't even do a lot with the gene splicing and it's still very entertaining. The human characters are also really funny! I've seen a lot of people mention getting bored midway through, or feeling like the game stalls out. What I found after a few restarts is that the game is way more fun for longer if you just take your time. This is a game for relaxing and enjoying the ride, not speeding through. There's really no time pressure here - you don't need to adopt new animals or use new research items immediately. Focus on transportation to build your income, and otherwise do whatever the heck you want. Build a giant hyena sanctuary and restore their wild population. Take an afternoon to do nothing but redecorate or move your enclosures around. Technically there's a completion point I suppose, but just do whatever you enjoy and progress when you feel ready.

_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: Let's Build A Zoo? More Like Let's Make Me Late For Work!As a kid, I loved sim/management type video games. Sim City, Sim Ant, Sim Life. Lots of sims. Sid Meyer's Railroad Tycoon! Later on, games like Pokémon came out, and like millions of other I was bitten by the collecting bug. Let's Build A Zoo brings management games and creature collecting games together in an amazing way. Not only are there 60 base animals to collect, but each animal has 10 breeds, or variants. 600 different animals may seem like enough (is it ever enough?), but with DNA splicing that number increased to over 300,000!Besides managing your zoo and breeding and collecting your animals, there are also morality choices you can make. Do you want to recycle your trash or burn it? Will you allow someone to paint a goose so you can call it a peacock? Use your animal pens to dispose a body?  Will you build wind turbines will you build a belt factory? As you increase your morality down the path of good or evil, more and more options open up.Between the mechanics, the pixel art style, and a development team that is eager to listen to and implement feedback, I give Let's Build A Zoo 5 hippos out of 5.

_childDocuments_.review: Insanely fun and addictive. Only gripe are the frequent crashes and losing hours of edits. _childDocuments_.review: I'd honestly give this game a 7/10, minus points for a number of quality of life issues, and the morality system. But im in late game now, im realizing how deep the veganism is, in a game about caring for animals, SOME OF WHICH ARE OBLIGATE CARNIVORES- Meaning there are nutrients they NEED from meat, that is not found in plants. Vegan diets work with humans because we're omnivores. 4/10The game has a cutesy art style, and i love the variety of colors, patterns, and shapes or styles to the animals. There was one hippo variant where, upon seeing it, i had a delightful 'OH LAWD HE COMIN'' moment. The fact that enrichment and decoration items work for all animals are both a curse and blessing, as it's amusing to see that very same hippo stand on a high beam, something in other zoo-based games would only be for monkeys and lemurs, but it also makes decorating the enclosures feel a little meaningless.The morality system is main reason why my review would have been 7/10- Because it's very rigid, even though in reality, morality is shades of grey, not black and white. Like, i could absolutely be the type of person to treat my animals extremely well and have a big focus on rescuing and conservation, but the employers get minimum wages, and visitors get the worst quality for food. But, that's fine, it's kind of normal for games to forget the monochrome in favor of being one-or-the-other, but... Why is animal processing bad, and farming good, only? The game excuses farming as a way of reducing carbon by transportation of food. Im actually getting a farm because it save money, which is absolutely not  ideal limited only to good people. This is the first sign of the veganism tint, and it gets a bit more transparent with animal processing. Now, i get the killing of animals being evil, but using animals that died of old age is still evil, apparently. Even though it not only would be saving on cost of buying carcasses, but ALSO. Save on carbon. Sounds pretty similar, wonder why. Not like i mentioned it a moment ago. And that's not even mentioning the MORAL alternative is literally BURNING the corpses. Which would then produce CARBON. Now, i'm at end game. In order to get a full 200 morality, i WILL need to make improbable meat, which makes the veganism agenda very, very transparent. Especially when the very research tile that unlocks the lab to turn beets into beef, even MENTIONS feeding lions the VEGETABLE based product. Now, yes, this is a game. But this is a game where diet has been a major thing, where if you're animals aren't on a very good diet, you'll get at least one newspaper, making you out to be a bad guy. So, even the mere idea of feeding a animal that requires at least 70% of their diet as meat, should be immoral. I wouldn't mind if there was a alternative option, to, say, make lab grown meat instead. in theory, lab grown meat in no different then real meat, except it doesn't requiring killing an animal, ignoring the whole, burning corpses which should be making carbon, instead of turning it to a good use.I'd like to add that i don't generally have a problem with vegans, or veganism. But when they try to force other people to conform to their ideals, i have a issue. And the whole, can't even use a elderly animal that died to feed the hyenas, but burning the corpse is okay, and farming is thing only GOOD people do, and the improbably lab; All these things very clearly paints the image that they believe vegans are morally better, and are REQUIRED to interact with and do, if you want the highest amount of moral points. Remember; Farmers churn up ground-dwelling animals, in order and in the process to ready their fields, so even crops are murder.

_childDocuments_.review: The game shows that a good zoo sim does not need high end graphics. I enjoyed it much more than Planet Zoo. It is much easier and more intuitive to use and as for the depth, you can decide for yourself how deep you want to dive. The animals are obtained by bartering with other zoos and have to fulfill certain characteristics, and the research system, with which you explore new decorations, stores and facilities, is very balanced. The game also lets you choose whether to play evil or good, although I personally never see zoos in real life as a good solution in general, but that's another topic.A perfect game for relaxing evenings without getting fits of rage because of setting fences. Yes, I'm talking about you, Planet Zoo.Oh, and there are capybaras. :3
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: This game is immaculate. I have never felt so stressed and calm simultaneously before. The pixel style animation reminds me of Pokemon on Nintendo, and the music just adds to the excitement. I genuinely get super giddy every time I have a new animal enter my zoo, and I have a newfound appreciation of zoo management because MY GOODNESS it is NOT easy. I love the fact that the game developers incorporated topical issues and real-life requirements such as having protesters, pollution management and paying off loans as well as wages. I don't know when or how it happened, but somewhere along the line I got addicted. The only things that are missing is co-op zoos (similar to the co-op farms found in Stardew Valley), and moderation on just how much enrichment is needed by certain animals like geese and bunnies (they are REALLY active in pro-creation to say the least) because it can get a little overwhelming. Other than that, everything (and I mean everything) is gorgeous! Such a fun game and you can tell a lot of time and love went into it. So glad the developers created this, and I would happily recommend it to anyone who enjoys light-hearted, strategic games.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is still a bit buggy.  There were a few times I had to chose a specific crisper combination or the game would crash.  Also my farmers decided to stop working and nothing I did, including firing/rehiring, rebuilding the farm and clearing the crops, would get them to do it again.  Also the game would randomly decide an area of fencing was on top of something without ever actually explaining what was going on.  So I just had random red X's showing up in some of my habitats.You can't see what you're researching out towards, so if you want a specific vendor or habitat, you basically have to spend research points shotgun-style to try and find them.  You can filter for "habitat" and even the hidden ones will light up, but that includes anything that goes in the habitats too.  You can't mix your morality, so you either have a normal zoo, or an 'evil' zoo.  Maybe there's more options on the immoral path, but the good path was very railroaded and the only interesting thing you got to do was kill a few people to save some animals, which... might not actually be moral?But ultimately, the overall reason I requested a refund, is that it's not particularly fun.  The animals all do the same thing, the hybrid animals are barely noticeable even though they're a huge selling point for the game.  Playing a 'collect them all' style just ends up with you sitting with nothing to do while pressing the fast forward button to see if your breeding pair will get the right baby this time.  If you want to make an efficient zoo, you can see how many buildings are put in a bad spot, but no way to actually see which buildings they are or why they're inefficient.  once you get a decent zoo started, your screen just gets overwhelmed by all the guest pop-ups so you can't even see your actual zoo in action.This has fantastic potential, and the idea of morality in a zoo game is fantastic, it just really didn't live up to my hope.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who likes zoo simulators, but always feels a bit let down by the missing animal-related goals, this is a really great game for me. The breeding trees are very easy to understand and very extensive, there really are tons of different animal types, variations and combinations. I love that. I love breeding in games.I did not have high hopes for this game seeing that it is from a very small studio, but it has far more content than I would have expected. The price is absolutely fair for what is offered. I did not encounter any bugs that I would have noticed.If you like zoo games, animal games or breeding mechanics, this game is definitely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: If you are on the fence about getting this game, jump down and buy it. I played the Beta and got a taste of the game and I loved it, but boy is the full game a 3 course buffet with a baked Alaska. This is much more than a simple "theme park sim"! There are so many options to splice up your game play. The morality scale is my favourite part, one game you can be this evil zoo keeper who dives into the black market, tricks their guests into paying more, and basically run a monopoly of a zoo business without a care of animal welfare. Another save you could be the golden goose who saves all the animals, reports all the bad guys and pretty much saves the world. Deciding which way to go has its benefits on either side with the research hub, depending on what you do there will be different things to unlock for your zoo. The animal breeding, splicing and cloning has so many cool aspects to it. This is a game you want to sit down with for a good chunk of time and let me tell you, you will never get bored. Everything in this game is so well thought out, to the visitors, the staff, the decorations, the shelter and trading system, the research tree... There is so much to this game! I can see myself playing this game for hours on end. So what are you waiting for???? Go build a zoo!

_childDocuments_.review: Do you want to build a zoo?Do you want cute sprites and no over-involved staff  needs?Do you want to be able to feed protesters to angry snakes?If yes, then this is the game for you!In Let’s Build a Zoo, you take over the running of a new zoo. Trade animals with other zoos around the world, breed new species variants, and take advantage of the CRISPR splicer to create new species altogether. The choice of how to run the zoo is up to you. Want to invest in breeding programs and conservation efforts? Go for it! Build sustainable farmland and green energy sources to cut down on expenditure? Sure! Or do you want to get cheap scamimals (a dog in a lion costume or a goose painted like a peacock for instance) and steal power and water  from the city to cut those costs? Sell salty snacks and expensive drinks to scam as much money as possible from your visitors? The choice really is yours. As you increase on either path,  you will unlock good or evil perk points to spend on improving your zoo.Let’s Build a Zoo offers so many different things to focus on. There are always areas that need at least some of your attention, but you still have the freedom to choose your own playstyle. You can focus on fulfilling quests for various areas of the zoo, doing research, discovering every animal variant, expanding the zoo, creating breeding programs to release back into the wild… the list goes on. Given this broadness, the game also has a great deal of replayability and is good to talk about with friends - it’s nearly impossible for two zoos to be the same.Updates to the game are still coming, with the latest one introducing dinosaurs (hell yeah!). Bugs also seem to be squished quite quickly, another point in Springloaded’s favour.My major gripe with this game is that there is an annoying amount of micro-managing for certain aspects. Mainly I have trouble with visitors throwing rubbish on the ground despite the presence of bins, and then needing to constantly look for rubbish clusters and create small cleaning zones for extra janitors even when the area’s already covered by a first janitor. Some of the calculations are also not explained very well - lighting and decorations, for example. They’re not hard to work out, but some extra info in a tutorial would be nice when you’re trying to work out why the visitors are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about the park being too dark or not pretty enough or whatever. The other annoyance is a common one of mine - that gaming trend of only being able to save once per day. FFS, people.Overall, though, Let’s Build a Zoo quickly found its place in my favourites list. I highly recommend giving it a try - or at least watching some let’s plays.Top 5 Pros	- ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ adorable	- Scamimals	- No staff drama, it’s all about the animals	- Unlocking the different species/variations is a lot of fun	- Having the ability to live out my mad biologist dreams and create strange abominationsTop 5 Cons	- Building successive zoos takes a long, long time	- The AI isn’t always very I	- Saving only once a day! Arg!	- Visitors and rubbish. The bin’s right there you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!	- You need to go to extremes to get the benefits - there’s no real middle pathWould I recommend:Hell yes. I love this game.(More reviews at

_childDocuments_.review: Overall an awesome game. Love the morally good vs evil routes/choices you can make, so much customization with your zoo, animals, enclosures and its quite addicting. The only thing I don't like is that according to the game eating animals is 100% evil, there are good ways to milk cows, get eggs from chickens but choosing to eat animals is always evil, which isn't right. There are sustainable, good ways to farm animals that this game just ignores, at least from what I can see from the 10 hours that I have played. I have a hobby farm of ducks and chickens for eggs, and rabbits for meat, pelt, and show/breeding that I am always working on to be more sustainable, and when the time comes the animal's deaths are quick and clean. It just rubs me the wrong way the way eating animals in this game is portrayed as bad (obviously eating endangered animals is bad but animals like domesticated, selectively bred farm animals do not exist in the wild).

_childDocuments_.review: When my partner gifted me this game I wasn't sure what to expect, but I feared the game might be a bit too cute.  I like cute, but often overly cute games come with a lack of actual gameplay.  Luckily, I was very wrong.  There is plenty to do and the game even has quite an edge to it as well.  The mechanics reminded me a bit of Theme Park from ages ago, but the morality aspects of the game adds a new spin.  Not to mention that the soundtrack is a complete win.  My partner and I were both feeling it the entire time I was playing.With that said, there are some criticisms to be had.  The game focuses heavily on making things suitable on a per quadrant basis, but does very little to explain this to you.  You can find information about having "unoptimized structures", but no information on how that was determined or how to fix it.  Hopefully with time, these things will be tweaked and made clearer.  In the meantime though, it's still an enjoyable experience and definitely worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Even with it being a bit buggy at times it is 1000% better then Planet Zoo. I wanted a zoo building game similar to the old ones. Planet zoo while nice graphics had a lot of issues. Having everything align was such a pain it was not worth it. Paths wouldn't go next to enclosures and even the first starting out exhibits raised the land around it to where it looked hideous. I spent near two hours trying to get one exhibit to look nice before refunding. For a long time I gave up on ever finding a zoo game until this game came along.Let's Build a Zoo is a fun zoo building game that has a nice twist with the morality system and the funny events you can get when playing. The devs of this game are still working on it and their discord is active. They plan on fixing a lot of the bugs along with making the Micromanagement better which is the main flaw of this game currently. But for 20$, just a fraction of what planet zoo and all it's DLC's cost I would say it is 100% worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: Who this game  for:1)  Anyone that likes Planet Zoo, but doesn't mind more cartoonish graphics2)  Anyone that likes management gamesAt first glance this seems like a childish zoo management game, but as you play you'll discover it is much more than that.  The look of the game is cutesy due to the colors used, the artstyle, etc., but the management portion is there - hiring staff, managing animals, researching new technologies, and other things.  I'd say that the game is a bit deeper than it initially appears and a young child probably would find it too much.I really want to make comparisons to Planet Zoo, but I don't have enough hours in either game to make such a direct comparison, but I will compare the early moments of each.  Both games have very different approaches to introducing you to them - Planet Zoo jumps right into building for the most part, while this game takes a more balanced approach by introducing you to things in a more logical manner.In Planet Zoo the tutorials are so long that you don't really feel like you're doing your own thing and if you skip them, well, things don't typically go so well.  In this game you have more freedom because while there are very similar mechanics to Planet Zoo, it doesn't seem so overwhelming initially.  You're building from the ground up and each step is presented to you without locking you into a pre-built zoo that isn't your own.Like Planet Zoo, this game does have a few issues - however, unlike Planet Zoo, I expect these devs will probably fix those issues.  The biggest issue I've come across so far is expanding an enclosure.  I  the game is attempting to do some sort of pathing check which slows down the actual resizing tool, but if you are editing an enclosure built along the very bottom of the screen it fails outright because it won't let you select the bottom edge (at least in my current play).So far I'm finding this game to be a lot more welcoming than Planet Zoo, while offering somewhat similar features - breeding, animal adoption/trading, research, etc., but I don't think Planet Zoo has DNA splicing, so I'm looking forward to seeing how that works.Alright, here's the breakdown so far: +  No crashes+  The graphics are more than serviceable, giving the game a distinct charm+  There appears to be quite a bit of complexity included here+  While initially limited, building out your zoo is fun+  Has moral choices that impact the story - be an evil zookeeper+/-  Music is okay - hoping they expand this+/-  You're stuck with the starting area/biome - not sure this changes later+/-  Initially the available animals are very limited - you'll need to trade for more+/-  Enclosure shapes are limited-  Resizing enclosures is hit or miss currently-  Feeding seems odd, sometimes I could max out their nutrition and other times I couldn't-  You can't buy excess food, you have to manually buy more if it gets too lowWhile I make a lot of comparisons to Planet Zoo, I don't have enough hours in either to say that one is better than the other - not even sure such a comparison  be made currently.  I'll continue to play both, but will say that I like the general vibe of this game more because it is more accessible.I hope they fix the issue with resizing enclosures, but the current fix is to move the enclosure, and then resize it.  I also hope they allow you to pick different locales for your starting zoo, so you can build in different biomes.  I'd also like to see an option to just get started without the tutorial - just add a sandbox mode with an option to toggle whether or not everything is unlocked or not.  Lastly, let's not forget the music - hoping for more options there as well.  Overall - the game is quite enjoyable thus far, with only the one minor bug to complain about that I've found.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like cozy management games with decorating, animals, and cheeky/dark jokes, then you should try this game out! The animals are adorable and you can breed different variations of one species or mix them up to create a new one, you can unlock new decorations to make your zoo as aesthetically pleasing as you'd like, and you can make a crap ton of money (for some reason I just love to watch those numbers go up in games). I thoroughly enjoyed the game until I got near the end. The story/challenges got repetitive and it became more of a "let's see how many animals I'll need to donate today in order to not have my zoo overflowing" kind of game. I obviously see the benefit in having the animals breed fairly quickly so that you can unlock different variations and new animals, but it got old fast. It got to a point where nearly half of my time playing the game was spent flipping a switch to make animals infertile and donating extras and it got annoying enough that I didn't even finish unlocking all of the animal types. I almost wish the animals were born infertile and you had to flip the switch to allow them to breed, but obvi that's not realistic. Outside of that though, the game was really fun and I totally recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr You'll spend more time in clunky, hard to read menus micromanaging your staff than you will with your animals.This game is so close to being amazing but it falls short. Why? Micro. Management. You'll spend more time doing boring and oftentimes annoying management tasks and keeping track of all your staff more than enjoying your animals and perfecting their enclosures. Remember how in Zoo Tycoon you hire a bunch of zookeepers and they just...do their job? Nah. Not here. It doesn't seem to matter how many you employ - which is a really tedious process here, by the way - animals are constantly going to be underfed and neglected. You can use the zoning feature to assign them to an exhibit, which helps to an extent, but you have to do it for every single zookeeper, making the entire process of hiring extra help a huge chore every time you need to do it.Janitors? Yeah, they're a pain to hire and set up too, while also not...doing their jobs a lot of the time? Also, every food/drink /merch stand requires fussing over hiring an employee, and after you unlock some more things in the research tab, you'll start getting nagged by more notifications that you can now hire more employees for each individual shop, which is especially obnoxious when it's been several hours and you thought you were done fussing with employees for all your shops.I DO like the morality system, it's a pretty unique mechanic for this type of game, though it does end up not feeling quite fleshed out enough. It is darkly amusing that you're given the choice to do things like  and so on. Speaking of which, the game definitely has a a sense of humor, but it's a dark one, which may or may not amuse you. Guests can make...unsavory comments about some of your animals, such as commenting that your adorable snakes and crocs might make nice belts or purses. Your millage will vary on whether or not it's funny or vaguely upsetting.Don't get me wrong, the game is fun and I do enjoy it. But adding a paid dlc instead of fixing or improving the whole menu and staff ordeal has really left a bad taste in my mouth.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, but I have a few quality of life suggestions that can make the game a lot easier to play. 1) The two UI size options are not enough, the text and images are so incredibly small on my particular device that I struggle sometimes to tell animals apart when seeing which to release etc. 2) An improvement to touch screen controls would be a huge boon, it's very difficult to select things currently using the touch screen, and as someone with arthritis this does mean I can't play for long stretches with a mouse. 3) The general UI can be very clunky to navigate repeatedly, which is more or less the brunt of what the game is. When inside certain menus like the Animals menu for Enclosures, you cannot click away and have to specifically select the X. That's not the case with other menus. It would seem small at first but since this is most of what you do in the game it gets to be a bit tiring. Another example is the amount of times you have to click to get to specific menus within menus- there's a lot of screen space on my version at least and I think it would be hugely beneficial to allow for certain things like Hiring to be accessible within one click. An option could be to make it so notifications of new hires available while recruiting are clickable, so you don't have to navigate to the staff menu and then to the menu for recruiting, and then click on them to see their stats and then choose whether to dismiss or keep and then tab back to assign your employee depending on the particular role. There is inevitably going to be a lot of menus in a game about management simulation but I feel like I've played a lot of sim games that find ways to make these menus quick to access- a navigation bar is on option, the ability to pin certain windows like Surveillance would be great, etc. 4) It would be an absolute godsend to have some sort of reference for how and why facilities are optimal or not optimal, and to also have a visual aid of some sort for that specific concern. When you get far enough into the game you have so many facilities that it becomes discouraging to try and make your park highly rated in facilities because you just don't know how to get it there. I've seen some guides but the info is limited and I really feel this should be part of the in game experience. _childDocuments_.review: edit: after almost 2 years of waiting, critical ux issues still weren't addressed. within those time span, however, they managed to release 2 dlcs... :/ skip this game.---5/10 . TL/DR: Let's build a zoo that introduces fresh ideas that work in the very monotonous zoo management scene. For the price, it is a great alternative to Planet Zoo. Unfortunately, it's far from achieving it's full potential due to the bad UX Design.Ok, so here's the review. Let's build a zoo has the typical zoo management mechanics (like, recruiting workers, buying and breeding animals, etc.) but it plays with fresh ideas that I don't often see in zoo management games (like, story progression & decision-making similar to Frostpunk) and it generally has a humorous, fun, and wacky tone to it! (hint: it involves making a chimera, and dealing with the mafia)Unfortunately, the UX is so bad... for someone who plays a lot of management games, i think UX and shortcuts are the things that make 50% of the management game I'm playing. And it's so frustrating seeing a game that has the potential to be so annoying to play with just because of the bad UX Design. I'll point out some of them in hopes that the devs will fix this in the future:1. no keyboard shortcuts to navigate between views. 2. It's missing a lot of key menus too, like shop lists, for example. 3. This game involves a lot of looking where your stuff is and trying hard to click on it (it's a tough job, especially for a cute 16-bit game where many things are small!). 4. For a game that focuses on building, I don't understand why a horizontal list is appropriate to display the build objects when as our tech tree grows more advanced, i unlock more objects. meaning i have to click the 'right' arrow multiple times. i don't understand why it's so hard to move items in this game, and why the hell do decor items not get sold when deleted? 5. Also it's hard as hell to create a zoo cage in this game... and if you create a zoo cage and forgot to add the gate, the game will take your hard-earned early money game as a punishment...6. Why can I only save during nighttime? Please change this... sometimes decorating takes a lot of time and I need to go somewhere, I want to save immediately after making such a radical change...And I could go on honestly...Final verdict? Buy on sale. You won't notice how annoying the missing shortcuts are until you played this game for at least 5 hours, so you won't be able to refund by the time you get annoyed by it. Your best chance is to buy on sale. The only thing that's keeping me from pressing the "Not Recommended" button is the game's potential, and how it's actually built upon mechanics that are fun and ideas that work.
