_childDocuments_.review: Okay, first of all, yes I do have 89 hours on the game as of me writing this, but since steam only has a Yes/No response about if we recommend it or not, I'm going to have to go with no. The game has good points, I know that I can stomach most of the bad stuff... for a while, but I really don't feel like I can in good faith recommend it to the wider audience. Let's try to break this down a bit.The good stuff:* The animals are cute, the pixel artstyle is overall quite well done for the aesthetic they're going for. It's bright and colorful and honestly it's a welcome change in today's gaming world filled with grey and brown "realism."* It's quite addictive, very easy to slip into the "one more day" mindset, especially if you're aiming to unlock specific research and get those sweet sweet little dopamine doses.* The writing can be quite fun, lots of little references and stuff. Not super deep and involving by any means, but it might get a chuckle or two out of you.And then there's the bad stuff.* Gods above and below, this game devolves into a micromanagement nightmare so quickly. The goal is to unlock 10 different variations of each animal specie by selective breeding, meaning that you'll feel pressured to keep certain amounts of variations on hand. Before long you'll get constant notifications about low water, low enrichment, enclosure size issues... and if you put things on contraceptives chances are it'll age and die before you've got the ideal mate to progress the unlocks. Now, there are nurseries specifically for breeding animals, so you could potentially put everything else on contraceptives and just breed what you need for the moment, but there are some issues with that too, because...* The park scoring system. Honestly this is a weird mess. One of the stats here is for animals and I think it wants you to keep as many animal variations on hand as possible? Which combined with the above becomes an inevitable population nightmare. It might also penalize you for keeping too many of a single variation in a pen, I'm not sure on that one though, the game does not elaborate in any manner whatsoever about how this works. Do you wonder what an unoptimized building is in that section of the score? Your guess is as good as mine.* The alignment system isn't too bad, but it does seem broken in some ways. I recently did a 200 Evil point run for the achievement and thought it would be a fun little challenge to do a redemption story. As it stands right now, I really do not recommend this. Part of that score is based on little moral choice popup events which seem to appear at random and let me tell you, getting that from 60 Evil back down to neutral and then 60 Good is going to take an eternity at best. It's just not worth trying to aim for a heartwarming little story about redemption, especially since...* Severance pay is what I meant when I said alignment is broken. This stat is the bane of my existence. I had to fire basically my entire workforce with no severance to get this stat to 20 Evil, and those were good stat worker's that I'd rather kept. Now, trying to redeem that stat is not working. At all. I tried to fire all my janitors and animal keepers later with full severance and it did not put a dent in that 20 Evil meter. To make this worse, I wonder if doing a Good run from the start is even a thing, haven't really tried it yet. The severance pay stat supposedly goes up by 1 for each week you haven't fired anyone if you've never fired anyone but in my DLC zoo (Yes I know, there was a big patch that made it sound like they'd fixed things, I hadn't played for several months, and I like dinosaurs) that stat hasn't gone up a single point despite several weeks of making very sure I never fired anyone.* Also, never firing anyone is such a weird requirement because, when you build a shop or facility of any kind, the game forces you to hire someone with potentially horrible stats. Want to get rid of them? You're not getting that passive severance score increase then (not that it works anyway, but still...)* The pathfinding can be so horrendous that it almost comes across as intentionally malicious at times.  You ARE going to have to line every path with decoration and buildings or visitors and employees will walk off it, and going on certain terrain slows them down/takes more energy from the visitors.  Just last night in watched in confusion as a visitor chose to stray off the path by one square for exactly three squares length before going back onto the path again since the gap was only so wide. It wasn't a potential shortcut to anything, it was just a shallow gap of no decoration there, making their actual path to wherever longer if anything. I've also seen an animal keeper walk three quarters around a block just because instead of taking the straight road down to the building they were going towards. It's weird.* This is already getting too long so let's make the last point an appropriate one. Namely research. Oh boy, this one is... something. Basically research is scattered all over the board seemingly at random. You need to unlock adjacent research to uncover ones you can't see yet. Simple? Well that random spread of things means you'll have to research all kinds of things just to get what you want, and researching things of a kind gives bonuses to that. Want to unlock all the plants and trees because their set bonus is increased decoration value? (I personally prefer to have this unlocked quickly so I know how much decorations I need to hit 100% in a sector) That's going to take a looong time. You can only have 2 researchers (you start with 1 and can research getting a second, good luck figuring out where that is on the board without a guide though) and you cannot build additional research buildings to hire more. Which is... Okay, it's dumb, It just really feels frustrating and slow for the sake of being slow. Some of the point requirements for individual unlocks get really high, and when you have to stop constantly to tend to animal populaition problems the game just comes to a crawl overall. It actually took me buying the DLC to REALLY notice just how padded the base game feels. The dinosaurs in the DLC has no specie variations, so population management becomes a lot easier (The animal score meter gets weird in the DLC, maybe because I only have one variation of each specie and numerous of them?) and the research needed for unlocks is a lot lower which speeds things up and just... feels better. My only actual grievance with the DLC is a lack of variations in shops and so far I haven't found a way to research having more than one shopkeeper per shop in it (those lines are getting long...)I honestly wish the base game was more chill like the DLC is.* Okay I lied, one more point. I'm not sure if it's because it's vacation times (about mid/late june right now, but the devs do not seem to be very active on the discussions forum at all, even the bugs and issues section has seen very little input from them lately. Maybe take a look at that if you're considering buying this game. A lack of good support in a game that does this poorly at explaining its mechanics is a problem.To finally close this up... Yeah, there you have it. It's fun for a while, but the problems pile up pretty quickly and makes it tedious and confusing. I'm hoping it improves 'cause the world does need more zoo keeping games but right now the flaws just makes me feel like I don't know who I can actually recommend this to. If you doubt me, take a look at the achievement statistics and how many players stuck around for the "unlock all research" or "complete the lions trade" which I assume is quite late game as I don't have it yet. Maybe get it on a sale if you are really curious.

_childDocuments_.review: The. Progression. Is. Too. Slow.If I had spent the same time in similar park sims, Roller Coaster Tycoon, Parkitect and so forth, I would have had something pretty neat to play with and look at. But the research in this game moves at a snails pace. It's infuriating. I'm doing all my tasks as they come up, I'm maintaining staff, prices and all that. But my park, after 89 mins or so is still just 4 enclosures with pigs, geese and rabbits. I have some food stands. I have a store house, a main office and a research building.That's about it. Maybe it was a bottleneck to be honest. Because the progression felt pretty normal up until that mark.I also don't really like the morality system being as restrictive as it is. I had good morality, bought some wind turbines for my park. Got my green energy, that's nice. But then some funny artist shows up and offers to make me a fake peacock using a good and paper mache. I'm like lol sure we'll play with that idea. BAM, suddenly, because of the morality system, the wind turbines I got suddenly stop working. Because apparently, they run on morality, not wind. Yes, if you lean in the opposing moral direction just enough in this game, it will outright disable the items you got from your initial decisions. That's honestly kinda dumb.I understand there should be a cost and trade for the morality system but to outright disable something you planned and paid for? What can I do, sell the turbines and just go back to normal energy because i got a fake bird? Meh!To summarize, I spent more time just looking at my screen than actually making decisions and playing the game. And I fast forwarded the timer as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Create your dream glue factory with a small horse petting zoo attached simulator.Seriously though a great value, with much more content and depth than I expected. I thought this would be just a little roller coaster tycoon copy with animals but the ability to play as either an ethical zoo and farm, or a nightmarish menagerie of animals on the way to the meat grinder will have me doing at least a few playthroughs to see everything. Way more than you think would be in a Zoo simulator. Farming your own food supply for animals and profit was also an unexpected bonus, as was being able to turn the plastic from my recycling bins into plastic toys I could sell. Recollecting your animals farts to run as cheap fuel. Be evil and steal your power from the city. Lots of thoughtful touches like this show this is a creative team (or individual?) who isn't just trying to crank out the bare minimum for a cash grab but is actually trying to make a game you'll replay for years. The Crispr gene splicing is also cool and something they didn't need to include.I'm currently 28 hours in and still have a long way to go in terms of the endgame, I'm still only occupying like 20% of my available land.Anyway I would highly recommend this game, and if it was complete the way it was I would feel I got more than my money's worth. Excited to see more as the game develops.4.5 Stars.DEVS IF YOU ARE READING HERE ARE SOME PROBLEMS I'M HAVING AS WELL-I don't like are the routing of the guests and workers, they sometimes choose inefficient paths or get stuck. Like Farmers resetting to the top of the field when harvesting instead of harvesting the next row as they walk back upwards. Why is it so hard for my zookeepers to find and clean up animal poop? I've got like a 10 man poop swat team in there and they're walking over massive festering piles of it and not finding any.  I just want my animals to experience a poop free like you know?-Make an option to maintain population in animal pens? I know you can disable pregnancy but then your population slowly ages and dies until you uncheck it. Basically at a certain point I'm sick of booming and busting on Geese and want to get on with managing my sick new bear population you know?-To the same point please make a check box to auto buy food at my store room. I'd rather just see the expense come out of my budget rather than have to forget and deal with animal starvation and protesters. -The interface and menus tend towards simplicity which is generally good and fits with the low pixel art style, but when managing a larger zoo this can become complicated. The worst thing is having to hire workers for each individual food stall on their own panel. When I have 40 food stalls it's like 3 menus and 6 clicks to hire each worker I need I'm basically not going to do it. Maybe there is a way to do it with heat maps I haven't figured out yet though.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically you manage a zoo, make it thrive. You set your goal, or just try to complete all of those Steam Achievements. Easy? My 42 hours gameplay says "No".This game maintain loosely similar concept of a mobile game called Disco Zoo: a zoo sim, pixel art, easter eggs, a little bit of mundanity here and there, and "collect 'em-all" goal - all of them in very widened extent.This game does NOT have a Zoo Tycoon-level of chill. This game is WAY harder. You'll probably spend your first hour wondering why you won't get animal species other than rabbits, and how you can get other animal stock if your starters are dying. The micromanagement in this game is crazy: you deal with animal overpopulation, a second later you deal with resigning staffs, then you deal with protesters complaining about dead animals, then you back on dealing with another animal overpopulation. Expect a similar complexity compared to Planet Zoo.And no, despite of cute art, this game is not for children. Its dark humor is currently way to evil for children IMO. Using monkey breastmilk for pretzel ingredient? Come on, man!Perhaps the most frustrating part of this game is UI. Lets compare it with Zoo Tycoon or Planet Zoo or other park management sims, and let me know how many click and mouse movement you need to manage a single random thing.Overall, this game is good but not perfect. It will give you balanced experience between chill and challenged. Go play it!

_childDocuments_.review: [7/10] Y'know, I really love sim games. As soon as I saw alpacas bouncing on trampolines I was sold. This is a really good little game, however it does have a plethora of flaws. The UI isn't the cleanest or easiest to navigate, some basic functions that have been suggested by the community (like a line or fill tool for floor tiles) haven't been implemented, a lot of the game isn't actually explained (maximising output on shops/workers, the higher-research buildings you unlock), a lot of the details of the game have no actual impact on the game yet (workers stats/efficiency), and the trash.The trash itself deserves its own paragraph. Eventually you'll get to a point that people will stop putting trash in bins regardless of how many or what type of bins you have. You will click on a bin, it will be 4% full (or something similar), and it'll be completely surrounded by heaps of trash because the guests haven't used it. This applies to EVERY bin. Suggested solutions are:- Unlock the research that lets janitors use all bins (because regular janitors can't use the recycling bins), however this doesn't always work.- Change the types of bins you're using, however this doesn't always work.- Try unzoning your janitors, however this doesn't always work.- Try zoning your janitors, however this doesn't always work.... Are you seeing a pattern here? I tried 'closing' (by blocking the park entrance and/or upping the ticket price to 100) the park to stop people adding to the trash while I let the janitors run around cleaning, soon as I opened the park it heaped up again. So I gave up and deleted all my shops because income isn't actually an issue for me at all. Everything is very cheap in the game.If you made it past that rant, well done. Overall though I'd still highly recommend it, its a brilliant little zoo game, I just hope they continue to develop the game further but we know there is a roadmap of updates they plan to keep up with in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: The game’s charm lies in its delightful absurdity. One minute, you’re rescuing animals from shelters, and the next, you’re deciding if painting a goose to look like a peacock is a good idea. Spoiler: it totally is. The moral choices add a layer of depth, making you ponder whether to be the benevolent zookeeper or the mischievous mastermind. Every decision has a ripple effect. Add extra chili to the nachos? Your guests will be thirstier, buy more drinks, and stay longer. It’s all about finding that sweet spot between profit and pandemonium.

That, or they didnt have the time/resources to complete it from the ground up on launch day. I played 21 hours and its a testament that yeah, theres definitely a fun game in there and I did have fun but in its current state, its absolutely a "wait for updates" kind of situation. Also have issues with the science system being flat instead of being marginally scalable sans one upgrade on the tree - reckon theres definitely space for a better system here. And money making and facility and shop optimising? Beyond me. And I tend to not skimp on tutorials in genres like these. That being said, absolutely keen on revisiting this with a few update revisions and at the very least, this is worth keeping on your wishlist until then. Oh, also I dont really feel like the SPLICR stuff adds much to the game especially when its so limited and when other more important parts of your zoo infrastracture require your money and especially your attention.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game! It takes zoo simulators to a unique new level, with a fun technology tree, complex maintenance of almost every aspect of your zoo, and fantastic replay ability with its morality pathways. It has a cute ass art style to boot. My only little nitpick is that, although the artwork is lovely, I do feel that the art on the title screen is incredibly jarring and is unrepresentative of the actual game. Would love to see a title screen that much better showcases the game's aesthetic style!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly amazing! And I lose track of time playing it!I've only owned the game for 3 days (so, launch day) and I've been playing it for roughly 6 hours a day. _childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: A humorous game about building and managing a zoo.Let’s Build A Zoo gives you a completely empty plot of land, tasking you with tasks you with constructing enclosures for various animals in order to attract paying visitors. You’re given quests by different people, guiding you through the basic game loop and nudging you towards trying out new features as they become available. Through all this, your main task is essentially to unlock more species and to expand your zoo further and further.You’ll of course also have to build a variety of structures for your visitors, adding food and drink stalls, benches, trash cans, signage and more to improve their stay. There’s also a wide variety of purely decorative items to improve your zoo’s appearance, which your customers are also looking out for. Animal enclosures should also be decorated and equipped with water access as well as enrichment objects. Additionally, you’ll have to hire zoo keepers, janitors, shop clerks and more to keep things running.New animals can either be adopted from a shelter, with a random assortment being available each day, or by trading with other zoos. These trades require you to provide a specific variation of one of the species already accessible to you. Each kind of animal has 10 variations, obtainable through breeding certain other variations. Unlocking enough of these variations will also allow you to genetically engineer creatures, mixing two regular animals to create a hybrid. While these hybrids don’t introduce special gameplay, they’ll attract visitors and frankly can be quiet fun, with many mixes looking rather ridiculous.There’s also a pretty expansive skill tree, allowing you to unlock upgrades for your zoo as time goes on. Most of these hold new variations of buildable structures as well as boosts to certain structures’ effects, However, there are also some completely new gameplay systems available to be unlocked. These are introduced by different side quests, getting you to try out the new stuff in order to mix up gameplay.Let’s Build A Zoo overall puts more emphasis on collecting than management, with you having to complete the animal roster, unlock each species’ variants and complete the skill tree. Additionally, each type of employee has a limited number of different variations, encouraging you to also collect different people. On the other hand, your animals and visitors require rather superficial maintenance you’ll rarely have to interact with. You can make adjustments to things like shop prices, product quality or animal diet, though with the number of shops, animals and more it takes a while to change everything, with little apparent effect gained from it.Through all this, Let’s Build A Zoo features a prominent Karma feature, allowing you to play in a good or evil way. Each of these feature unique unlockables, with the good path introducing basic farming and the evil one having you construct factories to process your animals. Quests also feature basic decisions based on this split, with certain quests only being available on one of the paths.Switching to the negative aspects, the game’s UI is far from perfect, with options often being nested way too deep and menu’s repeatably needing to be re-opened to perform basic tasks. Micro management in general becomes a problem in the late game, with some actions just eating way too much time. The game introduces a bit of automation systems to remedy this, though some of these don’t work well. Maintaining animal populations without overcrowding especially felt almost impossible for certain species, requiring constant manual intervention.AI also isn’t a strong suit of Let’s Build A Zoo, with certain employee types seemingly barely taking care of their work. Supply chains unlocked through the karma system also seem broken, with available materials simply not being delivered to relevant buildings. With the sheer number of guests and employees roaming around swiftly increasing as your zoo grows, performance also quickly starts to suffer in lieu of the game’s simple presentation.The game allows you to buy a second zoo, in which you can build much more freely. The skill tree starts out fully unlocked and karma system restrictions on buildings are removed. Similarly, all animals are already unlocked and quests are disabled, leaving you to just be creative. There’s also two DLCs, introducing dinosaurs as well as aquatic animals to the game. Each oif them also provides you with a new zoo, new structures and new quest lines. Gameplay-wise they play out much like the main game, though there are no more species variations as well as fewer quests and unlockables. This makes the experience as a whole feel blander and a bit too drawn out, though I still enjoyed my time with both DLCs.All in all, this is a decent game to play on the side and waste some time with.
_childDocuments_.name: Let's Build a Zoo

_childDocuments_.review: What if your morality matters when building a zoo?Don't let the cute artstyle fool you, this game can get pretty dark.Kill off your whole pen to replace all the animals with robots? (who don't need food/water) CHECK!Help the mafia dispose of their bodies by feeding them to your animals? CHECK!Purify your waste water and siphon electricity from the streetlights to save costs? CHECK!Set up a 'production line' to breed/clone your pigs like crazy and shove them into your bacon factory? CHECK!Sell off your animals to the black market? CHECK!And don't forget splicing DNA to combine animals and make (cute) monstrosities!But for the nature loving purists there's a path to take too, which takes you to clean energy and growing your own crops.Being a fairly new game this game still has some things that need to be improved/worked on. -Don't worry, the devs are on it!- There's some clunky menu screens for instance. Painting the landscape with a bigger brush doesn't always work as it should. And restocking food can/should be automated (maybe as a research option) But all in all there's a lot of fun and value to get out of this game. Either if you're going the good route or the evil route.PRO's- Cute but beautiful graphics (even my potato pc can handle this game)- Choices matter and can make a big difference- Morality system put's the Fable-games to shame- DNA splicing, have fun combining your own monstrosities- Run your zoo in ways you couldn't imagine running a zoo (painting animals to look like other animals etc.)- Funny remarks/quests and little easter eggsCON's- Clunky menu screens- Some functions don't work as they should (yet)- Finding specific decorations in the animal pens to move them can be a hassle- Saving at the end of a day might be off putting if you really really need to go somewhere (just keep playing)

_childDocuments_.review:
It's time to build a zoo! Let out your wild side, and create your own animal empire with this cute, expansive management sim. Import and breed rare creatures, hire the right staff, keep your visitors happy, and deal with plenty of weird and wonderful events. Then try your hand at DNA Splicing, and stitch together over 300,000 different types of animal, ranging from the majestic Giraffephant to the peaceful PandOwl!

Let's Build a Zoo lets you import a variety of animals from other Zoos around the world! Breed your animals and start families to expand your wildlife and fill your enclosures. But if that doesn't suit you... you could just create animals instead! With DNA splicing at your finger tips, you have the power to bind together over 300,000 different types of animal, creating monstrosities and oddities as you go! Ever wondered what a ChicKaka would look like? Now you can find out!

name: Haven Park
detailed_description: ' I'm getting older, my dear, and I'm not able to take care of the park any longer... Will you help me bring the life back into this place? ' Be Flint, who is doing his very best to keep his grandma's park up and running and make it a place for the campers to enjoy. Learn the camper's wishes and build whatever their hearts desire to attract even more quirky characters and look forward to whimsical conversations and quests. Get to know the campers and and learn more about the old stories surrounding the forest. Did someone mention a lost treasure? Haven Park is a place to relax, to enjoy and to make your own! Key Features Explore a tiny and peaceful open world and build cozy campsites at your own pace Plenty of quests and a heartfelt story keep you busy for 2-4 hours with many little secrets to uncover Learn new skills that help you make the campers even happier Meet lots of charming characters and learn their needs to make them fall in love with Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: I read a lot of reviews saying it's a blatant copy of The Short Hike and was wary, but I am happy to report that... it is, but in a good way. For me it doesn't feel like cheap 'steal the idea and make a copy' but more 'I loved Short Hike but wanted some extra elements there, so since I have the skill, I will MAKE my version, which has the bits I want' and it shows.It has the same general vibe - you are exploring a cute, vertical, quite well designed island, with uniquely stylized atmosphere, meeting quirky characters and doing stuff for them when collecting other stuff. The key shift that really make ♥♥♥♥ game its own is that Short Hike was all about exploring and freedom of flight and here it's all about 'renovating' the park island and making cute camps with collecting resources. It still has a final goal, a fun quests and can be 'done' in 2 hours, but if you want to max it out I bet 2-3 extra hours would be needed, and I very much intend do 100% this because it is simply... very pleasant. It lacks the witty charm of the Short Hike and isn't as unique visually, but it is still a fun, engaging game that is a soothing experience that I can wholehearteadly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game for my 6yo daughter. She only just started reading, and she can play this game on her own (unlike Alba, which requires lots of reading).She loves buying and setting up camp sites (I unlocked the entire game for her, and collected heaps of resources). Tip: If you looking for other games that doesn't require much reading: She plays Minecraft, Nickelodeon Kart Racers 2: Grand Prix, TMNT Shredder's Revenge, and Castle Crasher.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: So it's like Animal Crossing, except you’re the animal that's crossing!Finally. A Harvey Beaks game.You play as the most cutest chic in all the lands on a preschool adventure to enjoy a free -range life. You will never grow old, you will never lay an egg, the sun will forever shine and you will waddle to your hearts content into the setting sun. It’s the perfect story.I love the rise of open-world exploration and chill building/farming games lately! I'm thriving. I know they're not everyone's cup of tea. But, I have a soft spot for chill games like this.Every now and then, I need a calm and relaxing game to break up the massive collection of horror and adventure titles that are on my Steam library. It’s the kind of game that can almost have a healing effect on you, when being under extreme stress. Animal Crossing was that game for me back when the COVID19 pandemic started. Haven Park is to me an albeit shorter but equally soothing game experience at the current time. I also very much enjoy the way this little character wobblesThe campsite management is fairly engaging, which adds to the replayability, although that whole system feels like it goes against the chill vibes in some ways. It feels a little stressful trying to satisfy all of the guests' needs sometimes still, it’s a cute, relaxing game for the most part. Many other reviews accurately say that it's very similar to “A short Hike”, and yes this game has similarities, but also a lot of unique things!! It has its own charm, different from any other game I’ve played. Sometimes even quite an emotional game... l played it, it's fun, loved it! We need more games like this. Nobody is ever complaining about the 1000th same looking rpg, the same looking FPS or battle royal game. I'd like to see more of these relaxing stroll games come out. Overall, I think it's definitely a game worth checking out if you are a fan of "A Short Hike" and "Animal Crossing". With such a low price, it may just be the chill game missing on your library. What are you waiting for?9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Haven Par copied everything about A Short Hike, except the things that made A Short Hike great- namely, the flying, the memorable soundtrack, and the distinctive artstyle. What it adds is semi-fleshed out base-building, but it ends up being annoying. I found the characters grating, and whiny. Quite disappointing! Don't recommend sadly
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: 4h+ 2/10 1 Not yet, but you don't need any 1 on Astats No No No No No No No No difficulty option NoThis is such a sweet exploration game. You're on an island and are taking over the job of your grandmother to take care of the campers and camping sides on the island. You'll find your first camping side very quickly and have to find materials to build it up. What wasn't clear to me at first is that you see pictograms at the bottom of the game when standing on a camping side, that is the kind of buildings you should build to attract campers. After I figured it out, I always started with a campfire, because that seems logical right :P You'll meet quite a few campers, which most of them give you hints to other quests you can do. Most of the achievements are quite easy. You'll unlock them while playing through the game and while finding a few secrets along the way. The most challenging one at this moment is that you have to repair every lantern, route sign, and fence on the island. At this moment there is no tracking of which one you're missing, the developer is thinking about adding a tracking system after defeating the game, but it isn't in it at this moment. It took me 2,5h to find the missing item, so I would highly, very highly suggest that when you see something broken, fix it directly. Get the materials if you don't have them and go back to that one so you might end up getting them all already while getting through the main story. While finding the missing broken item was becoming a bit annoying after seeing the island already for so long, I had a lot of fun with this game.. it is so relaxing. No time pressure just walk around to explore, find crafting items and build up the island to blossom with tourists.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed this one, chill game to play on a hot summers day with a cold drink.Kinda gave me Animal Crossing vibes albeit a lot smaller in scope obviously, and an emphasis on exploration and designing cozy campsites.You work your way around a campsite in a state of disrepair fixing them up while keeping your guests happy. Some of the guests have little sidequests to do and there's always something to work toward, otherwise just running around collecting resources was nice just to soak in the ambience of nature.Fun little game that you can 100% in about 5 hours, we need more games like this, pick it up!
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Wholesome and adorable.Absolutely family friendly.I played the Demo during the June Steam NextFest, and really enjoyed myself during the approximately 2 hours I spent playing the Demo (which was only available then).Chill, casual, relaxing.So far, it seems entirely suited for younger children, with some help, perhaps. Older children and teens will have no issue with the game, IMHO.Adults will enjoy this game as well, if they are looking for exploration, crafting, and "city (park) building".Absolutely inspired by "A Short Hike", but not a complete clone.Controls are much better on this game than I found ASH to have. Keyboard (WASD) controls are less finicky, but this game does play much better with a controller.Very cute art style.No spoken words, just text and sounds on actions/interactions.Text is small, no scaling options that i could find, so that is a drawback for people who have vision issues or who depend on large text options.Lots to explore, many little 'hidden" areas you have to go outside of expected boundaries to find. Most contain resources to harvest, or give a view of other resources that you have to figure out how to get to.Some puzzle solving, none too difficult. Some will require a good bit of coins, and notes might be good to make sure you don;t answer the same question the wrong way more than once.Beta version just got an update (I am not in the Beta), so it looks like some new stuff is still coming. The game seems to autosave on exit, so it seems good for playing short sessions.My only real wishes would be text scaling and more info on the map such as unharvested resources, player position and a view of off-shore boundaries (there are invisible walls marked by buoys currently).Reasonably priced, even without the launch discount, for the amount of content and the number of things to do and find.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Few months ago, I kid around with my friend and asked for this game as a present. He gifted it for me, and I started playing it earlier this week and found myself enjoying this chill and short game.Positive things:• On visual department, the art style and direction are easy on the eyes, pretty atmospheric, and has cute character designs.• I like the chill ambiance and music in this game. Oh! I also love when Flint pews at the canyon! You can hear his echoes.• If you like short games, this game might be for you, it's short, concise, no fluff.• If you like chill adventure games like A Short Hike, this might be for you too!• You can customize camps located in various locations in this game. I wish I can customize my town as easy as this in Animal Crossing.• Meet cute and quirky animal characters along the way!Negative things:• This game is pretty chill. If you're looking for a challenge, this is not your game.• The animal characters are one dimensional, though understandable as this is a short game, not Animal Crossing.• The camera is fixed. This might hinder you looking at things behind cliff walls or something tall.• Not sure if the issue is only on my side, but I found the controls on the menu a little bit not responsive (I have to push X button twice in order for it to register).Overall, I love chill games like Haven Park, A Short Hike, and the like. If you like those kind of games, you should be getting this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Super cute little game, super relaxing. I loved the idea of fixing up the park, building campsites, talkin to Flint's grandma along the trail (although I wish we'd gotten more of that). The strongest element was definitely exploration. The island was well-designed and easy to traverse and there are enough unique points of interest to keep exploration exciting.Haven Park's inspirations are obvious, and unfortunately I don't feel that it stands out as its own unique thing. Nearly there, but not quite. I found it slightly lacking in almost every area -- sidequests, campsite building, island renovation, dialogue, everything fell a LITTLE bit short. The ideas were there, just underdeveloped. Would've loved to see them pushed further. I still really enjoyed the experience. Hoping to see more from Fabien Weibel in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the masterpiece that was A Short Hike, I wanted to look for another fun and cute exploration game. Lots of reviews and players suggested Haven Park. I gave it a try and was happy I did.Haven Park has you playing as Flint. He is talking with his grandma who used to be the ranger of the park. She is too old now to run the park and so the responsibility falls on Flint to do it instead. He's very nervous but, he'll do his best to be a good ranger like her.As stated previously, Haven Park is a exploration game with some management sim sprinkled in. As Flint, you'll be exploring the park, picking up materials like wood, metal, cloth, etc. to clean up the park. You'll use these materials to repair things as well as build campsites for visitors.As visitors enter campsites, they'll have requests of things they want built at the site. It usually means they want a place they can sleep, eat, an activity, and a decoration. There are a few things you can build for them to fulfill their requests and once you level up your skills. you can build more things as well as enhance some other abilities. On top of exploring and managing campsites, you can also take on quests! They usually require you to find hidden treasures and places located in the park to expand the lore. There are even fun interactions you can have with some of the visitors that genuinely put a smile on my face. If you focus on just the main quest, you'll finish the game pretty quickly, but doing the side quests and maintaining the campsites to %100 gives the game that extra little push to make it more fun.Despite the cuteness and short runtime, I do have some gripes with the game. It is so easy to get lost in this game. While there is a map, you'll have to go old school and use the park markers to try and locate where you are instead of a map icon showing you on the map itself. My second gripe is the inventory. Even when you get the bigger bag upgrade skill, you fill up pretty full and this can stop you from getting important quest items sometimes. It was annoying to get to a new area then have to backtrack a long way to a campsite just to build something to lighten my load. It would have been nice to have a storage trunk or something the player could access around the park to prevent that problem.Final verdict? This was a short and sweet game. It doesn't take long to finish and the twist ending was really beautiful. I didn't finish all the quests, but if I ever want to go back and finish them, it's nice to know there's still more for me to do in the park. I think 9 bucks is a perfect asking price for this game and it's fun for all ages especially if you're just looking for a chillaxing game to play. Thanks for reading!
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: as a huge fan of "a short hike" and other games that have been heavily inspired by it in some way (lil gator game, smushi come home, sable) i feel compelled to publicly argue that this is NOT a good comparison for this game. sure they both have a top down view and a cozy atmosphere, but there are hundreds of games like that and far fewer that focus on the pure joy of exploration and movement through a well designed space. haven park is essentially a checklist game in which you collect resources and use them to fill campsites with decorations. i would say it has far more in common with games like wytchwood, which is a cute game with a lot of good visual design elements, but both of them share an unfortunate emphasis on grinding for resources just to check a box, which is a fundamentally different focus than those games i mentioned earlier. even if that sounds like something you would be into i would say spend your time and money on a game like spiritfarer instead.if you like the idea of collecting resources and decorating a space and don't mind a little grind, this game may be for you. if you are like me and you resent any time a game asks you to go chop down 10 trees, steer clear and go play one of those other games i mentioned.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: To quote the game with its own words from the intro, a tiny exploration game. And yep, this definitely fits quite well as a classification. As some other people here already said, it reminded me a lot of A Short Hike vibe-wise, but mixed with a bit of crafting elements. Which means, you mostly walk around a medium-sized map, pick up materials here and there, talk to some NPCs, solve some side quests, and build up camps. I admit that after a while it starts getting a bit of repetitious (mostly because the building options are kind of limited in each camp), and yeah, it can be finished in a few hours, also there was too little music for my opinion, but I don’t know. Somehow the whole experience was indeed very relaxing for me, characters were cute, the little story it had was melancholic, and I guess this was what the game was aiming for in the first place. Also considering that this game was made by a single dev, seriously, the meditative journey I had and enjoyed just demands a clear positive rating from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: When i have first seen the game i thought "that looks kinda like Short Hike" And it is, but the gameplay is more focused on collecting resource and building camps than exploration only. Short Hike has a stronger story than Haven Park, but Haven never tries to be like Short Hike, they just have in some way the same background, and well both are incredibly wholesome and relaxing. definite a  game to play if your like those exact things, or had a blast with Short Hike.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: This game should be much more popular. It's similar to A Short Hike in where you get to explore a small map, but it's still different and unique. You get to decorate and build camps around the map, and repair items along the way with the materials you collect. There are also quests to do. It took me about 7 hours or less to complete all the achievements. Very cute game! Nice and relaxing to play. Wish I'd bought it sooner, instead of hesitating for so long. It turns out I loved it more than I thought I would.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: I feel a bit bad giving this a thumbs down because it's such a cute, wholesome game. But it just doesn't do it for me, and I usually love this little genre... I think the focus on resource collecting and levelling just works against everything. Moving around isn't fun, like in A Short Hike, and it's just not as heartwarming as something like Alba. I think there's better games to try if you want something like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: genuinely so good. i have a lot to say and i think the easiest way to make it make sense would be a list of pros and cons...pros:- cute!!! the artstyle is just so adorable and nice to look at. it's simple but very effective!- calming atmosphere <3 it's very pleasant- almost unlimited movement of the campsite furniture (tho that can be difficult sometimes. like if you want something to be perfectly straight, it's basically impossible because there is no grid)- dialog is funny, albeit limited, but that isn't really a problem for me- this can be a con to people who like the struggle/grinding for supplies, but the market allows for really easy access to resources if you get enough coins, which you are almost guaranteed to have if you check up on the food stalls regularly. it adds a lot of incentive to add markets to camps- the story is incredibly simple but i honestly didn't really expect a story so it was a pleasant surprise! it also made me very sad in a bittersweet way. - spoiler for two specific parts of the game: - exploring was really fun! just wandering around...admiring the scenery...very pretty and calmcons:- i encountered some glitches, but nothing game-breaking. just glitching through stuff sometimes. and sometimes dialog would be glitchy and that was really confusing at times.- the fire running out of wood is really annoying. i don't really get the point of that...? it doesn't add anything imo- in early game, getting around is really, really confusing. i am personally terrible at navigating as-is but having a map that doesn't show where i am was a huge struggle. i'd like it better if there was an option to have a little indicator as to where you are rather than just having to find a landmark and go off of that. maybe it's a silly complaint but it was definitely irritating to not have such a huge quality of life feature. i did get used to it after a while, though, but it was really terrible for the first couple in-game days.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this game! It is cute, cozy, heartfelt, and low-stress, which is everything I personally look for within the casual, indie-style genres. I normally never write reviews, however I felt as though this game deserved a few minutes of my time. I would highly recommended this game for those who are on the fence about purchasing it!
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: A really nice game for fans of A Short Hike.It doesn't feel original coming after it, though. It clearly states it's inspired by it, but it doesn't really add much to it. The first minutes were *really* hard for me, I was this close to getting a refund -- no background music generally (and when there's some, it's not too thrilling), no teleportation (although you can unlock a --very slow-- balloon to move around the island in the endgame), and the character moved at a snail's pace. You really should save your SPs to unlock the athletic skill after two level-ups. It makes the game playable and enjoyable, as opposed to annoying. One other issue I have is that it really seems like a prototype for a management game, but there's absolutely no point in doing more than the bare minimum asked to progress through the game. I'm sure you can ignore all camps, and happily go through all camps until you finish the game after a couple hours.Also, but I can only speak for the French version, it's full of typos and spelling mistakes. It hurts.Fabien, if you're reading this, please let me fix your text files...This game would usually get an 8 or 9/10 from me, but the aforementioned issues keep it away from greatness, for now. But at least it doesn't overstay its welcome. 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Haven Park is definitely the cutest and coziest game that I have been able to play this entire year.Your main objective is to run the park by fixing signs, lights, torches, and fences all around the map. While also finding every campsite and bringing it back to life for visitors to camp out at. To do those things, though, you'll need to venture out and find resources to build/fix these objects (or you can use the Marketplace to buy unlimited resources once you've unlocked the build.)You can also earn skill points to increase the amount of resources you can hold, how often you can find Mushrooms/Wood/Metal/etc., walk faster, see farther, and other useful skills to make the game smoother for your journey.There are multiple Main Quests, as well as some Side Quests, that you can do while talking to the visitors from the campsites. This made me feel more engaged to complete each quest and to make sure that I talked to everyone that I saw, so I didn't miss anything important!Plus you can go "Pew Pew" as many times as you want while running around, so that's a plus!  Be warned that there is no indicator on the map to tell you exactly where you are. You're able to see the number of different paths that you can take to get to a certain camp, but it can be a bit confusing if you're not familiar with the map.Overall, I found this game very comforting, relaxing, and very very cute. Thank you for reading this review!

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this are why I wish Steam had a star rating system or something in-between yes/no for recommending a game... It's alright for what it is. Obviously compared a lot to A Short Hike (which is perfect in every way), it falls short a lot of ways. The game can be buggy in some ways... I completed the last dialogue accidentally without going through the necessary pathway set to get to it. Keep in mind, there are only THREE dialogues that pertain to the "story". Now, it is catered to the "cozy" genre, so of course don't expect a whole lot, but it still feels somewhat empty on the whole "quest" aspect. Skill points are also integrated in the game, but just feel mundane and unnecessary. It also bothers me that you end up with ONE EXTRA SKILL POINT after you max out everything for some reason? The level system was just not needed. It's also incredibly easy to get lost at times and get left feeling like you're aimlessly wandering. The dialogue from the NPC's also just feel so empty, shallow, and give nothing of substance or charm... The "decorating" aspect also feels just as empty with EXTREMELY limited options to the point where every campsite looks the same.Overall, it still is cute at times and is a good break from stressful games. I feel like it could have been so much more if it had some tweaks and some extra additions. It's like a shell of something that could be great. Though I do say I would most likely never play it again as it doesn't seem to offer anything interesting enough to come back to. Everything considered, I still lean more towards "yes" for my recommendation. Just don't set your expectations high and enjoy it for what it is. 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who prefers horror, action rpgs, and fun multiplayer games: This title is FAR from my wheelhouse. However, I do enjoy the occassional, well done relaxing title, and that's what I got with Park Haven. Eight hours in, I managed to unwinc after a rough day in physical therapy [per my Grime review, I'm recovering from a bad med reaction and a sore that had a flesheating virus] or a ♥♥♥♥ Dead by Daylight session. The park itself is laid out fairly easy with plenty of side quests and hidden achievements to keep yolu playing (many of which are fairly simple). However, the last three camps end up a real pain in the ass to find, and I had to rely on guides posted here to guide me to the last two thanks to my horrible sense of direction.There are a few gripes, however. I constantly got stuck on trees and bushes with a few spots I had to jump over with nothing there. There is a map you use by referencing camp sites, landmarks, and mile markers. I just wish it showed your location for those of us who have crap navigational skills, but it isn't a necessary when you get more familiar with the park layout. Also the open twenty chests achievement seems glitched as I know I opened more than that in my time with the game.Overall, Park Haven is a fun, soothing park management themed game that can be a bit of a pain to navigate the further in you get. It did what I hoped it would do: Help me forget my problems or the last garbage team I was stuck with, and generally unwind enough to fall asleep. It's cutesy art style and gameplay makes it a short experience kids and adults alike will enjoy, especially fans of Animal Crossing or the recent Cozy Grove. If any of this strikes your fancy, or you're remotely interested, this title is definitely worth grabbing.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: If you're anything like me, you probably looked at the store page for this game and thought it was a clone of A Short Hike with some Animal Crossing thrown in to try and make it stand out. I was very pleased to find out that Haven Park, while it clearly takes inspiration from A Short Hike, and Animal Crossing, it still has its own ideas and very much is its own game, that is worth experiencing if you're a fan of either of those games, or wholesome games in general. While it doesn't do anything that will blow you away, every part of the game works together in a magical way to create an experience that will very much put a smile on your face and stick with you after the final credits roll.  The story of Haven Park is extremely simple, and that's fine since it's not the main focus of the game. You play as Flint, a young bird who is tasked with taking charge of the park from his grandmother. From there you are left to do as you please, repairing the run down park, building campsites, and helping campers. The more you repair and build, the more campers visit the park. These campers will give you more quests, and help flesh out the lore of the park. There's some touching dialogue between you and your grandmother but you only speak to her about 3 times. While the story is fine, it's nothing more than that. The focus of the game is very much on the exploration and rebuilding of the park.  Haven Park is a mix of gameplay elements that all come together quite nicely. As you run around exploring the park you can collect resources. These resources can in turn be used to repair signs, fences, torches, and other broken things around the park. They can also be used to build and decorate campsites. As you do these tasks you get experience and level up, granting you skill points which can be spent on things like moving faster and being able to carry more resources. The game rewarding the player for exploring was a nice touch. The building mechanic was quite limiting in what you could do with it, but there's enough items to make each campsite unique and fun looking. The exploration part of the game was where the game truly shined though. The park has plenty of variation in height, terrain, weather, and biomes where every section of park felt like its own unique area, encouraging the player to continue to explore. There was enough variety in things to do as well, with the game not being afraid to change the gameplay in different areas to keep things fresh, a very welcoming surprise. There is also a button that you can press at any time to make Flint say "Pew" and I think it might be the best game mechanic ever.  Haven Park isn't the most visually stunning game. In fact there isn't anything particularly unique or interesting about it, but yet the charm is so overpowering that it creates a feeling that few games can match. The vibrant colors of the day time, and the dark night illuminated by the torch in your hand create two contrasting looks to the game, each with their own unique vibe and charm. The character models are adorable and the music is top notch. I constantly found myself singing along to the tunes that fill the world. The constant differences in environments keep the player engaged, and every one is beautifully crafted.  Haven Park is a short game, that will most likely be finished in under 5 hours, and yet in this time it more than justifies it's price tag. For under $10, you get one of the most charming and enjoyable experiences I can remember from recent years. While it might not have the same emotional impact as A Short Hike, or the in depth building of Animal Crossing, it does have some of the most wholesome content out there. Flint's journey is very much one that is worth experiencing. For more reviews, follow my

_childDocuments_.review: Having played A Short Hike the same year as Haven Park, I was quick to notice that both games felt very similar - both games about anthropomorphic birds taking a hike across a nature location. However, Haven Park does not compare very favorably to its competitor. While A Short Hike has some okay-ish minigames and pretty strong movement mechanics, A Haven Park swaps those out for resource collection and simple structure building - and not for the better. The narrative is on the weaker side, but the focus is certainly more on exploration than on the story, so that's not really a bother. What I found very irritating were things like bugs, such as inputs not registering, and poor design decisions, like having to do platforming with platforms with different heights in an almost top-down view. In the end, I don't feel that A Haven Park was a very memorable game; just play A Short Hike instead.

_childDocuments_.review: There are plenty of reasons why Haven Park might not be your cup of tea. It’s on the short side – I have two save files, one at 100% completion, and I’ve still only clocked 6 hours. In that time, it’s a lot of walking, which some people will find annoyingly repetitive. And it’s hard to ignore that, despite its polished design, the game still has its share of rough patches.But I personally adored Haven Park. It’s a game that’s focused on feelings and experiences, and it delivers on through charming art and sound direction all the way down to meditative gameplay and a quaint story. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Shallow as a puddle, and barely wide enough to call it more than that. Way too many things were tried, and none succeeded even adequately. It's uninteresting, unengaging, and fails to be more than the sum of parts it was cobbled together from. It's not "burn it with fire" bad, but bad enough to tell you to look for something else.Haven Park tries to be multiple things at once. A mix of exploration adventure and park management, with a cutesy style and equally cute characters, and with some RPG elements sprinkled in. And sadly it more or less fails at each of these aspects.In retrospect I can't help but feel that the map is rather small and uninspired. There are a few different regions, gated off with single points of access from one to the next. The only reason to explore is to find more construction materials for the various camps, along with actually finding the camping spots in the first place. As far as I can remember there are no secrets to be found anywhere, apart from the few story-based fetch quests. Rewatching the trailer on the storepage here actually reminded me of the town put in the center of the map, which is completely deserted. No shops, no citizens, nothing. Just a mailbox for one of the fetch quests. Finally, one of the most infuriating things is that even if you unlocked new areas through the story, there are no shortcuts from one place to another. So if you accidentally fall off a cliff (there is no fall damage here or anything), you have to walk back to the earlier area and follow the path you unlocked, because that's literally the only way back up.The management aspect is a short-lived, one-and-done deal. Each camping spot has specific building types you need to place in order to attract more campers, each spot maxes out at 3 campers present (apart from I think one spot that only gets 2 campers), and once that point is reached there is no gameplay need to build anything again. Add to that the ability to gather money by putting up food stalls in the camps (often an early requirement anyway), and the market building that lets you buy and sell all the construction materials, and you don't have to worry with grinding out the materials you need for everything.The art style is simplistic. For me, it scratches the high end of being able to call itself "low-poly", with little to no personal charm to put itself apart. I'm struggling to come up with anything to say here, because everything just looks so generic. Things are easily recognizable for the most part, but that's about it. Things look how they are supposed to look, and that's fine, but nothing stood out to me as noteworthy.In terms of characters, there isn't much to say. There is Flint, the main character you play as, his grandma, and maybe one or two forgettable NPCs sprinkled across the map. Right now I only remember the bunny playing guard in the snow area. The campers seem to be completely generic, and fill no other purpose than to show the camps are actually getting used. (And to provide you money by buying food.) As intriguing as some of the lines may be, the immersion is quickly broken when different campers parrot the exact same words.The RPG aspect actually feels tacked-on. For pretty much every action you do, be it picking up materials or building things in the camp, you get rewarded with experience. There are experience levels going up to 10, and each level grants you skill points you can invest into skills. I can barely recall which skills are even offered, but I still remember that at level 10 you have enough points to buy all skills... and have a single skill point left over. I still remember that I saved up points for a skill that increases the amount of materials I get from debris lying around, but that's about as far as my memory goes on that. It's another system on the side that is barely worth interacting with.So far, the things I mentioned are more mediocre than outright bad. But there are two things that really rubbed me the wrong way. We are getting into light spoilery territory here, so some people may want to skip the following paragraphs.Just before reaching the end, you enter a cave system. Oh boy, that cave... This is the one and only place where you are put onto a different "map", and from how extensive it is, I fully understand why. The cave section consists of a series of trials, mazes, jumping puzzles, combination locks, stuff like that. It feels like a completely different game, and it dragged on for way too long. In multiple places I was either lost, not knowing where I was even supposed to go, or stumped by a riddle that turned out to have very obscure hints to its solution. There is even a rollercoaster-like mine cart ride somewhere in it, and in Steams discussion section there are multiple people saying they got stuck in a dip, with others explaining that they had forgotten to push forward to keep the momentum up. The cave was a slog and a confusing mess. It got even more infuriating as I fell off the final mountain and had to travel through the thing again just to get up there again.But the most damning part is clearly what has to be described as the story of this game. There are a total of three story beats in this game, three cutscenes playing at the very beginning, somewhere in the middle, and at the very end. Grandma tells Flint that she is getting old and that he should take over the park for her, followed by some generic advice and wisdoms. Grandma actually came off as haughty to me, and I had a hard time getting invested in her plight. That all culminated in the final cutscene, where  I laughed out loud at the absurdity of the scene. It was meant to be a heartfelt moment, and it gets ruined by what is either a translation error,  poor writing and choice of words, or indeed a confirmation of what a kind of person I imagined Grandma to be. To call this an anticlimax is an understatement. This is the very definition of butchering the ending.All those wanting to skip spoilers, you can come back now.All in all, I didn't enjoy my time in Haven Park. Steam tells me that I spent 4.5 hours in this game, and I think I can break that time down. The first hour was spent getting used to the game, trying to see what mechanics it has and how everything works. The second hour had me wondering whether there was any more to the game than what I've seen already. Hour three was just a mindless grind to finally get this over with. Hour four was spent in this annoying, tacked-on cave section. And finally, the last 30 minutes were spent grinding out the last bits for 100%. As you can tell, the corners of my mouth gradually decended further as I played, and now I am all too happy to put this game on the shelf and forget about it.Many other reviewers liken this game to A Short Hike, and I can't help but pull a face at that comparison. Superficially they are very similar, in that they play on an island you have to explore and feature a bird as protagonist. But that is where the similarities run thin already. In one you explore a national park, in the other you manage your own park. One lets you unlock more ways to travel places over time, while the other keeps you confined to the movement abilities you had from the start. One manages to fill the world with a whole host of individual and interesting characters, while the other is a dead waste with only the bare minimum of token NPCs. I could go on, but in the end it feels to me like comparing the TV series of The Last Airbender to the 2010 live action movie.

_childDocuments_.review: Haven Park is a cute little game. I enjoyed my time with it, but I think there could be some improvements to make it a  game. It feels like something is incomplete.It's kinda difficult to outline what exactly is missing, but I'll just write my thoughts.TL;DR: I *do* recommend Haven Park. If the trailer made you smile, you'll most likely enjoy it as I did. Get it on sale if you can. Rambling, incoming:The story element is short, with Flint helping his grandma fix the park. The few cutscenes were sweet. Some more details would have been nicer though to give it more emotional depth.You meet characters in each campsite and add buildings to suit their needs (tents, benches, etc). A few characters might give you a specific task. I didn't really connect at first that some of the quests were from these characters specifically.Maybe having a section in the notebook detailing the campsite's characters and their specific quests would give each area more personality.The use of XP and levelling up was great. You can level up fairly quickly and then use skill points to unlock skills in whatever order you want (running faster, finding more materials, etc). One skill is to get more buildings to put in the campsites.But it's just in two halves. You get one set of items when you begin and then you just unlock the rest in one go. Decorating feels a  unbalanced because of this. (And some areas are quite limited in space.)You also collect coins alongside materials. But after a certain point, the coins seem kinda useless. Maybe the extra buildings/decorations could have been bought using these coins. Or a few at a time could be unlocked with skill points. It might be a longer process but perhaps more rewarding after collecting those XP/coins.Fixing things around the island is mainly just signposts, fences and lights. I don't mind the repetition, though it was hard to spot the torches sometimes. The trailer shows Flint in a tractor but this is just superficial; you don't actually use the tractor to do anything. A bit of variety would be welcome - some light gardening tasks or some such thing would be nice.Most importantly, I think the music needs to have more of a presence. There are many times when there is no music in the background and there's an emptiness there. While it's nice to hear the nature sounds, music would make the overall feel of the game stronger. I feel a bit silly writing so much. But I think it's because there's a lot of potential in this game. Some things just need a bit of tweaking. There are many elements that are good and I think the developers did well to create a sweet environment.I would be interested to see what they have in store in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, quite simply, one of the loveliest feel-good games I've ever played.  the kids have completed every activity in this game many times over, as have I. _childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: A cute, simple, short game about taking ownership of a park and restoring it.  Simple crafting, plenty of exploring, a leveling system, and a charming story make it a relaxing experience.  If you liked things like "A Short Hike" or "Luna's Fishing Garden" then this is up your alley.In "Haven Park" you're flit, a cute bird who is taking over a park from his grandmother.  The park is in disarray, so you travel around, fix things up, build things, meet people, and occasionally talk to your grandmother as the plot advances.First thing you'll need to do is explore the colorful environment to find resources, things to repair, and campsites to build.  Your various adventures start netting you experience points that allow you to level up and get skills, and meet campers.Crafting is simple at camps - build the right things and people show up, do what makes them happy and more people show up. Some buildings generate income and provide other services, allowing you to make the camps pay off in more ways than one.  Campers may also give you some light quests or hint at requests.Otherwise as you journey you'll fix up various broken fences, signs, etc.  Some of these also help light your way (lamps) or provide guidance (signposts) and other services.You'll also get a few quests as you travel.  Nothing big, though some hunting and searching may be required.And that's it.  It's all simple, relaxing, accessible, but also provides a few moments of challenge and strategy.  In fact, sometimes you'll suddenly find something a bit more difficult or involved or weird than you expected.    There is a little inconsistency here, but the game charms you out of worrying about it for the most part.So is it good?  In that it achieves the very specific goals of the game - a short, comforting, relaxing game of crafting and wandering.  It's very engaging because there's always something to do, see, or find, so little of your time is wasted.  The only issues are occasional frustrating roadblocks and an at-times not that helpful map (until you figure out the way it works).  Still, the game achieves what it's aiming for, and does so in a surprisingly tight, engaging manner.So if you like "A Short Hike" and similar games, just buy it.  It's almost certainly for you.  If not, you may want to consider if this is up your alley.

_childDocuments_.review: Haven Park is a game similar to TOEM, Alba’s Wildlife Adventure and A Short Hike. In other words; it’s a wholesome game. You won’t be fighting anyone, it’s just you trying to help the people who come visit the park, to enjoy yourself and in this case to restore the park. No rush. But is it as good as these other games? To keep comparing them all the time is unfair. Every one of the aforementioned games has their own (graphical) style, charm and activities to do. But the genre is of course what connects these games to each other. However, for this review I won’t draw any more comparisons between those games. Haven Park can manage fine on its own. So let’s see what’s there to like and what’s there to dislike. The first thing you’ll notice is the cartoony graphics. They are cartoony, yet the environments are realistic, but instead of humans animals live in this place. After talking to your grandma you, a chicken, embarks on a quest to restore the park. You’ll do this by repairing things like sign posts and streetlamps, but also by finding empty camps and making them livable by placing tents, food stands and other things like campfires and even fireworks. After you place your first item, you’ll soon see that a park visitor will come. This will happen in a matter of seconds. Then you have to fulfill his requests so that he can actually live there while he resides in your park. Eventually a second visitor will come, and sometimes even a third one can arrive after fulfilling the needs of that second visitor.Park visitors can be talked to for more information, or to unlock quests. You’ll have a main quest to follow when you start the game, but there are optional quests that can be completed for money and other items that can be used to complete quests. It’s a fun idea, but the solutions to a riddle or the items needed are usually found close by in the vicinity.Things can be repaired and build by collecting things that are lying around the park. In this case you’ll need to collect wood, metal, cloths, coins and mushrooms. By building things likel food stands and marketplaces you can actually earn money (you have to do this manually) and trade the mushrooms that are otherwise useless for coins. Everything you pick up earns you experience. After having collected a specific amount you’ll level up and a result you can invest upgrade points in different categories. Think of things like unlocking more buildings or carrying more resources. You can level up to level 10, which is the max, and by then you’ll have enough points to unlock of all the available upgrades. One thing that bothered was the use of a zoom out upgrade. The camera is quite close to the character in the beginning, but you can actually put a point in a zoom upgrade that zooms out the camera so you have a better overview. It doesn’t affect your character in any way, but it does affect the game. I thought this was a very weird choice and I would even go as far as to call it terrible design, even if it is easy to unlock.Another thing that really bothered me was the usage of the X button (using a Xbox One S/X controller). You can build with X, but also talk with X. So when you’re building around a camp and you want to talk to a visitor you’ll frequently press the button and either open the wrong menu or the button doesn’t respond. Since you don’t actually use many other buttons one of these actions should’ve been mapped to a different button altogether. Again, that’s just a bad choice.The camera is something that on occasion also gets in the way, blocking the view when you need to have a clear view. Near the end is also a platforming section that is more frustrating than fun because of the imprecise controls (for this kind of gameplay, at least) and awkwardly placed camera.The park itself is made of a lot of forest, rivers, creeks and (snowy) mountains and it’s surrounded by the ocean. Most of the times you'll be walking on land, but there are also some opportunities for you to swim. But I guess it's not even 5% of the game.Playing through the game should roughly take three hours.Visually this isn't the prettiest game ever made but that's fine. It has a cozy feel to it, like you've been here many times before. The characters are reminiscent of the creatures from Animal Crossing, but even less detailed. The textures are simple but get the job done and the lighting is okay all things considered.There's no voice acting but the sounds are done well. I can't recall hearing any music. While there are definitely better wholesome games out there the fact remains that a wholesome game is supposed to make you play carefree and to make you feel good (about what you do). And so the game gets a recommendation. However, some of the technical issues can't be overlooked. For a game of this length it's unclear why the issues I have just listed weren't spotted and fixed. There's just no excuse if I'm being totally honest. So even though I recommend the game I urge you to try the three games mentioned at the beginning of this review first.

It is possible to fall off of a mountain, meaning you have to walk all the way back (which as mentioned is terribly slow). That might annoy me more than others, though.
