_childDocuments_.review: Here is a video of my review also showcasing some of the gameplay mechanics: About the Game:Haven Park, which released August 5, 2021,  is a cute nature adventure and management sim in which you play as Flint, an adorable little bird who is putting his all into taking care of his grandmother’s park and making it a place that campers will enjoy. It took me about 3 hours to complete and put me in the mind of games like A Short Hike. Flint is hesitant and afraid of this challenge, but with his grandmother’s love and encouragement he waddles his way to find his first first camp his confidence builds and he feels that maybe, just maybe he can make a camp to be proud of. General overview:Initially I felt that there wasn’t going to be much to do in this park as I completed the initial camp requests fairly quickly and easily…but as the campers started to appear, so did more requests. I felt pretty bad when a camper showed up in the middle of the night and had to sleep on the ground because I’d run out of resources to craft her a proper shelter. I vowed that none of my future campers would share the same fate…and at that point I was truly invested in making sure everyone had everything they needed and that they were truly happy. And hearing them tell me how much they enjoyed my park made me pretty happy too.  Game activities and quests:Most of the game follows a similar rhythm: find a new campsite, craft and decorate with the requested items, campers come, and you craft and decorate more. But that’s not all to the game. Some campers want to play mini games or they provide you information that might send you off on a side quest to discover a certain park feature or retrieve a particular item. It was a nice way to change up the pace now and again and give you other things to look out for. And I have yet to speak to how GORGEOUS this game is. The colors are so deep and bold and everything is so smoothly rendered. And when Flint splashes around in the water it just looks so cool and inviting that I wanted to jump in and swim with him!  Game progression:The map you are given is blank initially and sections only fill in once you find a new camp, which is encouragement to continue waddling around to find each one. As you travel through the park there will be other items to fix such as broken fences and light posts, all which require resources so be sure to grab every piece you see. Resources do respawn over time but it might take a while, so sometimes your campers will have to do without temporarily until you can get them what they need. Your skill also levels up as you complete tasks around the park, with you being able to trade in those skill points for new abilities along the way. Very helpful.  Heartfelt story:But between all of these tasks and quests and decorating and repairing, there is a heartwarming story between the love of a bird and his grandmother with a game ending that lingered with me long after the game was complete. I loved their moments together and it reminded me of the joy I have seeing my mother with my own son and how special that bond between the two is. I’m getting a big misty eyed just thinking about it. It gave Flint’s duties so much more significance and purpose and I quite enjoyed hearing other campers talk about her and how much they enjoyed the park under her care. And this, folks, is what really beautifully ties this game together in a way that makes it more than just a resource management sim or an exploration game, but a game with a heartwarming narrative that really helps you take pride in his park in hopes to continue to family legacy.  If you have some free time on a Sunday afternoon, this a wonderful way to spend the day. I enjoyed my time with little Flint and with the park and I have a couple of unfinished side quests that I’m about to hop back into and 100% this little adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Haven Park is like a short hike through a nostalgic trail, both alluring and bittersweet. As Flint, we take over our grandmother's position as caretaker of Haven Park and must go around and restore all the campsites to their former glory. Along the way we meet plenty of people and offer a helping hand where necessary, though all at our own pace.I did not stop playing until I reached Pilgrim's Peak, and then I realized I had been paying so much attention to the journey that I had not been thinking about where I had been heading.Haven Park is perfect to explore for a quiet afternoon or a rainy day, or really any time you just want to take something at your own pace.

_childDocuments_.review: this game makes me so happy <3 i spend a lot of time tinkering around with my campsites and interacting with NPCs. even after finishing the main objectives, i can see myself staying occupied for some time. the gameplay is simple but rewarding, and the atmosphere is soothing. my only complaints would be grindy travel. it's not in the traditional sense, and you feel like you're always progressing somehow. part of this issue might also be attributed to the size of the map, which is a lot larger than i thought it would be. thankfully you can raise your speed and jump stats eventually, which helps a bit. from the time i've put into it, i've fallen in love this game and think it was well worth the money. clearly won't appeal to everyone though. if you're not the type of person who enjoys decorating games or this cutesy/wholesome type of game in general i'd avoid it. otherwise i highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: As cozy games go, this is cozy. It is a peaceful little exploration adventure, running around an island, collecting resources, and building campgrounds. There is no time pressure. Resource limitations are short-term and fixed when more things spawn. You can make all the campers handy. Game complete in 3-4 hours, 100% completion in 4-5 hours.There are some limitations due to the simplistic controls, like guessing how to use the cranes in the mine (optional content). Repairing everything 100% will probably take a guide, because some broken things are hidden, in spots you would never notice, or just look like a branch. The hidden achievements are really hidden, and you would have no reason to guess that most of them exist.I had fun playing through the game. Pushing for the completionist 100% was probably not worth it, although it showed me a few details I had not noticed in passing.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Haven park is a really cute and relaxing game. It's good if you want to spend time walking around the map and setting up the camp sites. I have a few quests that get put into my journal. It's a good game to unwind from the day, but it doesn't have that much atmosphere to keep me in the game for more than a short play session.
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: Haven Park is kind of like Animal Crossing but kind of its own, check out my gameplay and review of this chill game. Review: So to summarise what I said in the video this game is very easy going wander around and collect resources to build up camp zones which you discover along the way. You have a decent amount of creative freedom in designing the camps and can also use the restaurants at these locations to generate extra coins. I found it super relaxing as similar to animal crossing you can't die or lose and conversations with the animals at the park are lighthearted and fun to read. You do have a main goal to reach the credits involving your Grandma but its hardly something that is ever forced on you as much as an over-looming goal to proceed towards. Speaking of goals there are side quests as well as goals involving the campsites to aim for, and I think in that regard the game is far more then just a collect items type of experience and more a relaxing one. You also can level up to level 10 which will happen as you play the game naturally allowing you to unlock new skills to help on your adventure. Graphically it looks amazing played in 4k with very sharp and beautiful colours. There is also a great variety of locations to max out that colour pallet too. Audio is also great but it doesn't have any voice overs, it doesn't need them though. And lastly control wise it is very simple with only a few buttons and your movement, you can jump, and interact with objects but that is pretty much it. I played with gamepad but it works with keyboard and appeared to work to some degree moving my character with the mouse. To conclude I found this to be a very enjoyable game to relax and play through and did so without checking the price first, when I saw how little the developers were asking it blew my mind as this for me at least definitely feels worth the $9. I would say take a look at the gameplay and if your into that kind of look and style of game totally by this.

_childDocuments_.review: fun little casual tycoon adventure all rounder. wish there was a sprint key or campsite fast travel.overabundant resources offset by market trading. intuitive puzzles. no replay incentive. no save scumming.good graphics and optimisation on old desktops, nice settings package.crashed a few times, but auto-saved at those precise moments.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever wanted to run your own holiday park? Well now you can with Haven Park - you play the part of a little chick, the grandson/daughter of someone, not sure who, but they're old and their partner has died, so now it's up to you to build the facilities and fix the broken stuff.You wander around the map and build the facilities and fix the broken stuff - and that's about it. You earn some experience points and can increase some skills (though there are not a lot of them), with useful things like being able to carry more resources, run faster, jump higher and find more stuff - and there's no blood or violence. You cannot build an axe and murder the people who decide to come and camp at the park, sadly. That perhaps would fun things up a bit.It's not unpleasant, it's probably not aimed at people who like 2D Fighters and Doom, but there's just not a lot to it, so things like Animal Crossing and My Time at Porta just have way more to them, and so should be played over this.I'm a little on the fence with this - it didn't crash the PC though, so this one gets 5 Hi-de-Hi out of 10 and a get it on sale recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Sweet and simple little game full of whimsy and wholesome moments. You are a little bird on a relaxing quest to repair and improve your grandma's extensive campgrounds in a majestic natural area full of rivers, mountains, and floating coins (the most majestic of all natural resources). You explore the map to find supplies and use them to set up campgrounds to make campers happy. Sometimes campers will give you little puzzles or quests to do, sometimes they just have funny things to say or challenge you to a staring contest. The barbecue stand sells grilled... chicken. ಠ_ಠ Flint's grandma's wholesome campground is a front for a cannibal cult. Oh well.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely LOVE Haven Park. I played the demo three times with 9 hours of gameplay and absolutely adored the graphics and storyline. Now I'm diving into the full game and I can't recommend this enough. If you're after a heartwarming, wholesome, calming but adventurous game look no further.The gameplay is about managing your grandma's campsites and exploring the vast wilderness, collecting materials and upgrading your camps to meet the visitors needs. There's a touching and adventurous story to keep you going through the game, or you can go on your own wandering around and exploring the forest.The NPC's add to the immersion and realism of the game and they wont hold back if your campsite is too boring or lacking in places to sleep! I'd love to see more dialogue in a future update. When you upgrade your skills by pressing tab, the character changes with your new skills i.e. if you upgrade your pockets your character will now wear a backpack. A little detail that goes far. I love the "pew pew" that the character makes, it adds a little cuteness into the game. I've found two minor errors so far - when setting off right at the start after speaking with grandma, if you don't follow the path by go towards the sign and tree trunk and instead go down and around the building, the game wont let you pick up anything until you go back to grandma and redo your steps and go towards the sign. Second minor glitch was when placing a flag arch it occasionally asks you to press "place" twice. Other than these two small things I haven't found any other errors which shows how well the game's made compared to other early access releases. If we're able to add more wildlife sounds into the game that would be great.Also, is there a way to turn off "birds eye view"?The price - I was pleasantly surprised to see this at only £6 which I believe is too cheap. Compared to other wholesome games I'd be happy to pay around £15+. I'm excited to find out more with the storyline as I play through more. I'm currently just enjoying taking my time and updating the campsites before continuing the story. The giant footprint/hand off the coastline is intriguing and can't wait to find out more / wait for more updates. Thank you developers for making such a calming, wholesome game. You can tell you've spent a lot of time making the game and it really shows in how well it plays,  10/10 !
_childDocuments_.name: Haven Park

_childDocuments_.review: The immediate point of comparison to  is the excellent , with both games putting the player in control of an anthropomorphic bird, exploring an island from an overhead perspective. However, beyond that there are significant differences, with  having a less well-defined overall goal, based primarily around restoring a somewhat dilapidated nature park and developing a number of campsites scattered around the area with a 'lite'  like approach, attracting (permanent) 'visitors' of whom a handful will set you a basic quest. Movement abilities are simple running and jumping, without any flight ability; a simple set of skill upgrades are split between those with an exploration focus and camp-building.With no real element of danger (the worst that you might encounter is falling from a height and having to climb back up) and a charming, cheerful approach to the scenario,  is an enjoyable, relaxing time to play through. It lacks the degree of polish and satisfying self-containedness of , but not meeting that high bar isn't an overly strong detractor.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Cozy game that fails to deliver anything beyond being “cozy.”Compared to  or , it’s bad, bland, boring, slow, and unfunny. Maybe it isn’t fair to compare it to the best the genre has to offer, and it did succeed in not stressing me out or boring me during my time with it which is a good thing for a cozy game but that’s a low bar.The story is literally three dialogues, which wouldn’t be a problem if the gameplay told the rest or was about something. You walk around the park, gather resources to fix it, and build amenities for visitors. They spend money, allowing you to buy more resources to build more amenities and fix more things faster. It sounds okay, and it is exactly that. The NPCs are unmemorable noncharacters; some offer fetch quests and tips on where things are. If you’re expecting interesting dialogue, there’s none. You can design your own camping spots, and while the options are very limited, it’s serviceable, I’m not expecting management game complexity. Walking around the park is slow and bothersome. You cannot really move vertically until the end of the game when you get a balloon, which takes forever to appear and is still slow and tedious, so you better not fall unless you want to backtrack half the map. There’s a leveling system with points and skills, but you can get them all at max level.I would trade base-building for actual characters and better writing, and it would be a good game. At least it's cheap.

_childDocuments_.review: In "Haven Park", you play as a young bird named Flint, whom is tasked with renovating and maintaining a large national park that was previously cared for by Flint's grandmother. Flint, now a park ranger, must make Haven Park a place that people want to visit and stay once again. The game is filled with cute amphomorphic animals like cats and dogs - similar to "Animal Crossing" - that require the player's attention. These characters are park visitors, and they must be provided with shelter, food sources, and other activities. The game unfolds much like how "A Short Hike" does, leading the player to a set destination, and adding obstacles/ new tasks along the way. In fact, "A Short Hike" might be game most comparable to "Haven Park". However, the way that the player must satiate park visitors is maybe most like how one pleases visitors in early "Zoo Tycoon" games. That is, certain facilities - food stalls, housing, etc., should be placed throughout the park.As your park visitors are mainly there to prompt you to provide them with facilities, they don't really feel very lifelike. There isn't "Animal Crossing: New Leaf" level of dialogue in this game, which is fine, but "Haven Park" could benefit from some more variety in character dialogue. The characters feel less lovable and more like customers as they are at the moment. It isn't that big of a deal, but some more unique dialogue would give more differentiation and intrigue. On that, more ways to decorate your campsites would be awesome. I basically kept giving everyone radios. With all of that said, the characters are adorable and it is nice to see new animals moving in :).The park is decently sized, actually bigger than I thought it would be. There are some traversing issues; climbing up the black tower is somewhat awkward for instance. But for the most part, the terrain and the movement is comfortable. One thing I did think about, however, is that there could be other ways of teaching your character how to run faster/ jump higher than just using skill points. For instance, in some "Pokemon" games, you get a bicycle to move faster. In "A Short Hike", you needed to do a side-quest to obtain running shoes. In "RuneScape", you can unlock rock climbing boots to better traverse mountains. You get the idea. I think this would make the early game even more enticing. Plus, it would give the player even more to unlock and do. Additionally, farming, fishing, or other kinds of activities would be wonderful additions! I know I've been 'recommending' a lot and not sounding very positive, but let me be clear to any prospective buyers or to any dev reading, this game is pretty darn enjoyable. If you enjoyed "a Short Hike", this game is that except you're establishing a park, not just exploring it. If you enjoyed games like "Firewatch" or "Moon Hunters", consider "Haven Park"; There's a lot of exploring to do. Although I think more could be done to make this game even better, I do believe this game deserves a big thumbs up. It was so clearly a passion project, and I can see the love put into making this game. I wish more games like this were released: quirky, cute, and not meant to be played for 600+ hours. I prefer quality over quantity, and I think many others do too. TL;DR: If you're looking for a short time-killer or just a game that calls back to better days, get this. Support an Indie developer, and have some fun too. Thank you, Fabien. I enjoyed your game and I'm definitely excited for any updates/upcoming projects from you :).P.S.pew pew

_childDocuments_.review: There was a point during the gameplay the review would've been positive, but overall it's really not a very positive experience to me. There's several little glitches, and by the end of things I was so frustrated it would've needed a really clean game experience to make up for it, and this game just doesn't offer that.-The buttons don't always register. Even on a menu, I often found myself pressing the same buttons over and over. The selection sound would even go off sometimes, but the menu wouldn't activate the selected option.-The game closes randomly. No error message, no specific action undertaken, it just would shut down on its own sometimes.-The Treasure Hunter achievement is bugged in some manner. It takes way more than 20 chests to complete. There is no tracker on steam nor in-game to check progress consistently even, so you have to guess how long it'll take to complete.As far as game play goes, it's fine. Cute, even. However, the game goes in about three different directions, and doesn't really shine in any one of them. The side quests don't really add to the game's story or further game play, unless they are necessary to complete a puzzle down the road. The mechanics of decorating campsites and making campers happy seems like something that was never finished, as it has no notable effect on the rest of the game. In fact, I think the only reason you really need to bother with campsites is to get enough resources to repair the broken park objects. Camper happiness doesn't seem to affect anything, and there's little of interest to place down. I suppose one caveat is that a few of the side quests aren't optional, as they are required to complete the game, so you would need to get at least one additional camper in a few areas. Otherwise, it's completely irrelevant.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute exploration/settlement-building game. Took me a little over 5 hours to 100% the game and feel like I've done pretty much all there is to do.The main point of the game is to restore the island park to its former glory by rebuilding its dozen or so campsites and fixing up the broken down fences and lamps by collecting resources scattered around the park. The map is decently sized and broken up by hills and cliffs, which makes it feel larger than it really is. The art style, interesting terrain, and sounds of nature make running around the island enjoyable and not too tedious. The campsites themselves are pleasantly unique with a variety of sizes and interesting locations. The settlement-building itself, however, felt a little lacking with a pretty small choice of buildings and decorations to fill the campsites, so it doesn't feel worth trying to build up the campsites very much. The side quests given by some campers give a little more to do, and that combined with some of their dialogue give the campers life so they don't all just feel like generic NPCs.Really the only downside I can think is that I wished I could build the campsites up more with more unique stuff, which I think would've given it much more playtime/replayability. But I guess just keep in mind that the campsites are more of a means to an end, while the game is more focused on the exploration/adventure part of the game, which is satisfying and done very well. So don't let this minor gripe keep you from playing.Overall, it's a cute, relaxing, short game. The $8 pricetag might be a tad high with the length of the game, but it goes on sale relatively frequently for around $5, which I think is definitely worth it. I'll probably rate it an 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Watch my 7 minute review here (or read at your own pace below): Here’s what I love about indie games - they come from all types of people, struggling with different problems, and all attempting to share a story or an experience with you, the player.  Fabien Weibel, the solo developer behind Haven Park, created the game as a way to stay sane during the COVID lockdown in 2020 and beyond, and I think you can clearly see that portrayed in this lovingly-crafted exploration title.  I’ll come back to the meaning behind this later in my review, so I do hope you’ll stick around.Gameplay-Haven Park, to me, is the epitome of a casual exploration game, in that there are no timers, no restraints on where you can go (well, almost no restraints), no certain progression of quests or tasks to complete before you can move on.  It’s truly just your young bird Flint, on a wobbly stroll through the woods to begin restoring the park and campsites after being neglected for a bit by his aging Grandma.  As you walk and pew pew pew your way around the charming landscapes that I’ll talk more about in a minute, you’ll pick up wood, metal, fabric, loose coins, and mushrooms?  You might be wondering what good are mushrooms in restoring a camp, but really, what good are coins for that matter when there aren’t any Lowe’s or Home Depot’s around.  But I digress.  As you wander, you’ll inevitably stumble across abandoned campsites, denoted by a chopping block with an axe, and a stone fire ring.  These campsites serve two purposes - First, they serve as the hubs where new visitors will come and enjoy the scenery too, and share stories with you as you sit around the blazing fire, or watch fireworks going off in the evening.  To attract these visitors, all you have to do is build what they want to see, as denoted in the bottom of your screen when in that camp.  There are different sleeping quarters, entertainment and food choices, and just some good old vanity decorations too.  I tried to keep my camps thematically consistent, like the beach camps had more palm trees, and all the tents matched at each site.  I loved the opportunity to craft each camp with a fresh slate, provided I had the right amount of materials, and if I didn’t have enough, it was only a minute or two of searching before I found more.  But the second purpose that these camps serve is that they unlock that portion of the map, which can be found in your journal.  And boy, what a helpful and charming map this is.  Once you’ve gotten bits of it filled in, it’s like when you go to a state or national park, and you take a look at all the trails available.  The trails on the map are even numbered, with stone pillars in the game to point out exactly where you are, since the map doesn’t show a character marker or avatar, which I think is a great choice.  In my opinion, it serves well to omit this character marker because it forces the player to make note of landmarks and memorable sights, and recall them while viewing the map.  Besides the campsites which you can restore, you’ll also find many other wonderful sights that I don’t want to spoil, and none of them are gated by needing certain skill levels or equipment.  Haven Park is truly an explore-at-your-own-pace kind of game, and I love it for that.Character Progression-While these don’t allow you to access new areas of the map or anything crazy, there is a simple leveling system in Haven Park which can be tracked in Flint’s lovely journal.  Your bird Flint gains xp by experiencing things in the park, whether that’s fixing a broken signpost or fence, or building a new grill for the campers, anything and everything the Flint does will work toward making him a more productive park ranger.  Upon reaching a new level, you’ll be given some points to allocate between different things like finding more of each resource, having better vision (or a bird’s eye view as the game calls it), or even just walking faster and jumping higher.  But do not fret, in the end, the only choice is in what order you select these skills, since by level 10 you will equip all the skills.  You can also view your inventory and read little notes regarding any of the objects you’re holding onto.  The journal is really well done and charming to look at, but if I’m being real, it’s a bit finicky to navigate, since you have to scroll up and down to get to either page in the skills and inventory.  I think a better solution would have been to use the triggers on a controller or certain keys to change the pages, and let the player navigate around the presented pages as they wish.  But let’s not dwell on trivial matters, there is a beautiful world to see and talk about!Art/Graphics-The hills are alive, not with the sound of music, although that is quite lovely, but they are alive with a fresh spring breeze blowing between the trees, with colorful blooms and mushrooms to pick and dandelions to blow, with waterfalls and beaches where you can swim and bask in the warm rays of the golden sun.  The more abundant scenery like the grass and water have great texture added to them, nothing looks overly smooth, but for a cartoony, low poly game, it’s one of the best I’ve seen in regards to holding my interest throughout.  I’m a person who likes to go on hikes and spend most of the time gawking not only at the big things like waterfalls and mountaintops, but someone who lays down on the ground to get a good look at a cool mushroom too, and Haven Park seems like just the place I would enjoy exploring.  In fact, I’ve often had dreams about an imagined campsite located in the mountains between two waterfalls, and I’m pretty sure I’ve found it in Haven Park.Music/Sound-Trust me, I am getting to the story, but first, the music and sound design is exactly what you would expect to hear in a park.  When you’re in the camp settings, there is some bright and warm music being played, like you would expect to hear at a beach-side barbecue, with some guitar, steel drums, and xylophone maybe?  All I can say for certain is that it’s cute and light, and sets the mood for welcoming new visitors to your camp!  However, when you are away from the crowds just meandering and exploring in the woods and shorelines, you’ll hear nothing but the sounds of nature.  Crickets and birds singing their respective songs, or just the muffled quiet of snow falling on a mountaintop while you pluck rare flowers.Story-So let’s talk (spoiler-free of course) about the story, which is quite sparse, but impactful even in small doses.  Your grandma is old and unable to take care of the park, so she begins passing on her wisdom to you in hopes that you will make for a good caretaker.  Really, you are her only candidate it seems, so you better not screw this up Flint!  But she mentions how even though she thought she was the caretaker for so many years, it is in fact the park, and the world of Haven Park, that has taken care of her for so long.  I’m not going to go any further guys, but I want to say this.  It’s been a long year and half inside, and I think many of us can relate to what I think Fabien, the developer, is getting at.  It’s hard to be alone, it’s hard to be stuck inside, and we all have those things we love which somehow keep us sane.  For me, it was backpacking and photographing cool stuff in the woods.  When that was taken away last year for the most part, I turned to video games as a means of finding an escape, someplace refreshing and comforting, and also to reviewing games on Youtube as a creative outlet and a way of sharing in a community.  Fabien turned to creating a game for the first time, to fully enveloping himself in a new project to share with the world, a new story that is timely and refreshing, and makes me want to go sit in a mountain meadow with my phone turned off and just lay in the cool grass and watch the clouds roll by.  So thank you Fabien, for sharing your imagination, th

_childDocuments_.review: It's more like a toy than a game most of the time. Took me less than five hours to grab all achievements.You're a weird fat bird with an enormous head (just like everything else on the island) and you walk around in order to collect things, which you do in order to build and fix things, which you do in order to please your  grandma, and that's pretty much it. The "story" is barely existant and the conclusion is obvious right off the bat; however, it didn't annoy me because there are only four important story-related interactions,  the opening and the ending sequence. There are  (and I cannot stress  enough) puzzle elements throughout the journey, but they're really simple so adjust your expectations accordingly. The dialogue with random NPCs was surprisingly diverse. You'd expect some annoying not-all-that-heart-warming junk that gets repetitive and annoying, but the expectations are nicely subverted here and instead we have a nitwit who thinks that a turtle stone is actually a stone turtle. I have to admit I chuckled slightly louder than it was socially acceptable.You actually have to be aware of your surroundings and use the map as if it was a real-world map. There's no magical floating spot on the map which represents your current location. There is no upgrade that will reveal a secret on the map. You have to actually read what the NPCs are telling you. If you've been paying the slightest bit of attention while exploring the island, you'll immediately understand the references made by quest givers.While it's certainly not a straightforward task to fix every single thing, I didn't even need a guide. The game is fair, and the handbook tells you if you've completled everything in each section of the island, so it never feels like there's too many things and that you'll never finish it. Before you know it, you've already done 75% and now you just can't resist spending one more hour to fix it all.My only complaint is that island looks mostly the same everywhere you go, with an obvious exception of one area covered with snow. It's hard to keep a mental image of an island when it all looks the same.The experience reminded me of Eastshade, but Haven Park is much shorter, easier, less memorable, and simpler in general. But it's fun enoughm for what it is, which always deserves a passing grade.

_childDocuments_.review: Teaboy's Basic(ish) Reviews....I read a lot of reviews when looking at games on Steam, and it quickly gets tiring – those who write involved, down to the micron scale reviews, although helpful, end up like looking at War & Peace when you’ve only got time for a quick 5 minute dump!  This is middle of the road and to the point – not easy for me as I tend towards sesquipedalian loquaciousness!  Vociferously Verbose?  Alright, verbal diarrhoea.  (Although I hate panning a developer’s work and all the time, effort and love they put into designing these – it is their life after all – this is my honest, personal opinion of my level of enjoyment.  Sorry devs!).  A note on time played:  My Steam clock does not seem to work properly, indeed, it even minuses time on occasion!  Plus, I have a tendency to wander off and leave games running at times, so time played may not be entirely accurate!  Teaboy’s Tonsil Titillators or Toenail Titbits!  (Rating)  Tonsil Tickler (Totally Tops):  The frenchy of which you always dreamt!  To quote a master, “She’s got a tongue like an electric eel and she likes the taste of a Man’s tonsils!”.  An absolute masterpiece and joy to play.  The Tits (Terrific):  Everyone loves playing with these!  Not THE best bit, but such fun on their own you can be lost for hours....mmmm.  What most games you really like score – perfection is so rare after all.   Torso Teaser (Taker of your Time):  It’s a flat stomach....sure it’s nice to look at, run your fingers over, slobber on a bit, sometimes that bellybutton gets your motor running....but it's just basically the corridor between the two ‘gaming rooms’.  The definitive ‘Meh’ - the middle ‘sideways thumb’ option for which everyone on Steam cries.  Todger/Tadger & (scroTum) Taters (Tedious):  Is it an ‘a’ or is it an ‘o’?  Who cares!  The meat can be fun to play with for about 5 minutes of your entire day, the rest it just hangs there and generally gets in the way of doing something else.  The main problem of course, is the two veg sticking to your inside thigh.  This is what this game feels like – the occasional/rare bouts of fun, the rest bobbing like a 19th century British Policeman (now you know why!).  Toenail Tornado (Total Toss):  A playthrough so appalling it’s like being trapped in a Turkish sauna with the ugliest, hairiest, fattest, sweatiest beast of a neolithic hominid who’s trimming his toenails using pliers and the splinters are reminiscent of a scene from the Normandy Landings.  My god how did this get released!?  Teaboy Touts (Score):  The Review:  The Tits!  Another calm, cute discovery game in the vein of A Short Trek which was my first and I still consider the master.  This one was fun and enjoyable, with just a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that kept it from the golden score.  Jumping.  Really annoying in certain sections.  Simple as that.  A tad unresponsive which is vital at edges and can cause frustration.  But this is a MINOR ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and should in no way deter you from this game!All the bits you've got to find and repair can be a Real pain to actually find, and nothing is logged on its overly simplistic map.  Even the marker stones are sometimes covered over by the campsite pictures!  So if you find one, but don't have enough wood or whatever, you will most likely forget where it is as there are so many!  And then those that are pretty much invisible due to the immovable camera - you start zoomed right in, can unlock a zoom out feature, but have zero control over camera after that.  Connected to the camera view, the balloon is an end game feature but you lose sight of the land, especially at night, and is soooo sloooow.  Frankly, its usefulness/helpfulness is questionable - other than getting to Pilgrim campsite.  Other than that though, the game is an enjoyable romp through relaxation!  The building of campsites is a bit too simplistic for my taste, but the game is Supposed to be like this.  It is extremely well put together, zero glitches at all for me bar entering the mine for the first time kicked me back to desktop, but it saves Precisely where you are when you close the game so I lost nothing.  You get to build a marketplace later on where you can sell/buy the materials you need which is a help, but would've been more so had it been early game - but then it would make the game far too easy!  A ton of thought has been put into this little gem, and it is WELL worth your purchase!  Try it with A Short Hike and see what you think.  Time On Frog Island is also a contender but had a 'carry only a single item at a time' issue which marred it a bit.  I've reviewed both.  Like these cutesy, cartoony but good graphics, flawless performance, simple but fulfilling, calm, adventure fetch quest build stuff type games?  Of course you do!  Buy this ;)  p.s.  I did leave this running whilst afk, so knock about an hour off my playtime!

_childDocuments_.review: Many of the negative reviews focus on how this is inferior to A Short Hike or Alba, so I'll start this off by saying that I did not enjoy or finish ASH and I finished but did not enjoy Alba.  What does that mean for this game?  Only that I'm coming at it from a no-prior-expectations POV.Unfortunately I still found it very unappealing.  You need to circle the map to find all the campsites, then again and again and again as you build up resources so you can fix things you had to bypass because you couldn't fix them, add items to camps that you couldn't afford to add, and, well, a couple of times I stopped to do something with a camper but they weren't even interesting enough to call diversions.The variety was pretty dull as well.  You're locked out of most stuff until you can gather quite a lot, and also get a special skill that's a fairly high point value.  So you build a campfire, then you can choose a camp or a teepee, a barbeque or an ice cream stand (very odd that these should be located individually per campsite and also that the campfire doesn't count as a place where you can get food?)Campers will tell you what they need by saying things like "I'm tired" or "I'm hungry".The map is very, very useless.  It doesn't show you where you are on it, and while it does have markers you can consult to figure out where you are, I found the paths on the map and the paths in the game didn't match up, and I'd end up going the wrong way as often as not.This game may be suitable for small children - I think it will depend on whether they can handle the jumping to get to some resources (or alternately be the kind of kid who doesn't get upset when they can't get something).  The look is cute and cartoonish, the resources respawn, and as mentioned, the campers are pretty up front about what the player needs to do for them.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to live in a national park?Click on my video for gameplay and to watch my first impressions as they happened. Haven Park puts you into the webbed feet of Flint, tasked with restoring Haven Park. Make pew sounds instead of quacks as you explore, design campsites to your liking, and meet campers eager to enjoy your hard work. It's a calming experience of getting lost repeatedly as you enjoy a short few hours of gameplay.... and that's really all there is to say. As a project by a solo developer, Haven Park is an adorable title. But as a game to consider buying, most people will choose to pass. Haven Park is about taking your time, smelling the flowers along the way, and not minding a very casual experience. It succeeds in those things, and I did enjoy my time with it, but I can't help but wish that there was more.
