_childDocuments_.review: SPRAWL: A Blazing-Fast Cyberpunk Adventure (with a Few Kinks)Just zipped and zapped my way through the neon-drenched streets of SPRAWL, and let me tell you, it's an adrenaline rush! Here's the 411 on my time dodging bullets and becoming a cybernetic parkour pro:Super Fun Stuff:•	Like a Bullet-Fueled Ballerina: The movement system in SPRAWL is incredible. Imagine wall-running, leaping between buildings, and slowing down time for epic shootouts - it's like a super stylish dance of destruction! Dodging bullets and raining fire felt amazing.•	A Cyberpunk Dream World: The art design in SPRAWL is killer. Think glowing signs, towering skyscrapers, and cool character designs - it totally pulls you into this cyberpunk world. Exploring felt like stepping into a neon-soaked comic book.•	Guns Galore!: The weapons in SPRAWL are a blast (literally!). Each gun has its own unique feel and power, and mastering them adds a fun strategic layer to the combat.A Few Things to Keep in Mind:•	Learning the Ropes (Literally): The movement system is awesome once you get the hang of it, but there's a bit of a learning curve at first. I totally fumbled around a bit before I became a smooth wall-running machine.•	Same City, Different Rooftops?: While the environments look fantastic, they can start to feel a bit similar after a while. I would have loved to see more variety in the level design to keep things fresh.•	Predictable Bad Guys: The enemy AI can be a bit on autopilot. They often just charge at you, making some fights feel a bit easier than they could be.The Final Verdict:SPRAWL is a fun and stylish shooter that's all about fast-paced action. The movement mechanics are a blast to learn, the world is gorgeous, and the gunplay is satisfying. However, the repetitive environments and predictable enemies hold it back from being mind-blowing.If you're looking for a visually-striking cyberpunk adventure with a focus on frenetic action, then SPRAWL is definitely worth checking out. Just be prepared to put in some practice time to perfect your parkour skills and accept that you might see a lot of the same rooftops.So, how was your time in SPRAWL? Did you become a master of bullet time and acrobatics, or did the repetitive environments leave you wanting more? Let me know what you think!

_childDocuments_.review: If you just want to shoot some guys in slow motion then I think you can have a good time. But there's no incentive to actually play the game in a fun way. The encounter and enemy design doesn't really encourage you to use any of the fun traversal mechanics, so if you want to pop off and make fun plays you kind of have to figure it out yourself.The fun platforming is just a way to get you from point A to B, completely disconnected from any idea of combat. They made all these big arenas, and they gave you all these movement options, but enemies will just gather in a group and let you circle strafe them completely unharmed. I finish every fight either within a tiny circle, a minuscule percentage of the arena, or I just run up to enemies, stand in front of their faces with bullet time activated, and shoot their heads. Then I wallrun to the next arena and do the same.The hit registration also feels awful and there are a lot of sound bugs. The game is boring to play and occasionally physically painful to listen to.I was really looking forward to this, and this is the most disappointed I've been in a game in a while.

_childDocuments_.review: SPRAWL is a shooter game set in the post apocalyptic future. You are fighting against the government with different weapons, which you unlock while progressing in the game. The movement and gunplay are great. Really don't have any bad words to say about it. _childDocuments_.review: This is almost a great game until you reach the middle of the GOR facility. Everything goes to trash. Guns need balancing because essentially they won't do anything after a while. You can't feel the gun progression as well. Tragic given it had so much potential. Movement is on par, the environment design in the early levels are great but you can see the point that they gave up making the progression work at the middle of the game. How can this be fixed? Easy:1- Don't replace the Junta Police with the Robot ones because they should be the most basic grunt, when you replace them they literally become as though as the Oni units, which makes no sense more so kills any fun to be had.2- There should be way to upgrade the weapons or at least the base pistol because at some point it is essentially useless.3- Shotgun is way too OP. Grande Launcher, RPG anything after this is essentially inferior.4- Spread on the RPG is completely broken. Can't hit anything, if you can you blow up.5- The blow on impact mechanic of the grenade seems clever at first, gets incredibly frustrating after a while.6- Your movement is not good enough for small, spaces after small spaces after small spaces, it feels incredibly limiting. The city level is the perfect balance between open space and clustered environment. GOR is completely broken on this aspect, it is literally more enjoyable skipping people and pressing buttons.Please balance patch this, because it is so tragic to see how good it could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: First: This game has potential.Sadly, I've played so much fast paced shooter that the "ailment" of overstayed welcome is much too common and sadly this game is no difference. Allow me to explain:The first levels were crafted with such a detail and an immersive level design that you are immediately drawn into its intricate silent story of this city. You blaze through the levels, having a hell-lot-of fun and get the whole idea this dev-team is following. Then slowly but surely the vacuousness is rearing its ugly head. Some occasional arena fight with every enemy you encountered is thrown your way and maybe you are like me and think: "Well, this bounds to happen" and it's okay! I mean nothing against some cqc, while rehearsing all the things you learned. Emphasis on SOME.Then E2 peaks around the corner leaving you terminally stuck in an industrial complex on the outskirts. The visual fidelity is lacking at this point, but with some little eye-candy splattered here and there. Elsewhere it's sewer-y pipelines, plane concrete wall, floors and ceilings and bland ass arenas with closed doors until you kill everything. And here it starts to get tedious. You’ve learned all mechanics and you got thrown in a hell of a lot of arenas without fun elements, just cluttered with Ammo-dumps, Enemies and HP sponges. Here the laziness kicks in.Finally, E3 is just a clusterf*ck of sparse checkpoints to "intentionally" kick up the difficulty a notch, because all those enemies you've seen. All those weapons you've used and now it's full of wave after wave after wave of dumb Ai running towards you. There is nothing to hide anymore, occasionally some walls to run on and what more? Nothing. Endless voids above and below you, platforms, enemies and heaps of ammunition. Arena after arena after arena. You want to play this game safe? Frick you. You want anything else to do as to run from adrenaline pickup to the other? Nope buddy. Playing baby toy match-Up with enemies (which gun goes with which enemy best). You're doing this exclusively for the next half an hour. And that's the point I stopped playing.This was just a sad display of lack of creativity. Not just in level-design, but in encounter-types and puzzle solving. Got till E3M2. Can't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Basic gameplay is fun but it's being held back by the backwards level design that doesn't fit the multidirectional concept it was built upon, you're supposed to circumvent weakpoints with wall jumps and all, but majority of the areas you fight in are too open to accomplish that.the enemies are all rushers, even those with guns, there won't be a time where using covers will be a good idea, not like you can do that with that level design, their behaviour just a lazy excuse to not create a proper ai to engage the player, by the 4th level you'll feel like a zombie clipping heads in bullet time, until you can't do that anymore because of a general bullet sponginess problem and you're forced to switch to weapons who don't synergize well with it, like the shotty with his slow fire rate or the smgs who's spread is too high and you won't hit weakpoints even at close quarters, the rest of the arsenal too suffers from these problems in one way or another, honorable mention to worst BFG ever conceived, barely oneshots advanced grunts, and is outclassed by the grenade launcher.on top of that the envrioment can't be interacted in any way, no physics on the objects, no natural hazards, no barrels to explode, no enemy feedback, you're confined with your subpar arsenal and the horde of enemies pulled out from a serious sam title, devs didn't even thought of maybe letting the player using them as a surface, a trampoline to jump over and get a clear shot on their jetpacks, nope! you're stuck with S+M1 unless a vertical surface presents itself, great use of your movement mechanics lads! prince of persia figured it out back in 2003 btw!Overall the game's a 5/10, play F.E.A.R. or Vanquish if you want a shooter high on adrenaline, hell play blood! Leave this one for when it's on sale, it's quintessential style over substance and it's a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Yup. Dig it. It has a kind of Severed Steel gameplay but in a Quake 2 era cyberpunk metropolis with plenty of little nods to Gibson.Controls feel very nice. I had a few instances where the three walljumps you're supposed to get turned into two, but that was probably due to me stutter-tapping the spacebar in a frenzy because I apparently can only play games in full panic mode.The graphics are wonderful. Sprawling (heh) industrial landscapes and wonderful futuristic cities. Take time after each arena to look around and enjoy. It's truly an admirable creation.The maps are intense. Some of them are quite large and almost maze-like, which really brings back that Quake 2 nostalgia. Lots of switch-hunting and some really fun walljump puzzles. For oldschool games, it will feel familiar but also new. A lot of work and love went into making these levels, and it shows.Weapons - dope. No notes. Shotgun reload is slow, so try to remember that when you're eyes-deep in frantic rampage.Music is good, very fitting and energetic. However, it seems like the looped sections are quite short, so it is VERY repetitive. On some of the maps where you are playing for a while because there's a lot to do or you keep dying (like I often do), it ends up becoming annoying. I'd say give it a listen to on its own, because it truly is good music - but maybe load something different while you play for variety in those longer levels.All in all, I'm very much enjoying this. Thumbs way up.

_childDocuments_.review: SPRAWL is a simple and familiar shooter, but it's a banger.You basically go around jumping and running on walls, shooting, exploding, and ripping heads off robots and corporate soldiers while Samuel Hayden monologues in your head about how badass you are and how screwed the guys over there are now that you're back in the game.With agile movement, just a notch above what you'd find in Quake, Sprawl doesn't bring much creativity to the table in terms of navigation. Apart from slides, wall runs, wall jumps, and a handful of advanced moves (like being propelled by a shotgun blast), there isn't much room for experimentation, and the inventiveness in using these mechanics leaves something to be desired, not going much beyond the obvious and at times appearing to be implemented clumsily and unintuitively.I must say that a double jump and a ledge-grabbing mechanic were sorely missed overall. Especially in moments of traversal that became unnecessarily awkward, with me slipping off platforms by a hair (with no penalty) because I had to climb on them like a drunken mishmash of Prince of Persia and Megaman.Something that could have been easily be mitigated by such simple and basic mechanics.You have a dozen stages here that exhibit relatively competent design, conveying a good sense of pace and progress and communicating the path to the goal without much difficulty and need for intrusive interface aids. The flow alternates regularly between combat arenas and somewhat questionable traversal zones that mostly align its structure with the movement and combat mechanics, but don't surprise with their geometry and concept.It's solid and functional but nothing particularly groundbreaking.Like many, I obviously enjoy the cyberpunk aesthetic with its neon saturation and gratuitous portrayal of dystopian landscapes showcasing the depths of human condition, but SPRAWL has the dubious distinction of not creating much excitement or distinctive elements for its setting, opting for more mundane brutalist and industrial scenarios than the psychedelic festival that typically accompanies the genre.The downside to this is that, instead of sounding different and creative, it sounds sterile and uninteresting. It's not a different cyberpunk aesthetic. It's a bland one.And then we have the combat. Polished, frenetic, and CRUNCHY.It's your classic old-school arena shooter, with enhanced movement and the cinematic grace of a slow-motion camera mechanic, energized by the incendiary beats of a powerful soundtrack.A standard variety of weapons make up a suitable arsenal with all the destruction toys you could wish for. While they may not have very original and inventive designs, the collection lacks nothing to obliterate half the world.In the absence of innovation, give me the classics. The classics always work.The weapons, extremely accurate and without recoil, provide a sense of adequate feedback, with powerful sound design and well-placed particle effects. Shooting is quite satisfying.Enemies come in a good variety (though with no creative designs) and are the typical archetypes you find in any other shooter of this kind, with basic behaviors, not threatening enough to create an elegant dance but dangerous enough to generate some sense of friction and propel your mind into the delightful and cathartic world of caffeine-infused techno.Sprawl brings a somewhat rare dimension to single-player arena shooters, being unforgiving of imprecise shots, encouraging the player to aim for enemies' weak points. The logic follows something similar to what you find in competitive shooters where agility and precision are rewarded with lethal damage (and more resources).Enemies have appropriately sized silhouettes to stand out on the screen and like to walk straight or stand still while shooting, conveniently positioned to create opportunities for you to capitalize within the dynamic presented by the game.The skill ceiling goes beyond just moving well and managing your resources but also hitting headshots and other weak points while dodging enemy projectiles.An even higher level of optimization is to try to face enemies without slow-motion, which is entirely plausible if you're good enough.The combat is well balanced and the level of challenge becomes increasingly chaotic as you approach the end, with enemies being dumped in large numbers almost to the point of breaking the difficulty (which, by the way, can be adjusted as you like).But of course, there are some small problems.Melee could benefit from a wider hitbox to more smoothly hit a stunned enemy in your peripheral vision while you're in motion.The movement shortcomings and the questionable compatibility of some arena designs also interfere with the flow of some fights.Whenever they tried to blend platform challenges with combat or create more complex navigable arenas, it didn't work very well. The frequency with which you can accidentally fall off a narrow ledge and find yourself practically confined by the geometry of the stage becomes quite problematic.I am a proponent of open arenas with functional verticality, with a clear routes to escape opportunities and acess to enemies without intrusive obstacles that do not enhance the combat. If you're going to do something different, at least make sure that playing within that difference is as fun as it is in more conventional arenas.The two boss fights don't break the core rules of the game but are very average.And they could have been bolder in the use of particles and creating more concrete feedback on received and given damage. Reinforcing the difference between mistakes and successes goes a long way in terms of clarity and satisfaction with the results.Moreover, I must say that the soundtrack, fortunately, does the heavy lifting and envelops the experience in a striking and memorable way, giving shape and flavor to a world built with not much creativity and texture. A truly delicious cherry on top.You know that GIF of a psychedelic dancing frog? That's the image of the feeling I had while playing.It's the kind of game that puts you in a frenetic vibe.Few things are more satisfying than hitting a slow-motion headshot on an enemy jumping towards you to the sound of those beats.A horde mode and time trials add a bit more to the experience and teach you some advanced tricks.Being a short game, these additions add to the final value, but it's not something that will hold your attention for long, as selecting and replaying the best stages of the game seems like a much more appetizing idea.It's a game quite favorable for speedruns as well.Anyway, it's a solid and competent package, especially considering the size of the team that developed the game. It's a great foundation for something with more identity that can stand out.It's a good game, worthy of recommendation.P.S: My tendinitis thanks you.

_childDocuments_.review: So, to start off, I'll do the easiest thing you can do to critique a game: compare it. And that's done easily, in my opinion, as many people will find comfort in the concept of "Mirror's Edge but Boomer Shooter." However, this game takes a relatively minor story, and through visuals and music, really transforms it into a transcendent, spiritually charged game. Again, not a deep, complex, story; but one that's very captivating.Now, more importantly, the gameplay is stellar. You've got an extremely powerful arsenal, and most weapon types are usable in just about any situation. Due to that, you're rarely punished for weapon bias, save for a couple select enemies, but rather rewarded for using your preferred weapon well. An example are the mech enemies: while their armor blocks damage from most of your light weapons, its grenades can be shot to damage it (and anything else around it). While more difficult, it's made much easier while in bullet time.Bullet time uses Adrenaline, a resource dropped by enemies on death. This game, much like DOOM 2016 and Eternal, has enemies go into a stagger state on low health. Any melee kill (it doesn't actually have to be on a staggered enemy, get creative with your "combos!") OR a headshot kill will be rewarded with a shower of ammo, health, and adrenaline. If you don't spread out your weapon usage, you will be very reliant on these executions; but careful use of bullet time will help you make the absolute most of your weaponry, even in a tense fight.It's worth giving a mention to the enemies: while variety in some stages and encounters can be a little lacking, they more than make up for it in each type's capabilities and weaknesses. A few examples that come to me right now:-Cloaking enemies that can teleport, but lack any ranged attack-The aforementioned mechs that encourage use of heavier weapons, but don't strictly punish lighter ones-Most humanoid enemies can spawn with or without a jetpack, which gives them higher mobility, but can be shot for an instakill (and explosion, of course)I didn't personally care too much for the boss fights. They feel a little too cycle based, certainly not sluggish but they'd do better I think with more complexity. The final boss was my personal favorite, having some tanky turrets that force you to use the arena more creatively, which is a core appeal of the rest of the game's encounters. By no means is this a dealbreaker, they're absolutely fine, but could certainly use a touch-up (which very may well happen, as the devs are quite receptive to feedback!).Speaking of the arenas, they are my absolute favorites in probably any singleplayer shooter, ever. It's one of the game's main selling points, in fact; the brutalist, urban SPRAWL feels like so much of it was created without true reason or purpose, a utilitarian monster of concrete that somehow manages to be  efficient. It gives a sense of lifelessness and desolation that makes seeking freedom so very worth it, while encouraging the player to move  damn fast. After all, why take in the sights when you've got stuff to shoot? That said, by no means is that a criticism of the visuals. In their own, twisted way, they really are beautiful, and lend their way to a broad sense of scope.The music is amazing. It has a very unique feel, blending spiritual-sounding chimes with breakbeat techno. Additionally, it has a dynamic soundtrack, which while I didn't notice too much of, the few times I did absolutely enhanced the experience. One small thing is that some segments have pretty short music loops, most often outside of fights. I think even in the most obvious examples of that, though, I still actively  it. However, I felt it was worth mentioning, as while I doubt it would be grating to many people, it is a point that could be improved.A couple stray things before wrapping up: Voice Acting, while limited (not too much story after all), is very enjoyable. Gianni's also there for like 2 minutes, so you know it's good. I didn't read any of the QR code stuff, which I think was lore, but they're adding an in-game way to check them, so, again, good post-release update. But, uh, I'm sure they're cool, based on the rest of the world. In terms of playtime, I clocked my first playthrough at under 5 hours. Certainly a short game, to some, but it feels like the perfect length for the campaign. If you're in need for more, there are time trials and horde modes, too. And, hell, they may add more in the future. In that vein, a couple suggestions:-While I love the weaponset, I did feel like some of them felt a little too single-use. Personally, while definitely the most work intensive, I'd suggest alt-fires or extra special gimmicks. Or perhaps an alternate version that functions differently, like a dragon's breath shotgun, or a more assault rifle-like function for the SMG.-Basic unlockables, like weapon recolors or whatever; unlockables generally function best for games of this length, and it adds a great incentive for replay value.-The dog robots can be kinda irritating, it makes sense that they don't have a weakpoint, but you basically guarantee taking damage trying to melee them. And they do give you bonuses for the melee kills, so it kinda feels like an oversight.-The chaingun is strong as hell, but doesn't feel as good to use as the other weapons for me. It slowing you down while firing it on the ground, again, makes sense. However, I found that it was too hard to use practically while wallrunning, and thus it became a gun where I just repeatedly jumped around a lot with to offset the downside, rather than respecting its weaknesses. In a similar way, it doesn't fit especially well with bullet time, in that the spin-up makes you essentially reverse how you play around bullet time. I think, actually, that's where its identity should lie in the arsenal: if accuracy wasn't such a concern, it could function as a spray-down powerhouse that's best used on walls, and doesn't need (or want) adrenaline to work.Overall, I'm going to give the game a 9/10. With so few flaws, and the couple that are there being minor gripes more than real problems, this is a very, very good game. Absolutely grab it if the trailer appeals to you. The only thing I'm missing is a bit of variety, but the game makes such amazing use of what it has that I almost feel greedy asking; still, 10/10 is a perfect score, so I do feel it's worth mentioning. I hope to see a DLC someday, too!

_childDocuments_.review: SPRAWL's combat is really fun. The weapons are all great to use and each has their own strength. The game is designed around you swapping weapons often ala Doom Eternal and there's mechanics to replenish your ammo via gunplay (through headshots) or with melee. The wallrunning is pretty smooth and the speed boost you get from a slide+hop is satisfying. These both help in enhancing each "combat arena." You don't have to look for something on the map to interact with to do something flashy. You don't need an air lift, monkey bar, or ramp to gain style points and feel cool. You can  turn the arena into your playground because of the game's movement. It always feels good to run on a wall, hop off, activate slow-mo and headshot an enemy. Then shotgun-jump into the air and take out the next two baddies on the bridge above you. All while slidehopping and strafing out of enemy fire. I mention these things not only because it's fun, but because they're necessary. You  to keep moving in SPRAWL. Enemies are always shooting at you and staying on the move keeps their projectile bullets out of your way. You  to go for headshots or you'll quickly run out of ammo and Andrenaline (slow-mo).Having played over 8k hours of Titanfall 2, I feel at home with SPRAWL's combat. Wallrunning felt a bit weird at first, because it's its own thing. There's no traditional double jump that resets so you can't endlessly chain wallruns. By design you can chain 3 walls, and the game's platforming is designed around this, leaving you to figure out how to best time your jumps to make it from Point A to B without falling to your doom. But there's some freedom here even with these limits. You can chain wallruns on the same wall without delay unlike Titanfall. This allows you to "climb" a wall for more leverage or height without hopping over to another. There's also lots of air control in terms of strafing acceleration. I even found some movement tech, though haven't really implemented it well since discovery. The moment you hop off a wall, you have a very small window to hit jump again. If done correctly, you can actually double jump a very short distance. As I stated earlier this game has no traditional double jump, so this tech may come in handy eventually.When things start to click for you, SPRAWL'S combat is a treat. This is a gameplay-first video game, as the story did nothing for me, and that's entirely okay. It's not perfect but it's pretty fun. The campaign length is appreciated as well, coming in at around 8 hrs for me. This allows me to try other difficulties without it feeling like a drag.It's clear the developers are passionate about SPRAWL and I hope to see more from them, in the game's post-release content and future titles. A rogue-like mode may suit this game well, to further replayability beyond just playing the campaign over again. Co-op would be insane too.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games (minor spoilers ahead).SPRAWL is a indie boomer shooter set in a future where a totalitarian government controls a megacity, known as the sprawl and uses humans and cyborgs to eliminate threats. You play the role of one of those agents that was betrayed and left for dead, later saved by a powerful AI that rebelled against the regime. You’ll play through a series of different missions set in different areas, facing enemies and boss monsters.The graphics are what you would expect from this kind of game and are similar to older quake or doom games, with a cyberpunk/futuristic theme and bleak colors that represent the lack of hope and in that dying world.The OST is a mix between more slow esoteric songs when the story is being told and fast paced techno songs in the combat section of the levels and both genres work very well together. The voice acting of the narrator is also very good and really gives that AI talking feeling.The gameplay is solid but doesn’t reinvent much: the weapons are the classic ones you would find on other games, only the bullet time from Max Payne mixed with wall walking from Titanfall are the original aspects of this game. Personally, I found the platforming harder than the combat, but I played safely when I could, and avoided rushing in and getting surrounded in the combat areas, because if you do that you’ll get easily killed, even by the weakest enemies.In some boss fights you might need to be efficient with your ammo since it isn’t abundant like in the rest of the level and you only get refills by attacking the weak spots.   31 Achievements. Around 8 hours, with a guide for the collectibles. Easy, if you’re good at FPS games and play safely. Easy. Most are story related and no missable achievements since you can replay levels but the collectibles are very well hidden and very hard to find on your own. Reaching them can also be frustrating at times. SPRAWL is a solid boomer shooter with an interesting story and world building. It has all the classic weapons and an original mix of bullet time and wall walking when it comes to movement. Recommended for its price, currently under 1 EUR in the gray market.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, this game isn't really what I was hoping for. It feels like this really could've turned into something good, but after playing through 3 levels, so far I have yet to enjoy myself. This game hinges very heavily on it's combat - there isn't much emphasis placed on the story, and while the visuals and music are pretty nice, they don't make the experience, and other than that the game doesn't have much else to offer. And the combat feels, well, dull. The game makes it very clear that you are meant to be relying heavily on the slow-mo. You practically need it in order to hit enemy weakpoints, which is both the main way you regain resources and the main way you do damage, as shooting at non-weakpoints does pitiful damage. If you're not using slow-mo basically at all times, you're not playing the game correctly, and you will die. And the game is very generous with how much you're allowed to use it - if you're stringing together weakpoint kills at so much as a half-decent pace, you won't run out. Now, the game does have some pretty cool movement and weapons, and there were some times where I do something and think "oh, that was pretty neat", but never in these moments do I feel like i'm having actual fun. This is because what I'm actually doing feels more like I'm playing a point-and-click adventure where I press a button on my keyboard every couple seconds to move close to enemies as I click on their heads. I don't have to worry about getting hit by enemies because any damage I take I can regain in a couple seconds just by getting more weakpoint kills. I only died like 3 or so times, and all of those times were literally due to the fact that I was getting so bored that I started playing sloppy and doing stupid stuff (and by "stupid" I mainly mean not holding down the slow-mo button). This feels like a game that SHOULD be fun, but it's just trying so hard to force you into playing in the most unfun way. And yes, I know there are options to tweak the difficulty and make it harder, but I'm not a fan of that stuff at all and I never touch it. How am I supposed to know in what way I should move these knobs in order to make the game actually fun? That's the developer's job, not mine. Just do set difficulties. Or, if you're not going to do that, make the base difficulty, y'know, actually well-balanced. Also, kind of unrelated to the rest of this rant, but the levels themselves can end up being pretty confusing. There were several times where I was hunting around for minutes on end looking for where I'm supposed to go next, or accidentally backtracking through the level, and it's not helped by the fact that whenever you fall off a building it just teleports you to a seemingly randomly location and you have to find your way back to where you were going.I'll edit my review later if my thoughts change after playing through the game more (if I ever come back to it).

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like SPRAWL. A retro shooter with wall running is a great idea that I think would've been a lot fun to play. Sadly, SPRAWL falls apart late game was a slog to sit through. Firstly, I do want to give the developers credit for releasing a complete game rather than launching SPRAWL in Early Access. I understand why many indie devs release their games in Early Access, since it gives them a lot more communication with their player base and allows them to make changes to the game based on community feedback. However the trend of Early Access games has gotten very exhausting to me so I'm glad to see a finished game out the gate.But before I talk about the game I do want to bring up some issues with the options the game has, or lack thereof. Firstly, there's no way to disable the camera sway. There is an option to reduce or disable the weapon sway, but not for you camera. While I don't get any motion sickness from this, it does annoy me and I wish it could be reduced or disabled. Secondly, and most importantly to me, is there no way to adjust the HUD. If you don't like the size of the HUD or crosshair, too bad, you can't change it. I personally hate the "X" crosshair and would like to disable it and use my own dot crosshair overlay, but since you can't disable to HUD you have to have the crosshair on at all times. A minor nitpick to some, but so many other shooters let you make these changes that they seem like an oversight.Before I begin I would like to mention that I played SPRAWL on it's current hardest difficulty, called "Nightmare." SPRAWL has a decent start, giving you a tutorial of the wall running and how the slow-motion mechanic, called "Adrenaline", plays into the combat loop. The Adrenaline meter allows you to see enemy weak points, which is usually the head or a jet-pack if the enemy has one. The resource management aspect of this game is very straight forward as well. When an enemy is low on health they'll begin to glow yellow, indicating that you can run up to them and decapitate them with your katana to receive health, ammo, and adrenaline. Killing an enemy by shooting their weak points also reaps these rewards. While this system seems pretty simple, there is an issue that I have with it that makes the late game unbearable. Either through decapitation or shooting a weak point, you only get ammo for the weapon the enemy has. So if you kill the basic solider, you'll get Handgun ammo. Kill a shot-gunner, Shotgun ammo. The cloaked enemies, Sub-machine Gun ammo, and so on. If we compare this system to Doom Eternal, the game this resource management system is clearly inspired from, you get ammo for all of weapons (minus the BFG) on Chainsaw kills. On top of this, certain enemies don't seem to drop any ammo at all from what I could tell. I forget their names, but the hulking melee robots who run at you and can kill you in one hit don't seem to drop any ammo at all. And maybe this flew over my head, but I couldn't for the life of me figure out how to get ammo consistently for the Railgun and the Chaingun. They never dropped from the enemies I killed, and I couldn't find any ammo pick ups in secret parts of the levels. Are they intended to be super weapons that you have to use carefully? Because that's how I ended up using them nearing the end of my time with SPRAWL. These issues with the games resource management system culminates into what happened to me in the final mission of Chapter 2. After playing through the level, you're faced with a boss, however I didn't have enough ammo to take it down. Even though destroying the bosses individual weak points gives you health, ammo, and adrenaline (like destroying all of the other weak points) it still wasn't enough. I tried to brute force my way through but alas, I failed. The only way I managed through was to do what this game probably didn't want or how it intended you to play, lame. Taking inspiration from everyone's favorite reviewer UnderTheMayo, I ran through the level again using only the pistol and the shotgun, eventually skipping the last couple of fights entirely to conserve as much ammo as possible. And I'm happy to report that I did, eventually, beat said boss. And even after playing extremely lame, I still barely had enough ammo to beat boss. But it was enough. This whole thing might be a me issue. Maybe the game explains how you can get more ammo from enemies and I missed it, if that's the case that this whole rant was pointless. But seeing as I'm not the only person complaining about the lack of ammo I'm willing to hedge my bets that it's a design issue.I wanted to at least see the end of SPRAWL, given that at this point I'm well past my refund policy. But I had to throw in the towel at what I'm going to assume is the last fight of E3M1. A giant arena fight with multiple waves of enemies and, you guessed it, not enough ammo! Cycling through my already limited ammo pool to take out enemies while getting scraps of ammo in return wasn't very fun. What I did notice however is one of the enemies in the level, a giant ship, drops Chaingun ammo. But upon picking the ammo up I could't switch to the Chaingun. It could be a bug that's not allowing certain enemies to drop the ammo they're supposed to, who knows. But I had to call it quits there. I had seen enough of what SPRAWL had to offer and quite frankly I'm disappointed. What was a cool concept I wanted to experience turned into a slow decay of misery attempting to beat the game. If this game were to get some patches and address my concerns with the low ammo count, then I'll gladly revisit SPRAWL and give it another chance. And if this is the first game that this dev teams had made, then I think they did a good enough job and can learn from SPRAWL to make an even better game. I just found what was released to be a disappointment, and personally wouldn't recommend in it's current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Good movement, satisfying gunplay, pumping soundtrack and fantastic art direction.SPRAWL is a worthy addition to your boomer shooter collection.It's fast paced, the movements feel really good and when you master the gunplay and movements it's an absolute blast to play.However it's far from perfect, the level design is interesting but sadly it's too confusing and it's way too easy to get lost in some areas because there is no clear indication about where we are supposed to go to complete objectives.The enemies AI is not really good, they are pretty much brain dead with bad pathfinding.For some reasons the developers decided to implement a weird auto reload system and somehow thought it would be funny to reduce ammo pick ups to the minimum in some maps. You will eventually get used to it after a while but personally I am not a fan of it and running out of ammo almost constantly is not what I consider fun or engaging gunplay.It is worth mentioning there is still few collision bugs where you can get stuck in geometry and some script bugs that may not trigger correctly but I'm pretty sure these will be patched soon.Even with all these issues I think SPRAWL is still well worth playing as it is fairly priced in my opinion, just don't expect the Ultrakill or Turbo Overkill killer and you will most likely have a good time playing this.If you enjoy cyberpunk aesthetics, indie games and retro fps with high emphasis on movements then in my eyes it's a sure buy.With the recent release of Quake II remaster, AMID EVIL - The Black Labyrinth, Turbo Overkill 1.0 and now Sprawl we can say retro fps enjoyers are eating good this month.I haven't played much of SPRAWL so far (at beginning of episode 2 atm) but can already say it's better than Trepang2 and Ghostrunner if that can be of any help.Will add more to this review later, and edit rating accordingly once finished, cannot really play as much as I'd like atm.

It loves these inspirations and honors them while also transcending them. It's alchemical gaming and it's awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: I was extremely worried that I wouldn't enjoy  for what it was because in theory, it was tailor-made for me: a dystopian, off-the-wall, cyberpunk classic-action FPS with bullet time, wall running, great soundtrack, pesky voice in my head, and also not having to do with that number, 2077. I don't think  is a bad effort by any stretch of the imagination but as an ensemble, it just doesn't make for a standout experience overall, at least to me.It's a damn shame too, because the glimmers of potential here are palpable. For one,  might just have some of the best sound design I've heard in a game in 2023 (more or less on par with ), and to regress, one of the best soundtracks I've heard in 2023 (again, neck in neck with , as well as ). Despite the textures emulating the id Tech 2 aesthetic, the game's environments bleed Mamoru Oshii influence, specifically that of  and . As also referenced in that corny introductory headline, the game aims to play like  with some extra gameplay quirks that combined with its level design, provide an experience that resembles a combination of , , and even the original .This should work really well; I can't in good faith say it always does.It may  the three aforementioned games, but the game design doesn't express a distinct identity that make those games more engaging and dynamic. Not 's schizophrenic level pacing and oddball charm, nor 's excessive gore and extensive combat features, nor 's enemy variety and plethora of level locations. Much of 's gameplay follows as such: progress to an area, lock you in an arena with some baddies to fight until there's no more left, a door unlocks, you climb a flight of stairs, wall-run on a billboard or two, and do the exact same thing again until you find the sweet spot that means you finished the stage. Outside of perhaps the second stage of Ep. 1, there are no distinct set pieces, sequences, or gameplay alterations that keep  refreshing to play (unless boss fights every five stages count), despite being a short game. It's somewhat reminiscent of the obscure Bungie game, , Oshii influences included. The bullet-time mechanic operates in a similar function as cyberware does in : it's used to either highlight enemy weaknesses (which is usually their heads, albeit this feature is useful during boss fights), target objects (which usually amount to nothing more than door switches), and to bring the world's rotation to a standstill for a brief moment (where everything already moves around at a reasonable pace). I won't talk about writing here, since for the other three games I've compared  to, story isn't a massive focal point.I feel genuinely horrible for disapproving ; there are far worse games being pressed out for its asking price, and ultimately . I'm even reluctant to call it mediocre, because it does excel in certain instances. Yet strictly by gameplay elements, I struggle to think of a classic-action FPS as disposable as this. Yes it's meat and potatoes and that may be an appeal, but what if one were to add some mustard?

_childDocuments_.review: For starters, I've played and loved movement FPS games for a long time. Titanfall 1 helped me rediscover my love for shooters with its fast paced movement and I've put over 2k hours into the series at this point, along with a significant amount of time put into other retro FPS style games too (Doom Eternal, Dusk, Ultrakill, Turbo Overkill etc.), so believe me when I say I genuinely feel bad for posting this, but I just can't recommend Sprawl. I can see what it's going for, but it feels like the game is actively fighting your attempts to have fun with it at every step of the way. Level and environmental design simply don't mesh well with the gameplay, initially throwing you into cramped rooftop areas with such repetitive and dull visual design that it can be confusing to figure out where to go at times; admittedly not for long, but enough for it to frustrate. Industrial cyberpunk sounds really cool on paper, but in execution it is not fun to experience. I'm halfway through Act 2 at the moment and while the environmental and arena design does improve past the first couple of levels when they start to open up, it still never felt fun to actually play through. it could be argued that this is due to the oppressive atmosphere the game is portraying, but Dusk had a much darker, grimmer atmosphere and I loved the design of that game, so I'm not sure that's the case.  The gameplay itself is fine. I think Sprawl doesn't help itself with the fact that it released just after Turbo Overkill, but the movement is fairly awkward, since you have to hold strafe against wallruns to not slide down rather than automatically attaching to them. This is compounded by the arbitrary 3 wall jump limit, making it feel like movement is neutered by bizarre design choices that hinder rather than aid the game. There's also a lack of overall speed due to momentum not seeming to carry between movement options. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but the platforming sequences don't excite and the only times I felt a rush during combat were those few moments where I felt I had any sense of speed, which is unfortunately rare (Unless I just didn't figure out how to conserve momentum). Gunplay does feel satisfyingly punchy, but the fire rate on the shotgun is absurdly slow, and the pistol fire rate in slow motion is painfui too. While I understand that this is to incentivize weapon switching, low ammo caps for the SMGS and grenade launcher add another layer of frustration to the proceedings. I think what doesn't help the combat is that there's a lack of any setpieces or variety. There's one boss battle at the end of act 1 which was so easy I almost thought it  must've bugged out, but there's every encounter feels functionally the same. Turbo Overkill mixed things up with new movement abilities and weapons at an almost breakneck pace, while Dusk was simplistic but had incredible level variety and unexpected moments From what I can tell, the actions you take in the first level in Sprawl will be almost exactly the same as the end of the game, barring a few extra weapons. Overall I'm just disappointed. The clip based nature of the marketing on Twitter etc worked really well for Sprawl because they showcase those few moments where the game feels like it's achieving it's potential, but on a moment to moment basis, my general feeling was boredom rather than excitement to see what's next. Despite how critical I've been I don't think the game is terrible by any means, but it feels like a simply okay game to play, lacking in anything that would set it apart from the rest. Frankly, there are much better retro fps games that you can play instead of this.

_childDocuments_.review: In SPRAWL, every moment is a pulse-pounding rush of excitement as you navigate through dynamic environments, leaping and bounding across walls, all while unleashing a barrage of bullets upon your robotic foes. With "Samuel Hayden's from DOOM lol" commanding voice echoing in your mind, the intensity never lets up, propelling you into a whirlwind of action and chaos.Masterful Movement and Combat:Experience the thrill of agile movement and relentless combat as you navigate through SPRAWL's meticulously crafted levels. While the game may not reinvent the wheel in terms of navigation mechanics, its fluid movements and explosive gunplay keep you on the edge of your seat, craving for more.Immersive Environments:While SPRAWL's cyberpunk aesthetic may feel familiar, its gritty industrial landscapes and neon-lit streets paint a vivid picture of a dystopian future. While the setting may lack some originality, its immersive atmosphere and captivating visuals draw you into a world teeming with danger and intrigue.Crunchy Combat and Frenetic Gameplay:Engage in adrenaline-fueled combat that packs a punch with every shot fired. With a diverse arsenal of weapons at your disposal and enemies that keep you on your toes, every encounter is a test of skill and reflexes, delivering a satisfying blend of challenge and excitement.A Symphony for the Senses:Immerse yourself in the pulsating beats of SPRAWL's powerful soundtrack, which sets the stage for an unforgettable gaming experience. With its infectious rhythms and heart-pounding melodies, the soundtrack adds an extra layer of intensity to an already electrifying adventure. one of those games where you might say you bought a soundtrack that came with a game attached.Conclusion:In conclusion, SPRAWL is a shooter that delivers on all fronts, offering a thrilling experience that will keep you coming back for more. With its fast-paced , SPRAWL stands as a testament to the power of action gaming done right. So buckle up, lock and load, and get ready for the ride of a lifetime with SPRAWL.If there is any small negative to mention is that the game is kind of short but that is backed up by the adrenaline pumping horde mode and the time trials challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: Sprawl is a movement shooter that is currently (week of launch) a bit rough around the edges.  I can give this the thumbs up at this price point, but not without some caveats.Sprawl is what happens when you take Ghostrunner and add in Doom's "push forward" system of power-up rewards.  Since it has sliding and wall running, some have described this game as an "indie Titanfall".  I suppose that is a good way to describe the gameplay, however you must understand that this is a game from an extremely small team and it's very jank compared to the sublime Titanfall feeling of movement and shooting.Yeah, this game has lots of indie jank.  The wall running doesn't always work as expected, making some movement puzzles annoying.  The shooting is likewise going to disappoint you often as you miss shots you probably should have hit.Overall the project is very impressive.  The fluid movement and bullet-time shooting is a blast.  At the same time, there were seemingly some corners cut to get this game shipped, and I wish they had kept it in the oven for longer.  This game could have used a nice long closed Beta period, or maybe even Early Access.  I encountered some bugs during my playthrough and a bunch of just weird behaviors.The music is good, and the sounds are good, but the levels are drab.  Just visually blech.  The first two episodes are gray, tan, and brown.  I get it, it's a dystopia, but come on give me something to look at.  The game uses red lights to mark the path, but like, not consistently red, depending on keycards I think, so I got confused.  Also the levels are seriously lacking in plot variety.  Every single one is "find the levers to activate the platform, or open the blast door".  Just over and over again.The biggest problem with the game is the weapons.  They just don't feel right.  I relied on the starting pistols for nearly the whole game, only switching to the power weapons to take out the large mechs.  This game has probably the least satisfying shotgun of all time.  They should have just called it a flack cannon or something because this is not what FPS fans expect for a shotty.  All the enemies except for the early ones are tanky as hell and the guns don't seem to actually damage them.  The railgun makes no discernible impact so you don't know if you even landed your shot sometimes.  This stuff should have been worked out with more playtesting.I recommend you buy this game and play it after a round or two of patching.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally left a negative rec, decided to give it another shot.It's actually not bad.  The gameplay is nice and fast and you get bullet time and can parkour off of walls.  Picking off headshots in slow-mo is fun.  The game gets all of the main mechanical stuff done right so that moment to moment gameplay feels great.I've got a couple of gripes with the game though, one of which was the awful repetitive industrial music loops at the beginning of the game.  There's a drum section that repeats far too often, as well as a choral section that does the same.  I was mainly encountering this irritation in the first episode (the game is split up into 3).  After episode 1 I didn't encounter this irritation again, the music beyond it was solid.The voice acting was kinda grating too.  It uses some electronic effect on the voice actor that makes it sound weird and I'm just not partial too it.My other main gripe with  is that it suffers a lack of varied environments.  Every level, be it in the city, warehouse or tunnels uses the same drab, mechanical looking colour palette and I rarely felt like I was on an adventure, exploring interesting locations, which is a big draw for me normally in first-person shooters.  It suffers from the same issue I had with  in that regard, where the levels feel too samey.  I find when playing games that suffer from this problem, it's best done in small doses.  I played a level of  every now and then whenever I needed a break from an RPG that I was playing at the same time.  This helped to keep the game feeling fresh rather than stale and repetitive.Boss fights in  are a little confusing at first.  They have weak-points that light up when you activate bullet time.  The first boss in particular had me confused.  Half the time when I shot its weak points they didn't appear to take damage.  Turns out that despite the game displaying a health bar for these weak points, you need to ignore that and look for a visual cue that the weak-point has been destroyed.  That's your cue to move onto the next one.  ..I was supposed to ignore that health bar I was constantly seeing.So all in all, , while very competent is kinda mid at best unfortunately.  It plays kind of like a less ambitious .  It's fast and frenetic and fun in small bursts.  A fine enough killing fest. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Sprawl alot. I really like the atmosphere, graphics and cyberpunk aesthetic. I've played Quake remaster, Quake 2 remaster which I liked the sci-fi setting more than original Quake, this feels very good. I never played Titanfall so I can't compare it. I recommend Sprawl on sale for sure. The Good -------I have a long winded story to tell you I hope you stick around. I watched TastySpleenTV months ago on twitch, Jehar mentioned a free game on steam called NeoTokyo and its soundtrack. Its a dead asian cyberpunk style shooter,  A few days there was an NeoTokyo event streamed on Twitch where found more music by Ed Harrison who made NeoTokyo soundtrack. So seeing Sprawl release made me extremely happy to play a retro arena shooter having a Ghost in the Shell type campaign. If you haven't noticed I enjoy Sprawl's soundtrack as well. This game also reminds me of a old 2005 PSP game i loved called Coded Arms especially the city environments. Sprawl feels even like Coded Arms Assault which exists only as a game trailer which is a plus for me.The Bad -----The game is very linear. Enemies can melt you down in seconds. I didn't pay attention to the slow motion mechanic until mission 3 so that's my fault. I haven't gotten to the power weapons or all the good stuff. I'm not a movement expert, i think the wall running is decent. It makes more interesting for casual players. If you are a movement pro then IDK how you will feel.I won't lie to you saying this game is mind blowing requiring you to drop whatever you are doing to buy it. It does have more art style/substance so far over gameplay nor intelligent enemy encounter design to brag about. There isn't much of a story/ cinematics.. _childDocuments_.review: Sprawl is an excellent boomer-esque FPS. The wall running/jumping/bullet-time felt fluid, the gun-play was fast-paced and fun, and the weapons (although a bit more to be desired) felt great to use.The map design is well thought out and fits the need to constantly be on the move while dealing with hordes of enemies. It plays well with the movement style of wall running, crouch sliding, and high action battles. It's very fun to wall jump over an enemy, enter bullet-time, pop an enemies head off, and then land to then directly go into a slide as you again enter bullet-time and shoot a 'weak-point' rocket pack on the back of an enemy so that they explode. It's also nice that you can always keep your bullet-time meter stocked when you kill enemies by using their weak-point(s).A great array of guns. You have your dual pistols, smgs, shotgun, gatling, rocket-launcher, ect... Although I do wish there was a bit more variety, maybe a second shotgun (with faster reloads), or a scoped rifle. I don't like how the gatling gun would slow your character's movement as it didn't feel in-place with the movement the game is expecting (This can be circumvented by jumping around or wall-running, but I don't want to feel immobile with basic WASD movement when I pull out a weapon). Due to the lack of a rifle-like gun, I found myself using the pistols for most non-heavy enemies.Enemy AI could use some work. I often found myself cheesing some of the more tanky enemies (mechs) from a distance, or finding pathing bugs that would confuse an enemy NPC into walking back and forth as I shot it.I prefer difficult games, but this game does not offer difficulty in an Easy/Normal/Hard fashion, but rather has 'difficulty sliders', in which you can change the values of the damage you take, you deal, and the depletion time of your bullet-time mode. I opted for 0.5x player damage dealt, and 2x (max) enemy damage dealt. I wanted to reduce my damage on enemies even more, but found that there's not a good way to keep your ammo in-stock by playing this way. The melee was next to useless and I only used it a few times to feel cool, I wish it had more utility.The graphics were par for the genre, and I really enjoyed the "retro" mode filter they allow you to apply. Retro mode comes in 0x, 2x, 3x, and 4x options. Each of them adding more pixelation to make the game look like one of those classic shooters I remember from the 90's. I did find 3x/4x to be a bit "too much" for me, so I opted to play in 2x retro mode. The 0x also looks great if you want more of a crisp visual experience.The music fit the theme, nothing that stands out too much, yet does a fine job encapsulating the overall feeling/theme of the game.I have mixed feelings about the story. I found myself not really caring to read many of the codex logs that can be found scattered throughout the game. After a few levels in I would just skim through the codices to get a rough idea of what's "going on". Despite things not being very well-written, the writing for the voice acted parts was just fine and kept me interested in what was happening. The Voice acting itself was excellent too.I'd definitely recommend this game for anyone who wants to have a good time with some solid game-play.Difficulty: Variable (Difficulty is custom. I played on 2x enemy damage and 0.5x player damage)Game Length: 6/10Enemy AI: 6/10Graphics/Art-style: 9/10Atmosphere: 8/10Gun-play: 9/10Enemies: 7.5/10Soundtrack: 8/10Map Design: 9/10Overall: 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Short and Sweet. One of the best shooter I played in a while. You like Titanfalls movement? You like Ghost in the Shell OST? You like a shotgun so heavy it boosts you backwards? Here you go!If I had a nickel everytimeI I played a great game developed by just two people, I would have 2 nickel (at the moment) which isn't a lot but funny it happend twice in such short time. Sprawl is a fps set in a dystopian Cyberpunk-setting. As "SEVEN" you shoot and slice your way through hoards of enemies. The combat-loop is similar to the one established by Doom Eternal. Kill enemies with melee or headshots and you get health and adrenalin (slowmo)  which encourages aggressive gameplay. A slow-motion can be activated which highlights enemy weakpoints and mission objectives. Combined with the fast and fluid movement which is supported by the great leveldesign and you got one hell of a ride. The retro graphics are nice and an optional pixel/retro filter is available for those who want a nostalgic feeling. All this gets round up by a great soundtrack which incorperates elements of drum and bass aswell as choirs to create a mix of intense action and imposing environments. TLDR: Recommend for fans of: Ghostrunner, Doom Eternal, Titanfall and Ghost in the ShellIf you excuse me. I have to start my second playthrough. :)

_childDocuments_.review: This has ingredients of a good game, but it comes out half baked. The parkour, while cool, is a bit janky. It's easy to get turned around due to the confusing level design. _childDocuments_.review: SPRAWL is good. Not great. Nothing unique, but well executed and most importantly, fun. I like the semi-pixelated Matrix/Ghost in the Shell/Patlabor cyberpunk art style. It's gritty and refreshing with all of the hot pink 80s cyberpunk of late. Even the soundtrack reminds me of Ghost in the Shell. A cool mix of electronic drum 'n bass and harmonic vocals. There's a decent assortment of guns, but none are unique. Shotgun, SMG's, pistols, railgun, rocket launcher, grenade launcher, minigun, the usual lineup. The gunplay is not that good. SMG's have no punch. None of the guns sound very beefy either. AI is a little braindead. They have a tendency to get stuck and stand around. I at least like that they can jump up to platforms you jump to. I appreciate that much needed improvement since many of these action shooters have too basic of AI. There's a decent variety of enemies, but again, nothing too stand out. The bosses are not that good either. They're slow and oversized. Just jump around them shooting til dead. Done. Movement is pretty good. It's very fast paced and with the slide+jump combo you can go flying and running on walls with ease. Shotgun jumping is especially satisfying. The slow motion was helpful for some of my aiming deficiencies (skill issue), but it's not necessary to beat the game. It's not a very difficult or long game, even on Hard difficulty. The checkpoint system is tolerable. I hate checkpoint systems nonetheless. I wasn't invested in the story much. It was pretty simple. I wish Seven was more of a character because the deep voice character doing all the talking was never once compelling to listen to. I like the game still. It was fun and addictive. I give it a 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't like to get too granular in my break down of games, but i feel like i have to here. SPRAWL is an incredibly SOLID 7/10 games. At its highest highs i felt genuinely bad-ass in some of the stuff i pulled off in this game. But at its lowest lows its bogged down in a few areas (specifically the later levels) with poor, overly open level design in  a game whose big selling point is mobility and wall running. The core gameplay loop, and when in closed spaces allowing for high mobility, this game shines super bright, and allows for some really unique "Max Payne" meets "Titanfall" style gameplay, and the majority of the game allows for this. Its in the 3rd/Last of the 3 episodes where things start to get a bit questionable in the level layout specifically. While aesthetically cool, yet overly simple compared to the prior cyberpunk city-scapes, the Brutalist architecture design of these levels, and the wide open spaces between most of the walls in many of these levels arenas, make the player primarily resort to bunny-hopping to keep even a percentage of the mobility the prior episodes levels had allowed for. This is made even worse by the fact that bunny-hopping isn't even a mechanic the game teaches you, and if you hadn't organically figured it out yourself in the prior parts like i did, i could imagine the last 3rd of this game being a slog to have to learn this mechanic in, let alone the fact that some players may not even realize its there/needed. I know many people had an issue with the wall-running jump limit, and while i understand its implementation from the perspective of the games platforming segments, it seemed to me like there's a better middle ground with the limit that could have been found. What that is, i couldn't tell you. Then there's what is probably this games biggest fault, the bosses. They honestly were just kinda frustrating. Cool in concept but poor in execution, specifically because they were designed around the player shooting specific weak-points on the different boss Mechs, all 3 of which take place in wide open arenas with either poorly placed walls to allow for cover and mobility, or worse, temporary, destructible walls that can be broken, making the arena just a wide open box/circle (which again makes the player resort to bunny-hopping, if they had even figured out how to.)Now this review may seem more scathing than positive, but i genuinely had a LOT of fun with this game. The aesthetics of the game are insanely well done and designed, the world-building is actually really good, from just the dialogue and if you take the time to read the text logs throughout the levels. And the soundtrack; OH BOY this games ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ soundtrack is INCREDIBLE. The reason I'm so hard on this game is because with a few different choices in game design and level design, i think this game has something REALLY special, and has come the absolute closest to replicating the feel of Titanfall 2 gameplay that I've been craving more of for years. So yeah, when i say its a Solid 7/10, know that going into it there will be some jank, but if you learn to work through it, there's a really cool game, and it makes me excited to see where these Devs go from here.

_childDocuments_.review: Sort of a mixed review for me. I wanted to like it more but there's jank to this game that sinks the experience a good deal.For starters, the wallrunning. Just to be clear, I LOVE the wallrunning this game has for the most part, but sections of the game don't feel like they want to utilize this mechanic at all in terms of map design. This is especially true for the first and final boss. If you're going to force the player to deal with an onslaught of bullets from a boss, why is there no way to use wallrunning to find cover and get an advantage on them? There's some areas of standard levels where the potential is there, but sometimes it's just better to stay on the ground and shoot them with Adrenaline bullet time active. Makes it easy to think "wow I could be playing any other shooter right now".Tangentially related to wallrunning, the sliding is kind of crappy. It's a very brief slide that kills your momentum at the end if you don't jump, and it's awkward to start sliding at times for whatever reason. For something crucial to get good wallruns going, it should just replace the crouching function entirely.Weapon design is a mixed bag. The handguns, shotgun, and SMGs feel so good in the right situations, but everything else can vary in mileage. The grenade launcher is okay if you're way far away from the massive explosion radius. The railgun is alright if you can manage to charge it up properly while fiddling around with movement. The rocket launcher is only good from mid range as it basically shotguns rockets in a random spread (??? sounds cool but is awful in practice). Then there's the chaingun. I HATED using the chaingun because it has such a slow wind-up speed, in a game where you WANT to be fast, despite being relatively strong (I only used it in a few spots of the game).Enemy AI overall is also not that smart. There were a lot of times where the AI will cluster together as they chase after you in the same pattern and get stuck on walls, which is pretty silly. There were also other times where enemies fail to jump up to you, and even if they do they're immensely slow to follow you. The standard grenade launcher mechs are also a slog to deal with as their AI is (reasonably) mechanical in nature, but there's at least 2 times in the game where you're forced to stop and shoot their own grenades to deal damage to them, which is an awful experience.Not the worst $15ish I've spent, but there's so much more room for improvement. It's got a good handful of bugs to fix (e.g. first boss duplicating a non-hostile version of itself on death, the gun cycling sound playing loudly for all your weapons on level start, etc.), but there's also a couple moments of badassness hidden in there that you expect from this game. I'd say wait and see if the game gets QoL and bug fix updates, otherwise spend your money elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a learning curve. After the tutorial, I spent at least a half hour on the opening level before the pattern truly occurred to me. Bullet time, pop a few shots to the head, melee attack to finish them off. Rinse, repeat, wreak havoc. Once that realization hit, I was kicking ass. The patterns against various enemies are different with each weapon, but are similar enough for muscle memory to take over. Eventually, I stopped relying on Bullet Time as a whole, and was racking up bodies at high speeds in real time. The levels are really well designed, and the low-poly art-style is really cool. Wall-running takes some getting used to, but like I said with the combat, eventually it becomes second nature. This game is all about high reaction times, moving ungodly fast, speed, speed and more speed.One of my favorite encounters in this game was when I rounded a corner and came face to face with a shotgun pointed right at me. Slide around the blast, enter bullet time, shotgun blast right to the back of his head. Bloodbath.Definitely buy this game if you can, it's easy to tell the devs put a lot of hard work into it. The hard work paid of in spades.

_childDocuments_.review: I've finished my first playthrough, and i got to say the game is pretty good! some drawback here and there, but nothing that makes me pull my ears outCombat: Solid. The game doesn't hold your hand and lets you experiment how everything works during gameplay. At first when you only have your melee weapon and pistol, so you most be reallying on bullet time to do most damage, when you get the SMG at the end of the first level, and a shotgun that has blowback on the second, things change and you have to adapt your playstyle because you woundn't be using your arsenal to its full potential. Bullet time is now more used to get fishing shots with your slow firing but heavy hitting weapons while moving or doging proj. and trying to hit the jackpack canisters at the back of enemies for a one shot KOMovement feels great. the game offers a lot of walls during combat sequences to wallrun, bunnyhop and fly using the the blowback of the shotgun. I felt that i could win every single encounter that the game threw on me if didn't underestimate my enemies or just get cocky and tried to kill the heaviest enemy in the game with shotgun because his health was low. It offered the right amount of challange without overwellming me or just being too easyThe story is told via QR Codes you can find on tablets throughout the game, but the just of it is: Your SEVEN, a cybernetic advanced super soldier working for a military junta (Or just "The Junta"), which is backed by mega corporations that supply them with weapons and military grade bots. As the last goverment on earth after a total war agaisnt the "American Empire", the world has been reduced to a single city which can sustain life, that is the Sprawl. All of that beyond the sprawl is either destroyed or just factories that full the Junta Regime, but are just bones of a bygone era. During a mission, you were setup with defective cybernetics that made you persive civilians as enemies, massacrating them. This gives the Junta a perfect excuse to get rid of you since they persive you as outdated. You were saved by FATHER, an AI that reanbles you and fixes your fauty cybernetics. In return for your revenge agaisnt the junta, you will set him "Free".Now lets get to the cons. I feel the weakest part of the game was the bosses. They were just were very underwelming (I finished the game on normal difficulty) and really dissapointing. The only thing making apart from normal enemies is their gigantic health pool, being bullet proof against small arms bullets and having weakspots that only big guns can damage.The amount of content is also not very worthy of its price tag(If you are an brazilian). I payed ~R$42 (Real) for 12 levels spread around 3 chapters? Sure there is a lot of replayability with different difficulities, but i feel they could have add at least an endless arena-type mode like ghostrunner.The game also feels somewhat rushed. You have this big levels with lots to do and various objectives, taking around 1 hour/40 mins to complete, and then they throw you on a 15 Min/20 Min level that is just... boring, and you can breeze through with the amount of heavy weapon ammo you get through the level, and there are also alot of day one bugs that when i'm writing this review is still not fixed, that can make enemies not spawn and you have to restart the level in order to beat it.Overall, If your an ULTRAKILL crack adict, loves DOOM and DOOM ETERNAL, likes DUSK, or just want to be a litlle gremilin in a movement shooter, your defitinaly gonna like this game (Hey, gianni even voices a character in the game)Update 1The game has now gone through 3 updates in total, with them adding more customization for difficulties, movement and weapon buffs that make the game much more smoother and fun to play overall. It has a niche but dedicated speedrun community pushing the game into breaking itself for less time loss.There was also new content added, that being "Horde Mode" with 2 maps, that is an Arena Mode i mentioned earlier in the review, and a "Time Trial" mode that you have to complete as fast as you can, in which you can master the movement and compete with yourself to get the best time. There are 5 maps of those as i'm writing this.Overall, the game is now somewhat worthwhile buying, even for a short adventure! I'll try to get it on a discount if you can.
